units.la: ENCHIRIDION hoc rei medicæ nostrū GASSARE doctissime, sub nomine tuo in lucē emittere uolui ut patrocinio tuo ac nominis tui authoritate munitū facili³ obtrectatorū ac virilitigatorū hominum calumnias contemneret. Nostrum autem appello, tum quia consilio meo diligentissimi typographi patrueles mei in vnum volumen libros hosce diuersos coniunxerunt, doctissimē omnes & arguta breuitate conscriptos: tum quia nōnihil in illis meū est meoq; studio perfectū. Nam BRvDI Lusitani libri Venetijs ante annos decem excusi, adeo ab imperitissimis librarijs depravati & male tractati erant, vt nulla nō pagina multis scareret mēdis, nō modo qui orthographiā attinent & tolerari facilē possut, innumeris, sed etiā quod ad sententiarū per puncstos & commata distinctionem: ita vt sæpissime nec initium nec finis sentētiæ appareret. Atpui vulgò fertur librum bene distinctum vice commentarij esse. Ego igitur cū superioribus annis libros hos legēdos mihi in manus sumpsissem, vt eorum lectione me exercerem atq; proficerem, obiter etiā istis vitijs mederi uolui, vt typographis aliquando diligentioribus tra derem. atq; hoc eo feci libentius quod Brudū ip sum Venetijs salutaueram, & homin em cū exfamiliari colloquio tum teftin onio doctoru rei me dicæ confuluifimu esse cognouerā : & publican- di etiam hos libros author ipsi hortatorq; fuerā, quod ipse præfixe Venete æditioni mea ad se epi- stola testatus est. Adhęc cum author verbis infini tiuis loco indicatiuorum frequenter vteretur, vt Greci interdu solent, hoc quoque mutaui, ut ni- hil eslet quod Lectore remoraretur, isque ita facili us iucundiusq; in solami ipsam rerum contépla- tione incumberet. Quæ certe in his Brudi nostri scriptis circa uictus rationem tum febriū ipsarum tum aliorū morborum, quibus plurimis febres ad hęret, uberrima eruditisimaque continetur. Non solum enim ueterum medicoruni, Hippocratis & Galeni præcipué sententias ordine enumerat, & interpretatur: sed recentiorum insuper circa uictū opiniones, quas uel scriptis mandarūt, uel opere ipso medici in diuersis Europæ regionibus alij aliter ostendūt, ad Hippocratis doctrinam ceu per sectissimū gnomonem & regulam refert atque exa minat: & uarios in usu mededi errores passim op- pugnat, non temere quidem illos aut leuiter, sed expositis pleruque & comissis vtrinque rationib; quotquot adferri poterant, concludit: ita ut meri tò felicissimū hunc diuini Hippocratis medicinæ parētis interpretem omnes huic arti initiati amā- re & ueneran debeant. Accepit ille rei medicæ sci- entiam uelut hereditariam à patre & auo doctissi mis clarissimisq; in Lusitania medicis: eiusdemq; usum ipse postea magna cum laude apud Lusita- nos, Britannos & Italos exercendo confirmauit. Sed hæc satis de Brudo.
units.tr: I wished, most learned Gassarus, to bring this Enchiridion of medicine of ours into the light under your name, so that, protected by your patronage and the authority of your name, it might be shielded against the slanders of quarrelsome and contentious men. I call it "ours" for two reasons: first, because my very diligent cousins, the printers, have joined these different books into one volume, all of them very learned and written with sharp brevity; second, because some part of them is mine and was completed by my own effort. For the books of the Lusitanian Brudus, printed at Venice ten years ago, had been so corrupted and mishandled by most unskilled copyists that almost every page was full of errors, not only innumerable ones in spelling, which can be tolerated easily enough, but also in the division of sentences by points and commas, so that very often neither the beginning nor the end of a sentence was apparent. Yet it is commonly said that a well-punctuated book is like a commentary. So when in previous years I had taken these books in hand to read, in order to train and improve myself by reading them, I wished in passing to correct these faults as well, so that I might hand them over to printers who would be more careful at some point. I did this more willingly because I had greeted Brudus himself at Venice, and had found him, both from familiar conversation and from the testimony of doctors of medicine, to be a most learned man. I had also been the one who urged the author to publish these books, as he himself attested in the letter he prefixed to my Venetian edition. Moreover, since the author often used infinitive verbs in place of indicative ones, as the Greeks sometimes do, I changed this too, so that nothing would hold the reader back, and he could more easily and pleasantly devote himself to the contemplation of the subject matter alone. Certainly in these writings of our Brudus there is a very rich and learned treatment of diet, both in fevers themselves and in other diseases to which fevers are often attached. For he not only sets out in order and explains the opinions of the ancient physicians, chiefly Hippocrates and Galen, but also measures against the teaching of Hippocrates, as if by a most certain gnomon and rule, the opinions on diet of more recent writers, which either they committed to writing or which physicians in various regions of Europe show by their practice, each in a different way, and he refers and examines them. He also everywhere attacks the various errors in the practice of medicine, not rashly or lightly, but generally sets out and weighs the reasons on both sides, as many as could be brought forward, and then reaches his conclusion. So deservedly all who have been initiated into this art ought to love and revere this most fortunate interpreter of divine Hippocrates, the parent of medicine. He received the science of medicine, as if by inheritance, from his father and grandfather, most learned and most distinguished physicians in Lusitania; and he himself later confirmed and exercised it with great renown among the Lusitanians, the British and the Italians. But enough about Brudus.

units.la: De IACOBO SYLVIO nihil dicam, quòd costantior clarioṙq; eruditionis eius ac præstan- tiæ in arte n stra fama per omnē Europam multis iam annis fit peruulgata, quàm quæ præconio nostro celebrari indigeat. Nihil etiam de incerto libelli DE PVLSIBVS, nihil de VASSAEO libelli de virinis authore, præter hoc vnū, nihil in hoc genere hactenus, quod istis præferre possim, me uidisse. Liber de pulsibus epitome est in pro lixos Galeni eiusdem argumenti libros. Liber de virinis, nō solum ea omnia quæ Actuarius habet, breuissimè proponit, sed alia etiam ex Hippocrate & Galeno addit.
units.tr: I will say nothing about JACOBUS SYLVIUS, since his learning and excellence in our art have for many years been so constant and so widely known throughout all Europe that they need no praise from me. Nor will I say anything about the anonymous little book On the Pulses, nor about Vassaeus's little book On the Powers, whose author is unknown; apart from this, I have not seen anything in this field up to now that I could set before those works. The book On the Pulses is an epitome of Galen's books on the same subject, set out at length. The book On the Powers not only briefly sets out everything that Actuarius contains, but also adds other things taken from Hippocrates and Galen.

units.la: Accipe igitur, uir clarissime, hilari fronte optimorum medicorum in unum ueluti manipulare librum inclusas vtilissimas lucubrationes, quas ego præstantiæ tuæ dedicandas imprimis existima ui, (præsertim cum ab authoribus ipsis in nullius nomen inscriptæ essent patroni,) vt & pro erudi-tione authoritateq; tua illas defenderes, & hoc ue luti pignus animi mei, quo te summopere propter virtutes tuas ac multa in me beneficia tua, & amo & suspicio, perpetuum tibi habe= res. Vale.
units.tr: Accept, therefore, most distinguished man, with a cheerful brow, these very useful studies, gathered into one volume like a bundle of the work of the best physicians. I judged that they should be dedicated above all to your eminence (especially since their authors had inscribed them under no one's name as patron), so that you might defend them by your learning and authority, and so that you might hold this as a pledge of my affection, by which I both love and respect you greatly, on account of your virtues and your many kindnesses to me, and will do so forever. Farewell.

units.la: DE PVLSI-SIBVS LIBELLVS EX GALENI LIBRIS COL-
units.tr: A LITTLE BOOK ON PULSES, GATHERED FROM THE BOOKS OF GALEN

units.la: lectus, ac uelut i in formulâ redactus, in candidatorum rei medicæ commo-ditatē, authore nostri seculi incerto, (Gallo, ut uidetur, quoniam liber Lu-tetiæ primum æditus est, anno Sa-lutis 1538.) sed diligentissi-mo doctissimoq; uiro.
units.tr: Gathered together, and as it were reduced into a small form, for the convenience of candidates in medicine, by an author of our age who is unknown (a Frenchman, as it seems, since the book was first published at Paris in the year of salvation 1538), but a most diligent and most learned man.

units.la: IN LIBRVM DE PVLSI-BVS praefatio.
units.tr: On the Preface to the Book on Pulses

units.la: QVOD medico optimum sit, vt prænotionem præsensionemque exerceat, clarè nobis ostendit bonorum omnium, quæ in re medicinali considerantur, author Hippocrates, quòd ob fœlicem prædictionis successum, sese medici arbitrio permittere audeat homines.
units.tr: That foresight and prediction are the physician's best exercise is clearly shown by Hippocrates, the author of all the good things considered in medicine, since on account of the happy success of prediction people dare to entrust themselves to the physician's judgment.

units.la: At cùm summa totius prognosticæ disciplinæ, tum moriturorum, tum convalituorum invehementiæ morbi ad ægrotantis virtute collatione consistat (nam vbi superior morbus fuerit, morietur æger: vbi inferior, non morietur) sintque tres genere facultates, totum animal gubernantes, vitalis scilicet, naturalis & animalis, habeatque vnaquæque sua, tum roboris, tum imbecillitatis signa, vitalis per arteriarum motus, naturalis per vrinas & deiectiones, animalis verò per functiones arbitrarias: de motibus arteriarum, quos pulsus vocant, primùm nonnihil referre optimum factu existimaui, cæteris in aliud tëpus non non absque ratione dilatis: nempe principa-tum ad ferenda de mutationibus, quæ in homi-num corporibus fiunt, indicia habuisse videtur de pulsibus disciplina. Ab ea enim in illis qui exactè ipsam possident, plures subo-riuntur præuidētiæ: præuidentia siquidē cum in-dicijs cōmunicat. Pulsus itaque alterationes, quæ in spiritu et nerueo genere fiunt, ostēdit: quòd arteriæ, quæ nerueas participauerūt tu-nicas, cōtineat eū, qui eas implet, spiritū. At cùm exquisitè quidē disciplinā eam tractaue-rit gloriosus sapientia & arte Galenus: sed forsan prolixius, quòd vnà cum opportune dictis, falsas etiā aliorū opiniones refellere co-actus sit: ob id sedecim ex libris, quos de pul-suū disciplina cōfecit, quæ candidatis medici-næ maximè cōferrent, collegi, et in breuiorē, quàm fieri potuit, redegi formulam.
units.tr: The whole sum of the discipline of prognosis rests on comparing the strength of the disease with the patient's strength, since the patient dies when the earlier disease prevails and does not die when the lesser one does. There are three kinds of faculties governing the whole animal: the vital, the natural and the animal. Each has its own signs of strength or weakness: the vital through the motions of the arteries, the natural through urine and excretions, and the animal through voluntary functions. I have thought it best first to say something about the motions of the arteries, which are called pulses, and to defer the others to another time, not without reason. The discipline of pulses seems to have been the chief source of indications for judging the changes that occur in human bodies. From it, in those who possess it accurately, many foresights arise, for foresight shares in the indications. Thus the pulse shows the alterations that take place in the spirit and the nervous kind, since the arteries, which share nervous coats, contain the spirit that fills them. Now, the glorious Galen treated this discipline exquisitely, with wisdom and skill, but perhaps rather at length, because alongside his apt statements he was also obliged to refute the false opinions of others. For this reason I have gathered from the sixteen books he wrote on the discipline of pulses those most useful to medical candidates, and reduced them to as brief a form as possible.

units.la: Est autem Pulsus, vt à definitione exordi-ar, motus præcipuè cordis, deinde arteriarū, quæ distensione et cōtractione mouētur à fa-cultate vitali, vt caloris natiui mediocritas retineatur, et in cerebro generetur animalis spiritus. Arteriæ adfectus uno tempore, simulatq; illa attollitur, plurimi attendendi:
units.tr: A pulse, to begin with its definition, is chiefly a motion of the heart and then of the arteries, which are moved by distension and contraction from the vital faculty, so that the moderate natural heat is kept up and animal spirit is generated in the brain. Many things must be attended to in the state of the artery at one time, as soon as it is raised up:

units.la: Distensionis quantitas.Mouentis eam facultatis, robur.Tunicæ status.Capedo interna.Qualitas & tempus motus.
units.tr: (1) the quantity of distension; (2) the strength of the faculty that moves it; (3) the condition of the coat; (4) the internal capacity; (5) the quality and tempo of the motion.

units.la: Arteria tres habente dimensiones, in singulis est distensionis quantitas. Hinc pulsuum differentiæ nouem.
units.tr: An artery, having three dimensions, has a quantity of distension in each. Hence there are nine differences of pulse.

units.la: Ex facultatis robore, siue ex ictus uel robo ris uitalis qualitate, differentiæ tres: Vehemens. Imbecillus vel languidus. Medius.
units.tr: From the strength of the faculty, or from the quality of the vital beat or force, three differences: vehement; feeble or languid; medium.

units.la: Ex tunicæ statu, tres: Durus. Mollis. Medius.
units.tr: From the state of the coat, three: hard; soft; medium.

units.la: Ex capedine interna, tres: Plenus. Vacuus. Medius.
units.tr: From the internal content, three: full; empty; medium.

units.la: Ex motus genere, siue ex ictus qualitate, tres: Celer. Tardus. Medius.
units.tr: From the kind of motion, or from the quality of the beat, three: quick; slow; medium.

units.la: Hæc quinque pulsuum genera in vno mo tu consistunt arteriæ. Cum præterea & pulsus duplex motus sit, geminam necessario habet quietem.
units.tr: These five kinds of pulse are all contained in the one motion of the artery. Since moreover the pulse is a double motion, it necessarily has a twofold rest.

units.la: Ex quietis ergo genere, uel temporis quietis quantitate, differentiæ tres: Rarus. Creber. Medius.
units.tr: From the kind of rest, or the quantity of time of rest, three differences: rare; frequent; medium.

units.la: Ex rhythmo, id est, modulo quodam, quæ pulsus omnis obtinet: Eurhythmus. Arhythmus.
units.tr: From the rhythm, that is, a certain measure which every pulse possesses: eurhythmic; arhythmic.

units.la: Arhythmi differentiæ tres: Pararhythmus. Heterorhythmus. Ecrhythmus.
units.tr: Three differences of arhythmia: pararhythmic; heterorhythmic; ecrhythmic.

units.la: Prædictis differentijs omnibus accidūt æqualitas & inæqualitas, tum in pulsu uno, tum in pluribus. hinc: Æqualis. Inæqualis.
units.tr: To all the aforesaid differences, equality and inequality belong, both in one pulse and in several. Hence: equal; unequal.

units.la: Accidunt & ordo & ordinis perturbatio, sed in pluribus solum. hinc: Ordinatus. Inordinatus.
units.tr: Order and disorder of order also belong, but in several pulses only. Hence: ordered; disordered.

units.la: Ex collectiua (quæ in pluribus pulsibus existit) in æqualitate: Æqualiter inæqualis.
units.tr: From the collective (which exists in several pulses), in equality: equally unequal.

units.la: Inæqualiter inæqualis.
units.tr: Unequally unequal.

units.la: Ex æquali inæqualitate: Miurus. Miurus deficiens. Miurus reciprocus.
units.tr: From equal inequality: Miurus; Miurus deficiens; Miurus reciprocus.

units.la: Ex inæquali inæqualitate. Intercurrens. Intermittens. Reciprocus deficiens: atque alij sine nomine plerique.
units.tr: From unequal inequality: Intercurrens; Intermittens; Reciprocus deficiens; and many others without a name.

units.la: Si inæqualitas in pulsu uno fuerit, ex motus inæqualitate duæ primæ differentiæ: Vna in vna arteria parte, sed non eodem tempore: Altera in pluribus. Primæ, tres. | Nam uel Motum quies interpellat: | Vel Motus est perpetuus, quanquam disparis velocitatis. | Vel est Reciprocus.
units.tr: If the inequality is in one pulse, from inequality of motion, there are two first differences: one in one part of the artery, but not at the same time; the other in several. The first kind gives three: either rest interrupts the motion; or the motion is perpetual, though of unequal speed; or it is reciprocal.

units.la: Si quies interpellat, differentiæ nouem.
units.tr: If rest interrupts, nine differences.

units.la: 5 A moderato, ad celeritatem.

units.la: 6 A moderato, ad tarditatem.
units.tr: 6 From moderate to slowness.

units.tr: If the motion is reciprocal, dicrotic pulses arise, that is, pulses striking twice.

units.tr: wormlike.

units.tr: ant-like, which is indeed unequal, though it does not appear to be.

units.la: Miuri fiunt in vna distensione, qui et innuen-

units.la: non videatur.

units.tr: or dicrotic.

units.la: Aut eandem obtinet partem,
units.tr: If distinct, in two ways:

units.la: Si eandem, tribus id modis:
units.tr: or interrupted.

units.tr: Either with interrupted motion,

units.la: Aut perpetuo,
units.tr: or perpetual,

units.la: Aut dicroto.
units.tr: or dicrotous.

units.la: Si distinctas bifariàm:
units.tr: or interrupted.

units.la: Aut motu continuo,
units.tr: Or with continuous motion,

units.la: Aut interciso.
units.tr: or intermittent.

units.la: Horum igitur generum, tot sunt singulares differentiæ, quot motus.
units.tr: Of these kinds, therefore, there are as many individual differences as there are motions.

units.la: Ex statu arteriæ inequalitas, in diuersis fit partibus solùm: & bifariam:
units.tr: Inequality from the seat of the distension of the artery corresponds to inequality in the quantity of distension, and in it are:

units.la: Aut continuo motu,
units.tr: vibrating pulse.

units.la: Aut intercisso.
units.tr: convulsive.

units.la: Et generis huius, tot erunt differentiæ, quot prædictæ.
units.tr: There are also other inequalities:

units.la: Inæqualitas à capedine interna, siue ab infusa materia, in diuersis fit partibus, non eadem:
units.tr: collective of frequency and rarity.

units.la: Vt de quantitate distensionis, dictu iam est.
units.tr: of frequency and rarity in one pulse.

units.la: Inæqualitas à sede arteriæ, distensionis, quantitatis inæqualitati, respondet: in qua sunt:
units.tr: collective of rhythm.

units.la: Vibratus pulsus.
units.tr: of rhythm in one pulse.

units.la: Convulsivus.
units.tr: There are also other pulses, of which later:

units.la: Sunt & aliæ inæqualitates:
units.tr: tremulous.

units.la: Crebritatis & raritatis collectiua.

units.la: Crebritatis & raritatis in pulsu uno.
units.tr: hectic.

units.la: Rhythmi collectiua.
units.tr: Rhythms collectively.

units.la: Rhythmi in pulsu uno.
units.tr: Rhythms in one pulse.

units.la: Sunt & alij pulsus, de quibus posteà:
units.tr: There are also other pulses, of which more later:

units.la: Tremulus.
units.tr: Tremulous.

units.la: Serrans vel serratus.
units.tr: Serrating or serrated.

units.la: Hecticus.
units.tr: Hectic.

units.la: NOMINVM ANTEDICTO- rum explicatio.
units.tr: Explanation of the aforementioned names.

units.la: DIstensio arteriæ, quæ & diastole, et relaxatio, & dilatatio dicitur, prior est pulsus motio: quæ trahit, nihil excernit. Contractio, quæ & systole, & cõstrictio dicitur, posterior: quæ excernit, nihil trahit. Quies, est tempus, quod motus sensibiles intercedit: & est duplex, supera, quæ & externa à distensione contractionem præcedit: Infera, quæ & interna à contractione distensionem.
units.tr: Distension of the artery, which is also called diastole, relaxation, or dilation, is the first motion of the pulse: it draws in and expels nothing. Contraction, which is also called systole or constriction, is the later motion: it expels and draws in nothing. Rest is the interval between the perceptible motions, and it is twofold: the upper rest, which comes after the distension and precedes the contraction, is external; the lower rest, which comes after the contraction and precedes the distension, is internal.

units.la: PVLSVVM:
units.tr: THE PULSE:

units.la: Magnus, vbi in longum arteria, & latum, & profundum distenditur:
units.tr: Large, when the artery is distended in length, breadth, and depth.

units.la: Longus, cùm in longum duntaxat:
units.tr: Long, when it is distended in length only.

units.la: Latus, cùm in latum:
units.tr: Broad, when in breadth.

units.la: Altus siue profundus, cùm in profundum.
units.tr: High or deep, when in depth.

units.la: Gracilis, in quo longitudinis dimensio, duabus reliquis præstat.
units.tr: Slender, in which the dimension of length surpasses the other two.

units.la: Tumidus vel turgidus, in quo duæ reliquæ longitudine præstant.
units.tr: Swollen or turgid, in which the other two surpass the length.

units.la: Paruus, breuis, angustus, humilis.
units.tr: Small, short, narrow, low.

units.la: Vehemens, qui valenter ferit tactum.
units.tr: Vehement, which strikes the touch forcefully.

units.la: Debilis, qui inualidè.
units.tr: Weak, which strikes feebly.

units.la: Durus, quum durior quàm natura ferat, arteria esse videtur:
units.tr: Hard, when the artery seems harder than nature allows.

units.la: Mollis, cùm mollior.
units.tr: Soft, when it is softer.

units.la: Plenus, qui arteriam corpulentiorem pleniorem-que ostendit, suppressionemque ipsius in humore tumidam.
units.tr: Full, which shows the artery larger and fuller, its compression swollen with fluid.

units.la: Vacuus, cùm elevato arteriæ, bullæ similis effici-tur.
units.tr: Empty, when on lifting it, it becomes like a bubble.

units.la: Celer, cùm pauco tempore, arteria distenditur: Tardus, cùm longo tempore.
units.tr: Quick, when the artery is distended in a short time; slow, when in a long time.

units.la: Creber siue frequens, cui breue quietis est tempus:
units.tr: Frequent or crowded, in which the interval of rest is brief.

units.la: Rarus, cui longum.
units.tr: Rare, in which it is long.

units.la: Rhythmus, est temporis distensionis ad tem-pus contractionis proportio, quæ in solis ve-hementissimis pulsibus reperitur.
units.tr: Rhythm is the proportion of the time of distension to the time of contraction, which is found only in the most vehement pulses.

units.la: Eurhythmus, id est consonus vel concinnus, qui rhythmum seruat, & pari constat pro-portione.
units.tr: Eurhythmic, that is, consonant or well-ordered, which keeps the rhythm and consists in equal proportion.

units.la: Arhythmus, id est, dissonus & incocinnus, qui rhythmum labefactat, & impari con-stat proportione.
units.tr: Arhythmic, that is, dissonant and ill-ordered, which breaks the rhythm and consists in unequal proportion.

units.la: Par, est proportio, vbi distensionis tempus contractionis tempori æquatur.
units.tr: Equal is the proportion where the time of distension equals the time of contraction.

units.la: Impar, si alterutrum eorum excedat, idque modò certis, modò incertis excessibus. Si certis, bifariam. nam aut dupla, vel tripla, vel aliis proportione: aut vt numeri ad numerū. Si incertis, trifariam: aut distensionis tempus est incertum, aut contractionis, aut vtrūq. Pararhythmus, qui rhythmum vicinae ætatis mutuatur.
units.tr: Unequal, if either exceeds the other, and this either by fixed or by unfixed excesses. If fixed, the case is twofold: either the proportion is double, triple, or some other, or it is as number to number. If unfixed, the case is threefold: either the time of distension is uncertain, or that of contraction, or both. Pararhythmic, which borrows the rhythm of a neighbouring age.

units.la: Heterhythmus, qui cuiusuis alterius.
units.tr: Heterorhythmic, which belongs to any other rhythm.

units.la: Ecrhythmus, qui rhythmum prorsus, nullius retinet ætatis.
units.tr: Ecrhythmic, which keeps no rhythm of any age whatever.

units.la: Aequalitas systematica, siue collectiua (id est, in pluribus pulsibus) est cum pares omnino maneant: & is pulsus absolutè æqualis dicitur: æqualitas in pulsu vno declaratur ex in æqualitate.
units.tr: Systematic or collective equality (that is, across several pulses) is when they remain entirely equal; and such a pulse is called absolutely equal. Equality in a single pulse is shown by the absence of inequality.

units.la: Inæqualitas collectiua, cum impares. Talesq; tum æqualitas, tum inæqualitas, in omnibus prædictis reperiuntur differentijs: vt pulsus, magnitudine æqualis & inæqualis: celeritate item & aliis.
units.tr: Collective inequality is when they are unequal. Both equality and inequality are found in all the aforesaid differences: a pulse may be equal and unequal in magnitude, likewise in speed and in the other respects.

units.la: Ordinatus, qui in circuitibus par est: Inordinatus, qui impar.
units.tr: Ordered, which is equal in its cycles; disordered, which is unequal.

units.la: Inæqualitas collectiua æquliter inæqualis, fit cùm pulsus æquam semper mutatione asse quuntur. vt, si primo pulsu, secundus minor sit: et tertius, ratio secúdo: et quartus, tertio: pari modo et sic deinceps: tales myuri existút
units.tr: Collective inequality that is equally unequal occurs when the pulses follow one another with a constant change: for example, if the second pulse is smaller than the first, the third bears the same ratio to the second, the fourth to the third, and so on in the same way. Such are the myurous pulses.

units.la: Myuri pulsus sunt, qui in arctu se colligút, & æquā semper mutationem assequuntur.
units.tr: Myurous pulses are those which contract into a narrow compass and follow a constant change.

units.la: Myuri deficientes, qui perpetuò diminuu-tur, & ad quietem prorsus recidunt.
units.tr: Failing myurous pulses are those which continually diminish and fall back altogether into rest.

units.la: Myuri reciproci, seu recurrentes, sunt qui ʋbi ad paruitatem aliquam desiuerunt, de intetegro augentur.
units.tr: Reciprocal or recurrent myurous pulses are those which, having ceased at some small size, increase again from the beginning.

units.la: Inæqualitas collectiua inæqualiter inæqualis est cū pulsus nulla prorsus inæqualitate retinent: et si aliquando ad tres vsq;, vel quatuor, vel quinq; habeant, posteà tamē amittut. Atq; vtrisq; adest ordo, vel ordinis perturbatio. Ordo scilicet, si circuitus aliquos seruent pares: ordinis perturbatio, si eos violent.
units.tr: Collective inequality that is unequally unequal is when the pulses keep no regular inequality at all; and if at times they have some order for three, four, or five pulses, afterwards they lose it. Both have order, or disturbance of order: order, if they keep certain cycles equal; disturbance, if they violate them.

units.la: Intercurrentes pulsus, fiunt ex inæqualitate crebritatis. Nēpe vt ad repellenda quæ molestant, maiores sæpe, & vehementiores, et celeriores siunt pulsus: ita quoq; & plures.
units.tr: Intercurrent pulses arise from inequality of frequency. Namely, to repel what troubles, the pulses often become larger, more vehement, and quicker, and also more numerous.

units.la: Intermittentes fiunt, cū haudquaquā mo-uetur uetur arteria. quod vocatur intermittere, sive in vnum pulsum, siue in plures inciderit: dissidentq; ab intercurrētibus: quòdin intercurrentibus, decertat cū noxiys causis facultas: In intermittētibus, hoc piget illa facere. Dissident itē, quòd intercurrētes, ex sola sint crebritatis inæqualitate: Intermittētes, ex in æqualitate raritatis & paruitatis: Raritatis quidē, quòd quies sit lōgissimè producta: Paruitatis uerò quòd distensio sit minimū dilatata.
units.tr: Intermittent pulses arise when the artery is not moved at all; this is called intermitting, whether it falls on one pulse or on several. They differ from intercurrent pulses: in intercurrent ones the faculty contends with harmful causes, whereas in intermittent ones it is loath to do so. They differ also because intercurrent pulses arise from inequality of frequency alone, while intermittent ones arise from inequality of rarity and smallness: of rarity, because the rest is greatly prolonged; of smallness, because the distension is dilated very little.

units.la: Reciproci deficientes fiūt, vbi duorū spacium, vel trium, vel pluriū etiam pulsuū, arteria cieri, non visa iterum agitari incipiat.
units.tr: Reciprocal failing pulses occur when, after the space of two, three, or even more pulses, the artery, not having been stirred, begins to be moved again.

units.la: Inæqualitas vnius pulsus, cū distensio quiete interpellatur, est quando celeriter primùm concitata arteria, deinde parua interposita quiete, tardè moueatur: ut patet in tabella nouem differentiarum.
units.tr: Inequality of a single pulse, when the distension is interrupted by rest, is when the artery, first quickly excited, then after a short interposed rest, moves slowly; as is shown in the table of nine differences.

units.la: Caprizans pulsus est, cùm diuisa per quietē distensione pars, post quietem robustior ante cedente videatur.
units.tr: The leaping pulse is when the part of the distension divided by rest appears stronger after the rest than before it.

units.la: Inæqualitas vnius pulsus, cū motus est perpetuō, sed disparis velocitatis, clara est ex tabellis pulsuum inæqualium.
units.tr: Inequality of a single pulse, when the motion is perpetual but of unequal speed, is clear from the tables of unequal pulses.

units.la: Inæqualitas vnius pulsus, cùm motus est reci procus, fit vbi arteria in occursu quasi repel litur, moxque redit.
units.tr: Inequality of a single pulse, when the motion is reciprocal, occurs where the artery is, as it were, repelled on meeting and soon returns.

units.la: Dicrotus pulsus, id est, bis feriens, fit vbi ar teriæ quam tangimus, partes duriores sint fri gidioresque, & ita difficilius etiam mouean tur partes vtrinque, quas non tangimus, ac deinde partem mediam præ ipsis in distensio ne concitatam, intrò retrahant, iterumq; se cum attollant: nempe vt bis tactus feriatur, est necesse.
units.tr: The dicrotous pulse, that is, the pulse that strikes twice, occurs where the parts of the artery we touch are harder and colder, so that the parts on either side, which we do not touch, are moved with more difficulty; then they draw the middle part inwards, which was excited in distension before them, and lift themselves up again. Thus it is necessary that the touch be struck twice.

units.la: Dicrotorum pulsuum differentiæ, in una sunt distensione, partem vnam inæqualitate occu pante.
units.tr: Differences of dicrotous pulses occur in one distension, one part being occupied by the inequality.

units.la: Inæqualitas, in pluribus arteriæ partibus, in vna distensione clara est ex antedictis.
units.tr: Inequality in several parts of the artery, in one distension, is clear from what has been said above.

units.la: Inæqualitas quantitatis distensionis, diuersas arteriæ occupans partes animadvertitur cre bro, et facillime percipitur, tum interrupta, tum continua, tum æqualiter, tum inæquali ter. In vna tamen arteriæ parte non recipit hanc inæqualitatem pulsus vnus. Myuri, in vna distensione fiùt, si duobus vel tribus adpositis digitis maior in prima parte arteriæ, vel vehementior aduertatur pulsus. In postremis verò, minor vel languidior: nem pe contentio paulatim remittitur, tantoque efficitur solito imbecillior, quantù est à principio remota.
units.tr: Inequality in the quantity of distension, occupying different parts of the artery, is commonly noticed and most easily perceived, whether interrupted or continuous, whether equal or unequal. In one part of the artery, however, a single pulse does not admit this inequality. Myurous pulses arise in one distension if, with two or three fingers applied, a greater or more vehement pulse is noticed in the first part of the artery, or a smaller or weaker one in the later parts: namely, the tension is gradually relaxed, and the pulse becomes weaker than usual in proportion as it is removed from the beginning.

units.la: Vndosus pulsus nomè habet, quòd veluti vn dæ exurgant in arteria, altera ab altera.
units.tr: The undulating pulse has its name because it rises in the artery like waves, one after another.

units.la: Vermiculans, quòd vermis gressui adsimilis sit. Fiunt autem hi, vbi id quod fluentis speciem habet, per arteriam subsistere videatur: mox iterum fluere, atque iterum retineri, atque hoc per totam accidere arteriam.
units.tr: The vermicular pulse is named because it resembles the movement of a worm. These arise when what has the appearance of flowing seems to stop in the artery, then flows again, and is again held back; and this happens throughout the whole artery.

units.la: Nam cùm singuli motus semper quiete terminentur, seriem veluti vndarum, vel vermis perreptantis, speciem contingit repræsentarì: id autem fit, cùm prima pars arteriæ primò descendit: deinde secunda, mox tertia, et ab hac quarta, cum eleuatione quadam vndosa: altera vnda, semper priorem excipiente. Differuntque hi pulsus sola quantitate.
units.tr: For since each individual motion is always ended by rest, it comes about that they present the appearance of a series, as it were, of waves, or of a creeping worm. This happens when the first part of the artery descends first, then the second, soon the third, and after it the fourth, with a certain wave-like elevation, one wave always taking up the one before. These pulses differ only in quantity.

units.la: Formicans, fit cùm multis amissis motibus, in vnu eumq; prorsus paruu terminetur. Succedit q; formicans vermiculanti, et vermicu lans vndoso: habetq; nomen a formica propter ipsius paruitatem, vel motus speciem.
units.tr: The formicant pulse occurs when, with many motions lost, it ends in one very small motion. It follows the vermicular and the undulating; and it has its name from the ant, on account of its smallness or the look of its motion.

units.la: Vibrati et conuulsiui fiunt, cum locu vnum arteria no teneat: sed sursum agitetur atq; deorsum, deserta naturali sede. Conuulsiui arteria in fidis modu sursum deorsumq; iactata.
units.tr: Vibrated and convulsive pulses arise when the artery does not hold one place, but is agitated up and down, having left its natural seat. The convulsive artery is tossed up and down like a plucked string.

units.la: Vibrati, cum arteria amplius cogitur vidistendi, vbi scilicet valida sit facultas, instrumentu durum & vrgeat vsus. Conuulsiuus ab affectu quem denotat, nomen habet.
units.tr: The vibrated pulse occurs when the artery is forced to stretch further, namely where the faculty is strong, the instrument hard, and use presses. The convulsive pulse takes its name from the affection it denotes.

units.la: Serratus, vel serrans, vel secans est, qui velut serre modo tactum ferit: nempe qui tangit, eam concipit imaginem, cum instrumentum inaequaliter durum occurrat: alia enim pars arteriae, attolli videtur: alia no, cum durior videatur.
units.tr: The serrated pulse, or sawing, or cutting, is one that strikes the touch as if with a saw: for the one who touches receives that impression when the instrument meets an unevenly hard surface; one part of the artery seems to be raised, another not, since it seems harder.

units.la: Tremulus pulsus, languidus simul et parvus, a tremore nomen habet.
units.tr: The tremulous pulse, at once feeble and small, has its name from tremor.

units.la: Inaequalitas crebritatis et raritatis collecti ua fit, vbi interualla per pulsus omnes, partim maiora, partim minora existunt. Inæqualitas crebritatis et raritatis in pulsu uno fit, si partes arteriæ omnes simul moueri coeperint, mox motæ minus æquis temporibus, iterum alteram simul distensionem inceperint.
units.tr: Collective inequality of frequency and rarity occurs where the intervals across all the pulses are partly longer and partly shorter. Inequality of frequency and rarity within one pulse occurs if all parts of the artery begin to move together, and then, having moved in less equal times, begin the next distension together again.

units.la: Inæqualitas rhythmi collectiua fit, cum proportio temporis ictus, ad tempus interualli variat.
units.tr: Collective inequality of rhythm occurs when the proportion of the time of the beat to the time of the interval varies.

units.la: Inæqualitas in pulsu uno, cum partes omnes arteriæ æquo tempore motæ sint, non æquo tamen quieuerint tempore.
units.tr: Inequality within one pulse occurs when all parts of the artery have been moved in equal time, yet have rested for unequal times.

units.la: DE PVLSVVM DIGNOTIONE.
units.tr: On the Recognition of Pulses.

units.la: Cum pulsum omnem tactu sentiri oporteat, tactu in pulsibus dignoscendis optimum esse conuenit.
units.tr: Since every pulse must be perceived by touch, it is fitting that touch be the best means of recognising pulses.

units.la: Optimus est, vbi nulla pars eius quo dani-maduerti possit, latet.
units.tr: The best touch is one in which no part of the pulse escapes notice.

units.la: Optimum pariunt: Natura. Meditatio. Applicandi modus.
units.tr: Three things produce the best touch: nature, practice, and the manner of applying the fingers.

units.la: Naturam apposi-tissimam esse oportet:
units.tr: The nature of the one touching must be very well suited to the task.

units.la: Quòd ut alius alio melius, vel deterius vi-det, ita et tangit. Manus item, quæ tangat non modò vt prompta sentiat oportet, verùm etiam mollis sit: nam sic motus vel minimos animaduertit.
units.tr: For just as one person sees better or worse than another, so too one touches better or worse. Likewise the hand that touches should not only be quick to perceive but also soft, for so it notices even the slightest movements.

units.la: Applicandi modus hinc necessarius:
units.tr: The manner of application follows from this:

units.la: Quòd manus hic firmius infigenda, illic leuius applicanda: vt in vehementibus & languidis constat pulsibus.
units.tr: The hand must be pressed down more firmly in one place and applied more lightly in another, as is established for strong and weak pulses.

units.la: Distensio manifestè dignoscitur, quanquã non secundum quamlibet eius partem:
units.tr: Distension is clearly recognised, though not in every part of it:

units.la: Tantum siquidem non sentitur, quantùm intercedit inter arteriæ primum impetum motus & ictus, vsque ad tactum nostrum.
units.tr: Indeed, that portion of the artery's first impulse of movement which lies between the beginning of the stroke and our touch goes unperceived.

units.la: Contractio non ita manifestè dignoscitur:
units.tr: Contraction is not recognised so clearly:

units.la: Neque enim cuiusuis contractio sentiri potest: nec quorum potest, æque omnium clara est. Contractionem sensibilem, habent pulsus omnes vehementes & magni: Languidorum verò, nullus.
units.tr: For the contraction of any pulse cannot be perceived, nor is what can be perceived equally clear in all cases. All strong and large pulses have a perceptible contraction; in weak pulses there is none.

units.la: Contractio dignoscitur:
units.tr: Contraction is recognised:

units.la: Ex vesicis, vtribus, follibus, & id genus instrumentis: si ipsa, materia vel humida, vel aërea impleueris.
units.tr: From bladders, bellows, wind-bags, and instruments of that kind, when you fill them with either moist or airy matter.

units.la: Contractionis dignotionem iuuant:
units.tr: The following help in recognising contraction:

units.la: Magnitudo, durities, tarditas.
units.tr: Size, hardness, slowness.

units.la: Magnitudo quidem: Nam si maximus fuerit pulsus, hac cognosces via: si tantum intelligas in contractionibus solere arteriam descendere, quantum in distensionibus ascenderit.
units.tr: Size, certainly: for if the pulse is very large, you will know it in this way: if you understand that in contractions the artery usually descends as far as it rose in distensions.

units.la: Durities ex rebus patet externis:Ut si æquis viribus, lapidem cuipiam impegeris: vel lignum, vel molle aliquid: nam contractiones, hoc clarius dignoscentur, quo violentioribus succedent distensionibus.
units.tr: Hardness is evident from external things: as if you struck a stone, or wood, or something soft, with equal force; for contractions are recognised more clearly the more violent the distensions that follow them.

units.la: Tarditas:Nempe quantum tempus auget recessus, tanto manifestiorem ostendit motum.
units.tr: Slowness: namely, the more time the recession takes, the clearer the movement it shows.

units.la: Contractionis præterea finis,Ut initium distensionis, est incognitus.
units.tr: Moreover, the end of contraction, like the beginning of distension, is unknown.

units.la: Quietum (quæ per accidens potius, quàm per se, pulsus partes sunt) dignotiones.
units.tr: The recognition of rest (which parts of the pulse are so by accident rather than in themselves):

units.la: Externa quidem dignoscitur:Si tactum citra vim vllam applicueris.
units.tr: External rest is recognised if you apply your touch without any force at all.

units.la: Interna,Ni vrgeatur, non cognoscitur. Nempe contractioni arteriæ tactus, constantissime adhærere debet: sed premere non licet, nisi in vehementibus: quo fit, ut in solis his, dignoscatur interna quies.
units.tr: Internal rest is not known unless it is pressed. For the touch must cling most steadily to the contraction of the artery, but it is permitted to press only in strong pulses; hence internal rest is recognised in these alone.

units.la: Longitudo dignoscitur: Si praeter pressum, omnem tactum admoue-ris: ergo qui tangit, omnino non premat: sæpe & leniter contrectet, & veluti suspendat manum.
units.tr: Length is recognised: if, apart from pressure, you apply every kind of touch; so the one touching must not press at all, but often and gently touch, as if holding the hand suspended.

units.la: Latitudo & profunditas,
units.tr: Breadth and depth,

units.la: Non vt in quadratis distinguitur: sed veluti in circulo. quaqua uniuersas latitudinis et profunditatis habere cogamur notiones: quod di stensio aliqua alta & angusta, alia humilis & lata, neque obstat, quin vt latitudine, et profunditate, sensu aliquando percipiamus: ita et circularem figurâ. Motus autem ab ascensu prohibitus, humilem efficit pulsum: in latitudinem inhibitus, angustu: in latum amplius exporrectus, latum. Profunditas, leniter tangentibus repræsentatur: & promptè quidem in pulsibus vehementibus.
units.tr: which are not distinguished as in squares but as in a circle. We are compelled to form general notions of breadth and depth, since a distension may be high and narrow, another low and wide; nor does it prevent us from sometimes perceiving by the senses breadth and depth, and likewise a circular shape. Movement hindered from rising makes the pulse low; restrained in breadth, narrow; extended more widely, broad. Depth is represented to those touching lightly, and readily so in strong pulses.

units.la: Pulsus temperati, qui omnium aliorum regula est, dignotio.
units.tr: Recognition of the temperate pulse, which is the rule of all others:

units.la: Optimam in primis constitutionem tibi inue nias: atque in co statu accipias, vbi pulsus à nulla externa causa immutatus sit. Externæ causæ sunt, ocium, exercitatio, ieiunium, cibus, bus, & similia. Arteria autem, in optimis naturis dilatatur, quoad vsus largiter imple atur, & nihil tunicæ offendantur.
units.tr: First of all, find for yourself the best constitution, and take it in that state where the pulse has not been altered by any external cause. External causes are idleness, exercise, fasting, food, drink, and the like. The artery, in the best natures, is dilated as far as it is fully filled, and the coats are not offended at all.

units.la: Magni & parui dignotio:
units.tr: Recognition of large and small:

units.la: Inuêta optima natura, cognitaq; in illa, tum corporis, tum distensionis arteriæ magnitudi ne, existimes arteriã hac maiorem, maiorem in natura optima esse habiturã distensionem: quam si tantam reperias, quantã fore conie-ceris, sic moderatus erit pulsus: si maiorẽ vel minorem, magnus erit vel paruus.
units.tr: Having established the best nature, and known in it the size both of the body and of the artery's distension, you should judge that a larger artery will have a larger distension in the best nature; if you find it as large as you conjectured, the pulse will be moderate; if larger or smaller, it will be large or small.

units.la: Arteriæ autẽ magnitudo, in optima natura deprehenditur, aut per dissectionem, quæ casu, vel industria fiat: aut colligendo ex signis optimæ constitutionis. Vel sic:
units.tr: The size of the artery in the best nature is discovered either by dissection, whether done by chance or by design, or by inferring from the signs of the best constitution. Or thus:

units.la: Tu pulsus optimæ naturæ memor: si in alterũ incideris, colligere poteris, vtrũ is maiores, vel minores habeat arterias, deinde & distensionis magnitudinem: & ex consequenti coniectare, an magnus, an paruus, an moderatus sit pulsus.
units.tr: Keeping in mind the pulse of the best nature, if you come upon another, you will be able to gather whether it has larger or smaller arteries, then also the magnitude of the distension, and from this conjecture whether the pulse is large, small, or moderate.

units.la: Celeris pulsus dignotio.
units.tr: Recognition of the swift pulse.

units.la: Ex sola is motus qualitate dignoscitur: quo scilicet pacto, ex locis discedat. Nam qui celerius discedit, celerem dicunt: qui tardius, tardum.
units.tr: It is recognised from the quality of the movement alone, namely in the manner by which it departs from its places. For those that depart more quickly are called swift, those more slowly, slow.

units.la: Vehementis & duri dignotio:
units.tr: Recognition of the vehement and the hard:

units.la: Ii siquidem in comprimendo tactu cognoscuntur: quo autem distent inter se modo, cognosces, si quid vehementia à duritia distet, cognoueris. Cognosces autem, si duri proprium sciueris esse premere: vehementis autem, euertere. Id quod ostendunt fluuiorum decursus, & venti magni, quos vehementes appellant: nempe hi euertunt, non premunt: Lapides verò & ligna quæ dura sunt, premunt & contundunt.
units.tr: These are recognised in the pressing of the touch; but you will know in what way they differ from one another, if you have understood how vehemence differs from hardness. You will know this if you have learned that it is proper to hardness to press, but to vehemence to overturn. This is shown by the courses of rivers and great winds, which they call vehement: these indeed overturn rather than press; but stones and wood, which are hard, press and bruise.

units.la: His utrisque conuenit ictus uiolentia:
units.tr: The violence of the stroke is common to both of these.

units.la: Est enim in distensione arteriæ quidam veluti ictus, qui, cùm tangimus, tactum ferit: & qui comes esse videtur, non duri tantùm & vehementis: verùm & magni, & celeris, et alti, & connulsiui, & vibrati. Duri quidem, quòd arteria dura, tactum contundat: Vehementis, quòd veluti euertat: Magni, quòd magnitudine distensionis plurimum progrediatur: diatur: Celeris, quòd qua fertur celeritate, ue hementer impellat: Alti, quòd veluti subeat ac intret: Conuulsiui, quòd ob tensionem & grè arteria moueatur: Vibrati, quòd ob vibrationem tensionis, simul duritiei & celeris occursus speciem præbeat.
units.tr: For in the distension of the artery there is a certain stroke, as it were, which strikes the touch when we feel it; and it seems to be a companion not only of the hard and the vehement, but also of the great, the quick, the high, the convulsive and the vibrating. It is hard, because the artery, being hard, bruises the touch; vehement, because it as it were overturns; great, because by the magnitude of its distension it advances very far; quick, because it strikes forcefully with the speed with which it moves; high, because it as it were rises up and penetrates; convulsive, because the artery is moved with difficulty on account of its tension; vibrating, because, owing to the vibration of its tension, it presents at once the appearance of both hardness and a quick onset.

units.la: Pleni simul & uacui, Dignotiones nunc sileo, quòd tales non agno scere videatur Galenus, tanquam tactui nõ subiectos.
units.tr: Full and empty together: I pass over the differences here, because Galen does not seem to recognise such things, as they are not subject to touch.

units.la: Rhythmus dignoscitur, Moderata digitorum applicatione, ne quid externi interpellent motus: dignosciturque in solis vehementissimis pulsibus: & si qualitatem motus distensionis contuleris, cũ qualitate motus contractionis: id quod patet ex tabula, in qua sunt sex concursuum formæ.
units.tr: Rhythm is discerned by applying the fingers moderately, so that nothing external interferes with the motion; and it is discerned only in the most vehement pulses. And if you compare the quality of the motion of distension with the quality of the motion of contraction, (as is evident from the table in which the six forms of concourse are set out).

units.la: DE CAVSIS PVLSVVM.
units.tr: ON THE CAUSES OF PULSES.

units.la: Pulsum uariantes causæ, duplices:
units.tr: The causes that vary the pulse are of two kinds:

units.la: Generatrices.
units.tr: Generating.

units.la: Alteratrices. Generatrices, quæ & continentes dicuntur, quòd pulsuum essentiam contineant: Vsus. Facultas. Instrumentum. Vsus: Caloris refrigerium. Fuliginis ex succornm adustione, excretio. Spiritus animalis nutritio. Facultas: Vitalis. Instrumentum: Arteria. Alteratrices causæ, duplices: Præcedentes. Externæ. Præcedentes: Humorum, Crassitudo. Abundantia. Lentor. Acredo. Externæ: Balnea. Hyems. Aestas. Frigus. Calor. Ocium.
units.tr: Altering. The generating causes, also called containing causes, because they contain the essence of the pulses, are: use, faculty, and instrument. Use: cooling of the heat; excretion of soot from the burning of the humours; nourishment of the animal spirit. Faculty: vital. Instrument: the artery. The altering causes are of two kinds: preceding and external. Preceding: the humours, in respect of thickness, abundance, viscosity and sharpness. External: baths, winter, summer, cold, heat, idleness.

units.la: Otium.
units.tr: Idleness.

units.la: Exercitatio.
units.tr: Exercise.

units.la: Cibus, & similia.
units.tr: Food, and the like.

units.la: Quosnā pulsus usus efficiat, si solus euariet, facultate & instrumetis in eode manētib. statu.
units.tr: What pulse the use produces when it alone varies, with the faculty and instruments remaining in the same state.

units.la: Calor itaq; in temperato homine, si solus auctus fuerit:
units.tr: Heat, then, in a temperate man, if it alone is increased:

units.la: Maiores et celeriores facit, atq; vnà cum calore, ad maximam vsq; distensione augebuntur arteriæ: & tunc maximi fient.
units.tr: Makes the pulses larger and quicker; and together with the heat the arteries are enlarged to the greatest distension, and then they become greatest.

units.la: Calor maximam superans distensionem:
units.tr: Heat exceeding the greatest distension:

units.la: Celerrimos.
units.tr: Very quick.

units.la: Extremè incensus:
units.tr: Extremely inflamed:

units.la: Creberrimos: nam crebritatis causa vna, est prioris actionis defectus.
units.tr: Very frequent: for one cause of frequency is a defect of the preceding action.

units.la: Refrigeratio in eodem homine:
units.tr: Cooling in the same man:

units.la: Primum, paruos: deinde, tardos & postremò, raros.
units.tr: First small, then slow, and finally rare.

units.la: Plurimum progressa:
units.tr: Having progressed very far:

units.la: Rarissimos, quanquàm non tardissimos: & minimos, ob virtutem.
units.tr: Very rare, though not the slowest; and smallest, on account of weakness.

units.la: Vsu et facultate simul euariātib. quatuor cōiugia:
units.tr: With use and faculty varying together, there are four pairings:

units.la: Facultas imbecilla, calor igneus: facultas imbecilla, refrigeratio: increscētes, calor et facultas: facultatis robur, & caloris defectus.
units.tr: Weak faculty with fiery heat; weak faculty with cooling; heat and faculty increasing; strength of faculty with deficiency of heat.

units.la: Facultas ualde imbecilla, & calor igneus:Parvos, tardos, & creberrimos.
units.tr: Faculty very weak, and fiery heat: small, slow, and very frequent.

units.la: Modice imbecilla, & calor igneus:Aeque crebros: sed in distensione & motu, moderatos.
units.tr: Moderately weak, and fiery heat: equally frequent, but moderate in distension and motion.

units.la: Facultas imbecilla, & refrigeratio:Parvos, tardos, sed non creberrimos.
units.tr: Weak faculty, and cooling: small, slow, but not very frequent.

units.la: Prostrata omnino:Minimos, intermittentes frequenter, & deficientes.
units.tr: Utterly prostrate: smallest, frequently intermittent, and failing.

units.la: Modice infirma, & ualida refrigeratio:Crebros.
units.tr: Moderately weak, and strong cooling: frequent.

units.la: Calor & facultas: increscentes:Quàm vehementissimos, maximos: sed non celerrimos, neque creberrimos aperte.
units.tr: Heat and faculty increasing: as vehement as possible, greatest, but not quickest, nor clearly most frequent.

units.la: Facultatis robur, & caloris defectus:Moderatos, magnos, tardiores, & bene rarðs: maximè, vbi polleat refrigeratio.
units.tr: Strength of faculty and deficiency of heat: moderate, large, slower, and fairly rare, especially where the cooling prevails.

units.la: Arteriæ sola mollities, seclusis aliis causis, paritMaiores, celeriores, & raros.
units.tr: Softness of the artery alone, other causes set aside: larger, quicker, and rare.

units.la: Durities sola:Minores, tardiores, crebros.
units.tr: Hardness alone: smaller, slower, and frequent.

units.la: Durities cum caloris innati refrigeratione:Minores iusto, & tardiores.
units.tr: Hardness with cooling of the innate heat: smaller than is right, and slower.

units.la: Duritiés refrigeratione superior:Minores quàm tardiores, crebriores.
units.tr: Hardness superior to cooling: smaller, slower, and more frequent.

units.la: Refrigeratio uincens:
units.tr: Cooling prevailing:

units.la: Tardiores quàm minores, & rariores.
units.tr: Slower than smaller, and rarer.

units.la: Durities & refrigeratio, pares:Minores tantò, quantò tardiores.
units.tr: Hardness and cooling equal: smaller in proportion as they are slower.

units.la: Durities insignis, & pauca omnino frigiditas:Creberrimos.
units.tr: Marked hardness and very little coldness: very frequent.

units.la: Durities pauca, & frigiditas multa:Rariores quàm minores.
units.tr: Little hardness and much coldness: rarer than smaller.

units.la: Mollitudo & calor pares:Magnos & celeres, non statim tamen crebros: nisi distensionis magnitudinem, vsus superet.
units.tr: Softness and heat equal: large and quick, not at once frequent, unless the use exceeds the magnitude of the distension.

units.la: Mollitudo calore superior:Maiores quàm celeres.
units.tr: Softness superior to heat: larger than quick.

units.la: Calor mollitudine superior, bifariam est:Vel ita abundat calor, vt vsum actio complere nequeat.
units.tr: Heat superior to softness is twofold: either the heat so abounds that the action cannot satisfy the use;

units.la: Vel,Vsus satisfacit.
units.tr: Or the use is satisfied.

units.la: Si primum:Celeriores quàm maiores.
units.tr: If the first: quicker than larger.

units.la: Si secundum:Æque magnos atque celeres.
units.tr: If the second: equally large and quick.

units.la: Calor cū duritie, trifariam est. Nam uel:Vterque multum à natura discedit.
units.tr: Heat with hardness is threefold. For either both depart greatly from nature;

units.la: Vel,Calor est immodicus, & materia non valde dura.
units.tr: Or the heat is immoderate, and the matter not very hard;

units.la: Vel, Durities præpollet.
units.tr: Or the hardness predominates.

units.la: Si primum: (mos.
units.tr: If the first:

units.la: Celerrimos creberrisimosq, nō tamē mini-
units.tr: Very quick and very frequent, yet not the smallest.

units.la: Si secundum:
units.tr: If the second:

units.la: Maiores & celeres.
units.tr: Larger and quick.

units.la: Si tertium:
units.tr: If the third:

units.la: Paruos.
units.tr: Small.

units.la: Mollitudo frigiditate superior:
units.tr: Softness superior to coldness:

units.la: Magnos.
units.tr: Large.

units.la: Frigiditas superior:
units.tr: Coldness superior:

units.la: Paruos.
units.tr: Small.

units.la: Mollitudo & frigiditas pares:
units.tr: Softness and coldness equal:

units.la: Moderatos: neque enim quicunque moderati sunt, continuò & naturales existunt.
units.tr: Moderate: for those that are moderate are not at once natural either.

units.la: Durities cum imbecilla facultate:
units.tr: Hardness with weak faculty:

units.la: Paruos, tardos, & crebros.
units.tr: Small, slow, and frequent.

units.la: Cum robusta:
units.tr: With robust faculty:

units.la: Paruos, crebros, nec tardos: imò longè interdum iusto celeriores.
units.tr: Small, frequent, not slow; indeed sometimes far quicker than is right.

units.la: Mollitudo cum robore:
units.tr: Softness with strength:

units.la: Maiores prioribus, tardiores & rariores.
units.tr: Larger than the former, slower and rarer.

units.la: Cum infirmitate, bifariam est:
units.tr: With weakness, twofold:

units.la: Vel æquus vtriusque simulque modicus, à natura est deflexus:
units.tr: Either equal and moderate in both at once, deflected from nature;

units.la: Vel,
units.tr: Or,

units.la: Valde immodicus.
units.tr: Very immoderate.

units.la: Si primum:
units.tr: If the first:

units.la: Moderatos, & plane naturales.
units.tr: Moderate, and plainly natural.

units.la: Si secundum:
units.tr: If the second:

units.la: Paruos, tardos, crebros.
units.tr: Small, slow, frequent.

units.la: Mollitudo superior:
units.tr: Softness superior:

units.la: Moderatos.
units.tr: Moderate.

units.la: DE COMPLICATIONIBVS causarum omnium continentium, quae octo numero existunt.
units.tr: On the combinations of all the containing causes, which are eight in number.

units.la: Priores duae:
units.tr: The first two:

units.la: Remissis facultate & vsu instrumentis, modo mollibus, modo duris.
units.tr: With the faculty and use of the instruments relaxed, the instruments now soft, now hard.

units.la: Duae alterae:
units.tr: The other two:

units.la: Languida facultate, vsu aucto, instrumentis que, vel mollibus, vel duris.
units.tr: With the faculty languid, use increased, and the instruments either soft or hard.

units.la: Duae aliae:
units.tr: Two others:

units.la: Valida facultate, remisso vsu, & variante instrumentorum differentia.
units.tr: With the faculty strong, use relaxed, and a variation in the difference of the instruments.

units.la: Duae reliquae:
units.tr: The remaining two:

units.la: Valida facultate, aucto vsu, et variantibus instrumentorum differentiis.
units.tr: With the faculty strong, use increased, and varying differences of the instruments.

units.la: Priores duae:
units.tr: The first two:

units.la: Paruos, et tardos: sed crebros, vel raros, pro instrumentorum differentia, et quantitate of fensionis causarum continentium, aut sngularum, aut binarum, aut vniuersarum.
units.tr: Small and slow, but frequent or rare according to the difference of the instruments and the degree of offence of the containing causes, whether single, paired, or all together.

units.la: Languida facultas, aucto vsu, & duro in-strumento:
units.tr: Languid faculty, increased use, and hard instrument:

units.la: Ad crebritatem vergentes, deinde ad parui-tatem, postea ad tarditatem.
units.tr: Tending first to frequency, then to smallness, and afterwards to slowness.

units.la: Languida facultas, aucto vsu, & molli in-strumento, si permultum augeatur vsus, cæ-teris non multum à natura deflexis:
units.tr: Languid faculty, increased use, and soft instrument, if the use is increased greatly while the other things do not much deviate from nature:

units.la: Iusto maiores, sed non perinde celeres: crebri-ores item iusto.
units.tr: Larger than is right, but not equally quick; likewise more frequent than is right.

units.la: Vsus & facultas, à natura paululum deflē-ctentes, & instrumentum ualdè molle:
units.tr: Use and faculty slightly deviating from nature, and a very soft instrument:

units.la: Ad mediocritatem accedentes.
units.tr: Approaching the moderate.

units.la: Vsus & instrumenta non multum deflecten-tia, & facultas uehementer laborans:
units.tr: Use and instruments not much deviating, and the faculty greatly labouring:

units.la: Paruos, crebros, & modicè tardos.
units.tr: Small, frequent, and moderately slow.

units.la: Valida facultas, minor vsus, & durum in-strumentum:
units.tr: Strong faculty, lesser use, and hard instrument:

units.la: Minores, non tardiores, nec crebriores ne-cessario.
units.tr: Smaller, not slower, nor necessarily more frequent.

units.la: Valida facultas, ualde remisso vsu, & duris modicè instrumentis:
units.tr: Strong faculty, greatly relaxed use, and moderately hard instruments:

units.la: Minores, tardiores, rariores.
units.tr: Smaller, slower, rarer.

units.la: Instrumentorum uicijs, uicium vsus uin-centibus:
units.tr: With defects of the instruments, the defect of use overcoming:

units.la: Paruos abundè, crebros & tardos minus.
units.tr: Small in abundance, frequent and slow less so.

units.la: Valida facultas, aucto vsu, & molli instru-mento:
units.tr: Strong faculty, increased use, and soft instrument:

units.la: Magnos, celeres, & crebros non semper, sed imodice' aucto vsu.
units.tr: Large, quick, and frequent, not always, but when use is increased immoderately.

units.la: Aucto insigniter usu, & instrumento parū duro:
units.tr: Use notably increased, and instrument a little hard:

units.la: Maiores iusto, celeriores, & crebriores.
units.tr: Larger than is right, quicker, and more frequent.

units.la: Causa utraq; æquo discedente interuallo, neq; admodum longo:
units.tr: Cause of each departing at an equal interval, and not very long:

units.la: Naturalibus pares, sed celeriores, & crebriores.
units.tr: Equal to the natural, but quicker and more frequent.

units.la: Vsus & instrumenta, insigniter offensa:
units.tr: Use and instruments notably offended:

units.la: Celeriores moderatis, sed minores, & crebriores.
units.tr: Quicker than the moderate, but smaller and more frequent.

units.la: MAGNVM itaq; pulsum pariunt:
units.tr: Therefore they produce a GREAT pulse:

units.la: Valida facultas, caloris copia, & mollia instrumenta.
units.tr: Strong faculty, abundance of heat, and soft instruments.

units.la: Paruum,
units.tr: Small:

units.la: Contraria: nempe aut virtutis imbecillitas, aut vsus remissio, aut instrumentorum durities.
units.tr: The contraries, namely either weakness of power, or relaxation of use, or hardness of the instruments.

units.la: Longum simpliciter & proprie dictum:
units.tr: Long, simply and properly speaking:

units.la: Totius corporis gracilitas, duritics cutis, durities instrumenti, et facultatis imbecillitas.
units.tr: Slenderness of the whole body, hardness of the skin, hardness of the instrument, and weakness of the faculty.

units.la: Latum:
units.tr: Broad:

units.la: Facultas aliquo modo deficiens, latitudo locorum arteriæ insignis, & grauitas arteriæ ex superiore accedens loco. Grauitatis huius rationem habet rugæ cutis: ut in senibus, gra cilibus & recens iudicatis. Sæpius etiam hu miditates, & præsertim si ipsa arteriarum cor pora, his diluta fuerint, ut in hyderis.
units.tr: Faculty somewhat deficient, notable breadth of the places of the artery, and heaviness of the artery arising from its upper position. This heaviness has as its cause the wrinkles of the skin, as in old men, slender people, and those recently judged. Also, more often, moistures, especially if the bodies of the arteries themselves have been diluted by them, as in dropsy.

units.la: Altum parit:
units.tr: Deep produces:

units.la: Arteriæ distensio in magnitudinem coarctata, locis arteriæ circumiectis, tumorem hunc non capientibus.
units.tr: Distension of the artery, constricted in size, the places around the artery not receiving this swelling.

units.la: Longū, latū, & altū primæ tabellæ pulsus:
units.tr: Long, broad, and deep, of the first table of the pulse:

units.la: Gracilitas aduentitia, si tanta, quanto pul-sus est maior.
units.tr: Adventitious slenderness, if as great as the pulse is larger.

units.la: Calor & gracilitas, si non tanta.
units.tr: Heat and slenderness, if not so great.

units.la: Calor solus, si eadem habitudine fuerit cor-pus.
units.tr: Heat alone, if the body is of the same habit.

units.la: Calor duplo auctus, si corpus crassius euase-rit.
units.tr: Heat doubled, if the body has become thicker.

units.la: Longum, latum, moderatum:
units.tr: Long, broad, moderate:

units.la: Notæ superiores, & cutis arteriæ summè in-cumbentis rugositas: perinde atq; membrum peruertas, ut pars superior inferior sit.
units.tr: The above marks, and the roughness of the skin lying most closely over the artery; just as if the limb were reversed, so that the upper part becomes the lower.

units.la: Longum, latum, humilem:
units.tr: Long, broad, shallow:

units.la: Superiores notæ, arteria mole obiectorū cor-porum valde onerata, imbecillior vna facul-tas, & summè mollis arteria. Longum,moderatum,altum:
units.tr: The above marks, the artery very burdened by the mass of the bodies lying over it, the one faculty weaker, and the artery very soft.

units.la: Restricta in obliquum arteria, propter multitudinem, vel crassitiem, vel duritiem posi torum inter arteriam & tactum corporu. Longum,moderatum,moderatum:
units.tr: Long, moderate, deep: The artery constricted obliquely, on account of the multitude, thickness, or hardness of the things placed between the artery and the touch of the body.

units.la: Gracilitas corporis solito maior. Longum,moderatum,humilem:
units.tr: Long, moderate, moderate: Slenderness of the body greater than usual.

units.la: Gracilitas longu, & humile profunditas, ob causam paulo ante memoratam, imminuta. Longum, angustum,altum:
units.tr: Long, moderate, shallow: The slenderness of the length, and the shallow depth diminished, for the cause mentioned a little before.

units.la: Superiores notæ & latitudo restricta. Longum,angustum,moderatum:
units.tr: Long, narrow, deep: The above marks, and breadth restricted.

units.la: Corporis macies, & constricta in latum arteria. Longum,angustum,humilem:
units.tr: Long, narrow, moderate: Emaciation of the body, and the artery constricted in breadth.

units.la: Corporis macor. Hunc, si neque durus, neq; valde languidus, gignit refrigeratio. Moderatum,latum,altum:
units.tr: Long, narrow, shallow: Wasting of the body. If this is neither hard nor very languid, cooling produces it.

units.la: Arteriæ ex sua sede migratio, uel arteriæ sub profunda carne utrinq; occultatio, et quæ in media parua parte sublimis extet. Moderatum,latum,moderatum:
units.tr: Moderate, broad, deep: Migration of the artery from its own seat, or concealment of the artery deep beneath the flesh on both sides, and what stands out high in a small central part.

units.la: Causæ prioris, & causa profunditatem humi lians. Moderatum,latum,humilem:
units.tr: Moderate, broad, moderate: The causes of the former, and the cause lowering the depth.

units.la: Membri inuersio: nempe aut moderatus omnino videtur, aut magnus: si moderatus, altitudo compressa est, & producta ob molliciem latitudo: si magnus, plurimùm compressa est altitudo.
units.tr: Moderate, broad, shallow: Inversion of the limb. Namely, it seems either wholly moderate or large. If moderate, the height is compressed and the breadth produced on account of softness; if large, the height is very much compressed.

units.la: Moderatum, moderatum, altum: Naturalis conformatio, & naturalis sedis mutatio.
units.tr: Moderate, moderate, deep: Natural conformation, and natural change of seat.

units.la: Moderatum, moderatum, moderatum: Moderata omnia.
units.tr: Moderate, moderate, moderate: All moderate.

units.la: Moderatum, moderatum, humilem: Compressa profunditas cum cæteris moderatis.
units.tr: Moderate, moderate, shallow: Compressed depth, with the other things moderate.

units.la: Moderatum, angustum altum: Conformationis proprietas, aut latitudo arteriarum in obliquum compressa.
units.tr: Moderate, narrow, deep: Peculiarity of conformation, or breadth of the arteries compressed obliquely.

units.la: Moderatum, angustum, moderatum: In obliquum contracta arteria, profunditatem humiliat.
units.tr: Moderate, narrow, moderate: The artery contracted obliquely lowers the depth.

units.la: Moderatum, angustum, humilem: Corporis gracilitas.
units.tr: Moderate, narrow, shallow: Slenderness of the body.

units.la: Breuem, latum, altum.
units.tr: Short, broad, deep.

units.la: Conformationis proprietas, aut situs arteriæ distorsio.
units.tr: Peculiarity of conformation, or distortion of the position of the artery.

units.la: Breuem, latum, moderatum:
units.tr: Short, broad, moderate:

units.la: Impedita altitudo, moderatum.
units.tr: Hindered height, moderate.

units.la: Breuem, latum, humilem:
units.tr: Short, broad, shallow:

units.la: Praeter easdem causas, quae latum & humilem pariunt.
units.tr: Besides the same causes which produce broad and shallow.

units.la: Breuem, moderatum, altum:
units.tr: Short, moderate, deep:

units.la: Praeter easdem causas, quae moderatum latitudine, & altum pariunt.
units.tr: Besides the same causes which produce moderate breadth and depth.

units.la: Breuem, moderatum, moderatum:
units.tr: Short, moderate, moderate:

units.la: Causae eaedem.
units.tr: The same causes.

units.la: Breuem, moderatum, humilem:
units.tr: Short, moderate, shallow:

units.la: Causae eaedem, & quae altitudinem deprimunt.
units.tr: The same causes, and those which depress the height.

units.la: Breuem, angustum, altum: & breuem, angustum, moderatum:
units.tr: Short, narrow, deep: and short, narrow, moderate:

units.la: Naturalis conformatio, aut situs arteriae per uersus.
units.tr: Natural conformation, or position of the artery across.

units.la: Breuem, angustum, humilem:
units.tr: Short, narrow, shallow:

units.la: Quae paruum efficiunt.
units.tr: Those things which make it small.

units.la: Vehementem pulsum parit:
units.tr: Produces a vehement pulse:

units.la: Mouentis arterias facultatis robur.
units.tr: Strength of the faculty moving the arteries.

units.la: Debilem:
units.tr: Feeble:

units.la: Infirmitas.
units.tr: Weakness.

units.la: Durum:
units.tr: Hard:

units.la: Arteriae duritia.
units.tr: Hardness of the artery.

units.la: Arteriae duritiem:
units.tr: Hardness of the artery:

units.la: Siccitas in ardentissimis febribus: constrictio a frigore, vel per frigidae intempestiuum potum, vel per balneas similes, ex pomis refrigerantibus, intempestiue, vel praeter modum ingestis: ex his quæ multum pituit & frigida gi-gnere solent.
units.tr: Dryness in the most burning fevers; constriction from cold, either through untimely drinking of cold drink, or through similar baths, or from cooling fruits taken untimely or beyond measure, and from those things which commonly produce much phlegm and coldness.

units.la: Tensio ex convellentibus affectibus, ingen-tibus inflammationibus, & scirrhis. Mollem pulsum:
units.tr: Tension from convulsive affections, huge inflammations, and scirrhi. Soft pulse:

units.la: Arteriæ mollicies, & humiditas. Plenum:
units.tr: Softness and moistness of the artery. Full:

units.la: Humorum copia, aut nimia cibi, vel potio-nis vini redundantia. Vacuum:
units.tr: Abundance of humours, or excessive food, or an overflow of drink of wine. Empty:

units.la: Fames, aut inanitio. Celerem:
units.tr: Hunger, or emptiness. Quick:

units.la: Facultatis robur, caloris abundantia, vel u-sus vrgens, & instrumentorum mollicies. Tardum:
units.tr: Strength of the faculty, abundance of heat, or urgent use, and softness of the instruments. Slow:

units.la: Contraria. Crebrum:
units.tr: The contrary. Frequent:

units.la: Facultatis imbecillitas, copia caloris, & in-strumentorum durities. Rarum:
units.tr: Weakness of the faculty, abundance of heat, and hardness of the instruments. Rare:

units.la: Contraria. Rhythmos mutant:
units.tr: The contrary. They change rhythms:

units.la: Distensionis & contractionis vsus. Nem-pe in ætatibus ad iuuentutem vsque, in qui-bus multa est humorum consumptio, distien-sio fio à contractione parum vincitur: in seni-bus, in quibus paucissima est talis consum-ptio, distensionis tempus, contractionis tem-pore maius est.
units.tr: Use of distension and contraction. Namely, in ages up to youth, in which there is much consumption of humours, the distension is little overcome by contraction; in old men, in whom such consumption is very slight, the time of distension is greater than the time of contraction.

units.la: Ordinatos, & inordinatos pariunt.
units.tr: They produce ordered and disordered pulses.

units.la: Inæqualitatū causæ, quòd omnes inæquales sint. Sed quæ ordinatos pariunt, fixæ sunt, et perpetuæ: quæ inordinatos, non fixæ, varian-tes, nec in vna manentes, vel magnitudine, vel specie, vel loco.
units.tr: Causes of inequalities, since all are unequal. But those which produce ordered pulses are fixed and perpetual; those which produce disordered pulses are not fixed, but vary, and do not remain in one state, whether in size, kind, or place.

units.la: Pulsus inæquales pariunt, aut Opilationes: Aut, Instrumentorum compressiones: Aut, Humorū abundantia, ad facultatem collata: Aut, Cordis inæqualis intemperies.
units.tr: They produce unequal pulses, either by Obstructions; or by Compressions of the instruments; or by Abundance of humours in proportion to the faculty; or by Unequal intemperature of the heart.

units.la: Inæqualitatem collectiuam, quæ nunquam usus uariationi aperte succedit:
units.tr: Collective inequality, which never openly follows upon a variation of use:

units.la: Cordis intemperies.
units.tr: Intemperature of the heart.

units.la: Instrumentorū, vel facultatis vitia. Nem-pe aut opilationibus, aut cōpressionibus, aut duritia, aut nimÿs humoribus, ad facultatem collatis vitia incurrunt. Facultas itaq;, si omnibus imperat instru- mentis, pulsus facit,
units.tr: Defects of the instruments or of the faculty. Namely, defects arise either from obstructions, or compressions, or hardness, or humours too abundant in relation to the faculty. Therefore, if the faculty commands all the instruments, it makes the pulse,

units.la: Æquales.
units.tr: Equal (pulses).

units.la: Si infirma per se, non ita crebrò:
units.tr: If the faculty is weak in itself, though not so often: (the pulse) makes unequal (beats).

units.la: Inæquales facit.
units.tr: Makes unequal.

units.la: Si ualida, & humorum copia opprimatur, aut plane contumacia habeat instrumeta:
units.tr: If it is strong, but is overwhelmed by a quantity of humours, or the instruments are plainly stubborn:

units.la: Inæquales.
units.tr: Unequal.

units.la: Si imbecilla parum:
units.tr: If it is slightly feeble:

units.la: Minores, languidiores, sed non myuros.
units.tr: Smaller, weaker, but not "myurus" (wave-tailed, dwindling).

units.la: Si imbecilla magis, ut digitorû applicatio facultati oneri sit:
units.tr: If it is more feeble, so that the application of the fingers is a burden to the faculty:

units.la: Myuros.
units.tr: Myurus.

units.la: Si resurgat, & uelut sese recolligat,
units.tr: If it rises again, and as it were gathers itself together,

units.la: Myuros reciprocos:
units.tr: Myurus reciprocus (alternating).

units.la: Si non,
units.tr: If not,

units.la: Myuros prorsus deficientes.
units.tr: Myurus altogether failing.

units.la: Facultatem uiciant:
units.tr: The following vitiate the faculty:

units.la: Inedia, vigilia, solicitudines, mœrores, uacuationes immodicæ per aluum, vel vrinas, vel vomitum, vel uterum, vel profluuium sanguinis, vehementes dolores, vel singulares, vt quem stomachicum vocant, & quæ cordis, vel arteriarum creant intemperiem, siue in succis, vel solidis continentur, siue foris antecedant.
units.tr: Fasting, sleeplessness, anxieties, sorrows, excessive evacuations by the bowel, or by urine, or by vomiting, or by the womb, or by a flux of blood, violent pains, or single ones, such as what they call stomachic, and those which produce an intemperature of the heart or arteries, whether they are contained in the juices or in the solids, or precede from outside.

units.la: Instrumenta uiciant:
units.tr: The following vitiate the instruments:

units.la: Humor offusus, inflammatio, abscessus, scirrhus, sanguinis abundantia, & maxime crassi, vel lenti, & opilationes.
units.tr: A poured-on humour, inflammation, abscess, scirrhus, abundance of blood, especially thick or sluggish blood, and obstructions.

units.la: Cordis autem inaequales intemperies, pulsus etiam inaequales pariunt, cum scilicet aliae calidiores, aliae frigidiores: ac hae omnino mu-tae, alia abundantia excrementorum confusae, non eodem omnes impetu, ad manus ferun-tur: sed hae anteuertunt, illae cunctantur. Nam calidiores si motui praesint, maturior simul & celerior, & maior fiet distensio: si frigidae, serior, tardior, & minor.
units.tr: An unequal intemperature of the heart, moreover, produces unequal pulses, namely when some (parts) are hotter and others colder; and these, altogether changed and confused by an abundance of excretions, are not all carried to the hands with the same impetus: but some get ahead, others linger. For if the hotter ones preside over the motion, the distension will become earlier, quicker and larger at the same time; if the colder, later, slower and smaller.

units.la: Intercurrentes facit:
units.tr: The following produce intermittent (beats that come in between):

units.la: Facultas valida, copia humorum, vel instrumentorum opilatione impedita.
units.tr: A strong faculty, a quantity of humours, or the instruments impeded by obstruction.

units.la: Intermittentes:
units.tr: Intermittent (pulses):

units.la: Facultatis infirmitas, & instrumentorum valida opilatio, compressio, aut constrictio.
units.tr: Weakness of the faculty, and strong obstruction, compression or constriction of the instruments.

units.la: DE CAUSIS INAEQUALITATIS unius pulsus, & primum cum distensionem quies interpellat.
units.tr: On the causes of the inequality of a single pulse, and first when rest interrupts the dilation.

units.la: Celerem itaq;, deinde parua interposita quiete tardum pariunt:
units.tr: Hence a quick pulse, followed after a short interval of rest by a slow one.

units.la: Vsus urgens. Facultas obsequens. Instrumentorum vitium: Vel, Humorum insignis abundantia. Instrumentorum uitium: Valida obstructio. Compressio violenta. Celere utrinq;, & ante, & post quietem: Facultas robur attollens, & seruans, & cum humorum copia pugnans. Caterae differentiae, ex his patent. Caprizantem pariunt: Humorum immodica copia.
