units.la: 4. Virtutis debilitatem.
units.tr: 4. Weakness of strength.

units.la: In mediocrium, b. Minorem debilitatem. Cum concaufis, a. Abscessum futurum.
units.tr: In moderate cases: b. lesser weakness. With concauses: a. an abscess to come.

units.la: a. Virtutis debilitatem, quæ ad tantam imbecillitatem peruenit, ut ob uehementiam causarum affligentium, necessariarum actionum oblita fit.
units.tr: a. Weakness of strength, which reaches such great feebleness that, because of the violence of the afflicting causes, it forgets its necessary actions.

units.la: b. Minorem debilitatem, quòd natura minus afflicta fedatiore existente febre. Abscessum futurum, superfluis ad locum abscessus transmigrantibus.
units.tr: b. Lesser weakness, because nature is less afflicted, the fever being milder. An abscess to come, as superfluities migrate to the site of the abscess.

units.la: Concaufæ sunt quas adiutrices dicunt, ut in longis morbis hyberna aeris caliditas, iniudicabilis conditio, motus ægritudinis erraticus, atque ægri uirtus mediocriter debilis. Tenuissima & vehementer alba, Vasorum obstructionem insignem, Indecentem frigiditatem & cruditatem. Spicea & subspicea, Minorem obstructionem, quanquam nō minorem cruditatem. Aurea & crocea, Obstructionem minorem, sed cruditatem. Rubea vinea passea, Putredinem in venis, Cruditatem. Longas vigilias.
units.tr: Concauses are what they call helpers, such as, in long diseases, the wintry heat of the air, an unjudgeable condition, the wandering motion of the illness, and the patient's moderately weak strength. Very thin and intensely white: a marked obstruction of the vessels, unseemly coldness and crudity. Straw-coloured and somewhat straw-coloured: a lesser obstruction, though no lesser crudity. Golden and saffron: a lesser obstruction, but crudity. Red, vine-coloured, raisin-coloured: putrefaction in the veins, crudity. Long vigils.

units.la: Quoniam genus omne prædictarum urinarum hypostasi, scilicet priuatarum, nō uno tingatur colore, cum alia uehementer, alia mediocriter alba sit, alia spicea & alia aurea, & ita de alijs : unaquæque rei alicuius signum existit, ut iam antedictum est, atq; hinc causæ etiam manifestæ.
units.tr: Since the whole kind of the aforesaid urines with a hypostasis, namely those deprived of contents, is not tinged with one colour, but some are intensely white, others moderately white, others straw-coloured, others golden, and so on, each is a sign of something, as has already been said, and hence the causes also become manifest.

units.la: HYPOSTASIS DIGNOSCITUR.
units.tr: HYPOSTASIS IS RECOGNISED.

units.la: Quantitate, Substantia, Colore, Lævitate, Æquabilitate. Hypostasis optima & naturalis, Mediocri substantia & quantitate, Alba, a. Lævis, b. Æqualis, c. Diu perdurans, & in morbis per totum mor bi tempus.
units.tr: By quantity, substance, colour, smoothness, evenness. The hypostasis is best and natural: of medium substance and quantity, white, a. smooth, b. even, c. lasting long, and in diseases lasting through the whole course of the disease.

units.la: a.b.c.Lævem dicit continuam & nō dispersam: Æqualem uerò, id est, singulis suis partibus sibi si milem. In morbis per totum tempus dicitur, nam sæpius contingit, hodie ut quis inculpatè mingat, cras uerò uel sequente nocte culpatè: deinde tertia die manè inculpatè, uesperi autem culpatè. Sed urinæ huiusmodi, uenas nonnihil coctum, aliud insctum continere indicant.
units.tr: By a, b and c he means smooth as continuous and not dispersed, and even as similar in each of its parts to the others. "Through the whole course of the disease" is said because it often happens that one urinates without fault today, but tomorrow or the following night with fault; then on the third day without fault in the morning, but with fault in the evening. Urines of this kind indicate that some matter in the veins is somewhat cooked and something else is uncooked.

units.la: Pauca,
units.tr: Few,

units.la: a. Inediam, b. Exercitationes, c. Obstructiones, d. Coctionis tarditatem.
units.tr: a. Fasting, b. Exercise, c. Obstructions, d. Slowness of concoction.

units.la: a. Inediam, nempe si decens nutritio defecerit, deficient & superflua.
units.tr: a. Fasting: namely, if proper nourishment fails, the superfluities also fail.

units.la: b. Exercitationes, nempe per eas attenuantur su perfluitates, & per occultas uaporationes descen- dunt, & ita pauca redduntur contenta.
units.tr: b. Exercise: by it the superfluities are thinned and pass down through hidden evaporations, and so little is left as contents.

units.la: c. Obstructiones, nempe sola tenuia transeunt, & crassa adhærent.
units.tr: c. Obstructions: namely, only the thin things pass through, and the thick ones stick.

units.la: d. Coctionis tarditas pauca reddit contenta ex causa manifestiore.
units.tr: d. Slowness of concoction yields little contents, from a more evident cause.

units.la: Multa,
units.tr: Many,

units.la: Nutrimentum multum, Coctricis virtutis robur.
units.tr: Abundant nourishment, and strength of the concocting power.

units.la: Nempe si alimenta abundauerint, ualeatq; concoctrix facultas, multa coquentur, multaq; erunt superflua.
units.tr: Namely, if food has been plentiful and the concoctive faculty is strong, much will be concocted, and much will be superfluous.

units.la: Tenuis,
units.tr: Thin,

units.la: a. Caloris natiui in tertia concoctione debilitatem. b. Crudorum humorum tenuationem robora ta genuina caliditate.
units.tr: a. Weakness of natural heat in the third concoction. b. Thinning of crude humours by a robust native warmth.

units.la: a. Caloris debilitatem, ob frigiditatem, ita ut contenta ad mediocritatem peruenire non possint.
units.tr: a. Weakness of heat, from coldness, so that the contents cannot reach a moderate state.

units.la: b. Crudorum humorum tenuationem, cum scilicet attenuauerit dissipaueritq; omnem crassitudinem materiæ, quæ in venis erat ob humorum cruditatem. Id autem cognoscCes: nam si modicè matu iam uacuaueris, ipsa contenta citò eleuantur, atq; læuitatis dissimilis redditur: non facilè autem eleuantur quæ ex caloris debilitate fiunt.
units.tr: b. Thinning of crude humours, namely when it has thinned and dissolved all the thickness of the matter which was in the veins because of the crudity of the humours. You will recognise this: if you have voided a moderate amount once it is already ripe, the contents are quickly lifted up and become unlike in smoothness; but those which arise from weakness of heat are not easily lifted.

units.la: Crassa,
units.tr: Thick,

units.la: a. Crudorum humorum in venis manentium amputationem,
units.tr: a. Cutting off of crude humours remaining in the veins,

units.la: b. Sequestrationem iudiciariam.
units.tr: b. Judicial sequestration.

units.la: a.b. Duo hæc sæpius in urinis uisuntur, sed de his distincte pronunciandum. Primum enim appa-rere solet in principio & augmento febris, & sæpius liquore urinæ improbi coloris existente. Id quod & artifices ipsos fallit, existimantes hypostasin bonam esse quòd alba sit: sed talis hypostasis in æqualis est & non læuis: item uiscea est, & muccosa est. Secundum frequentius fit post statum & uigorem, neque eiusmodi hypostasis cum improbi coloris liquore.
units.tr: a, b. These two are seen more often in urines, but each must be pronounced on separately. The first usually appears at the beginning and increase of a fever, often while the liquid of the urine is of a bad colour. This even deceives the practitioners themselves, who think the hypostasis good because it is white; but such a hypostasis is uneven and not smooth; likewise it is viscous and mucous. The second occurs more often after the state and vigour of the disease, and such a hypostasis does not come with a liquid of bad colour.

units.la: Vehementer alba,
units.tr: Vehemently white,

units.la: Pus, aut crudi humoris ramenta continet.
units.tr: Contains pus, or fragments of crude humour.

units.la: Hæc item distinguenda, nempe pus male olet, & glutinosum est: crudus humor proprie dictus puri colore & crassitie tantum similis, sed non male olet neque est uiscosus. Neque tamen talis crudus humor subsidet tantum in urinis eorum, qui ex crudorum multitudine febriunt: uerùm quoque & sanorum, qui laboribus sese dedentes cibos durios & ægrè coctiles ingerunt. Differtque is humor ab humore pituitoso, quòd pituitosus crudus & frigidus existit,non tamen crassus. Hæc Galen. in 1. alimentorum.
units.tr: These too must be distinguished. Pus smells bad and is glutinous; crude humour, properly so called, resembles pus only in colour and thickness, but it does not smell bad and is not viscous. Nor does such crude humour settle only in the urines of those who run a fever from a multitude of crudities, but also of healthy people who, given to labours, take in hard foods that are barely concocted. And this humour differs from a phlegmatic humour in that the phlegmatic is crude and cold, yet not thick. Galen says these things in the first book of On Foods.

units.la: Subspicea & spicea,
units.tr: Somewhat straw-coloured and straw-coloured,

units.la: Bilem mediocrem in tertia coctione, aut ciborum biliosorum inculcationem.
units.tr: Moderate bile in the third concoction, or the intake of bilious foods.

units.la: Bilea,
units.tr: Bilious,

units.la: Bilem rubram.
units.tr: Red bile.

units.la: Subrubra & rubra,
units.tr: Somewhat red and red,

units.la: Cruditatem ob rubræ bilis excessum,
units.tr: Crudity from an excess of red bile,

units.la: Sanguinis non exquisitè confecti abundantiam.
units.tr: An abundance of blood not properly concocted.

units.la: Cruenta, id est, veluti cruore suffusa,
units.tr: Bloody, that is, as if suffused with gore,

units.la: Sanguinem inelaboratum ob multitudinem, vel virtutis debilitatem.
units.tr: Blood not worked up, from its quantity or from weakness of power.

units.la: Omnia hæc ex prædictis satis constant.
units.tr: All these are sufficiently clear from what was said before.

units.la: Veneta livida & nigra,
units.tr: Venous, livid and black,

units.la: Vitalis virtutis remissionem & mortificationem,
units.tr: Remission and mortification of vital power,

units.la: Sanguinem mortificatum,
units.tr: Mortified blood,

units.la: Influxum nigri humoris.
units.tr: An influx of black humour.

units.la: Rationes quoque horum iam in coloribus urinarum sunt explicatæ.
units.tr: The reasons for these have already been explained in the colours of urines.

units.la: Orobiæa, id est, orobo similis,
units.tr: Orobic, that is, like orobus (vetch),

units.la: Magnam in hepate ipso factam inflammationem, tionem, vt in Nicostrati vxore in epidemiorum quarto.
units.tr: A great inflammation made in the liver itself, as in the wife of Nicostratus in the fourth book of the Epidemics.

units.la: a. Corporis totius liquefactionem,
units.tr: a. Liquefaction of the whole body,

units.la: b. Renum solorum.
units.tr: b. of the kidneys alone.

units.la: a. b. Absumpto adipe caro liquescit, atq; hinc tales apparent subsidentiae. At si in febribus apparent, affectum denotant uniuersi corporis: si no adsit febris, renum duntaxat. Praeterea si urina cruda fuerit, totius corporis est uitium: si cocta, renum est aegritudo.
units.tr: a, b. When the fat is consumed, the flesh liquefies, and hence such sediments appear. But if they appear in fevers, they denote a fault of the whole body; if no fever is present, of the kidneys only. Moreover, if the urine is crude, the fault is of the whole body; if it is cooked, it is a disease of the kidneys.

units.la: Furfurea, id est, furfuri tritici bene moliti similis,
units.tr: Bran-like, that is, like the bran of well-ground wheat,

units.la: a. Febrem in profundis vasis flammeam & colliquantem,
units.tr: a. A fever in the deep vessels, flaming and melting,

units.la: b. Vesicae affectum.
units.tr: b. An affection of the bladder.

units.la: a. b. Absumptis adipe & maiore carnis parte, ita utiam profunditatem carnis obsideat flammea caliditas, fiunt furfureae subsidentiae angustiores qui dem lamineis, sed crassiores: id quod & in uesicae accidit morbis. Sed corporis uitium cum febre & urinae cruditate est, uesicae uitium sine febre & cu urinarum concoctione, Aetius in quinto.
units.tr: a, b. When the fat and most of the flesh are consumed, so that a fiery heat besieges the depth of the flesh, bran-like sediments arise, narrower than the lamina-like ones but thicker; this also happens in diseases of the bladder. But a fault of the body goes with fever and crudity of the urine; a fault of the bladder occurs without fever and with a concoction of the urines. So Aetius, in the fifth book.

units.la: Laminea seu foliata aliys, id est, laminis seu foliys similis,
units.tr: Lamina-like or leaf-like, that is, like thin plates or leaves,

units.la: a. Febrem in partibus solidioribus infixam,
units.tr: a. A fever fixed in the more solid parts,

units.la: b. Vesicae affectum.
units.tr: b. An affection of the bladder.

units.la: a. b. Vbi solidae partes affectae fuerint, & primum quidem superficiariae, fiunt in urinis laminea: id quod etiam uesica contingit affecta. Sed si febris fuerit, & urinæ cruditas fuerit, & urinarum cruditas, uitium est corporis totius: sunt enim laminæ huiusmodi, si Galeno credimus, superficiales partes uasorum resolutorum, & quæ contabuerunt. Si uero febris non fuerit, & urinæ coctio fuerit, & dolor, uitium est uesicæ.
units.tr: a, b. When the solid parts are affected, and first of all the superficial ones, lamina-like sediments form in the urines; this also happens when the bladder is affected. But if there is fever and crudity of the urine, it is a fault of the whole body: for such laminae, if we believe Galen, are the superficial parts of dissolved vessels which have decayed. But if there is no fever, the urine is cooked, and there is pain, it is a fault of the bladder.

units.la: Pultacea seu farina hordei crasiori si-milis, quæ Græcè crimnodes, id est, quæ crimna, hoc est, grandiusculas effractihordei impolentis rectas partes, ob inexquisitam in mola domitu-ram, repræsentat:
units.tr: Pulpy, or like coarse barley meal, which in Greek is crimnodes, that is, which presents the larger broken straight parts of unpolished barley, owing to imperfect grinding in the mill:

units.la: a. Sanguinis crassi torrefactionem,
units.tr: a. Roasting of thick blood,

units.la: b. Vehementem partium solidarum colliqua tionem.
units.tr: b. Vehement melting of the solid parts.

units.la: a. b. Si candida fuerit, solidæ partes colliquatur: si rubra, sanguis affatur autore Aetio.
units.tr: a, b. If it is white, the solid parts are melting; if red, blood is being burnt, according to Aetius.

units.la: Conualituris febrientibus,
units.tr: In febrile patients likely to recover,

units.la: a. Longam ægritudinem.
units.tr: a. A long illness.

units.la: Non conualituris,
units.tr: Not likely to recover,

units.la: b. Citam mortem.
units.tr: b. A quick death.

units.la: a. b. Primum constat ex tertio tertij epidemiorum ægro. Secundum ex primo primi epidemiorum Sileno.
units.tr: a, b. The first is from the patient in the third book of the third Epidemics; the second from Silenus in the first book of the first Epidemics.

units.la: Pinguis & adipofa,
units.tr: Fatty and oily,

units.la: Pinguedinis & carnis liquefactionem.
units.tr: Melting of fat and flesh.

units.la: Si multa & separata seu inæqualis, renum ipsorum uitium ostendit: si minor & minus separata dispersaque, locorum remotiorum. Hæc Auicenna.
units.tr: If there is much of it and it is separated or uneven, it shows a fault of the kidneys themselves; if less, less separated and dispersed, a fault of more remote places. So Avicenna.

units.la: a. Saniosa, Instrumentorum meiendi vlcus.
units.tr: a. Pus-like: an ulcer of the urinary organs.

units.la: b. Muccosa,
units.tr: b. Mucous,

units.la: Crassum humorem in corpore multum, aut ex instrumentis vrinæ egredientem,
units.tr: Much thick humour in the body, or coming out from the urinary organs,

units.la: c. Crisim ischiadis, aut dolorum iunctura-rum,
units.tr: c. A crisis of sciatica, or of the joint pains,

units.la: d. Temperaturam frigidam.
units.tr: d. A cold temperament.

units.la: Fermenti infusi frustulis similis,
units.tr: Like pieces of infused leaven,

units.la: e. Stomachi debilitatem & mesarei,
units.tr: e. Weakness of the stomach and mesentery,

units.la: Lactis vsum & casei.
units.tr: Use of milk and cheese.

units.la: a. De saniosa satis ex antedictis constat.
units.tr: a. What is pus-like is sufficiently clear from what was said above.

units.la: b. Muccosa notissima euadit ex his qui calculo uesicæ laborant, aut obnoxij sunt.
units.tr: b. Mucous becomes quite well known in those who suffer from, or are liable to, bladder stone.

units.la: c. Quod crisin ischiados indicet, id constat, si aleuetur postea æger.
units.tr: c. That it indicates a crisis of sciatica is clear if the patient is afterwards relieved.

units.la: d. De temperatura frigida iam dictum est.
units.tr: d. The cold temperament has already been discussed.

units.la: e. Stomachi postea dixit debilitatem & mesaraei significari ab ea, quæ est similis frustulis fermenti infusi: non enim notabile uentris uitium emendat hepar.
units.tr: e. He said afterwards that weakness of the stomach and mesentery is signified by the sediment like pieces of infused leaven: for the liver does not correct a notable fault of the belly.

units.la: a. Arenosa, Lapidem in renibus vel vesica. Cineritia, Phlegma adustum, Pus propter longam moram mutatum. c. Sanguinea, Hepatis debilitatem, Vulnus in urinæ canalibus.
units.tr: a. Sandy, a stone in the kidneys or bladder. Ash-coloured: adust phlegm, pus changed by long delay. c. Bloody: weakness of the liver, a wound in the urinary passages.

units.la: a. Primum ita distingue, si rubra in renibus est, si alba in uesica.
units.tr: a. Distinguish the first thus: if it is red, it is in the kidneys; if white, in the bladder.

units.la: c. Tertium item distingue, si uehementer mixta sit, uitium est hepatis: sin minus, in urinæ canalib.
units.tr: c. Distinguish the third likewise: if it is strongly mixed, it is a fault of the liver; if less so, it is in the urinary passages.

units.la: QVÆ DE hypostasi dicta sunt, eadem de enæoremate & nubibus sunt intelligenda, nisi quod in biliosis morbis nulla habeatur hypostasis vel prorsus minima: quibus satis est, si enæorema vel nebulam habuerint. In hoc etiam distat, quod hypostasis si bona sit, primum obtineat bonitatis locum: enæorema secundum, & nebula tertium. Et si mala sit hypostasis, primum habet locum malitiæ: enæorema secundum, & nebula tertium. Præterea enæoremata materiam tetigisse hypochondria, viscera, & pectus arguunt: nubes vero affectum in capite esse.
units.tr: What has been said about the hypostasis is to be understood equally of the enaorema and of the clouds, except that in bilious diseases there is no hypostasis, or only a very minimal one; for these it is enough if they have an enaorema or a cloud. They also differ in this: if the hypostasis is good, it holds the first place for goodness, the enaorema the second, and the cloud the third. And if the hypostasis is bad, it holds the first place for badness, the enaorema the second, and the cloud the third. Moreover, enaoremata show that matter has reached the hypochondria, the viscera and the chest; clouds show that the affection is in the head.

units.la: IVDICIVM EX VRINAE CIRculo vel corona, quae per vrinae ambitum circumcurrit.
units.tr: JUDGEMENT FROM THE CIRCLE OR CROWN OF THE URINE, which runs round the rim of the urine.

units.la: Corona nulla fit, Si humores pari virtute fuerint. Alba corona in vrinis aureis & rubris, vineis & aliis, Naturam coepisse humoribus dominari. In viridi & passea si deterior, Humorum dominium. a. Spumea, Sensuum internorum perturbationem, ViscLeos humores, Flatum in ventriculis cerebri.
units.tr: No crown forms if the humours are of equal strength. A white crown in golden and red urines, and in vinous and other colours, shows that nature has begun to dominate the humours. In green and pale urine, if the crown is worse, it shows the dominion of the humours. a. Foamy crown: disturbance of the internal senses, viscous humours, wind in the ventricles of the brain.

units.la: Saepius coronae colores apparent ab urinarum colore declinantes, aliquando cum illis conuenientes. Si declinent ad bonos, urinae coloribus malis existentibus, bonum indicant: si uero deteriores sint quàm urinae colores, mali sunt existimandi. Si ergo boni, natura coepit humoribus dominari: si mali, humores uictores sunt.
units.tr: The colours of the crown often differ from the colour of the urine, and sometimes agree with it. If they incline towards good colours while the urine's colours are bad, they indicate good; but if they are worse than the colours of the urine, they are to be judged bad. So if they are good, nature has begun to dominate the humours; if bad, the humours have won.

units.la: a. De spumea in significatione ex bullis uidebimus.
units.tr: a. We shall see what the foamy crown means from the bubbles.

units.la: IVDICIA EX HIS QVAE in superficie urinae innatant, & primum de
units.tr: JUDGEMENTS FROM THOSE THINGS THAT FLOAT ON THE SURFACE OF THE URINE, and first concerning

units.la: bullis his quæ post quietam, & prorsus refrigeratam manent vrinam, quæ si-gna sunt spiritus adul-terini.
units.tr: the bubbles that remain after the urine has been left to rest and has thoroughly cooled, which are signs of adulterine spirit.

units.la: a. Bullæ albæ vel albis similes coronæ ambitum occupantes, Paruum aut nullum capitis dolorem.
units.tr: a. White bubbles, or bubbles like white ones, occupying the rim of the crown: little or no headache.

units.la: Cum vrina tenui & contentis non prorsus concoctis, Caloris naturalis imbecillitatem.
units.tr: With thin urine and contents not fully concocted: weakness of natural heat.

units.la: Cum crassa, Spiritum vrinæ familiarem.
units.tr: With thick urine: a spirit natural to the urine.

units.la: Cum vrina tenui & hypostasi priuata, Renum obstructionem.
units.tr: With thin urine and no sediment: obstruction of the kidneys.

units.la: b. Bullæ solam coronâ integra serie occupantes, & vrinæ concolores, Maiorem capitis affectionem, & dolorem non mediocrem.
units.tr: b. Bubbles occupying only the crown in an unbroken series, and of the same colour as the urine: a greater affliction of the head and no small pain.

units.la: Et quo intensius aureo colore, eò Maiores dolores.
units.tr: And the more intense the golden colour, the greater the pains.

units.la: c. Versus mediam superficiem concedentes, Remissionem doloris,Fluxum ad pulmones in sanis & ægris.
units.tr: c. Bubbles that move towards the middle of the surface: remission of pain, and a flux to the lungs in the healthy and the sick.

units.la: Maiores & absque ordine per matu-lam dimissæ,Dolores qui præcesserunt diminui.
units.tr: Larger ones, without order, discharged through the flask: the pains that went before are diminished.

units.la: In sanis,Spiritus frigidos.
units.tr: In the healthy: cold spirits.

units.la: d.Bullæ in vrinæ superficie palantes,Multam naturæ debilitatem.
units.tr: d. Bubbles wandering on the surface of the urine: great weakness of nature.

units.la: e.Bullæ si cum febre apparuerint, & præcesserint,Dolores capitis non modicos.
units.tr: e. Bubbles that appear with fever and come before it: headaches that are not mild.

units.la: Cum vrina tenui,Deiectiones.
units.tr: With thin urine: evacuations.

units.la: Cum crassa,Modestiores.
units.tr: With thick urine: milder ones.

units.la: f.Bullæ in febribus non pridem visæ,Naturam concoctioni indulgere.
units.tr: f. Bubbles seen in fevers not long ago: nature yields to concoction.

units.la: Bullæ densiores in vrinis,g.Seminis fluxum,h.Senum & vesicæ angustiam,i.Frigidam renum ægritudinem.
units.tr: Denser bubbles in urines: g. a flux of semen; h. narrowness of the bladder and kidneys; i. a cold disease of the kidneys.

units.la: Bullæ cum corporibus capillorum modo crassis,
units.tr: Bubbles with bodies like hairs, only thick,

units.la: Renum colliquamenta.
units.tr: Colliquations of the kidneys.

units.la: Cum in tribus concoctionibus spiritus flatuo-fos gigni contingat, eorumq; non semper eadē fit, tum quantitas tum qualitas, (nanq; alij multi, alij pauci, alij crasiores, alij tenuiores, alij calidi, alij frigidi) sane ut de nebulis & enæoremate diximus, quod scilicet partes corporis respondentes affectas ostendant: ita cum bullæ adusq; urinæ superficiem cocesserint, spiritus in corpore ascedisse usq; ad caput demonstrabunt: & quo maiores bullæ, eo spiritus materialis minus, & consumptibilior: quo minores & densiores, eo spiritus materialior neq; facile consumptibilis, quoniam a materia crassiore & glutinosiore fiat. Sunt itaq; bullæ signa spiritus flatuosi adulterini, quæ & colore, & locis quos occupant, distinguuntur.
units.tr: Since in the three concoctions windy spirits happen to be generated, and their quantity and quality are not always the same (for some are many and others few, some thicker and others thinner, some hot and others cold), just as we said about clouds and enaorema, which show the affected parts of the body that correspond to them, so when bubbles have risen to the surface of the urine, they will demonstrate that the spirit has ascended in the body as far as the head. The larger the bubbles, the less material and the more consumable the spirit; the smaller and denser they are, the more material the spirit is, and not easily consumed, since it is made from a thicker and more glutinous matter. Bubbles are therefore signs of spurious windy spirit, and they are distinguished both by their colour and by the places they occupy.

units.la: a. De albis autem bullis quid significent, satis constat ex dictis.
units.tr: a. What the white bubbles signify is sufficiently clear from what has been said.

units.la: b. Quæ integra serie occupant coronam, & urinæ sunt coloris, a forti sunt causa, & eo deteriores quo color urinæ deterior: nam si sparsim in corona essent, debiliorem indicarent dolorem.
units.tr: b. Those that occupy the crown in an unbroken series and are of the colour of the urine arise from a strong cause, and they are worse the worse the colour of the urine; for if they were scattered over the crown, they would indicate a weaker pain.

units.la: c. Quæ uersus superficiem mediam concedunt, remissionem doloris ostendunt, materia iam evaporata quæ dolorem faciebat, aut iam ad pulmones defluxa. Talis defluxio potest fieri & in sanis ipsis.
units.tr: c. Those that move towards the middle of the surface show a remission of pain, the matter that caused the pain having now evaporated or already flowed down to the lungs. Such a flux can occur even in healthy people.

units.la: d. Si maioris & absq; ordine per matulam diuidantur, dolores qui præcesserunt dissolui arguūt, quod maiores sint, crassiore scilicet & glutinosiore materia iam in aliam quæ absumptibilior sit transmutata, nempe concocta & obedientiore redita. Et (ut summatim dicam) bullæ quo minores & densiores, atq; circa solam circumcurrerint coronam nam, eò plures, potentiores, & crasiores demonstrant spiritus quò verò contrariæ magis, eò spiritum imbecillitas, & disperditio promptius indica tur. Quæ præterea ex bullis dolorem capitis often dunt, quædam totam coronam occupant, & totius capitis dolorem indicant: aliæ dimidiam coronā, & medietatis capitis dolorem arguunt: & reliquæ ex proportione.
units.tr: d. If they are larger and are discharged without order through the flask, they indicate that the pains which preceded have dissolved, because they are larger; the thicker and more glutinous matter has by then been changed into another that is more consumable, namely concocted and rendered more tractable. And (to speak briefly) the smaller and denser the bubbles, and the more they run only around the crown, the more numerous, powerful and thick they show the spirits to be; but the more they are the opposite, the more promptly is weakness and dispersal of the spirit indicated. Moreover, among the bubbles which show headache, some occupy the whole crown and indicate pain in the whole head; others occupy half the crown and indicate pain in half the head; and the rest in proportion.

units.la: d. Multam naturæ debilitatem à palantibus bullis significari ait, & maximè quidē, quò plures fuerint oppilationes, & crudorum copia humorum.
units.tr: d. He says that wandering bubbles signify great weakness of nature, and most of all when there are more obstructions and a greater abundance of crude humours.

units.la: e. Si bullæ cum febribus appareant, certissimæ sunt ex prædictis notæ.
units.tr: e. If bubbles appear with fevers, they are most certain signs, from what has been said above.

units.la: f. Si non pridem uisæ, quòd natura concoctioni indulgeat est manifestum: hinc sæpenumerò satis esse possunt, ut appareant signum bonum concoctionis.
units.tr: f. That nature is yielding to concoction is evident if they were seen not long ago; hence very often they may suffice to appear as a good sign of concoction.

units.la: g. Seminis fluxum præterea à densioribus bullis indicari ait, motione circa uasa seminaria facta, & flatu ad urinas missō. Id quod quotidie adnotamus in eo morbo, quo magna hominum pars qui publicè indulgent veneri fatigatur. Morbū hunc uocant urinæ ardorem, qui uerè est profluuium sE minis.
units.tr: g. He says that a flux of semen is further indicated by denser bubbles, from movement made around the seminal vessels and wind sent into the urine. This we note every day in that disease by which a great part of men who openly indulge in Venus are worn out. They call this disease heat of the urine, which is truly a flux of semen.

units.la: h. Renum item & uesicæ angustiam, motione sicet ob locorum angustiam facta, & hinc generato flatu.
units.tr: h. Likewise narrowness of the kidneys and bladder, from movement made because of the narrowness of the places, and wind generated from this.

units.la: i. Quòd et frigida renum ægritudo indicetur, docuit nos Hippoc. 7. partic. aphor. 34. aph. Renū coliquamenta, uel (ut alij dicunt) seminis segmenta.
units.tr: i. That a cold disease of the kidneys is indicated, Hippocrates taught us: Hippoc. 7. partic. aphor. 34. Colliquations of the kidneys, or (as others say) segments of the semen.

units.la: IVDICIVM SVPER EXTERNIS quibusdam, quæ innatant in humore vrinæ.
units.tr: IVDICIVM SVPER EXTERNIS quibusdam, quæ innatant in humore vrinæ.

units.la: Pinguitudo veluti Aranea supra hærens, Corporis totius vel solorum renum colliquationem. Puncta velut olei iniecta, Idem. Si parumper appareant & se resoluerint, Nihil difficilis indicant. Si perseuerauerint, Colliquationis principium.
units.tr: Fatness, hanging on the urine like a spider, indicates a melting of the whole body or of the kidneys alone. Points like oil dropped in, the same. If they appear a little and dissolve, they indicate nothing serious. If they persist, the beginning of a melting.

units.la: Hæc notiora sunt, quàm ut explicari debeant. Veluti capilli, a. Ciborum crassorum vsum, Renum vehementem caliditatem.
units.tr: These are better known than they need explaining. Like hairs, a. The use of thick foods, a very great heat of the kidneys.

units.la: a. Ciborum crassorū usum, ut orobi & casei. Id habetur 4. particula, Aphor. 76. Veluti caruncula, Renum vlcerationem.
units.tr: a. The use of thick foods, such as bitter vetch and cheese. This is found in the fourth part, Aphorism 76. Like a little caruncle, an ulceration of the kidneys.

units.la: In eodem loco habetur. Fructulum album punici grano simile, Renum liquefactionem.
units.tr: The same is found in the same place. A white little fruit like a grain of pomegranate, a melting of the kidneys.

units.la: Hoc Auicenna. Arenæ non residentes & ad ruborem declines,
units.tr: This is Avicenna. Sands that do not settle and tend towards redness,

units.la: Hepatis adustionem.
units.tr: a burning of the liver.

units.la: Non solum id accidit, ut non resideant, imo & matularum parietibus tenaciter hæreant: quasi diceres urinas ipsas manifesto in lapides cocrescere.
units.tr: This does not only happen so that they do not settle; indeed they cling stubbornly to the walls of the urinals, as if you were to say that the urines themselves coagulate visibly into stones.

units.la: Squamulæ,
units.tr: Scales,

units.la: Vesicæ exulcerationem & erosionem.
units.tr: ulceration and erosion of the bladder.

units.la: Hippocrates quarta particula Aphorismorum, aphorismo octogesimo primo.
units.tr: Hippocrates, fourth part of the Aphorisms, aphorism 81.

units.la: Furfurea,
units.tr: Scurfy,

units.la: a. Vesicæ scabiem,
units.tr: a. Scabbing of the bladder,

units.la: b. Vel venarum, vel
units.tr: b. Or of the veins, or

units.la: Vrinalium meatuum.
units.tr: of the urinary passages.

units.la: a. b. Hæc ita distingue, si tenuis fuerit urina, venarum scabies indicatur, quarum tunica patitur ob febrem ardentem: si non tenuis, prima tunica vesicæ patitur. Id etiam accidit cum sanguis ob ardores comburitur. Galen. 4. particula Aphor. Aphorismo 77.
units.tr: a. b. Distinguish thus: if the urine is thin, a scabbing of the veins is indicated, whose coat suffers because of a burning fever; if it is not thin, the first coat of the bladder suffers. This also happens when the blood is scorched by heat. Galen, fourth part, Aphorism 77.

units.la: Pus,
units.tr: Pus,

units.la: Renum vel vesicæ ulcerationem.
units.tr: an ulceration of the kidneys or bladder.

units.la: Thrombi sanguinis vel grumi cum urinæ stillicidio,
units.tr: Clots or grumes of blood with a dribbling of urine,

units.la: Laborem circa vesicam.
units.tr: trouble around the bladder.

units.la: Hæc quoque ex prædictis nota.
units.tr: These also are known from what has been said above.

units.la: Substantiæ inæquales,
units.tr: Unequal substances,

units.la: Fortem corporis perturbationem.
units.tr: a strong disturbance of the body.

units.la: Superante enim natura omnia æqualiter unitæ sunt:pugnante uerò cum noxijs causis, quæ obedi unt & concoquuntur aliam habent formam : quæ uerò renituntur aliam. Galen. 7. partic. Aphor. Aphor. 33.
units.tr: For when nature prevails, all things are united equally; but when it struggles against harmful causes, those which yield and are concocted take on another form, and those which resist take another. Galen, seventh part, Aphorism 33.

units.la: Vrina fermentata, Crudorum humorum perturbationem & agitationem.
units.tr: Fermented urine, indicating a disturbance and agitation of the crude humours.

units.la: Cum in terra acetum acre effusum fuerit, protinus intumescens sursum, quasdam terræ partes sursum tollit, fitq; compositum quoddam ex terrestri substantia, & aceti humiditate, & ex facto uaporoso spiritu. Simile contingit cum atra bilis in terram effusa fuerit: nempe & in utroque spirituosa quædam motio euidenter fieri uidetur ei similis, quæ in feruente musto apparet. Simile quoque & in pa nibus quotidie fieri uidetur, cum remixta aquæ tritici farina mixto illo & fermento, mediocriter macerari permiserint, fermentatio fieri uidetur fusa si mul, & intumescente, quæ fermentatur substantia. Vrinæ similiter quæ fermentantur, ut prorsus notabilem crassitiem habeant opus: deinde & in ea leuem quandam efferuescentia: quodq; pars spirituosa motione nacta, tumorem habeat maiore, quàm cum excerneretur. Hæc Gal. in 2. prorrhetici.
units.tr: When sharp vinegar is poured onto earth, it immediately swells up and lifts some parts of the earth upward, and a certain compound is formed from earthy substance, the moisture of the vinegar, and a vaporous spirit produced. Something similar happens when black bile is poured onto the ground: in both cases a spirited motion is clearly seen to occur, like that which appears in fermenting must. Something similar also seems to happen daily in bread, when, after the wheat flour has been mixed again with water and that leaven, they let it steep moderately; fermentation seems to occur, the substance that ferments being poured out together and swelling. Likewise, urines that ferment must have a thick substance that is quite noticeable, and in them a certain slight effervescence; and the spirituous part, having gained motion, has a greater swelling than when it was excreted. Thus Galen, in the second book of the Prognostics.

units.la: Vrinæ suppressio,
units.tr: Suppression of urine,

units.la: a. Vesicæ imbecillitatem, b. Inflammationem, Tumorem, c. Obstructionem,
units.tr: a. weakness of the bladder, b. inflammation, swelling, c. obstruction,

units.la: Aegrum vesicæ sensum.
units.tr: a sensation of a sick bladder.

units.la: a. Vesicæ imbecillitatem, uesica ea quæ continen tur exprimere non potente.
units.tr: a. Weakness of the bladder, the bladder being unable to expel what it contains.

units.la: b. Inflammationem & tumorem, meatu angu-stiore reddito.
units.tr: b. Inflammation and swelling, the passage being made narrower.

units.la: c. Obstructionem, ob sanguinis thrombum, uel crassum humorem, uel lapidem, uel pus, quod ab hepate uel renibus, aut aliquo alio inferiore mem bro excernitur.
units.tr: c. Obstruction, from a clot of blood, or a thick humour, or a stone, or pus, which is discharged from the liver or kidneys, or from some other lower member.

units.la: Vrinæ suppressio in sanis accidit, aut ob negoti-orum importunitatem, aut in concionibus, aut foro iudiciario, aut in somnis si diutius continue-rint mictionem: nempe uesicæ uis obuoluens ex immodica repletione uel tensione afficitur.
units.tr: Suppression of urine occurs in healthy people either from the importunity of business, or during sermons, or in the law court, or in sleep, if they hold back urination for too long at a stretch: namely, the bladder's retaining force is affected by excessive filling or tension.

units.tr: END.

units.la: MORBORVM INTERNORVM PROPE OMNIVM CURATIO, BREVI METHODO COMPREHENSA, EX GALENO PRAECIPVE, ET MARCO GATTINARIA: PER IACOBVM SYLVIVM MEDICVM SELECTA.
units.tr: THE CURE OF ALMOST ALL INTERNAL DISEASES, COMPRISED IN A BRIEF METHOD, CHIEFLY FROM GALEN AND MARCO GATTINARA: SELECTED BY JACQUES DUBOIS, PHYSICIAN.

units.la: IACOBI SYLVII AD LECTOREM praefatio.
units.tr: James Sylvius's preface to the reader.

units.la: CUM METHODVS curatoria in uniuersalibus tantum constituta, neminem perfecte scientem reddere queat, nisi in particularibus eadem exerceatur, mihi precium operæ facturus uideor, si post methodi therapeuticæ Galeni interpretationem a nobis absolutam, iam in morbis prope omnibus curandis auditorem exerceamus. Id quod si Galenus præstitisset, ac perfecisset, quod in methodo eadem locis aliquot obiter, & exemplis non ita multis attingit: in libris uero de compositione Medicamentorum secundum partes, non paulo plenius expresisit, cassus erat futurus noster hic labor: quo morborum prope omnium, præcipue internorum, curationem perstringere statuimus. Hi enim cognitu, & curatu sunt multo quam externi difficiliores, & magna ex parte periculosiores.
units.tr: Since the method of curing, when laid down only in general terms, cannot make anyone thoroughly skilled unless it is practised on particular cases, I seem to be doing a worthwhile job if, after the interpretation of Galen's therapeutic method, which we have completed, we now train the student in the cure of almost all diseases. This labour of ours would have been unnecessary if Galen had done, and completed, what he touches on only in passing, with not very many examples, in his method in several places; and if in his books on the composition of medicines by parts he had set it out somewhat more fully. We have resolved to go through the cure of almost all diseases, especially internal ones. For these are more difficult to recognise and treat than external ones, and for the most part more dangerous.

units.la: Quam in rem cum mihi ordine a cæteris obserua to, & breuitate luculenta aptus esse uideretur Marcus Gattinaria, ne post tot celebres medicos idem saxum uoluerem, eius ipsius opera, uti malui, quam ingenium fruستra nouo labore, & parum ne cessario excruciare. Quanquam habeo mihi scriptum eiusdem farinæ opus, sed multo, multoque prolixius, ob morborum causas, signaque, ac remediorum multitudinem. Sed auditori iam in morborum omnium, tum causis tam internis, quam externis, tum signis exercitato satis nunc factura ipsorum curatio est putata: breuis illa quidem, dem, sed tamen perspicua, quantum licuit: ut qua qua uersum facile circunferri posset, ne medicus adhuc rudior remediorum sylua destitueretur, & curandi ordine: interea dum magistros alios cum mutos, tum uel maxime uocales consuleret. Tamen quoniam non pauca in Gattinaria redundabant, seculi sui quodam errore: plaeraque etiam multum desiderabantur: illa ablegauimus, haec ex Galeno suffecimus. adhaec, orationi cultum aliquem uelut induximus. Poteram uero libellum hunc etiam multo breuiorem contrahere, si initio statim, uictus rationum differentias, & remediorum uacuantium, & reuellentium, & repellentium, & eiusmodi aliarum causarum salutem efficientium, fusius expresissem: postea in curationibus singulis ad hos, ceu fontes, lectorem remisissem: sed inexercitato lectori continua haec oratio erit clarior, utilior, & paratior, & tam crebra repetitione familiarior. Quo etiam accedit: quod morbi prope singuli proprium aliquid in dictarum causarum generibus prope singulis habent; quod manifestius singulatim adscriptum patet, quam si semel tantum cum alijs confusum legeretur.
units.tr: For this purpose, Marcus Gattinaria seemed to me suited, since he is observant in his ordering and clear in his brevity, and so that I should not roll the same stone after so many famous physicians, I preferred to use his work rather than waste my talent on a new labour and needlessly torment myself. Although I have by me a work of his of the same kind, it is much, much more long-winded, on account of the causes and signs of diseases and the multitude of remedies. But the cure of all diseases, both their internal and external causes and their signs, is now judged sufficient for a student already practised in them: that treatment is indeed brief, yet clear as far as was possible, so that it could easily be carried about in the pocket, and the physician, still rather raw, would not be left without a forest of remedies, and would have an order for treatment while he consulted other teachers, both silent and, above all, vocal. Yet since not a few things in Gattinaria were excessive because of an error of his age, and many things were much lacking, we have dismissed the former and supplied the latter from Galen. In addition, we have given the discourse a certain polish. I could indeed have condensed this little book even further, if at the outset I had set out at length the differences of dietary regimens and of remedies that purge, revulse, repel, and bring about health by similar means, and then in the individual cures had sent the reader back to these as to sources. But for an inexperienced reader this continuous discourse will be clearer, more useful and more ready to hand, and more familiar through such frequent repetition. To this is added the fact that almost each disease has something peculiar of its own within almost each of the said kinds of causes; this appears more plainly when noted separately than if it were read once only, mixed together with the others.

units.la: Vale.
units.tr: Farewell.

units.la: MORBORVM INTERNORVM propè omnium curatio, Breui Methodo comprehensa, ex Galeno præcipuè, & Marco Gattinaria, per Iacobum Syluiũ Medicum selecta.
units.tr: The cure of almost all internal diseases, summarised in a brief method, chiefly from Galen and Marco Gattinaria, selected by Jacob Sylvius, physician.

units.la: CEPHALALGIA SANGVINEA curatur sex remediorum generibus.
units.tr: Sanguineous headache is cured by six kinds of remedy.

units.la: ICTVS ratione refrigerante, & siccante: ut, aëre cubiculi aquilonem spectantis, non solem & per euripos immisso, & refrigerato, floribus, & foliis salicum vitium, iuncorum, arundinum per aream sparsis, vt docet Galenus lib.9. & 10. Methodi: turba hominum etiam ingredi prohibita, quæ hali tu & transspiratu aërem calefacit, non solum inficit: Vt, cibo, pane loto, hordeaceo, miliaceo, piscibus carne friabili præditis, fruͤctibus austeris, oleribus, intybi, & cichorij, & lapathi generibus, portulaca, cucumere, cucurbita.
units.tr: First, by a cooling and drying method: for example, in a bedchamber facing north, not facing the sun, with cooled air admitted through channels, and with flowers and leaves of willow, reeds and rushes scattered over the floor, as Galen teaches in books 9 and 10 of the Method. Crowds of people are also to be kept out, since their breath and perspiration heat the air and not only foul it. For food: bread that has been washed, barley and millet dishes, fish with tender flesh, sharp fruits, and herbs: endive, chicory, the kinds of sorrel, purslane, cucumber, and gourd.

units.la: Condimento ex omphacio, aceto, succo aranciorum, ranciorum, aut limonum, aut citreorum, aut oxalidis: potu aquæ pluuiæ, aut cum hordeo coctæ: vel si vino est omnino, propter consue tudinem, virium imbecillitatem, & morbi paruitate, vtendum, sit oligophorum, et imbecil lum, aquosumq;, ac etiam aqua multa dilu tum, et his omnibus actu frigidis: &, si opus calfactis, deinde refrigeratis: ut lib. 7. Meth. Galeni, nisi ventriculi intemperies frigida obsistat. Vt, quiete corporis, & animi, aut saltem motibus vtriusq; remissis, et paucis: somno item parciore, venere autem nulla, nec ira, nec furore.
units.tr: For seasoning: verjuice, vinegar, juice of oranges, bitter oranges, lemons, citron or wood sorrel. For drink: rainwater, or barley water. If wine must be taken at all, because of custom or weakness of strength or the mildness of the illness, let it be light, weak, watery, and well diluted with much water, and all of these cold in their action; and if needed, warmed and then cooled again, as in book 7 of Galen's Method, unless a cold condition of the stomach stands in the way. For rest: of body and mind, or at least movements of both kept moderate and few; likewise sleep kept moderate; no sexual intercourse, no anger, no fury.

units.la: 2. SECTIONE vena primum interna, seu basilica, aut communis, si plenitudo est: dein de cephalica lateris dolentis: aut, si totum ca put æque dolet, dextri: qua sanguis causa do loris reuellatur deorsum, & foras vacuetur, ad duo, tria, quatuor vascula, trium vnc. ca pacia, pro scopis à Galeno scriptis, lib. 2. rat. victus acutorum. lib. 9. meth. & alibi passim.
units.tr: 2. By bloodletting: first from the internal vein, or the basilic or common vein, if there is plethora; then from the cephalic vein on the painful side; or, if the whole head aches equally, from the right. In this way the blood is drawn away from the cause of pain downward and emptied outward, into two, three or four small vessels holding three ounces each, for the purposes written by Galen in book 2 of On the Diet in Acute Diseases, book 9 of the Method, and passim elsewhere.

units.la: 3. AFFLUENTEM in caput sanguinem, repellentibus admotis, non frigidis tantum actu, & potestate, sed etiam astringentibus, ut valentius materiam in vicinas partes regerant, & simul caput roborent: ne tam prompte nouam fluxionem admittat, sed in partes imbecillas magis remittat: qualia sunt aqua, & hac valentior, sed crassior succus rosarum, intybolum, lapathorum, plantaginis, portulacæ, semperuiui, lactucæ, solani: singula per se, vel mista secum, aut cum aceto, vt altius in caput descendant. Quam in rem iuuat multum ex alto hæc torrentis in modum illidere sincipiti: nempe rarior, raso, & lanea, aut pannea corona cincto, ne humor hic prompte diffluat, & corpori reliquo sit molestus. Addi potest prædictis oleum rosatum, vt eius vncia vna, aceti albi vnciæ duæ miscentur aquæ, aut succi rosarum, vel aliorum vnciis quatuor. Possunt & panni humoribus his actu maxime frigentibus imbuti, raso sincipiti tandiu admoueri, donec inca lescant, quando noui horum loco sunt substituendi. Repellentibus autem his abstine infebribus: quia febrilem vaporem transpirare vetant.
units.tr: 3. Repelling blood that flows to the head, by applying repellents that are not only cold in action and power but also astringent, so that they drive the matter more strongly into neighbouring parts and at the same time strengthen the head, so that it does not so readily admit a fresh flux but rather sends it on into weaker parts. Such are water, and a stronger but thicker juice of roses, of endive, of the docks, plantain, purslane, houseleek, lettuce, and nightshade, each alone or mixed together, or with vinegar, so that they penetrate deeper into the head. For this purpose it helps much to strike the forehead with these, like a torrent: namely, with a thin, shaved head wrapped in a woollen or linen cloth, lest the humour flow away too quickly and trouble the rest of the body. Rose oil may be added to the above: one ounce of it with two ounces of white vinegar, mixed with four ounces of water, or of rose juice, or of the others. Cloths soaked in these liquids, which are most strongly cooling, may be laid on the shaved forehead for as long as they stay cold; when they warm, fresh ones must be put in their place. But abstain from these repellents in fevers, because they prevent the feverish vapour from passing off by perspiration.

units.la: Lib. 8. metho. in dia ria ab eftu Li. c. ph. p vetant, & ob id febres augent. abstine item, si tota in caput fluxit materia, quam repel- lentia valentius impingent: ac denique, si ce- phalalgia cum catarrho est calido, quæ com presşa materia augerent astringentia.
units.tr: Book 8 of the Method... abstain likewise if all the matter has flowed into the head, which repellents would drive back more forcibly; and finally if the headache comes with a hot catarrh, which astringents would make worse by compressing the matter.

units.la: 4. PVRGANTE bilem flauam turgentem, aut turgenti proximam, medicamento cholagogo, uti mox audies: nam quæ in sanguine erat naturalis, inflammata est.
units.tr: 4. To purge the yellow bile that is swollen, or close to swelling, with a cholagogue medicine, as you will hear shortly; for what was natural in the blood has become inflamed.

units.la: adde, quod sanguinis ita ob transpirationem ipsius prohibitam, calfacti portio tenuior in bilem flauam promptè transit, ut crassior multo post in melancholiam. Sed quo postea parcior gignatur ex sanguine, vel alimentis quoti dianis dulcibus bilis flaua, caliditas eius & acrimonia, & ne tam promptè in caput repat leuitas, & tenuitas, refrigerantibus edo manda nonnihil est: qualia sunt, syrupus violatus, rosatus, intybi, oxalidis, omphacij, acetatus simplex, aut (si magna eius est caliditas) syrupus granatorum, aut limonum, aut ex cort. citri acido: omnium in id validissimus, cum subduplo aquarum intybi, lactucæ, cichorÿ, plantaginis, portulacæ, lupuli, (quæ miscella iulepus vulgo medicorum dicitur.) Buglossi quoq; aqua, licet tepera ta sit, quia tamen roborat cor, his est idonea: sed in principio, fluente adhuc materia, etiam astringentes syrupos, & aquas dare præstat, vt acetatum, rosatum, granatum, ex succo oxalidis: quòd sanguinem crassant, ad fluendumque ineptiorem reddunt, et meatus, per quos fluit, astringunt.
units.tr: Add that when perspiration is blocked, the thinner part of the blood, once heated, passes quickly into yellow bile, and the thicker part much later into melancholy. But so that less yellow bile is afterwards generated from the blood or from daily sweet foods, and so that its heat and sharpness, and the lightness and thinness that so readily rise into the head, are checked, a little should be eaten of cooling sweetmeats, such as syrup of violets, syrup of roses, syrup of endive, of sorrel, of verjuice, or plain vinegar syrup, or (if the heat is great) syrup of pomegranates, of lemons, or acid syrup of citron peel. Most powerful for this is the mixture of two parts water of endive, lettuce, chicory, plantain, purslane and hops with one part syrup, which is commonly called a julep by physicians. Bugloss water, though lukewarm, is also suitable for these cases, because it strengthens the heart. But at the start, while the matter is still flowing, it is better also to give astringent syrups and waters, such as vinegar syrup, rose syrup, pomegranate syrup, and sorrel juice, because they thicken the blood, make it less apt to flow, and tighten the passages through which it runs.

units.la: Dantur autem huiusmodi iulepi ab vncijs tribus ad vncias sex, septem, octo: horis duabus ante cibum, vel etiam alios pastus: quandiu videbitur in sanguine ac bile flava alteranda: in pituita vero apparan da, pluribus consequenter diebus: in melancholia plurimis. Purgabitur autem prunorum & tamarindorum, ana vncia vna in aquæ vncijs trib. quatuor, cocta: cui adde expressum drach. duarum, vel vnc. semiss. myrobalanorum citrearum in aqua intybi infusæ. Valentiora sunt, sed potestate calida, ob idparum tuta in hoc affectu calido scammoniata hæc, electarium de psyllio, & rosatum Mesuæ E.
units.tr: Such juleps are given in doses from three to six, seven or eight ounces, two hours before food or other meals, for as long as the blood and yellow bile seem to need altering; in phlegm they should be given for several days in succession, and in melancholy for very many days. The purge is made of prunes and tamarinds, one ounce of each, boiled in three or four ounces of water, to which is added the strained juice of two drachms, or half an ounce, of citrine myrobalans infused in water of endive. Stronger, but hot in their power, and therefore less safe in this hot condition, are these scammony preparations, the electuary of psyllium, and Mesue's rose preparation.

units.la: de
units.tr: concerning

units.la: Causa est lib. Hipp. de nat. hu ma. & lib. meth. 14. de succo rosarũ Nicolai: Diapruni solutiui u-triusq;, à drachmis tribus ad drachmas qua-tuor, quinq; sex in robustis, & duris corpo-ribus, qualia rusticorum, nautarum. His æ-quipollent pilulæ aureæ Nicolai, & aggrega-tiue à Mesue inuentæ, datæ à drach. vna, seu scriptulis duobus ad scriptula quatuor.
units.tr: The reason is in Hippocrates' book On the Nature of Man, and in Nicolaus' book 14 of the Method, on rose juice. Solutive diaprunum of either kind, from three drachms up to four, five or six, in robust and hard bodies, such as those of country folk and sailors. Equal in effect to these are the golden pills of Nicolaus, and the aggregative pills invented by Mesue, given from one drachm, or two scruples, up to four scruples.

units.la: 5. MATERIAM biliosam, & sangui-neam in capite reliquam, clementer digeren-tibus, quale fuerit fotus capitis ex feminibus althææ, lini, fœnigraeci, floribus chamæmeli, meliloti in aqua sufficienti coctis: vel ex oleo chamæmeli, vel gallo, columbo, hepate, pul-mone magni animalis natura, præ calido ad-huc, admoto.
units.tr: 5. To disperse gently the bilious and bloody matter remaining in the head, such as a fomentation of the head made of seeds of marsh mallow, flax and fenugreek, and flowers of chamomile and melilot, boiled in enough water; or with oil of chamomile; or with a pigeon, a cock, the liver or the lung of a large animal, applied while still warm.

units.la: 6. INTEMPERIEM calidam in capi-te ab his humoribus calidis relictam, sanan-tibus frigidis, qualia sunt dicta repulsoria re-media: vt, oxyrhodinum ex olei rosati vnc. vna, & aceti vnc. semis. & aquæ rosarum, plantaginis, oxalidis, solani: vel harum, ac si milium succi vnc. quatuor, quæ ex pano capi-ti, vt frigeat, admouenda sunt. oleum rosarũ inunctum vel per se, vel cum mucagine semi-nis psyllij, idem præstat.
units.tr: 6. The hot intemperature left in the head by these hot humours is to be healed with cooling remedies, such as the repelling remedies described above: for example, oxyrhodinum made of one ounce of rose oil, half an ounce of vinegar, and rose, plantain, sorrel or nightshade water, or of these together, or four ounces of millet juice, which are to be applied to the head on a cloth so that it cools. Rose oil, rubbed on either alone or with the mucilage of psyllium seed, does the same.

units.la: CEPHALALGIA BILIOSA CVRA-tur sex ijsdem præsidiorum generibus.
units.tr: Headache from bile is cured by the same six kinds of remedies.

units.la: VICTVS ratione refrigerante, et hu-mectante, ob id gigni prohibente, aut genitam temperante bilem flauam, omnium quæ in corpore sunt calidissimam & siccam: qualis victus ratio febricitantibus omnibus est salubris indicatione à febri sumpta.
units.tr: By a regimen of diet that cools and moistens, which prevents bile from being generated, or, if it has been generated, tempers the yellow bile, which is the hottest and driest of all the things in the body. Such a dietary regimen is wholesome for all feverish patients, as indicated by the fever itself.

units.la: Vt, aëre frigido, humido qualem arte & in dustria machinari docet Galenus lib. metho. 9. & 10. calidis omnibus prohibitis, et in cu-biculum illatis refrigerantibus et humec-tantibus plantis, & liquoribus paulo ante re-citatis.
units.tr: Such as: a cold, moist air, which Galen teaches us to contrive by art and industry (Methodus, books 9 and 10); all hot things being forbidden, and cooling and moistening plants and liquors, just recited, being brought into the bedroom.

units.la: Vt, potu aquæ, aut vini aquosi, et aqua mul-ta diluti, aut pomatij, pyratij, imbecillis. Fru-ctibus etiā crudis, pomis, pyris acidis, lactu-ca, portulaca, intybis, oxalide, spinacio, lac-te, caseo recenti, melca, aphrogalacte, pane loto, vel hordeaceo, tenero, piscibus, aut par-tibus animalium nervosis.
units.tr: Such as drinking water, or watery wine diluted with a great deal of water, or pomatium or pyratium, which are weak. Also raw fruits, apples, sour pears, lettuce, purslane, chicory, sorrel, spinach, milk, fresh cheese, melca, aphrogalacte, bread soaked in water, or tender barley bread, fish, or the sinewy parts of animals.

units.la: Vt, quiete, somno etiā longiore, animi tran-quillitate, aut hilaritate, fuga iræ, curarum, mœroris, studiorum, amorum.
units.tr: Such as rest, sleep, even a longer one, tranquillity or cheerfulness of mind, avoiding anger, cares, grief, study and love.

units.la: 2. BILIS flauæ impetum, furoresque ob-tundentibus, frigidis remedijs sumptis & ad motis.
units.tr: 2. To blunt the onset and fury of yellow bile, by taking and applying cold remedies.

units.la: 3. BILEM ipsam turgentem & velut su-riosam purgante medicamento, vt myroba-lanorum citrearū vncia dimidia infusa vn-cijs tribus aquæ, cui tamarindorum, & pru-norum ana vncia vna fuerit incocta, addita ad saporis gratiam sacchari, vel (si febris ad-est) syrupi violati vncia, vel dimidia, vel etiam integra.
units.tr: 3. To purge the swollen bile itself, as if it were raging, with a purgative medicine: for example, half an ounce of finely powdered citrine myrobalans infused in three ounces of water, in which an ounce each of tamarinds and plums has been boiled. Add sugar to taste, or, if there is a fever, an ounce, half an ounce, or even a whole ounce of syrup of violets.

units.la: Vt, rha barbaro tenuiter puluerato à dra-chma dimidia ad drachmam vnam & dimi-diam, aquæ intybi vncijs tribus dissoluto, ad dita syrupi violati vnc. vna, vel taleatim se sto à drach. vna ad drachmas tres, & horis decem, aut circiter infuso aquæ intybi vncijs tribus, deinde valenter expresso, cui miscere potes diaprunum simplex, vel solutiuum vel electarium aliud cholagogum prius dictum, sed minuto tunc rha barbaro.
units.tr: Such as rhubarb of Barbary, finely powdered, from half a drachm to a drachm and a half, dissolved in three ounces of chicory water, with an ounce of syrup of violets added; or cut into slivers of one to three drachms and steeped for about ten hours in three ounces of chicory water, then strongly pressed out. To this you may add simple diaprunum, or a solutive or another electuary, a cholagogue mentioned before, but then with less rhubarb.

units.la: Vt catapotijs aureis Nicolai, vel aggregatiuis à Mesue inuentis, pituitā quoq; purgātib.
units.tr: Such as the golden pills of Nicholas, or the aggregative pills invented by Mesue, which also purge phlegm.

units.la: 4. QVÆ omnia vacuando etiā reuellunt deorsum materiam in caput ruentem, et præter hæc, secta lateris eiusdem vena paucisanguinis vacuatio: cucurbitulæ item omoplatarum interuallo affixæ, primum leues, deinde cum scarificatu, per quas si rursus vacuare libet, oleum etiam cum sale scarificatis partibus, ne glutinentur illinendum.
units.tr: 4. All these, by evacuating, also draw down the matter rushing to the head. Besides these, there is opening a vein on the same side to draw a little blood, and likewise cupping-glasses placed between the shoulder blades, first without scarification and then with it. If one wishes to evacuate again through these, oil mixed with salt should be smeared on the scarified parts, so that they do not stick together.

units.la: 5. REPELLENTIBVS à capite fluentem in id materiā, vt oxyrhodino, & ceteris prius dictis, nisi febris adest, aut tota bilis iam fluxit, aut cephalalgia est cum catarrho calido, vt prædiximus.
units.tr: 5. Remedies that repel the matter flowing into the head from above, such as oxyrhodinum and the others mentioned before, unless there is fever, or all the bile has already flowed out, or the headache is with a hot catarrh, as we have said.

units.la: 6. INTEMPERIEM calidam in capite relictam alterantibus frigidis ex alto in fluxum incipiti, aut etiam capiti reliquo admotis, aut potius per nares attractis, tum prædictis, tum odoramentis frigidis, vt aqua rosata, oxycrato: nā quæ foris capiti occurrant frigida, ipsum densant, ob id calidum vaporem transpirare prohibent. Materia autem biliosa, quia ob leuitatem, raritatem, tenuitatem facile exhalat, huius reliquias digeren tibus vix vnquam opus fuerit.
units.tr: 6. Applying cooling alterants to the head, which are cooling remedies to be applied to the scalp at the beginning of a flow, or also to the rest of the head, or better drawn up through the nostrils, both cooling remedies of this kind and cooling perfumes, such as rose water and oxycrate; for cold things that meet the head from outside thicken it and so prevent the hot vapour from escaping through perspiration. But biliary matter, because of its lightness, rarity and thinness, easily evaporates, so there is hardly ever any need to digest its remnants.

units.la: Quod si remedijs istis cephalalgiæ biliosæ vehementia non vincatur, ad narcotica, id est, stupefacientia sensum tactus, ob id modo quo dam dolorem sedantia, veniendum erit, sed caute applicanda sunt, nec ita valentia, nec diu hærere permittenda sunt, præsertim capiti parti principi, & natura frigidæ: quia multos ita sopiuerunt, etiam partibus aliis indita vt postea nunquam sint expergefacti.
units.tr: But if the violence of biliary headache is not overcome by these remedies, one must have recourse to narcotics, that is, agents that numb the sense of touch and thereby, in a certain way, calm pain. They must be applied cautiously, neither too strong nor allowed to remain long, especially on the head, the principal part and cold by nature, because they have lulled many to such a sleep, even when applied to other parts, that they never afterwards woke up.

units.la: CEPHALALGIA PITVITOSA IISdem causarum salubrium generibus curatur.
units.tr: Phlegmatic headache is cured by the same kinds of wholesome causes.

units.la: VICTVS ratione calfaciente & siccante, vt, aere æstiuo: & si est hyems, calfacto, & siccato per ignem luculentu, ac suffitus aromatum, vt cinamoni caryophyllorum & aliorum similiter calidorum siccorum: Vt, pane fermentato & salso, anisato, vel melathiato, vel aromatato uel sacchara to, uel biscocto, carnib. musculosis animalium & natura non excrementosorum, & præte rea probè exercitorum, assis et sumptis cum sinapio, vel simili viribus condimento, oleri bus, apio, saluia, hyssopo, satureia, thymo, maiorana, aromatum catalogo. Vino genero so, calentibus herbis, aut aromatibus medi-cato, sed parco, præsertim purgato iam cor-pore. Omnia autem hæc alimenta sint pauca & rara, quum inedia etiam huic causæ sit salubris, non solum victus iste tenuis & te-nuans.
units.tr: A regimen of diet that warms and dries, such as summer air; and if it is winter, air warmed and dried by a bright fire, and fumigations of aromatics, such as cinnamon, cloves and other similarly hot and dry things. Such as bread leavened and salted, flavoured with anise, or with honey, or spiced, or sweetened, or twice-baked; meats of muscular animals, not excrementitious by nature, and moreover well exercised, roasted and eaten with mustard or a similar condiment of strong power; herbs such as celery, sage, hyssop, savory, thyme, marjoram, from the catalogue of aromatics. Wine of a generous kind, with warming herbs or medicated with aromatics, but sparingly, especially once the body has already been purged. All these foods should, however, be few and rare, since fasting is also wholesome for this cause, and not only this thin and thinning diet.

units.la: Vt, motu celeri, robusto, vehementi totius corporis ieiuni, præsertim aëre calido sicco.
units.tr: Such as: vigorous, strong, violent movement of the whole body while fasting, especially in hot, dry air.

units.la: Vt, vigilijs, ira, curis, mœrore, & simili-bus animi affectibus, corpus omnino siccan-tibus & sæpe calfacientibus, si non per se, per aliud tamen.
units.tr: Such as: wakefulness, anger, cares, sorrow, and similar affections of the mind, which dry the body thoroughly and often warm it, if not directly then by some other means.

units.la: 2. PITVITAM fere crassam & lentam
units.tr: 2. Phlegm that is generally thick and viscous

units.la: expulsioni apparantibus, incidentibus, tenu-antibus, tergentibus, primum clementiori-bus, qualia mel rosatum, oxymeli Galeni & simplex, syrupus acetatus simplex. deinde uà lentioribus: vt, oxymelite composito, oxy-melite
units.tr: for those preparing it for expulsion, thinning, cutting, and cleansing; first with the milder kinds, such as rose honey, Galen's oxymel, both plain, and simple vinegar syrup. Then with the thicker kinds, such as compound oxymel, oxymel

units.la: Lib. 2. de san. tuen. melite scillitico, syrupo ex duabus aut quin-que radicibus, aut ex stœchade cum duplo a-quarum capiti familiarium, maiorana, sabi-na, bethonica, saluia, melissophylli, quæ die-bus quatuor, quinque, sex; continenter vbi sumpta (nam pituita ægrè apparatur) ad cle-menter vacuantia transeundum. Deinde post illorum vsum in dies aliquot, iterum purgan-dum: ligni gataci decoctum cum floribus car-dui benedicti, in id est efficacissimum.
units.tr: Lib. 2. de san. tuen. squill oxymel, a syrup of two or five roots, or of stoechas with twice the quantity of the herbs that are friendly to the head: marjoram, savory, betony, sage, and balm. Take these for four, five, or six days in a row. Once taken (for phlegm is hard to bring forward), pass on to remedies that purge gently. After using those for some days, purge again with a decoction of guaiacum wood with flowers of blessed thistle; this is most effective for the purpose.

units.la: 3. PVRGANTIBVS cœptam appara-ri per blandiora pituitam, primum etiam cle-mentioribus: vt, pilulis ex hiera Gal. assaie-ret Auic. elephanginis Mesuæ, mastichinis Conciliatoris sumptis hora somni, à drach-ma dimidia ad scriptula duo per se, uel ad scri-ptulum vnum cum agarici trochiscati scrip-tulo vno, per quarum vsum postridie ad mu-nia consueta ire licet.
units.tr: 3. For phlegm that has begun to be drawn out by gentler means, use milder purgatives first: for example, pills of Galen's hiera, which Avicenna tested, the elephangine pills of Mesue, or the mastic pills of the Conciliator. Take them at bedtime, from half a drachm up to two scruples on their own, or one scruple with one scruple of agaric troches. After using these, one may return to ordinary duties the next day.

units.la: Apparata deinde exactius pituita per va-lentius coquentia, tota si fieri potest euellen-da & vacuanda medicamentis etiam valen-tioribus: ut pilulis ex agarico, fœtidis, coccijs
units.tr: Then, once the phlegm has been more thoroughly prepared by stronger digestives, it should be pulled out and evacuated entirely if possible, using stronger medicines too: for example, pills of agaric, fetid pills, and coccias

units.la: L Rasis à drachma vna, ad drachmam vnam & dimidiam, non cum Rasi ad drachmas duas & dimidiam: quòd regionum frigidarū corpora, quàm calidarum minus sint densa, dura, robusta, medicamentis resistentia.
units.tr: of Rhases, from one drachm to one and a half drachms, not with Rhases up to two and a half drachms. This is because bodies in colder regions are less dense, hard, and robust, and so less resistant to medicines than those in warmer ones.

units.la: Pilulis his æquipollent electuariū Indu, & diaphœnicum etiam cholagogum ad vncia dimidiam, vel etiā in robustissimis integram cum decocto herbarum capitalium maiora-ne, bethonicæ, lauri, & c. Sunt qui pilularū, cocciarū verbi gratia, drachmæ semissem et scrup. indi drachmas duas, eodem decocto di soluunt et propinant: sed pilulæ longa in ven-triculo mora diutius, & à remotioribus at-trahunt, quàm potiones: quippe quæ ventri-culo promptè elabantur.
units.tr: An electuary of Indus and cholagogue diaphoenicum, equal in effect to these pills, may be given in a dose of half an ounce, or even a whole ounce for the very robust, with a decoction of the chief head herbs: marjoram, betony, laurel, and so on. Some dissolve and give pills of coccias, say half a drachm, and two drachms of Indian in the same decoction. But pills linger longer in the stomach and draw from more remote parts than drinks do, since drinks pass quickly out of the stomach.

units.la: Vacuata sic, etiā aliquoties à capite pitui-ta, reliquum tamen aliquid omnino post pur-gationes istas manet vacuandum sternutato-rijs & errhinis: primum blandioribus, vt a-qua vel succo maiorane, betæ foliorū aut ra-dicum: deinde valetioribus si opus est: vt pul-uere piperis, struthij, ellebori albi cum succo bethonicæ, melissophylli, rutæ, radicis cyclamini, apophlegmatismis etiam ex mansu mastiches, quarum nostratium clibano siccatarum, baccarū oxyacanthes, pirethri, staphidos agriæ, gargarismatis: denique ex purgante aliquo prius dicto in aqua quapiam capitali soluto, præterquam quod apophlegmatis mata & gargarismata sunt noxia propensis ad catarrhos & affectus alios pulmonis & thoracis, ob id in his vitanda.
units.tr: Even after phlegm has been evacuated from the head in this way, several times, some of it still remains and must be cleared after these purgations, using sneezing powders and errhines. Begin with gentler ones, such as water or juice of marjoram, beet leaves, or roots; then, if needed, stronger ones: powder of pepper, ostrich (struthium), and white hellebore with juice of betony, balm, rue, or cyclamen root; also apophlegmatisms made by chewing mastic, of the kind dried in our ovens, with berries of barberry, pellitory, and wild staphisagria; and finally gargles. Then purge with some purgative mentioned earlier, dissolved in some head-friendly water. Apophlegmatisms and gargles are harmful for those prone to catarrhs and other ailments of the lungs and chest, and so they must be avoided in such cases.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBVS deorsum pituitæ sursum ruetis impetu.
units.tr: 4. For drawing back phlegm that is rushing downward with force upward.

units.la: In quibus præter dicta nunc purgantia, sunt etiam acres balani, & clysteres, partium extremarum vinicula dolorifica, frictiones validæ & diuturnæ, iam inde ab omoplatis inferna versus. Fotus earundem partium ex decocto plantarū capitalium, ex cuius vncijs decem, vel etiam libra vna, et hieræ picræ Gal. vnc. dimidia, vel etiā integra, saccari rub. vnc. duabus, olei chamæmeli vncijs tribus, salis communis drachmis duabus clyster modicè acer fieri potorit: acriores aut post dicetur in apoplexia, epilepsia, caro. Balani autem acres ex melle, & sale, acriores mistis purgantibus prædictis fient.
units.tr: Besides the purgatives just mentioned, the remedies here include sharp cupping-glasses, enemas, painful ligatures on the extremities, and vigorous, prolonged frictions, beginning from the shoulder blades and working downward. A fomentation of these parts may be made from a decoction of the chief herbs, with ten ounces, or even a whole pound, of Galen's hiera picra, half an ounce or even a whole ounce, two ounces of red sugar, three ounces of chamomile oil, and two drachms of common salt. This makes a moderately sharp enema; sharper ones are described below for apoplexy, epilepsy, and caro. Sharp cupping-glasses are made from honey and salt, and they become sharper when mixed with the purgatives named above.

units.la: Cucurbitulæ etiam inter scapulio & cerui cibus affixæ, in id salutares sunt: nec inutilia sunt repellentia, vt lib.13. meth. in lethargo.
units.tr: Cupping-glasses placed between the shoulder blades and the neck are also useful for this purpose. Repellents are not useless either, as in Lib. 13 of the Method, on lethargy.

units.la: Pituitam à capite reliquam dissipantibus, vel sumptis (vt diamosci dulcis, vel amari Mesuæ, vel pliris arcotic. Nicolai drachmis duabus, vel theriaces aut mithridatij veteris drachma vna semel in hebdomade sumpta mane, horis septem ante cibum: vel acoro codito, vel confectione ex acoro tota sua sub statia in id efficaci, horis duabus ante cibum per se, aut cum aqua maiorana, bethonica, saluia, vel alterius capitalis facultate simi-lis) vel admotis vnctionibus, irrigationibus, fotibus, cataplasmatis, emplastris, sacculis, odoramentis, ac reliquis topicis remedijs, ex oleo anethino chamæmeli, liliorum, costino, balanino, ex decocto capitalium prædictorum in lixiuio, euphorbio, castoreo, quæ etiam in aurem tuto à Galeno immittuntur, ne capiti cum
units.tr: To dispel the phlegm that remains in the head, use either things taken internally, such as sweet diamoschus, or bitter diamoschus of Mesue, or two drachms of the pills of Nicholas' arcoticon, or a drachm of old theriac or mithridate taken once a week in the morning, seven hours before food; or prepared sweet flag, or a confection of sweet flag, with its whole substance, which is effective for this, taken two hours before food by itself or with marjoram, betony, or sage water, or some other head-friendly herb of similar power. Or apply, externally, ointments, irrigations, fomentations, cataplasms, plasters, sachets, perfumes, and other topical remedies: oils of dill, chamomile, lilies, costus, and balanus, decoctions of the chief herbs mentioned above in lye, euphorbium, castoreum (which Galen also safely puts into the ear), so that you need not fear applying them to the head with

units.la: Auicen. cociliator Acorus sit indicus non no-stras. cum aliis applicare formides: ex pomo odorifero, maiorana, stœchade, caryophyllis, cinamomo, & c. cum cera constante: quæ omnia capiti admouenda sunt ventriculo vacuo: nam à pleno vim magnam vaporum calore suo in caput traherent. Hæc autem cum caput pituita non modò purgent, sed etiam intemperiem eius frigidam humidam (à qua actionum imbecillitas pendet) emendent: etiam capitis partes roborant, temperaturæ sci licet pristinæ ipsas restituendo, & ratione eadem in aliis affectibus, quos materia aliqua intemperata creat.
units.tr: (Avicenna; the Conciliator: the acorus is the Indian kind, not ours) with other things: scented apple, marjoram, stoechas, cloves, cinnamon, and so on, with firm wax. All these should be applied to the head when the stomach is empty, for if it were full, the heat of the stomach would draw great force of vapours up into the head. These remedies not only purge the head of phlegm but also correct its cold and moist constitution, from which weakness of its functions depends. They also strengthen the parts of the head by restoring their original temperament, and by the same reasoning they serve in other ailments that some intemperate matter produces.

units.la: Cephalalgia ex capitis consensu cum toto corpore in febribus, cùm sit harum symptoma, his persanatis cessat, nec remedia postulat, nisi ob vehementiam frontalia ex oxyrhodino, populeo vnguento, albuminibus applicare cogamur, et frigida quædam ore continere: non autem sincipiti repellentia applicamus, vt ante in cautionibus repellentium in cephalalgia sanguinea diximus. Si autem critica sit cephalalgia, præsertim crisi per vomitum, aut hæmorragiam impendente, re medijs non eget, nisi forte his quæ vomitum, aut sanguinis fluorem è naribus celerent, & promoueant: de quibus posteà.
units.tr: Headache arising from the sympathy of the head with the whole body in fevers is a symptom of those fevers, and it ceases once they are cured; it needs no remedy of its own. Only if its severity forces us should we apply frontal remedies of oxyrhodinum or poplar ointment, or egg whites, and hold cooling things in the mouth. We do not apply repellents to the forehead, as we said earlier in the cautions about repellents in sanguine headache. If, however, the headache is critical, especially when a crisis by vomiting or a threatened haemorrhage is coming, it needs no remedy, unless perhaps those that speed and promote vomiting, or a flow of blood from the nostrils. These will be discussed later.

units.la: CEPHALALGIA PER CONSENSVM.
units.tr: HEADACHE BY CONSENT.

units.la: CEPHALALGIA ex capitis sympathia et cōsensu cum partibus subiectis, vt ventriculo, curatur prospiciendo ante omnia parti primario affectæ, & quæ caput consensu tandem afficit. Deinde ipsi capiti: vt, si in ventriculū effusa bilis flaua, vapori bus in caput sublatis cephalalgiā faciat, danda est cibus frigidus astringens, vt panis ex vino granatorū, vel omphacio: & ita in aliarum partium affectibus posteà dicendis, caput consentiens lædentibus. Capiti autem succurritur primū per astringentia ipsum roborantia, ne talē doloris causam recipiat: deinde per ea quæ iam receptā in ipsum dispositionē abigant: vt, refrigerantia, si calida intemperiem conceperit: caput calefacientia si frigidam, vti prius à nobis est dictum.
units.tr: Headache arising from the sympathy and consent of the head with the parts beneath it, such as the stomach, is treated by attending first of all to the part primarily affected, which in the end also affects the head by consent, and then to the head itself. Thus, if yellow bile poured into the stomach causes headache by sending vapours up into the head, one should give cold, astringent food, such as bread with pomegranate wine or verjuice. So too in the affections of other parts, to be described later, which affect the head by consent. The head is helped first by astringents that strengthen it, so that it does not receive such a cause of pain, and then by things that drive away the disposition already received into it: cooling remedies if it has taken on a hot intemperature, and warming ones if a cold one, as we said before.

units.la: CEPHALALGIA AB AESTV.
units.tr: HEADACHE FROM THE SUN.

units.la: CEPHALALGIA ex mora sub so-le immodica curatur ægrū à solis radio defendentibus, si adhuc sub sole est: victu ite refrigerante & admotis capiti frigidis prius dictis, quæ receptam in ipsum dispositionem calidam profligent.
