Quia tamen capitis calor cucurbitulæ modo trahit, quod tractum iam est partim dictis refrigerantibus & astringentibus repellendum, partim frictionibus, ligaturis & aliis revellendum: partim si quid materiæ post hæc superfit digerendum, reme diys ante dictis, præcipuè in cephalalgia pituitosa: si vero corpus impurum sit, aut plethoricum, vacuandum, ne huic cephalalgiæ succedat diaria, aut synochus non putris, aut putris, aut synoches, aut aliqua ex intermittentibus, id quod vere ipso in adolescentibus maximè quotannis observamus.
units.tr: Headache from excessive time under the sun is treated by keeping the patient out of the sun's rays, if he is still under it, with a cooling diet and cold applications to the head, as mentioned before, which dispel the hot disposition received into it. Yet because the heat of the head draws like a cupping glass, what has already been drawn should be repelled partly by the cooling and astringent things mentioned, partly revelled away by friction, bandages and other means, and partly digested if any matter remains after these, by the remedies mentioned before, especially in pituitous headache. If the body is foul or plethoric, it should be evacuated, lest a daily, a non-putrid or putrid synochus, or some intermittent fever follow this headache, which we commonly observe in young people every year in spring.

units.la: Cephalalgia à frigore externo calidis capiti admotis et sumptis curatur, qualia multa diximus in cephalalgia pituitosa. Curatur item mora sub sole donec dolor desinat, si homo nec plethoricus est, nec cruditate laborat, nec humorem prauum in ventriculo, præsertim ipsius cauitate habeat.
units.tr: Headache from external cold is treated by applying and taking warm things, of which we have said many in the discussion of pituitous headache. It is likewise treated by remaining in the sun until the pain ceases, if the person is neither plethoric, nor suffering from indigestion, nor has a bad humour in the stomach, especially in its cavity.

units.la: Cephalalgia à vini generosi etiam largius poti vaporibus calidis multis, vt per ebrietatem, curatur, prohibito vaporum ascensu in caput, & vacuatis his qui iam sunt in caput recepti, restitutaque pristina capitis temperie. Prohibemus vaporum ascensum naribus inspirantes & expirantes ore aperto, aqua, cydonijs, fructibus etiam crudis, vel si cocti sint, refrigeratis: & omnibus his vel denora tis, vel ore retentis: vacuatio item vino vomitu, aut potius (quia vomitus replet cerebrum his quæ vomuntur, & sanguine vasis thoracis immodicè compressis, à ventriculo sursum ad os suum faciente impetum) deiectione per balanos, iniectiones etiam acres, aut per admota vmbilico purgantia: sumptis etiam catapotijs aliquod Rufi, vel ex hiera, vel similibus, motu corporis recti clementi adiuuante. Quod autem in caput iam repsit, quæ sit vaporosum, facilè resoluetnr dictis prius remedijs in digerendis cephalalgiæ pituitosæ reliquijs, & frictionibus artuum, ligaturisq; ac ambulatione, & reliqua partium inferna rum & brachiorum exercitatione. Vitalis simul his quæ nouo vapore caput replere & inde dolorem ciere possunt, qualia sunt men- tha, crocus, multis etiam moschus et odores cæteri vehementes, & vapore multo, & ca lido replentes instrumenta olfactus atque a- deo continuos ipsis ventres cerebri omnes et cerebrum ipsum. Adde cephalalgiam à con- tusione, vulnere, percussu.
units.tr: Headache from generous wine, even when drunk rather freely, with many hot vapours, as in drunkenness, is treated by preventing the ascent of the vapours into the head, by evacuating those already received into it, and by restoring the head's former temperament. We prevent the ascent of vapours by breathing in and out through the nose with the mouth open, by water, quinces, and even raw fruits, or cooked ones if they are cooled, and by all these either cold or held in the mouth. Evacuation is likewise done by wine-induced vomiting, or rather (because vomiting fills the brain with what is vomited, and with blood, when the vessels of the chest are excessively compressed, driving an impulse from the stomach upward to the mouth) by purging through suppositories, sharp enemas, or purgatives applied to the navel; also by taking some pills of Rufus, or of hiera or similar ones, with gentle upright bodily movement helping. What has already crept into the head and is vaporous will easily be dissolved by the remedies mentioned before for digesting the remnants of pituitous headache, and by friction of the limbs, bandaging, walking, and exercise of the lower parts and the arms. At the same time, avoid those things which can fill the head with new vapour and provoke pain, such as mint, saffron, much musk, and other strong odours, and instruments of smell that fill with much hot vapour, and indeed all the ventricles of the brain and the brain itself. Add headache from a blow, a wound, or a knock.

units.la: SCOTOMATIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: TREATMENT OF SCOTOMA.

units.la: SCOTOMA & vertigo vel corpori neutro impendent, tuncque illis prophy- lactice artis pars, id est, præcautrix prouidet augeri causam prohibendo, vel iamiá homi- nem conflictant, tunc artis parte curatrice est opus, quæ præsentem causam morbumq; abigat genitum. Causa enim effectrix morbo rum, prima est cum perseuerat auferenda, vt recte Galeno visum est. Quæsi externa est, vt corporis in gyrum circumactio, æger quie scat: si corporis ita circumacti, vel rotarum aspectus intueri hæc desinat, si ebrietas, clysteré potius quàm vomitu ventriculus vacuetur, extrema fricentur & ligentur, aliisq; auxiliis à capite vapor auertatur. Si verò in terna est, vt motus spirituum immodicus et inordinatus, quiescat in aëre obscuro: nam lux ipsos spiritus exagitat: sumantur frigida, vt saccharí rosati, syrupi rosati, ribes, granatorum, cydoniorum vncia vna, cum aquæ rosarum, lactucæ, plantaginis vnc. duabus, quæ spirituum motus turbulentos sedent ac sistant.
units.tr: Scotoma and vertigo either threaten a body that is still free of them, and then the prophylactic part of the art, that is, its preventive part, provides for stopping the cause from growing; or they already trouble the person, and then the curative part of the art is needed, which drives away the present cause and the disease it has produced. For the efficient cause of diseases, when it persists, is the first thing to be removed, as Galen rightly thought. If the cause is external, as the turning of the body in a circle, let the patient rest: if he has been turned around, or let him stop gazing at the sight of wheels; if it is drunkenness, let the stomach be emptied by an enema rather than by vomiting; rub and bind the extremities, and by other aids turn the vapour away from the head. But if the cause is internal, as an immoderate and disordered motion of the spirits, let him rest in a dim air, for light stirs up the spirits itself: let him take cooling things, such as rose sugar, rose syrup, currants, pomegranates, and one ounce of quinces, with two ounces of rose water, lettuce, and plantain, which calm and stop the turbulent motions of the spirits.

units.la: Foris etiā applicentur quæ fluentem in caput materiam repellant, qualia prius dicta sunt: caput quoque roboretur, & quæ ex intemperie relicta in eo est imbecillitas castigetur remediis ante descriptis.
units.tr: Outwardly let there also be applied things that repel the matter flowing into the head, such as were said before. The head should also be strengthened, and the weakness left in it by the intemperature should be corrected with the remedies described before.

units.la: Si verò causa eius vel præsentis, vel impendentis sit sanguis, secta, vt in cephalalgia sanguinea dictum est, vena vacuetur: si pituita aut humor alius, prædictis etiam auxilijs purgetur.
units.tr: If, however, its cause, whether present or impending, is blood, let a vein be opened, as was said in the discussion of sanguine headache; if it is phlegm or another humour, let it be purged with the aids already named.

units.la: PHRE-
units.tr: PHRE-

units.la: CVRATIO. PHRENITIDIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE. THE CURE OF PHRENITIS.

units.la: PHRENITIS erysipelas est menin-gum cerebri, morbus omnino acutissimus symptomataq; saeuissima inuehens, ob idstatim ipso principio curandus, vt Hippo. imperat Apho. 10.lib.4. Medicari in valde acutis, si materia turget eadem die: tardare enim in talibus malum est: & remedijs etiam valentissimis, quod idem iußit Aph.6. lib.1. Extremis morbis extrema exquisite remedia optima sunt.
units.tr: Phrenitis is an erysipelas of the membranes of the brain, a most acute disease that brings on very savage symptoms. For this reason it must be treated at once, from the very beginning, as Hippocrates commands (Aphorisms 10, book 4): "In very acute diseases one must treat on the same day if the matter swells, for delay is harmful in such cases." And even with the most powerful remedies, as the same author ordered (Aphorisms 6, book 1): "In extreme diseases, extreme remedies are the best."

units.la: Si igitur morbo ineunte vocaris, cum eius pars iam sit genita, pars gignenda: genita curabis, materiam quae fluxit per resoluentia et alia vacuando: gignendam autem sublata eius causa prohibebis, ne absolutum fiat erysipelas. Id quod si iam est, dubia est salus, frustraque à medicis forè auxilium expectatur. Augeri autem & procedere affectum prohibebis auxiliorum quinque generibus.
units.tr: If therefore you are called at the beginning of the disease, when part of it has already arisen and part is yet to arise: you will treat what has arisen by evacuating the matter that has flowed in, by resolvents and other means; and you will prevent what is yet to arise by removing its cause, so that the erysipelas does not become full-blown. If it is already full-blown, safety is doubtful, and help from physicians is vainly expected. You will prevent the affliction from increasing and advancing by five kinds of remedies.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione tenui & refrigerante, & astringete: vt aqua hordei, seu potione ptissanæ, ptissana colata, & non colata seu tota, ut iubet Hippocra. lib. de rat. victus in morbis acutis: vel potius paulo pleniore (praesertim hac in regione cibo largiori assueta) ne aegrum inedia enecuisse accuseris: ut, cremore alicae, vel hordei farina cum aqua cocta, addito granatorum, limonum, aranciorum, citreorum, cydoniorum succo aut omphacio, aut aceto, aut simili, quibus humores densati & coacti in caput aegrius confluant. Aër si frigidius natura non est, industria (ut ante docui) refrigeretur & humectetur aqua rosarum, aceto & similibus per aream sparsis, quiescat, ac in caeteris faciendis uti et sumen dis, admouendis, educendis quae refrigerant, deligantur, haecque potissimum primis quatuor diebus.
units.tr: 1. DIET, with a thin, cooling and astringent regimen, such as barley water, or a drink of ptisan, strained or unstrained, as Hippocrates orders in his book On the Regimen in Acute Diseases; or rather a somewhat fuller diet (especially in this region, where people are accustomed to richer food), lest you be accused of having starved the patient: such as gruel of spelt or barley flour boiled with water, with added juice of pomegranates, lemons, oranges, citrons or quinces, or of unripe grapes, or with vinegar or the like, by which thickened and coagulated humours reach the head with more difficulty. If the air is not naturally cool, let it be cooled and moistened by effort (as I taught before), with rose water, vinegar and the like sprinkled about the room; let him rest; and in the other procedures, use, apply and withdraw those things that cool, and these chiefly during the first four days.

units.la: 2. AVERTENTIBVS: ut, secta vena cephalica, aut si magna est plenitudo, vena cubiti interna priore, post hanc cephalica. Quod auxilium omni phrenitidi etiam vere & ex syncera bile, non solis phlegmonwdes est salubre, ut ipsi etiam craniifracturae, quatenus sanguinem cum aliis humoribus a meningi-
units.tr: 2. DIVERTING: as by opening the cephalic vein, or, if the fullness is great, the internal vein of the arm first and the cephalic after it. This help is salutary in every phrenitis, not only the phlegmonous kind but also the true one from pure bile, and likewise in fracture of the skull, inasmuch as it draws blood with other humours away from the membranes

units.la: Vere phrenitidi phleboto mē negat Gētilis ne bilis furiat, impat Matth. Gradi, avertendi nō uacuā di gratia. meningibus in ytroque affectu, ob sensum tactus exactum valde dolentibus attractum, & phlegmonas minantem reuellit, non quatenus vacuat, nisi phrenitis sit phlegmonwdes, id est à sanguine cum bile misto. In affectibus enim solum biliosis vacuatio sanguinis bilem cohibentis, & contemperantis, ipsam bilem furere et feruere permittit, si multus scilicet vacuetur, quantus scilicet in sanguineis affectibus: non autem si paucus, ut dum auersionis solius causa & transpirationis sanguinem paucum vacuamus: cui etiam si bilis feruor aliquis superueniat, maius tamen ex erysipelatis generatione per auersionem illam prohibita emolumentum consequimur, quàm sit incommodum bilis inflammationi exiguæ succedens. Quid quòd Auicennas etiam largum sanguinem mittendum imperat, nisi cautio quædam maxima prohibeat? quibus verbis omnino missum vult, nisi magna aliqua occasione prohibemur. Vena igitur secta reuellemus quamprimùm, etiam ventriculo pleno: nam in talibus tardare malum est, periculumque est ne erysipelas absoluatur interea dum cibus in ventriculo per coqui & descendere debet. Quam ventris in serioris vacuationem omnino expectamus, aut tardantem maturamus in morbis mitioribus, antequam venam secemus vacuationis, aut revulsionis, aut alterius alicuius causa.
units.tr: Gentilis denies that one should bleed in true phrenitis, lest the bile rage; Matthaeus Gradi commands it, for the sake of diverting, not of evacuating. In either condition the membranes, which are very painful because of the exact sense of touch they possess, and which threaten inflammation, are drawn away by bleeding, not insofar as it evacuates, unless the phrenitis is phlegmonous, that is, from blood mixed with bile. For in purely bilious conditions, evacuation of the blood, which restrains and tempers the bile, allows the bile itself to rage and boil, if the blood is drawn in large quantity, as it is in sanguine conditions; but not if it is drawn in small quantity, as when we draw a little blood for the sake of diversion and transpiration alone. Even if some heat of bile should follow upon that, we still gain a greater advantage, by preventing the generation of erysipelas through that diversion, than the harm of the slight inflammation of bile that follows. What of the fact that Avicenna also orders a large amount of blood to be let, unless some great caution forbids it? By these words he clearly wants it let, unless we are prevented by some major circumstance. Therefore we will open a vein and divert as soon as possible, even with a full stomach; for in such cases delay is harmful, and there is danger that the erysipelas may become complete in the meantime, while the food in the stomach must be digested and move downward. We certainly do not wait for the stomach to be emptied later, nor do we delay in milder diseases before opening a vein for evacuation, or for revulsion, or for some other reason.

units.la: Sanguinem nanque interdum mittimus alias ob causas, vt ad precautionem: quod lib. de morborum curatione per phlebotomen docet Gal. & ad cognoscendam sanguinis naturā, vt in febre quartana & alijs affectibus melancholicis Gal. lib. 1. ad Glauconem, & in elephantiasi, vt pernoscamus, an vsus, in illis, in hac corruptus sit sanguis.
units.tr: For blood is sometimes let for other reasons, as a precaution, which Galen teaches in his book on the cure of diseases by phlebotomy; and to learn the nature of the blood, as in quartan fever and other melancholic affections (Galen, book 1, To Glaucon), and in elephantiasis, to find out whether in these cases the blood is corrupted.

units.la: Auertunt etiā cucurbitulæ ceruicibus, & omoplatis affixæ: artuum item frictiones, ac ligaturæ ad articulos dolorificæ. Medicamēta denique cholagoga vel clementia, vel, si corpus robustuum est, valentia: vt, Elect. rosatū, Elect. de succo rosarum, diaprunum scammoniatum à drachmis tribus ad drach. quatuor: pilulæ itē aureæ, vel aggregatiuæ à drachma chma una adscript. quatuor, non apparata prius materia, quia turget, aut vacuari sua-pte natura est habilis maximè, nec morbus dat inducias. Auertut et enemata etiā clemen-tia ex vnc. decè vel lib. vna decocti maluæ, violæ nigræ, hordeiana ad Ma. vnū, additis decocto huic cassiæ fistulæ sescuncia, saccha-ri rub. vnc. vna, olei violati vncijs tribus, sa-lis communis drachmis duabus: sed potentius acria, ex prædicto decocto accipiēte pro cas-sia diapruni scammoniati vel alterius. E. prædicti drach. sex vel vnc. vnam.
units.tr: Cupping glasses applied to the neck and shoulder blades also divert, as do rubbing of the limbs and painful ligatures at the joints. Finally, cholagogue medicines, either mild or, if the body is robust, strong: such as Electuary of Roses, Electuary of Rose Juice, diaprunum scammoniatum from three drachms up to four; likewise golden pills or aggregative pills, from one drachm up to four, without first preparing the matter, since it is swelling, or is by its nature readily evacuated, and the disease allows no respite. Enemas also divert, the mild ones made from ten ounces or a pound of decoction of mallow, black violet and barley, with a mallow base added to this decoction: one and a half ounces of cassia pulp, one ounce of red sugar, three ounces of violet oil, two drachms of common salt. But stronger, sharper ones are made from the said decoction, taking diaprunum scammoniatum or another in place of cassia: six drachms or one ounce of the aforesaid.

units.la: 3. REPELLENTIBVS à supernis par-tibus materiā fluentē, qualia, frigida astrin-gentia, vt oxyrhodinum ex aceti parte una olei rosati duabus, aquæ rosatæ quatuor, vel aliud ex prædictis in cephalalgia vel sincipi-ti inflicta, vel capiti admota, vel collo ex pā-no aliquo circumpositā vt vias contrahant, per quas materiæ ascendunt, & materias ip-sas cogant, crassent, & ad motum ineptas reddant. Sed omnia hæc omnia hæc antè mu-tanda quàm incaluerint. Eodem pertinent caphura, acetum, aqua rosarum, odorata & naribus imposita, vel etiam auribus: vel horum loco aqua, aut succus plantaginis, solani, semperuiui, oleum rosatum.
units.tr: 3. REPELLING the flowing matter from the upper parts, with cold astringents such as oxyrhodinum, of one part vinegar, two parts rose oil and four parts rose water, or another of the above preparations, applied to the forehead in headache, or to the head, or wrapped around the neck with some cloth, so that they contract the passages through which the matters ascend, and thicken the matters themselves, rendering them unfit to move. But all of these must be changed before they warm up. To this class belong camphor, vinegar, and rose water, smelled or placed in the nostrils, or also in the ears; or in their place, water or juice of plantain, nightshade, houseleek, or rose oil.

units.la: 4. INTEMPERIEM capitis calidam à bilis contactu relictam, & viarum per quas ascendit laxitatem, corrigentibus frigidis et astringentibus: vt, syrupo rosato & granatorum, cum duplo aquæ rosarum, solani, plantaginis, buglossi sumpto mane, & post cœnam, vt cum vaporibus à cibo elatis cerebrum petant: admotis quoque aliis prius dictis in cephalalgia calida.
units.tr: 4. CORRECTING the hot condition of the head left by contact with bile, and the looseness of the passages by which it rises, with cooling and astringent agents: such as rose syrup and pomegranate syrup with twice the amount of rose water, nightshade, plantain and bugloss, taken in the morning and after supper, so that they reach the brain together with the vapours raised from food; also applying the other remedies mentioned earlier for hot headache.

units.la: 5. DIGERENTIBVS materiam siqua adhuc in meningibus superest crassior, aut impactior, & quæ prædictis remediis non est vacuata: qualia sunt prius dicta in cephalalgia sanguinea, & biliosa, & pituitosa: sed ex his moderatiora primum applicada sunt, quæ si non sufficiant, ad valentiora transfibitur, de quibus etiam nunc agemus. Si enim phrenitis iam facta est, ac absolutum erysipelas, nec hec amplius in generatione est, materiam in tumore coactam vacuare oportet, vt in tumoribus cæteris: symptomata etiam castiga re. Porrò vacuabitur partim sumptis myro balanis, rha barbaro, pilulis, & aliys in cephalalgia sanguinea & biliosa dictis: partim admotis capiti temperatè calidis: vt, columbo, capo, æluro, catulo velsimili animalculo vino per spinam secto, & exenterato, vt a vita calet: vel arietis pulmone aut hepate, si militer ab animali calente, & aliys in melancholia dicendis.
units.tr: 5. DIGESTING the matter, if any thicker or more clogged remains in the membranes and has not been evacuated by the aforesaid remedies: such as those mentioned earlier for sanguine, bilious and phlegmatic headache. But of these, the milder should be applied first, and if these do not suffice, one passes on to the stronger, which we will now discuss. For if phrenitis has already developed and the erysipelas is complete, and it is no longer being generated, the matter gathered into a swelling must be evacuated, as with other swellings; the symptoms must also be checked. This evacuation will be effected partly by taking myrobalans, rhubarb, pills and the other things mentioned under sanguine and bilious headache; partly by applying to the head moderately warm things, such as a pigeon, a capon, a cat, a puppy or a similar small animal, split along the spine and gutted while still warm with life; or a ram's lung or liver, likewise from a warm animal, and others to be mentioned under melancholy.

units.la: Symptomata autem phrenitidis maxima sunt, insomnia, & ischuria. Somnum igitur conciliabis somniferis omnibus etiam opiatis: vt, Philonis antidoto, vel opio ipso sumpto aut admoto, sed pauco, & mistis calenti bus obtuso, modo vires valeant, nec æger sit senex, in his enim opiata exiguas caloris natiui reliquias extinguere periclitantur. Ob id etiam dysenterico & aliter laboranti, si vir tus est imbecilla, opij vsum recte Auic. formidauit. Satis igitur sit syrupum papaueris, aut violatum, cum aqua lactucæ sumere, vn guentum autem populeum admouere.
units.tr: The greatest symptoms of phrenitis are sleeplessness and suppression of urine. You will therefore procure sleep with all soporifics, even opiates: such as Philo's antidote, or opium itself, taken or applied, but in small amount and mixed with warm and blunting things, provided the strength is sound and the patient is not old; for in these cases opiates risk extinguishing the small remaining traces of natural heat. For this reason Avicenna rightly feared the use of opium in dysentery and in other sufferers whose strength is feeble. It is therefore enough to take syrup of poppies or of violets with lettuce water, and to apply populeon ointment.

units.la: Vrinā verò suppressam promouebis vreticis remedijs: vt, oleo scorpionum pubi illito e regione vesicæ, sua proprietate his affectibus idoneo: item titillata digitis virga et perinæo ipso adsedem vsque: admota etiam dictis partibus cocta parietaria, & fotu harum partium facto ex ipsius decocto.
units.tr: But suppressed urine you will promote with diuretic remedies: such as oil of scorpions rubbed on the pubes opposite the bladder, which by its property suits these affections; likewise a rod titillated with the fingers, and the perineum itself as far as the anus; also applying cooked pellitory to the said parts, and fomenting these parts with its decoction.

units.la: APOPLEXIAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: Treatment of Apoplexy.

units.la: APOPLEXIAE omnis præsertim fortis, ex magna respirationis noxa se prodentis, curatio admodum quàm difficilis est, quòd affectus sit grauissimus, & à quo ægri perquam pauci liberantur: id quod parentibus prædicendũ tibi est, si quem tractandum suscipias remedijs, quæ iuuare possint, sed ante omnia cum apoplecticus mortuo sit persimilis: an adhuc viuat his aliquot signis à respiratione sumptis, cognosces.
units.tr: The treatment of apoplexy, especially of the strong kind that shows itself by a great impairment of breathing, is very difficult, because the affection is most grievous and few patients are ever freed from it. You must tell the relatives this beforehand if you undertake to treat anyone with remedies that might help; but above all, since an apoplectic person is very like a dead one, you will learn from the following signs, taken from respiration, whether he is still alive.

units.la: 1. LANA carpta, aut gosapium similiter carptum, vel accensa candela huius ori naribus admota: vel cyathus aqua plenus pe​ctori, si mouetur, respirationis, & per hanc vita certissimum sit indicium: quòd respira- tio à vita, & vita à respiratione separari non potest.
units.tr: 1. Carded wool, or cotton similarly carded, or a lighted candle, brought close to the mouth and nostrils; or a cup full of water placed on the chest, to see whether it is moved by breathing. Through this, life is shown most certainly, since breathing cannot be separated from life, nor life from breathing.

units.la: Respirationem quoq; & vitâ testatur spe culum terfissimum: ori & naribus admotû, si maculatur & velut caligine obducitur. Quanquam verò nullum in apoplecticis vi-ta indiciû appareat, ante tamen tres exactos dies non sepeliantur: quòd horû plurimi præ-sertim mulieres, & qui corde sunt minus ca lido reuixisse sunt visi, quorum exempla tibi passim suppetunt.
units.tr: A very clean mirror also bears witness to breathing and life: if it is brought close to the mouth and nostrils and is clouded over or covered as with a mist. Although no sign of life appears in apoplectics, they should not be buried before three full days have passed, because many of them, especially women and those whose heart is less warm, have been seen to revive, and examples of this are readily available to you.

units.la: APOPLEXIAE SANGVINEAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: Treatment of Sanguine Apoplexy.

units.la: APOPLEXIA autem magna ex parte sanguinea est, aut phlegmatica: sanguinea verò tribus remediorum generi-bus curatur.
units.tr: Apoplexy is for the most part either sanguine or phlegmatic. Sanguine apoplexy is treated by three kinds of remedies.

units.la: 1. AVERTENTIBVS: vt, secta ve-na primùm basilica, præsertim si magna est plenitudo, deinde cephalica et corporis totius frictionibus: ligaturis artuum dolorificis, lotionibus calidis: cucurbitulis primum leuibus, deinde cum scarificatu affixis in collo in plenitudine mediocri, in maiore, partibus primum infernis.
units.tr: 1. Revulsives: that is, first let blood from the basilic vein, especially if there is great plethora; then from the cephalic vein; frictions of the whole body; tight bindings of the limbs that cause pain; warm baths; cupping-glasses, at first without scarification, then with scarification, applied to the neck in moderate plethora, and in greater plethora, first to the lower parts.

units.la: 2. VACVANTIBVS materiam quae iam fluxit in cerebrum, & ipsius ventres corpusque obstruit: vt, secta vena cephalica vel frontis, quâ affectus capitis omnes a sanguine persanare affirmat. Auic. in cap. de cephalalgia. Secat etiam in apoplexia Rasis venas iugulares, non imitandus, quod periculo hæc non vacet phlebotomia. Nam collum ante sectionem fricare & ligare expedit, vt iugulares tumore & tensione se prodant: quæ res cerebrum magis replet affectumque auget, nisi emolumetum maius ex vacuatione hac, quàm incommodum ex ligatura causeris, præsertim cum etiam in vena frontis secanda collum sit stringendum, si tunc minor superest copia. Sectis item his iugularibus venis a medio vel casu, hæmorrhagia fit multa, & quæ ægerrimè cohibetur, vixque vlcus glutinatur tur: quòd vinculo idoneo astringi pars hæc non ferat sine suffocationis & apoplexiæ aut gendæ periculo, soloque digito sectioni horas multas appresso sanguis sistitur, et sectio glutinatur pice, & emplastricis alijs ægrè adhærentibus citra deligaturam.
units.tr: 2. Evacuants, to draw off the matter that has already flowed into the brain and obstructs its ventricles and the body: that is, let blood from the cephalic vein or the vein of the forehead, by which Avicenna, in his chapter on headache, asserts that all affections of the head are cured by blood-letting. Rhazes also opens the jugular veins in apoplexy; this is not to be imitated, because this bleeding is not free from danger. For it is useful to rub and bind the neck before the section, so that the jugulars show themselves by swelling and tension; this fills the brain more and increases the affection, unless you judge the advantage from this evacuation to be greater than the harm from the ligature, especially since the neck must also be bound when the vein of the forehead is to be opened, if a smaller amount then remains. Likewise, when these jugular veins have been opened either by design or by accident, a great haemorrhage follows, which is most difficult to check, and the wound scarcely closes; because this part cannot bear a suitable ligature without danger of suffocation and of apoplexy or of gangrene, and the bleeding is stopped only by pressing a finger on the incision for many hours, and the incision is closed with pitch and other plasters which stick poorly without a bandage.

units.la: 3. INTEMPERIEM à sanguinis calidi copia partem alterantibus, sumptis, et sub finem curationis admotis: vt, aceto, & oleo rosato.
units.tr: 3. Alterants that correct the intemperature arising from an abundance of hot blood, taken internally and applied near the end of the cure: for example, vinegar and oil of roses.

units.la: Quæ quamuis etiam initiò ad repellendum conducerent, tuta tamen non sunt, præsertim his qui ad obstructiones sunt propensi, vtpote quas hæc remedia, vijs à se contractis, & materia nonnihil crassata, prompte vel excitant, vel iam factas geminant.
units.tr: Although these might at first serve to repel, they are nevertheless not safe, especially for those prone to obstructions, since these remedies, by contracting the passages and somewhat thickening the matter, either readily provoke obstruction or double what has already occurred.

units.la: APOPLEXIAE PITVITOSAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: Treatment of Phlegmatic Apoplexy.

units.la: APOPLEXIA autem pituitosa curatur quatuor auxiliorum generibus.
units.tr: Phlegmatic apoplexy is treated by four kinds of aids.

units.la: 1. AVERTENTIBVS, vt acribus et caput & pituitam respicientibus enematis, quale quod hieram picram, aut hac multò valentiorem hieram Logadij, & cætera pi tuitam vacuantia recipit, vt accipias saluiæ, rorismarini, maioranæ, foliorum lauri, origa ni, calaminthes, stœchados ana Ma. vnum, coque in aqua sufficienti. Decocti huius libra vni adde hierę picrę vnc. vnā, aut hierę Lo gadij vnc. Dimidiam, sacchari rub. cassiæ fi stulæ ana vnc. vnā, olei chamæmeli, vel lau rini, vel rutæ vnc. tres, salis gemmæ drach. di midiam iniice clysterc: id enim validum satis & capiti familiare.
units.tr: 1. Revulsives, such as sharp enemas that act upon the head and the phlegm, of the kind that receives hiera picra, or the much stronger hiera of Logadius, and other purgatives of phlegm. Take of sage, rosemary, marjoram, bay leaves, oregano, calamint, and stoechas, one handful each, and boil them in enough water. To one pound of this decoction add one ounce of hiera picra, or half an ounce of hiera of Logadius, one ounce each of red sugar and cassia pulp, three ounces of oil of camomile, or of laurel, or of rue, and half a drachm of rock salt; inject this as a clyster, for it is strong enough and suited to the head.

units.la: Idem prestant, sed infirmius, balani digitos sex longæ, ex melle et prædictis hieris valen tibus, ac etiam colocynthide compositis, vt ex puluere hierę picrę drach. sex, vel hierę Logadij drach. tribus, salis gemmæ drach. vna, ellebori agarici ana scriptulo vno, colo cynthidos script. dimidio, fiant balani filo, an tequam indantur, ligandæ, vt cum opus erit retrahi possint. Iuuant quoq; cucurbitulæ na tibus, lumbis, & omoplatis affixæ, et præter has totius corporis frictione, & ligaturæ ar tuum dolorificæ: ac etiam testium, vt horum dolore maximo expergificata facultas obstruentem, materiâ expellat. Quæ omnia sæpe sunt repetenda, si prius nondum contulerint.
units.tr: Balls of the same kind, but weaker, do the same: six fingers long, made of honey and the aforementioned strong hieras, and also compounded with colocynth, for example six drachms of powder of hiera picra, or three drachms of hiera of Logadius, one drachm of rock salt, one scruple each of white hellebore and agaric, and half a scruple of colocynth. Make them into balls, tied with thread, so that they can be pulled out when needed before they are inserted. Cupping-glasses applied to the nostrils, loins and shoulder-blades are also helpful, as well as frictions of the whole body and painful bindings of the limbs; and also of the testicles, so that the faculty, roused by their very great pain, may expel the obstructing matter. All these things must often be repeated, if they have not yet produced an effect.

units.la: 2. PITVITAM non apparatam (quia morbus hic acutissimus inducias apparandi non permittit) vacuantibus etiam valentibus et largioribus medicamentis, ob id quod virtus expultrix multum est sopita, & mea tus angustiores redditi, partibus scilicet eorū refrigeratis in seq; cōcidentibus, cùm nec amplius per ipsos sanguis cum calore & spiritu permeat. Talia fuerint pilulæ coccïæ, ex euphorbio, fœtidâ, à scriptulis quatuor ad sesquidrach. syrupo stœchados, & aquâ saluiæ dissolutæ, ut devorari possint, cum apoplectici omnes motus naturales & animales (ut idem de vitalibus intelligas dictum) habeat prostratos.
units.tr: 2. Evacuants, even strong and rather large medicines, for phlegm not yet prepared (since this most acute disease does not allow time for preparing it), because the expulsive power is much dulled, and the passages have become narrower, their parts being chilled and collapsing afterwards, since blood can no longer pass through them with heat and spirit. Such would be the pills of cocci, made of euphorbium and stinking asafoetida, from four scruples to a drachm and a half, dissolved in syrup of stoechas and sage water, so that they can be swallowed, since every apoplectic has his natural and animal motions (and you should understand the same said of the vital ones) prostrated.

units.la: Vacuabis ex capite ipso dictis prius in cephalalgia pituitosa sternutamentis & errhinis atque ubi adsepaululum redierit, gargarismatibus, et apophlegmatis, quæ motu voluntario egent ut in usum veniat: quāuis dentes, gingiuas, linguam, palatum, ore à nobis aper to ijsdem fricare liceat.
units.tr: You will evacuate from the head itself, by the sternutatories and errhines previously described in phlegmatic headache, and when the patient has recovered a little, by gargles and apophlegmatics, which need voluntary motion to be of use; although it is permitted to rub the teeth, gums, tongue and palate, with the mouth opened by us, with the same.

units.la: 3. MATERIAE reliquias digerentibus, & simul caput roborantibus, partim sump-tis, ut confectionis anacardinae scriptulo vno (quae calore vehementi etiam febrem excitat) ut acoro vero condito, confectione ex acoro vero per se in ore retentis, vel etiam denoratis cum aquis capitalibus: partim admo tis capiti raso, oleis liliorum, ex spica, ex euphorbio, ex costo (quod capiti etiam familiare est) emplastro Mesuae ex sinapi phoegnimon & vesicas excitante, & valenter ad cutim trahente, suffitu quoque castorij & odoramentorum similiter valentium, cataplasma tis, fotibus ex valenter calidis, siccis capitalibus post vacuatum diligenter, ut praedixi, corpus totum atque adeo caput ipsum. Si soluatur apoplexia, ei solet succedere paralysis.
units.tr: 3. Remedies that digest the remnants of the matter and at the same time strengthen the head, partly taken internally, such as one scruple of the confection of anacardium (which by its vehement heat also excites fever), or true acorus preserved in sugar, or the confection of true acorus alone, held in the mouth, or even swallowed with the capital waters; partly applied to the shaved head: oils of lilies, of spikenard, of euphorbium, of costus (which is also suited to the head), Mesue's plaster of mustard, which raises blisters and inflammation and draws powerfully to the skin, also fumigation with castoreum and similarly strong perfumes, poultices, and fomentations with strongly warm and dry capital waters, after the whole body and indeed the head itself has been carefully evacuated, as I have said. If the apoplexy is loosened, paralysis usually follows it.

units.la: CARI CVRATIO.
units.tr: Cure of Caros.

units.la: CAROS, id est, somnus longus, et gravis, affectus cerebri aut primarius, proprius aut per consensum maximè cū ventriculo, vterque à causa vel interna, vt intemperie frigida humida sola vel cum materia (qualis infantibus sæpe accidit, præsertim aëre frigido humido et in eo diu educatis) vel externa vt esu fungorum vel frigidis potesta te venenis, vt opio, cicuta largius sumptis.
units.tr: Caros, that is, a long and heavy sleep, is an affection of the brain, either primary, proper, or through sympathy, most often with the stomach. Each arises either from an internal cause, such as a cold and moist intemperature alone or together with matter (as happens often to infants, especially when they are reared in cold, moist air for a long time), or from an external cause, such as eating mushrooms or taking poisons with cold power, such as opium or hemlock, in excessive amounts.

units.la: Si proprius est cerebri affectus & primarius, curatur vt apoplexia & cephalalgia pituitosa. Si à pituita est (id quod ferè est) aut sanguinea, si à larga in capite sanguinis copia. Curatur autem illa solis calfacientibus tam sumptis, vt diamoscho dulci & amaro, acoro vero condito, confectione veri acori, & anacardina: quàm admotis, vt oleo spicæ, costino & cæteris prædictis: etsi à sola intemperie frigida, vel etiam humida sine materia fiat. Si per consensum cum parte aliqua, vt ventriculo, ob materiam aliquam, aut multitudine vires opprimentem, aut frigiditate humida stupefacientem fit caros: parti materiam transmittenti prius est prospiciendum vacuatione illius materiæ, & prouidentia, ne similem vel in se gignat, vel aliunde recipiat, in cerebrumq; transmittat: deinde cerebro recipienti prospiciemus vacuando quod iam recepit, & roborando: modisq; omnibus pro uidendo ne talem deinceps materiam recipiat. Quae quibus remedijs perficipossint, prius abunde in cephalalgia diximus.
units.tr: If the affection is proper to the brain and primary, it is cured like apoplexy and phlegmatic headache. If it arises from phlegm (which is usually the case) or from blood, if from a large abundance of blood in the head. It is cured, however, by warming things taken internally, such as sweet and bitter diamoschum, acorus prepared with sugar, the confection of true acorus, and anacardine, and by those applied externally, such as oil of spica, costus and the other things mentioned above; this holds even if it arises from cold intemperature alone or from moist intemperature without matter. If caros arises through sympathy with some part, such as the stomach, because of some matter that either overwhelms the strength by its quantity or stupefies by its cold moistness, then first one must provide for the part that transmits the matter by evacuating that matter, and by taking care that it neither generates a similar matter in itself nor receives it from elsewhere and sends it on to the brain; then we shall provide for the receiving brain by evacuating what it has already received and by strengthening it, and in every way take care that it does not afterwards receive such matter. As to the remedies by which these things can be accomplished, we have already said enough under headache.

units.la: Si autem materia sit deleteria vt narcotica in ventriculo, non solum calidis est oppugnanda, sed suis alexipharmacis tota sua substantia contrarijs & in illa expellenda agentibus, quae horum singulis propria a Dioscoride & aliis describuntur.
units.tr: If, however, the matter is deleterious, like a narcotic in the stomach, it must be attacked not only with warming remedies, but with its own alexipharmics, whole in their substance, which act against it and expel it; these are described for each of them by Dioscorides and others.

units.la: Auertentibus etiam vtendum est, ac materiam attolli astrictione sua prohibentibus, sed calidis actu et potestate: vt hiera ex aloe, rha barbaro, myrobalanis.
units.tr: Derivatives also must be used, and the matter must be drawn up by means of agents that prevent its retention by their astringency, but with warming action and power, such as hiera made with aloes, rhubarb and myrobalans.

units.la: Excitandus postremo aeger est valentibus, tum reuulsionibus per purgatia, balanos, clysteres in apoplexia dicta: per frictiones quoq; & ligaturas dolorificas, & cucurbitulas: tum vulsis naribus, auribus, barba, capillis, sternutamentis, odore aceti acrimonia mordentis dentis, & materia aliquid siccantis.
units.tr: Lastly the patient must be roused with strong measures: by revulsions through purgatives, balanos, and clysters, as described for apoplexy; also by friction, painful ligatures, and cupping glasses; then by pulling the nostrils, ears, beard and hair, by sneezing powders, and by the smell of vinegar, which bites with sharp acridity, and of something that dries the matter.

units.la: CATALEPSEOS CVRATIO.
units.tr: Cure of Catalepsy.

units.la: CATALEPSIS Galeno ab intem perie cerebri frigida sicca fit, dicta vul go medicorum congelatio, à catoche seu so-pore vigilante diuersa affectio: quòd catale-psis spiritus animales à frigido sicco velut co-cretos, & ad actiones suas ineptos habet si-ne materia: catoche autem seu sopor vigilans gignitur à bile flava largiore, cum pituita e-tiam largiore in cerebro permistis: quarum illa calida sicca, vigilias: hæc frigida humida somnum inducit, magis & minus pro vin-centis materia quantitate & qualitate.
units.tr: Catalepsis, according to Galen, arises from a cold and dry intemperature of the brain; it is what physicians commonly call congelation, and it is a different affection from catoche or waking sopor. For catalepsis has the animal spirits, as if congealed by cold and dryness, and unfit for their actions, without matter; catoche or waking sopor, however, is produced by a larger amount of yellow bile, with a larger amount of phlegm also mixed in the brain. Of these, the former, being hot and dry, induces wakefulness; the latter, being cold and moist, induces sleep, more or less according to the quantity and quality of the matter that prevails.

units.la: In accessione æger pristinam partium figu- ram retinet, rigidis videlicet neruis, & frigi-do sicco velut concretis, vt si prius sedebat, sedens permanet: si genua flexerat, genibus flexis permanet: si os apertum erat, apertum manet, ac oculis manet apertis, musculo illo visum fugiente, qui palpebra superiorem ape-rit, rigido manente: sensu quoque omni, & motu priuantur, spiritu animali in singulis partibus, non solo cerebro, ab intemperie frigida sicca concreto, & ad permeandum nervosa corpora, ac etiam mouendum inepto. Ob id somnus in hac non est, quod spiritus animalis totus a neruis in cerebrum non revocatur, sed in hac ut caro manet quaedam respiratio, ab illæsis adhuc quibusdam spiritibus, ob vitæ necessitatem respirationi potissimum servientibus. Quanquam vero hæc cum apoplexia communem habet sensus & motus privationem, tamen in apoplexia spiritus sunt integri: per obstructionem vero ventriculorum cerebri, in partes nervosas sentiendi, & movendi facultatem conuehere prohibetur, quo fit, ut partes laxæ & resolutæ maneant, & corpus situm, ac partium figuram priorem commutet: in catalepsi autem spiritus ipsi sunt affecti, & velut concreti, ob intem periem ipsorum frigidam siccā: ob id ad vim sentiendi et movendi in partes nervosas transvehendum inepti, sed quibus locis sunt intercepti manent quieti, et hæ partes rigidæ fiunt. Catalepsis curatur calidis moderatè & humectantibus sumptis & admotis, vt fotibus ex oleo sesamino, iasmino, chamæmeli, addita etiam in singulas horum libras euphorbij vnc. vna: ex oleo etiam liliorum calorem natiuum proprietate sua viuificante, vim alexiteriam contra hoc malum sortita: ex decoëto item chamæmeli, meliloti, saluiæ, maiorana, &c. capitalium in vino.
units.tr: During the attack the patient keeps the former shape of his parts: the nerves, namely, being rigid and as if congealed by cold and dryness, so that if he was sitting before, he remains sitting; if he had bent his knees, he remains with knees bent; if his mouth was open, it remains open, and his eyes remain open, the muscle that raises the upper eyelid, which keeps the sight, remaining rigid. All sense and motion are also taken away, the animal spirit in the individual parts, not only in the brain, being congealed by cold dry intemperature and unfit to pass through the nervous bodies and even to move them. Therefore there is no sleep in this condition, because the whole animal spirit is not called back from the nerves into the brain; but in this there remains a certain breathing, like a living flesh, from some spirits still unharmed, which serve chiefly for breathing, for the necessity of life. Although this condition shares with apoplexy a general loss of sense and motion, yet in apoplexy the spirits are intact; rather, through the obstruction of the ventricles of the brain, the faculty of sensing and moving is prevented from being conveyed into the nervous parts, whence it happens that the parts remain lax and loosened and the body changes its position and the former shape of its parts. In catalepsy, however, the spirits themselves are affected and as it were congealed, because of their cold dry intemperature; therefore they are unfit to be conveyed into the nervous parts with the power of sensing and moving, but they remain quiet in the places where they have been intercepted, and these parts become rigid. Catalepsy is cured by moderately warming and moistening things, both taken internally and applied externally, such as fomentations of sesame oil, jasmine, and chamomile, with one ounce of euphorbium added to each pound of these; also of lily oil, which by its own property revives the native heat and has an alexiteric power against this evil; likewise of a decoction of chamomile, melilot, sage, marjoram, etc., and of the chief herbs in wine.

units.la: Hæc post auersionem materiam resoluunt, sed vide ne aceto aut similiter siccante remedio, vitales spiritus paucos in corde relictos absumas, & extinguas. A mitioribus ergo incipienda fusio, ad valentiora paulatim, si est opus, deinde transeundum: qualia fuerint oleum quod dixi, euphorbiatum, rutaceum, ex spica, costinum, laurinum: & vini optimi & aromatici potus, quale est maluaticum, & quod νιέξον igneum seu fuluum, quo catalepsim sanasse se dicit Gal. lib. 3. Simplicium.
units.tr: These things resolve the matter after derivation; but take care not to waste and extinguish the few vital spirits left in the heart with a vinegary or similarly drying remedy. The pouring-on should therefore begin with milder things, and proceed gradually to stronger ones if need be: such as the oil I mentioned, euphorbium oil, rue oil, spica oil, costus oil, laurel oil; and drinks of the best and aromatic wine, such as Malvasia, and the fiery or tawny wine which Galen, in the third book of the Simples, says cured him of catalepsy.

units.la: Vinum nanque huiusmodi virtutem quandam viuificandi obtinet. Auic. cap. de delete rijs frigidis. Catalepseos autem curatio plenius ex melancholiæ curatione intelligetur.
units.tr: For wine of this kind has a certain power of reviving. Avicenna, chapter on cold poisons. The cure of catalepsy will be understood more fully from the cure of melancholy.

units.la: PARALYSEOS CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF PARALYSIS.

units.la: Paralysis curatur quinq; remediorum generibus.
units.tr: Paralysis is cured by five kinds of remedies.

units.la: VICTVS ratione calfaciente & siccante, & ob hoc pituitæ generationē prohibente, vt aëre calido sicco per ignem lu culentum, suffitum ex caryophyllis, & aliis similibus. Caue tamen ne initio fluente scili cet materia multum calfacientibus materiā colliques, & fusam calore per vias à calore eodem latiores redditas ad fluendū magis pro noces. Vt cibis calidis siccis natura & arte, vt perdicibus, auiculis aßis, vel frixis, pane biscocto, & si vis anisato, melanthiato, sac charato. Vt cæteris denique sumendis, admo uendis, educendis, faciendis facultate quandā naturalem calfaciendi & siccandi sortitis.
units.tr: (1) Diet, using warming and drying foods, which also prevents the generation of phlegm: dry warm air from a bright fire, fumigation with cloves and similar things. Beware, however, that at the start, while matter is flowing, you do not use very warming things that melt the matter; once it is melted by heat, it flows more harmfully through the passages that the same heat has widened. Use warm, dry foods, natural and prepared, such as partridges, small birds roasted or fried, twice-baked bread, and, if you like, bread flavoured with anise, nigella or sugar. Finally, use other things to be taken, applied, drawn out or made, which by their natural quality warm and dry.

units.la: 2. PITVITAM coquentibus, & ad ex pulsionem incidendo, tenuando, tergendo pa rantibus, primo quidem triduo, aut quatri duo clementioribus, vt mellis rosati colati se scuncia cum duplo aquarū saluiæ & betho nicæ: deinde purgato blandius corpore, melle rosato, aut oxymelite simplici, aut syrupo acetoso, simplici par pondus syrup. stœchados cum aquis prædictis, aut similibus miscebitur, pauloque valentius purgabitur: postremò syrup. stœchados solo cum dictis aquis vtendum: deinde valentius multo vacuandu, & in his tamen vt purgantibus, & victus ratione, & ( vt summatim dicam) cæteris affectuum mitiorum remedijs, ad dies quatu or primos mitioribus auxilijs vtendum, paulatim ad valentiora deinde transeundum, vt etiam paulo ante dixi. Quamuis autem acetum & acetata omnia ad pituitam crassam tenuandum & lentam incidendum sit efficax, quia tamen neruis quorum affectus paralysis, nocet, vt frigida et mordacia cætera: ob id eo rarius et parcius vtendu, præsertim solo: additu enim mel rosatum noxa ab eo prohibet. Vacuantibus paratam per dictos syrupos pituitam, primùm vt dixi, clementioribus, vt pilulis de hiera, agarico, elephangi-nis, assaieret, mastiche, quæ etiam partes roborant. Agaricu item trochiscatu per se quidem ad scriptula quatuor dabis: cum drach. autem dimidia aliquarum ex dictis pilulis, ad scriptula duo, ut in cephalalgia pituitosa praedictum est: his postea pilulae valentiores vsurpandae sunt foetidae Mesue, & coccie Ra sis, aut de sagapeno, de opopanace, de euphor bio omnium valentissimae raro admodum vtendae: pilulae tamen sua in ventriculo mora longiore diutius a remotis partibus trahunt, ob id optatiores sunt alia quauis medicamen torum forma in affectibus partiu remotaru.
units.tr: (2) For those who digest phlegm and prepare it for expulsion by cutting, thinning and cleansing: at first, for three or four days, with milder remedies, such as half an ounce of strained rose honey with twice as much water of sage and betony. Then, once the body has been purged more gently, rose honey, or simple oxymel, or simple vinegar syrup, or the same weight of syrup of stoechas with the said waters or similar, is mixed in, and the purge is a little stronger. Finally, syrup of stoechas alone with the said waters is to be used. After that the body is to be emptied much more strongly. In all this, both the purgatives and the diet, and (to speak briefly) the other milder remedies for these affections, are to be used for the first four days, and then one gradually moves on to stronger ones, as I said a little before. Although vinegar and all vinegared preparations are effective for thinning thick phlegm and cutting viscous phlegm, yet, because they harm the nerves whose affection is paralysis, as do other cold and biting things, they are to be used more rarely and sparingly, especially alone; for adding rose honey prevents the harm from them. For purging the phlegm prepared by the said syrups, first, as I said, use milder things, such as pills of hiera, agaric, elephantine pills, and mastic, which also strengthen the parts. Give agaric troches alone, four scruples; or, with half a dram of some of the said pills, two scruples, as was said in the discussion of phlegmatic headache. After these, the stronger pills are to be used: the foetid pills of Mesue and the coccic pills of Rhazes, or those of sagapenum, opopanax and euphorbium, the most powerful of all, to be used very rarely. Nevertheless, pills stay a longer time in the stomach and so draw more slowly from remote parts; for this reason they are more desirable than any other form of medicine in affections of remote parts.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBVS in contraria materia, qua ad spinalem medullam defluit, ut praeter dicta nunc purgantia, clysteribus, sternutatoriis, errhinis, apophlegmatismis, gargarismatis ante dictis: vtendum aute post multas corporis totius vacuationes.
units.tr: (4) For those turning away matter that flows toward the spinal marrow: besides the purgatives just mentioned, use clysters, sternutatories, errhines, apophlegmatisms and gargles, as described before; but these should be used after many evacuations of the whole body.

units.la: 5. RELIQVAM materiam digerentibus, & simul cerebrum, & partes alias ab hac materia laesas roborantibus, applicantes parti primario affectae, non his quae animali facultate ad sensum & motum necessaria priuantur, ob superiorum partium affectum:
units.tr: (5) For digesting the remaining matter, and at the same time strengthening the brain and other parts harmed by this matter, applying remedies to the primarily affected part, not to those parts that are deprived of the animal faculty necessary for sensation and motion, on account of the affection of the upper parts:

units.la: Vt Galenus quendam ex casu à curru digi- tos habentem resolutos, sanauit emplastro di gitorum spinali medullæ admoto: qua parte offensa, neruus qui ad illos digitos ferebatur, ex dolore phlegmonem, & ab ea obstructio nem, quæ spiritum ad digitos ferri prohibe ret, contraxerat. Adde quod mitia digeren tia, vt sæpe iam diximus, prima sunt explo randa: vt, oleum chamæmeli, oleum vulpi num Mesuæ ad neruorum affectus efficax: po stea valentiora: vt, oleum de spica, costinũ, de terebinthina Mesuæ, philosophorum eius dem, aqua vitæ, & vnguentum ex puluere lumbricorum terræ, olla in clibano siccato rum, ex galange, piperis ana vnc. tribus, cũ libris tribus mellis despumati: id in affectib. neruorum resoluendis mirè efficax expertus est Gattinaria: & succum treos, castoreum, emplastrum Mesuæ ex sinapi: sed hæc valen tia parti diutius non adhæreant, ne vrant, aut phlegmonem accersant. Explorabis igi tur sæpe illorum effectum, vt intelligas quan do illis abstinendum sit. Balnea quoq; aquarũ medicamentosarum, præsertim sulfurearum, & nitrosarum, et horum lutum parti primario affectæ admotũ, sunt in hunc affectum efficacissima. Sumatur autem semel in hebdomada drach. vna theriaces veteris, aut mithridatij diamoschi dulcis, aut amari, aut acori veri conditi, aut confectionis de acoro, aut drach. duæ olei ex acoro in dies sumptæ: stœchas quoq; saluberrima in id est, quia cerebrum valde calefacit, et siccat: pulueris etiam hieræ aureus vnus, piperis aurei duo calfaciunt, siccant, resoluunt.
units.tr: As Galen cured a man who had his fingers loosened after a fall from a chariot, by applying a plaster to the spinal marrow. When that part was struck, the nerve that ran to those fingers had, from the pain, contracted a phlegmon, and from that an obstruction which prevented the spirit from being carried to the fingers. Add that mild digestives, as I have often said already, are to be tried first: such as oil of chamomile, and Mesue's oil of foxes, which is effective for affections of the nerves. Afterwards stronger ones: such as oil of spike, costus, Mesue's oil of turpentine, the aqua vitae of the same philosopher, and an ointment made of powder of earthworms, pot-dried in an oven, with galangal and pepper, three ounces of each, and three pounds of skimmed honey. Gattinaria found this wonderfully effective in loosening nerve affections. Also juice of treos, castoreum, and Mesue's plaster of mustard; but these strong things should not stay on the part for long, lest they burn or bring on a phlegmon. You will therefore often test their effect, so that you understand when they must be avoided. Baths of medicinal waters, especially sulphurous and nitrous ones, and their mud applied to the primarily affected part, are most effective for this affection. Take one dram of old theriac, or of sweet or bitter diamoschus mithridate, or of candied true acorus, or of the confection of acorus, or two drams of oil of acorus taken daily, once a week. Stoechas is also most wholesome for this, because it greatly warms and dries the brain. One aureus of powder of hiera and two of golden pepper also warm, dry and resolve.

units.la: Postremo chamæpytis in paralysim et ischia dem, quo voles modo sumpta et admota, est efficacissima multorum experientia.
units.tr: Finally, chamaepitys against paralysis and sciatica, taken or applied in whatever way you wish, is most effective, as the experience of many shows.

units.la: CONVVLSIONIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF CONVULSION.

units.la: Conuulsio præsertim ex repletione & maximè pituitosa, aliis frequentior, curatur sex auxiliorum generibus.
units.tr: Convulsion, especially when it arises from repletion, and most of all from phlegm, which is more common than other kinds, is cured by six kinds of help.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione calida sicca prius dieta, in cephalalgia pituitosa, & apoplexia & paralysi.
units.tr: 1. DIET of a warm and dry regimen, described earlier, in phlegmatic headache, apoplexy and palsy.

units.la: 2. COQVENTIBUS spituitam, & expulsioni apparantibus, primum clementibus ad dies quatuor, quinque, deinde clementer vacuantibus: post valentius apparantibus et vacuatibus, ut locis prædictis est abundè demonstratum. Quod præceptum est intelligendum, vbi morbus est moderatior, nec symptomata inuehit multum formidanda. Sienim est vehementior, ac dolorem affert magnum qui vires prosternat, citra coctionem vacuandum est, etiā potentibus remedijs: ne si coquamus, interea vires deficiant & ægermoriatur. Quæ verò blandè & potenter coquant & vacuent ibidem scripsimus.
units.tr: 2. Where phlegm is being concocted and prepared for expulsion, first give gentle purges over four or five days, then purge more gently; afterwards, when it is ready, purge more strongly, as has been fully shown in the places cited above. This rule applies where the disease is milder and the symptoms are not very alarming. If the disease is more violent and causes great pain that prostrates the strength, evacuation must be made before concoction, even with strong remedies, lest while we wait for concoction the strength fail and the patient die. How to concoct and evacuate gently yet effectively, I have written about in the same place.

units.la: 3. PVRGANTIBVS paratam vt dixi materiam, si morbus dat inducias, vel nõ apparatam, si acutissimus est. Talia fuerint pilulæ fœtidæ & coccię valentes multum: valentiores autem pilulæ de sagapeno & opopanace: quæ tamen viribus, ob magna symptomata, vel alia occasione imbecillis non sunt devorandæ: vel si potionem ægermauult, da infusum agarici, agaricū trochiscatum, diaphœnicon, scrupu. Indum & similia dissolue decocto capitali ex abrotono, radice acori, saluia, &c. quæ vim medicamenti ad caput & neruos deducunt.
units.tr: 3. For purging, use matter already prepared, as I said, if the disease allows a respite; if it is very acute, use matter not yet prepared. Such would be the stinking pills and the strong coccus pills; stronger still are the pills of sagapenum and opopanax. However, if the patient is weak, because of severe symptoms or some other circumstance, these should not be swallowed. Or, if the patient prefers a draught, give an infusion of agaric, troches of agaric, diaphoenicon, a scruple of Indian [rhubarb] and similar things, dissolved in the principal decoction of southernwood, sweet flag root, sage, etc., which carries the force of the medicine to the head and nerves.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBVS materiam ad inferna, vt clysteribus ex prædicto decocto, frictionibus, errhinis, sternutatoriis, gargarismatibus, apophlegmatismis, post legitimā totius vacuationem.
units.tr: 4. To divert the matter downward, after complete evacuation has been properly carried out, use clysters made from the aforementioned decoction, frictions, errhines, sneezing powders, gargles and apophlegmatisms.

units.la: 5. RELIQVIAS materiæ neruis affixæ (quæ spasmi causa est continens) digerentibus, vt vnctionibus cum oleo liliorum, & (nisi febris adest) vulpino, costino actu calidiore: aut potius in his oleis, vel decocto catuli ex oleo, vel vino, vel aqua saluiæ, partium conuulsarum balneo. Vnguentum quoque de bdellio in spasmo efficacissimum, & pelles lup… porum, vulpium, melidum (taxones vocat) felium, veruecum & similium animalium, ac hepeta, pulmones à viuis animalibus, vt vita calent conuulsæ parti admota quandiu calebunt, & catuli viui & in dorso sècti cum compositi. Confert etiam partem in bouem, aut veruecem, aut aliud maius animal reces cæsum immissam continere quandiu animal calebit. Præstantissimum quoque est, conuul sas partes oblinere adipe anseris pinguis exen terati, & cato minutim concisso, ac lardo ve teri, myrrha, thymo & reliquis capitalibus, & calentibus medicamentis, farti & consu ti, & tosti: non eo qui primus defluet, sed qui secundus: excipiantur autem cadula aceto al bos vis destillato semiplena, & eodem aceto anser percoquatur, adepsque aceto supernatans collectus, priori addatur.
units.tr: 5. To digest the remnants of matter that cling to the nerves (which is the cause of the spasm), use ointments such as anointing with oil of lilies and, unless fever is present, fox oil, of a warmer kind like costus; or better still, bathe the convulsed parts in these oils, or in a decoction of puppy in oil, or in wine, or in sage water. An ointment of bdellium is also most effective against spasm, as are the skins of wolves, foxes, badgers (which he calls taxones), cats, rams and similar animals, and the livers and lungs taken from living animals, applied to the convulsed part while they remain warm with life; also live puppies split along the back, applied together. It is also useful to hold against the part a freshly slaughtered ox, ram or other larger animal, split open, as long as the animal stays warm. It is also most excellent to anoint the convulsed parts with goose fat, rendered from fat goose, and with the cat, minced finely, and with old lard, myrrh, thyme and the other principal and warming remedies, stuffed and sewn in, and roasted: not the fat that first runs out, but the second. The flasks should be filled halfway with vinegar distilled from white wine, the goose should be cooked in that same vinegar, and the fat that floats on the vinegar, collected, should be added to the former mixture.

units.la: Cucurbitulas item parti conuulsæ applicare salubre est, leues quidem si paruus est spasmus: cum scarificatione vero, si magnus: alio qui largiore materia in partem multum con uulsam attracta, nec vacuata plenitudo, co- uulsionis causa geminatur, & conuulsio fit lethalis, adhæc pars conuulsa si vlcus abest, æstate media iuuene bene carnoso, frigida aqua perfusa caloris intro à frigore compulsi, reuocatione sanatur. Febrem quoq; epheme ram excitasse seculo Auicenæ, ob victus par simoniam & corporum puritatem fuit salu-bre, nunc suspectum est remedium, ob id non tentandum: quia huius ætatis corpora plenio revictu multum excrementosa sunt reddita, ob id ad febres putridas opportuniora, in quas diariæ in talibus prompte degenerant, quæ homines sæpe interimut. Ne igitur febre à te excitata hominem perijsse calumnientur propinqui, potius quàm spasmo, à febri excitanda abstine.
units.tr: It is also wholesome to apply cupping glasses to the convulsed part: light ones if the spasm is slight, but with scarification if it is great; otherwise, if more matter is drawn into the affected part and the fullness is not evacuated, the cause of the convulsion is doubled and the convulsion becomes lethal. Moreover, if the convulsed part has no ulcer, in midsummer, on a young and well-fleshed person, the part may be drenched with cold water, and the heat driven inward by the cold is restored and cured. To have provoked an ephemeral fever, which in the age of Avicenna was a wholesome remedy by reason of regimen and purity of the body, is now a suspect remedy, and so is not to be attempted; because the bodies of this age, having been made very excrementitious by overfull living, are more liable to putrid fevers, into which diaries easily degenerate in such people, and which often kill them. So, lest your kinsfolk accuse you of having caused a man's death by a fever you provoked, rather than by the spasm, abstain from provoking fever.

units.la: Balnea quoque purgato rite toto corpore præsertim naturalia: vt, sulfurea, salsa, alumino-sa, laudantur multum: & quæ à nobis ex sulfure, sale, alumine in aqua coctis fiunt, ac etiam ex decocto herbarum cerebralium, maiorana, salui-a, betonica, chamæmeli, rorismarini, aut ex sanguine bubulo ab animali calē te: dum enim à singulis partibus materiæ reliquias resoluent, nullum erit periculum, ne fusa à balneo in partem distentam confluat.
units.tr: Baths are also greatly praised, especially natural ones, once the whole body has been properly purged: sulphurous, salt and aluminous baths. And those we make from sulphur, salt and alum boiled in water, and also from a decoction of cephalic herbs such as marjoram, sage, betony, chamomile and rosemary, or from fresh bull's blood: for while these dissolve the remnants of matter from each part, there will be no danger that the fluid poured out of the bath will flow into the distended part.

units.la: Suffitum quoque, et vaporem prædicti decocti per lapides ignitos, præcipuè pyrites, aut lateres coctiles in cacabū iniectos excepisse toto toto corpore sub papilione, ne vapor expiret, confert.
units.tr: It is also beneficial to take a fumigation and vapour of the aforesaid decoction, through glowing stones, especially pyrites or baked bricks thrown into a cauldron, while the whole body is kept under a tent, so that the vapour does not escape.

units.la: Sumenda vero quae etiam resoluant, & roborent: vt, acorus verus conditus, diacorū, diamoschum dulce & amarum, quotidie ad drach. duas: theriace vero, & mithridatios, fortiora tantū semel in hebdomade, vna drachma sumantur: aut si quotidie, parciora: vt scriptulo vno, semidrachma. Confectio quoque anacardina si febrem vis excitare, vt dixi, periculosa est. Opopanacem quoque & castoreum dat Auicen. post cibum, vt ab eo vis ipsorum obtundatur: non autem ante, ne cito ad hepar permeantia ipsum laedant, quāuis & sumptum & admotum castoreum ne minem vnquam laeserit Galen. etiam si odore deleterium apparet.
units.tr: Remedies that both dissolve and strengthen should be taken: such as preserved true sweet flag, diacorum, sweet and bitter diamoschum, two drachms daily; but theriac and mithridatium, which are stronger, only once a week, one drachm; or if taken daily, smaller doses, such as one scruple or half a drachm. The confection of anacardium, if you wish to provoke fever, as I said, is dangerous. Avicenna also gives opopanax and castoreum after food, so that their force may be blunted by it; not before, lest, passing quickly to the liver, they harm it. Yet Galen says that castoreum, whether taken or applied, has never harmed anyone, even though it smells deleterious.

units.la: 6. SYMPTOMATA
units.tr: 6. SYMPTOMS

units.la: corrigetibus praecipuè dolorem sæpe tam intolerabilem, vt clamantes audire ac sese modis miseris intorquentes ac iactantes spectare sit luctuosum. Identidem igitur balneo tradantur ex oleo communi temperatè calido, tum per se, tū ei incoquendo femen lini fœnigraeci, folia malua viola, vel lumbricos, & hos iam coctos, probe tritos, parti imponere cataplasmatis modo. Si vero diuites sint, balneum ex oleo vulpino cui vetusto vulpes aliquot ætate florentes viuæ sint incoctæ. In his autem balneis mora longior vires resoluit. Mox igitur dolore sedato in lecto reclinandi: & cum repetet, balneo reddendi. Anodynum quoque decoctum capitis lanati & intestinorum vermecis & omasorum aliorum. Si autem conuulsio à sanguine est, vena secta vacuetur sanguis, sed parcior quàm ipsa copia exigat, ne vires symptomati occursurae deijciantur: satius enim est hic, vt alibi passim, vacuationem partiri, quàm semel quantum necesse est vacuare. Si à bile est flaua, vacuetur mox cholagogis prius dictis. Si ab atra, apparetur, vt dictum est, ac vacuetur.
units.tr: They are treated mainly for pain, which is often so intolerable that it is painful to hear them cry out and to watch them writhe and toss themselves about. Repeatedly, therefore, they should be put in a bath of common oil, moderately warm, either alone or with linseed, fenugreek seed, mallow and violet leaves, or earthworms boiled in it. These, once cooked and well ground, are applied to the part as a poultice. If the patient is wealthy, use a bath of fox oil, in which several living foxes of advanced age have been boiled. A longer stay in these baths weakens the strength. Once the pain has subsided, the patient should be laid to rest in bed, and when the pain returns, he should be returned to the bath. An anodyne decoction of the head of a sheep, of earthworms and of other tripe is also useful. If the convulsion arises from blood, let blood be drawn from a vein, but less than the amount itself requires, so that the strength needed to meet the symptom is not cast down. For here, as elsewhere throughout, it is better to divide the evacuation than to empty all at once what is necessary. If it arises from yellow bile, let it be evacuated soon with the cholagogues mentioned above. If it arises from black bile, let it be prepared as said, and then evacuated.

units.la: Si à flatibus (quæ cito & fit & desinit) his resolutis præsertim frictione cum pannis calentibus, aut vnctione aliqua digerente adhibita, cessat, nisi etiam pituita flatuum mater fit vacuanda. Si conuulsio ab inanitione, ac siccitate est, curatur humectantibus omnibus causis salubribus, vt tum medicamentis tum alimentis, vt iusculis carnium succulentis, optimis carnibus contusis, tandem vino dilutiore. Initio enim materias in neruos penetrare facit. Balneum item ex capitibus & in testinis veruecum & oleis clementibus: a balneo autem conuulsam partem illinit, & astringit, et roborat Auic. oleo rosato, aut cucurbitino, ne humiditas balneo quaesita exhalet.
units.tr: If it comes from wind (which both begins and ends quickly), it ceases once the wind has been dispersed, especially by rubbing with warm cloths or by applying some digestive ointment, unless phlegm, the mother of wind, is also to be evacuated. If the convulsion arises from exhaustion and dryness, it is treated by moistening through all wholesome means, both by medicines and by foods, such as broths rich in meat, well-pounded good meats, and finally a rather diluted wine. For at the start it causes the matter to penetrate the nerves. Likewise a bath of sheep's heads and intestines and soothing oils; after the bath he anoints and binds the affected part and strengthens it with Avicenna's rose oil or gourd oil, so that the moisture drawn in by the bath does not evaporate.

units.la: Si conuulsio est ab ictu, aut animalium venenosorum, id venenum extrahe, parti punctae admoto ano galli, aut gallinae deplumato. Suctu enim ani venenum extrahet: sunt qui rostrum eius tunc comprimant, vt ano etiam respiret. Scabiosa quoque cum vitello oui in cataplasmatis speciem pertrita, & admota venenum secreto quodam opere extrahit, ob id etiam bubonibus pestiferis efficaciter imponitur. Capa item cruda vel cocta, et capa succus punctae parti admotus venenum extrahit. Idem praestat cucurbitula cum scarificatu parti punctae affixa, & theriaca apposita, quamuis ex quo venenum pellit, intra corpus protrusura videtur non foras attractura.
units.tr: If the convulsion comes from a bite or from venomous animals, draw out the poison: apply to the wound the anus of a cock or a hen, plucked. For by suction the anus will draw out the poison; some press its beak at that time so that it may also breathe through the anus. Scabious, pounded with egg yolk into the form of a poultice and applied, also draws out poison by a certain hidden action, and for this reason it is effectively applied to plague buboes. Likewise a raw or cooked capon, and the juice of a capon applied to the wound, draws out the poison. The same is achieved by a small cupping-glass with scarification applied to the wound, and theriac applied on top; although, by the very fact that it drives out the poison, it seems likely to push it further into the body rather than draw it outward.

units.la: Si conuulsio sit neruo puncto a ferro acuto, punctura sit aperta, ut sanies expiret: si angustior sit, ferro aperiatur, ne sanies retenta ibi putrescat. Vnguentum multum siccans et digerens tenuium partium imponitur apostolorum dictum, & hoc fortius vnguentum basilicon.
units.tr: If the convulsion is due to a nerve pricked by a sharp iron, the puncture should be opened so that the pus may escape; if it is too narrow, it should be opened with iron, so that the pus retained there does not putrefy. A strongly drying and resolving ointment of fine parts is applied, the one called Apostolicon, and a stronger ointment, the basilicon.

units.la: Quia verò punctis neruis dolor interdum ad est vehementissimus, sedetur terebinthina oleo rosato mista, qua caeterarum partium nervosarum dolorem a casu, vel causa alia mirè compescit, vel fotu partis ex oleo cui terrae lumbrici fuerint incocti: ac ex ijsdem tritis cataplasma est efficacissimum. Panis quoque calidus, calido lacte infusus, & cataplasmatis modo impositus valde anodynus est. Quod si nullis remedijs vincatur dolor stupefacientibus tactum vtendum est: vt, pane cum decocto coćło papaueris albi, & si opus est, cum opio ipso.
units.tr: Since the pain from a pricked nerve is sometimes most severe, it is calmed with turpentine mixed with rose oil, which wonderfully relieves the pain of other nerve injuries, whether from a fall or some other cause, or by fomenting the part with oil in which earthworms have been boiled; and a very effective poultice is made from the same worms when ground. Warm bread soaked in warm milk and applied as a poultice is also very soothing. If the pain is not overcome by any of these remedies, narcotics that numb the sense of touch must be used, such as bread with a decoction of white poppy, and if needed, opium itself.

units.la: Quòd si nullis remediȷs conuulsionem hanc potes compescere, neruum transuersum secare præstiterit, quàm homine certæ morti occumbere: sed periculum mortis ex neruo punćto, vix vnquam superueniet, si statim ab initio Galeni præcepta sequaris.
units.tr: But if you cannot check this convulsion by any remedy, it is better to cut the nerve across than for the man to die a certain death. Yet danger of death from a pricked nerve will scarcely ever follow, if you follow Galen's precepts from the very beginning.

units.la: EPILEPSIAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: TREATMENT OF EPILEPSY

units.la: EPILEPSIA vel imminet, vt ferè pueris ad eā opportunissimis, tunc parte artis præcautrice opus est, vt in accessionis intermissione: vel iam prehendit & nunc hominem fatigat, tunc curatione proprie didća indiget. Si recens natus est infans, conuul sus vbi experrectus & accessione solutus erit, capiat in dies antequam lac sugat saccha rum album, cum oleo sesamino, vel amygda larum dulcium, vel butyro mistum in electa rij mollis formam ad purgandos humores prauos, ex ventriculo, et intestinis, à quibus elati vapores praui, epilepsiam his afferunt: deinde sumant in dies cochlearium vnum sy-rup. de cichorio sine aqua. Vel manna, vel al-bi tartari puluis, vel nitri, si eius est potestas, vel lapidis Iudaici, lacti cocto misceatur: vbi autem ambulare coeperint, cum suo lorio: sic medicus quidam filios principis cuiusdam à morte vindicauit, quae priores eius liberos epilepsia suffulerat. Paeoniae, maris praesertim, radix transuersim secta corona modo consu-ta, collo appensa, vel quouis modo alio gesta ta, vt odoretur tamen, proprietate sua epile-psiam praesente sanat, vel impendentem prohi-bet: smaragdus quoque, & corallium col-lo appensum, vt hodie fit à multis, praesidium est optimum. Iaspidem viridem appensum sic, vt stomachi regionem tangat, stomachum roborare scribit Galenus.
units.tr: Epilepsy either threatens, as it most often does in children, when the preventive part of the art is needed during the interval between attacks; or it has already seized and now wears the man down, and then it needs its proper treatment. If the infant is newly born, when the convulsion has ended and the attack has passed, let him take, each day before he sucks milk, white sugar mixed with sesame oil, or sweet almond oil, or butter, formed into a soft electuary, to purge the bad humours from the stomach and intestines, from which the bad vapours rising up bring on epilepsy: then let him take daily a spoonful of syrup of chicory without water, or manna, or white tartar powder, or nitre, if he can take it, or Jewish stone, mixed with cooked milk. When they begin to walk, use it with its strap. Thus a certain physician saved the sons of a prince from death, when epilepsy had carried off the prince's earlier children. The root of peony, especially the male kind, cut crosswise and sewn like a crown, hung at the neck, or worn in some other way, though it only has to be smelled, by its own property cures epilepsy when present or prevents it from threatening. Emerald too, and coral hung at the neck, as many do today, is an excellent safeguard. Galen writes that a green jasper hung so that it touches the region of the stomach strengthens the stomach.

units.la: Ab infantibus etiam prohibebis omne obiectum sensus insigne & subitum: vt, sonitus vehementes, strepitus, terrores: cum Matthaei Gradi filius infans, repentino tubarum clangore epilepticus euaserit, & alij no pauci à causis similibus, quidam à lapsu scalarum Nutrix quoque infantis à venere lac ipsum corrumpente abstineat, & crapula, & cibis malis cæteris á; prauum lac gignentibus.
units.tr: You must also keep infants away from every striking and sudden object of the senses, such as loud sounds, noises and frights; when the infant son of Matthaeus Gradus became epileptic from the sudden blare of trumpets, and not a few others from similar causes, some from a fall down stairs. The infant's nurse too should abstain from sex, which corrupts the milk, and from gluttony and other bad foods that produce bad milk.
