units.la: In ipsa igitur intermissione causa epilepsiam genitura, quæ fere est pituita, abigetur quinque auxiliorum generibus.
units.tr: During the interval itself, therefore, the cause that produces epilepsy, which is mostly phlegm, is to be driven away by five kinds of aid.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione calfaciente & siccante, vt aëre cubiculi aut lecti alterato per ignem luculentum et suffitus cum caryophyllis, cortice citri, rore marino, maiorana, salvia, stœchade & similibus: caue tamen ne copia vaporum, aut caput repleat, aut materiam exagitet. Cibus & potus sit paucus, nec vaporosus, præsertim cœna: nam ex alimento multo vapor multus tollitur qui accessionem epilepticam, & alia capitis vitia accersit. Vitet apium vulgi, & caprarum grandium carnes, quia vtrunque proprietatem habet excitandi, & detegendi epilepsiam, vti odor bituminis, iecur caprinum & hircinum assum, & sumptum, Galen. u. simpl. licet capreoli, quia facile coquuntur, sumi possint.
units.tr: 1. Diet, arranged to warm and dry: for example, by changing the air of the bedchamber or bed through a bright fire and fumigations with cloves, citron peel, rosemary, marjoram, sage, stoechas and similar things. Take care, however, that the quantity of vapours neither fills the head nor stirs up the matter. Food and drink should be sparing and not windy, especially at supper; for much food gives off much vapour, which brings on an epileptic attack and other ills of the head. Let him avoid common celery and the flesh of large goats, since both have the property of stirring up and bringing out epilepsy, as does the smell of bitumen; goat's liver, roasted and eaten (Galen, Simpl. v.). Roebuck may be eaten, since it is easily digested.

units.la: Vitentur herbæ frigidæ humidæ, lactuca, portulaca & similes: sumantur autem calidæ, saluia, maiorana, & præter cæteras hyssopus, quasola decoctis & cibis largiter mista testatur Serapio se multos curasse. Vinum quoq; quia epilepsiam facit, vitetur præsertim multum: paucum autem & aromatites aut aliter calidum permittitur, præsertim assuetis eo citra capitis, aut ventriculi noxam vti, nisi corporis, aut aëris intemperies calida prohibet.
units.tr: Cold and moist herbs should be avoided, such as lettuce, purslane and the like; warm ones should be taken, such as sage, marjoram, and above all hyssop, which Serapion testifies he used to cure many, when boiled and mixed generously with foods. Wine too should be avoided, especially in quantity, because it brings on epilepsy. A little wine, however, that is aromatic or otherwise warm, is allowed, especially for those accustomed to it, provided it does no harm to the head or stomach, unless a hot disorder of the body or air forbids it.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM scilicet pituitam coquentibus: vt, melle rosato, oxymelite simplici, composito, scillino, syrup. stœchad. cum aquis capitalibus, præcipuè hyssopi & his per dies 6. 8. 10. continuos apparanda est materia.
units.tr: 2. Ripening the matter, namely the phlegm, with rose honey, simple oxymel, compound oxymel, squill oxymel, syrup of stoechas, together with head waters, especially hyssop water. The matter is to be prepared in this way for six, eight or ten successive days.

units.la: 3. PHLEGMAGOGIS, vt hieræ picræ simplicis, mellitæ drach. sex, agarici recenter trochiscati drachma vna cum aqua hyssopi: vt, pilulis elephanginis, mastichinis, et in robusto hyera, fœtidis, coccijs, cum agarico pituita à capite potèter vacuante. In ace cessione aut si nimis est molesta, aut diuturna pilularum fœtidarum & cocciarũ ana scri-ptula duo vel ana drac. dimidia, ex aqua hys sopi soluta dari possint si maius nihil interce dat, vel diaphœnici, aut E. indi ỽncia dimi-dia, aquis capitalibus soluta. Melius autem extra accessionem parata, vt dixi prius, ma teria medicamentis purgantibus vti.
units.tr: 3. Phlegm-purgers, such as simple bitter hiera, honeyed, six drachms; agaric freshly made into troches, one drachm, with hyssop water; or elephantine pills, mastic pills, and in a robust patient hiera with stinking pills and coccia, with agaric, which powerfully purges phlegm from the head. During an attack, or if it is too troublesome or lasting, two scruples each of stinking pills and coccia, or half a drachm each, dissolved in hyssop water, may be given, if nothing greater stands in the way; or diaphoenicon, or half an ounce of elaterium dissolved in head waters. It is better, however, to use purgatives on the matter when it has been prepared outside an attack, as I said before.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBVS materiam de orsum balanis, clysteribus, friction ibus, liga turis, apophlegmatismis, errhinis dictis in pa ralysi & apoplexia. 5. RELIQVAM in cerebro materiam resoluentibus, & cerebrum frigidum humi dum calfaciendo, & siccando roborantibus, ne similem materiam postea generet: ỽsque vel sumptis, vel admotis: sumptis quidem a-coro vero condito, diacoro, diamoscho dulci & amaro, pliris arcotico Nicolai, medica-mento ex scilla, quod ad præcauendam epile-psiam præstantissimum est. Scilla autem æsti ua purgata, incisa cũ melle in vase vitreo ob structo insoletur dies 40. horis singulis ver-tendo, ut omnia sol tãgat. Post dies hos liquor
units.tr: 4. For those who divert the matter downwards: baths for the feet, clysters, frictions, ligatures, apophlegmatisms and errhines, as described under paralysis and apoplexy. 5. For those who dissolve the remaining matter in the brain, and who warm the cold brain while moistening it and strengthen it by drying, so that it does not generate similar matter afterwards: either taken internally or applied externally. Taken internally: compound acorus, diacorum, sweet and bitter diamoschum, the pills of Nicolaus' arcoticum, and a medicine of squill, which is most excellent for preventing epilepsy. Squill, cleansed in the summer sun, is cut up with honey, placed in a closed glass vessel, and set in the sun for forty days, turning it each day so that the sun reaches all of it. After these days the liquor

units.la: vi solis solutus ad electarium id componendum est capiendus quod Rasis describit libro primo continentis. & Auic. in curatione epilepsiae. electarium quoque a Rasi in epilepsia hac curanda descriptum, multos ab epilepsia curasse plerique medici testantur. Nicolaus quoque Florentinus quendam quadragenarium ab infantia ad hanc usque aetatem epilepticum sanasse affirmat hoc electario quod recipit herba paralysis (quae costus, piperella herba sancti Petri, vel Pauli quoque vulgo dicitur) quantitatem idoneam minutim concisam et caryophyll. paeoniae, pirethri ana portiones aequales cum melle sufficienti fac electarium, sumendum in dies ad cochlearium unum, vel theriaca, aut mithridatios semel in septimana sumantur. Sunt & quae epilepsiae tota sua substantia repugnant, ruta, paeonia praesertim mas saepe sumpta, & modis omnibus admota, & odorata.
units.tr: which the sun has dissolved is to be taken for making the electuary that Rhazes describes in the first book of his Continens, and that Avicenna gives in the treatment of epilepsy. Many physicians testify that the electuary described by Rhazes for curing epilepsy has cured many from the disease. Nicolaus of Florence also affirms that he cured a certain forty-year-old man, epileptic from infancy until this age, with the following electuary, made from herba paralysis (commonly also called costus, piperella, the herb of St Peter or St Paul): a suitable quantity, finely cut, with equal portions of clove, peony and pellitory, and enough honey to make an electuary. It is to be taken daily, one spoonful at a time, or theriac or mithridate once a week. There are also things wholly opposed to epilepsy in their whole substance: rue, and peony especially the male, often taken, applied in every way, and smelled.

units.la: Vesica quoque apri urina plena, & cum hac clibano siccata, puluerata cochleario uno quotidie sumpta, est efficax multum, et cornu cerui, & smaragdus collo appensus, corium a fronte asini, castorium laseris, Parthici succus, seu assa foetida sumpta, & suffi ta etiam accessionem finiunt. Lapis quoque, praesertim versicolor in ventriculo pullorum hirundinis inuentus, corio vituli tectus & in argenteo vasculo appensus collo, maxime quosdam adiuuit. Cranium quoque maris in mare, foeminae in foemina vstum, donec sit albissimum & pulueratum, potu quotidiano epilepsiam sanare testis est Gerardus a Salo, & Galenus lib.11.simpl.de ossibus. In infantibus ergo, si a prauo est victu, vt cerebro porrorū esu, curatu facilis est: in adultis vbi confirmata est, & cerebro propria, aegrè curatur: quin & curari in his posse Gordonius negat: si verò est per consensum cum partibus subiectis, etiam diuturna curatur.
units.tr: A bladder of a wild boar filled with urine, dried together with it in an oven, powdered and taken one spoonful each day, is very effective. Also a stag's horn, and an emerald hung around the neck; the hide from an ass's forehead; castoreum; the juice of laserwort (Parthian); or asafoetida taken or fumigated, also end the attack. A stone, especially a many-coloured one found in the stomach of swallow chicks, covered with calf's skin and hung around the neck in a little silver vessel, has greatly helped some people. The skull of a male burned in a male, or of a female in a female, until it is very white and powdered, is taken daily in drink; Gerardus a Salo and Galen (book 11 of the Simples, on bones) bear witness that it cures epilepsy. In infants, if it arises from a bad diet, such as eating leeks, which harm the brain, it is easily cured; in adults, where it is established and rooted in the brain itself, it is cured with difficulty; indeed Gordonius denies that it can be cured in these. If, however, it comes by sympathy with the parts beneath, it is cured even if long-standing.

units.la: Si a sanguinis copia est, seca venam cephalicam: postremo si opus erit, venam frontis.
units.tr: If it arises from an abundance of blood, open the cephalic vein; finally, if need be, the vein of the forehead.

units.la: Si a melancholia est, cura vt phlegmaticam, sed remedijs in melancholia dicendis.
units.tr: If it arises from melancholy, treat it as phlegmatic, but with the remedies to be given for melancholy.

units.la: Si per consensum cum parte aliqua subieiecta, elato ad cerebrum ex ea vapore prauo & venenoso accessionem committente, stricta fiat deligatura, si in artubus est, quae via vapori praecludat: post accessionem vero, ex parte ipsa luem ipsam vacua, etiam si opus est, partem ipsam vlcerando, vt Gattinaria quendam epilepticum sanauit aperto per cauterium tumore in coxa, & osse quod simul computruerat ablato, & parte illa putri sanie diligenter purgata.
units.tr: If it comes by sympathy with some part beneath, when a noxious and poisonous vapour rises from that part to the brain and brings on the attack, a tight ligature is to be applied, if it is in the limbs, to cut off the vapour's passage. After the attack, the poison itself is to be drawn off from that part, even if need be by ulcerating the part itself, as Gattinaria cured a certain epileptic by opening a swelling in the thigh with a cautery, removing the bone that had rotted at the same time, and carefully cleansing that part of its putrid matter.

units.la: Si per consensum cum stomacho, curatur vt epilepsia phlegmatica.
units.tr: If it comes by sympathy with the stomach, it is treated as phlegmatic epilepsy.

units.la: In ipsa autem accessione materiam a cerebro auerte, siue propria sit, siue per consensum, clysteribus, balanis, frictionibus, ligaturis, cucurbitulis, apophlegmatismis, errhinis, suffitu etiam castorij, assa foetida, paeoniae radicis & seminis.
units.tr: During the attack itself, divert the matter from the brain, whether it is proper to the brain or by sympathy, by clysters, baths, frictions, ligatures, cupping-glasses, apophlegmatisms, errhines, and also by fumigation with castoreum, asafoetida, and peony root and seed.

units.la: Item ruta trita, & succus eius in nares trunda immissus per se, vel cum castorio: paeonia assa, & similibus est praestantissima ad finiendam accessionem.
units.tr: Likewise, crushed rue, and its juice put into the nostrils on a tampon, either alone or with castoreum; roasted peony, and similar things, are most excellent for ending the attack.

units.la: INCVBI CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE TREATMENT OF INCUBUS.

units.la: INCVBVS ab incubando quod pondus quoddam nobis incumbere, & supra nos stare putamus, respirationem opprimens, & ob id vocem impediens Græcis ἐφιάλτης, id est insultor. Fit ore ventriculi, aut pituita crassa, lenta, aut ciborum præsertim durorū copia oppresso, resupino præsertim corpore. Curatur purgatione ventriculi per hieram picram, & victu tenui ac tenuante.
units.tr: INCUBUS, from "incubare" (to lie upon), because we think some weight lies on us and stands over us, oppressing the breathing and thereby hindering the voice; the Greeks call it ephialtes, that is, "assailant". It arises from the mouth of the stomach, or from thick, sluggish phlegm, or when the body is oppressed by a surplus of food, especially hard food, chiefly when lying on the back. It is cured by purging the stomach with hiera picra, and by a light and attenuating diet.

units.la: MELANCHOLIAE MORBI CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE TREATMENT OF THE DISEASE OF MELANCHOLY.

units.la: ANTEQVAM ad melancholiæ morbi curationē accingamur, pauca quædam monendus est lector: primùm ne solus ad melancholicos adeat, nec ad hos propius accedat, & ipsorum manus, pedes, os observet: nam horum multi mente constare initio videntur, sed mox depravata ratione me dicos & alios violant. Secundo loco observandæ sunt melancholici phantasiæ, quarum quibusdam ad curationem seruiendum est, ut si quis ranas se in ventre multas habere imaginetur, concedendum est: promittasque ranas illas te expulsurum facile, modo is tecum consenserit: cumque hominem purgaris, deie ctionibus iube ab assidentibus ranas vivas clam immitti, ostendendas mox ægro. Sic enim falsa apprehensione deposita facilius curabitur. Adde quod quibusdam est blandiendum: alii iurgandi, & verberandi, & ligandi, ne sibi aut aliis manus violentas inferant: omnisque ferri præcipitiq; potestas auferenda, custodibusq; robustis nunquam destituantur.
units.tr: BEFORE we set about the treatment of melancholy, the reader must be warned of a few things. First, he should not approach melancholics alone, nor come too near them, and he should watch their hands, feet and mouth; for many of them seem at first to be sound in mind, but soon, their reason being corrupted, they attack both physicians and others. Second, the fancies of melancholics must be observed, and some of them must be humoured for the sake of the cure: if someone imagines that he has many frogs in his belly, one should agree, and promise that you will easily expel those frogs, provided he has agreed with you. And when you have purged the man, have those attending secretly put live frogs into the evacuations, to be shown to the patient at once. For thus, with the false notion put aside, he will be cured more easily. Add that some must be flattered, others scolded, beaten, or bound, lest they inflict violent hands on themselves or others; and every opportunity of iron or of a precipice must be taken away, and they must never be left without strong guards.

units.la: Porro melancholia, generibus remediorum quinque sanatur initio: nam confirmata ægre admodum sanatur. Auic.
units.tr: Moreover, melancholy is cured at the start by five kinds of remedy; for once established it is cured with great difficulty. Avicenna.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione humectante, & temperata potius quam calida: ut, aere per vapores decocti malua, althaea, viola, per odores gratos, sed blandos: ut, cibis humectantibus, capis, gallinis, phasianis, hœdis, veruecibus elixis, non assis nec frixis: adiecta portulaca, lactuca & similibus: ut, somno conciliando frictionibus, fotu partium extremarum diuturno, turno, & capitis modico, ex decocto lactu-cæ, foliorum salicis, se. papaueris albi, se. lactucæ, syrup. papaueris post cœnā dato, fron-te & temporibus vnctis oleo violato, & nymphææ, vng. populeo: clysteribus ex simili materia, per quæ si somnus non cōciliatur, ad opiata transi clementia, præsertim viri-bus imbecillis.
units.tr: 1. DIET should be moistening, and temperate rather than hot; the air should be made with vapours of decocted mallow, marshmallow and violet, with pleasant but soothing odours; the food should be moistening: capons, hens, pheasants, kids and wethers, boiled, not roasted or fried, with purslane, lettuce and the like added. To induce sleep, use frictions, a long warm bath of the extremities, and a short one of the head, with a decoction of lettuce, willow leaves, white poppy and lettuce, and a syrup of poppy given after supper; the forehead and temples anointed with violet oil, water-lily, and poplar ointment; clysters of similar material. If sleep is not induced by these, pass on gently to opiates, especially when the strength is feeble.

units.la: 2. MELANCHOLIÆ apparanti-bus syrup. de pomis simpl. & compos. de fumaria, de thymo, de epithymo cum duplo aquarum buglossi vtriusque intybi, scolopendriæ, fumariæ, lupuli.
units.tr: 2. For those preparing for melancholy: syrup of apples, simple and compound, of fumitory, of thyme, of epithymum, with twice the amount of water of bugloss, of both endive, of scolopendrium, fumitory, and hops.

units.la: 3. VACVANTIBVS melancholiam primùm lenibus: vt, epithymo per se ad drac. duas, vel infuso ad vnc. dimidiam in sero lactis præsertim caprini: myrobalanis similiter sumptis. Deinde valentioribus: vt, folliculis sennæ, lapide armeno, lapide cyaneo correctis, ut in compositionibus docetur: Hamech confectione, pilulis indis, pilulis de lapide cyaneo ad scriptula quatuor, cum syrupo violato vel alio humectāte. Secta basilica sinistra sanguis si niger apparet, mittatur quantum videbitur: si tenuis & clarus, mox sistatur.
units.tr: 3. For emptying melancholy, first with gentle agents: epithymum alone, two drachms, or infused, half an ounce in whey, especially goat's whey; myrobalans likewise taken. Then with stronger ones: senna leaves corrected with Armenian stone or lapis lazuli, as taught in the compositions; the confection of Hamech; Indian pills; pills of lapis lazuli, up to four scruples, with violet syrup or another moistening syrup. Let the basilic vein of the left arm be opened: if the blood appears black, let it be drawn as much as seems fit; if thin and clear, stop it at once.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBUS a cerebro & corde ad partes ignobiles, ut partium externarum fotu ex aqua calida, frictionibus, ligaturis, cucurbitulis sine scarificatu, balanis clysteribus acribus: ut, ex lib. vna decocti thymi, epithymi, fumariæ, lupuli, polypodij, sennæ, cum cassiæ, saccha. rubri ana vncia vna, olei violati vncia vna dimidia, salis communis drach. duabus.
units.tr: 4. For diverting matter from the brain and heart to the ignoble parts: fomentations of the external parts with warm water, frictions, ligatures, cupping-glasses without scarification, and sharp clysters, such as: from one pound of a decoction of thyme, epithymum, fumitory, hops, polypody, senna, with cassia and red sugar, one ounce each; olive oil of violet, one and a half ounces; common salt, two drachms.

units.la: 5. RELIQVIAS resoluentibus sumptis: ut, diabuglosato, diaborraginato, & valentioribus. Diamoscho dulci & amaro, Electuario de gemmis Mesuæ, Electuario laetificante Rasis, Electuario Conciliatoris: addito his saccharo violato: & admotis, ut epithemate cordiali ex florum borraginis & buglossi ana Ma. vno been albi & rubri, ana drachmis duabus caryophyll. drachma vna simul mistis: et balneo totius & capitis ex malua, althaea, viola, capitibus, & intestinis veruecum: no tamen diuturno, ne vires deiciat.
units.tr: 5. For resolving the remainders, take: diabugloss, diaborage, and stronger ones; sweet and bitter diamoschum, the electuary of gems of Mesue, the cheering electuary of Rhazes, the electuary of Conciliator, with violet sugar added; and apply: as a cordial epithem of flowers of borage and bugloss, equal parts, white and red beeswax, two drachms each, and one drachm of clove, all mixed together; and a bath of the whole head with mallow, marshmallow, violet, the heads and intestines of wethers; not for a long time, lest it weaken the strength.

units.la: CATHAR-
units.tr: CATHAR-

units.la: CATARRHI CVRATIO.
units.tr: CATARRHI CVRATIO.

units.la: CATARRHVS recte curabitur si ante spectes an causa, & catarrhi materia eadem remedia indicent ac requirant, ut si ambo sint, vel calida, vel frigida, vel si amborum indicationes pugnant, ob id remedia postulant contraria, ut si catarrhi materia est calida, a frigore comprimente destillans: aut frigida a calore liquante. In hoc enim complexu pugnantium indicationum vrgentioris maior est habenda ratio, altero tamen non neglecto.
units.tr: A catarrh is rightly treated if you first consider its cause, and whether the remedies that the nature of the catarrhal matter indicates and requires are the same for both. If both are hot, or both cold, the remedies are the same. If the indications of the two conflict, they call for contrary remedies, as when the matter of the catarrh is hot and drips from a cold that compresses it, or cold and dripping from a heat that liquefies it. In such a mixture of conflicting indications, greater regard must be paid to the more urgent, though the other should not be neglected.

units.la: Catarrhus autem curatur sex remediorum generibus.
units.tr: A catarrh is treated by six kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione in calida materia refrigerante, in frigida, calfaciente. Vitenturque in illa auster, affectus animi inflammantes, cibi calidi, odores vegeti: in hac septentrio, somnus longior, & supino corpore. Dormiat autem in ventrem magis, ut catarrhus in nares fluat: commune utrique ex apta corporis figura remedium.
units.tr: 1. REGIMEN of life: in hot matter, cooling; in cold matter, warming. In the former case avoid the south wind, passions that inflame the mind, hot foods and pungent odours; in the latter avoid the north wind, long sleep and lying on the back. The patient should sleep rather on the belly, so that the catarrh runs into the nostrils. This posture of the body is a remedy common to both.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM apparantibus, id est, tenuantibus crassam, initio mitioribus, qua-lia sunt mel rosatū, syrup. glycyrrhizæ cum duplo aquæ saluiæ, hyssopi, vel decoctipecto-ralis ex glycyrrhiza, vuis passis, myxis, zi-ziphis, & similibus compositi: sed proceden-te affectu valentius incidentia & tenuantia vtenda, & primò mitiora: vt syrup. de dua-bus radicibus: post efficaciora: vt, syrup. de hyssopo, de prassio, tandem syrup. de stœcha de cū aqua saluiæ, hyssopi, bethonicæ, vel po-tius decocto pectorali cum ficis, passis, gly-cyrrhiza, adianto, præsertim sisputum pro-mouere libet.
units.tr: 2. PREPARING the matter, that is, thinning what is thick. At first use milder things, such as rose honey, syrup of liquorice with twice its weight of water of sage or hyssop, or a pectoral decoction of liquorice, raisins, jujubes, ziziphus and similar ingredients. But as the condition advances, use more powerful cutting and thinning remedies, milder ones first: for example syrup of the two roots; afterwards more effective ones, such as syrup of hyssop and syrup of horehound; and finally syrup of stoechas with water of sage, hyssop and betony, or better a pectoral decoction with figs, raisins, liquorice and maidenhair, especially when one wishes to promote expectoration.

units.la: Si autem materia est lenta, & glutinosa, oxymeli simplex & compositum. Nam bilis flauæ vacuatio est facilis: pituitæ verò præ-sertim crassæ & lentæ etiam à ventriculo, difficilis sine incisione, & detersione: atræ bi-lis difficilior.
units.tr: If the matter is viscid and glutinous, use oxymel, simple or compound. Evacuating yellow bile is easy. Phlegm, especially thick and viscid phlegm, even from the stomach, is difficult to evacuate without incision and cleansing. Black bile is more difficult still.

units.la: 3. PVRGANTIBVS materiam, calidam quidem: vt, pilulis aureis, agoregatiuis, à drachma vna ad scriptula quatuor, electa-rio ex succo rosarum, rosato, diapruno scam-moniato, moniato, à drachmis tribus ad drach. quatuor: frigidam verò: vt, pilulis coccijs, & de agarico: quæ etiam crassam materiam à pulmonibus vacuant: Electario autem indo & diaphœnico ad vnciam dimidiam: quæ etiam calidam materiam vacuât, vti & phleboto mia, si corpus est robustum, præcalidum, sanguine abundans: aut si cynanche, aut pleuritis à tali catarrho impendet, nisi materia revellatur per venæ sectionem: aut si febris catarrho adest, quæ humores immodicè calfaciat: aliâs non facienda in catarrho sanguinis vacuatio, quia cerebrum partem exanguem & frigidam, frigidiorem reddit.
units.tr: 3. PURGING the matter. If it is hot, use golden pills or aggregative pills, from one drachm up to four scruples, or an electuary of rose juice, rosate, or diaprunum with scammony, from three to four drachms. If it is cold, use coccine pills and pills of agaric, which also evacuate thick matter from the lungs; or an electuary of indum and diaphoenicum to half an ounce, which also evacuates hot matter. Phlebotomy is also used if the body is robust, very hot and full of blood, or if quinsy or pleurisy threatens from such a catarrh, unless the matter is drawn off by opening a vein, or if a fever accompanies the catarrh and heats the humours excessively. Otherwise bloodletting is not to be done in catarrh, because it makes the brain, which is an exsanguine and cold part, colder.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBVS: vt, frictionibus, ligaturis extremorum, cucurbitulis in natibus, & spathulis: errhinis ex aqua violarum, vel hordei, in calida materia, quæ nares dilatent, vt viam dent liberam materiæ per has effluxuræ: in frigida autem errhinis ex aqua maioranæ, succo foliorum & radicum betæ, decocto melanthij, & his fortiore succo ireos, et cyclamini: sternutamentis etiâ ad nares trahentibus: sed amborum vsus, nō est tutus ante coctam per quietem & medicamenta materiam, & factas totius vacuationes, quòd ambo catarrhi materiam exagitant, & motu ipso coqui prohibent. Arcula nus quoque cauterio in commissura coronali imposito, materiam larga per vlcus semper apertum salubriter vacuat: Alij apertionem post aurem faciunt.
units.tr: 4. DIVERTING the matter: for example by rubbing, by ligatures on the extremities, by cupping-glasses on the buttocks and by scarifications. In hot matter use errhines of water of violets or barley, which dilate the nostrils to give the matter a free path to flow out through them. In cold matter use errhines of water of marjoram, juice of beet leaves and roots, decoction of melanthium, and the stronger juice of iris and cyclamen. Sneezing-powders that draw toward the nostrils also serve. But the use of both kinds is not safe before the matter has been concocted by rest and medicines and total evacuations have been made, because both stir up the matter and, by that very motion, prevent it from being concocted. Arculanus also, by placing a cautery on the coronal suture, drains the matter well through an ulcer that is always kept open. Others make the opening behind the ear.

units.la: 5. CATARRHVM sistentib.et incrassantibus, quando scilicet ab eo largiore, suffocationis periculum impendet, aut ab eo acrio re, & tenuiore excoriato: aut ab vtroq; tussis aspera & insomnia: alioqui sistendus non est, nec materia in cerebrum partem principem regerenda.
units.tr: 5. STOPPING and thickening the catarrh. This is done when, namely, there is danger of suffocation from its excessive quantity, or from its acrid and thin nature, which excoriates, or from both, when there is harsh cough and sleeplessness. Otherwise it is not to be stopped, nor is the matter to be driven back into the brain, the principal part.

units.la: Sistunt autem astrictione sua bolus Armenia, spica, thus, gummi iuniperi, mastiche: nec pectori nocent præcipuè spica: adhæc materiam crassant & præter hæc etiam succus glycyrrhizæ, syrup. eiusdem & violarum in lep. violatus, saccharum violatum, penidia, diatragacanthum, syrup. papaueris, eclegma eiusdem diacodium, trochisci bechici in ore retenti: cum aliorum quaedam deuorentur & suffiantur: ut, thus, gumi iuniperi, mastiche: quaedam gargarizentur: ut, syrupi cum aqua rosarum, oxalidis. cetera ex Mesue repete.
units.tr: Remedies stop it by their astringency: bole armenian, spikenard, frankincense, gum of juniper, mastic. Nor do they harm the chest, spikenard especially. They also thicken the matter. Besides these, there are juice of liquorice, syrup of liquorice and of violets, lambative of violet, candied violet, penidia, diatragacanth, syrup of poppy, eclegma of the same, diacodium, and bechic troches held in the mouth. Of the others, some are swallowed and some are fumigated, such as frankincense, gum of juniper and mastic; some are gargled, such as syrup with rose water and oxalis. Seek the rest in Mesue.

units.la: Si aut tussis aspera cum insomnia praedictis no vincitur, pilulae de cynoglossa Mesuae sunt dandae, quae ad omnes morbos catarrho succedentes valere ei dicuntur quia opiatae sunt: sed his non vtendum, nisi affectus curatione deplorata.
units.tr: If, however, a harsh cough with sleeplessness is not overcome by the aforesaid remedies, pills of cynoglossum of Mesue are to be given. These are said to be good for all diseases that follow catarrh, because they are opiate. But they are not to be used unless the affliction has been given up as hopeless by treatment.

units.la: 6. AFFECTVS catarrho succedentes sanantibus: ut, obstructione ossium ethmoidum, quam decoctum lentium iuuat, & synanchen etiam impendentemigni impedit, ut phlebotome fluentem materiam auertes.
units.tr: 6. AFFECTIONS that follow catarrh are cured: for example, obstruction of the ethmoid bones, which a decoction of lentils helps. It also prevents the quinsy that threatens, if you divert the flowing matter by phlebotomy.

units.la: Si autem catarrhi materia est frigida, interim peries cerebri frigida est corrigenda, sicque roborandum cerebrum, sacculis ex saluia, maiorana, milio, thure, sale: & lotione capitis ex vino aromatico, vel maluatico, addedis etiam caryophyllis, pipere, zingibere: lotione item ex lixiuio, cui plantae capitales incoctae fuerint: sumptis quoque Elect. diamoscho dulci & amaro, pliris arcotico, theriaca. Si autem materia est calida, frigidis utendum syrupis, conserwis, & admotis oleis, & unguentis frigidis.
units.tr: But if the matter of the catarrh is cold, the coldness of the wall of the brain must meanwhile be corrected, and the brain thus strengthened with little bags of sage, marjoram, millet, frankincense and salt, and by washing the head with aromatic or malmsey wine, adding also cloves, pepper and ginger; likewise by washing with lye in which the head plants have been boiled. Also take electuary of sweet and bitter diamoschus, pliris arcoticum, and theriac. If the matter is hot, cooling syrups, conserves, and cooling oils and ointments should be used, applied to the part.

units.la: OPHTHALMIAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE TREATMENT OF OPHTHALMIA.

units.la: OPHTHALMIA non vera, est in temperies oculi calida, cum rubore exiguo sine tumore, a causa externa excitari solita: ut, fumo, sole, humorum ex corporis motu agitatione, qua causa ablata, si corpus est purum, quiescere solet. Iuuatur autem multum aere frigido, lacte mulieris puerum lactantis cum albo ovi & aqua rosarum agitaro: Haec enim humores ab oculis repellunt, et horum motum sistunt.
units.tr: A false ophthalmia is a warm disposition of the eye, with slight redness and no swelling, usually brought on by an external cause, such as smoke, sun, or agitation of the humours from bodily movement. When that cause is removed, and the body is sound, it usually settles down. It is greatly helped by cold air, and by bathing the eye with a mother's milk (from a woman nursing a boy) mixed with egg white and rose water. For these drive the humours away from the eyes and stop their movement.

units.la: Si a casu aut percussione initium est fluxionis, eadem adhibe: si incrementum, rosarum, & seminis fœnigraeci decoctum, ut rosis repellas fluentem materiam, & fixam resoluas fœnograeco: si vigor est, fœnumgraecum solu: si rubor paruus superest, ouum ad duritiem coctum. coctum, & calens admotum reliquias poten-ter digerit, remedium etiam vulgo probatis-simum, uti & pomum putre vel coctum, et calens admotum, modò non sit adstringens.
units.tr: If the flux began from a fall or a blow, apply the same remedies. If it is increasing, use a decoction of roses and fenugreek seed, so that the roses repel the flowing matter and the fenugreek dissolves what has settled. If there is still inflammation, use fenugreek alone. If a slight redness remains, use an egg boiled hard and applied warm. The boiled egg, applied warm, powerfully disperses what is left over; it is also a remedy commonly regarded as very reliable. So too is a rotten or cooked apple applied warm, provided it is not astringent.

units.la: Ophthalmia vera, est phlegmone oculi tu-nicæ cohærentis à sanguine, aut bile flava pro-veniens: curatur autem sex remediorum ge-neribus.
units.tr: A true ophthalmia is an inflammation (phlegmone) of the eye's coat, which is attached to the eye, arising from blood or yellow bile. It is treated by six kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione refrigerante: ut, aë-re frigido natura, vel industria nostra sparsis per aream aquis, & partibus plantarum re-frigerantibus: & obscuro, quia lumen humo-res commouet, spiritusque resoluit.
units.tr: 1. REGIMEN by cooling methods: by cold air, whether given by nature or by our own effort, with water sprinkled over the courtyard, and with cooling parts of plants; and by darkness, because light stirs up the humours and dissolves the spirits.

units.la: Ut, victu tenui, quo partes inanitæ auidi-us quod habent humorū retineant, ne ad ocu-lum confluant. Vinum interdicitur ad usque declinationem: tunc permittitur cum Hippo. & Galen. lib. 6. Aph. 31. quando venæ oculi sanguine crasso sunt plenæ, sine totius plenitu-dine: & oua, carnes, reliqua sanguinem au-gentia. Ut, somno per quem oculus quiescit à motu & dolore, quibus fluxio trahitur: per somnum quoq; magis quieti sunt humores.
units.tr: By a thin diet, by which the emptied parts draw in more eagerly whatever humour they hold, so that it does not flow to the eye. Wine is forbidden until the decline, and then it is permitted, as Hippocrates and Galen teach (Aph. 6.31), when the veins of the eye are full of thick blood, though the whole body is not full; and eggs and meats, and other foods that increase the blood, are avoided. Sleep too, during which the eye rests from movement and pain, by which the flux is drawn; and during sleep the humours are also more at rest.

units.la: Vt fuga animi affectuum, qui humoribus in flammandis coducunt, ut caeteris refrigerando prohibentibus phlegmonem gigni, vel si coepta est, augeri.
units.tr: By avoiding the emotions of the mind, which gather humours into inflammation, so that other things, by cooling, prevent a phlegmone from arising, or, if it has begun, from increasing.

units.la: 2. FLUENTEM sanguinem auertentibus, ut sectione venae cephalicae lateris eiusdem, nisi magna plenitudo prius venam cubiti internam, aut communem secari suadeat, horis octo aut circiter interpositis. Extrahatur autem in iuuene carnoso, sanguineo, robusto, vere largior: ut medicamento purgante, clysteribus, partium extremarum frictionibus, fotu ex aqua calida, ligaturis dolorificis cucurbitulis sine, vel potius cum scarificatione in spathulis & brachijs summis.
units.tr: 2. By drawing off the flowing blood: by opening a vein of the head (cephalic vein) on the same side, unless great fullness first suggests opening the internal or common vein of the arm, with an interval of about eight hours. The blood should be drawn more freely in a young man who is fleshy, sanguine and robust, and in spring: by a purgative medicine, by enemas, by rubbing the extremities, by a fomentation of warm water, by painful bindings, by cupping-glasses without scarification, or rather with scarification, on the shoulder-blades and upper arms.

units.la: 3. REPELLENTIBVS fluentem materiam admotis fronti, si fluxio fit per venas & arterias extra cranium, ut fere fit, cum tunica haec a pericranio producatur: qualia sunt aqua rosarum, plantaginis, solani, albumen ovi, oleum rosatum, acetum, cortices granatorum, balaustia et similia, cataplasmatis modo admota, ut vias contrahant per quas fluit materia. Si autem per venas & arteri as intra cranium materia fluat, nocent hæc repellentia, cùm materiam versus nervos o- pticos impingunt: repellimus autem gosapio, aqua lactuca, aut potius rosata imbuto, ocu- lis superpositta, ligatura deinde laxa & com primentis media adhibita.
units.tr: 3. By repelling the flowing matter: apply to the forehead, if the flux comes through the veins and arteries outside the skull, as usually happens, since this coat is drawn from the pericranium; such things as rose water, plantain, nightshade, egg white, rose oil, vinegar, pomegranate rinds, balaustines and the like, applied in the manner of a poultice, so that they contract the passages through which the matter flows. But if the matter flows through the veins and arteries inside the skull, these repellents do harm, since they drive the matter towards the optic nerves. In that case we repel it by means of a sponge soaked in water of lettuce, or rather in rose water, laid over the eyes, and then a loose binding that presses gently is applied.

units.la: Oculo aut ipsi immittimus aquam rosarū albo ovi permistā: vel lac ex mamma emul- gemus: collyria quoque, vel sicca, vel liqui- da in cote medica ex aqua rosarum, vel similï pertrita, ex corallio rubro, gummi arabico, tragacantho, pompholyge, cerussa, lotis, ne oculū morsu suo lædat. Quibus si dolor nō uin citur, etiā opij, vel opiati aliquid ad sensum tactus oculi stupefaciendū additur, aut quod repellendi simul & stupefaciēdi facultate pol let: ut aqua rosarum cui incoctum sit semen papaueris albi, etiam addito ovi albo immis- sa oculo per se, vel ex mica panis eo decocto imbuta. Quæ si dolorem non leniant, trochi- scis albis Rasis ex aqua rosarum solutis vten dum, si dolor est vehementissimus nullis cedens remedijs: alias ne vtaris, quia cum va lenter stupefaciant, spiritus crassos reddunt, & facultatem visoria infirmant. Ob id nar coticorum vsus semper Galeno fuit suspectus Aph.31.lib.6. & alibi passim: praecipue in oculo & partibus capiti vicinis frigidis natu ra & etiam morbo.
units.tr: We put into the eye itself rose water mixed with egg white, or we squeeze milk from the breast. Also collyria, either dry or liquid, prepared on a medical stone with rose water or something similar, made of red coral, gum arabic, tragacanth, pompholyx, white lead (cerussa), and lotus, so that they do not harm the eye by their bite. If pain is not relieved by these, something of opium or an opiate is added to numb the sense of touch in the eye, or something that has both the power to repel and to numb: for example rose water in which white poppy seed has been boiled, with egg white added, poured into the eye by itself, or with bread crumb soaked in that decoction. If these do not ease the pain, white troches of Rhazes dissolved in rose water should be used, if the pain is most severe and yields to no remedies; otherwise do not use them, since, though they numb strongly, they thicken the spirits and weaken the power of sight. For this reason the use of narcotics was always suspect to Galen (Aph. 31, book 6, and elsewhere passim), especially in the eye and in parts near the head, which are cold by nature and also in disease.

units.la: 4. MATERIAM crassam apparantibus in cacochymia, syrupis granatorum, oxalidis, acetato simplici, rosato, de ribes cum aqua rosarum, oxalidis, plantaginis.
units.tr: 4. PREPARING the thick matter in cacochymia, with syrups of pomegranates, sorrel, simple acetate, rose, and dried gooseberries (de ribes) with rose water, sorrel and plantain.

units.la: 5. EVACVANTIBVS materiam, vt myrobalanis, pilulis aureis, aggregatiuis, & electario rosato de succo rosarum. Secta etiam vena cephalica lateris dolentis ad partem cubiti externam, non autem secto cum quibusdam ramo vena communis inter indicem & pollicem, nisi longius vis auertere.
units.tr: 5. EVACUATING the matter with myrobalans, golden pills, aggregative pills, and rose electuary made from rose juice. Also by opening the cephalic vein on the side of the painful part, on the outer side of the arm; or, if you wish to draw it away further, by opening a branch of the common vein between the index finger and thumb, which some use.

units.la: 6. RELIQVIAS materiae ex oculo vacuatibus: vt, decocto seminis fœnigraeci, vel meliloti, ex spongia, vel linteo molli oculis admoto.
units.tr: 6. CLEANSING the remnants of matter from the eye: for example, with a decoction of fenugreek or melilot seed, applied to the eyes with a sponge or soft linen.

units.la: Balneum quoque in declinatione salubre cum humohumores sunt acres, authore Galeno: In principio autem noxium, quia materiam liquat, & meatus dilatat, fluxionemque hac ratione geminat. Vinum autem quale, & quantum, & quando, & qua ophthalmiæ differentia sit salubre: ut, balneum, fomentum, venæ sectio, purgatio pulchrè Galen. distinguitur aph. 31. lib. 6. & alibi passim: aloës drac. una, aquæ foeniculi uncia una, si soluatur, & oculo applicetur, ipsum roborat, reliquias siccat & absumit: sarcocolla quoq; aqua rosarum, vel potius lacte muliebri soluta, et oculo immissa coquit materias, & digerit: ouum quoque coquendo duratum, ut calet, oculo impositum: trochiscus etiam seu puluis citrinus.
units.tr: A bath also is wholesome in the decline when the humours are sharp, according to Galen. At the beginning, however, it is harmful, since it liquefies the matter and dilates the passages, and so doubles the flux. As to which wine, how much, when, and in which kind of ophthalmia it is wholesome, as well as bathing, fomentation, venesection and purging, Galen distinguishes these beautifully in Aph. 31, book 6, and elsewhere passim. Aloes, one dram, with one ounce of fennel water, if dissolved and applied to the eye, strengthens it, dries up and consumes the remnants. Sarcocolla dissolved in rose water, or better in mother's milk, poured into the eye, concocts and disperses the matter. An egg boiled hard, applied to the eye while warm; also the citrine troche or powder.

units.la: VISIONIS IMBECILLAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: Treatment of Weak Vision.

units.la: VISIONIS imbecillæ causa, vel oculo est propria in ipsoque existit, vel à partibus subiectis communicatur, in hacque curanda scopi sunt duo seruandi: prior est partis, vel totius affectus imbecillam visionem
units.tr: The cause of weak vision either belongs to the eye itself and exists in it, or is communicated from the parts beneath it. In curing it, two aims must be kept. The first is to heal the affection of the part, or of the whole body, that makes the vision weak. For example, if the stomach suffers in sympathy, one must first look to it, using a laxative rather than an emetic if purging is needed.

units.la: P faciens, sanandus: ut si ventriculus consensu laboret, est illi ante prospiciendū dieectoryș potius quàm vomitoryș si purgatione opus est. Si corpus atrophia defectum imbecillam visionem facit, ut in hecticiś, nutritione instaurandum: ut ex sanguine bono auctiore, largior fiat spiritus animalis & visorius.
units.tr: If the body is wasted by atrophy and so weakens the vision, as in hectic fevers, it must be restored by nourishment, so that from more abundant good blood a fuller animal and visual spirit may be produced.

units.la: Alter scopus est, oculi curatio per contraria causas, ut si est siccior, is cum capite humectatur lacte, lacte ebutyrato, decocto maluas, al thaas, vel capitis, pedum intestinorum verue cis, idq; longo tempore: quia intemperies sicca vix etiam diuturnis auxilijs emendatur. Si ab alio oculi partium vitio est visio imbecilla, id sanandum est.
units.tr: The second aim is the cure of the eye by contrary means. If the eye is too dry, it should be moistened with the head, using milk, buttermilk, a decoction of mallows, marshmallow, or of the head, feet or intestines of animals, and this for a long time, since a dry intemperament is hardly corrected even by lasting remedies. If the weak vision comes from a fault in another part of the eye, that must be healed.

units.la: Si vitium est oculo proprium, et ab humore largiore, quinq; remediorum generibus curatur.
units.tr: If the fault belongs to the eye itself and arises from an excess of humour, it is cured by five kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. VICTVS
units.tr: 1. Diet

units.la: ratione tenui & siccante: ut aëre natura partis anni, & ventorum sicco, aut industria per ignem luculentum, per suffitus aromatum, ut caryophyllorū, foliorum siccorū rorismarini, maiorana, lauri. Ut proba cibi et potus parci coctione in ventriculo: quæ fiet, si donec cibus prior percoctus descenderit, nouus non injiciatur. Descendisse conjcies ex coctricis robore et alimento panco, tenero, grato, conciso, contuso, præmanso, coctu facili: non descendisse, ex contrarijs: adhæc ructibus, gravitate ventriculi, aut morsu, aut tumore. Ex crudo enim alimento vapor crudus in caput elatus oculo nocet, multo magis ex cruditate nidorulenta acer vapor.
units.tr: Diet should be thin and drying, both in the air, according to the nature of the season and the dry winds, or by diligent use of a bright fire, and by fumigations of aromatics such as cloves, dried rosemary leaves, marjoram and laurel. Let the food and drink be good and sparing, so that they are well concocted in the stomach. This will happen if no new food is put in until the earlier food has been fully digested. You may guess that it has gone down from the strength of the digestion and from food that is small in quantity, tender, pleasant, finely cut, crushed, pre-chewed and easy to cook; if it has not gone down, you will see the opposite, along with belching, heaviness of the stomach, colic or swelling. For raw food sends a raw vapour up into the head, which harms the eye, and far more does sharp vapour from indigestion that gives off a smoky stench.

units.la: Si ciborum natura variorum vsum paslu eodem vitabis, nisi coctu faciles primos, difficiliores secundos sumas, vt illi simulatq; cocti erunt, viam aliis parent iam coqui in superiore ventriculo cœptis, in fundo percoquen dis: qui si priores sumantur, cum tempus longum ad coctionem sui postulent, exitu per pylwam prohibent alios coctu faciles in superiore ventriculo iam diu percoctos & putre scentes, ex hisque vapor multus, & natura varius in caput effertur.
units.tr: If you cannot avoid the use of various foods, at least avoid eating them all at one meal. Take first the foods that are easy to cook and afterwards those that are harder, so that as soon as the first are cooked they open the way for the others, which are only beginning to be cooked in the upper stomach and must be digested in the lower. If the hard foods are taken first, since they need a long time for their cooking, they block the passage through the pylorus, and the easy foods, already long cooked and rotting in the upper stomach, cannot get out. From these a great deal of vapour, varied in kind, is sent up into the head.

units.la: Si ante expletam famem, cibo et potu abstineas, quia victus tenuis, vt inedia, per accidens vacuat & siccat.
units.tr: If you abstain from food and drink before hunger is satisfied, a thin diet, such as fasting, empties and dries by accident.

units.la: Si post pastus ea sumas quæ vapores in ca-put efferri prohibent: vt, panem tostum, co-riandrum tostum, vel conditum, cydoniatū, trypheram ob myrobalanos: vel quæ oculum roborant, vt fœniculum: id quod serpentum & bufonum nos exemplum docuit. Oculo-rum enim aciem ex mora hyberna in cauer-nis imbecillam affrictu fœniculi recreant. Ra-pæ etiam tota sua substantia visionem iuua-re creduntur: & viperarum, vt opus est, pa-ratarum caro: sed aqua cui incoquuntur, sæ-pe abiecta, si edatur: quo modo elephantici curandi est edenda: quanquam in his aqua non sit mutanda, & possint gallinæ hiis car-nibus prius nutritæ donec deplumentur, edi ab elephantiacis, vt post Matthæum Gradi fecisse se Gattinaria confirmat.
units.tr: If after a meal you take things that prevent vapours from rising into the head, such as toasted bread, toasted or preserved coriander, quince preserve, or trifera for the sake of the myrobalans; or things that strengthen the eye, such as fennel. The example of serpents and toads teaches us this, for after their winter sleep in caves they restore their weakened sight by rubbing on fennel. Turnip, in its whole substance, is also believed to help the vision. So is the flesh of vipers, prepared as needed, though the broth in which it is boiled is often thrown away, if one eats it. In this way it is to be eaten by lepers, though in this case the broth is not to be changed; and hens nourished on these meats before they are plucked may be eaten by lepers, as Gattinaria confirms that he did after Matthaeus Gradi.

units.la: Si denique somnus nec sit diurnus, nec di-turnus: si quoque aluus quotidie per se, aut à medico adiuta descendat ne teter vapor à ster-core in cerebrum elatus, animalem spiritum vitiet. Omitto quæ sumpta aut admota co-ctionem
units.tr: If no labour of body or mind is added, but only some gentle walking, by which the food descends only into the bottom of the stomach; also, a larger drink, because it stirs the contents, hinders digestion.

units.la: {a} ... Ệionem iuuant, vt grana piperis, mastiches, iuniperi integra aliquot inter epulas aut post eas sumpta, catellus, aut venter pueli non falcile sudantis foris applicatus, aut palma manus, aut simile aliquid.
units.tr: Galen writes, in book 1 of On the Foods, that eating much lentil helps weak sight caused by a large moisture.

units.la: Si labor etiam corporis, aut animi nullus accedat, sed tantum mollis quædam deambulatio, qua cibus insundum ventriculi tantum descendat: potus etiam largior, quia fluctuationem facit, coctionem impedit.
units.tr: If no labour of body or mind is added, but only some gentle walking, by which the food descends only to the bottom of the stomach, and if the drink is too abundant, because it causes agitation, this hinders digestion.

units.la: Esu multo lentis, visionem ab humiditate larga imbecillam iuuari scribit Galenus lib. 1. aliment.
units.tr: Galen, in book 1 of On the Faculties of Foods, writes that the vision weakened by a great moisture is helped by eating much lentil.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM apparantibus: melle rosato initio, oxymelite simplici: deinde syrup. stœchados cum aqua hyssopi, saluiæ & similibus ante iam sæpe repetitis.
units.tr: 2. To prepare the matter: first rose honey, then simple oxymel; afterwards syrup of stoechas with water of hyssop and sage, and the other remedies often repeated before.

units.la: 3. MATERIAM eandē vacuantibus, primùm pilulis elephanginis cum agarico trochiscato: vel mastichinis cum eodem, vel de hiera simplici aut composita, vel pilulis lucis Mesuæ: vel pilulis sine quibus etiamsi calida sit materia: postremo cum materia radicitus est vacuanda, coccijs, vel fœtidis à drachma vna ad scriptula quatuor.
units.tr: 3. To empty the same matter: first the elephantine pills with troched agaric, or mastich pills with the same, or simple or compound hiera, or the pills of light of Mesue, or pills without which, even if the matter is hot, it must finally be removed by the root, with coccia or foetid drugs, from one drachm up to four scruples.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBVS ad partes in fernas, aut posticas, vt capitis reuersi pexu multo occipitium versus: vt, clysteribus, balanis, ligaturis, frictionibus, fomento extremorum ex decocto capitali, apophlegmatismis, errhinis, cauterio post aures, vel in commissura coronali, cuius vlcus apertum diu tenendum est: vel in collosetone (quem vocât) injixo. Cutem autem colli forcipe apprehendimus donec sensus tactus abeat: postea acu filum aliquod crassum habete perforamus, vt in vulnere ablata acu filum maneat, quod vlcus diu apertu seruat, ac per id materiæ multæ vacuationem moliatur. Diuitibus autem quidam fili loco ablata acu anulum aureum æqualem apertum immittunt, postea ne excidat, eius extrema adducunt, & identidem quotidie dimouent, vt dolore & attritu materiam trahat & vacuet multam, mane & vespere quotidie tergendo.
units.tr: 4. To turn the matter away to the lower or back parts, as when the head is combed much towards the back of the skull; by clysters, suppositories, ligatures, frictions, fomentation of the extremities with a decoction of the head, apophlegmatisms, errhines, a cautery behind the ears or in the coronal suture, whose ulcer must be kept open for a long time; or by an issue placed in the so-called collosetone. The skin of the neck is grasped with forceps until feeling is lost; then we pierce it with a needle and leave some thick thread in the wound, so that when the needle is withdrawn the thread remains, keeping the ulcer open for a long time and so effecting a large evacuation of matter. Some rich people, instead of a thread, put in a level, open gold ring after removing the needle; afterwards, lest it fall out, they draw its ends together and move it every day, so that by pain and friction it draws out and empties much matter, wiping it morning and evening each day.

units.la: 5. ROBORANTIBVS partem, reliquias quias materiæ tergentibus & resoluentibus: sumptis quidem, vt nuce moschata (qua vna in dies mane sumpta, visionem recuperat Mesues) myrobalanis cepulis conditis duabus bis aut ter in hebdomada sumptis ad roborandu, pliris arcotico, acoro vero condito, diacoro ad cochlear vnum, seu drach. duas, mane & vespere hora somni, mithridatio, diamoscho dulci & amaro: admotis autem oculo, vt em plastro Mesuæ succo & aqua fœniculi, collyrio Mesuæ ex succo fœniculi in vase æneo per residentiam purgato, qui cum saccharo & melle & foliis auri & state insoletur, sæpe & leniter transfuasando excrementosum subsidens abjiciatur: vt, aqua Arculani destillata capitello ex fœniculo, verbena, rosis, chelidonio, ruta.
units.tr: 5. To strengthen the part and to wipe away and dissolve the remaining matter: taken internally, such as nutmeg (of which Mesue records that a single one taken each morning restores the vision), myrobalans, two preserved onions taken twice or three times a week to strengthen, Pliris arcoticum, preserved calamus, diacorum to one spoonful or two drachms, morning and evening at bedtime, mithridate, diamoscum sweet and bitter. Applied to the eye: Mesue's plaster with juice and water of fennel; Mesue's collyrium of fennel juice, purified in a bronze vessel by settling, which is to be exposed to the sun with sugar, honey and gold leaves, and often and gently strained, the sediment being thrown away; likewise the water of Arculanus distilled from fennel, verbena, roses, celandine and rue in a still.

units.la: Vt, collyrio Gentilis in consilijs, ex pompholyge vero & stibio lotis: quod cum aqua fœniculi mirè siccat oculo immissum.
units.tr: Such as Gentilis's collyrium in his Consilia, made with washed pompholyx and stibium; which, with fennel water, dries the eye marvellously when applied.

units.la: Vt Gerardi de Salo puluere ex pica vsta cum aqua fœniculi.
units.tr: Such as the powder of Gerard of Salo, made of burnt magpie with fennel water.

units.la: Vt Serapionis liquore torrendo cadente ex hepate vrsi prius in frusta dissecto, & inter posito inter hac piperc longo.
units.tr: Such as the liquid of Serapion, distilled from bear's liver, first cut into pieces and placed between them with long pepper.

units.la: Vt felle gallinæ, perdicis, piscium plurimorum. Animalium autem rapacium, & aliorum natura calidorum: vt, leonis, canis fellacrius: suis autem, veruecis, agni clementius: piscium fel est clementissimum: reptilium verò & aliorum venenosorum felle nemo unquam tuto vtatur. Felle autem quouis in oculum instillato adsit medicus: vt si rodendo dolet, obtundat aqua rosarum affusa oculo: vel oui albo, vel lacte: aut pannum lineum horum aliquo mersum applicet. Vsus autem emplastrorum in oculo parum tutus est, nisi sint moderata: & frequenter eximendo, ipsorum corpus explores.
units.tr: Such as the gall of hens, partridges and many fishes. Of the gall of rapacious animals and of others of hot nature, that of the lion and of the dog is sharper, while that of the pig, ram and lamb is milder, and fish gall is the mildest of all. But no one ever uses the gall of reptiles or of other poisonous creatures safely. Whatever gall is dropped into the eye, let the physician be at hand: if it causes pain by gnawing, let it be blunted by rose water poured on the eye, or by egg white or milk, or he may apply a linen cloth dipped in one of these. The use of plasters in the eye is not very safe unless they are moderate, and by frequently removing them you should examine their substance.

units.la: SUFFUSIONIS CURATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF SUFFUSION.

units.la: HYPOCHYMIA, id est, suffusio, et affectus in quo visa suffusorum visis similia apparent, remedijs egent similibus genere, sed illud valentioribus. Vterque hic affectus proprio oculi vitio contingit, aut per consensum eius cum cerebro, aut ventriculo aut parte alia: tunc parti primario affectæ pro spiciendum, vt pituita ex ventriculo, apparata est purganda, si ea vapore suo visioni officit: si bilis in ventriculo visa vapore exci tat, ea mox vomatur, si æstas est, ac æger facile vomit, nec pulmonicus est: alioqui deiici enda potius est cholagogis: deinde oculo prospiciendum, quibus dicemus remedijs.
units.tr: HYPOCHYMIA, that is, suffusion, and the affliction in which things seen appear like the visions of those suffering from suffusion, need remedies similar in kind but stronger. Both conditions arise either from a fault of the eye itself, or through its sympathy with the brain, the stomach or another part. Then the part primarily affected must be looked to. If phlegm from the stomach, once prepared, hinders sight with its vapour, it must be purged. If bile in the stomach, stirred up by vapour, is present, it must be vomited at once, provided it is summer, the patient vomits easily and is not consumptive. Otherwise it should rather be drawn off with cholagogues. Then the eye must be attended to, with the remedies we shall describe.

units.la: Si autem suffusio iam adest, eaque iam ab soluta: acu puncto ad angulum paruum oculo deturbetur, modo nec liquidior sit, nec tenacius oculi tunicis adhæreat, sed mediocri sit consistentia, quam oculo aliquandiu com presso, facile observabis. Si vero nondum ab soluta sit, quinq; his remediorum generibus curatur.
units.tr: If the suffusion is already present and already ripened, it is pushed down with a needle into the small corner of the eye, provided it is neither too liquid nor adheres too tenaciously to the coats of the eye, but is of moderate consistency. You will easily judge this by pressing the eye for a while. If it is not yet ripened, it is treated with five kinds of remedies.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione calida sicca (quia materia eius est vaporosa vel aquosa) vt ære æstiuo, qualem arte, & igni, & suffitibus moliri oportet, si desit. Vt, victu tenui & tenuante: quin & ieiunium atque abstinentia plurimum est huic chronico affectui salubris, vel Avicenæ testimonio: quòd si die semel comedisse his non sufficit, saltem leuius cœnent. Vino & iusculis abstineant: in aliis quoq; summendis, admouendis, faciendis, educendis, calida sicca sunt deligenda.
units.tr: 1. DIET: warm and dry (because its matter is vaporous or watery), like summer air, which must be produced by art, by fire and by fumigations if the season lacks it. The diet should be thin and attenuating. Indeed fasting and abstinence are very beneficial for this chronic affliction, on the testimony of Avicenna: but if one meal a day does not suffice, at least dine more lightly. Let them abstain from wine and broths. In other things to be taken, applied, done and evacuated, warm and dry things are to be chosen.

units.la: 2. AQVOSAM materia coquentibus, vt melle rosato: & si lentor aliquis adest, oxymelite simplici, syrup. stœchados, cum duplo aquarum fœniculi, maiorane, ad dies nouem, aut circiter: quin et sacculus lineus puluere maiorane plenus, oculo & naribus admotus multum iuuat hunc affectum Avicenna, & practicis aliis.
units.tr: 2. Things that concoct watery matter, such as rose honey; and if some viscosity is present, simple oxymel, syrup of stoechas, with twice as much water of fennel and marjoram, for about nine days. Indeed a linen bag filled with marjoram powder, applied to the eye and nostrils, greatly helps this affliction, as Avicenna and other practitioners say.

units.la: 3. AQVOSAM hanc materiam vacuantibus pilulis lucis vtriusq; in id efficacibus, & coccijs à drachma vna, adscriptula quatuor, agarico trochiscato, pilulis de agarico: pilulæ etiam tres mastichinæ, vel elephangine, vel de hiera, vel assaieret dormitum ituris sumendæ, sunt salubres: neque munia consueta, postridie impedient, vt prædictæ.
units.tr: 3. Pills of aloes of both kinds, which are effective for evacuating this watery matter, and coccus berries, one drachm, with four (scruples) added, agaric troches, pills of agaric. Three mastich pills, or elephangine, or of hiera, or of assaret, to be taken by those about to go to sleep, are wholesome; and they will not impede the usual duties the next day, as the ones mentioned above.

units.la: Toties autem vacuada est materia hæc, donec in totum curatus sit affectus, non solum se-mel, mel, bis, ter, quater.
units.tr: So often must this matter be evacuated, until the affliction is wholly cured, not only once, twice, three times, four times.

units.la: Phlebotome aut raro facienda, ne per hanc cerebrum refrigeratum, aquas largius cumu let, ac in oculum transfundat.
units.tr: Phlebotomy should be done rarely, lest through it the cooled brain pour out waters more abundantly and transfuse them into the eye.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBVS praeter dictas vacuantiones: acribus clysteribus et balanis, frictionibus, & fotibus per aquam calente partium extremarum, et harum ligaturis dolorificis: phoenigmo quoque et cauterio in coronali, aut prope aures, aut setone, quem vocant, cervicibus affixo e regione oculi affecti & cucurbitulis, primum leuibus, deinde cum scarificatu: manus saepe & diu clausas, si tenebis in lecto, vel alibi, ut largius sudent, et sudorem crebro terseris, omnia capitis et thoracis vitia materialia multum iuuat.
units.tr: 4. REVULSIVES, besides the said evacuations: sharp clysters and baths, frictions, and fomentations of the extremities with hot water, and ligatures of these that cause pain; also the phoenigmus, and a cautery on the crown of the head, or near the ears, or a seton, as they call it, fixed in the neck opposite the affected eye; and cupping glasses, first without scarification, then with it. Keeping the hands often and long clenched, if you hold them so in bed or elsewhere, so that they sweat more freely, and wiping the sweat frequently, greatly helps all material faults of the head and chest.

units.la: 5. MATERIAE reliquias dissoluetibus, & dissipantibus, partim sumptis hora somni, ut cum cibi vapore vis eorum in cerebrum & oculos rapiatur: vt, drachmis duabus confectionis humain laudatae a Mesue capite de visus imbecillitate: partim admotis: corpore tamen toto atque adeo capite ipso exquisitè vacuato. Nam hæc in oculum vapores nouos, & aquas largiores, qua vi dige runt, etiam traherent. Admonentur autem primò clementiora (quo ipse oculus sensu tactus exacto præditus, paulatim etiam valentioribus remedijs assuescat) vt, fœniculi, ruta aqua, vel succus per resident[?]ia purgatus: aqua ex melle destillata: Hæc enim mirè terget albuginem ac maculas oculi, & facici. Idem præstat puluis sacchari candi à multis probatus. Sagapenum quoque ad hypochy-fes resoluendas admotum, efficacissimum do-cet Auic. cap. de sagapeno: quod verum probabis ipsum dissoluens vino granatorum, vel aqua rosarum, fœniculi, mellis destillati, & lacte, & albo oui cum saccharo cando, vt oculus sagapeno soli paulatim assuescat. Idem præstat Auicennæ puluis capitum hirundinum: eandem siccat vrina pueri nondum polluti cum pauco fœniculo destillata, vt seruari diutius incorrupta possit, nec oleat grauiter. Balsamum quoque ob eius penuriam vsurarum, eas etiam siccat, et oculum sanitati pristinæ restituit. Ossis sepiæ puluis oculo immissus, aquas illas tergęt. Quibus si non cedit malum, valentiora sunt tentanda: vt, fella primùm mitiora, qualia piscium, suûm, agnorum, gallinarum, perdicis: deinde etiam acriora: vt, aluiû prædacearum, accipitris, aquilæ, falconis, et item viperæ & aliorum reptilium: sed hæc venenosa cũsint, suspecta mihi omnino sunt, nec vtenda censeo: etiam si tunc aquam sæpe mutatam, & cum theriaca, vel alio alexipharmaco ore contineas, ne in ventriculum aut pulmones, id venenum per magni canthi & palati foramen penetret: præsertim cùm valentia satis fel taurini, fel bouis, fel apri, nobis ad manum sint.
units.tr: 5. Things that dissolve and disperse the remnants of the matter, partly taken at bedtime, so that their force is carried with the vapour of food into the brain and eyes, such as two drachms of the confection of humanity praised by Mesue in the chapter on weakness of sight; partly applied. Yet the whole body, and especially the head itself, must be thoroughly evacuated first. For these would draw in new vapours and more abundant waters, which they have digested by force. Milder things are to be applied first, so that the eye, endowed with the sense of touch, may gradually grow accustomed to stronger remedies: such as fennel, rue water, or juice purified by settling, and water distilled from honey. For this wipes clean the whitish film and spots of the eye and the (cataract) marvellously. Powder of candied sugar, approved by many, does the same. Sagapenum also, applied to dissolve hypochymas, Avicenna shows to be most effective, in his chapter on sagapenum. You will prove this true by dissolving it in wine of pomegranates, or rose water, fennel, distilled honey, milk, and white of egg with candied sugar, so that the eye gradually grows accustomed to sagapenum alone. The powder of swallows' heads, according to Avicenna, does the same. Urine of a boy not yet grown, distilled with a little fennel, dries these too, so that it can be kept longer uncorrupted and does not smell strongly. Balsam, on account of its scarcity, also dries them and restores the eye to its former health. Powder of cuttlefish bone put into the eye wipes those waters away. If the ailment does not yield to these, stronger things must be tried: first milder galls, such as those of fish, pig, lamb, hen and partridge; then even sharper ones, such as those of birds of prey, the hawk, eagle and falcon, and likewise of the viper and other reptiles. But since these are venomous, I consider them wholly suspect and do not think they should be used, even if you then hold water, often changed, with theriac or another antidote in the mouth, lest that poison penetrate through the opening of the great canthus and palate into the stomach or lungs. This is especially so since strong enough galls of bull, ox and boar are at hand for us.

units.la: HEMORRHAGIAE E NARIBVS CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE TREATMENT OF NOSEBLEED.

units.la: Sanguinis per nares profluuium criticum non sistendũ, nisi copia uires immodice prosternat: non criticum autem sistitur quatuor remediorum generibus.
units.tr: A critical nosebleed should not be stopped, unless its quantity immoderately prostrates the strength. A non-critical one is stopped by four kinds of remedy.

units.la: VICTVS ratione refrigerante, & astringète vias per quas fertur sanguis: ut, aere in id parato per acetum & aquam rosarum, folia vitis, rubi, salicis, nymphaeę, violarum. Ut cibis ex omphacio, vino granatorum, aranciorum, limonum paratis & sumptis: & his glutinosis, quales sunt, pedes & capita vituli, veruecis, & aliorum animalium: caseus recens, pinguis, opus pistorium, praesertim ubi sanguis est biliosus, & tenuis. Oua item praesertim dura, quia sanguinem paucum & crassum gignunt, praesertim parte alba: sorbilia autem & tremula largiorem & liquidiorem, praecipuè vitellis: ob hæc illis ut carnibus, hac praesente causa abstine: aqua item chalybata sanguinem astringit mi sta potui, & coctis in hac obsoniys: ut denique ipsa corporis & animi quiete, quod utri usque motus humores exagitat, ad fluendûque concitat.
units.tr: DIET: a cooling regimen that also astringes the passages through which the blood flows. For example, air prepared with vinegar and rose water, and vine leaves, bramble, willow, water lily and violets. Foods prepared and taken from unripe grapes (omphacium), pomegranate wine, orange and lemon. Also glutinous foods such as calves' feet and heads, mutton and the parts of other animals; fresh, fatty cheese; and pastry, especially where the blood is bilious and thin. Eggs likewise, especially hard-boiled ones, since they produce little thick blood, particularly from the white. Soft-boiled and runny eggs produce more and more liquid blood, especially from the yolks. For these reasons, while this cause is present, abstain from them as from meats. Likewise chalybeate water astringes the blood, if drunk mixed in, and so do things cooked in these sauces. Finally, rest of body and mind, because motion of either agitates the humours and drives them to flow.

units.la: 2. AVERTENTIBVS, in quibus spes curationi praecipua uersatur: ut, brachiorum & crurum ligaturis dolorificis, frictionibus, fotibus ex aqua calente, cucurbitulis hypochondrio è regione naris sanguine fluentis appositis, positis, & inter scapulio sine scarificatione: vel, si opus est, cum ipsa: vt phlebotome in id efficacissima ad fluoris impetum in contraria revocandum: secetur autem vena basilica, aut cephalica, aut communis lateris eiusdem. Timorem quoque incussisse confert, cyathis aquae frigidae duobus, tribus, interuallo iniectis in faciem aegri incogitantis, vel alia ratione: per eum enim calor cum sanguine & spiritu ad cor revocatur. Sed vide ne sit epilepsiae obnoxius, vel viribus omnibus prostratus.
units.tr: 2. REVULSIVES, in which the chief hope of cure lies: for example, tight ligatures of the arms and legs, rubbing, fomentations with warm water, and cupping glasses applied to the hypochondrium on the side of the nostril that is bleeding, and placed between the shoulder blades, without scarification or, if need be, with it. Phlebotomy is also most effective for turning the flow back in the opposite direction; the basilic or cephalic vein, or the common vein of the same side, should be opened. It also helps to cause fright by suddenly pouring two or three cups of cold water on the face of the patient, who is not expecting it, or by some other method, for through this the heat is drawn back to the heart together with the blood and spirit. But take care if he is subject to epilepsy or utterly prostrated in strength.

units.la: 3. SANGVINEM sistentibus & cohibentibus sumptis vel admotis, nunc frigidis tantum sanguinem velut glaciantibus, et ob id ad fluendum ineptiore reddentibus, viasque densantibus, et contrahentibus, per quas sanguis fluit: vt lactuca, portulaca, & alimentis alijs refrigerantibus: adhaec mannae vncia vna, vel sescuncia, syrupi rosati, oxalidis, cydoniorum, granatorum praesertim vbi tenuior sanguis: vel si is etiam inflammatus est, syrupi omphacij, limonum, acidae partis citri, cum duplo aquarum plantaginis, rosarum, oxalidis, solani, & cum scriptulis duobus, aut drachma una trochiscorum terrae lemniae sigillatae, vel trochiscorum electri: quae etiam in nares immitti possunt tusa, & frontis applicari: & praeter haec, si necessitas vrget, hyoscyamo, opio, & opiatis recentibus: sed a mitioribus incipiendum: & impense frigida capiti frigidae parti, sed principi ne adhibe, quia sanguinem & spiritum animalem glaciant ac extinguunt. Nunc etiam astringentibus, & vasa, sive oribus hiantia, sive tuni cis rariora, sive rupta, vel incisa, vel erosa vnientibus, & contrahentibus: ut, rosis, balaustijs, gallis, malicoro, rhu: nunc emplasticis & meatus obstruentibus: ut, farina molet-rinarum tenuissima, aloe, oui albo, caseo, gypso, muccaginibus. Nunc escharoticis, quae vrendo escharam gignunt, quae crusta hiatui vasorum est operculi vice: ut, calce viva, face vini vsta, sed potius chalciti & chalcantho, & similiter astringentibus, simul & vrentibus, vt ab his eschara valentius here-at, reat, quae ab aliis effecta prompte cadit, & aucto hiatu haemorrhagiam maiorem, et periculosiorem revocat Galenus lib. 5. method. Nunc his quae sanguinem sistunt tota sua sub stantia, seu proprietate occulta, & nobis ignota ante experientiam: ut succo basilici, porri, urticae, veltritis ipsorum foliis in nares immissis (misto tamen his impense calidis refrigerante aliquo, ut caphura) stercore asini recente in nares cum bombace immisso, vel ipsius siccati puluere in nares per calamum efflato: puluere item sanguinis columbae, vel limacum simul cum testa assatarum, similiter efflato, aut cum oui albo subacto: cerebelis gallinarum, iaspide.
units.tr: 3. Those that stop blood, taken internally or applied externally. Some merely chill the blood, as if freezing it, and so make it less apt to flow, and they thicken and contract the passages through which the blood runs: for example lettuce, purslane and other cooling foods. Besides these: manna, one ounce or six scruples; syrup of roses, sorrel, quinces and pomegranates, especially where the blood is thinner; or, if it is also inflamed, syrup of unripe grapes, lemons, and the acid part of citron, with twice the quantity of waters of plantain, roses, sorrel and nightshade; and two scruples or one drachm of lozenges of sealed Lemnian earth or of amber lozenges. These may also be pounded and put into the nostrils, and applied to the forehead. Besides these, if necessity presses, henbane, opium and fresh opiates, but one should begin with milder remedies. Apply cold things often to the head, but not to the principal part, because they freeze and extinguish the animal blood and spirit. Then there are astringents, which join and contract vessels that gape, or are rarer in their coats, or are ruptured, incised or eroded: for example roses, pomegranate flowers, galls, pomegranate rind and sumac. Then there are plasters that obstruct the passages: very fine flour of meal, aloes, egg white, cheese, gypsum and mucilages. Then escharotics, which by burning produce an eschar, a crust that serves as a lid over the gaping vessels: for example quicklime, burnt lees of wine, but rather chalcitis and chalcanthum, and similarly astringents that also burn, so that the eschar formed by them holds more firmly. An eschar made by others falls off promptly, and with the opening enlarged it brings back a greater and more dangerous haemorrhage, as Galen says in book 5 of the Method. Then there are those remedies that stop blood by their whole substance or by a hidden property, unknown to us before experience: for example juice of basil, leek or nettle, or their fresh leaves rubbed into the nostrils (mixed, however, with some cooling agent such as camphor, since they are very hot); fresh dung of an ass put into the nostrils with cotton, or its dried powder blown into the nostrils through a reed; likewise powder of pigeon's blood, or of slugs roasted with their shells, similarly blown in or kneaded with egg white; cerebella of hens; jasper.

units.la: Nunc stupefacientibus (vbi scilicet facultate praedictorum omnium victa, salus deplorata est) quae sanguinem glaciant, ut athanasia recente, Philonis antidoto a drachma dimidia ad drachmam unam. Haec quoque sommnum conciliant, & hoc etiam modo fluorem sedant. Refrigerantia autem & astringentia non solum sumenda, aut naribus sanguine fluentibus immittenda: sed fronti quoque & vertici capitis, & collo, & inter scapulio, et lumbis, & testibus, et hyppochondrio na rem fluentem respicienti, applicāda, ex bom bace aut linamentis in hæc mersis, & modi- cè expressis. Adhæc vertici ex alto torrentis modo hæc illidi, vel incidere est multò efficacius, vti & aquam è stillicidio in verticem illabi. Galenus autem ad hæmorrhagiam eti am arteriæ, aloën, & thus cum oui albo subigit, & pilis leporum mollißimis excipit. Sunt qui per bolum armeniam, & sanguinē draconis, & oui albumina, idem præstant: nec vereare aloën: foris enim admota glutinat, licet sumpta venarum ora aperiat Mesuæ: cum nihil sumptū et foris admotū vires habeat easdem, vt in Mesue probaui. Qua au tem vi sanguinem sistat papyrus gestata, cui ex sanguine ipso fluente inscriptū sit, consumatum est, Theologis relinquo: & item bur sa pastoris collo appensa, sed quæ genibus flexis ante sit collecta, cum oratione dominica, & salutatione angelica ter dicta, & oratione.
units.tr: Then narcotics, where the power of all the aforesaid remedies has been defeated and safety despaired of. These freeze the blood, such as fresh athanasia, or Philo's antidote, from half a drachm to one drachm. These also induce sleep, and in this way too allay the flow. Cooling and astringent remedies should not only be taken or put into the bleeding nostrils, but also applied to the forehead, the crown of the head, the neck, between the shoulder blades, the loins, the testicles, and the hypochondrium facing the flowing nostril, from cotton or linen soaked in them and lightly squeezed. Moreover, to dash these onto the crown from a height, like a torrent, or to let water drip onto the crown from a dripping source, is much more effective. Galen, for haemorrhage of an artery, mixes aloes and frankincense with egg white and receives the mixture on the softest hares' fur. Some do the same with Armenian bole, dragon's blood and egg white. Nor need you fear aloes: applied externally it glues, although taken it opens the mouths of the veins, according to Mesue, since what is taken and what is applied externally do not have the same powers, as I proved in Mesue. As for the power by which a papyrus carried on the person, on which is written with the blood itself flowing, stops blood, I leave that to the theologians. Likewise a shepherd's purse hung at the neck, gathered before the knees are bent, with the Lord's Prayer and the angelic salutation said three times, and a prayer.

units.la: Gal. lib. 3. temper. ratione adiecta, Concede deus cũ tuo precioso sanguine, etc. apud Nicolaum Florentinũ.
units.tr: Galen, book 3 of Temperaments, with the reason added: "Grant, God, through your precious blood," etc., among Nicolaus Florentinus.

units.la: 3. CAVSAM hæmorrhagiæ auferentibus: vt, medicamentis cholagogis, si biliosus & acer et mordax is fuerit: vel glutinantibus remedijs, si vas apertum est: & cæteris, quæ abundè docet Galen. lib. 5. meth.
units.tr: 3. Those that remove the cause of the haemorrhage: for example cholagogue medicines, if the blood is bilious, sharp and biting; or glutinating remedies, if the vessel is open; and the others which Galen teaches at length in book 5 of the Method.

units.la: CYNANCHES CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF QUINSY.

units.la: Cynanche nondum absoluta, si resoluenda est, sex remediorum generibus curatur, hisque statim initio potentissimis: quia morbus acutis. ut Aphor. 4. & 24. lib. 1. & Aphor. 10. lib. 4.
