units.tr: A quinsy not yet fully formed, if it is to be resolved, is treated with six kinds of remedy, and these from the very start, since the most potent are needed because the disease is acute, as in Aphorisms 4 and 24 of book 1 and Aphorism 10 of book 4.

units.la: VICTVS ratione phlegmonem augeri prohibente: hoc est, tenui & refrigerate: vt, aëre frigido: vt, vnius diei vel biduî inedia, si vires ferre poterunt: vel saltem solo cremore ptissanæ, vel amylo aqua hordei soluto: in potu autem aqua hordei, iulepo rosato, vino granatorũ, vel similibus liquidis, et deglutiri facilibus. Vini aut et ouorũ abstinentia, quod hæc sanguinem augent & calfaciunt, præsertim vinum, & horum vitelli.
units.tr: DIET, to prevent the inflammation from increasing: that is, thin and cooling food, such as cold air; a fast of one or two days, if the strength can bear it, or at least only the cream of ptisan, or starch dissolved in barley water. For drink, barley water, rose julep, pomegranate wine, or similar liquids that are easy to swallow. Abstain from wine and eggs, since these increase the blood and warm it, especially wine and the yolks.

units.la: 2. AVERTENTIBVS sanguinis ad laryngem fluentis impetum, ob id phlegmone ipsam augeri prohibentibus, vt phlebotome ad lepothymiam, si vires valent, & corpus plenum est: alioqui eam partiri est satius. Secatur autem Galeno primum cephalica: deinde vbi fluxio cöstitit, ea quæ sub lingua est: Arabibus verò, si plenitudo magna subest, vena malleoli prima inciditur, post hanc interna, vel communis, deinde cephalica: qui ordo, vt parum efficax, sic admodum ægro molestus fuerit. Auertimus etiam purgatio- ne, si à sanguine syncerore nö sit, sed aliys humoribus largis misto: vt, succo fructuum, cum Rasi (valentibus enim medicamentis purgantibus humores agitare prudenter metuit Avicen. præsertim principio, ne ad locum affectum largius fluant) vel prunorum, tamarindorum ana sescuncia cocta, in vnc. octo aquæ, ad tertiæ partis consumptionem, expresso sci licet huic adiecta mannæ bonæ sescuncia. Auertimus etiam clysteribus, sed ob febrim acutam clementioribus: quæ si mitior est, vt in Archigenes apud Aetium saʒta medio cri sectione, partita sanguinis uacuatione m facit: damnat saʒta ad leipothymiam, ut per quam in hoc affectu prompta fluxio in pulmones rat, & periculum minetur. in cynanche pituitosa, & externa etiam, valentioribus. Revellunt etiam cucurbitulæ spathulis affixæ, & brachijs prius imis, deinde summis, si plenitudo maior adest: frictiones item valenter comprimentes manuum condylos, & earundem et pedum fotus ex aqua calente.
units.tr: 2. To turn aside the flow of blood running to the larynx, and so prevent the inflammation from increasing: phlebotomy, to the point of fainting, if the strength allows and the body is full; otherwise it is better to divide the bleeding. Galen cuts first the cephalic vein, then, when the flow has stopped, the vein under the tongue. But the Arabs, if there is great fullness, first open the vein of the ankle, after this the internal or common vein, then the cephalic. This order, as it is little effective, is also very troublesome for the sick person. We also turn the flow aside by purging, if the matter is not pure blood but mixed with other copious humours, such as juice of fruits, with Rhazes (for Avicenna fears prudently that powerful purgatives stir up humours, especially at the beginning, lest they flow more freely to the affected place), or of plums and tamarinds, half an ounce of each boiled in eight ounces of water until a third is consumed, the strained liquid having added to it half an ounce of good manna. We also turn the flow aside by enemas, but gentler ones because of the acute fever; and if the fever is milder, as Archigenes in Aetius, bleeding in part and partly evacuating the blood, he condemns frequent bleeding to fainting, since in this condition a sudden flux into the lungs is apt to occur and threatens danger. In quinsy with phlegm, and external quinsy too, stronger enemas may be used. Cupping glasses fixed to the shoulder blades also draw revulsion, and first to the lower arms, then the upper, if there is greater fullness; likewise rubbings that press firmly on the knuckles of the hands, and foot baths in warm water.

units.la: 3. MATERIAM ad musculos laryngis in quibus fit cynanche, fluentem repellentibus, & augeri cynanchen ob id prohibentibus, frigidis, & astringentibus leniter gargarizatis, aut potius donec incaluerint, relictis in vltimis faucibus, quæ partem roborent, et vias contrahant, per quas affluit materia: vt plantaginis, solani, lactucæ, oxalidis, rosarũ, nucum viridium, mororum, granatorũ, succo potius quàm aqua ex his destillata, vel syrup. granatorum, rosato, oxalidis, omphacij vel omphacio ipso: diacaryo, diamoro simplici, diacodio, aceto præsertim cum aqua simplici vel rosata: & his omnibus actu frigidis. Foris autem repellentia ne adhibe, quia materiam intro ad partem inflammatã protruderent, sed post principium clementer digerentia: ut, oleum chamaemeli, amygdal. dulcium: quando etiam gargarismatis repellentibus aliquid miscetur detergens, ut caeteris internarum partium phlegmonis: ut quae ab his sani es tenuis resudat, tergeatur.
units.tr: 3. MATERIAL flowing to the muscles of the larynx in which the quinsy arises is to be repelled, and the quinsy is to be prevented from growing; for this, use cold and astringent gargles, lightly applied, or rather, until they have warmed, leaving at the very back of the throat those that strengthen the part and contract the passages through which the matter flows in: of plantain, nightshade, lettuce, sorrel, roses, green walnuts, mulberries, pomegranates, using their juices rather than waters distilled from them, or syrup of pomegranates, of roses, of sorrel, or of unripe grapes, or the unripe grapes themselves; diacarydion, simple diamoron, diacodion, vinegar, especially with plain or rose water; and all these are truly cold. Do not apply repellents externally, since they would push the matter inward toward the inflamed part, but after the beginning apply gently digesting remedies, such as oil of chamomile and sweet almonds. When a cleansing ingredient is mixed into the repelling gargle, as in other inflammations of the internal parts, the thin matter that oozes out of the sound parts is also wiped away.

units.la: 4. MATERIAM apparantibus, frigidam, ut melle rosato, oxymelite simplici, syrup. oxalidis, cum aqua absinthij, quae repellit, digerit, & tergct sine manifesto calore: biliosam vero, ut quae fere turget, statim vacuare licet.
units.tr: 4. MATERIAL that is preparing: cold matter is to be treated with rose honey, simple oxymel, syrup of sorrel, or with wormwood water, which repels, digests and wipes away without obvious heat; but bilious matter, which tends to swell, may be evacuated at once.

units.la: 5. MATERIAM vacuantibus: ut, sectione venae, primum cephalicae dextrae, nisi sinistra parte laryngis, angina magis saeviat: deinde ubi fluxio constitit, eius quae sub lingua est, quam si priorem secueris, ad partem affectam tracta materia phlegmonem augebis, quanquam rustici quidam parum excrementosi, eam saepe solam secant, sed vix unquam initio cum tardi sint ad remediorum usum. Secanda autem omnino in angina sic vena est, etiamsi corpus atque adeo caput purum tibi videatur. Vt purgantibus materiam calidam, vt pilulis aureis vel polychrestis, vel electario de succo rosarum, vel myrobalanis, aut ipsarum infuso, frigidam verò pilulis de agarico, & aliis prius dictis in pituitosis capitis affectibus.
units.tr: 5. MATERIAL that is to be evacuated: by bleeding, first the right cephalic vein, unless the quinsy rages more on the left side of the larynx; then, when the flow has stopped, the vein under the tongue. If you open the first and draw the matter toward the affected part, you will increase the inflammation, although some rustics with little superfluity often open only the latter, but they hardly ever do so at the beginning, since they are slow to use remedies. Indeed, in quinsy the vein must always be opened, even if the body, and so the head, seems clean to you. Purge the hot matter with golden pills or polychrest pills, or with electuary of rose juice, or with myrobalans, or their infusion; the cold matter with pills of agaric and the others mentioned earlier for phlegmatic affections of the head.

units.la: 6. MATERIAM laryngi impactam coquentibus et dissipantibus: partim gargarismatis ex decocto vuarum passarum, ficuum passarum, dactylorum, chamæmeli, fœnigræci, croci: addito etiam melle rosato, vel diamoro composito: nam simplex principio convenit, vt lac incremento, partim admotis: vt oleo chamæmeli, liliorum, amygdalarum dulcium per se, aut cum farina se. fœnigræci, lini, vel cum nido hirundinum, si vis, prius cocto ex vino albo: is enim tota substantia hunc affectum iuuat, vt pulvis ipsarum hirundinum, cum Auic. paratarum, & stercus humanum, & caninum ex ossibus album: vtrunque Gattinaria cum melle bono in fauces quoque efflat, et filu laneu purpura tinctum, & quo postea vipera est strangulata, collo cynanchici circundatum: filum quoque multum cum cineribus, aut lixiuio coctum, & collo, vt calet, circundatum. Hæc autem omnia sunt vtenda, vbi fluxio constitit, in statu scilicet ipso, & præcipuè in declinatione, non principio, vel incremento inflammationis.
units.tr: 6. MATERIAL lodged in the larynx is to be cooked and dissolved: partly by gargles made from a decoction of raisins, dried figs, dates, chamomile, fenugreek and saffron, with rose honey or compound diamoron added; for simple honey suits the beginning, as milk suits the increase. Partly by applying, as external remedies, oil of chamomile, of lilies, of sweet almonds alone, or with meal of fenugreek or linseed, or, if you wish, with swallows' nests first boiled in white wine. For the whole substance of the nest helps this condition, as does the powder of the swallows themselves, prepared as Avicenna directs, and human dung and white dog dung from bones; Gattinaria also blows both of these, with good honey, into the throat. Also a woolen thread dyed purple, with which a viper was afterwards strangled, wrapped around the neck of the quinsy patient; also a thread boiled much with ashes or lye, and wrapped warm around the neck. All these things are to be used once the flow has stopped, namely in the very state of the disease, and especially in its decline, not at the beginning or during the increase of the inflammation.

units.la: Si autem cynanche resolui nequeat (quæ tamen curandi ratio est optatior) suppurantibus est coquenda: emplastro ex farina se. lini, & fœnigræci: deinde abscessus est rumpendus, mansio & deglutio duriore crusto panis, vel immisso altius digito, vel si cerni potest, scalpello: tuncque inclinato capite, ne in pulmones ruat pus, effluere permittendum est: vlcus melle rosato, & aqua hordei tergendum: postremò glutinandum, bolo armenia, sanguine draconis, & thure.
units.tr: If, however, the quinsy cannot be resolved (though this method of cure is the more desirable), it is to be ripened with suppurants: a plaster of meal of linseed and fenugreek. Then the abscess must be burst; the patient chews and swallows a harder crust of bread, or a finger is inserted deeper, or, if it can be seen, a scalpel is used. Then, with the head inclined so that the pus does not run into the lungs, it must be allowed to flow out. The ulcer is to be cleansed with rose honey and barley water; finally it is to be closed with a glutinant, Armenian bole, dragon's blood and frankincense.

units.la: TVSSIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE TREATMENT OF COUGH.

units.la: TVSSIS tot modis curatur, quot causas habet varias: si enim fit à causa externa, ea prius ablata, dispositio partibus respiratorijs spiratorijs ab ea causa impressa, est abigenda. Si vero fit per consensum partium spirita lium cum alijs primario affectis: praesertim quae ab illis motis mouentur, vt ventriculo, hepate, liene, & si gurgulio, aut caput destil let, primum his est succurrendum: deinde si qua dispositio partibus respiratorijs inhaesit, tolleda: si a pleuritide est, aut peripneumonia per harum phlegmonarum curationem post dicendam prospicitur: vt si a pure collecto in thorace, aut pulmone est tussis, curationem eius in empyemate audies: si a rupta in pulmo ne vena, in sputo sanguinis: si a catarrho, is tibi ante est curandus, vt dixi. Si autem tussis est ob alium proprium partium spiritalium affectum, id est intemperies calida, frigida, humida, sicca, vel sola, vel cum materia: omnis per contrarium corrigenda. Si enim frigida sola, calidis sumptis, & admotis: vt dia moscho dulci, amaro, & alijs calidis, ouo sor bili, & vino, reliquaque victus ratione calida: quae si imbecilla est, etiam anhelitus cohi bitio sanat: pulmone, per retentam expirandā materiam fuliginosam calfacto, & spiritu cohibito in omnes arctos meatus penetrante, lib. 5. symp. Similiter intemperies calida frigidis, humida siccis, sicca humidis curatur.
units.tr: Cough is treated in as many ways as it has various causes. If it arises from an external cause, that cause must be removed first, and then the disposition that the cause has impressed on the respiratory parts must be driven out. If, however, it arises through sympathy of the respiratory parts with other parts that are primarily affected, especially those that are moved by the parts they move, such as the stomach, liver, spleen, or when the head discharges into the throat, these must be helped first. Then, if some disposition has taken hold of the respiratory parts, it must be removed. If the cough comes from pleurisy or peripneumony, provision is made for it by the treatment of these inflammations, which I will describe later. If it comes from pus collected in the chest or lung, you will hear its treatment under empyema. If it comes from a ruptured vein in the lung, it is treated under spitting of blood. If it comes from catarrh, that must be treated first, as I said. But if the cough is due to some other affliction peculiar to the respiratory parts, namely a hot, cold, moist or dry intemperament, whether alone or with matter, it is to be corrected in every case by the contrary. If it is cold alone, warm things are to be taken and applied, such as diamoschum dulce, amarum and other warm remedies, a yolk of egg with wine, and the rest of the diet warm. If this is weak, even restraining the breath cures it, when the lung, heated by the sooty matter retained that should be breathed out, and the restrained breath penetrating into all the narrow passages (book 5, Symposiacs). Likewise a hot intemperament is cured by cold remedies, a moist one by dry, and a dry one by moist.

units.la: Si autem tussis ab intemperie cum materia calida frigida excitatur (id quod frequentius accidit, & ob id à Rasi tractatur) sex remediorum generibus curatur.
units.tr: If, however, the cough is excited by an intemperament with hot or cold matter (which happens more often, and for that reason is treated by Rhazes), it is cured by six kinds of remedies.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione calida, si materia est frigida: frigida, si calida, vt in catarrho diximus.
units.tr: 1. DIET of the opposite kind: warm if the matter is cold, cold if it is hot, as we said under catarrh.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM fluere paratam apparantibus, crassam quidem tenuantibus, & lentam incidentibus, & tergentibus: calida vero & tenuem frigidis, crassantibus, sed lenientibus vias, non autem materiam pulmoni affingentibus, & inculcantibus: vt syrupis pectoralibus, violato & zizyphorum: si tamen humor calidus acer insomniam pariT, vt saepe fit hora somni capiat syrup. papaueris vnc. vnā, syrup. violati, aut zizyphorum vnc. dimidiā cum duplo aquæ violarū, vel decocti hordei, vel prunorum, tamarin-dorum, myxorum, zizyphorum se.fri.communium, vel bibat tunc aquæ frigidæ per se, aut saccharatæ, vel decocti hordei vncias quatuor, quinque, sex: hæc enim omnia materiam calidam aut frigidam tenuem, crassant. Si vero frigida est materia & crassa, dabis syrup. glycyrrhizæ, mel rosatum etiā terforium: syrupum hyssopi terforium magis, & syrup. marrubij, maxime horum omniū tergentem cum duplo aquarū scabiosæ, hyssopi, prassij, fœniculi, adiantorum, vel decocti horum simplicium & glycyrrhiza, dactylorum: quod etiam per se (dulce enim est) mane calens dari potest.
units.tr: 2. For those preparing matter to flow: thinning the thick matter, and cutting and cleansing the viscid; but for hot and thin matter, cooling, thickening, yet soothing the passages, and not adding and forcing matter onto the lungs; such as pectoral syrups, violet and jujube, if the hot sharp humour causes sleeplessness, as often happens, let him take at bedtime one ounce of poppy syrup, half an ounce of violet or jujube syrup with twice the amount of violet water, or of decoction of barley, or of plums, tamarinds, quinces, or common jujubes; or let him drink then plain cold water, or sweetened water, or four, five or six ounces of barley decoction. For all these thicken hot or cold thin matter. But if the matter is cold and thick, you will give licorice syrup, rose honey, also a cleansing syrup, and hyssop syrup, more cleansing, and horehound syrup, especially the most cleansing of all these, with twice the amount of waters of scabious, hyssop, parsley, fennel and maidenhair, or a decoction of these simples with licorice and dates. This can also be given by itself, warm, in the morning, since it is sweet.

units.la: 3. PVRGANTIBVS materiam: calidam quidem, cassia, manna, electario rosato Mesuæ, scrup. de succo rosarum, diapruno scammoniato, pilulis aureis, vel polychrestis à drachma vna adscript. quatuor: sed scammoniata & similiter valentia vitabus æits, & ægri natura calidiore frigidâ vero pilulis coccijs, de agarico: quib. sumptis nocte, domi postridie manendum est: non item si horasom ni mastichinas, elephanginas, ex agarico trochiscato, ex hiera simpliciaut copositasumpseris. Cum autem ægrè hæc purgatoria àpul monibus vacuent, Auic. & Rasis in hoc affectu purgationibus abstinet, ob distantiam pulmonis, & asperarum arteriarum ab intestinis, & negatam viarum communitatem: purgando autem à capite fluxuram materiam commodant.
units.tr: 3. For those purging matter: hot matter with cassia, manna, Mesue's rose electuary, a scruple of rose juice, diaprunum scammoniatum, golden pills, or polychrest pills, four drachms each; but avoid scammony and similarly strong things for those whose nature is hotter, and for the cold, coccine pills and agaric. After taking these at night, one should remain at home the next day. This does not apply if you have taken mastic, elephant or agaric troches, or hiera simplex or composita at bedtime. Since these purgatives empty only with difficulty from the lungs, Avicenna and Rhazes abstain from purges in this affliction, on account of the distance of the lung and the rough arteries from the intestines and the lack of a common passage. They recommend, however, that purging draws the matter away from the head.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBVS prædictis purgantibus & errhinis, & cæteris eiusdè classis remedijs, prius sæpe declaratis.
units.tr: 4. Diverting, by the aforementioned purgatives and errhines and the other remedies of the same class, already often explained.

units.la: 5. MATERIAM pulmonibus concep-tam, expui facilem reddentibus ( in quo studio curationis pars est præcipua) calidam quidem et tenuem pulmonibus immersam crassantibus, ut efflatione expellatur, nō autem tussim ob tenuitatem eludat, nec dissiliat: talia sunt eclegmata quædam lenta: ut, de papaue-re, & diacodion, saccharum violatum, ju-lep, et syrupus violatus, tragacanthū, scrup. diatragacanthi, decoctum hordei saccharatum: tum: quæ cochleari sumpta in fauces, paula- tim deglutiuntur, ut portio eius quædam in asperam arteriam decerret, uti nobis edenti-bus & bibentibus cibi & potus portio tenuior eodem transfertur: vel potius inspira-tu violento in asperas arterias trahantur, et aliquanto post tussi reiciantur: foris autem thorax oleo violato inungendus: si autem frigida est materia, sumat eclegma sanum & expertum, vel ex pulmone vulpis scriptum à Mesue in curatione phthisis, mirum in pulmone roborando: syrupum glycyrrhizæ: sumat autem sæpe, ut prius cochlearîo per se, vel cum decocto vuarum passarum, ficuum, glycyrrhizæ, & aliorum pulmonariorum: sumat item penidia scrup. diairis Nicolai ad ciceris magnitudinem. Foris autem illinat oleum amygdalarum dulcium per se, aut etiam cum butyro recenti non salso, & croco pauco, vel etiam oleo, & muccagine semi. lini, fœnigræci, malvæ, althææ.
units.tr: 5. Making the matter gathered in the lungs easy to expel (in which care lies the chief part of the treatment): warm and thin matter that is immersed in the lungs is to be thickened, so that it is expelled by breathing out, and not eluded by the cough through its thinness, nor scattered. Such are certain soft electuaries: for example, of poppy, diacodion, violet sugar, julep, violet syrup, tragacanth, a scruple of diatragacanth, and sweetened barley decoction. These are taken with a spoon into the throat and gradually swallowed, so that some part of them runs down into the rough artery, just as a thinner portion of food and drink passes there when we eat and drink. Or rather, they are drawn into the rough arteries by a forceful inhalation and some time later are coughed up. Outwardly, the chest is to be anointed with violet oil. But if the matter is cold, let him take a sound, tested electuary, either the one written by Mesue from fox lung in the treatment of phthisis, which is marvellous for strengthening the lung, or licorice syrup. He should take it often, as a spoonful by itself, or with a decoction of raisins, figs, licorice and other lung remedies. He should also take penidia, with a scruple of Nicholas's diairis, the size of a chickpea. Outwardly let him smear sweet almond oil alone, or also with fresh unsalted butter and a little saffron, or with oil and mucilage of linseed, fenugreek, mallow and marshmallow.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM reliquam digerentibus, ut trochiscis, & suffitibus Rasis à Matheo Gradi expertis.
units.tr: 2. Treating the remaining matter by digesting it, with lozenges and fumigations, as Rhazes taught and Matthaeus Gradi tested.

units.la: ASTHMATIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF ASTHMA.

units.la: ASTMA, id est, anhelatio à pituita crassa trachęas arterias obstruente. (Nam quæ à sanguine fit angustia, & inde spirandi difficultas, in sputo sanguinis: quæ à peripneumonia in capite de ipsa, quæ ab vlcere pulmonis, in capite de phthisi: quæ à luxatis intro spinæ spondylis, capite de gibbositate dicetur) curatur sex remediorum generibus.
units.tr: Asthma, that is, breathlessness caused by thick phlegm obstructing the windpipe. (The narrowing that comes from blood, and the resulting difficulty in breathing, is dealt with under spitting of blood; that from pleurisy under pleurisy itself; that from an ulcer of the lung under phthisis; and that from the vertebrae of the spine displaced inward under gibbosity.) It is cured by six kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione calida sicca: vt, aëre: vt cibo, carnibus scilicet tostis vel assis, non pinguibus neque neruosis: vt, potu in parsu quidem parco, post pastus autem nullo, etiam si vehementer sitiatur ob cordis calorem minus quàm exigit, refrigeratum. Potus enim tunc ventriculo distenso diaphragma premit, & respirandi auget difficultatem: potest tamen bibere vbi cibus prior ventriculum iam egressus est. Potest verò etiam prius os potu lauare, & gargarizare, & liquoris sputum promouentis aliquid in asperas arterias inspiratu trahere.
units.tr: 1. DIET: the regimen should be hot and dry, in air, in food (namely roasted or grilled meats, not fatty or sinewy), and in drink, taken sparingly during the meal and not at all afterwards, even if one is very thirsty because of heat of the heart, and cool. For drink taken when the stomach is distended presses on the diaphragm and increases the difficulty of breathing. One may drink, however, once the previous food has left the stomach. One may also first rinse the mouth and gargle with liquid, and draw a little of a liquid that promotes spitting into the windpipe by inhalation.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM in cerebro, pulmone, vel partibus aliis transmittentibus collecta, apparantibus: calfacientibus, humectantibus, incidentibus, tenuantibus, tergentibus. Ne vero calidis multum initio vtere, quia tenui resoluto crassum expuitioni ineptum relinquunt. ne etiam in hoc affectu chronico ijsdem continenter vtere: quia quibus remedijs natura assuescit, ea contemnit, quod ab assuetis non fiat passio. Adhaec quamuis haec medicamenta qualitatibus manifestis conueniant: diuersam tamen habent proprietatem occultam, qua haec illis corporibus, illa aliis magis conueniant & conferant. Sunt e-nim medicamentis cum corporibus totius substantiae proprietates, & familiares, & repugnantes, quae sola experientia noscuntur. Conueniunt igitur syrupi glycyrrhizae, hyssopi, prassij, & his valentiores, de duabus, & de quinque radicibus: oxymeli item simplex, compositum, & valentius scilliticum cum duplo aquarum hyssopi, foeniculi, vel decocti radicis helenij, vuarum passarum, daEtylorum, adiantorum, & caeterorum thoracicorum.
units.tr: 2. MATTER gathered in the brain, the lungs, or other parts that transmit it: the remedies should be warming, moistening, cutting, thinning, and cleansing. At the start, do not use hot remedies in large amounts, because they dissolve the matter into thin fluid and leave the thick part unfit for expectoration. Nor should you use the same remedies continuously in this chronic condition, because the nature grows used to remedies and disregards them, since the complaint is not caused by what it is accustomed to. Moreover, although these medicines agree with manifest qualities, they have different hidden properties, by which some suit and benefit some bodies more than others. For medicines have properties of their whole substance in relation to bodies, some familiar and some hostile, which are known by experience alone. Thus syrup of licorice, of hyssop, and of horehound suit, and the stronger ones made from the two roots and the five roots; likewise simple oxymel, compound oxymel, and the stronger squill oxymel, with twice the quantity of water of hyssop, fennel, or decoction of elecampane root, dried grapes, dates, maidenhair, and other chest remedies.

units.la: 3. MATERIAM si multa est, purgantibus (si enim tam pauca est, vt per sputa ex cerni possit, purgatione non opus est) vt, agarico trochiscato, pilulis ex agarico Mesuae (is enim cerebrum, thoracem, pulmones, tacito consensu mirè purgat) pilulis coccijs pituitâ à cerebro vacuantibus per se à drachma vnâ ad script. quatuor, vel ipsarum, & pilularum ex agarico, aut agarici trochiscati ana scrip. duobus, vel scrup. indo ad semunciam, vel ex presso drach. duarum agarici, cum salis gemmae, & zingiberis ana scriptulo vno, decem horis infusarum in aquae hyssopi, & scabiosae quantitate sufficienti, addendo scrup. indi drachmas duas, syrupi glycyrrhizae vnciâ vnam. Vt tamen à pulmonibus tandem attrahant purgatoria, in pilulis sunt efficaciora, vt quae mora in ventriculo longa à remotis partibus attrahunt. Conueniunt & asthmatiâ catarrho pilulae aromaticae, de hiera simplici, vel composita, cum agarico semper, ut omnium simul dentur scriptula quatuor, quarto aut sexto quoque die, hora somni. Potest etiam elleborus & colocynthis, aut potius hiera diacolocynthidos his tandem exhiberi, parata multum materia, ut facilius evacuetur. Saepe autem repetenda purgatio est ob morbi longitudinem, modo ne purges dum vt lut in pulmone feruet, et exundat sursum materia per quosdam paroxysmos, & saepe certis periodis repetentes.
units.tr: 3. If the matter is abundant, use purgatives (for if it is so little that it can be seen to come out in spit, there is no need for purging). For example: lozenges of agaric, the pills of agaric of Mesue (for it purges the brain, chest and lungs remarkably by a hidden sympathy), pills of Cocci that draw phlegm from the brain, given alone from one drachm up to four scruples; or of these and of pills of agaric, or of agaric lozenges, two scruples each, or from one and a half scruples up to half an ounce; or a pressed extract of two drachms of agaric with one scruple each of rock salt and ginger, infused for ten hours in a sufficient quantity of water of hyssop and scabious, adding two drachms of indigo and one ounce of syrup of licorice. Purgatives work more effectively in pills, so that they may finally draw matter from the lungs, since they remain a long time in the stomach and draw from remote parts. In catarrhal asthma, aromatic pills of simple or compound hiera are also suitable, always with agaric, so that four scruples of the whole mixture are given every fourth or sixth day at bedtime. Hellebore and colocynth, or rather hiera of colocynth, may finally be given as well, when much matter has been prepared so that it may be evacuated more easily. The purging must often be repeated because of the length of the illness, provided one does not purge while the matter seethes and rises up in the lung in certain paroxysms, which recur at fixed periods.

units.la: Accessionis enim tempore medicamento purgante materiam non agitabis, ne largius in pulmones fluat, & suffocet, sed blande spu tum tunc pronocabis, aut per cucurbitulas, paulo supra renum situm affixas, & recto corpore revelles materiam ad arterias asperas truncum, confertim ruentem, & suffocationis periculum afferentem.
units.tr: For at the time of an attack one should not stir up the matter with a purgative medicine, lest it flow more copiously into the lungs and suffocate the patient; instead, one should then gently provoke spitting, or draw the matter away by cupping glasses applied a little above the loins, with the body held upright, from the trunk of the windpipe, where it rushes in and brings danger of suffocation.

units.la: 4. AVERTENTIBVS remedijs: vt
units.tr: 4. Remedies that divert: for example,

units.la: errhinis, apophlegmatismis, causticis, & caeteris ante in catarrho & tussi descriptis.
units.tr: errhines, apophlegmatisms, caustics, and the others described earlier under catarrh and cough.

units.la: 5. SPVTA promouentibus, hoc est, thoracem roborătibus, arterias asperas dilatan
units.tr: 5. Expectorants, that is, those which bring up sputum, strengthen the chest, and dilate and cut through the rough arteries

units.la: R tibus, & incidentibus: hisq; vel simplicibus: vt, glycyrrhiza, vuis passis, ficis siccis, myxis zizyphis, adiatis, hyssopo, scabiosa, rad. helenij, aristolochiæ rotundæ, foliys, & seminæ vrticæ, & cæteris dulcibus, nitrosis, salsis, amaris, acribus: vel compositis ex his, et similibus syrupis, electarijs, eclegmatis: quale ex brassica & ex pulmone vulpis factum, ab omnibus scriptoribus celebratur proprietate pulmones iuuare, vti pulueris ericij sylvestris drach. duæ sæpe sumptæ. Radix quoq; ari cruda, vel potius elixa, aut sub cineribus assata, trita, & syrupis thoracicis mista, sputum efficacissime promouet: si eius, exempli gratia, semuncia cum eclegmatis de pino: & de pulmone vulpis, ana drachmas sex, cū syrup. glycyrrhizæ misceantur: cui addunt quidam vuas passas purgatas, ficus, dactylos, penidia, hyssopum, adiantum. Foris autem corpus linatur oleo amygdal. dulcium, butyro recenti, cum pauco croci, et linteis asperis mollisculè fricetur, vt per poros apertos aliquid materiæ exhalet.
units.tr: ...tting, and incisive remedies, either simple ones, such as liquorice, raisins, dried figs, jujubes, maidenhair, hyssop, scabious, the root of elecampane, round birthwort, the leaves and seed of nettle, and other sweet, nitrous, salty, bitter and sharp ones; or compounded from these and similar syrups, electuaries and linctuses. Of this kind is the linctus made from cabbage and fox's lung, which all writers celebrate for its property of benefiting the lungs, and the powder of wild hedgehog, two drachms, often taken. The root of arum, raw, or rather boiled or roasted under the ashes, then pounded and mixed with thoracic syrups, promotes sputum most effectively: for example, half an ounce of it mixed with six drachms each of the pine linctus and the fox-lung linctus, together with syrup of liquorice. Some add to this cleaned raisins, figs, dates, penidia (pine-nut sweetmeats), hyssop and maidenhair. Externally, the body is anointed with oil of sweet almonds and fresh butter, with a little saffron, and rubbed gently with rough linen cloths, so that some of the matter may exhale through the open pores.

units.la: 6. SICCANTIBVS & dissipantibus materiæ reliquias suffitu cū thure, sulphure purgato, et etiā arsenico: quod mirū in idGentilis prædicat, etiā si sit deleterium, et ob id vix vtendū, nisi rite castigetur: sumptis etiā theriaca, mythridatio, diamoscho dulci & amaro, pluris arcotico, & similibus.
units.tr: 6. Drying agents, which dissipate the remnants of the matter by fumigation with frankincense and purified sulphur, and even with arsenic, which Gentilis praises as remarkable for this purpose, although it is poisonous and therefore hardly to be used unless it is properly corrected; also taken are theriac, mithridate, sweet and bitter diamoscum, arcoticum in more than one form, and similar remedies.

units.la: PLEVRITIDIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: PLEURISY: ITS CURE.

units.la: Pleuritis uera, & resolui, & sputis perpurgari apta, curatur sex remediorum generibus: phlegmonem augeri prohibentibus, & quod eius iam est genitum resoluentibus.
units.tr: True pleurisy, which can be resolved and purged by expectoration, is cured by six kinds of remedy: those that prevent the inflammation from increasing, and those that dissolve what has already been generated.

units.la: VICTVS ratione ad quartum vsque diem tenuis, si vires ferre possunt, vt potione ptissanæ, velptissana tota, aut colata, seu aqua hordei, & hordeato curiose cocto, vt voluit Hippoc. deinde ad septimum vsque pane loto, vt salis & fermenti calor tollatur, & ex aqua alia percocto, portione butyri & sacchari exigua, ad saporis gratiam adiecta: posl diem septimum, amygdalatum panis, aut hordeū, ex iure pulli coctū.
units.tr: As regards diet, keep it thin until the fourth day, if the strength can bear it: a drink of ptisan, whether whole or strained, or barley water, and barley gruel carefully cooked, as Hippocrates advised. Then, until the seventh day, bread soaked in water so that the heat of salt and leaven is removed, and bread cooked in other water, with a small portion of butter and sugar added for flavour. After the seventh day, almond bread or barley cooked in chicken broth.

units.la: {*} Hippoc. deinde ad septimum: note placed beside text as printed. Vini autem loco bibat decoctum hordei, vel aquam saccharatam. Vinum autem nunquam ante declinationem: quod si vires nimis collabuntur, paulo pleniore victu vtendum est: vt, pullorum, uel aliarum carnium contuso cum mica panis, vel expresso, vel consummato, quod vocant, idest, carnibus per se, aut cum pauca aqua in phiala vitrea coctis in vase alio aqua feruentem habente. Vinum autem ob consuetudinem, aut viriu imbecillitatem dare si cogaris, sit imbecillum, dulce, aut aqua saccharata dilutum: nisi in hepate, aut liene sit phlegmone, aut saltem obstructio, quae dulcia omnia excitant, & geminant.
units.tr: {*} Hippoc. deinde ad septimum. In place of wine, let him drink a decoction of barley or sugared water. Wine should never be given before the decline of the fever. But if the strength collapses too far, a somewhat fuller diet must be used: crumb of bread pounded with chicken or other meats, or pressed, or what they call "consummated", that is, meats cooked by themselves or with a little water in a glass flask set in another vessel of boiling water. If you are compelled to give wine because of habit or weakness of strength, let it be weak, sweet, or diluted with sugared water, unless there is inflammation, or at least obstruction, in the liver or spleen, since all sweet things stir up and redouble these.

units.la: Dormiat æger in partem affectam, vt maiore ipsius calore sic quæsito, phlegmones materia largior resoluatur, & indolentior sit decubitus. Aluus sit facilis: animi affectus tollantur, & cætera phlegmonem augere potentia.
units.tr: Let the patient lie on the affected side, so that by the greater heat thus sought, the larger matter of the inflammation may be dissolved, and the lying will be less painful. Let the bowels be kept easy. Let the emotions be calmed, and whatever else tends to increase the inflammation.

units.la: 2. AVERTENTIBVS materiam incrementum phlegmones facturam: vt, sectione venæ cubiti internæ lateris eiusdem: aut si non
units.tr: 2. Diverting the matter that would increase the inflammation

units.la: non apparet, cōmunis: sed presso tunc cephalicæ ramo, vt ex sola interna vacuetur: pro virium robore (quas alioqui morbus acutus, sæua symptomata, victus tenuis deiciunt) ætate, morbi magnitudine, ad caloris vsq; mutationem: vt lib. 2. victus rat. acutorum docent Hipp. Galen.
units.tr: By bleeding the vein of the inner elbow on the same side, or if that does not appear, the common vein; but then pressing the branch of the cephalic, so that the blood is drawn from the inner vein alone. The amount depends on the strength (which the acute disease, severe symptoms and thin diet otherwise wear down), on age and on the magnitude of the illness, and it is to be continued until the change of heat, as Hippocrates and Galen teach in book 2 of the Regimen of acute diseases.

units.la: Auertunt etiam cucurbitulæ inguinibus affixæ, & hypochondriis: frictiones, & ligaturæ, & fotus calidi artuum, & balani, clysteres, sed clementes: quòd pleuritidi fluor alui saepe superuenit, idemq; periculosus.
units.tr: Diversion is also achieved by cupping-glasses fixed to the groins and flanks; by friction and bandaging; by warm fomentations of the limbs and by warm baths; and by enemas, but gentle ones, because a flux of the bowels often supervenes on pleurisy and is dangerous.

units.la: 3. MATERIAM apparantibus crassam (tenuis enim biliosa præsertim à qua pleuritis frequentius fit: quia feré turget, mox est vacuanda) & thoraci familiaribus, & sputum facilè reddentibus, calidam quidem vt syrup. violato, zizyphorum cū duplo aquæ hordei, vel aquæ coctæ & saccharatæ: syrupi autem acetati quanquam eadem præstat, thoraci tamē nocent: syrup. intybi, rosarum, cydoniorum, hepatici magis sunt quàm thoracici. Lactuca autem et portulaca valenter refrigerando, sputum prohibent. Vtêris etiā decocto violarum, zizyphorum, myxorum, hordei, cum syrup. glycyrrhizæ, zizyphorū post tertium aut quartum diem.
units.tr: 3. For matter that is being prepared, thick (for thin matter, especially bilious, from which pleurisy arises more often, swells and must soon be evacuated), and for remedies that are suited to the chest and readily bring up sputum: warm ones such as syrup of violets, jujubes with twice the amount of barley water, or of boiled and sweetened water. Syrup of vinegar, although it does the same, nevertheless harms the chest. Syrups of endive, roses and quinces are more for the liver than for the chest. Lettuce and purslane, being strongly cooling, check the sputum. You may also use a decoction of violets, jujubes, mallows and barley, with syrup of liquorice and jujubes, after the third or fourth day.

units.la: 4. MATERIAM parti inflammatæ assi xam vacuantibus, vt dicta phlebotome ad coloris sanguinis mutationē, vt medicamento purgante, si materia ad ventrem repat: purgante autem non valenter, nec astringendo, sed tantùm leniendo. Vitanda igitur scam moniata, licet Gal. lib. 2. rat. victus acutorum, hieram quæ colocynthidem recipit, propinet, & Hipp. ibidem elleborum, & peplium valentia medicamenta, quòd illorum ætate clementia nondum erant inuenta, qualia sunt cassia, ad sescunciam cum decocto thoracico sumpta. Vitandæ etiam myrobalani citreæ, licet sint cholagogæ: quia immoderatius astringunt. Eadem ratione rhabarbarum hic damnat Arcul. rhabarbari tamen drachmæ duæ vel tres, cū pauca spica minutim concisa infusæ, aut potius nostro more sine spica, horis decem vel duodecim in aqua violarū, & Scan is cut off at the bottom of the text block. & scabiosæ, et valenter expressæ cum cassia re centis drach. quinq; vel sex : vel cum mannæ bonæ vnc. vna, tutò potantur diuitibus : vel mannæ vnc. duæ vel tres, dissoluantur decocto thoracico, additis quinq; vel sex drach. syrup. violati & glycyrrhizæ.
units.tr: 4. For matter attached to the inflamed part, in order to empty it: the aforesaid phlebotomy until the colour of the blood changes; a purgative medicine if the matter tends towards the bowels, but a purgative that is not strong, nor astringent, only gently laxative. Therefore scammony is to be avoided, although Galen in book 2 of the Regimen of acute diseases gives hiera which contains colocynth, and Hippocrates in the same place gives hellebore and peplium, strong medicines, since in their time gentler ones had not yet been discovered. Such remedies are cassia, taken to a sescuncia (an ounce and a half) with a thoracic decoction. Myrobalans of citrine are also to be avoided, although they are cholagogue, because they astringe too strongly. For the same reason Arculanus condemns rhubarb here. Nevertheless, two or three drachms of rhubarb, infused for ten or twelve hours in water of violets and scabious with a little spikenard finely cut, or better, in our custom, without spikenard, and strongly pressed, with five or six drachms of fresh cassia, or with an ounce of good manna, may be safely taken by the wealthy. Or two or three ounces of manna may be dissolved in a thoracic decoction, with five or six drachms of syrup of violets and liquorice added.

units.la: 5. SPVTVM materiæ pleuritidem committentis, & in pulmones exudantis, facile & fluidũ reddentibus aliis atq; aliis, per varia eius phlegmones tempora: vt, syrupo violato, & zizyphorum ad quartum circiter diem: deinde syrup. violati vnc. vni miscea-tur semuncia syrup. glycyrrhizæ : semper eo magis augendi quo propior est status, violato interim proportione diminuto, cum aquæ saccharatæ, aut decocti hordei vnc. tribus.
units.tr: 5. The sputum that causes the pleurisy and exudes into the lungs is made easy and fluid by various other remedies, varied according to the different stages of the inflammation: for example, syrup of violets and jujubes up to about the fourth day; then one ounce of syrup of violets is mixed with half an ounce of syrup of liquorice. This is always increased as the state approaches its height, while the syrup of violets is meanwhile reduced in proportion, with three ounces of sugared water or barley decoction.

units.la: Ore etiam retenta, sputũ promouet: saccha-rum album, saccharum candum, et violatũ, iulep violatum, pilulæ albæ, hypoglottides, diatragacanthum per se, aut iulepo violato exceptum: diabuglossatum quoque ad cordis robur. His ad diem quartum perfectis syrup. glycyrrhizæ per se, vel eclegma de pino. Si autem febris est vehemens, minus calidis vtendum est. Foris quoque ad quantum vsque diem illinitur ceratum ex cera & oleo violato, & amygdalarum dulcium, postea ex amygdalino solo, vel chamæmelino.
units.tr: Also, medicines held in the mouth promote sputum: white sugar, sugar candy and violet; violet julep, white pills, hypoglottides, diatragacanth by itself or taken with violet julep; and diabuglossate too, for the strength of the heart. When these have been carried through to the fourth day, syrup of liquorice alone, or an electuary of pine kernels. If the fever is severe, less warming remedies should be used. Externally also, up to the fifth day, a cerate of wax and violet oil and sweet almond oil is smeared on; afterwards, of sweet almond oil alone, or of chamomile.

units.la: 6. MATERIAM reliquam digerentibus: admotis linamentis, vnguentis, cataplasmatis, emplastris: fotu item per spongiam ex decocto chamæmeli, meliloti, furfuris: vel per vesicam eodem decocto plenam, aut frixo cum pauco vino, milio, & furfure. Qui fotus initio adhibiti, si materia est tantum flatulenta, flatibus resolutis dolorem sedant. Si autem est vera pleuritis, materia largiore tracta, eam augent: ob id initio, vel non tentandus, vel minimum diu hic fotus, & primum colli, ali, aliquanto post partis dolentis.
units.tr: 6. For digesting the remaining matter: apply linen rags, unguents, poultices and plasters; likewise fomentation with a sponge soaked in a decoction of chamomile, melilot and bran, or through a bladder full of the same decoction, or fried with a little wine, millet and bran. These fomentations, if applied at the start when the matter is only flatulent, relieve the pain by dissolving the wind. But if it is true pleurisy, with a larger quantity of matter drawn to the part, they increase it. Therefore at first either this fomentation should not be tried at all, or only for the shortest time, first on the neck, then on the armpit, and somewhat later on the painful part.

units.la: Olea fuerint idonea, amygdal. dulcium, & chamæmelinū, & cataplasma ex farina aut muccagine, se. lini, fœnigraeci, maluæ, althææ, & radicum, floribus chamæmeli, meliloti.
units.tr: Oils should be suitable: sweet almond oil and chamomile oil, and a poultice of flour or mucilage of linseed, fenugreek, mallow, marshmallow and roots, with chamomile and melilot flowers.

units.la: Si autem pleuritis suppuretur, eadem olea cum butyro recenti, & adipe gallinaceo co-ctionem
units.tr: But if the pleurisy suppurates, the same oils, with fresh butter and hen's fat, promote the concoction

units.la: Hippo. & Gal. lib. 2 rat. uictus acutorum. ctionem promouent. Tussis frequens abscessum rumpet, & vociferatio, & vomitus, et sternutamentum, & vehemens corporis concussio, & tulacha herba. Aqua deinde saccharata, vel hordei decoctum ulcus tergêt: si febris autem est remissior, etiam hydromeli, vel aqua ex melle destillata, & decoctum cicerum rubrorum.
units.tr: Hippocrates and Galen, book 2 of the Regimen of acute diseases. promote the concoction. A frequent cough will break the abscess, and shouting, vomiting, sneezing, and a violent shaking of the body, and the herb tulacha. Then sugared water or a decoction of barley cleanses the ulcer; if the fever is milder, also hydromel, or water distilled from honey, and a decoction of red chickpeas.

units.la: Vlcus denique glutinabunt, bolus armenia, terra lemnia, adscript, vnum, & caetera in phthisi dicenda.
units.tr: Finally they will close the ulcer with Armenian bole, Lemnian earth, as prescribed, and the other remedies to be described under phthisis.

units.la: Si autem pleuritis notha est, cucurbitulis, & phœnigmon excitantibus, foras magis trahatur, coquatur, rumpatur, tergeatur, glutinetur.
units.tr: If, however, the pleurisy is spurious, it should be drawn further outwards with cupping-glasses and remedies that excite phoenigmon, then concocted, broken open, cleansed and closed up.

units.la: PERIPNEVMONIAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF PERIPNEUMONIA.

units.la: PERIPNEVMONIA, remedijs prope ijsdem, quibus pleuritis curatur: quae autem vtrique curandae sunt propria, abunde docet Auicennas.
units.tr: Peripneumonia is cured with almost the same remedies as pleurisy. Avicenna teaches fully what is proper to each to be cured.

units.la: SPVTI SANGVINIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF SPITTING OF BLOOD.

units.la: VICTVS ratione refrigerante, siccan te, astringente: vt, aere, inspersis humi herbis, aqua rosarum, aceto, rosis, santalis, caphura, ijsdemque odoratis.
units.tr: Diet should be cooling, drying and astringent: the patient should be in air with herbs strewn on the ground, and use rose water, vinegar, roses, sandalwood, camphor, and the same scented things.

units.la: Vt cibo tenui, potius quàm multo, ad biduū aut triduum: sed praeterea emplastico & glutinoso: vt, cremore ptissanæ, lactè cocto cum amylo, aut farina hordei: inspersis vtriq; malorum punicorū granis, panibus azymis, piscibus glutinosis: vt, anguilla, cyprino, tinca, extremitatibusque animalium, & partibus aliis neruosis, cartilaginosis, pinguibus, caseo recenti non salso (nam vetus calet) quæ sanguinem crassant, & ora vasorum illitu suo obturent.
units.tr: The food should be light rather than plentiful, for two or three days, and besides this also soothing and glutinous: such as barley gruel, milk boiled with starch or barley flour, sprinkled with pomegranate seeds, unleavened breads, and glutinous fish such as eel, carp and tench. Also the extremities of animals and other sinewy, cartilaginous and fatty parts, and fresh cheese that is not salted (for old cheese is hot). These thicken the blood and, by coating them, close the mouths of the vessels.

units.la: Lentes quoq;, lac acidū, milium, panicum, oryza, quatenus siccant & astringunt huic affectui sunt salubria, & quæ etiam refrigerant: vt, lactuca, plantago, cucurbita, portulaca, etiam trita, & ore retenta. Aqua ferrata, aut chalybata per se, aut cum iulep.rosato: fato: aut (si vires sunt imbecillæ, & vini sem per consueti cupiditas) vino austero, crasso: alioqui abstinendum vino est. Ex eadem aqua omnia eius alimenta coquenda. Vt, quiete corporis & animi, & silentio, & somno fluxus omnes cohibente.
units.tr: Lentils too, sour milk, millet, panic grass and rice are wholesome for this condition, inasmuch as they dry and astringe, as are those which also cool: such as lettuce, plantain, gourd and purslane, also crushed and held in the mouth. Iron or steel water, either alone or with rose julep, or (if the strength is weak and there is a habit of always taking wine) thick, astringent wine. Otherwise wine must be avoided. All his food should be cooked in that same water. He should also keep quiet in body and mind, observe silence, and sleep, which checks every flux.

units.la: 2. AVERTENTIBVS sanguinem à vena aperta, vel rupta, vt secta cubiti vena interna missio sanguine frequente, vt tertia quaque hora, vel quoties necesse est: sed pau co, si iam multus est reiectus: si vero paucus, et æger plethoricus est: etiā paulò largiore, ex vena poplitis, aut malleoli: vt mesibus in mulie re provocatis: vt, cucurbitulis coxæ, et natibus, & inguinibus affixis: vt, partium infernarum, & manuum frictionibus, ligaturis dolorificis, fotibus ex aqua calida: nam calor & dolor attrahunt.
units.tr: 2. TURNING the blood away from a vein that is opened or ruptured: such as bleeding frequently from the inner vein of the elbow, every third hour or as often as necessary, but little if much has already been discharged. If little has been discharged and the patient is plethoric, somewhat more may be taken, from the vein of the popliteal region or of the ankle, as when menses are provoked in women. Cupping glasses are applied to the hip, buttocks and groins; the lower parts and hands are rubbed; painful ligatures are used; and fomentations of warm water. For heat and pain attract.

units.la: 3. SANGVINEM æquantibus, & ad humorum 4. ipsum constituentiu proportionem iustam reducentibus. Vt victu tenuiore & parum nutriente, si sanguis ipse est largior, si biliosus est & acer, ac mordax, syrupo vtendum rosato, ex oxalidis succo, ex omphacio, ex succo granatorum, cydoniorum, myrteo, cum duplo aquarum oxalidis, plantaginis, rosarum, portulacæ, solani: quæ omnia bilis vim obtundant, & simul astringendo fluorem sanguinis cohibeant. Deinde bilis vacuanda non scammoniatis, sed astringendo cholagogis, vt myrobalanorum citrearum drachma una, & dimidia, cum semuncia syrupi violati, vel rosati, vel eorundem uncia dimidia, aquis prædictis infundenda, & cum cassiæ uncia una, vel semuncia, vel rhabarbari drachma una & dimidia, cum Mesue.
units.tr: 3. EQUALISING the blood and restoring the just proportion of the humours that constitute it. For example, by a thinner diet with little nourishment, if the blood itself is too abundant, or if it is bilious, sharp and biting. A rose syrup should be used, made with sorrel juice, unripe grape juice, pomegranate and quince juice, and myrtle, with twice the amount of waters of sorrel, plantain, roses, purslane and nightshade. All these blunt the force of the bile and at the same time, by astringing, restrain the flow of blood. Then the bile should be purged not with scammony but with astringent cholagogues: for example, one and a half drachms of citrine myrobalans, with half an ounce of violet or rose syrup, or half an ounce of the same, infused in the aforesaid waters, and with one ounce or half an ounce of cassia, or one and a half drachms of rhubarb, with Mesue.

units.la: Si pituita aquosa, mistis melle rosato, & syrupo rosato cum aqua betonicæ, & absinthij etiam astringente, parata vacuctur myrobalanis cepulis, vel rhabarbaro, vel turbith sive zingibere: cum hoc enim pituitam crassam vacuat, sine eodem aquosam & tenuem.
units.tr: If the phlegm is watery, it should be prepared with rose honey mixed with rose syrup and water of betony, and also with astringent wormwood, and purged with myrobalans, onions, rhubarb, turbith or ginger. For with this it purges thick phlegm; without it, watery and thin phlegm.

units.la: 4. GLVTINANTIBVS vlcus, aut oris hiatum contrahentibus, & ob id sanguinem sistentibus, statim cum ægrum accedis, adhibendis, ne sanguis immodicè fluat:
units.tr: 4. AGGLUTINANTS, which close an ulcer or the gaping of a mouth (of a vessel) and therefore stop the blood, should be applied at once, as soon as you approach the patient, so that the blood does not flow excessively:

units.la: Vt, portulaca mansa, & ore retenta: Hæma tita lapidis aureo vno sumpto: corallo albo, vsto potius quàm rubro: cornu cerui vsto, à drachma vna ad sesquidrach. bolo armenia, terra lemnia sigillata, ad drach. vnam hora somni: balaustijs, malicorio, seminibus myrtorum. Nam vlcus glutinant, fluxum astrin gunt, catarrhum tenuem crassant & obtun dunt. Tragacanthum autem, gummi arabi cum, mastiche suo lentore glutinant, & va sis hiatum opplent. Composita idem præstan tia sunt, trochisci ex terra sigillata, troch. ex electro, ex spodio ad drach. vnā cum syrup. vel aquis astringentibus.
units.tr: For example: chewed purslane, held in the mouth; haematite stone, one gold-weight taken; white coral, calcined rather than red; calcined deer's horn, from one drachm to a drachm and a half; Armenian bole; Lemnian earth, sealed, one drachm at bedtime; balaustines, pomegranate rind, myrtle seeds. For these glue ulcers, astringe the flux, and thicken and blunt thin catarrh. Tragacanth, however, and gum arabic, with mastic, glue by their viscosity and fill the gaping of the vessels. Compound preparations have the same effect: troches of sealed earth, troches of electrum, troches of spodium, one drachm with syrup or astringent waters.

units.la: Antidotus Philonis, vel hac mitior atha nasia Nicolai, primis quatuor diebus etiā ef ficaciter sumuntur contra catarrhum tenu em: & vt frigore suo, partes sanguine fluen tes contrahat. In idem sanguis hirci non con cretus proprietate sua valet Auicen. & cen taurium eidem, et Conciliatori, & Disco- rid. à drach. vna, ad drachmas duas.
units.tr: Philo's antidote, or the milder one of Nicolaus, taken effectively for the first four days against thin catarrh, and so that by its coldness it contracts the parts that are bleeding. For the same purpose, goat's blood not coagulated is effective by its property, according to Avicenna. Centaury likewise, according to the Conciliator and Dioscorides, from one drachm to two drachms.

units.la: Syrupi quoque, rosatus, cydoniorum, myr tinus, granatorum, ribes per se, vel cum aquis rosarum, portulacæ, & similibus: vel etiam cum drachma una, nunc cornu cervi, nunc lapidis hæmatitæ, nunc trochiscorum prædicto rum, ne uni assuescat natura.
units.tr: Syrups too: rose, quince, myrtle, pomegranate and currant, alone or with waters of roses, purslane and the like; or also with one drachm of something, now deer's horn, now haematite stone, now the aforesaid troches, lest nature grow accustomed to one.

units.la: Hæc vero etiam suppresso fluxu continuan da, ne repetat: Eclegma quoque ex sacchari rosati, tragacanthi ana unc. una, boli armeniæ, cornu cervi, balaustij, gummi arabici, ana drachma una: excipe syrup. violato: glutinat. Illinatur foris thorax, oleo chamæmeli, vel amygdalarum dulcium, potius quam rosato, myrtino, cum aqua scabiosæ, potius quam solani, vel portulacis, ne hæc astringendo sanguinem intro compellant, & sputum sanguinis redintegrent.
units.tr: These things must be continued even after the flux has been suppressed, lest it return. Also an electuary of rose sugar and tragacanth, one ounce of each, with Armenian bole, deer's horn, balaustines and gum arabic, one drachm of each; mix it with violet syrup, and it glues. Let the chest be smeared outside with oil of chamomile or of sweet almonds rather than rose or myrtle oil, and with water of scabious rather than of nightshade or purslane, lest these, by astringing, drive the blood inward and renew the spitting of blood.

units.la: 5. SYMPTOMATA, præcipue sanguinis in pulmone et arteriis asperis concretionē corrigentibus: ut, oxycrato, oxymelite simplici, cōposito, scillitico ad uncias duas, cum aqua oxalidis, si tussis abest: si vero adsit, aceto cum prouocante abstinendum est.
units.tr: 5. Remedies for the symptoms, chiefly those that correct the thickening of blood in the lungs and the rough arteries: for example, oxycrate, simple or compound oxymel with squill, two ounces, with water of sorrel, if there is no cough. If cough is present, vinegar with an expectorant should be avoided.

units.la: Theriaces quoq; drachma una & dimidia cum aqua hyssopi, et scabiosæ, vel diacurcu-mæ drach. duæ, vel coaguli leporis script. vnū per se, vel drach. dimidia cum aqua hyssopi et scabiosæ. Si tussis quoque molesta adsit, curetur vt dictum in catarrho & tussi.
units.tr: Theriac too, one and a half drachms with water of hyssop and scabious, or two drachms of diacurcuma, or one scruple of hare's rennet alone, or half a drachm with water of hyssop and scabious. If troublesome cough is also present, it is to be treated as said under catarrh and cough.

units.la: PHTHISEOS CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF PHTHISIS.

units.la: Phthisis, id est, ulcerosa pulmonum dispositio curatur (si curabilis est) quinque remediorum generibus.
units.tr: Phthisis, that is, an ulcerous condition of the lungs, is cured (if it is curable) by five kinds of remedy.

units.la: VICTVS ratione, si febrem & emaciationem spectes, refrigerante, humectante: si vlcus causam mali, calida sicca. Sit igitur calido, frigido temperata, sed siccior vlceris gratia, nisi indicatio a febre præpolleat, & minus siccantia exhiberi cogat: tamen a causa præsente, vlcere scilicet sumpta indicatio magnarum est virium, ob id Gal. phthisicos mittebat Thabias vbi aër erat siccior, & sanabatur. Cibi autem sint coctu faciles, quòd calor nativus phthisico est imbecillus: sint item boni, & multi alimenti, vt corpus emaciatum instaurent: sed liquidi & tenues: vt vias phthisicorum ob siccitatem contractas facilius subeant, et penetret: ob febrim quoque refrigerent nonnihil, & ob vlceris saniem, detergant, & ob solutionem continui, glutinent. Quas dotes omnes habet lac: facile enim coquitur, ac omnium quae alimenti gratia sumimus, lac, butyro et caseo multum nutrit: optimum optimi est succi: sero casei & butyri liquidum est, subfrigidum est: vt, cap. 20. lib. 5. simpl. terget saporedulci butyrosae substantiae, & acrimonia seri: glutinat caseo, & eodem, ac butyro est em plasticum. Lac autem asininum & caprinum frigidum magis & tergens: quia serosius, omnium, vaccinum plenius nutrit, & valen tius glutinat, quia butyrosius & caseosius: muliebre autem ad omnia simul est praestan tissimum. In singulis autem praedictis lactis differentijs, potes singulas eius facultates augere, aut minuere idonea victus ratione ipsius animalis: vt, lactuca, portulaca, cichorio nutritum, refrigerans magis lac habet: foeniculo, hyssopo, adianto, hordeo, terget magis: rubi, lentisci, salicis, vitis folijs: glutinat potentius, & c. à Gal. scripta, lib. 7. metho-de lacte asinino, & lib. 3. alimen. & 1. sanita-tis tuenda. Sumatur autem mane ieiunis, ho-ris tribus, aut quatuor ante cibum, vnc. qua-tuor primum: quas si recte confecerit, postri-die quinque, sex vncias, & sic diebus conse-quentibus auctum, si bene concoquat, vsque ad lib. vnam. Sumat autem ex mamilla, aut minimum diu extra propria cōceptacula mo-ratum (illic enim vt sanguis & semen prom-ptissimè corrumpitur) per se, aut cum pauco melle, vel saccharo, & sale, ne in ventricu-lo acescat. à lacte hausto, ne dormiat, ne cor-rumpat, nec corpus exerceat motu aut fricti-one, ne crudum lac in corpus trahat.
units.tr: DIET, chosen by reason. If you look to the fever and the emaciation, it should be cooling and moistening; if you look to the ulcer as the cause of the evil, it should be warming and drying. So it should be tempered between warm and cold, but drier for the sake of the ulcer, unless the indication from the fever predominates and forces the use of less drying things. Yet the indication drawn from the present cause, namely the ulcer, is one of great strength, and for this reason Galen used to send phthisics to Thabias, where the air was drier, and they were cured. Food should be easy to digest, because the native heat of a phthisic is weak. It should also be good and rich in nourishment, to restore the emaciated body, but liquid and thin, so that it may more easily reach and penetrate the passages contracted by dryness. Because of the fever it should also cool somewhat, because of the pus of the ulcer it should cleanse, and because of the broken continuity it should bind. Milk has all these qualities. It is easily cooked, and of all the things we take for nourishment, milk, together with butter and cheese, nourishes greatly; it is the best of the best juices. The whey of cheese and butter is liquid and somewhat cooling; as Galen says in book 5 of the Simples, ch. 20, it cleanses by the sweet taste of the buttery substance and the sharpness of the whey. It binds through the cheese, and in the same way the butter is agglutinating. Ass's milk and goat's milk are cooler and more cleansing, because they are more watery; cow's milk nourishes more fully and binds more strongly, because it is richer in butter and cheese; but women's milk is by far the most excellent in all respects. Within each of the kinds of milk just named, you can increase or reduce its particular powers by a suitable diet for the animal itself: milk from animals fed on lettuce, purslane or chicory is more cooling; that from animals fed on fennel, hyssop, maidenhair or barley is more cleansing; that from animals fed on leaves of bramble, mastic, willow or vine binds more powerfully, and so on, as Galen wrote in book 7 of the Method, on ass's milk, and in books 3 of the Foods and 1 of the Preservation of Health. It should be taken in the morning, fasting, three or four hours before food, four ounces at first; if the patient digests this well, five or six ounces the next day, and so on in the following days, increasing to a pound if it is well digested. It should be taken straight from the teat, or at least from milk that has not stood long outside its proper vessels (for blood and semen are most quickly corrupted there), either plain or with a little honey, sugar and salt, so that it does not turn sour in the stomach. After drinking the milk, the patient should not sleep, nor should he corrupt it, nor exert the body by motion or rubbing, lest he draw raw milk into the body.

units.la: Salubria etiam sunt iura multum succulen-ta, ex carnibus caporum, phasianorum, per-dicum, cum amygdalis, glycyrrhiza, semini-bus frigidis, bolo armenia, saccharo rosato. Ex hisque & similibus, velut bucella, aut marcipanes, & similia, parua mole multum nutrientia. Cicera etiā ex iure prædicto mul-tum cocta, sunt multi nutrimenti, & ob lentore diuturni, cancri fluuiatiles, limaces, testudines, et ex limacibus aqua capitello destillata. Potus sit praeditus ijsdem facultatib. quibus est cibus: vt, vinum album tenue, non vaporosum: quidam potus solius lactis sunt persanati, vt testatur Rasis lib. 4. continentis, quod erit praestantius, si chalybs, aut ferrum candens in eo fuerit extinctum. Cetera sumenda, admonenda, facienda, educenda, eodem spectant, quo aer, cibus, potus.
units.tr: Broths rich in juice are also wholesome, made from the flesh of capons, pheasants and partridges, with almonds, liquorice, cooling seeds, Armenian bole and rose sugar. Also from these and similar things, such as little cakes or marzipan, which in small bulk give much nourishment. Chickpeas cooked much in the aforesaid broth are very nourishing and, because of their viscosity, lasting; also river crayfish, snails, tortoises, and water distilled from snails in a still. The drink should have the same qualities as the food: for example, thin white wine, not heady. Some phthisics have been completely cured on nothing but milk, as Rhazes testifies in book 4 of the Continens; this will be even better if a steel or red-hot iron has been quenched in it. Everything else to be taken, advised, done, or evacuated, bears on the same aim as air, food and drink.

units.la: 2. CAVSAM phthisis abigentibus, quae sit catarrhus, curetur, vt diximus, si vas ruptum curetur, vt in sputo sanguinis habes, si humor in pulmonibus erodens, apparetur & vacuetur.
units.tr: 2. To drive out the CAUSE of phthisis, which is catarrh, it should be treated, as we said: if the vessel is ruptured, it should be treated as you have it in spitting of blood; if a humour is eroding the lungs, it should be attenuated and evacuated.

units.la: 3. VLCVS pulmonis tergentibus dulcib. & amaris: vt, syrupo glycyrrhizae, hyssopi, praesij, melle rosato cum aqua scabiosae dupla, vel adianti, foeniculi, hyssopi, vel decocto pectorali: si vero febris vrget, cum decocto violarum glycyrrhizae, se. frigidorum communium, myxorum, detur syrup. violatus, rosatus, mel rosatum, aqua saccharata, vel parum mellita, decoctum cicerum rubrorum lac cum saccharo violato.
units.tr: 3. ULCER of the lung should be treated with sweet and bitter things, for example syrup of liquorice, hyssop, or horehound, rose honey with double the amount of scabious water, or with maidenhair, fennel and hyssop, or a pectoral decoction. If fever presses, give violet syrup, rose syrup, rose honey, sugared or lightly honeyed water, a decoction of red chickpeas, or milk with violet sugar, together with a decoction of violets and liquorice, that is, of the common cold remedies and mucilages.

units.la: 4. VLCVS carne implentibus, & gluti nantibus, quae duo naturae sunt opera, si ipsi- us impedimenta tergendo sordem, & siccan do saniem sustuleris: maxime vsu crebro sac chari rosati, sed pauci: hoc enim terget sac- charo, & rosarum amara substantia, sac- charo nutrit, rosis refrigerat, & glutinat. Cum igitur id vnu omnia complectatur, qui bus eget hic affectus, non abs re Rasis: et A- uicennas plurimos phthisicos sacchari rosati vsu persanatos affirmant: id quod si recès est, acrimoniae particeps est, eaq; potentius ter- get. Si verò glutinatione magis opus est, quia sputum adhuc cruentum est, non purulentum, vetus dabitur cum bolo armenia, vel sangui ne draconis: quorum astrictione, si materia pul moni affigitur, sumatur syrup. glycyrrhizae, vel hyssopi cum decocto pectorali, aqua sca- biosae, & similibus.
units.tr: 4. ULCER that fills with flesh and binds together, which are two works of nature, will be achieved if you remove its obstacles by wiping away the foulness and drying up the pus, above all by frequent use of rose sugar, but in small amounts. For this cleanses by its sugar and the bitter substance of the roses, nourishes by its sugar, cools by the roses, and binds. Since this one remedy embraces all the things this condition needs, Rhazes was not wrong, and Avicenna and many others affirm that many phthisics were completely cured by use of rose sugar. If this is taken in the proper way, it shares in sharpness and cleanses more powerfully. But if more binding is needed, because the sputum is still bloody and not purulent, the old remedy is given with Armenian bole or dragon's blood. If, by their astringency, matter clings to the lung, take syrup of liquorice or hyssop with pectoral decoction, scabious water and similar things.

units.la: Sunt praeterea quae phthisi prosunt totius sub stantiae proprietate: vt, pulmo vulpis, et ericij siccatus & pulueratus, & ex pulmone vul-pis, eclegma Auic. liquidum. Quibus etiam catarrhosis animalibus, & inde phthisi mul-tum obnoxijs, herba quedam est cognita, ho-minibus ignorata: cuius vsu vicus in pulmo-ne ouis glutinatum inuenit Auenzoar: sunt enim, vt idem ex Hermete scribit, plantis et metallicis corporibus facultates, quas si ho-mo cognitas haberet, ea faceret, quæ magico-rum putantur.
units.tr: Moreover there are things which help phthisis by the property of their whole substance: for example, the lung of a fox, and of a hedgehog dried and powdered, and the liquid electuary of fox lung given by Avicenna. There is also a certain herb known to catarrhal animals, which are therefore much liable to phthisis, but unknown to men, by the use of which Avenzoar found an ulcer in the lung of a sheep healed. For, as the same writer says from Hermes, plants and metallic bodies have powers which, if men knew them, they would make what are thought to be the works of magicians.

units.la: 5. SYMPTOMATA corrigetibus: vt alui fluorem, ob coctricis & retentricis ven-triculi, & aliarum partium facultatis imbe-cillitatem: vt, puluere à Rasi descripto, et dia-rhodo Abbatis, ventriculum, hepar, & ali-as partes male nutritas roborante. Emaciati-onem vero etiam phthisews symptoma corri-guntaqua carnium, iura prædicta. Si vero phthisis omnino est insanabilis, vel non tra-ctanda, vel blande, & callus per siccantia excitandus est, quod mulieri furnariæ phthi-sicæ dicit accidisse Matthæus Gradi: inspira-to enim sæpe furni aëre sicco, vlcus occaluit, vixitque vixitque postea annos viginti octo.
units.tr: 5. SYMPTOMS are corrected: for example, the flux of the bowels, by means of the weakness of the faculty of the stomach and of the other parts that retain and hold; for example, by the powder described by Rhazes and by the Abbot's diarrhodon, which strengthens the stomach, liver and other poorly nourished parts. Emaciation, which is also a symptom of phthisis, is corrected by broths of meats, the aforesaid soups. But if phthisis is wholly incurable, or not to be treated, it should be treated gently, and the callus should be roused by drying things; this, Matthaeus Gradus reports, happened to a baker's wife who had phthisis: for, breathing often the dry air of the oven, her ulcer hardened over, and she lived twenty-eight years afterwards.

units.la: PALPITATIONIS CORDIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF PALPITATION OF THE HEART.

units.la: Cordis palpitatio, seu tremor quinque praesidiorum generibus ex Avicenna & Rasi curantur.
units.tr: Palpitation of the heart, or trembling, is cured by five kinds of remedies, according to Avicenna and Rhazes.

units.la: VICTVS ratione, si à causa est calida refrigerante (vt aëre alterato frigidis odoribus, oxycrato, rosis, aqua rosarum, caphura: addito vino odorifero pauco, aut moscho, aut ambra aut alio calente, vt frigida ad cor promptius penetrent) à causa vero frigida, calfaciente: vt, aëre alterato, roremarino, maiorana, origano, ambra, moscho, & similiter calidis odoramentis. Aëris enim ratio praecipua est habenda, vt qui inspiratus ad cor mox penetret, citoque iuuet, vel noceat.
units.tr: Regimen: if the cause is hot, it should be cooled. Use altered air with cold odours, oxycrate, roses, rose water, camphor, with a little fragrant wine added, or musk, or amber, or some other warm substance, so that the cold things may penetrate the heart more readily. If the cause is cold, it should be warmed: use altered air, with rosemary, marjoram, oregano, amber, musk, and similar warm perfumes. For the air we must chiefly consider, since what is breathed in reaches the heart at once and either helps or harms it quickly.

units.la: Cibi quoque in calida refrigerentur, oxalide, aceto, omphacio, succo aranciorum, citrorum, limonum Avicennae laudatorum in febribus acutis. Vitetur vinum praesertim generosum, & vaporosum: si imbecillo est ob consuetudinem vtendum, diluatur aqua, decocto hordei, vel alio refrigerante, aut bibat decoctu coriandri praeparati, cum iulep. violato, aut rosato. Similiter caeteris sumendis, admouendis, educendis, faciendis prius saepe dictis, contra causam pugnandum est.
units.tr: Foods too should be cooled if the cause is hot: sorrel, vinegar, verjuice, juice of oranges, citrons and lemons, which Avicenna praised in acute fevers. Wine should be avoided, especially strong and vaporous wine. If it must be used because of habit in a weak patient, let it be diluted with water or with (the end of the italic) decoction of barley or another cooling drink, or let him drink a prepared decoction of coriander with violet or rose syrup. In the same way, with the other things to be taken, applied, evacuated and done, which have been said often before, we must fight against the cause.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM apparantibus, & tenuantibus crassam: calidam quidem, frigidis: frigidam vero calidis: sed ambobus moderatis ne corpus princeps, & vitae fons, ab immoderate tam calidis quam frigidis in contrariam intemperiem praecipitetur. Sed in calida, frigidis aromata quaedam calida (ut dixi) miscenda: quae frigidorum aditum sibi densando praecludentium vim ad cor ipsum deducant, nisi magnum sit cordis incendium, ut in causo. Tunc enim solis frigidis pugnandum, quales trochisci de caphura Rasis in tremore cordis: alioqui crocus, et pauca quaedam aromata cum Auic. & Mesue illis sunt miscenda.
units.tr: 2. For those who prepare the matter and thin the thick humour: if it is hot, use cold remedies; if it is cold, hot ones. But both should be moderated, so that the body, the chief and fount of life, is not thrown by excessive heat or excessive cold into the opposite disorder. In hot cases, certain warm aromatics (as I said) should be mixed with the cold remedies, which by thickening the passage of the cold substances that block it, carry their power to the heart itself, unless the burning of the heart is great, as in a cause of this kind. For then we must fight with cold remedies alone, such as the troches of camphor of Rhazes for trembling of the heart; otherwise saffron and a few aromatics are to be mixed with them, according to Avicenna and Mesue.

units.la: Materia igitur crassam, calidam tenuando apparant: syrup. violatus, intybi, ex succo oxalidis, ribes, acetosus: & si valentius refrigerandum, syrup. maxime cardiaci, ex succo to acido limonum, aut potus citrorum, cum aqua rosarum, portulacæ, lactucæ, intybi, solani, plantaginis: quibus se multos curasse affirmat Matthæus Gradi. Frigidam verò & pituitosam incidunt, tenuant, tergent, mel rosatum, oxymeli simplex, compositum, squillitícum: & si valentioribus est opus, syrup. de duabus vel quinque radicibus cum aqua betonicæ, scabiosæ, melissophylli, quæ sanguinem cordis, humore melancholico expurgat. Eodem pertinet syrup. pectorales, glycyrrhizæ, hyssopi, prassij: syrupus quoq; de thymo, epithymo, de pomis à Mesue scriptus in melancholia: syrup. fumariæ cum aquis buglossi utriusq; fumariæ, scolopendrij, quod ut prædicta efficax est ad purgandos humores melancholicos & adustos.
units.tr: Therefore, to thin and prepare the thick matter when it is hot: violet syrup, endive syrup, sorrel juice syrup, currant syrup, and vinegar syrup; and if a stronger cooling is needed, the syrup most suitable for the heart, made from juice of lemon's sour juice, or a drink of citrons with rose water, purslane, lettuce, endive, nightshade, and plantain, with which Matthaeus Gradi affirms he cured many. But for cold and phlegmatic matter, use things that cut, thin and cleanse: rose honey, simple and compound oxymel, and squill oxymel; and if stronger remedies are needed, syrup of the two or five roots with water of betony, scabious and balm, which cleanses the blood of the heart of melancholic humour. To this belong the chest syrups of liquorice, hyssop and horehound; also the syrup of thyme, epithymum and the fruit syrup written by Mesue for melancholy; the syrup of fumitory with waters of bugloss and both fumitories and of scolopendrium, which is as effective as the aforesaid for cleansing melancholic and burnt humours.

units.la: 3. VACVANTIBVS materiam, calidam quidem, rhabarbaro à drachma vna ad sesquidrach. puluerato: infuso autem à drach. duabus ad drachmas tres, in aqua intybi: bilem quoq; vacuant myrobalani citreæ: addi-tis vbique etiam cordialibus, ne cordi noxa inferatur: ob quam scammoniata sunt vitan da. Frigidam vero materiam, praesertim pituitosam vacuabis diaphoenico electario indo, myrobalanis cepulis, agarico etiam cordiali Auic. Si autem materia melancholica sumus vacuaturi, confectio Hamech, Mesuae pilulae ex lapide cyaneo, pilulae Indae dentur. Vena quoque basilica secetur, dextra qui dem si palpitatio a sanguine est: sinistra vero si a vapore spirituoso largiore in ventriculo cordis sinistro: si autem palpitatio urget multum, vacuamus nondum apparatam materiam.
units.tr: 3. To evacuate the matter when it is hot, use rhubarb from one drachm up to a drachm and a half in powder, or in infusion from two drachms to three drachms, in endive water. Bile is also evacuated by citrine myrobalans. Cordial remedies should be added everywhere, so that no harm is done to the heart; for this reason scammony is to be avoided. To evacuate cold matter, especially phlegm, you will use the electuary of diaphoenix, Indian myrobalans, squill, and also cordial agaric of Avicenna. If we are going to evacuate melancholic matter, let the confection of Hamech, Mesue's pills of lapis lazuli, and the Indian pills be given. The basilic vein should also be opened: the right if the palpitation comes from blood, the left if it comes from a greater spirituous vapour in the left ventricle of the heart. If the palpitation presses hard, we evacuate matter not yet prepared.

units.la: 4. MATERIAM a corde ad partes ignobiles auertentibus, praesertim dum symptomata ipsius urgent: ut, secta vena malleoli, frictionibus, & ligaturis dolorificis partium extremarum, clysteribus, cucurbitulis.
units.tr: 4. To turn the matter away from the heart toward the ignoble parts, especially while its symptoms press: as by opening the vein of the ankle, by frictions and painful ligatures of the extremities, by enemas and by cupping-glasses.

units.la: 5. COR ipsum roborantibus, & intemperiem ipsius corrigentibus, etiam per dicta omnia auxilia miscendis: calidam quidem frigidis: frigidam vero calidis, & ijs vel sumptis, vel admotis: sumantur vero simplicia in frigida: vt, buglossus, zedaria, doronicum, melissophyllon, citri cortices & semen, moschus, ambra, caryophylla: Composita, diabuglossatum, diaborraginatu, scrup. de gemmis, diambra, diamoschon dulce & amarū Mesuæ, scrup. Conciliatoris differentia 196. confectio de hyacintho Auic. regibus et principibus dicata.
units.tr: 5. To strengthen the heart itself and correct its disorder, these remedies are to be mixed with all the aforesaid aids: warm ones with cold, and cold ones with warm, and these are either taken or applied. Simple remedies to be taken when it is cold: bugloss, zedoary, doronicum, balm, citron peel and seed, musk, amber, cloves.
