Compounds: diabuglossum, diaborago, powder of gems, diambra, sweet and bitter diamoschon of Mesue, the scruple of the Conciliator's differentia 196, the confection of hyacinth of Avicenna, dedicated to kings and princes.

units.la: Admoneantur autem medio thoraci epithemata ex lib. vna aquarum melissophylli, buglos. vtriusque, & rosati aromatici vnc. vna, cum cinamomo, caryophyl. nuce moscha ta, et aliys simul calefactis cum panno lineo. Ex ijsdem pulueratis moscho, ambra, ligno aloës, been vtroq, corrallio omni, fragmentis cordialibus, floribus buglosi, melissophylli, sacculi ex panno conchiliato consuti et calfacti, medio quoque thoraci applicentur. Ex ijsdem pulueribus cum ladano, & cera, pomum odoretur continenter. In calida verò causa sumantur diarhodon abbatis Nicolai, & commune Mesuæ, scrup. trium santalorū, saccharum rosatum, & violatum, trochisci caphura Mesua: aut si magna est caliditas Rasis sine croco. Simplicia item, spodium, caphura, rosa, viola, acetum, corallia, santala, margarita, mire cardiaca omnia. Admoue- antur autem epithemata ex prædictis, cum aquis rosarum, violarum plantaginis, oxali dis:pomum quoq; aut sacculi ex ysdē. Si autē tremulus iste motus cordis a veneno est, aut vermibus postea tractabitur.
units.tr: Let there be applied to the middle of the chest plasters made from one ounce of the water of balm, of both bugloss, and of aromatic rose, with cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg and others, warmed together and applied with linen cloth. From the same powders, musk, amber, aloes wood, both behen, all coral, cordial fragments, flowers of bugloss and balm, and a little sack sewn of purple cloth and warmed, let them also be applied to the middle of the chest. From the same powders with ladanum and wax, let an apple be continually scented. In hot cases let there be taken the diarrhodon of Abbas, the Nicholas's, and the common one of Mesue, three scruples of sandalwood, rose and violet sugar, and the troches of camphor of Mesue; or, if the heat is great, Rhazes' without saffron. Simple remedies likewise: spodium, camphor, rose, violet, vinegar, coral, sandalwood, pearls, all of them wonderfully cordial. Plasters made from the aforesaid, with rose waters, violet, plantain and sorrel waters, should be applied; likewise an apple or sacks of the same. If this trembling motion of the heart comes from poison or from worms, it will be treated afterwards.

units.la: SYNCOPES CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF SYNCOPE.

units.la: SI SYNCOPE adest, spirituum in partibus externis paucorum resolutio prohibenda est aqua frigida, aut rosata, faciei & aliis partibus nudis inspersa: nisi syncope sit a causa frigida, vel ab alui fluore, quem frigida materias intro comprimens augeret. Vbi autem syncope est ab æstu, aut febris incendio resolutis spiritibus, saluberrimum est aqua frigida, aut rosata per se, vel cum aceto faciem rigare, & spiritus nutrire odoribus bonis, nisi syncope est a præfocatione ex vtero. Tunc enim graviter olentia, sed ori stomachi grata, naribus sunt adhibenda. Spi-ritus autem non solis odoribus bonis, & vi-no aromatico instaurandi sunt: sed etiam o-uis sorbilibus, carnibus bonis, & ex his a-qua, aut iure, intritis, contusis, concretis, analepticis. Aeger item a syncope, hoc est, virium omnium lapsu praesente est revocan-dus, & spiritus intro conculcati foras sunt euocandi frictionibus partium extremarum ligaturis dolorificis, vellendo nasum, auri-culas, pilos: sternutatoriis, cucurbitulis in coxis, & spathulis: si autem syncope est, ob magnam spirituum largam vacuatione inani-torum penuriam, frictionibus, & dictis nunc remediis abstinendum: quietique aeger permittendus, hausto vino, & odoribus ad-motis.
units.tr: If syncope is present, the dissolution of the spirits in the outer parts, which is the cause of the fainting, must be checked: by sprinkling cold water or rose water on the face and other bare parts; unless the syncope comes from a cold cause, or from a flux of the bowels, which cold would thicken and so make worse by driving the matter inward. But where the syncope arises from heat, or from the spirits being dissolved by the fire of a fever, it is most wholesome to bathe the face with cold water or rose water alone, or mixed with vinegar, and to nourish the spirits with pleasant odours; unless the syncope comes from suffocation of the womb. For then strong-smelling things, though agreeable to the mouth and stomach, should be applied to the nostrils. The spirits are to be restored not only with pleasant odours and aromatic wine, but also with egg-based sorbile foods, good meats, and broth or water in which these have been steeped, crushed, boiled down, and made into restoratives. Likewise the patient who is present with syncope, that is, with a collapse of all the strength, must be recalled, and the spirits driven inward must be called out again by rubbing the extremities, by painful ligatures, by plucking the nose, ears and hair, and by sneezing powders, cupping glasses on the thighs, and spatulas. But if the syncope arises from a great loss of spirits through the emptying of the body and a lack of them, the rubbing and the remedies just mentioned are to be avoided; the patient is to be allowed to rest quietly, with wine drunk and odours brought near.

units.la: Syncopes curationem singulis causis debi-tam, ex Gal. lib. 1. ad Glauc. & lib. meth. 12. repete.
units.tr: The cure of syncope, suited to each cause, is to be taken from Galen, in the first book to Glaucon and the twelfth book of the Method.

units.la: CHOLERAE MORBI ACVTI CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF ACUTE CHOLERA MORBUS.

units.la: CHOLERA morbus est cum vomitu, et deiectione biliosa deiciuntur tanto saepe impetu, ut inanito simul spiritu multo vires langueant, & tremor cordis, ac syncope saepe succedant, & mors: ob id morbis acutis adnumeratur Hippocrati. Curatur autem remediorum generibus quatuor.
units.tr: Cholera morbus is a disease in which there is vomiting and bilious purging, and the discharges come with such violence that the strength fails from the great loss of breath, and trembling of the heart, fainting, and often death follow. For this reason Hippocrates counts it among the acute diseases. It is cured by four kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione varia in affectu incipiente, & procedente, & ob symptomata succedentia. Affectu incipiente, sit aer calido frigido temperatus, parum luminosus: nam lumen & calor humores exagitat, & spiritus resoluit: tenebrae contra sedant, & quietos reddunt: frigus vero quanquam spiritum resolui prohibet, quia tamen materias intro ad ventriculum & intestina ex ipsius corporis habitu protrudit, noxium est. Odoribus bonis spiritus nutriantur & instaurentur. Cibus detur paucus, coctu facilis, si virium prostratio impendet. Si autem oppressio tantum & aggrauatio, cibo abstineatur. Ventriculus autem ad vomendum & deiciendum effusus, ante cibum est roborandus, admotis si materia frigida & pituitosa est, calidis: vt oleo de spica, menthæ, absinthij, mastichini, nardini, vel vnguentis, ex ijsdem oleis et puluere menthæ, absinthij, mastiches, spicæ nardi, caryophyllorum cinamomi, cardamomi, galangæ, nucis moscatæ, xylaloës, & pauca cera, vel fotibus ex ijsdem in vino rubro austero incoctis: si calida, frigidis: vt oleo violato, rosato, cydoniorum, myrteo & puluere rosarum, violarum, santalorum, corallij, balaustiorum, malicorij: factis ex his linimentis, vnguentis, fotibus pro varia ægri gratia. Sumptis quoque roboratur, in frigida quidem calidis: vt, syrup. de mentha, mina cydoniorum aromatica, syrup. cydoniorum cum aromatibus Mesuæ, syrup. de corticibus citri grato et cardiaco, ob id idoneo, si etiam adest syncope. In calida verò frigidis: vt syrup. & iulepo rosato, de ribes, de granatis, de limonibus, de acida citri parte, datis à duobus aut tribus cochlearibus ad quatuor, & non multo post cibo coctu facili, & grato, etiam si parum affectui conueniat: vt, aqua carnium perdicis, vituli, agni: quæ quomodo sit facienda, docet Auic. Detur etiam vua pensilis siccata: si appetitur contusum, ouaforbilia cum succo limonum, aranciorum in calida: cum cinamomo autem, cardamomo, pauco vino puro in frigida. Odor quoque pullorum tostorum, & aliorum ita conditorum instaurat vires, ac appetentiam excitat. Potus sit: in frigida, vinum generosum, odoriferum: id enim omnium celerrime vires instaurat, præsertim si syncope adsit: in calida autem, vinum granatorum. Vitentur autem quæ causas has augere possunt, et animi affectus, qui materias intro trahunt: vt, mœror, timor, cura.
units.tr: 1. DIET, varied according to the stage of the disease, whether it is beginning, advancing, or accompanied by the symptoms that follow. In the beginning stage the air should be tempered with warmth and cold, and dimly lit, for light and heat stir up the humours and loosen the spirits, whereas darkness calms and quiets. Cold, though it prevents the spirits from being loosened, is harmful nonetheless, because it drives the morbid matter inward toward the stomach and intestines by the constitution of the body itself. Good odours nourish and restore the spirits. Food should be given sparingly and be easy to digest if there is a threat of collapse of strength; but if there is only oppression and aggravation, the patient should abstain from food. The stomach, weakened by the vomiting and purging, must be strengthened before food. If the matter is cold and phlegmatic, apply warm remedies such as oil of spike, of mint, of wormwood, of mastic, of nard, or ointments made from these same oils, and powder of mint, wormwood, mastic, spikenard, cloves, cinnamon, cardamom, galangal, nutmeg and xylaloes, with a little wax, or fomentations of the same steeped in strong red wine; if the matter is hot, use cold remedies such as oil of violets, of roses, of quinces, of myrtle, and powder of roses, violets, sandalwood, coral, pomegranate flowers and pomegranate rind. These are made into liniments, ointments and fomentations, according to the patient's condition. The stomach is also strengthened by things taken internally: in cold cases warm ones, such as syrup of mint, the aromatic quince conserve, the syrup of quinces with the aromatics of Mesue, syrup of citron peel, which is pleasant and cardiac and therefore suitable if there is also a faint; in hot cases cold ones, such as syrup and julep of roses, of barberries, of pomegranates, of lemons, and the sour part of citron, given in doses of two or three spoonfuls up to four, and not long afterwards an easily digested and agreeable food, even if it fits the condition poorly, such as broth of partridge, veal or lamb, the preparation of which Avicenna teaches. Dried hanging grapes may also be given, and if the patient desires it, crushed eggs with lemon or orange juice in hot cases, but with cinnamon, cardamom and a little pure wine in cold cases. The smell of roasted chicks and other birds seasoned in this way also restores strength and stirs the appetite. As for drink: in cold cases a generous, fragrant wine, for this restores strength more quickly than anything else, especially if there is a faint; in hot cases pomegranate wine. Avoid whatever can increase these causes, and the emotions of the mind which draw the matter inward, such as sadness, fear and anxiety.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM in ventrem receptam vacuantibus, vomitu, aut potius deiectione, vtro natura repet. Vomitum igitur iuuabis sola aqua tepida: vt quæ nec materiam nouam attrahat, neque repertam foueat, sed temperet & vacuet. Remedio est eadem ventriculo à bile flaua in ipsum ruente oppresso, vel roso: in vtroque autem affectu per se detur, non cum oleo aliquo, vt quod ventriculum culum & intestinum relaxet.
units.tr: 2. The matter received into the belly is to be evacuated, by vomiting or rather by purging, whichever way nature tends. Vomiting, then, you will help with plain warm water alone, since it neither draws in new matter nor fosters what is already there, but tempers and empties. The same remedy suits a stomach oppressed or corroded by yellow bile flowing down into it; in either condition it should be given by itself, not with any oil, since oil relaxes the stomach and intestine.

units.la: Potes aquæ tepidæ miscere syrupū acetosum ad saporis gratiam, non ad incidendum, aut tenuandum, quòd materia in hoc affectu non sit crassa, lenta: aqua saccharata, aut decoctum hordei, aquæ loco propinari potest. His tamen astringentia non miscenda (nisi virium cadentium imbecillitas id suaderet) quia materiam ventriculo contumacius affigūt. Cùm verò aqua sit flatulēta, illi incoque vel misce cumini semunciam, vel circiter, aut niī tri drach.ij. Ea autem ad vomitum quàm ad nutrimentum multò largior est bibenda, vt ea copia retentrix grauata expultricem mox stimulet. Si autem materiæ ad sedem feruntur, eas iuuamus, si vires valent, cassia, vel manna, vel rhabarbaro in substantia, vel decocto myrobalanorum: non autem valentiore, quod materiæ ad fluendum sunt paratæ. Si verò vires sint imbecillæ, sunt firmandæ: post humores abundantes familiari ipsis medicamento purgandi.
units.tr: You may mix a sour syrup into warm water to make it pleasant to taste, but not to cut or thin the matter, since in this condition the matter is not thick or viscous. Sugared water or a decoction of barley may be given in place of water. Astringents, however, should not be mixed in (unless the weakness of failing strength suggests it), because they fix the matter more stubbornly to the stomach. Since water causes flatulence, add to it about half an ounce of cumin, or three drachms of anise. The water should be drunk in a larger quantity for vomiting than for nourishment, so that the bulk of it, weighing down the retaining organ, may soon stimulate the expelling one. If, however, the matter is moving toward the bowel, we help it, if the strength allows, with senna, manna, or rhubarb in substance, or with a decoction of myrobalans; but not with a stronger purge, since the matter is already prepared to flow. If the strength is feeble, it must be fortified first, and only after the excess humours is it to be purged with the medicine suited to them.

units.la: 3. MATERIA Mà toto corpore in ventrì
units.tr: 3. MATTER falling from the whole body into the stomach

units.la: culum & intestina ruentem apparantibus, & vacuantibus, si aquosa aut biliosa: si autem corrupta & maligna turgeat, sine appa ratu vacuantibus: si benigna est, in contrari um auertentibus (quibus etiam vtendum est vbi ventrem nimium fatigat aquosa aut biliosa) vt balneo ad cutim trahente, ligaturis dolorificis, frictionibus. Venter etiam inferior per sumpta & admota astringentia, & refrigerantia, si calida est materia, roborandus, & vix claudendæ, ne tam prompte fluxionem recipiant: præsertim vbi pro copiæ ratione iam præcessit vacuatio.
units.tr: and intestines: if it is watery or bilious, prepare it and evacuate it; if it is corrupt and malignant and swells, evacuate it without preparation; if it is benign, turn it the other way, using what draws to the skin, such as a bath, binding ligatures, and friction (these should also be used where the watery or bilious matter overly wears out the belly). The lower belly should be strengthened by astringents and refrigerants taken internally and applied externally, if the matter is hot, and it should scarcely be closed, lest it receive the flux so promptly; especially where evacuation has already gone before in proportion to the amount.

units.la: 4. SYMPTOMATA in hoc affectu sæuissima corrigentibus: vt, sitim, aqua hordei, iulepo rosato, succo, & syrupo granatorum: vt spasmum ex inanitione, litu, vel fotu, vel balneo, ex oleo violato, si causa est calida: liliaceo, si frigida, & cæteris in spasmo dictis: vt, vomitum immoderatum sistentibus, cucurbitula ad fundum ventriculi affixa, vel cataplasmate ex pane, vino rub. astringente, & pulvere mastiches, cinamomi, absinthÿ, absinthij, menthae, caryophyllorum: vel si causa est calida, aceto, aut vino granatorum, puluere malicorij, balaustij, & similium frigidorum astringentium.
units.tr: 4. The most violent symptoms in this condition are to be corrected: thirst, by barley water, julep of roses, juice and syrup of pomegranates; spasm arising from exhaustion, by anointing, fomenting, or bathing with oil of violets if the cause is hot, with lily oil if it is cold, and by the other remedies named under spasm; immoderate vomiting, by checking it with a small cupping glass applied to the bottom of the stomach, or with a plaster of bread, astringent red wine, and powder of mastic, cinnamon, wormwood, mint and cloves; or, if the cause is hot, with vinegar or pomegranate wine, powder of pomegranate rind, pomegranate flowers, and similar cold astringents.

units.la: IMBECILLITATIS VENTRICVLI CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF WEAKNESS OF THE STOMACH.

units.la: IMBECILLITAS ventriculi curationem propriam non requirit, sed cessat, morbo, eius causa, profligato. Nullum enim symptoma, qua symptoma est, aliquid indicat. Si enim ventriculus est imbecillus à tumore praeter naturam, curato tumore, imbecillitas, tumoris symptoma cessat: eodem modo in aliis eius affectibus, quos dolor & imbecillitas sequuntur. Quae vero imbecillitas ventriculi à magno aut longo morbo reuale scentibus adest, ea roborantibus qualitate, tum manifesta, tum occulta corrigenda est. Si enim imbecillus est ventriculus ab intemperie calida, per refrigerantia curatur, & contrà: similiter in aliis intemperaturis, tam simplicibus quàm compositis, tam solis quàm cum materia est faciendum. Non autem sem-
units.tr: Weakness of the stomach does not need a cure of its own, but ceases when the disease that causes it has been overcome. For no symptom, as a symptom, indicates anything by itself. If the stomach is weak from a swelling contrary to nature, then once the swelling is cured the weakness, being a symptom of the swelling, ceases. It is the same with its other affections, which are followed by pain and weakness. The weakness of the stomach that is present after a great or long illness must be corrected by strengthening qualities, both manifest and occult. If the stomach is weak from a hot intemperature, it is cured by cooling remedies, and the reverse holds for a cold one. Similarly with the other intemperaments, whether simple or compound, whether alone or with matter, the same must be done. Not, however, always

units.la: T per in ventriculo imbecillo vtendum calidis, siccis, astringentibus: quem errorem praeceptoribus suis appingit Gal. lib. 7. meth.
units.tr: Nor should hot, dry and astringent remedies always be used on a weak stomach. Galen, Method. lib. 7 [Gal. lib. 7. meth.] charges his own teachers with this error.

units.la: Si imbecillus est ventriculus ab intemperie frigida, humida ex cruditate, coctioni prospiciatur exercitatione, somno, taciturnitate, et silentio: & admotis calorificis siccantibus: sed in primis sumptis, alimentis quidè delicatis, coctu facilibus paru humidis, medicamentis vero materiam apparantibus, incidendo, tenuando, tergendo: deinde vacuantibus vomitu, aut potius deiectione. Similiter à morbo reualescentibus, stomachus laxior, frigidior curatur syrup. stomachicis, quorum praestantissimi sunt, syrup. absinthij Ro. etiā hepar roborans: syrup. seu miua cydoniorum aromatica, syrup. menthae, cū dupla aqua menthae, & absinthij praecipuè, vel fœniculi, bethonicae: cum scrup. rosato Galeni, scrup. diaromaton Mesuae, galanga puluerata cum vino albo sumpta, vel in pilulas cū syrup. menthae, vel similí, formata, per horam vnā ante cibum, & diagalanga secreto quibusdam remedia remedio, praesertim ad flatus ipsius resoluen- dos: scrup. ex xylaloë, zingiberis conditi radi ce vna mane sumpta, vel theriacæ, aut mi- thridatij drachma vna semel in septimana, granis piperis 6. 7. 8. integris (ne puluerata ad hepar rapiantur: quòd fere calidum est, qui- bus ventriculus est frigidior) hora ante cibu̅ dimidia deuoratis. Corallium etiam proba- tur, praesertim cum imbecillus est ventricu- lus ab intemperie calida: quia ipsum est frigi dum: & tunica interior ventriculi gallina- rum, quam vt ventrem mergi, & struthio- camelì damnabis cu̅ Galen. Per admota quo que ventriculus est firmandus, & dolor se- dandus: in frigida quidem causa, per calida: vt, oleum de spica, mentha, absinthio, masti che: vt, vnguenta, vel cerata, vel emplastra: ex ijsdem oleis, cera et aromatibus stomachi- cis: vt, nucem moschatam, xylaloën, caryo- phylla, galangam, mastichen, mentha, absin thium: forma remediorum saepe mutata, ne vni assuefacta natura eius vires contemnat, ab eoⸯ nihil patiatur. Ob id etiam foueri potest ventriculus paulò ante pastus, spongia imbu-ta vino aromatico, cui incocta sint mentha, absinthij, schœnanti ana Ma. vnus, cinamo-mi, ciperi, calami aromatici ana drachmæ duæ, mastiches, nucis moschatæ, ana drach. vna. Post hunc verò fotum poris ab eo aper-tis, salubriter prædictis oleis partem illines. Bombax quoque bene carptus, eodem vino aromatite mersus & siccatus: deinde pulue-ribus prædictorum aromatum farctus, in epi-thema ventriculi, forma scuti consutum, te-ctum, ligatum imponatur: vel ex ijsdem sac-culi.
units.tr: If the stomach is weak from a cold intemperature, moist because of crudity, digestion should be helped by exercise, sleep, quiet and silence, and by applying warming and drying things. But first, the foods taken should be delicate, easy to digest and rather dry; medicines should prepare the matter by cutting, thinning and cleansing, and then evacuate by vomiting or, better, by stool. Likewise, for those recovering from illness, a loose and cold stomach is cured with stomachic syrups, of which the most excellent are: syrup of wormwood (Rosatus), which also strengthens the liver; aromatic syrup or mixture of quinces; syrup of mint, with twice the amount of mint water, and especially of wormwood, or of fennel or betony; with Galen's rose pill (scruple), Mesue's diaromaton (scruple), and powdered galangal taken with white wine, or formed into pills with syrup of mint or the like, one hour before food. Diagalanga is, for some, a secret remedy, especially for dispelling its wind. A scruple of xylaloes and one piece of preserved ginger root is taken in the morning, or theriac or mithridate, one drachm once a week, with six, seven or eight whole grains of pepper swallowed half an hour before food. (Powdered forms should not be drawn to the liver, which is almost hot, while the stomach is colder.) Coral is also approved, especially when the stomach is weak from a hot intemperature, since it is cold. The inner membrane of the gizzard of hens, which you will reject as you would the stomach of a crane or ostrich, is likewise rejected, following Galen. The stomach is also to be strengthened and its pain eased by applied remedies, warm ones if the cause is cold: such as oil of spike, mint, wormwood, mastic; ointments, or cerates, or plasters made from the same oils, wax and stomachic aromatics: such as nutmeg, xylaloes, cloves, galangal, mastic, mint and wormwood. The form of the remedies should often be changed, so that the nature does not become accustomed to one and despise its powers, and suffer nothing from it. For this reason the stomach may also be fomented shortly after eating, with a sponge soaked in aromatic wine, in which have been boiled mint, wormwood, schoenanthus, one handful each, with cinnamon, cyperus, and aromatic calamus, two drachms each, and mastic and nutmeg, one drachm each. After this fomentation, when the pores have been opened, rub on a portion of the aforesaid oils, which are healthful. Cotton wool, well carded, soaked in the same aromatic wine and dried, then stuffed with powders of the aforesaid aromatics, sewn into the shape of a shield, covered and tied, may be applied as a plaster to the stomach; or a little bag made of the same.

units.la: Pueri quoque carnosi non facilè sudantis venter admotus, calore suo coctionem poten-ter adiuuat, & catulus pinguis, & palma manus, si carnosa est: decubitus quibusdam probatur, principiò in latus dextrum, vt ad fundum ventriculi carnosius, & ob id cali-dius, & ad coquendum valentius, alimentū descendat: deinde in sinistrum, vt hepar ven-triculum amplectatur, & suo calore ipsius coctionem iuuet: postremò absoluta coctione, rursus rursus in dextrum: ut tum per pylorum fundo insertum os ventriculi infernum chylus excernatur in ecphysin, & tenuia intestina distribuendus per venas mesaraicas in hepar. Quibus tamen hepar calidius, salubre non est primo in dextrum cubare, nec diu, nisi consueuerint. Si vero causa mali calida est, sumantur frigida haec: syrup. cydoniorum, rosatus ex succo oxalidis, de ribes cum duplo aquae rosarum, plantaginis, oxalidis: diarhodon abbatis, aut commune, scrupu. trium santalorum, conserua rosarum, saccharum rosatum, caro cydoniorum. Sumantur autem horis tribus ante pastus: quae omnia praeter oxalidem, astringendo quoque laxam a calore partem roborant. Admouenda, aut oleum rosatum, cydoniorum, myrteum per se, vel cum rosis, balaustijs, malicorijs, santalis, spodio, corallio: forma linimenti, vel alia. Caue autem ne ventriculum partem natura frigida, immodice refrigeres, & sic vim eius coctricem prosternas. Quauis enim ventriculi intemperies calida & frigida, aequè citò curentur, utraque per sibi contraria: non tamen &que tuto: tutius enim calefacis quàm refrigeras. Si imbecillus est ventriculus ab intempe rie sicca, curatur uti febris hectica humectantibus: ut, lacte, balneo ex decocto malua, viola nigra, lactuca, capitibus, & intestinis veruecum, vino imbecillo, fuluo, diluto, herbis humectantibus.
units.tr: The belly of a child who is fleshy and does not sweat easily, when applied, powerfully aids digestion by its own warmth; so too a fat pad, and the palm of the hand, if it is fleshy. Some approve of lying down in various positions: first on the right side, so that the food may descend to the bottom of the stomach, which is fleshier and therefore warmer and more able to digest; then on the left, so that the liver embraces the stomach and helps its digestion by its warmth; finally, when digestion is complete, again on the right, so that the chyle may then pass through the pylorus, inserted at the bottom, and out of the lower mouth of the stomach into the ecphysis [ἔκφυσις], and the thin intestines distribute it through the mesaraic veins to the liver. Yet for those whose liver is hotter, it is not healthful to lie on the right side at first, nor for long, unless they are accustomed to it. But if the cause of the evil is hot, these cold things should be taken: syrup of quinces; rosatum made from the juice of sorrel; of ribes with twice the amount of rose water; of plantain and sorrel; the Abbot's diarhodon, or the common one; three scruples of sandalwood; preserved roses; candied rose petals; quince flesh. They should be taken three hours before food. All these, except sorrel, also strengthen the part relaxed by heat, by their astringency. Apply either rose oil, quince oil or myrtle oil by itself, or with roses, pomegranate flowers, pomegranate rind, sandalwood, spodium, or coral, in the form of a liniment or otherwise. Take care, however, not to cool immoderately a part that is cold by nature, and so overthrow its power of retention. For although a hot and a cold intemperature of the stomach are cured equally quickly, each by its contrary, it is not equally safe: it is safer to warm than to cool. If the stomach is weak from a dry intemperature, it is cured, as in hectic fever, with moistening remedies: such as milk; baths of decoction of mallow, black violet, lettuce, the heads and intestines of a ram; weak, tawny, diluted wine; and moistening herbs.

units.la: DOLORIS VENTRICVLI CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF PAIN OF THE STOMACH.

units.la: DOLOR ventriculi magna cura, praecipuo? studio placandus, quòd is actionem habet chylosin, seu alimenti in chylum mutationem toti corpori communem, seu quo chylo in sanguinem mutato, partes corporis omnes nutriuntur. Fit autem hic dolor ut alius quiuis ab alteratione subita, aut solutione continui. Alteratio ipsa intemperiem facit calidam aut frigidam (nam duae reliquae vix per se sunt dolorificae) aut solam, aut cum materia. Si intemperies est cum materia, curatur quinque remediorum generibus.
units.tr: PAIN of the stomach needs great care and especial zeal to soothe it, because the stomach performs chylosis, that is, the change of food into chyle, which is common to the whole body, and by which, once the chyle is changed into blood, all the parts of the body are nourished. This pain arises, like any other, from a sudden alteration or from a solution of continuity. The alteration itself produces either a hot or a cold intemperament (the other two hardly cause pain by themselves), either alone or together with matter. If the intemperament is accompanied by matter, it is cured by five kinds of remedy.

units.la: i.VI.
units.tr: i.VI.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione contraria ipsi materiæ: vt, calida, aromatis, &c. in frigida: frigida, vt vino granatorum, &c. in calida, ut paulò ante fusius diximus.
units.tr: 1. DIET contrary to the matter itself: for hot matter, cold foods, such as aromatics, etc.; for cold matter, hot foods, such as wine of pomegranates, etc., as we explained more fully a little above.

units.la: 2. SEDANTIBVS dolore statim vtendis, quòd ventriculus sensu est tactus exacto præditus: præsertim ore suo: qualia sunt; quæ causam ipsam, hoc est, materiam dolorificam ventriculo expellunt vomitu, aut deiectione: si verò altius in ventriculi tunicas sit recepta materia, ante apparanda est incidentibus, tenuatibus, tergentibus, quàm vacuari possit: ac interea vt sedetur dolor, adhibe anodyna, quæ temperatè calida sunt, & fere humida, partem relaxant, materiæ aliquid digerunt, tensionem minuunt: vt, fotus cum impleta vesica, vel cū spongia imbuta decocto chamæmeli, meliloti, sæ. lini, fœniculi: vel linamentū, ex oleo lini, chamæmeli, anethi: vel vnguentū, ceratum, emplastrū, simili materia cōstans: vt, farina sæ. lini, fœniculi, radice althææ. Cyathi etiā duo, aut tres, seu vnc. tres vel quatuor et dimidia decocti chamæmeli potu mire iuuant. Quæ si vincan-tur, & vires dolor prosternit stupefacienti-bus sumptis, vt opiatis zazanea Mesuæ ad drachmas duas, vel athanasia Nicolai à dra-chma vna, ad sesquidrach. vel Philonio Ro-mano, Auic. valentissimo à semidrach. ad drachmam vnam. Illa enim somnum cocili-ant, per quem vires instaurantur, nec dolor sentitur. Virtute autem forti adhuc dentur, imbecilla, ne dentur: quia reliquum calorem extinguerent.
units.tr: 2. SOOTHING remedies, to be used at once against the pain, because the stomach has a sense of touch that is especially exact, above all in its mouth. Such are those which expel the cause itself, that is the painful matter, from the stomach by vomiting or purging. But if the matter has lodged deeper in the coats of the stomach, it must first be prepared with incisive, thinning and cleansing agents before it can be evacuated. Meanwhile, to calm the pain, apply anodynes which are moderately warm and fairly moist, which relax the part, digest some of the matter, and lessen the tension: for example, a fomentation with a bladder filled with warm liquid, or a sponge soaked in a decoction of chamomile, melilot, linseed and fennel; or a linen cloth with oil of linseed, chamomile and dill; or an ointment, cerate or plaster made of similar materials, such as flour of linseed and fennel with root of marshmallow. Two or three cups, or three and a half to four ounces, of decoction of chamomile drunk also helps wonderfully. If these fail and the pain overcomes the strength, it is struck down with stupefying drugs taken internally: for example, the opiate zazanea of Mesue, two drachms; or the athanasia of Nicolaus, from one drachm to a drachm and a half; or the Philonium Romanum of Avicenna, very strong, from half a drachm to one drachm. For these bring on sleep, through which the strength is restored and the pain is not felt. They are to be given only when the strength is still robust; when it is weak they must not be given, because they would extinguish the remaining warmth.

units.la: 3. MATERIAM parantibus, calidam quidem refrigerantibus, & si affluit in ven-triculum bilis, etiam astringentibus: vt, sy-rup. ex succo oxalidis, acetato, rosato, grana-torum, cichorij, intybi, violato cum aquis oxalidis, rosarum plantaginis, solani, cicho-rij, intybi. Frigidam vero et pituitosam (qua-lis plurima esse consueuit) melle rosato, oxy-mel. simpl. vel (si valentiore opus est) com-posito & scillite cum aqua bethonicæ, sal-uiæ, maiorana: syrup. autem & aqua absin-thij pontici, pituitam affigit tenacius ventri-culo culo: bilem vero indidem deturbat: absinthium vulgare, utrunque humorem potenter deturbat: sed malum est stomacho: quia minimum astringit, uti & seriphium. Melancholicam denique syrup. thymi, epithymi, fumariæ cum aquis fumariæ, scolopendriï datis ad dies octo. Si à sanguinis copia dolet ventriculus, vena basilica dextra secta sanguis mitta tur quantum indicationes suadent.
units.tr: 3. Preparing the matter: cooling agents for the hot kind, and, if bile flows into the stomach, also astringents: for example, syrups of sorrel juice, of vinegar, of roses, of pomegranates, of chicory, of endive, of violets, with waters of sorrel, roses, plantain, nightshade, chicory and endive. For the cold and phlegmatic kind (which is very common), use honey of roses, simple oxymel, or, if a stronger one is needed, compound oxymel of squill, with water of betony, sage and marjoram. Syrup and water of Pontic wormwood bind phlegm more tenaciously to the stomach but drive bile out of it; common wormwood powerfully drives out both humours, but it is bad for the stomach because it astringes only slightly, as does seriphium. Finally, for melancholic matter, syrup of thyme, of epithymum and of fumitory, with waters of fumitory and hart's tongue, given for eight days. If the stomach hurts from a plethora of blood, the basilic vein of the right arm is opened and blood let as far as the indications suggest.

units.la: 4. MATERIAM vacuantibus, sed clementibus: & quorum uis hepar nō transcendat: vt, hiera picra bilem & pituitam à ventriculo, & venis mesaraicis, ac sima hepatis tantum purgante: non autem scammoniatis, & aliys trahentibus etiam à remotis partibus: vt, turbith, agarico. Hiera loco, præsertim vbi ventriculi intemperatura est calidior, cassia, manna, cum pauco rhabarbaro, myrobalani citreæ vsurpentur.
units.tr: 4. Evacuating the matter, but gently, and with purgatives whose force does not reach beyond the liver: for example, hiera picra, which purges bile and phlegm from the stomach, the mesenteric veins and the upper part of the liver only. Not scammony and other drugs that draw even from remote parts, such as turbith and agaric. In place of hiera, especially where the intemperament of the stomach is hotter, cassia, manna with a little rhubarb, and citrine myrobalans are used.

units.la: Vomitus quoque ex aqua tepida, bilem flauam sursum ad os ventriculi repentem vacuat. Quibus si malum non vincitur, etiam diaphœnico vtendum, cuius vis attractrix hepar quoque non superat, licet scammonium, & turbith recipiat, sed quorum vis lentore & astrictione dactylorum, amygdalorum, penidiorum, & aliorum cohibetur. Eadem ratione tutum est diacydonium scammoniatum, in quo vis calidorum carne cydonia obtunditur. Idem præstant pilulæ ex hiera simplici & composita, elephanginæ, mastichinæ Conciliatoris.
units.tr: Vomiting induced by warm water also evacuates yellow bile creeping up to the mouth of the stomach. If the trouble is not overcome by these, diaphoenicon must also be used. Its drawing force does not surpass the liver, although it contains scammony and turbith, because their force is restrained by the viscosity and astringency of dates, almonds, pine nuts and others. By the same reasoning diacydonium with scammony is safe, in which the force of the hot purgatives is blunted by the quince pulp. The pills of simple and compound hiera, elephangine and the mastichine of the Conciliator do the same.

units.la: 5. INTEMPERIEM abigentibus, calidâ frigidis, & contrà, tam sumptis, quàm admotis dictis capite superiori. Si verò ventriculus dolet à flatibus, si qua ipsos materia fovet, apparanda & vacuanda: deinde flatus dissoluendi, primùm clementioribus: ut, temperatè calidis, ut chamæmelo melilloto: deinde valentioribus, ut baccis lauri, allijs: ut Gal. lib.7. & 12. meth. anisfo, cumino, galanga cũ vino aromatite, aut cretico dulci, seu malua tico, vel diacumino, diagalanga, dianisfo, & valentiore his confectione ex baccis lauri.
units.tr: 5. Removing the intemperament by hot remedies for cold and cold for hot, both taken and applied, as described in the chapter above. But if the stomach hurts from flatulence, and if some matter feeds the wind, that matter must be prepared and evacuated. Then the flatulence is dissolved, first with gentler agents, moderately warm ones such as chamomile and melilot; then with stronger ones, such as laurel berries and garlic and onions, as Galen says in books 7 and 12 of the Method; also anise, cumin, galangal with aromatic wine or sweet Cretan wine or Malvasia, or diacuminum, diagalangal, dianisum, and, stronger than these, the confection made of laurel berries.

units.la: PHLEGMONES VENTRICVLI CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF INFLAMMATION OF THE STOMACH.

units.la: PHLEGMOME ventriculi curatur ut phlegmone pulmonis, & phrenitis principio scilicet repellentibus & auertentibus materiam: deinde additis etiam digerentibus: in statu his prope solis. Astringentia enim & partē roborantia resoluentibus semper miscenda in ventriculo, ut hepate, ob actionis eius necessitatem. Si resolui non potest, quod tamen est longe optatius, coquentibus est suppuranda: et ulcus, ubi abscessus erupit, tergendum, siccandum, carne implendum, cicatrice tegendum, remedijs quae docent Rasis, Auic. & alij.
units.tr: INFLAMMATION of the stomach is cured as inflammation of the lungs and phrenitis are, that is, at the beginning by repelling and turning away the matter, then adding also digestives; in the established stage, almost only these. For astringents and part-strengthening agents must always be mixed with the resolvents in the stomach, as in the liver, because of the necessity of its function. If it cannot be resolved (which is much more desirable), it must be brought to suppuration by ripening agents. The ulcer, where the abscess has burst, must then be cleansed, dried, filled with flesh and covered with a scar, by the remedies taught by Rhazes, Avicenna and others.

units.la: SINGVLTVS CVRATIO.
units.tr: Treatment of the Individual Case

units.la: SINGVLTVS curatione recipit variam pro causa varia. Si enim est à causa externa (id quod raro accidit) ut aëris calidi aut frigidi occursu: hac ablata, & ægro in aërem contrarium translato, facile cessat: si verò iam dispositionem reliquit ea, contrarijs quoque oppugnanda sumptis & admotis. Si verò fit à materia in ventriculo corrupta, aut cibo crassiore: si sursum repat, & æger facile vomat, vomitu expellatur: si ad fundum ventriculi, clysteribus lenientibus, aut etiam purgantibus medicamentis, cassia, manna, hieræ mellitæ &c. vna diaphœnico à drach. tribus ad drach. quatuor vacuetur, deinde ventriculus roboretur, partim admotis oleis, menthæ, absinthij, maslitches, & unguentis, ceratis, emplastris, reliquisque dictis in ventriculi imbecillitate, partim sumptis: vt aromatico rosato, caryophyllato, zingiberè condito, & aliis prius dictis.
units.tr: The treatment of a single case varies with its cause. If the cause is external (which seldom happens), as from meeting hot or cold air, then removing that cause and moving the patient into air of the opposite kind usually brings the trouble to an end. If, however, the disposition has already been left behind, it must be attacked with contraries, both taken and applied. If it arises from corrupt matter in the stomach, or from coarser food, then: if it creeps upward and the patient vomits easily, let it be expelled by vomiting; if it lies at the bottom of the stomach, let it be emptied by soothing clysters or by purgative medicines, such as cassia, manna, honeyed hiera, etc., with diaphoenicon, from three drachms to four drachms. Then the stomach is to be strengthened, partly by applying oils, mint, wormwood, mastic, ointments, cerates, plasters, and the other remedies described for weakness of the stomach, and partly by taking such things as aromatic rosewater, clove-flavoured or ginger-preserved remedies, and the others mentioned earlier.

units.la: Si fit à sensu tactus ventriculi exquisitiore, vel re aliqua mordaci: vt, acribus, cæpa, allio, porro, sinapi, pipere, zingiberè: hæc vacuentur deiectione, aut vomitu ex aqua dulci, vel hordei tepida, largiore quidem quàm potus gratia, non tamen tam copiosa, vt mox vomitum moueat: aliquandiu enim retenta, melius purgabit ventriculum: postea ventriculus roborandus saccharo rosato, violato, iulepo rosato, violato, diarhodo & cæteris tam sumptis, quàm admotis, in ventriculi imbeimbecillitate descriptis. Si à flatibus est (vt plurimum fit) decoctum menthæ & cumini, & aliorum Rasi scriptorum, ad vnc. quatuor sumptum, est salubre: adhæc semen anisi, cumini, castorij, baccæ lauri, dianisum, diacyminum diagalanga, elect. de baccis lauri cum vino bono sumpta. Cucurbitula quoque ventriculo, vel etiam umbilico admota, miraculi modo affectus flatulentos ventris infe-rioris derepente mitigat, aut tollit. Somno etiam longiore coquat venter materiam flatulentam: decoctum quoque chamæmeli, melilo-ti, anethi, pulegij, calaminthes, origani, abrotoni, se. ameos, fœniculi, baccarum lauri in vino albo, vel aqua, & pauco vini albi, odoriferi flatus potenter dissipat, si spongia hoc imbuta decocto, aut vesica eodem semiplena ventriculo admoueatur: illitus etiam ex oleo chamameли, liliorum, de spica, & ex his cum aliys, unguenta cerata, emplastra: filum quoque cum cineribus frixum, linteo in volutum vtiliter admouetur, vel ipsi cineres per se frixi in scutella ex lixiuio vel vino aromatico, vel potius aqua vitæ super carbones ne flammam concipiat: Balneo quoq; si vires valent, et ieiuni sint, multùm iuuantur. Sternutatio quoq; & cohibitus anhelitus, quia cor calidius efficit et vicinas partes suppressis in ipso fumidis excrementis, coquit, aut dissipat flatus singultum excitantes: id quod etiã vulgò fieri videas. Si ab hepatis phlegmone est, illa prius curanda. Si aut singultus est à materia in ventriculo contenta, curatur quinque remediorum generibus.
units.tr: If it arises from an excessively acute sensitivity of the stomach's surface, or from some biting substance, such as sharp things like onion, garlic, leek, mustard, pepper, or ginger, these are to be evacuated by a downward discharge, or by vomiting induced with sweet water or warm barley water. The dose should be larger than a drink, but not so copious as to bring on vomiting at once; for if it is retained for some time, it will cleanse the stomach better. Afterwards the stomach must be strengthened with rose sugar, violet sugar, rose or violet julep, diarhodon, and the others described under weakness of the stomach, both taken and applied. If it comes from wind (as it most often does), a decoction of mint and cumin, and of the other remedies Rhazes describes, taken in a quantity of four ounces, is wholesome. Besides these, seed of anise, cumin, castoreum, bay berries, dianisum, diacuminum, diagalanga, and electuary of bay berries taken with good wine are useful. A small cupping glass applied to the stomach, or even to the navel, miraculously and suddenly eases or removes flatulent affections of the lower belly. Also, a longer sleep lets the stomach digest flatulent matter. A decoction of chamomile, melilot, dill, pennyroyal, calamint, marjoram, abrotanum, spignel, fennel, and bay berries, in white wine or water with a little white wine, powerfully disperses fragrant wind, if a sponge soaked in this decoction, or a bladder half full of it, is applied to the stomach. Ointments, cerates, and plasters, smeared on with oil of chamomile, of lilies, of spikenard, and of these with others, are also useful. A cloth folded and warmed with ashes fried in it, or the ashes themselves fried alone in a dish with lye or aromatic wine, or better still with brandy over coals, lest it catch fire, is also usefully applied. A bath too, if the strength allows and the patient is fasting, gives much help. Sneezing also, and holding the breath, since they make the heart warmer and, by compressing the neighbouring parts, cook or disperse the smoky excrements shut up within, or disperse the winds that provoke hiccups; you may see this happen commonly enough. If it comes from inflammation of the liver, that must be treated first. If the hiccup comes from matter contained in the stomach, it is cured by five kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione contraria ipsi materiæ.
units.tr: 1. DIET, arranged against the matter itself.

units.la: 2. APPARANTIBVS materia: pituitosam melle rosato, syrup. de duabus radicibus, cum aquis supra scriptis. Melancholicã deniq; syrup. de pomis, thymo, epithymo, cum aqua scolopendrij, fumariæ, & cæteris. Si autem bilis est, vt pituita tenuis, promptè vacuatur, nisi altius in tunicas ventriculi infarcta sint: tunc sequere Galenum.
units.tr: 2. WHEN the matter is rising: for phlegmatic matter, rosewater honey, syrup of the two roots, with the waters written above. For melancholic matter, finally, syrup of apples, thyme, epithymum, with water of hart's tongue, fumitory, and the others. But if it is bile, and it is thin like phlegm, it is quickly evacuated, unless it has become lodged more deeply in the coats of the stomach; in that case follow Galen.

units.la: 3. MATERIA Msic paratam vacuantibus, sed clementibus, & quorum vis hepar non transcendat capite superiori scriptis.
units.tr: 3. MATTER that has been prepared, to be evacuated, but gently, and with remedies whose force does not pass beyond the liver, written above under the heads.

units.la: 4. REME-
units.tr: 4. REMEDIES

units.la: Gal. Aph. 22. li. 5. & apho. 17. lib. 7.
units.tr: Galen, Aphorisms 22, book 5, and aphorism 17, book 7.

units.la: Li. 7. met. 4. REMEDIIS materiam reliquam ventriculo tenacius affixam excutientibus: ut, vomitu, sternutamento Hippocra. lib.6. Aph.13. clamore, saltu, equitatione in equo succussatore: aqua etiam faciei clam & repente infliƈta: quia timorē efficit, quo calor intrò retractus coquit & dissipat. Parū autem probandus est potus largior aquæ frigidæ, nisi æstate media, iuuene bene carnoso, in assueto, in causa calida: quamuis etiā ut tenuum, sic frigidam causam dissoluere possit. Syrup. de papauere datur ad cochlearia duo interdum deploratis ad obtundendum ventriculi sensum, uel semen papaueris albi tusum cum aqua lactucæ, uel eius seminis, & se. lactucæ, & se. hyoscyami albi decoctum. Quæ leuia, si non sufficiunt, philonium Romanum sumatur, quod partim frigidis simplicibus stupefacit, partim calidis resoluit.
units.tr: Book 7 of the Methodus, chapter 4. REMEDIES that shake loose the remaining matter that clings more tenaciously to the stomach: such as vomiting, sneezing, Hippocrates, Aphorisms 6, 13, shouting, jumping, riding on a jolting horse; also cold water suddenly and secretly flung in the face, because it causes fear, by which the heat, drawn inward, cooks and disperses the matter. A large drink of cold water is little to be recommended, except in midsummer, in a young man of good flesh, accustomed to it, and when the cause is hot; although it may dissolve a cold cause as well as a thin one. Syrup of poppy is given, two spoonfuls at a time, sometimes even to those despaired of, to blunt the sensitivity of the stomach, or white poppy seed pounded with lettuce water, or a decoction of that seed, lettuce seed, and white henbane seed. If these mild remedies are not enough, let Philonium Romanum be taken, which partly stupefies with its simple cold ingredients and partly dissolves with its warm ones.

units.la: 5. INTEMPERIEM ab humore relictam à calido, calidam, à frigido, frigidam tollentibus contrarijs. Si sicca est, iusculis instaurantibus, & nutriendo humectantibus:
units.tr: 5. An intemperament left by moisture: contraries are used to remove a heat-derived intemperament if it is hot, and a cold-derived one if it is cold. If it is dry, restore it with broths, and moisten it by nourishing it:

units.la: illitu quoque ventriculi, & spondylorum, & propinquorū, ex oleo violato, vel amygdal. dulcium.
units.tr: also by anointing the stomach, and the spine, and the neighbouring parts, with oil of violets or of sweet almonds.

units.la: APPETENTIAE IMMODERATAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: IMMODERATE APPETITE: CURE.

units.la: Appetentia immoderata, vel est ab inanitione, qualis ex longo morbo reualescentibus fere aduenit: quibus cibo pauco, & frequenti, sed coctu facili opus est, nec pingui. Nam multus, quia non coquitur, corrumpitur: pinguia, vt iura, carnes, quia ventriculum laxant, nauseam potius excitant, & prosternunt appetentiam illam immoderatam. Si à ventriculi imbecillitate, curetur vt dictum est. Si ob hepatis calorem vehementius distribuentem: post, qua ratione curatur, dicetur. Si ob humorem melancholicū à liene ad os vētriculi largius transmissum, qui os ventriculi immodicè contrahat & exugat, dicetur in affectibus lienis. Si à lumbricis omnia vixdum devorata depascentibus excitetur: audies in affectu hoc intestinorum. Si à pituita multa frigida, acida, uen-
units.tr: Immoderate appetite arises either from emptiness, as commonly happens to those recovering from a long illness. Such people need little food, taken often, but easy to digest and not rich. A large meal goes bad because it is not digested, while rich foods such as broths and meats relax the stomach, provoke nausea rather, and overthrow that immoderate appetite. If it comes from weakness of the stomach, it is cured as has been said. If it comes from the heat of the liver distributing too vigorously, the method of cure will be stated afterwards. If it comes from melancholy humour sent in larger amounts from the spleen to the mouth of the stomach, which contracts and draws off the mouth of the stomach excessively, it will be discussed under the affections of the spleen. If it is aroused by worms that devour everything hardly swallowed, you will hear of it under the affection of the intestines. If it comes from much cold, acid phlegm, ven-

units.la: Gal. lib. 4 uius part. uentriculum, ac praesertim ipsius os infestan te, curatur quinque remediorum generibus.
units.tr: Galen, lib. 4 uius part. In the stomach, and especially in its mouth when it troubles it, it is treated by five kinds of remedies.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione calida, sicca, omnibus pituitosis affectibus communi, praeter quae quod acria: vt, cepae, allia, porra, sinapi, & acida, pituitae incidendae, tenuandae, tergendae prosunt: sed appetentiam excitant, ob id in hoc affectu fugienda: aliis tamen pituitosis sunt salubria.
units.tr: (1) DIET: planned by a warm, dry diet, common to all phlegmatic affections, except for the sharp foods: such as onions, garlic, leeks, mustard, and the acids, which help to cut, thin and cleanse phlegm. But these stir up appetite, and so are to be avoided in this affection; yet they are wholesome for other phlegmatic conditions.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM apparantibus saepe dictis.
units.tr: (2) MATERIAL: to be prepared by the methods often mentioned.

units.la: 3. PHLEGMAGOGIS frequenter etiam ante scriptis.
units.tr: (3) PHLEGM-DRAWING remedies, also often written about before.

units.la: 4. MATERIAE reliquias resolucntibus etiam saepe antea descriptis: vt, famè tho rexis, id est, meripotio soluit Hippocrati. Vi{a}num autem generosum post cibos pingues largius, imperat Gal. ad fluctuationem & vomitum. Auic. vero idem vinum ante cibum propinat, vt materiam coquat.
units.tr: (4) Remedies that dissolve the remnants of the matter, also often described earlier: for example, hunger, which Hippocrates calls meripotio, and the stroke of the diet. Galen prescribes generous wine in larger amounts after rich meals, to cause flushing and vomiting. Avicenna, however, recommends the same wine before food, so that it may digest the matter.

units.la: 5. APPETITVM prosternentibus, vt ventriculi corpus laxum reddentibus, qualia sunt pinguia iura, & cibaria omnia: vt, oryza cum pinguibus cocta. Si autem ab intemperie calida ventriculi, alimenta corrumpantur, coctu difficilia offerantur: vt, castanea, bubula, suilla, panis silignites, cremor alica, & similia. Cum autem calor appetentiam prosternat, non debet haec causa recenseri inter eas quae appetentiam caninam excitant.
units.tr: (5) Remedies that overthrow the appetite, by making the body of the stomach lax, such as rich broths and all foods of that kind: for example, rice cooked with fat. But if the food goes bad from hot intemperament of the stomach, foods hard to digest are offered: for example, chestnuts, beef, pork, rye bread, gruel of spelt, and the like. Yet since heat overthrows appetite, this cause should not be counted among those that stir up a ravenous appetite.

units.la: DOLORIS HEPATIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: PAIN OF THE LIVER: CURE.

units.la: DOLOR hepatis sedatur, vt ventriculi et aliarum partium dolor, per remedia causae dolorificae contraria, mistis semper quae partis robur conseruent: quod hepar, vt ventriculus actionem toti corpori communem habet. Si igitur dolet ab intemperie sola, haec contrariis corrigitur, tutius tamen frigida per calida, quam contra. Si cum materia est, vt in phlegmone, scirrho, obstructione, per remedia singulis his affectibus dicata, post dicenda.
units.tr: Pain of the liver is calmed, like pain of the stomach and other parts, by remedies contrary to the cause of the pain, always mixed with those that preserve the strength of the part, since the liver, like the stomach, has an action common to the whole body. If therefore it hurts from intemperament alone, this is corrected by contraries, though cold by hot is safer than the reverse. If matter is involved, as in phlegmon, scirrhus or obstruction, it will be treated afterwards, by remedies dedicated to each of these affections.

units.la: PHLEGMONES HEPATIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: INFLAMMATION OF THE LIVER: CURE.

units.la: HEPATIS phlegmone diligenter curanda, ob principis ipsius partis actionem toti corpori communem: cauendum et ne intempestiue & immodicè refrigerando, aut resoluendo, aut copia humorum laborem in scirrhum abeat haec phlegmone: id quod sex auxiliorum generibus prouideremus.
units.tr: The phlegmon of the liver must be treated diligently, because of the action of this principal part common to the whole body. Care must also be taken lest this phlegmon, by cooling untimely and excessively, or by resolving, or by a plenty of humours, pass into a scirrhus; we shall provide against this with six kinds of aid.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione tenui & refrigerante, & ita sanguinem ad fluendū ineptiorem reddente: vt, aëre frigido natura, vel nostra industria, cremore hordei, vel iusculis cum pane loto, fuga vini, carnium, ouorum, & caeterorum sanguinem augentium, & calefacientium.
units.tr: (1) DIET: planned on a thin, cooling regimen, which makes the blood less apt to flow: for example, cold air, whether by nature or by our care; gruel of barley, or broths with washed bread; avoidance of wine, meats, eggs, and all things that increase the blood and warm it.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM ad hepar fluere paratam, & malum auctuntam reuellentibus, vt secta interna vel communi vena dextra missō sanguine quantū vires ferre possunt, ac morbi causa, & magnitudo postulat: vt ligaturis, frictionibus, cucurbitulis in artus ipsos impactis.
units.tr: (2) MATERIAL that is ready to flow to the liver and increases the evil: draw it away by opening an internal vein or the common right vein, letting blood as far as the strength can bear and the cause and magnitude of the disease require; also by ligatures, frictions, and cupping-glasses applied to the limbs themselves.

units.la: 3. FRIGIDIS styptis repellētibus materiam ad hepar fluentem, et fluxura prohibentibus astriĉtis hepatis poris, & meatibus angustis: sed mitioribus vtendum, ne vis hepatis contractis obstructionem in eo excites, & ne immoderatius refrigerando ex phlegmone scirrhum efficias, morbu, aut insanabilem, aut sanatu difficilem: ne item saniem ex phlegmone hepatis, vt pleuræ & aliarum partium internarum resudantem vacuari prohibeas, & in hepar regeras: sed modice tergeas: ne denique bilem flauam ita compingas, & folliculi fellis stomachorum orificia sic cōtrahas, vt bilis in folliculum recipi nequeat. Sint igitur clementer frigida, & styptica: hisque misceantur quæ modice aperiunt & tergent: siue sumantur, vt syrup. rosatus ex hepatica, ex eupatorio vero, ex succo oxalidis, cydoniorum cum aqua solani, intybi, oxalidis, foliorum & radicum plantaginis, quæ refrigerat, siccat, astringit sanguinis pro fluuia, & si quid aduratur, refrigerat, addita aqua cichorij, adianti albi, quæ etiam aperit & terget: siue admoueantur: vt, litus ex oleo rosato, et cydoniorum: vt fotus ex aqua rosarum, plantaginis, solani cum linteo: ut sacculi ex tribus santalis, malicorio, balaustijs, rosis tritis, additis caphuræ granis quatuor, aut sex, si valentiori remedio est opus.
units.tr: (3) COLD astringents that repel the matter flowing to the liver and prevent its flux, by constricting the pores and narrow passages of the liver; but milder ones must be used, lest the power of the liver, contracted, produce an obstruction in it, and lest by cooling too immoderately you turn the phlegmon into a scirrhus, a disease either incurable or hard to cure. Likewise, do not prevent the pus from the liver's phlegmon, which exudes to the pleura and other internal parts, from being evacuated, and so sent back into the liver; but purge it gently. Finally, do not so bind the yellow bile, nor so constrict the orifices of the gall bladder's ducts, that the bile cannot be received into the gall bladder. Let the remedies therefore be gently cooling and astringent, and mixed with things that open and cleanse moderately, whether they are taken, such as rose syrup with hepatica, with eupatorium, with juice of sorrel, quince with water of nightshade, of endive, of sorrel, of the leaves and roots of plantain, which cools, dries and binds the flux of blood, and, if anything is burnt, cools it; with the addition of water of chicory and white maidenhair, which also opens and cleanses; or whether they are applied, such as a poultice of rose and quince oil; a fomentation of rose water, plantain and nightshade with linen; or little bags of three sandalwoods, pomegranate rind, myrobalans, crushed roses, with four or six grains of camphor added, if a stronger remedy is needed.

units.la: Si autem sanguis est pituitosus, sumendum est mel rosatum, cum syrup. rosato & aqua absinthij: admouendaque cum dictis frigidis calida: ut, absinthiū, schœnanthum, mastiche: sine fotus est faciendus, his coctis aut destillatis: sine sacculi ex his parum tritis: sine litus ex oleo absinthij mastichino.
units.tr: But if the blood is phlegmatic, honey of roses is to be taken, with rose syrup and wormwood water; and warm things are to be applied together with the cooling ones, such as wormwood, camel's hay (schoenanthum), mastic; either a fomentation is to be made of these, boiled or distilled; or little bags of these lightly crushed; or a liniment of mastic and wormwood oil.

units.la: 4. MATERIAM coquentibus mistā, additis tamen semper astringentibus ad partis principis robur seruandum: ut, syrup. rosato, ex succo oxalidis, de ribes. Si pituita adest, mel detur rosatum, oxymeli simplex, syrup. de duabus & quinqueradicibus: præsertim si phlegmone erit in gibba hepatis, et coctaiam sit, & corpus reliquum purum: si melancholia, syrup. fumariæ, & de pomis simplex.
units.tr: (4) MATERIAL mixed with things that concoct, always adding astringents to preserve the strength of the principal part: for example, rose syrup, sorrel juice, and of barberries. If phlegm is present, honey of roses is given, simple oxymel, and syrup of the two and five roots; especially if the phlegmon is on the convex part of the liver and the rest of the body is clean; if melancholy, syrup of fumitory and simple syrup of apples.

units.la: 5. MATERIAM illam vacuātibus clemeter: per deiectionem, si phlegmone simam hepatis partem obsidet: vel si gibbam, mouen tibus vrinam, si pauca est vtrobique materia: si enim multa, etiam per intestina est suspectata purgatio Galeno. Cassia igitur, manna, & rhabarbari infusum bilem (si abundat) vacuando sunt salubria, quia non trahunt a longinquo, nec materias exagitando ad fluendum incitant.
units.tr: (5) Gently evacuate that matter: by stool if the phlegmon besieges the flat part of the liver, or, if the convex part, by urine-provoking remedies, if the matter is small in amount on either side. For if it is abundant, Galen suspects purging even through the intestines. Therefore cassia, manna, and an infusion of rhubarb are wholesome for emptying the bile (if it abounds), because they do not draw it from afar, nor stir up matter to flow by agitating it.

units.la: 6. RELIQVIAS materia digerentib. mistis tamen styptics: vt, absinthio potico, rosis, mastiche, schoenatho, spica nardi. (Pars enim hac opus habet toti corpori commune, & ad vitam necessarium) cum chamaemelo, meliloto, anetho, althaea, sive decoctum ad fovendum hypochondrium dextrum facere libet, sive ex his tritis sacculum, sive linimentum, vel vnguentu ex oleo lilij, chamaemeli, anethi, absinthij.
units.tr: (6) For dissolving the remaining matter, mix with astringents: for example, Pontic wormwood, roses, mastic, camel's hay, spikenard. (For this part needs what is common to the whole body and necessary for life.) With chamomile, melilot, dill, marshmallow; or it is pleasing to make a decoction for fomenting the right hypochondrium; or from these lightly crushed, a little bag; or a liniment or ointment of lily oil, chamomile, dill, and wormwood.

units.la: 7. INTEMPERIEM a materia reliquam fere calidam a sanguine & bile corrigentibus frigidis: vbi scilicet phlegmone resoluetibus est persanata. Si enim suppuratur (quod dolores et febres tunc intensiores declarant rant) coctio hæc nobis iuuāda cataplasmate ex decocto ficuum siccarum, vuarū passarū, althææ, maluæ, se. lini & fœnigræci, cum butyro, oleo, amygdal. dulcium, adipe gallinæ, anseris. Abscessum deinde rumpēs motu violento, qualis in saltu, vomitu, tussi, sternuta mento fit: postea tergebis per vretica: vt, decoctum cicerum rubrorū, vel hordei cū mul sa, vel aqua saccharata, si vlcus est in gibba: per cassiam verò, mannam, serum lactis caprini, & alia aluum deiicientia, si est in sima. Postremò vlcus est glutinandū cum bolo armenia, sigillo lemnio. Si autē hepar obdu-ruit, molliatur emplastro meliloti Mesuæ vel malua, althæa, farina lini, fœnigræci, butyro, cerato, œsypato Philagrij apud Mesuem: adhæc œsypus ipse cum oleo amygdalarum dulcium, vel butyro, mirè scirrhos emollit: qui si sint exquisiti & absoluti, sunt insanabiles in hepate, & cæteris partibus.
units.tr: (7) Correct the remaining intemperament, which is almost hot, from blood and bile, with cooling remedies: when the phlegmon has been thoroughly cured by resolving remedies. For if it suppurates (which the then more intense pains and fevers declare), we must aid that concoction with a poultice of decoction of dried figs, raisins, marshmallow, mallow, linseed and fenugreek, with butter, oil, sweet almonds, and fat of hen or goose. Then, when the abscess is ruptured by a violent motion, such as occurs in leaping, vomiting, coughing or sneezing, afterwards cleanse it by diuretics: for example, a decoction of red chickpeas, or barley with honey, or sugared water, if the ulcer is on the convex part; but by cassia, manna, goat's whey, and other laxatives, if it is on the flat part. Finally the ulcer is to be glued together with Armenian bole and Lemnian sealed earth. But if the liver has become hard, it is to be softened with a plaster of melilot according to Mesue, or of mallow, marshmallow, linseed meal, fenugreek, butter, cerate, and oesypum of Philagrius according to Mesue; besides, oesypum itself with oil of sweet almonds or butter wondrously softens scirrhi; which, if they are exquisite and complete, are incurable in the liver and in the other parts.

units.la: IMBECILLITATIS HEPATIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF WEAKNESS OF THE LIVER.

units.la: HEPATIS, vt aliarum partium imbecillitas, à quauis intemperie insigni fit: per contrariaque corrigitur, additis clementer aperientibus: quod fere simul adest obstructio à congestis in eo per imbecillam sanguificationem excrementis: additis etiam modicè astringentibus, quæ partis principis robur: præsertim à calore solutum, aut soluendum tueantur. Sint præterea tenuium partium, tergeant, leniant, vt dicta excrementa vacuent.
units.tr: Weakness of the liver, like that of the other parts, arises from some marked intemperance, and is corrected by contraries, with gently opening remedies added. Obstruction usually accompanies it, from excrements gathered in the liver through weak blood-making, so slightly astringent remedies should also be added, to preserve the strength of the principal part, especially when it has been loosened by heat or is about to be. Moreover, the remedies should be of thin parts, to cleanse and soothe, so that these excrements may be evacuated.

units.la: Quas vires habent terebinthina, cinamomum, vuæ passæ, pistacia, schœnanthum, spica nardi, absinthiu ponticu: quamuis enim caleant, sunt tamen ob id salubria, quod fere hæc imbecillitas ab intemperie frigida fit, vel primo, vel succedente calori immodico, & ob id hepatis sanguinem, & spiritum, & calorem natiuum dissipanti: si tamen calor adhuc subest, vitentur calida, & vuæ passæ hepati tota substantia familiares: acidæ (quales nobis clibano coctæ) sumantur loco dulcium: vt quæ etiam dysenteriam hepaticam sanent. Tam intybus quoque & hepar par lupi, quàm caro limacum, hepatis intem periei, tum calidæ, tum frigidæ, salubris est tota sua substantia, ablato limacum lentore multis lotionibus & frictionibus in lixiuio calido, vel aqua calida, sali aut arenis mista: frigida enim durescunt. Aqua etiam ex li- macibus destillata mane ad vncias sex sum- pta, hepar imbecillū mirè roborat, et phthi- sicis gracilibusque est remedio: absinthium ponticum idem promittit, vt etiam solo ipsi- us vsu hydrops sanetur: cuius species omnes drachmis duabus diacurcumæ mane cum li- quore aliquo, vt aqua absinthij sumptis, sa- nari scribit Auicen. Aqua hordei intempe- riem hepatis calidam post febres biliosas re- lictam persanat. Dialaccæ etiam cochlear vnum, hepar roborat. Δι' οἰνῶς, Galen. lib. 8. c. ph. p. cap. 14. dysenteriam hepaticam sanat Auicennæ & aliis multis probatus pastillus. Rhabarbarum hepatis vita, & aliorum medicamentorum frænum, bis in hebdomada sumptum ad drachmam vnam dysenteriam hepaticam secreto quorundam inuento persanat. Idem possunt trochisci de rhabarbaro, bis quoque in hebdomada sumpti à drachma una ad drachmas duas: & trochisci de rosis, vel de eupatorio cum syrup. absinthij, eupatorij, vel aquis similibus: saepe enim mutanda sunt medicamenta in affectu hoc longiore, ne natura partis vni assueta, eius vires contem nat. Quod si aliquod horum sit paulo calidius, temperabis aqua cichorij, intybi, & alia rum seridis specierum: spodium quoq; et diarhodum abbatis, & commune, & scrup. trium santalorum Nicolai. Quod si facultas hepatis coctrix est imbecilla, salubria sunt calida humida: si retentrix, sicca: quia tamen una partis alicuius facultate naturali imbecilla, reliquae debiles esse consueuerunt, ob id medicamentum compositum, omnes istas facultates naturales roboret oportet: ut, electuarium triu santalorum, syrup. de eupatorio vero, vel de absinthio pontico seu Romano, ad iectis simplicibus medicamentis, quae facultates quaesitas sortita sint, qualia & abunde sunt dicta, & dicentur posteà.
units.tr: Turpentine, cinnamon, raisins, pistachio, camel's hay (schoenanthus), spikenard and Pontic wormwood have the following powers. Although they warm, they are nonetheless wholesome for this weakness, because it arises mostly from a cold intemperance, either at first or following on excessive heat, which dissipates the blood, the spirit and the natural heat of the liver. If heat still lies beneath, however, hot things should be avoided. Raisins, which are wholly familiar to the liver in their whole substance, should be taken in place of sweet things in their acid form (such as those baked in an oven), since these also heal hepatic dysentery. Chicory too, and the liver-herb called par lupi, as well as the flesh of slugs, are wholesome in their whole substance for liver intemperance, whether hot or cold, provided the slimy mucus of the slugs is removed by many washings and rubbings in warm lye or warm water, mixed with salt or sand, since cold slugs harden. Water distilled from slugs, taken in the morning in an amount of six ounces, greatly strengthens a weak liver, and is a remedy for consumptives and the thin. Pontic wormwood promises the same, so that dropsy may be cured by its use alone. Avicenna writes that all its kinds, taken in the morning in two drachms of diacurcuma with some liquid such as wormwood water, are cured. Barley water cures the hot intemperance of the liver left after bilious fevers. A spoonful of dialacca also strengthens the liver. Diaoinos [Δι' οἰνῶς], Galen, book 8, chapter 14, cures hepatic dysentery; the lozenge approved by Avicenna and many others also cures it. Rhubarb, the life of the liver and a bridle on other medicines, taken twice a week to the amount of one drachm, cures hepatic dysentery by a secret discovered by certain people. Troches of rhubarb, likewise taken twice a week, from one drachm up to two drachms, can do the same, as can troches of roses, or of eupatorium, with syrup of wormwood, of eupatorium, or similar waters. For medicines in this longer affliction must often be changed, lest the nature of the part, accustomed to one, despise its powers. If any of these is somewhat too hot, you will temper it with chicory water, endive water and other similar species; likewise spodium, the abbot's diarhodon, the common one, and the electuary of three sandalwoods of Nicolaus. If the digestive faculty of the liver is weak, warm moist remedies are wholesome; if its retentive faculty, dry ones. Yet because when one natural faculty of a part is weak the others are usually weak too, a compound medicine ought to strengthen all these natural faculties: such as the electuary of three sandalwoods, and syrup of eupatorium or of Pontic or Roman wormwood, with simple medicines added that have obtained the faculties sought, as has been said at length, and will be said later.

units.la: ICTERI
units.tr: ICTERUS (JAUNDICE)

units.la: ICTERI CVRATIO.
units.tr: The Cure of Jaundice

units.la: Icteri uaria est curatio pro causis uarijs: qui autem est à bilis copia, hepatis, & uenarum intemperiem calidam sequente, curatur quatuor auxiliorum generibus.
units.tr: The cure of jaundice varies with its various causes. The jaundice that arises from an excess of bile, with a hot intemperance of the liver and veins, is treated by four kinds of remedies.

units.la: VICTVS ratione refrigerante, humectante.
units.tr: Diet: a regimen that cools and moistens.

units.la: 2. BILEM, si crassior est, & tenacior apparantibus: ut, syrup. ex succo oxalidis, granatorum, omphacij, limonum, citrorum, intybi, cichorij, violarum, rosarum cum duplo aquarum solani, plantaginis, lactucæ, oxalidis, intybi, cichorij.
units.tr: 2. Preparing the bile, if it is thicker and more tenacious: for example, a syrup of the juice of sorrel, pomegranates, unripe grapes, lemons, citrons, endive, chicory and violets, and of roses, with twice the amount of water of nightshade, plantain, lettuce, sorrel, endive and chicory.

units.la: 3. CHOLAGOGIS, ut cassia, manna, electario rosato, vel de succo rosarum, diapruno scammoniato, rhabarbaro, vel pulue rato, vel, si timetur obstructio, infuso. Venæ etiam sectione, si toti corpori est communis intemperies, & si non est suspitio, ne bilis largior, calidior, tenuior furiosa turgeat, cum sanguis aliorum humorum sit velut frænum & retinaculum.
units.tr: 3. Cholagogues, such as cassia, manna, rose electuary or electuary of rose juice, diaprunum scammoniatum, rhubarb, either powdered or, if obstruction is feared, as an infusion. Also bloodletting from the vein, if the intemperance is common to the whole body, and provided there is no suspicion that the bile, being more abundant, hotter and thinner, may swell into fury, since the blood of the other humours acts like a bridle and rein.

units.la: 4. INTEMPERIEM calidam, quæ ictlerum regignere possit, tollentibus sumptis & admotis, frigidis & tenuibus prædictis. Horis enim duabus ante pastus vacuata ex hepate bile (alioqui retenta putreret, febresque augeret, vel gigneret) hypochondrio dextro applicetur pannus lineus mersus his: aquæ intybi lib. vna, aquæ rosarum roborantis vncijs duabus aut tribus, aceti ad penetrandum vncia vna, spicæ scriptulo vno, vel croci granis quatuor, ad calorem partis sanguificæ tuendum, santalorum, spodij ana drac. vna: fiat epithema hepatis vel cordis calidi: cui tamen cordi hæc omni tempore applicari possunt: quia coctionis instrumentum nō est, additis tamen aquis buglossi, been vtroque, caphura, caryophyllis, ligno aloës, croco multum cardiaco: sed his tribus quæ calent, manu parcissima. Sumuntur verò conserua violarum, rosarum, &c alia nunc dicta in apparanda bile. Si verò ictlerus est ab obstructione per bilem crassam aut pituitam, curatur remediorum generibus quatuor.
units.tr: 4. Against the hot intemperance, which can give rise to jaundice, use the cooling and thinning remedies mentioned above, both taken and applied. For two hours before meals, once the bile has been evacuated from the liver (otherwise, if retained, it would putrefy and increase or cause fevers), a linen cloth soaked in the following is applied to the right hypochondrium: one pound of endive water, two or three ounces of strengthening rose water, one ounce of vinegar to help it penetrate, one scruple of spikenard or four grains of saffron to preserve the warmth of the blood-making part, and santal and spodium, one drachm each. Make this an epithem for the liver or the warm heart. It may be applied to the heart at any time, since the heart is not an organ of digestion, with the addition of water of bugloss, both kinds of balm, camphor, cloves, aloeswood and a good deal of cardiac saffron; but of the three warming ingredients, use a very sparing hand. The conserves of violets and roses, and the others mentioned just now for preparing the bile, are taken. If, however, the jaundice arises from obstruction by thick bile or phlegm, it is treated by four kinds of remedies.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione tenuante, aperiente, calfacalfaciente minus, si à bile est obstructio, quàm si à pituita.
units.tr: 1. Diet that thins, opens and warms, but less if the obstruction is from bile than if it is from phlegm.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM apparantibus, vt syrup. incidentibus, tenuantibus, aperientibus, primo mitioribus: vt dictis, & de bizantijs cum aceto: deinde de duabus radicibus, postea de quinque: & item melle rosato, syrup. eupatorij cum aqua cichorij, asparagi, lupuli, fœniculi, apij, cassuthæ, eupathorij: purgato prius ventriculo per cassiæ drach. decem, vel mannæ vnc. duas, vel diaphœnici drach. mas duas, tres, vel pilularum elephanginarum scriptu. quatuor, ne prædicti syrup. materijs multis & crassis à ventriculo in hepar tractis obstructiones augeant.
units.tr: 2. Preparing the matter with syrups that cut, thin and open, milder at first, such as those mentioned, and that of bizantia with vinegar; then that of the two roots, afterwards that of the five; likewise rose honey, and syrup of eupatorium with water of chicory, asparagus, hops, fennel, celery, cassutha and eupatorium. First purge the stomach with ten drachms of cassia, or two ounces of manna, or two or three drachms of diaphoenicon, or four scruples of elephant pills, so that the aforementioned syrups do not increase the obstructions by the many thick materials drawn from the stomach into the liver.

units.la: 3. BILEM crassam, & mistam eipituitam vacuantibus: vt, agarico potenter obstructa liberante: vt rhabarbaro ad drach. duas, vel tres infuso horis decem, vel duodecim in aqua cichorij, vel intybi, & pauco vini albi odori, & fortiter expressso: cui in robustis addere potes agarici trochiscati drach. vnam, & ad saporis gratiam iulepi violati unciam unam: vel diaphœnici, aut scrup. indi unc. dimidia, vel hierœ simplicis, cū melle, unc. una, agarici trochiscati drachma una. Clysteribus etiam acribus, & quorum vis intestina tenuia attingat, est opus: quibus etiam citetur aluus alioqui his pigrior, quia bilis ad eam ferri fere desijt propter obstructionem. Vena quoq; secatur, vel basilica vel salvatella vulgo dicta, inter minimum & annularem digitum media dextræ manus: præsertim cum bilis sanguini est mista: sic enim humores in hepate fixi agitantur, stationem deserunt, & obstruere desinunt.
units.tr: 3. Evacuating thick bile and bile mixed with phlegm: for example, with agaric, which powerfully frees obstructions; or with rhubarb, two or three drachms, infused for ten or twelve hours in water of chicory or endive with a little light white wine, and strongly pressed out. To this, in robust patients, you may add one drachm of troches of agaric, and one ounce of violet julep for the sake of taste; or half an ounce of diaphoenicon or of Indian powder; or one ounce of simple hiera with honey and one drachm of troches of agaric. Sharp enemas are also needed, whose force reaches the thin intestines, by which the bowel, otherwise sluggish, is also stimulated, since bile has almost ceased to flow down to it on account of the obstruction. The vein is also opened, either the basilic or what is commonly called the salvatella, between the middle and ring fingers of the right hand, especially when the bile is mixed with blood. For in this way the humours fixed in the liver are stirred up, leave their station and cease to obstruct.

units.la: 4. MEATVS aperientibus syrupis, & aquis prius dictis materiam apparare: præterea radicibus quinque apij, fœniculi, asparagi, rusci, petroselini lotis, & ad dimidias ex aqua coctis: adhæc foliorum rhaphani contusorum decoctum, vel eo gratior aqua inde destillata matutinis quatuor, sumpta ad unc. quatuor. Lumbrici quoque siccati & sumpti cū vino albo, & saccharo ad saporis gratiam, à nesciente ne auersetur, icterum sanant nant Auic. & aliys permultis, vi quadam secreta. Idem puluis cum syrup. de bizantijs in pilulas formatus, quæ auri foliis intectæ sumantur: & postridie bibat serum caprinum. Idem præstat Auic. stercus canis ossibus tantum pastī: præsij item decoctī ex vino albo tenui vnciæ quatuor saccharatæ matutinis aliquot potæ, omnem icterū sanant: vel vnc. quatuor decoctiperfecti cicerum rubrorū, & radicum asparagi.
units.tr: 4. Preparing the matter with the opening syrups and waters mentioned before; moreover with the five roots of celery, fennel, asparagus, butcher's broom and parsley, washed and boiled down by half in water; also a decoction of crushed horseradish leaves, or the water distilled from them, which is more pleasant, taken in the morning, four ounces at a time.
