Dried earthworms, too, taken with white wine and sugar for the sake of taste, so that the person who does not know what it is is not put off, cure jaundice, says Avicenna and very many others, by a certain secret power. The same powder formed into pills with syrup of bizantia, to be taken wrapped in gold leaf, and the next day he should drink goat's whey. Avicenna offers the same with the dung of dogs fed on bones alone. Likewise a decoction of horehound in thin white wine, four ounces sweetened, drunk several mornings, cures all jaundice; or four ounces of a thoroughly boiled decoction of red chickpeas and asparagus roots.

units.la: Capræ item prius nutritæ herbis aperientibus, fœniculo, apio, petroselino, rusco, lupulo, eupatorio, asparago, lactis lib. tres, accipiant noctē vna seminis cnici pugillū vnum: postridie caseosa eius substantia separata serum potu iterum liberat Auic. Idem præstant aperientia hæc, dialacca, diacucurma, diacalaminthe, à drachmis duabus, ad drachmas quatuor, et trochisci rhabarbari, eupatorij, rosarum, ad drachmā vnam cum aquis prædictis, mutata sæpe remedij forma, ut in cæteris affectibus diuturnis: ne vni natura assuescat, sed semper in id fiat mutatio, quod affectus et affectæ partis natura et aëris expostulat. Cutis aut & oculorum color flavus tollitur, partim mouetibus vrinas dictis, partim admotis balneo ex decocto chamæmeli, meliloti, & similium: balneo item sulfureo, & aëre calido, cæteris q; poros aperientibus, & humorem tenuantibus, foras q; trahentibus, et sudore vacuantibus. Oculo aut conse runt sternutamenta, quia materiam excutiunt, & acetū calidum odoratum: vt eius va pore apertis poris materia exhalet. Eisdem initio aqua rosarum applicari potest, ne adeo tingantur: aliys autem temporibus hæc, & c. astringentia sunt noxia.
units.tr: Goats, too, first fed on opening herbs (fennel, celery, parsley, butcher's broom, hops, eupatorium, asparagus), three pounds of milk, and take in the evening one handful of cnicus seed. The next day, when the cheesy substance has been separated, the whey drunk again frees them, says Avicenna. The following opening remedies do the same: dialacca, diacucurma and diacalaminthe, from two drachms up to four drachms, and troches of rhubarb, eupatorium and roses, one drachm, with the waters mentioned above. The form of the remedy should often be changed, as in other long-lasting affections, so that the nature does not grow accustomed to one thing, but the change is always made to what the nature of the affection and of the affected part and of the air demands. The yellow colour of the skin and eyes is removed, partly by moving the urine as said, partly by applying baths of a decoction of chamomile, melilot and the like; also by a sulphur bath and warm air, and by other things that open the pores, thin the humour, draw it outwards and empty it by sweat. For the eyes, sneezing is helpful, since it shakes out the matter, and warm vinegar with a pleasant smell, so that by its vapour the matter may exhale as the pores are opened. At the beginning, rose water may be applied to the eyes so that they are not so stained; but at other times these and other astringents are harmful.

units.la: Si aut icterus est niger, curatur vt præcedens, sed remediys melancholiæ debitis: de quibus in lienis affectibus.
units.tr: If the jaundice is black, it is treated as the preceding kind, but with remedies for melancholy suited to it, which are discussed under the affections of the spleen.

units.la: OBSTRVCTIONIS HEPATIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF OBSTRUCTION OF THE LIVER.

units.la: Hepatis obstructio a materia multa, crassa, lenta, curatur remediorum generibus quatuor.
units.tr: An obstruction of the liver caused by much thick, sluggish matter is cured by four kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione tenui & tenuante, præsertim vbi multus & crudus est succus: post coctionem vero vino albo tenui, capparibus, radicibus petroselini, cichorij, apij, fœniculi, vitentur autem vina crassa et dulcia omnia, & acerba & cruda, etc. crassum & lentum succum gignentia: somnus ite diurnus, præsertim mox à cibo, et diuturnus.
units.tr: 1. DIET, of a thin and attenuating kind, especially where the juice is abundant and crude. After digestion, a thin white wine, capers, and roots of parsley, chicory, celery and fennel. Thick and sweet wines, and all sour and raw foods, which generate thick, sluggish juice, should be avoided, etc. Sleep by day, likewise, should be avoided, especially straight after food, and long sleep too.

units.la: 2. POST purgatum per cassiam, aut hieram picram, aut pilulas elephanginas ventri culum, incidentibus, & tenuantibus, & tergentibus materiam: vt, melle rosato, oxymelite, syrup. bizantiorum, radicum duarū aut quinque, eupatorij cum aquis fœniculi, cassu tha, eupatorij, asparagi.
units.tr: 2. AFTER purging with cassia, or hiera picra, or elephantine pills, the bowels should be opened with remedies that cut through, thin and cleanse the matter: such as rose honey, oxymel, syrup of the Byzantines, decoction of two or five roots, and of hemp agrimony with fennel water, dodder, hemp agrimony, and asparagus.

units.la: 3. MATERIAM obstruentem vacuantibus: vt, venæ basilicæ dextræ sectione, omni magnæ obstructioni hepatis, etiam initio statim competenti: præcipue si à sanguine est, aut etiam pituita cum sanguine mista, aut etiam sola. Cùm enim materias exagitet, loco que moueri cogat sanguinis missio, obstructioni hepatis, etiam à pituita confert: et post hanc diaphœnicon, indum, ad drachmas quatuor cum decocto radicum asparagi, fœ niculi, rusci, petroseleni, apÿ, & similiu: vel agarici trochiscati drachmæ duæ aquis fœni culi, asparagi, & similium, cum pauco salis gemmæ, ut actio eius sit vegetior, infusæ ho ris decem: vel rhabarbari drachmæ duæ aut tres ÿsdem aquis cum pauco vino albo odo- ro infusæ, addita, si opus est, drachma vna diaphœnici vel agarici trochiscati: pilulæ eti am de rhabarbaro, cum pauco diarhodo ad calorem earum remittendum.
units.tr: 3. EVACUATE the obstructing matter: by opening the right basilic vein. This suits every great obstruction of the liver, even at its very start, especially if it arises from blood, or from phlegm mixed with blood, or even from phlegm alone. For since bloodletting stirs up the matter and forces it to move from its place, it helps an obstruction of the liver even when it comes from phlegm. After this, give diaphoenicon, the indum, four drachms with a decoction of roots of asparagus, fennel, butcher's broom, parsley, celery and the like; or two drachms of troches of agaric, infused for ten hours in waters of fennel, asparagus and the like, with a little rock salt, so that its action is more vigorous; or two or three drachms of rhubarb infused in the same waters, with a little fragrant white wine, adding, if needed, one drachm of diaphoenicon or of troches of agaric. Also pills of rhubarb, with a little diarrhodon, to temper their heat.

units.la: 4. VIAS iam purgatas, aperientibus, fri- gidis quidem, sed tenuantibus in materia cali da, vt bile crassa, qualia sunt intybus horten sis & agrestis, cichorium, & omne seridis, sonchi, hieracij, chondrillæ genus: syrup. ci- chorij à Nicolao scriptus, cum rhabarbaro, aqua foliorum, & radicum plantaginis, de- coctum quinque seminum communium fri- gidorum, rhabarbarū. Si frigida autem est materia, calydis syrupis, & aquis ante dictis in secundo remediorū genere, aperiendum. Si vtraque misceatur, temperatis: vt, lupo sali- stario, vuis passis, glycyrrhiza, adiato albo, trochiscis rosarum, vel eupatorij: vel calidis & frigidis prædictis certa mensura mistis: vt, dialacca, diacucurma, praßij decoctum, trochisci, rhabarbari cum aqua cichorij, inrybi, diarhodo. Si ob vasorum hepatis, & in his extremis osculorum angustiam obstructio fit, hac percurata vitentur crassa, lenta, multa alimenta, motus, balneu, studium: somnus mox à cibo. Si ab hepatis imbecillitate, illi prospiciatur vti ante scripsimus.
units.tr: 4. NOW that the passages are cleared, open them with aperients that are cold but thin, suited to matter that is hot, such as thick bile: endive, wild chicory, chicory, and every kind of sow-thistle, sowthistle, hawkweed and chondrilla. Syrup of chicory as described by Nicolaus, with rhubarb, water of plantain leaves and roots, and a decoction of the five common cold seeds, and rhubarb. If the matter is cold, open with the chalybeate syrups and the waters mentioned earlier in the second class of remedies. If both kinds are present, use tempered remedies: such as lupine flour, raisins, liquorice, white iris, rose troches, or agrimony; or a set measure of the aforesaid hot and cold remedies mixed: such as dialacca, diacurcuma, decoction of prasium, troches, and rhubarb with chicory water and diarrhodon. If the obstruction comes from narrowness of the vessels and of the tiny openings at their ends, then, once this has been treated, avoid thick, sluggish, abundant foods, exercise, bathing and study, and sleep straight after food. If it comes from weakness of the liver, provide for that as we have written above.

units.la: HYDROPIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF DROPSY.

units.la: Hydrops ascites curatur tribus remedio rum generibus.
units.tr: Dropsy of the belly (ascites) is cured by three kinds of remedy.

units.la: VICTVS ratione calida sicca: quoniam causa eius tumoris in ventre continens, & propinqua, est aqua frigida humida: adhæc hepatis actio, scilicet sanguificatio frustrata est ab intemperie frigida, licet eam intemperies calida sanguinem & spiritum resoluendo excitet interdum: tuncq; minus calidis pugnandum est, quàm dum à frigidis causis abolita est sanguificatio. Viuat igitur in aere libero, calido, sicco, natura, partis anni, aut nostra industria, ignibus luculentis, suffitibus aromatum. Cibi condiantur pipere, caryophyllis, & similibus aromatis: sed ij si vires valent, sint pauci, vt calor natiuus aquas illas interea resoluat. Vinũ sit album tenue, sed paucum: vinosum tamen, ni si à causa sit calida. Aquam verò ne spectet quidem, quod siti inexpleta cum torquentur, visa illa ad bibendum incitantur.
units.tr: DIET of a warm and dry kind, since the cause of this swelling in the belly, the containing and immediate cause, is cold, moist water. Moreover, the liver's action, namely the making of blood, is frustrated by cold intemperance, although warm intemperance sometimes stirs it up by dissolving blood and spirit. So one must contend less with warm causes than when the making of blood has been destroyed by cold ones. Let him live in open, warm, dry air, whether by nature, by the season of the year, or by our own care, with bright fires and fumigations of aromatics. Foods should be seasoned with pepper, cloves and similar spices, but if his strength allows, let them be few, so that his natural heat may meanwhile dissolve those waters. Wine should be white and thin, but in small amounts, yet vinous unless the cause is hot. He should not even look at water, since, tormented by unquenchable thirst, they are driven to drink whatever they see.

units.la: Exercitatio & vigilia largior quiete, & somno est salubris, nisi magna ex tumore spi randi difficultas prohibeat.
units.tr: Exercise and wakefulness are more wholesome than rest and sleep, unless great difficulty in breathing from the swelling prevents them.

units.la: 2. AQVAS hydropem excitantes, vacuantibus primò purgatorijs: vt, sero laćtis caprini, rhabarbaro, hepar etiam roborante, agarico hepati innoxio, succo brassicæ marinæ (quam soldanellam vulgus, arabes cachitam vocant) citra molestiam: hydragogæ, et hepar roborante. (Quæ duo effećta in hydrope curando sunt necessaria) ac etiam faciei maculas tergente. Datur autem à drachmis tribus ad quatur Myrobalanis citreis etiam in causa calida: sagapenum item in catapotia Mesuæ formatum drachma vna, valentius purgat quàm brassica marina. Radicum quo que ireos syluestris, aut ex loco sicciore, purgatarum, lotarum, & tritarum succus resi-dendo purgatus, quarto vel sexto quoque die sumptus: primò ad drachmas duas, tres, tan-dem ad vnciam vnam, seu cum Gordonio, quantum dimidia oui testa contineri potest, aquas valenter purgat, & curabilem omnè ascitem persanat. Intercedentibus verò die-bus hepar roborabis succo vel aqua, prassij, absinthij, cassuthæ: his etiam omnibus aquas hydropis purgantibus miscenda sunt hepar roborantia: aut post illa sunt sumenda: datur etiam eius succi semuncia cum syrup. capil. vene. vel si friget cœlum cu syrup. absinthij, aut prassij vncia vna, et vini albi parui vnc. duabus, vel decoctum ireos diebus nouem, horis tribus ante cibum datur: vel radicis hu ius taleolæ decem, vino albo, imbecillo mace-rantur noctè: postridie vinum ipsum mane bibitur diebus aliquot magno successu. Fiant autem vacuationes aquarum parcæ, sed frequentes, ut interim roboretur natura. Thy- melaea quoque (mezereon arabes vocant) et ex ea electarium Mesuæ drach.duabus sumptum, magna molestia multas aquas vacuat, nocetq; hepati: ob id non vtendum: nec daph-noides, quam laureolâ vocant: succus quoq; cucumeris agrestis siccatus, elaterium vocant, omnium purgantium durantissimus: nâ Plinio etiam centum annos integer feruatur: euphorbij quoq; grana octo, et pilulæ de euphorbio Mesue, vna parua pilula, datæ etiam in quartana, & arthritide frigida, multu vacuant, sed clementia sunt tutiora: vt, agaricus, rhabarbarum, brassica marina, iris. Venam vero in hydrope ne seca, quia intemperiem frigida hepatis vacuato sanguine auxeris, nisi hydrops sit à suppressis mensibus, aut hæmorrhoidibus, sanguine vtrinq; vacuari consueto, in vasa, & hepar regurgitante, et calorem eius natiuum præ copia, et crassitie, & qualitate sæpe aliena strangulante. Quamquam autem in ascite & tympanite interdum rubra sit vrina, non ob id vena secanda est, quia talis fit ob imbecillitatem facultatis hepatis coquendo secernentis. Si hydrops est ab hepatis tumore aliquo praeter naturam, is ante est curandus, ut ante est praeceptum.
units.tr: 2. THE WATERS that provoke dropsy: first evacuate with purgatives, such as whey of goat's milk, rhubarb, agaric, which strengthens the liver and does it no harm, and juice of sea cabbage (which the common people call soldanella and the Arabs cachitam), without discomfort. These are hydragogues that also strengthen the liver, two effects that are necessary in curing dropsy, and they also cleanse facial blemishes. Myrobalans, citrine, are given from three to four drachms, even when the cause is hot. Sagapenum likewise, formed into Mesue's catapotia, one drachm, purges more strongly than sea cabbage. Also the juice of wild iris roots, purged, washed and ground, allowed to settle and then taken every fourth or sixth day: first two or three drachms, then at last one ounce, or, with Gordonius, as much as half an eggshell can hold. It powerfully purges the waters and cures any curable ascites. On the intervening days, strengthen the liver with juice or water of prasium, wormwood or dodder. All these water-purging remedies should be mixed with liver-strengthening ones, or taken after them. Also give half an ounce of its juice with syrup of maidenhair, or, if the sky is cold, one ounce of syrup of wormwood or prasium with two ounces of thin white wine. Or a decoction of iris is given for nine days, three hours before food. Or ten slices of this root are steeped overnight in weak white wine, and the wine itself is drunk the next morning for several days with great success. Evacuations of water should be sparing but frequent, so that nature is strengthened in the meantime. Thymelaea too (the Arabs call it mezereon), and Mesue's electuary taken in two drachms, drain many waters but cause great discomfort and harm the liver; so it is not to be used. Nor is daphnoides, which they call laureola. Nor is the juice of wild cucumber, dried, called elaterium, the most violent of all purgatives, for Pliny says it keeps whole for a hundred years. Also eight grains of spurge, and Mesue's pills of spurge, one small pill, given even in quartan fever and cold arthritis, purge a great deal, but gentle remedies are safer, such as agaric, rhubarb, sea cabbage and iris. Do not open a vein in dropsy, because by evacuating blood you would increase the cold intemperance of the liver, unless the dropsy comes from suppressed menses or haemorrhoids, which are customarily evacuated by blood on either side, into the vessels and the liver, which often regurgitates and, through excess, thickness and a frequently alien quality, strangles its natural heat. Although in ascites and tympanites the urine is sometimes red, the vein must not be opened on that account, because this happens through weakness of the liver's faculty of concocting and secreting. If the dropsy comes from some swelling of the liver beyond its natural state, that must be treated first, as was taught above.

units.la: 2. SECVNDO, vreticis & aperientibus inter purgatoria sumptis: ut, syrup. bizantiorum, duarum & quinque radicum cum aqua, aut decocto absinthij, fœniculi, praßij, cassuthæ.
units.tr: 2. SECOND, take diuretics and aperients among the purgatives, such as syrup of the Byzantines, of the two and five roots, with water or a decoction of wormwood, fennel, prasium and dodder.

units.la: 3. TERTIO, per insensilem transpiratum resoluentibus: ut, ventris solius insolatu, aut in arenis calentibus impositu, aut balneo ex vrina pueri biliosi, aut suffitu per mensam, foramen ventri recipiendo æquale habentem, facto ex decocto saluiæ, maioranæ, rorismarini, pulegij, chamæmeli, anethi, origani, calaminthes, stœchados, foliorum lauri, salis, aluminis, sulphuris in vini albi, & lixiuij, ana libras octo: impositis sæpe lapidibus ignitis, ne frigescat. Ne autem vapor disperdatur, dolio suffitus materiam continenti, aut panno denso prohibe. Ventri etiam applicare possis sacculos, arena, sale, alumine, sulphure plenos, vel oleum lilij, anethi, vel pulverem seminis anisi, baccarum lauri, et similium: vel ex his & stercore caprino, aut vaccino à vacca adhuc calido cataplasma: vel vnguentum agrippæ, vel limaces cum testa tritos cataplasmatis modo, donec per se cadant, admonere. Postremò ventris incisione aquas emittere licet, vbi cætera nihil profuerunt, si æger est iuuenis & robustus: nec tamen vniuersim vacues, sed particulatim per dies aliquot.
units.tr: 3. THIRD, dissolve it by insensible perspiration: for example, by sunning the belly alone, or laying it on hot sand, or by a bath of the urine of a bilious boy, or by a fumigation through a stool with a hole fitted to the belly. This is made from a decoction of sage, marjoram, rosemary, pennyroyal, chamomile, dill, oregano, calamint, stoechas, bay leaves, salt, alum and sulphur, in white wine and lye, eight pounds of each, with hot stones often placed in it so that it does not cool. To keep the vapour from escaping, shield the fumigation with a barrel holding the material or with a thick cloth. You may also apply to the belly small bags full of sand, salt, alum or sulphur, or of oil of lily or dill, or powder of anise seed, bay berries and the like; or a poultice of these with goat or cow dung still warm from the cow; or Agrippa's ointment; or snails crushed with their shells, applied as a poultice until they fall off by themselves, as I advise. Finally, incision of the belly to let out the waters is permitted when the other measures have done no good, if the patient is young and robust. Yet do not drain him all at once, but in portions over several days.

units.la: Aperitur autem ad musculum obliquum ascendentem dextrum, si hepar primario est affectum: sinistrum verò si lien cute prius deorsum reuulsa, vt post incisionem locum naturalem repetens, hiatum obturet, ne aqua largior effluat, vel immisso siphone in hiatu: aqua autem quotidie bis, aut ter siphonis operculo ablato mittatur, ægro interim roborato cibis delectis, & condituris analepticis: vt dialaccæ drachmis duabus mane sumptis: vel diacucurma, cum aqua intybi, absinthij, cassuthæ, & cibis calidis modicè humidis, tenuibus, coctu & distributu facilibus: aut si causa est calida, electario trium santalorum, diarhodo abbatis. Hepar quoque lupi, & rhabarbarum, & trochisci ex eo hepar mire roborant, bis in hebdomada dati ad dra chmas duas, & alia quae tota sua substantia hepar roborant. Electarium de vino, syrup. de bizantijs, si calida est causa, si vero frigida, syrup. absinthij cum aqua prassij, cassutha, eupatorij.
units.tr: The incision is made over the right oblique ascending muscle if the liver is chiefly affected, or over the left if the spleen is. First the skin is pulled down, so that after the incision it returns to its natural place and closes the opening, lest too much water flow out; alternatively a siphon is inserted into the opening. The water is drawn off once or twice a day, or three times, with the cap of the siphon removed, while the patient is meanwhile built up with choice foods and analeptic preparations: for example, two drachms of dialacca taken in the morning; or diacucurma with water of endive, wormwood and cuscuta, and warm foods that are moderately moist, thin, and easy to cook and digest. Or, if the cause is hot, an electuary of three santals, or diarhodon abbatis. The liver of wolf, rhubarb, and troches made from it greatly strengthen the liver, given twice a week in doses of two drachms, as do other things that strengthen the liver by their whole substance. An electuary of wine, and syrup de bizantijs if the cause is hot; if cold, syrup of wormwood with water of leek, cuscuta and eupatorium.

units.la: HYDROPS TYMPANITES CVRATVR.
units.tr: Treatment of Tympanitic Dropsy

units.la: VICTVS ratione, vt praedictus hydrops calida, sicca, & flatus resoluen te, & fuga eorum omnium quae flatus gignunt, fame, siti, exercitatione.
units.tr: Regimen: the dropsy just described is hot and dry and dissolves wind, so avoid all the things that generate wind; also hunger, thirst and exercise.

units.la: 2. FLATVS ipsos dissipantibus medicamentis, & aquas, pituitasque flatuum fomites vacuantibus ante dictis & dicendis. Flatus autem dissipant, ventri impositi calentes sacculi ex milio, panico, sale, cinere, furfure, & sulphure: spongiae item vel panni mersi decocto chamaemeli, meliloti, origani, calaminthes, & similiter resoluentibus: vesica eodem decocto plena.
units.tr: 2. Wind is dispelled by medicines that disperse flatulence and by those that purge the water and phlegm which feed it, as mentioned above and below. Warm little bags filled with millet, panic grass, salt, ashes, bran and sulphur, placed on the belly, disperse wind; likewise sponges or cloths soaked in a decoction of chamomile, melilot, marjoram, calamint, and similar warming remedies; or a bladder filled with the same decoction.

units.la: Cucurbitula quoque magna cu larga flamma, bis, terue vmbilico imposita sine incisione mire flatus in colico dolore, & tympania resoluit. Galanga, cyminu, diagalanga, diacyminum, diamoschus salubriter sumuntur, et scrup. de baccis lauri drach. tres, vel semucia clysteribus miscetur factis ex ruta, saluia, ana ma. vno, florum chamemeli, meliloti, ane thi, centauri parui, chamedryos, ana pug. vno, se. anisi, cymini ana drachma duabus coctis in lixiuio, aut vino, aut hydro mel, aut aqua fabrorum, addita hiera picra semuncia, et olei anethi, aut ruta, vncijs tribus: balani quoq; ex dictorum puluere, misto cum melle cocto ad consistentiam idoneam. Ventrem quoque linteis calidis fricuisse bonum est, vt apertis poris tenuati flatus exhalent: melius cum manibus carnosis, & calentibus, & admotis animalium visceribus natu ra sua calidis.
units.tr: A large cupping glass with a broad flame, applied twice or three times to the navel without incision, wonderfully dissolves wind in colic and tympany. Galangal, cumin, diagalangal, diacuminum and diamoschus are taken with benefit; also three drachms of powdered laurel berries, or half an ounce, mixed into enemas made from rue and sage, one handful each; flowers of chamomile, melilot, dill, and lesser centaury, one handful each; and chamedrys; two drachms each of anise and cumin seed, boiled in lye, or wine, or hydromel, or smiths' water; with half an ounce of hiera picra added, and three ounces of dill oil or rue oil. Balls made of the powder of the aforesaid, mixed with honey boiled to a suitable consistency, are also good. It is also good to rub the belly with warm linen cloths, so that with the pores opened the thinned wind may escape; better still with fleshy, warm hands, and with the warm entrails of animals applied, which are naturally warm.

units.la: 3. DISPOSITIONEM hepatis, cau sam
units.tr: 3. Removing the disposition of the liver, the cause

units.la: fam mali, tollentibus: ijs scilicet, quæ illi dispo sitioni sunt contraria, & hepar roborant: de quibus sæpe prius est dictum.
units.tr: of the disease, by those things which are contrary to that disposition and strengthen the liver; these have often been mentioned before.

units.la: Raro autem hydropis species sunt simplices, sedferè secum implexæ.
units.tr: Pure forms of dropsy are rare, but they are usually mixed together.

units.la: Hydrops sarcites (qui & anasarca, et hypo sarca, et leucophlegmatias dicitur) curatur victus ratione, ut hydropes dicti, calida sic-ca: ut, aëre æstiuo, natura vel industria, fuga frigidi, humidi: qualis pluuius, nebulosus. Ci-bo pauco, raro, ob coctricis & sanguificæ fa-cultatis imbecillitatē coctu facili, sed euchy-mo, aut tenui potius quā crasso: ut, vino fla-uo, sed pauco, carnibus delectis, vitellis ouo-rum recentium sorbilibus, pane duro, aut bis coéto: vino, si opus est, mersó, et aspersó in-terdū puluere cinamomi, caryophyllorū, ga-lagæ, macis, anisi, amomi, laccæ lotæ: aut per hunc puluerem vino aliquoties colato.
units.tr: Dropsy with swelling of the flesh (also called anasarca, hyposarca, or leucophlegmatia) is treated by regimen in the same way as the dropsies already described, hot and dry: namely, by a summer air, by natural or deliberate avoidance of what is cold and moist, such as rainy or misty weather. The diet should be sparing and infrequent, because of the weakness of the digestive and blood-making faculties; the food should be easy to cook, producing good chyle rather than thick humour, such as yellow wine, but in small amounts; choice meats; the yolks of fresh eggs to be sipped; hard bread, or twice-baked bread; wine, if needed, with the bread dipped in it; and sometimes sprinkled with powder of cinnamon, cloves, galangal, mace, anise, amomum and washed lac; or wine strained several times through this powder.

units.la: Exercitatio quæ sudorem excitet conti-nenter tergendum, est salubris, si vires va-lent, aut eius vice frictio multa, mollis, aut mediocris: vigiliæ item & affectus animi, et
units.tr: Exercise that brings on sweat, to be wiped off continually, is healthful, if the strength allows; or in its place much soft or moderate rubbing. Likewise wakefulness and emotional disturbances, and

units.la: 2. MATERIAM pituitosam per carnem & habitum corporis totum sparsam, primum apparatibus dictis in ascite: ut, mel le rosato, oxymelite simplici, syrup. duarum & quinque radicum, cum aqua absinthij, foeniculi, cassuthae per dies quinque, aut sex: diutius enim apparanda, quam ascitae materia fluxilis et liquida, ventriculo propinqua, & hepati. Deinde vacuantibus: ut, hierae picrae mellitae uncia una, vel eiusdem semuncia cum agarici trochiscati drachma una, vel pilularum de rhabarbaro drac. duabus, quarto quoque die sumptis: (pituitam enim, & ex hac putrefacta bilem purgant, & hepar roborant) vel rhabarbari, & agarici trochiscati, ana scrip. duobus septimo quoque die sumptis, vel diaphoenico, scrup. indo. quamuis scammonium hepati noxium est: post ea autem scammoniata dantur, quae noxam emendent, aut potius cum his vel ante hac, quae noxam prohibeant: in quibus enim affectibus hepar imbecillum est, quae ipsum laedant, ledant, fugienda sunt: vt scammonium, ellebORUS, colocynthis: quibus si coacti vtimur, diebus consecuturis ea demus, quae ipsum roboret, & noxam corrigant, vel potius ante: propinanda autem simul quae prohibeant. Vacuandum est autem saepe, quia affectus est longus, & solui contumax. Bilem vero in hydrope vacuari nolunt quidam, quòd ea calida sicca pituitam frigidam humidam coërceat & emendet: nisi forte hydropi complexa sit febris biliosa, aut pleuritis. Tunc enim vt in complicatis affectibus contraria remedia indicantibus, vrgentioris maior est habenda ratio, non neglecto tamen altero. Venae autem sectio quanquam omni hydropi est noxia, maxime tamen tympaniae, medio modo ascitae, minimum hyposarcae: quia in hac hydropis specie, minus quàm praedictae duae maligna (tympanias enim pessimus, ascites amborum est medius) cùm in venis continea tur, vt in aliis duobus sub peritonaeo, aliquid eius cum sanguine vacuatur, praesertim sia- nasarca est a suppressis mensib. aut haemorrhoidibus. Vacuatur item materia hæc vre-ticis: vt syrup. bizantiorum, & succo prassij vel decocto eiusdem, aut radicū petroselini, apij, fœniculi, rusci, asparagi. Cantharides au-tem vitandæ, quia flatulentæ, & vesicam vlcerāt. Foris admota materiam hanc resol-uunt: sol æstiuus nudo corpori occurrens, aut arenæ ab hoc calfactæ, cinis ex vino frixus, laconicum, suffitus per lapides ignitos, ex de-coctis in vino, foliis lauri, anetho, origano, abrotono, saluia, roremarino, & similibus. Balneum quoque salsum, nitrosum, alumino sum, sed sulphureum naturale, aut etiam ar-tificiale: salubre etiam ægrum mensæ incuban-tem immittit in clibanum extracto pane te-pentem, sic tamen vt caput sit extra præsur-nium, ne calido aëre suffocetur.
units.tr: 2. The phlegmy matter spread through the flesh and the whole body is to be treated first with the preparations mentioned under ascites: for example, honey of roses, simple oxymel, syrup of the two sorts of five roots, with water of wormwood, fennel and cuscuta, for five or six days; for this matter must be prepared for longer than the fluid and liquid matter of ascites, which is closer to the stomach and the liver. Then purgatives: for example, one ounce of honeyed hiera picra, or half an ounce of it with one drachm of troched agaric, or two drachms of rhubarb pills, taken every fourth day (for they purge phlegm and the bile that rots from it, and strengthen the liver); or rhubarb and troched agaric, two scruples each, taken every seventh day; or diaphoenicon, two scruples. Although scammony is harmful to the liver, scammonies are given afterwards which correct the harm; or rather they are given with or before these things, which prevent the harm. For in diseases where the liver is weak, the things that injure it, such as scammony, hellebore and colocynth, must be avoided; if we are forced to use them, on the following days we give those things which strengthen the liver and correct the harm, or better, we give them beforehand; those that prevent the harm should be given at the same time. Purging should often be repeated, because the disease is long and resists being dissolved. Some men do not want bile purged in dropsy, because bile, being hot and dry, restrains and corrects the cold, moist phlegm; unless perhaps a bilious fever or pleurisy is joined to the dropsy. For then, as in complicated diseases where contrary remedies are indicated, the more urgent condition must be given greater consideration, without neglecting the other. Bloodletting, although harmful in every dropsy, is most harmful in tympany, moderately harmful in ascites, and least harmful in hyposarca; because in this kind of dropsy it is less malignant than the two just mentioned (for tympany is the worst, and ascites is midway between the two). Since the matter is contained in the veins, while in the other two it lies under the peritoneum, some of it is drawn off with the blood; especially when the anasarca comes from suppressed menses or haemorrhoids. This matter is also drawn off by urine: for example, syrup of the Byzantines, and juice of leek or a decoction of it, or decoctions of parsley root, celery, fennel, butcher's broom, and asparagus. Cantharides should be avoided, because they cause wind and ulcerate the bladder. Applied externally, they dissolve this matter: summer sun falling on the bare body, or sand warmed by it, ashes fried in wine, a Laconian bath, fumigation over hot stones with leaves of bay, dill, marjoram, dittany, sage and rosemary boiled in wine, and similar things. Also a salty, nitrous, aluminous bath, but a natural sulphurous one, or even an artificial one. It is also healthful to place the patient, sitting at table, into an oven from which the bread has just been removed and which is still warm, with the head kept outside the opening, lest he be suffocated by the hot air.

units.la: 3. DISPOSITIONEM hepatis, ana sarcæ causam, rollentibus, vt obstructionem, vt tumorem præter naturam, vt intemperi-em aliquam simplicem vel compositam, im-becillitatis effectricem, sanantibus cōtrarijs: vt intemperiem frigidam oppugnabimus e-lectario lectario dialacca, diacucurma, absinthio, eupatorio, rhabarbaro, trochiscis de rhabarbaro per se, aut cum puluere diarhodi, si calor metuitur.
units.tr: 3. Removing the disposition of the liver, the cause of anasarca, by those things which remove obstruction, unnatural swelling, or any simple or compound intemperature that produces weakness, healing by contraries: for example, we will combat cold intemperature with the electuary of dialacca, diacucurma, wormwood, eupatorium, rhubarb, troches of rhubarb alone, or with powder of diarhodon if heat is feared.

units.la: DOLORIS SPLENIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: Treatment of pain in the spleen

units.la: DOLOR splenis si ab intemperie est sola calida, frigida, humida, sicca, simplici vel composita: contrariis æqualibus sumptis & admotis est alterãda: vt pars ad temperiem iustam redeat: quam rem victus ratio in sumendis, admouendis, educendis, et faciendis, abundè præstabit. Si verò est ab intemperie cum materia, calida quidem, vt melancholiæ, tribus remediorum generibus curatur.
units.tr: If the pain of the spleen arises from a simple intemperature, whether hot, cold, moist or dry, or from a compound one, it is to be altered by contraries taken and applied in equal measure, so that the part returns to its proper temperature. A regimen of diet will largely accomplish this, in what is taken, applied, evacuated and done. But if the intemperature is accompanied by matter, hot as in melancholy, it is treated with three kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. MATERIAM apparantibus syrup. fumariæ, epithymi, acetato, intybi, cum aqua intybi, oxalidis, fumariæ.
units.tr: 1. To prepare the matter, use syrup of fumitory, of epithymum, the acetated syrup, of endive, with endive water, of wood sorrel, and of fumitory.

units.la: 2. EANDEM vacuantibus, vt pilulis aureis aggregatiuis, folliculis semnæ, scrup. hamech.
units.tr: 2. To evacuate the same, use the aggregative golden pills, folliculi of senna, and scruples of hamech.

units.la: 3. RELIQVIAS resoluëtibus, et parte roborantibus, sumptis quidem: vt, diarhodo abb.scrup.trium santalorum, saccharo rosa to, & prædictis syrupis, & aquis: admotis vero oleo rosato, violato, vel aqua plantagi nis, rosarum, violarum, cum ipsarum pulue- re. Si autem materia est pituitosa, aut succus melancholicus, apparanda est sape dictis pri us auxilijs, sed valentioribus, quàm si in he- pate esset simils affectus, quod lien à ventri- culo per venas mesaraicas longius abest: ob id ipsius remedijs acetum est miscendum, vt si causa est calida, syrup. acetatus: si frigida, oxymeli simplex, compositum, scilliticum, de radicibus duabus, quinque. Post vacuan- da agarico, hiera picra Gal. diaphœnico. In- temperiem vero splenis frigida tollent, sum- pta quidem, theriaca, diamoschum dulce & amarum, scrup. aromaticum rosatum, scrup. ex baccis lauri: admota vero decoctum ru- ta, anethi, pulegij, calaminthes, chamæmeli, se. anisi, cumini, ex spongia, aut vesicæ impo- situm: post id, oleum capparum, rutæ, anethi. Si dolor est à tumore præter naturam calido: ut phlegmone, auertenda est fluxio, secta ba- silica
units.tr: 3. To dissolve the remainders and strengthen the part, use as things taken: diarhodon abbatis, three scruples of sandalwood, rose sugar, and the aforementioned syrups and waters; as things applied: rose oil, violet oil, or water of plantain, roses and violets, with their powders. But if the matter is phlegmatic, or a melancholic juice, it must be prepared by the aforesaid aids, yet stronger ones than if the same affection were in the liver, because the spleen lies farther from the stomach by way of the mesenteric veins. For this reason vinegar must be mixed into its remedies: if the cause is hot, acetated syrup; if cold, simple oxymel, compound oxymel, squill oxymel, or oxymel of the two roots and five. After evacuation, use agaric, hiera picra (Galen), and diaphoenicum. Indeed, the cold intemperature of the spleen is removed by these: taken, theriac, sweet and bitter diamoschus, aromatic rose-scruples, and scruples of laurel berries; applied, a decoction of rue, dill, pennyroyal, calamint, chamomile, anise, cumin, placed on a sponge or bladder; after this, oil of capers, rue and dill. If the pain arises from a hot preternatural swelling, such as a phlegmon, the flux must be turned aside: the left basilic vein is opened, unless suppression of the menses or of the haemorrhoids has provoked that phlegmon, for then the vein of the ankle or of the ham is to be opened, and the swelling is to be repelled externally by applying cold things, such as rose oil, violet oil, their waters, and that of plantain, and this at the beginning of the flux.

units.la: Lib. meth. II. silica sinistra, nisi mensium suppressio, aut hæmorrhoidum eam phlegmonem excitarit: tunc enim secanda vena malleoli, aut poplitis, repellendum q; foris admotis frigidis: vt, oleo rosato, violato, aqua ipsorum, & plantaginis: idque in principio fluxionis. In augmento autem repellentibus frigidis, & parū astringentibus, misce pauca quædam leniter digerentia: vt, oleum chamæmeli, amygd. dulcium. In statu digerentibus magis agendum: vt, decocto chamæmeli, meliloti, althæa se lini, fœnigræci, oleo amygdal. dulcium, capparis, in varias medicamenti formas compositis: sed caue ne duresscere paratū lienem obdures: ac ex ipsius phlegmone scirrhum excites, valentius & intempestiuus, vel refrigerando, vel digerendo. Postremò vacuata omni materia pars roboranda oleo mastichi no, & rosato. Si autem splenis est tumor durus, vt ferè fit, ab humore melancholico, curatur tribus etiam remediorum generibus.
units.tr: Lib. meth. II. In its increase, however, use cold repellents with a little astringency, mixed with some gently digesting things, such as chamomile oil and sweet almond oil. At its height, more must be done with digestives, such as a decoction of chamomile, melilot, marshmallow, flax, fenugreek, with sweet almond oil and caper oil, made up into various forms of medicine. But take care lest, by cooling or digesting too strongly or at the wrong time, you harden a spleen that is preparing to harden, and provoke a scirrhus out of its own phlegmon. Finally, when all matter has been evacuated, the part is to be strengthened with mastic oil and rose oil. But if the spleen has a hard swelling, as usually happens from melancholic humour, it is treated likewise with three kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. POST victus ratione ex curatione melancholiæ morbi repetitam: his quæ materiā
units.tr: 1. After the regimen of diet, the treatment of the melancholy disease being repeated: these are the things which must be prepared so that the melancholic matter can be expelled.

units.la: melancholicam expelli apparant: vt, syrup. thymi, epithymi, fumariæ, de pomis, et simul acetatis, syrup. acetato simpl. oxymelite aliquo (nam in liene & carnosis partibus scirrho affectis, tutus est aceti usus Gal.) cum duplo aquarum scolopendrij, asplenij, fumariæ, tamaricis. Quæ omnia tota substantia lienem iuuant re probata sunt. Ob id vinum ijsdem aquis diluunt: vel vase ex tamarice continent antequam bibant, vel vino macerant folia aut cortices: præsertim radicum tamaricis: hæc.. multos dies sumenda: quia humor hic apparatu & purgatu difficilis.
units.tr: Such as syrup of thyme, of epithymum, of fumitory, of apples, and at the same time acetated syrups; simple acetated syrup, or some oxymel (for in the spleen and in fleshy parts affected with scirrhus, the use of vinegar is safe, according to Galen), with twice the amount of waters of spleenwort, ceterach, fumitory and tamarisk. All these, in their whole substance, have been proved to help the spleen. For this reason they dilute wine with these waters, or keep it in a vessel made of tamarisk before drinking, or steep leaves or bark in the wine, especially of tamarisk roots. These are to be taken for many days, because this humour is difficult to prepare and purge.

units.la: 2. VACVANTIBVS melancholicum succum: vt confectione hamech, pilulis fumariæ, indis, lapidis armeni, vel cyanei, à drach. vna ad script. quatuor, myrobalanis indis, cum epithymi drach. ij. & oxymelite. Frequenter autem materia hæc tum apparanda, tum vacuanda est: propter dictam priùs causam.
units.tr: 2. To evacuate the melancholic juice: such as the confection of hamech, fumitory pills, Indian pills, pills of Armenian or blue stone, of a dram of each to four scruples, Indian myrobalans, with two drams of epithymum and oxymel. Frequently this matter must be both prepared and evacuated, for the reason stated earlier.

units.la: 3. TVMOREM durum mollientibus, et digerentibus: vt vnguento ex medulla cruris cerui, aut vituli, adipe anseris, gallinæ, oleo amygdal. dulcium: vt, emplastro de meliloto, vt ceratis Mesuæ œsypatis, vt hammoniaco in aceto communi, vel scillitico soluto, addito oleo amygdal. dulciū, vel capparum: quod remedium est efficacissimum, vt vnguento ex succo, vel substantia tota radicis bryoniæ, aut cyclamini, cum oleis prædictis & cera pauca facto: quod efficacissimum post vicla alia est, ac certiss. Vt fotu ex decocto florum geniste, radicum capparis, foliorum tamaricis, scolopendrij, asplenij, ex spongia vel vesica impositò: vt, butyro liquato, & subacto diu, cum hoc decocto: & deinde spleni illito.
units.tr: 3. To soften and digest a hard swelling: such as an ointment made from the marrow of a stag's or calf's shank, goose or hen fat, and sweet almond oil; such as a plaster of melilot; such as the ceratum of Mesue, the cypress ointments, or ammoniacum dissolved in common vinegar or in squill, with the addition of sweet almond oil or caper oil, which is a most effective remedy; such as an ointment made from the juice or whole substance of the root of bryony or of cyclamen, with the aforesaid oils and a little wax, which is most effective and most certain after the other things. Likewise a fomentation of a decoction of broom flowers, caper roots, tamarisk leaves, spleenwort and ceterach, applied on a sponge or bladder; and, with this decoction, butter melted and worked for a long time, and then smeared on the spleen.

units.la: DOLORIS COLICI CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE TREATMENT OF COLIC PAIN.

units.la: COLICVS dolor citò curandus, quia ob vehementiam vires maximè prosternit. Si verò est mitior, & dat inducias, clystere primùm vacua: vt viam aperias, per quam facienda est vacuatio, etiam si aluus est libera: deinde purga medicamento, phlegmagogo, si pituita est causa: cholagogo, si bilis eo refusa, vel attracta ab eo in ventrem materia, & libero exitu prohibita, ad partes principes sursum regurgitant. Si autem intestinis solis haerent, medicamento opus est, cuius vires hepar non superent: ut hiera picra. Si vero materia est rodens & mordax, & ulcerans: clystere blando lava, & dolorem mitiga. Si pituitosa & flatuosa, etiam scammonio & turbith: cum cibo, vel mitioribus aliis sumpta, sunt remedio. Dum autem materia est crassa, lenta frigida, multa, quae valenter calfaciunt sumpta, iniecta, admota, flatibus excitatis tensionem, & ab ea dolorem augent: ut etiam docet Galenus libro methodi septimo, & duodecimo. Sumpto autem clystere, aeger in partem magis dolentem cubet. Si autem iniectio recipi in intestina per flatus prohibetur, habe fistulam biforem: ut foramine uno, materiam injicias, altero flatus foras erumpant. Si balanis utendum, sint longae digitos circiter septe: ut, penitius vim suam immittat. Quod si dolor his non cedat, & sit maximus, narcoticis utendum, praesertim
units.tr: Colic pain must be treated quickly, because its violence above all prostrates the strength. If it is milder and allows some respite, first empty the bowels with an enema, to open a way through which the evacuation is to be made, even if the bowel is already open. Then purge with a phlegm-expelling medicine if phlegm is the cause, or with a bile-expelling medicine if bile has flowed back, or if matter drawn from the bile into the belly and blocked from free exit is regurgitating upward to the principal parts. If the matter sticks only in the intestines, a medicine is needed whose strength the liver will not overpower, such as hiera picra. But if the matter is gnawing, biting and ulcerating, wash it out with a mild enema and soothe the pain. If it is phlegmatic and windy, pills of scammony and turbith, taken with food or with other milder things, are a remedy. But when the matter is thick, sluggish, cold and abundant, medicines that warm strongly, whether taken, injected or applied, stir up flatulence and increase the tension and pain from it, as Galen also teaches in the seventh and twelfth books of the Method. After the enema has been given, the patient should lie on the side that hurts more. If the injection is prevented from entering the intestines by wind, use a double-holed tube, so that you inject the matter through one opening while the wind escapes through the other. If you must use suppositories, let them be about seven fingers long, so that they send their force more deeply. But if the pain does not yield to these and is very great, narcotics must be used, especially if the matter is hot.

units.la: Gal. lib. 2. meth. ubi pulchra e colicu do lore cura di ratio. fertim si materia est calida. Si enim frigida est, vsu narcotic. crassior euadit, & contumacior expelli, malumque paulò post grauius sæuit, siue pituita erat, siue flatus.
units.tr: Galen, Method book 2, where he gives a fine account of the treatment of colic pain (the running head is garbled in the scan). Especially if the matter is hot. For if it is cold, by the use of narcotics it becomes thicker and more obstinate to expel, and the trouble, a little later, rages more severely, whether it was phlegm or wind.

units.la: Foris autem admouentur narcotica empla stri forma: intro autem recipiuntur probè ca stigata: vt, philonium, theriaca recens: sed victis prius remedijs omnibus alijs, & parua mensura.
units.tr: Narcotics are applied externally in the form of a plaster, but taken internally only when well prepared, such as philonium or fresh theriac, and only after all other remedies have been tried, and in a small amount.

units.la: Dolor igitur imprimis est sedandus prædi-ctis remedijs causam auferentibus, quâ desi-ta, dolor cessat: materia interdum prius appa-rata, & posteà vacuata: interdum ad vomitū reuulsa, resolutáue per admota. Quòd si dolor vehementer vrget: admotis, aut iniectis pri-mò pugnandum est anodinis, hoc est, calidis moderatè, vel nō vltra primum gradum (vt partem materiæ clementer digerant, neque no-uam, vel attrahant, vel ex pituita ibi con-tenta excitent) & humidis, vt partes laxa-tæ tensioni magis obediant: ob id minus do-leant.
units.tr: Therefore the pain must first be calmed by the remedies mentioned above, which remove the cause; when the cause is gone, the pain ceases. Sometimes the matter is first prepared and afterwards evacuated; sometimes it is drawn back to the vomit, or dissolved by applications. But if the pain presses hard, one must first fight it by applying or injecting anodynes, that is, things moderately warm, or not beyond the first degree (so that they gently digest part of the matter and do not draw in fresh matter or stir up the phlegm contained there), and moist, so that the relaxed parts yield more readily to the tension and therefore hurt less.

units.la: Qualia sunt, decoctum seminis, & foliorum
units.tr: Such are a decoction of the seeds and leaves of

units.la: lini, fœnigræci, foliorum malua, althæa, anethi, fœniculi, florum chamæmeli, meliloti, et similium: vel clepsydra ex alto ventri vndiq; lana munito affusum, vel potius ex magna spongia expressa, aut in vesica admotum. Fomentus item cum simili spongia, aut vesica exoleo communi, lini, chamæmeli, anethi: fercus etiam vaccinum vtiliter admouetur: filum item ex lixiuio cum cineribus coctum, calidum admotum: insessus ventris totius inferioris per semihorā in balneo ex dictis plantis cocto. Mora nanque in ipso, vires dolore, inedia, vigiliis fractas nimis deiceret: ob id interea dum infessu dolor placatur, olfaciat aromata, & suaues alios odores ad virium robur: manus etiam & pedes lauet aqua rosarum, & vino aromatico.
units.tr: flax, fenugreek, the leaves of mallow, marshmallow, dill, fennel, the flowers of camomile and melilot, and similar things; or a clyster poured from a height onto the belly, covered all round with wool, or rather a large sponge wrung out in it, or applied in a bladder. Likewise a fomentation with a similar sponge or bladder soaked in common oil, of flax, camomile or dill. Warm dung is also usefully applied, and a cloth boiled with ashes in lye, applied warm. Also a sitz bath for the whole lower belly for half an hour in a bath of the said herbs boiled. For delay in the bath itself would wear out the strength, which is already broken by pain, fasting and sleeplessness. Therefore, meanwhile, while the pain is calmed by the sitz bath, let him smell aromatics and pleasant odours to strengthen his powers; let him also wash his hands and feet with rose water and aromatic wine.

units.la: Clystere item iniicitur decoctiprædicti, vel iuris pinguis, vel olei chamæmeli, vel nucum vel lini, quod efficacissimū est lib. vna, cum cassia et saccha. ana vncia vna, vitellis duobus ouorum. Sumuntur verò decoctum, vel aqua destillata chamæmeli, ius galli, aut gallinæ, lina, aut simile pinguo, cū multo croco. Quibus victis & viribus deficientibus, narcotica injiciuntur potius quàm sumuntur, præsertim causa calida: nam frigidam augent, sive pituita est, sive flatus: sitq; dolor non multo post sævior. Clysteribus ergo prædictis misce philonij Romani drachmas duas, tres: videlicet illinè balanis filum habentibus, ut tempestiue retrahantur: nam mora calorem natiuum interdum extinguunt, & occidunt caro vel apoplexia. Opium etiam castorio flatus dissipante, sibi maximè contrario cor rectum, interdum victis prædictis inditur.
units.tr: A clyster of the aforesaid decoction is also given, or of rich broth, or of oil of camomile, walnut or flax, which is most effective: one pound with one ounce each of cassia and sugar, and two egg yolks. Let the decoction, or distilled water of camomile, chicken or hen broth, or a broth of similar richness, be taken with plenty of saffron. When the patient is already worn out and his strength fails, narcotics are injected rather than taken, especially in a hot case; for in a cold one they increase the trouble, whether it is phlegm or wind, and the pain soon becomes fiercer. So add two or three drachms of Roman philonium to the above clysters, but only as a suppository of the kind with a tube, so that it can be withdrawn in good time; for delay may extinguish the natural heat, and a patient may die of a stroke or apoplexy. Opium too, with castoreum to disperse the wind (which is very much opposed to it in the heart), is sometimes given once the above have failed.

units.la: Vinum quoque aromaticum clystere injectum in materia frigida, & flatu, salubre est. Si sumi ea est necesse, egothea, aut fortior athanasia à drachma vna ad sesquidrachmas, vel his valentius philonium ad drachmam vnam dantur.
units.tr: Aromatic wine injected as a clyster is also wholesome in cold matter and in wind. If it is necessary to take something by mouth, use egotheon, or the stronger Athanasia, from one drachm up to a drachm and a half; or philonium, which is stronger than these, in a dose of one drachm.

units.la: Tutissimè autem horum drachma vna, vel scriptula quatuor sumuntur cum purgantibus: vt, hierę picrę Galen. mellitæ drach. sex, diaphœnici drachmis duabus, scrup. indi drachma una: nā calida opij vim frangunt, & ipsum mox vacuant cum parte materiæ: opium contrà calidorum violentiam obtundit, & tamen agit, sed moderatius. Ea mistio medicorum probatissimis maximè probatur in colico dolore vehementi, quòd tuta sit & efficax. Tota verò substantia colicos iuuant, stercus lupi ossibus nõ præ mansis plenum, aut ipsius intestinum collo appensa: castorium etiam caliditate & siccitate idoneum: lumbricorum terræ, vel cornu cerui drachma una, cū vino albo pota: scorpiones assati per se calculum quidem renum frangunt, motis verò vrinis auertunt materiam, & sic colicum iuuant: tanti tamen momenti in id non sunt, vt sumi debeant. Ossium messpilorum drachma una cum semine anisi cum vino sumpta calculum frangit, & colicum dolorem sedat: secretum quorundam remedium. Si autem à pituita est dolor colicus victus rationem pituitosis affectibus debita seruet: ventrem leniat dictis clysteribus: sumat etiam blandum phlegmagogum, vt hic ram picram Galen. diaphœnicon, electarium indum. Apparetur deinde oxymelite aliquo, vel syrup. radicum duarum, aut quinque, iterum purgetur, sed valentius: vt, hieræ mellitæ vnc. vna, diaphœnici drach. duabus, vel scrup. indi: quanquam materia in vijs istis capacibus non magnopere eget apparatibus: præsertim vbi magnus dolor non dat inducias, nisi materia sit multum crassa, lenta, infarta, etiam hiera diacolocynthidos vacuanda. Reliquæ postremò resoluuntur oleis chamæmeli, lilij, anethi, rutæ, cum se. cumini, anisi, fœniculi, baccis lauri, cum abrotono, pulegio. Sumitur aromaticum rosatum, scrup. de baccis lauri, diagalanga, diacyminum, diamoschum. Si succus est biliosus (quod rarum est) aut melancholicus, vacua dictis clysteribus. Sumat cassiam, mannam, terebinthinam ad vnciam vnam, vel ius galli antiqui cum polypodio, anisso, fœniculo, vel agarico, turbith pro varijs scopis coctiad dissolutionem: ad vncias octo, vel decem sumatur. Si dolor in colo sit à phlegmone, cura phlegmonem, vt dixi saepe. si à vermibus, post audies. Si à malo situ, vel hernia, elatis cruribus suc cusso corpore per crura reddatur loco suo. Si à flatibus, leniora primùm tenta, quæ flatus dissipent: præsertim cùm adest materia flatu fouens: vt puluerem anisi, cū vino dabis: valentiora, diacyminum, diagalangam scrup. de baccis lauri. Cucurbitula magna loco dolenti affixa mirè leuat, & repente clyster ex oleo nucum, vel rutæ, cum hierâ, terebinthinæ, scrup. de baccis lauri ana uncia dimidia, valens est, etiam si pituita subest.
units.tr: Most safely, one drachm or four scruples of these is taken with purgatives, such as hiera picra of Galen, six drachms of honeyed, two drachms of diaphoenicon, and one drachm of Indian scruples. For the warm ingredients break the force of the opium and soon empty it out along with part of the matter, while the opium, on the other hand, blunts the violence of the warm ones, and yet still acts, but more gently. This mixture is most highly approved by the most approved physicians in severe colic pain, because it is safe and effective. The whole substance of the following also helps colics: wolf's dung full of undigested bones, or the intestine of the animal itself hung round the neck; castoreum too, suitable for its warmth and dryness; one drachm of earthworms, or of hart's horn, drunk with white wine; scorpions roasted by themselves indeed break up kidney stone, and by moving the urine they turn away the matter, and so help the colic; yet they are not of such importance for this that they ought to be taken. One drachm of the bones of medlars, taken with aniseed and wine, breaks up stone and calms colic pain: a secret remedy of certain people. But if the colic pain comes from phlegm, let the patient keep to the diet due to phlegmatic conditions; let him soften the belly with the clysters mentioned; let him also take a mild phlegm-expeller, such as Galen's hiera picra, diaphoenicon, or Indian electuary. Then let him be prepared with some oxymel, or syrup of two or five roots, and purge again, but more strongly: for example, one ounce of honeyed hiera, two drachms of diaphoenicon, or Indian scruples. Although matter in these channels does not greatly need preparations, especially where great pain allows no respite, unless the matter is very thick, sluggish and clogged, in which case it must be evacuated with hiera of diacolocynth. Finally, the rest is dissolved with oils of camomile, lily, dill and rue, with cumin, aniseed and fennel seed, bay berries, with southernwood and pennyroyal. Take rose aromatic, a scruple of bay berries, diagalanga, diacuminum, diamoschum. If the humour is bilious (which is rare) or melancholic, empty it with the clysters mentioned. Let him take cassia, manna, and turpentine, one ounce, or the broth of an old cock with polypody, anise, fennel, or agaric, and turbith, boiled to dissolution according to the various aims; eight or ten ounces are to be taken. If the colic pain comes from inflammation in the colon, treat the inflammation, as I have often said; if from worms, you will hear about that later. If it comes from a bad position or a hernia, the body is to be shaken with the legs raised, and returned to its place through the legs. If it comes from wind, first try milder things that disperse wind, especially when there is matter that feeds the wind: for example, you will give powdered aniseed with wine; stronger ones are diacuminum, and diagalanga with a scruple of bay berries. A large cupping vessel applied to the painful place relieves wonderfully, and a sudden clyster of walnut or rue oil, with hiera, turpentine and a half-ounce each of bay berries, is effective even if phlegm is present underneath.

units.la: FLVORIS ALVI A CATARRHO CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF FLUX OF THE BOWELS FROM CATARRH.

units.la: FLVOR alui à catarrho, vel acri, & pungente & salso, vel vitreo, vel acido, vel insipido, vel dulci, ex cerebro ruente, nunc per œsophagum in ventriculum: nunc per mesaraeum in intestina: nunc in vtraque qui vim retentricè, vel qualitate, vel quantitate molestat: aut lubricam, & ad continendum ineptam reddit. Hunc autem indicant catarrhus, vel præcedens, vel etiam dū præsens capitis grauitas ex austrino flatu, sta-tu pluuio, somno diuturno, victu intempera-to, cerebri intéperie frigida, sensus fluxionis ab ægro perceptus. Curatur quomodo asse-ctus cæteri ex fluxione profecti, prospiciēdo scilicet imprimis parti fluxionem transmittē ti cerebro ipsi, per dicta prius remedia in ca-tarrho. Deinde partibus fluxionem recipien-tibus: vt, ventriculo per remedia ante dicta in ventriculi imbecillitate, materiam scilicet primùm apparantia: deinde vacuantia: vt, hiera picra, diaphœnicum, scrup. indum. Postremò reliquias dissoluentia, & ventrem totum roborantia: vt sotus ex absinthio, ro-sis, mentha, spica, roremarino, pulegio, ca-laminthe, galanga: caryophyllis in uino aro-matico coctis, ut ex ijsdem sacculi, cataplas-mata, unguenta cum oleo mastichino, absin-thÿ, menthæ: spicato, ut cerata stomachi-ca: ut sumpta aromaticum rosatum, garyophyllatum, diagalanga, zingiber conditum.
units.tr: A flux of the bowels from catarrh, whether acrid and pungent, or salty, or glassy, or sour, or insipid, or sweet, flows down from the brain: sometimes through the gullet into the stomach, sometimes through the mesentery into the intestines, and sometimes into both; it disturbs the retentive power, either in quality or in quantity, or makes the bowel slippery and unfit to retain its contents. It is indicated by catarrh, either preceding or still present, by heaviness of the head from a south wind, a rainy season, long sleep, intemperate diet, a cold intemperature of the brain, and by a sensation of flux perceived by the patient. It is cured in the same way as other affections arising from flux, that is, by first providing against the flux passing into the brain itself, by the remedies previously described for catarrh. Then, for the parts receiving the flux: as with the stomach, by the remedies mentioned earlier for weakness of the stomach, which first prepare the matter, then evacuate it, for example hiera picra, diaphoenicum, and scruples of Indian (rhubarb). Finally, dissolving what remains and strengthening the whole belly: for example, a fomentation of wormwood, roses, mint, spikenard, rosemary, pennyroyal, calamint and galangal; caryophyllum boiled in aromatic wine; from the same ingredients sachets, plasters, and ointments with mastic oil, wormwood and mint; spikenard, as a stomachic plaster; and taken internally, aromatic rose, clove-infused, diagalanga, and ginger preserved in sugar.

units.la: LEIENTERIAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: The Treatment of Lienteria

units.la: ΛEιευτεγίᾳ, id est lævitas, & lubricitas intestinorum, sed etiam ventriculi, sit ubi ventriculus à re quapiam, vel mordaci, vel grauante sic irritatur, vt eam expellere cupiat. Res verò mordax & rodens, vel medicamentum est per se, aut cum cibo sumptū, vel alimentorum corruptela, vel excrementa mordacia in ventrem à corporis habitu de fluentia, aut in ipso genita: vel mordax indicatur ob vlcera ventriculi, & intestinorū, ab humore acri, & tenui excitata, aphthis in ore similia.
units.tr: Lienteria [λειεντερία], that is, smoothness and slipperiness of the intestines, and also of the stomach, occurs when the stomach is irritated by some biting or burdensome thing, so that it wishes to expel it. The biting and corroding thing is either a medicine taken by itself or with food, a corruption of the food, or biting excrements that flow into the stomach from the constitution of the body or are generated in the stomach itself. A biting cause is indicated by ulcers of the stomach and intestines, excited by a sharp, thin humour, similar to aphthae in the mouth.

units.la: Grauatur autem à copia alimenti, vel excrementi, vel ob imbecillitatē coctricis, aut retentricis, aut vtriusque, ex intemperie natam. Vnde fit vt alimentum celeriter deiciatur, quale & quantum est assumptum.
units.tr: It is burdened, however, by an excess of food or excrement, or by weakness of the concocting or retaining faculty, or of both, arising from an intemperature. Hence it comes about that the food is quickly voided, in the same state and quantity as it was taken.

units.la: Nam Lienteria ventriculi affectus est qua lis diabetes renum, & vesicæ: fit etiam interdum resoluto sphincter e intestini recti. Est quando pituita multa & glutinosa, ventriculum & intestina intus sublinens, lubricum facit ventrem. Noscitur facile causa quaevis praedicta per responsa aegri, & symptomata unamquamque causam peculiariter sequentia: ut excreta purulenta, aut cruenta, ulcus indicant: et dolor ab acribus sumptis, aut injectis: qua parte ulcus est, magnus: si medicamentum violentum aeger sumpsisse dicatur, aut cibum largiorem, vel coctu difficilem, aut crudum, aut frigidum immodice. Curatur contrariis causae remediis: si enim a cibo multo coctu difficili, vel corruptibili: paucum coctu facilem, vel non facilem corruptu impera: si a frigidis, calida. Si corrupta est materia in ventriculo, vomitu ex aqua tepida vacuetur, vel deiectione per mannam, cassiam: si est in intestinis, clystere educatur.
units.tr: For lienteria is an affection of the stomach, as diabetes is of the kidneys and bladder. Sometimes it also happens through a loosening of the sphincter of the rectum. Sometimes abundant and viscid phlegm, coating the stomach and intestines within, makes the belly loose. Each of the causes mentioned can easily be recognised from the answers of the patient and from the symptoms that follow each cause in its own way: purulent or bloody discharges indicate an ulcer, and pain after acrid things have been taken or injected indicates the same, and where the pain is great, there is the ulcer. If the patient says he has taken a violent medicine, or a larger amount of food, or food hard to digest, or raw, or excessively cold, that also points to the cause. It is cured by remedies contrary to the cause: if it comes from much food that is hard to digest or easily corrupted, order little food that is easy to digest or not easily corrupted; if from cold things, warm ones. If the matter in the stomach has become corrupt, let it be emptied by vomiting with warm water, or by evacuation with senna or cassia; if it lies in the intestines, let it be drawn off by an enema.

units.la: Si ob materiam multam ventriculo affixam, quod saepe contingit: curatur quatuor remediorum generibus.
units.tr: If it is due to much matter attached to the stomach, which often happens, it is treated with four kinds of remedies.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione incidente, tenuante, tergente: ut, salsis, amaris, acribus.
units.tr: 1. Diet, adapted to cut, thin and cleanse: such as salty, bitter and sharp foods.

units.la: 2. PITVITAM parantibus saepe dictis.
units.tr: 2. Remedies that prepare the phlegm, as often said above.

units.la: 3. VACVANTIBVS vomitu, aut potius deiectione, nisi materia ad os uentriculi erumpat: qui si non sufficit, addatur deiectio per medicamentum a longinquo non trahens: ut, hieram picram, diaphoenicon, pilulas masticbinas, elephanginas, de hiera: qua etiam salubris est, si ambigis, an pituita, uel bilis uentriculum offendit: utrunq; enim uacuat.
units.tr: 3. By evacuating with vomiting, or rather with purging, unless the matter breaks out at the mouth of the stomach. If this does not suffice, let purging be added with a medicine that does not draw from afar, such as hiera picra, diaphoenicon, mastic pills, elephangine pills, from the hiera; which is also wholesome if you are in doubt whether phlegm or bile offends the stomach, for it empties both.

units.la: 4. VENTRICVLVM roboratibus sty pticis & intemperiem frigidam tollentibus calidis: admotis quidem, oleis absinthij, menthae, masticiches, ex spica illitis: & item unguentis, ac ceratis, tum ex his, tum ex pulue re absinthij, menthae, masticices, schoenatho, cipero, galanga balaustijs, malicorio, cinamomo, caryophyllis, calamo aromatico: ac denique fotu cum spongia ex uino nigro austero, cui praedicta fuerint incocta. Sumptis autem, aromatico rosato, diacymino, diagalanga, zingibere condito, myrobalanis, cepulis conditis duabus in hebdomada ante cibu, diacydonio cum saccharo et aromatibus. In causa uero calida, sine aromatibus: cochlearibus bus, etiam duobus miuæ, cydoniorum aromaticæ ante cibū: syrupo menthæ, absinthij. Hæc enim coëtricem uim & retentricem roborant. Coriandrum quoq; cibum in uentriculo ualenter continet. Auicen. Si uerò Lienteriæ causa est calida, similiter uictus ratione, sed frigida oppugnetur: deinde materia expelli facilis uacuetur, myrobalanis citreis tritis, uel infusis. Postremò intemperies calida tollatur frigidis, & pars roboretur styptici: ut, iulep. rosato, syrup. & saccharo rosato, syrup. cydoniorum, granatorum, scrup. diarhodo abba. scrup. trium santalorum. Si Lienteria est ab ulceribus, quales aphthæ sunt in ore, tergean tur, & cicatrice tegantur remedijs aphtharum, aut phthisewos. Si à flatibus, curetur remedijs colicis. Si à dolore uentriculi, remedia prius scripta habes.
units.tr: 4. Strengthening astringents for the stomach, and warm remedies to remove cold intemperature: applied, indeed, as oils of wormwood, mint and mastic, anointed with spica; likewise ointments and plasters, both of these and of powder of wormwood, mint, mastic, schoenanthus, cyperus, galangal, pomegranate flowers, rind of pomegranate, cinnamon, cloves, and aromatic calamus; and finally fomentation with a sponge in austere black wine, in which the aforesaid have been boiled. Taken internally: aromatic rose electuary, diacyminum, diagalanga, ginger preserved in sugar, myrobalans, two preserved onions a week before food, quince preserve with sugar and spices. In a hot cause, without spices: two spoonfuls, also of small quince preserves with spices, before food; syrup of mint, of wormwood. For these strengthen the concocting and retaining power. Coriander also holds food firmly in the stomach. Avicenna. But if the cause of lienteria is hot, let it be similarly treated by diet, but opposed with cold remedies; then let the matter be emptied, which is easily expelled, with citrine myrobalans, crushed or infused. Finally, let the hot intemperature be removed with cold remedies, and the part strengthened with astringents: such as julep of roses, syrup and preserve of roses, syrup of quinces, of pomegranates, two scruples of diarhodon abbatis, two scruples of three santals. If lienteria comes from ulcers, such as the aphthae in the mouth are, let them be cleansed and covered over with a scar by remedies for aphthae or phthisis. If from flatulence, let it be treated with colic remedies. If from pain of the stomach, you have the remedies written earlier.

units.la: DYSENTERIAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: The Treatment of Dysentery

units.la: Dysenteria, id est intestinorum difficultas ab ulceribus, remediorum generibus quatuor curatur.
units.tr: Dysentery, that is, difficulty of the intestines from ulcers, is treated with four kinds of remedies.

units.la: VICTVS ratione, si materia est calida, ut feré fit, refrigerante: ut, cibis parùm acidis ad excitandam appetentiâ per consensum prostratam) vitentur autem acetum, salsa acria: quia ulceribus hæc sunt mordacia) ijsdem paucis ut partes largiori almen to destitutæ, contumacius quem habent humorem, retineant: neque ita prompte intestinis dolore ulceroso trahentibus permittant. Sint quoque cibi actu frigidi, ut appetentiam inuitent, & natura inter se similis, non diuersæ aut contrariæ: & euchymi, & coctu faciles, ob ventriculi imbecillam coctricem, & retentricem. Tales enim citò cocti prompte distribuentur: quales sunt, testes gallinaceorum, hepata gallinarum, ova sorbilia: nã liquidiora ventre leniunt, dura ægrè coquuntur: aqua carnis, contusum carnium, milium, far, panicum, oryza, super tegulam ignitam assata, lentes excorticatæ, lac acidum (quod fit lacte per noctem serenam in aëre depositò et deinde ebutyrato) lapidibus, aut ferramentis ignitis ter, quater vstulatum. Vinum aut nullum bibatur, aut styptricum, idemq; aqua chalybata dilutum, vel decocto se.coriandri vel baccarum rhois, vel oxyacanthæ, addito si vis saccharo rosato, quod per se, vt iulep. rosatum, etiam salubre est.
units.tr: Diet: if the matter is hot, as it usually is, let it be cooling: such as foods not too acid, to rouse the appetite that has been prostrated through sympathy; let vinegar and sharp salty things be avoided, since these are biting to ulcers. Let the same foods be given in small amounts, so that the parts deprived of a larger nourishment may retain the more stubborn humour they hold, and so that they do not too readily let it pass into the intestines, which draw it in with ulcerous pain. Let the foods also be cold in action, so as to invite appetite, and similar in nature to one another, not different or contrary; and let them be of good juice and easy to concoct, because of the weak concocting and retaining power of the stomach. For such foods, quickly cooked, are promptly distributed: such as the gizzards of poultry, the livers of hens, eggs to be sipped; for the more liquid things soothe the belly, while hard things are digested with difficulty. Meat broth, pounded meat, millet, spelt, panic grass, rice, roasted on a hot tile, peeled lentils, sour milk (which is made from milk left overnight in a clear air and then deprived of butter), roasted three or four times on stones or hot irons. Let no wine be drunk, or only an astringent one, and likewise diluted with chalybeate water, or with a decoction of coriander or of barberries, or of berberis, adding, if you like, rose sugar, which is wholesome in itself, like julep of roses.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM dysenteriæ causam vacuantibus, vt bilem, causam eius crebrio re in regionibus calidis, myrobalanis citreis, tritis ad sesquidrach. vel, ad semunc. infusis in aqua calida: deinde ter feruefactis, & valenter expressis, cum syrup. aut iulepi rosati vncia vna, ad tollendam asperitatem, aquæ plantaginis, buglosi q.s. Sunt qui rhabarbarum quoque exhibent: quod alij cur damnet, non video: vitentur autem scammoniata omnia. Sunt qui corticum myroba. cepulan drachmas tres, citrearum drach. duas, vuarum passarum drach. vnam, spicæ parum, trita macerant aqua absinthij, plantaginis, buglosi: duodecies feruefaciunt: vbi refrixerunt, manibus fricant, valenter exprimunt, addut catholici drac. duas rhabarbari drac. semissem. Vbi verò processit multùm morbus, & bilis multa, tum à natura, tum à nobis est vacuata, et venter inferior astrictio-
units.tr: 2. Those who purge the matter that causes dysentery, such as bile, which is very frequent in hot regions, use yellow myrobalans, rubbed to a scruple and a half drachm, or to half an ounce, steeped in warm water, then boiled three times, strongly pressed, and given with an ounce of syrup or julep of roses to take away the harshness, with plantain water and bugloss water as needed. Some also give rhubarb, though I do not see why others condemn it. All scammony preparations should be avoided. Some steep three drachms of chebulic myrobalans, two drachms of yellow myrobalans, one drachm of raisins, and a little spikenard, all ground, in wormwood, plantain and bugloss water; they boil it twelve times, and when it has cooled, they rub it with the hands, press it strongly, and add two drachms of catholicon and half a drachm of rhubarb. But when the disease has advanced far and much bile has been evacuated, both by nature and by us, and the lower belly needs a greater astringency...

units.la: Z ne maiori indiget, magna rhabarbari, potius quàm rhabarbarum ipsum, super tegulam ignitam sæpe vertendo assatam, est salubre, et paratu facile. Secundo aut tertio die refrigerando bilem crassantia, & obtundentia dantur: vt, syrup. intybi, violatus, cum aqua plantaginis. Vbi verò processit, nec tàtus est metus retinendæ materiæ, syrup. rosatus, cydoniorum cum aquis rosarum, plantaginis: iterum myrobalanis citreis, et rhabarbaro, partim integro, partim assato purgamus: deinde ieiu nis hepar fouemus decocto santalorum, rosis, spodio cum aqua rosarum, intybi: additis tandem aliis quoq; astringentibus. In his autem regio nibus septentrionalibus, ex aëre et victus gene re à pituita vitrea, & salsa, tinesmi, et dy senteriæ magis fiunt, vel in ventre genita, vel in ipsum corriuante ex capite, aut corpore vniuerso. Phlegmagogis curatur. Si autem ab atra bile inceperit, cur lethalis sit Hippocrati, docet Galen. aph. 24. lib. 4.
units.tr: Z not so much, but a large amount of rhubarb, roasted on a hot tile and turned often, is better than rhubarb itself, and is easy to prepare. On the second or third day, thickening and blunting remedies that cool the bile are given, such as syrup of endive and violet with plantain water. But when it has advanced, and there is no great fear of retaining the matter, we purge again with syrup of roses, quince syrup with rose water and plantain water, yellow myrobalans, and rhubarb, partly whole and partly roasted; then we foment the stomach while fasting with a decoction of sandalwood, roses, and spodium with rose water and endive, and finally add other astringents as well. In these northern regions, from the air and the manner of life, tenesmus and dysentery arise more often from glassy and salty phlegm, either generated in the belly or flowing down into it from the head or the whole body. It is treated with phlegm-purgers. But if it begins from black bile, Galen, in aphorism 24 of book 4, teaches why it is lethal according to Hippocrates.

units.la: 3. VLCERA sanantibus, sed prius lotis à bile, vel mucco mordaci intestinis, per iniectiones
units.tr: 3. ULCERS are to be healed, but first they must be cleansed of bile or biting mucus in the intestines, by injections:

units.la: stiones ex aquæ hordei libra vna, vitellis duo bus, sacchari rubri vnc. vna. Quæ interdum curandæ dysenteriæ sufficiunt: interdû post eas, emplasticis opus est, internam intestinorû su perficiem contra fluentis materiæ morsum, ccu tectorio quodam, et crusta armantibus: ex albumine ouorum, gummi arabico, adipis caprini, ana semunc. olei rosati, vnc. duas, ne adeps citò concrescat, boli armenicæ, traga-canthi ana vnciam vnā, cum vncijs decem aquæ hordei, si lauandum & tergendû: vel tantundem iuris pinguis carnium, si vim em plasticam maiorem volumus: addito etiam butyro recenti, insalso, et succo plantaginis. Post iniectiones emplasticas, ne acres materi as lentore suo retineant, et affigant intestinis: lauatoria iterum opus est, sicq; vicissim. Vbi materia mordax constitit, ac fluere desijt, so lusq; sanguis fluere perseuerat: sarcoticis, & glutinantibus, & cicatricem ducentibus in-iectionibus vtendum est, ex libra vna deco-ctiro sarû, balaustiorû, malicorÿ, rhois, oxya canthæ, vuarû, gallarû, se. coriādri: addendo boli armenicæ, sanguinis draconis, terræ lem- nia, thuris, ana drach. vnā, vel trochiscorum ex terra lemnia, drach. duas cum vitellis ouo rum duorum. Si autem ulcus est profundum, pus multum reijciens, tergendum est clistere ex decocto furfuris frumenti, vel ligni gaiaci, vel cicerum rubrorum, vel ex hydromelite, vel sero lactis caprini, vel lotio: vel, si valen tius vis, ex lixiuio: vel ex vino rubro subdul ci tergente, & roborante, addendo melli s ro sa. vncias duas. Si valentiore opus est, muria piscium salsorum, aut oliuarum colymbadum. Interdum & valentissimis vtendum: vt, tro chiscis ex arsenico. Si autem diligenter deter seris, natura carne implere, glutinare, & ci- catrice tegere per se poterit. Quòd tamen vt promptius faciat, inuanda est clysteribus sic cantibus, & astrigentibus: vt, decocto len- tium, rosarum, balaustiorum, addendo bolum armenicam, terram lemniam: non omissis ta men interea tergentibus.
units.tr: Injections of one pound of barley water, two egg yolks, and one ounce of red sugar. These are sometimes enough to cure dysentery. Sometimes, after them, emplastic remedies are needed to coat and crust the inner surface of the intestines and arm it against the bite of the flowing matter. Take the white of eggs, gum arabic, and goat's fat, half an ounce each; two ounces of rose oil, so that the fat does not set too quickly; Armenian bole and tragacanth, one ounce each. Use these with ten ounces of barley water if the bowel is to be washed and cleansed, or with the same amount of broth from fatty meat if we want a stronger emplastic force. Add also fresh unsalted butter and juice of plantain. After the emplastic injections, washes must be used again, and so on alternately, lest the sharp matter, by its stickiness, stay and cling to the intestines. When the biting matter has settled and stopped flowing, and only blood keeps flowing, one must use injections that cleanse, glue together, and bring on a scar. Take a decoction of one pound of sorrel, pomegranate peel, pomegranate rind, sumac, oxycantha, grapes, oak galls, and coriander seed, and add Armenian bole, dragon's blood, Lemnian earth, and frankincense, one drachm each; or lozenges made of Lemnian earth, two drachms, with two egg yolks.
