If the ulcer is deep and discharges much pus, it must be cleansed with an enema of decoction of wheat bran, or of guaiacum wood, or of red chickpeas, or of hydromel, or of goat's whey, or of a wash; or, if you want something stronger, of lye; or of a cleansing and strengthening red wine, with two ounces of rose honey added. If a stronger remedy is needed, use the brine of salted fish or of pickled olives. Sometimes even the strongest agents must be used, such as lozenges of arsenic. But if you take care that nature itself can fill the wound with flesh, glue it together, and cover it with a scar, it will manage by itself. Yet to make it do so more quickly, it should be helped with enemas that both bind and astringe, such as a decoction of lentils, roses, and pomegranate flowers, with Armenian bole and Lemnian earth added, without leaving out in the meantime the cleansing remedies.

units.la: 4. FLVOREM astrigentibus, ne mate ria etiam benigna, vacuatione multa ob uia rum
units.tr: 4. ASTRINGENTS TO CHECK THE FLUX, lest even benign matter, through much evacuation caused by the looseness of the passages, should cast down the strength.

units.la: rum laxitatem, uires deiciat: maligna autem & corrupta non est retinenda, ne febrem augeat, & alia symptomata graviora excitet. Sumuntur in id sacharum rosatum corallio rubro mistum, cydoniorum sine aromatibus, syrup. cydoniorum, trochisc. ex spodio cum se oxalidis drach. vnâ. Hæc si non sufficiunt, narcoticis dolor sedandus, somnus conciliandus, & materia ceu glacianda, ut adfluendum sit ineptior: modo uirtus non sit imbecilla, ne calorem exiguum illa extinguat. Sumitur autem athanasia à drachma vna ad scriptula quatuor, vel clystere immittitur etiam drachmis tribus: balani quoq; ex lycio à Rasi descripta cum filo sedi imponuntur, ut tempestiue retrahi possint, ne symptomata afferant prius scripta. Admouetur autè ven trioleum cydoniorum, myrteum, mastichinum, insperso deinde puluere corallij, rosarũ, mastiches, boli armenicæ, sanguinis draconis In idem efficacissimum est emplastrum Mesuæ, diaphœnicum calidum, in frigida: frigidum, in calida causa dysenteriæ. Vapor etiam vini austeri per scoriam ferri, ferrumue igni tum elatus, ac sede receptus saluber est: eode vino vel re similiter astringente, manus & pedes fouere, ventri etiam fluenti robur tandem magnum sæpe affert: maius, cataplasma ex pane medio tosto, vino austero extincto, addito butyro vsto, ol. astringentibus, super data mastiche. Si à solis intestinis sine vlcere fluor est, curetur clysteribus vires habentibus easdem cum remedijs per os sumptis, cum à ventriculo solo fluebat materia.
units.tr: But malignant and corrupt matter must not be retained, lest it increase the fever and bring on other more serious symptoms. For this one takes rose sugar mixed with red coral, quince preserve without aromatics, quince syrup, and lozenges of burnt spodium with sorrel seed, one drachm. If these are not enough, the pain must be calmed with narcotics, sleep must be brought on, and the matter must, as it were, be frozen so that less unsuitable matter flows to the part, provided the strength is not feeble, lest it extinguish the little warmth that remains. Athanasia is taken in doses from one drachm up to four scruples, or it is also injected in an enema in doses of three drachms. Also, acorn-shaped pills of lycium, as described by Rhazes, are placed on a thread at the anus, so that they can be drawn out in good time, lest they cause the symptoms described above. Next is applied the ventriole of quince, myrtle, and mastic, and then powder of coral, roses, mastic, Armenian bole, and dragon's blood is sprinkled on. The plaster of Mesue is very effective for the same purpose: the warm diaphoenicon when the cause of dysentery is cold, and the cold when it is hot. Likewise the vapour of astringent wine, passed through the scoria of iron, or iron heated in the fire and received into the seat, is wholesome; and bathing the hands and feet with the same wine, or with some similarly astringent thing, often at last brings great strength to the fluxing belly. Greater still is a cataplasm of the middle of toasted bread, soaked in astringent wine, with burnt butter and astringent oils added, and mastic sprinkled on top. If the flux comes from the intestines alone, without ulcer, it should be cured by enemas having the same strength as the remedies taken by mouth, since the matter flowed only from the stomach.

units.la: TINESMI CVRATIO.
units.tr: TENESMUS: TREATMENT

units.la: TINESMVS, vehemes et inanis deiciendi appetitus, qualis fere adest dysenteriæ prædictæ, ob materias mordaces, ad intestini recti finem hærentes: bilem scilicet, aut pituitam salsam vel vitream, vel aliter mordacem, ad sedem solum desidentem.
units.tr: TENESMUS is a vehement and useless urge to expel, such as usually accompanies the dysentery described above, owing to biting matters that cling to the end of the rectum: namely bile, or salty or glassy phlegm, or some other biting matter that settles only at the seat.

units.la: Curatur à bile, clystere lauatorio, ex decocto hordei, saccharo, vitellis ouorum: si à pituita, ex decocto cicerum, sero lactis, melle rosato: si à stercore durato est, molliatur sumptis & iniectis: si à tumore, curetur vti eius partis natura, & tumoris postulat. Si à frigore est, vel flatibus, quadra mensarum calfacta sedi admota, remedio est: sacculi item ex chamemelo, & verbasci floribus calidi suppo- nantur vtiliter, vel eadem vino incocta, ex pressa, sedi applicentur calida, & ventri. Si tinesmus à repletione est, sinatur: saluber enim est. Si ab imbecilla retentrice, roboretur prae dictis astringentibus. Si à partibus corporis calore immodico liquatis, calor mitigetur. Si fluor est immodicus, sistitur, vtrius. Si dolor implacatus vrget, balanus indetur ex lycio, vt prius: vel athanasia sumatur.
units.tr: It is treated against bile with a washing clyster of barley decoction, sugar and egg yolks; if from phlegm, with a decoction of chickpeas, goat whey and rose honey; if from a hardened stool, it is softened by taking and injecting remedies. If it comes from a swelling, let it be treated according to the nature of that part and what the swelling requires. If it comes from cold or wind, a warmed square of cloth applied to the seat is a remedy; likewise bags of chamomile and mullein flowers, warm, are usefully placed beneath, or the same flowers boiled in wine, pressed out, are applied warm to the seat and belly. If the tenesmus comes from repletion, let it be left alone, for it is wholesome. If it comes from a weak retentive faculty, strengthen it with the astringents mentioned above. If it comes from parts of the body melted by excessive heat, let the heat be moderated. If the flux is excessive, it is checked, as described. If an unrelenting pain presses, a suppository of lycium is inserted, as before, or athanasia is taken.

units.la: FLVORIS ALVI CVRATIO.
units.tr: TREATMENT OF FLUX OF THE BOWELS.

units.la: SI FLVOR est à lienis obstructione, vel imbecilla vi tractrice, curatur vt dictum est in dolore splenis: vt, admoto oleo cappa- rum, lilij, genistae, sumpto tamarice, aspleno, scolopendrio, capparibus: purgato item corpore per myrobalanos indas. Si ab hepate est, illius affectus, obstructio, phlegmone, scirrhus imbecillitas tractricis, vel retentricis, vel co‐ctricis ab intemperie, ante est corrigendus i‐doneis remedijs in horum affectuum curatio ne prædictis. Si igitur hepar obstructu à ma‐teria frigida, ita vt deiectiones sint chylosæ, ea paretur expulsioni per syrup. cichorij Ni‐colai, radicum duarum, aut quinque, cum a‐quis aperientibus absinthij, prasij, apij, fœ‐niculi, cassuthæ: si vero materia est calida, obtundatur dicto syrup. intybi, rosato, & a‐quis cichorij, intybi: postea vacuabimus rha barbaro infuso per se, aut etiam cum agari‐co, vitantes scammoniata, & alia hepati noxia.
units.tr: If the flux comes from an obstruction of the spleen, or from weakness of the drawing power, treat it as described under pain of the spleen: apply oil of capers, lily and broom, and take tamarisk, spleenwort, scolopendrium and capers. Then purge the body with Indian myrobalans. If it comes from the liver, first correct the liver's affection (obstruction, phlegmon, scirrhus, or weakness of its drawing, retaining or concocting faculty from bad temperament) with suitable remedies, as in the treatment of these affections above. So if the liver is obstructed by cold matter, so that the stools are chylous, prepare the matter for expulsion with syrup of chicory of Nicolaus, with two or five roots, together with opening waters of wormwood, prasium, parsley, fennel and cassutha. If the matter is hot, temper it with the said syrup of endive, rosewater, and waters of chicory and endive. Afterwards we will purge with rhubarb infused by itself, or even with agaric, avoiding scammony and other things harmful to the liver.

units.la: Postremò intemperies tollatur, heparq; ro‐boretur, nunc trochiscis de lacca, de rhabar‐baro, nunc diacurcuma, diacalaminthe, à drach. vna ad drach. duas: nūc aliys atq; aliys. Nam in affectu diuturno varietate remedio‐rum, etiam idem pollentium, vicissim vten‐dum, ne natura vni assueta & familiaris, vi res eius contemnat. Sed caue ne materias in hepate compingas, & retineas his roboran‐tibus: tibus: nec foris illinas hypochondrio dextro frigida, astringentia: quia sanguinem cogunt, & hepatis calorem reliquum extinguunt, & hominem occidunt. Si ab imbecillitate est hepatis, eius curatio prius est scripta: hepar enim roborandum est in dysenteria hepatica, per ea quae causae sunt contraria: ut, frigida, incalida: calida, infrigida causa: ut pistacia, cubebas, & ex his electarium: hepar lupi quoque est praestantissimum, mane ad cochlearis mensuram sumptum. Vuae item passae pinguis passim Avicennae commendantur, ita ut dulces, causa frigidae: acidae vero, calidae tribuantur. Dysenteriam enim hepaticam, etiam sola sanant ablatis tamen feminibus, cum astrictione opus non est. Eadem trita et creta sac charo mista fiunt salubres, misto, si vis, spodio, vel aliis hepati familiaribus: ut, hepatica, rhabarbaro. Quod si in dies scriptulo uno vel in hebdomadas drachma una sumatur, est in idsaluberrimum: & syrup. absinthij, et absinthium cibo, potu, in idem optimum: tro chisci etiam Ἀλί οἶνος, id est, de vino Galeni, & Auic. causa praesertim frigida: si calida autem est causa, miscentur ei sporiu, trochisci sporij, species, diarhodi abb. et scrup. trium santalorum, syrup. cichorij, Nicolai. Si vero fluor sit biliosus ab hepate, syrup. intybi, & byzantiorum cum aqua intybi, cicchorij: trochisci de sporio cum se. oxalidis, diarhodon abb. vel commune, scrup. trium santalorum. Si sanguineus est, fluere aliquantisper permittatur: post sistatur, ut alius sanguinis fluor quiuis immodicus. Si virulentus est, seu cum sanie calida, (ἰχωρας vocat Gal.) intem peries calida hepatis, sumptis et admotis praedictis in debilitate hepatis mitigetur. Si pus inest hepati rupto abscessu, tergetur aqua hordei saccharata, vel cicerum decocto: deinde glutinatur per dicta prius in dysenteria.
units.tr: Finally, remove the bad temperament and strengthen the liver, sometimes with troches of lac and of rhubarb, sometimes with diacurcuma or diacalaminthe, from one drachm to two drachms, sometimes with one remedy, sometimes with another. For in a long-lasting affection, the remedies should be alternated, even those of equal power, lest nature, accustomed and familiar to one, come to despise its effect. But take care not to pack matter into the liver and hold it there with these strengtheners, and do not smear cold astringents on the right hypochondrium from outside, because they constrict the blood, extinguish the liver's remaining heat, and kill the patient. If the flux comes from weakness of the liver, its treatment has been written above: the liver must be strengthened in hepatic dysentery by things that are contrary to the causes, as cold to hot, and hot to cold: such as pistachios, cubebs, and an electuary made from these. Wolf's liver is also most excellent, taken in the morning in a spoonful. Fat raisins are commended everywhere by Avicenna, the sweet ones being assigned for a cold cause and the sour ones for a hot cause. For they cure hepatic dysentery even by themselves, with the seeds removed; astringency is not needed. The same raisins, rubbed and mixed with sugar and chalk, become wholesome; add, if you like, spodium or other things familiar to the liver, such as hepatica and rhubarb. If one scruple is taken each day, or one drachm each week, this is most wholesome. Syrup of wormwood, and wormwood in food and drink, are also best for the same. Troches called [Ἀλί οἶνος], that is, "of wine," of Galen and Avicenna, are good, especially for a cold cause. If the cause is hot, mix with them troches of sporium, the species, diarrhodon abbatis, and three scruples of sandal, and syrup of chicory of Nicolaus. If the flux is bilious from the liver, use syrup of endive and of the Byzantines with water of endive and chicory; troches of sporium with juice of wood sorrel; diarrhodon abbatis or the common kind, and three scruples of sandal. If the flux is bloody, let it run for a little while, then stop it, as with any immoderate flux of blood. If it is virulent, or with hot sanies (Galen calls it ichor), the hot intemperature of the liver is to be mitigated by the things mentioned, taken and applied in the weakness of the liver. If there is pus in the liver from a ruptured abscess, cleanse it with barley water sweetened with sugar, or a decoction of chickpeas; then bind it with the things mentioned before for dysentery.

units.la: Si diarrhoea est a cibo largiore, sumatur parcior: si a corruptibili, sumat bonum & euchymum, coctu, & corruptu difficilem: si ab vnctuoso, sumat astringentē. Si materia corrupta est iam in intestinis, vacuetur clystere communi cum cassia vnc. vna. Si in ventriculo adhuc
units.tr: If the diarrhoea comes from too large a meal, take less food. If it comes from corruptible food, take something good and wholesome, cooked, and hard to corrupt. If it comes from oily food, take an astringent. If corrupt matter is already in the intestines, empty them with a common enema with one ounce of cassia. If it is still in the stomach,

units.la: Fluxus ci balis vulgo. adhuc restat: hierę picrę, vel casię vnc. v-na, vel mannę vnc. duabus: vel pilularū ele-phanginarū script. quatuor. Postremò ven-triculi intēperies corrigatur: calida, vt sump-ptis pepo nibus: frigida per sumpta: vt, syrup. absinthij, menthæ, aromaticū rosatum, dia-galangam, diacyminū, et similia: admota aut olea mastichinum, absinthij, menthæ: vel em-plastra, vel vnguenta, & alia in ventriculi imbecillitate dicta. Si fluit alvus, ventre per frigus aëris perfrigerato: curetur calidis om-nibus sumptis & admotis vt prius.
units.tr: still remains: one ounce of hiera picra or of cassia, or two ounces of manna, or four scruples of elephant pills. Finally, correct the stomach's intemperature: if it is hot, by taking pepones; if cold, by taking syrup of wormwood, mint, aromatic rosewater, diagalanga, diacuminum and similar things; apply oil of mastic, wormwood and mint, or plasters, ointments and the others mentioned for weakness of the stomach. If the bowels flow because the belly has been chilled by the cold air, treat it with all the hot things, taken and applied as before.

units.la: ISCHVRIAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: TREATMENT OF ISCHURIA.

units.la: ISCHVRIA, id est, vrinæ suppressio: cu-ratur per ea quæ causæ ipsius sunt contra-ria: vt, frigida, calida sumpta: iniecta intesti-nis, et meatui vrinario: et admota imo ven-tri: vt, olea, vnguenta, cataplasmata empla-stra, sacculos. Si ab obstructiõe supprimitur, inquirenda est, et curanda obstructionis cau-sa: vt, tumor præter naturā, caruncula, gru-mus sanguinis, pituita crassa, calculꝰ: is enim cōminuēdus est, aut cubāti supino succussatis cruribus in vesica regerendus: vel cathetere vel cādela cerea oleo intincta, vel digiti cōdy lo per perinæum celeriter acto sedē versus. Sive rò in meatu iam totus inciderit, trahēdus est fuctu virgæ, dilatato prius meatu per insessum, vel fotum, vel alia: deducendus quoque est digito in sedē immissō, si illic hæret: si vero ad perinæum, condylo celeriter per id à sedē scrotum versus acto, potius quàm tunc re pellendus in vesicam, vbi in calculum insignem posset grandescere, & forte vix postea in meatum vrinarium incidere. Si à pituita, pure, grumo sanguinis obstruitur, syrup. duarum & quinque radicum, vel eupatorij cum aqua fœniculi, apij, petrosæ: tenuentur & incidantur hæ materiæ, vel theriaca veteri cū vino albo tenui. Si causa sit renum aut hepatis affectus, ei prospiciendū est, ablata ischuriæ causa. Si lotium non excernitur, prouocandum primùm mictoribus: ut, compressione imi uentris, balano acri, & sale aliquo acuta immissa sedi, cui vesica incumbit: pediculo quoque in virgæ initium immisso, qui motu titillet, expulsricemque uim sopitam, irritet, uel eius loco portiuncula cepæ, uel alii, uel similiter acrium: frictione etiam perinæi, & uirgæ prope ignem: hæc si non sufficiunt, pectini illinatur oleum scorpionum, & lilii per se, uel cum syslmbrio aquatico frixa: uel imponatur helxine frixa in id efficacissima: regula quoque calfacta uino bono calente irrigata, herbis etiam prædictis, aut simili bus impositis cruri alligetur: adhæc epiploon recens exectu, ut ab animali calet, imo uentri impositum. Valetior est fotus imi uentris ex spongia cum origano, calaminthe, pulegio, abrotono, sabina, mentastro: & insessus ex prædictorum decocto: quod etiam clystere iniectum cum oleo liliorum, scorpionum, hiera uel benedicta est optimum. Sumuntur ite syrup. radicum duarum uel quinque, uel harum decoctu, syslmbrij aquatici, rubiæ, baccarum iuniperi: quæ etiam sanguinem mictu prouocant Dioscor. ut sabina, & drachma una testæ purgatæ oui à quo pullus exclusus est, est efficacissima potu. Cantharides uerò etiam alis, & capitibus ablatis ob vehemen-tia venenosam fuge: tutior est aqua rhapha-ni. Si à grumo sanguinis est, da potandum o-xy. aliquod, vel lepor. coagulum.
units.tr: Ischuria, that is, suppression of urine, is treated by means contrary to its causes: for cold causes, take hot things, inject them into the intestines and the urinary passage, and apply them to the lower belly, such as oils, ointments, cataplasms, plasters and little bags. If it is suppressed by an obstruction, the cause of the obstruction must be sought and treated: a swelling beyond nature, a caruncle, a clot of blood, thick phlegm, or a stone. A stone must be crushed, or pushed back into the bladder by lying supine with the legs shaken, or with a catheter or a wax candle dipped in oil, or by driving a knuckle quickly through the perineum toward the seat. If the stone has already fallen entirely into the passage, it is to be drawn out with a probe, after the passage has first been dilated by a sitz bath, a fomentation or other means. It is also to be pushed down with a finger inserted into the rectum, if it sticks there. But if it is stuck at the perineum, drive it quickly from the seat toward the scrotum with a knuckle, rather than push it back into the bladder, where it might grow into a notable stone and afterwards hardly fall into the urinary passage again. If it is obstructed by phlegm, pus or a clot of blood, take syrup of the two or five roots, or of eupatorium, with water of fennel, parsley and rock-parsley; these matters are thinned and cut through. Or take old theriac with thin white wine. If the cause is an affection of the kidneys or liver, provide for that, once the cause of the ischuria has been removed. If the urine is not passed, it must first be provoked with diuretics: by pressing the lower belly, by a sharp suppository, and by some salt inserted into the seat, against which the bladder lies. Also insert a small stalk at the beginning of the penis, which, by its motion, tickles and rouses the expelling force that has been dulled, or in its place a piece of onion, or other similar sharp things. Rub the perineum and penis near the fire. If these do not suffice, smear oil of scorpions and of lily, alone or fried with water mint, on the pubes; or apply fried helxine, which is most effective for this. A rule warmed and moistened with good hot wine, with herbs as above or similar things placed on it, is tied to the leg. Also place on the lower belly a fresh caul cut from an animal, while it is still warm. A fomentation of the lower belly made from a sponge with marjoram, calamint, pennyroyal, southernwood, savin and mint is stronger, and so is a sitz bath made from a decoction of the same herbs. This, injected as an enema with oil of lilies and scorpions, with hiera or benedicta, is best. Also take syrup of the two or five roots, or a decoction of them, with water mint, madder and juniper berries, which also provoke urine, as Dioscorides says, and savin. One drachm of the calcined shell of an egg from which a chick has hatched is most effective as a drink. But avoid cantharides, even with their wings and heads removed, because of their violent venom; radish water is safer. If it comes from a clot of blood, give something sour to drink, or hare's rennet.

units.la: CALCVLI IN RENIBVS PRAE-CAVTIO.
units.tr: Precaution against kidney stones.

units.la: LAPIS in renibus gigni prohibetur: pri-mò fuga eorum quæ pituitam calculi ma-teriam in corpore augent, qualia sunt alimen-ta crassa, frigida, lenta: vt, caseus omnis, præ-sertim glutinosior, ex lacte: reliqua, panis a-zymus, animalium partes pingues et albæ: vt extremitates, intestina: aues aquaticæ: cibus largior, & ab hoc venus, somnus, labor, bal-neum: sumendi enim cibi euchymi, & parci-us quàm pro appetentia. Secundò, pituitâ no-bis imprudentibus genitam, ne adrenes ruat, ad intestina retrahemus clysfere leniente, bis in hebdomadas iniecto, vel caßiæ vncia v-na in hebdomadas sumpta, vel potius tan-tundem diacaßiæ, quod ex caßia, & saccha-ro, & decocto glycyrrhizæ, & baccarû ha-licacabi fit, vel terebinthinam ab semunc. ad vnciam, pane missali in vinum merso inuolu tam, vel iure capi solutam, & liquatam. Nam ventriculum, intestina, renes, vesicam purgat, nullo partium harum detrimento. Vel pi lula vna elephangina in dies, vel alternis die bus sumpta.
units.tr: A stone is prevented from forming in the kidneys. First, one must avoid those things that increase phlegm, the matter of stones, in the body: such as thick, cold, and sticky foods, for example all cheese, especially the more glutinous kind made from milk; also unleavened bread, and the fatty and white parts of animals, such as the extremities and intestines; water birds; a rich diet, and from it Venus, sleep, labour and the bath. For food should be taken in moderate amounts and sparingly, rather than as much as the appetite craves. Secondly, since phlegm generated without our knowledge may flow down into the kidneys, we draw it back to the intestines by means of a gentle enema, injected twice a week, or by taking one ounce of cassia each week, or rather as much diacassia, which is made from cassia, sugar, a decoction of liquorice and the berries of the Halicacabus; or turpentine, from half an ounce to an ounce, wrapped in a crust of white bread soaked in wine, or dissolved and melted in broth. For it cleanses the stomach, intestines, kidneys and bladder without harm to any of these parts. Or take one elephantine pill daily, or every other day.

units.la: Tertiò, materiam pituitosam si qua in rene hæsit, ne in eo lapidescat, expellemus vreti cis: vt decocto cicerum, præsertim cum gly cyrrhiza et saccharo ab vncijs sex ad octo, accepto pridie medicamento leniente ex cas sia: id enim decoctum, renes & vesicam mul tum terget ciceribus, glycyrrhiza, saccharo. Idem pollet ius galli decrepiti saccharatum, & aqua lactis caprini, & parietariæ deco ctum, vel aqua, vel succus resi dendo purga tus, & saccharatus. Nam vias vrinarias ter get, vrinamque prouocat.
units.tr: Thirdly, if any phlegmy matter has lodged in the kidney, lest it turn to stone there, we shall expel it by way of the ureters: for example, with a decoction of chickpeas, especially with liquorice and sugar, from six to eight ounces, after a gentle purgative of cassia has been taken the day before. For this decoction cleanses the kidneys and bladder thoroughly, with the chickpeas, liquorice and sugar. The broth of an old hen with sugar has the same power, as do water of goat's milk and a decoction of pellitory of the wall, or its water or juice, purged by settling and sweetened with sugar. For it cleanses the urinary passages and promotes urine.

units.la: Quarto, calorem renum, calculi causam effectricem temperamus, admoto renibus in ter duas telas cerato Galen. refrigerante, vel santalino, vel ex cera alba, & oleo vio lato, uel nymphæato, uel cucurbitino: sed post quartam partem horæ ablato, & aliquoties in die dum refrixit, reddito: tepidum tamen aëre frigido applicandum est. Vitamus autem astringentia, ne uÿs astrictis materias retineant. Aëri externo lumbos quoque aperimus: pelles, plumas colorifica cætera lumbos tangere prohibemus.
units.tr: Fourthly, we moderate the heat of the kidneys, the efficient cause of stones, by applying to the kidneys, between two cloths, a cerate that cools, as Galen describes, or one of sandalwood, or one of white wax and violet oil, or of water lily, or of gourd; but it should be removed after a quarter of an hour and reapplied several times during the day while it cools; it should nevertheless be applied warm rather than in cold air. We avoid astringents, lest they retain the matter within. We also open the loins to the external air; we forbid skins, feathers and other warming things to touch the loins.

units.la: CALCVLI RENVM CVRATIO.
units.tr: The Cure of Kidney Stones.

units.la: CALCVLVM uero in renibus concretum, & iam dolentem, præcipuè si in ureteribus est, expellimus ipsum frangentibus, uias lubricantibus, aperientibus, dilatantibus, & urinas mouentibus: sumpto prius ad uias lubricandas caßiæ bolo cum oleo recens extracto ex amygdalis dulcibus, non rancidis: ne illa materiam crassam ex ventriculo & primis venis adrenes trahant. Calculum autem frangunt quædam qualitate manifesta: vt, pulegium ureticum, & anastomaticum, calaminthe, origanum, lithospermum, saxifraga vulgaris: decoctum radicis graminis, secretum quibusdam remedium: amygdalæ amaræ, nuclei cerasorum, persico rum mansi, vel triti cum vino albo degluti ti, aqua ex fabarum siliquis destillata, deco ctum cicerum rubrorum, apij, fœniculi, pe trofelini, ruscj, asparagi, malvæ, bismalvæ: sed hæ diutius coquendæ sunt. Alia calculum frangunt in renibus tota sua substantia, seu proprietate occulta. Lapis Iudaicus sapore in cundo præditus, pulvis leporis cum pelle in furno siccati: pulvis item ex osse calcanei le porini, vitrum septies ignitum, & toties a qua saxifragiæ extinctum. Pulvis item lapi dis cancrorum, & limacum, & spongiæ, et lumbricorum terræ: & mandibularum lucij, secretum quibusdam remedium. Dantur au tem ad drachmam unâ cum vino albo, vel aqua aliqua prædicta, aut decocto calculum frangente: vel cum aqua raphani, apij, petro selini, aristolochiæ longæ, baccarum halica cabi, spinæ albæ, saxifragiæ: pulvis quoque scorpionis ad scriptulum dimidium, valenter frangit calculum.
units.tr: But to expel a stone already formed in the kidneys and causing pain, especially if it lies in the ureters, we use remedies that break it up, lubricate the passages, open and dilate them, and move the urine. First, to lubricate the passages, a bolus of cassia is taken with oil freshly pressed from sweet, not rancid, almonds, so that these do not draw thick matter from the stomach and the first veins to the kidneys. Some things break the stone by their manifest quality: pennyroyal (ureticum and anastomaticum), calamint, marjoram, lithospermum, common saxifrage; a decoction of couch-grass root, a remedy kept secret by some; bitter almonds, cherry kernels, and peach kernels, chewed or ground and swallowed with white wine; water distilled from bean pods; a decoction of red chickpeas, of celery, fennel, parsley, butcher's broom, asparagus, mallow and marshmallow, though these must be boiled for longer. Others break the stone in the kidneys by their whole substance or hidden property: Jewish stone, which has a sharp taste; powder of a hare's skin dried in an oven; likewise powder of a hare's heel bone; glass heated seven times and quenched each time in saxifrage water; likewise powder of crayfish stones, of snails, of sponge, and of earthworms; and the jaws of a pike, a remedy kept secret by some. They are given in a dose of one drachm with white wine, or one of the waters mentioned above, or a decoction that breaks the stone, or with water of radish, celery, parsley, long birthwort, winter cherry berries, white thorn, or saxifrage. Powder of scorpion, half a scruple, also breaks the stone powerfully.

units.la: Ossis humani ex sepulchro limatura ex vi
units.tr: Scrapings of human bone from a sepulchre, drunk in

units.la: a no pota, dolorem renum sedare mox, quibus-dam probata est. Lapide quoque exectum vel excretum àrene, renalem: à vesica, vesicale calculum frangere potu quibusdam putatur: quanquam id Galenus mendacium affirmat. Cortex lauri potus Auicenæ idem potest: omnibus autem drach. vna siccati sanguinis hirci, quem quadrimum, & diebus aliquot ante nutritum herbis prædictis, tam vreticis quàm calculum frangentibus, potumque vino maluatico, vel similiter aromatico. Deinde Augusto mense decollaueris, sanguinemq; medium, non primum, nec postremum, scutellis multis collectum, dum cocretus est, tesselatim sectu siccaueris in vmbra. Sed ex hirco, vulpe, lupo, & similibus, vuis, calentem adhuc sanguinem haurire præstantius fuerit: quod nonnullos magno successu tentasse audio, nulloque periculo: addebant enim aliquid coagu-li, ne in ventriculo glaciaretur. Auicula quoque motacilla seu cauda tremula vulgo dicta, furno siccata, in id efficacissima creditur. Item quæ vulgo gallorum messengua dicitur: citur: bethonica quoq; seu cestrum Galenus. Composita autem calculum frangentia sunt: iustinianum Nicolai, à drachma vna ad drachmas duas cum vino albo calido, vel aquis dictis ieiuno data, lithon tripon, id est calculum perforans, & frangens, dialacca, electarium de cineribus scorpionū. Clysteres quoq; anodyni sunt salubres, ex libra vna decocti foliorum malua, bismalua, parietaria, chamaemeli, meliloti, adianti, se. fœnigraeci, cum multo butyro recenti, vel adipe gallinæ, vel oleo amygdalarum dulcium vel amararum: vel si flatus adsunt, anethino, cum caßiæ vncia vna, benedictæ simplicis Nicolai, & olei scorpionum, ana semuncia: vel clyster ex solo oleo communi cum se. anisi. Largior autem quàm libra iniectio, renes premendo est dolorifica magis, ob id vitanda, sed frequentia copiam suppleas. Lumbis autem illinantur oleum scorpionum, amygdalarū dulcium, amararum ana semuncia cum adipe gallinæ, butyro recenti, cæspo: vesica etiā plena decocto chamaemel, melilo, malua, althæa, helxin, vel
units.tr: a dose, are proved by some to calm kidney pain at once. A stone also removed or passed from the kidney as gravel is called renal; from the bladder, vesical. Some think that drinking something breaks a bladder stone, although Galen calls this a lie. Laurel bark drunk does the same, according to Avicenna. But for all of these, one drachm of dried goat's blood is used, from a goat fed for four days, and for some days before, on the herbs mentioned above, both diuretic and stone-breaking, and drunk in mallow wine or some similarly aromatic wine. Then, in August, cut the goat's throat and collect the middle of the blood, not the first nor the last, in many dishes; when it has congealed, cut it into squares and dry it in the shade. But it is better to drink warm blood from a goat, fox, wolf, or similar animals, which, as I hear, some have tried with great success and no danger, for they added a little rennet so that it would not freeze in the stomach. The little bird called the wagtail (motacilla, or tremulous tail as it is commonly named), dried in an oven, is believed to be most effective for this. Likewise the plant commonly called cock's messenger, and betony, or cestrum, according to Galen. The compound stone-breaking remedies are: Nicolaus' iustinianum, from one drachm up to two drachms, given fasting with warm white wine or the waters mentioned; lithon tripon, that is, the stone-piercing and breaking remedy; dialacca; and an electuary of scorpion ashes. Clysters too are useful anodynes, made from a pound of boiled leaves of mallow, marshmallow, pellitory, chamomile, melilot, maidenhair, and fenugreek, with plenty of fresh butter, or hen's fat, or oil of sweet or bitter almonds. Or, if there is wind, a clyster with dill, one ounce of cassia, Nicolaus' simple blessed thistle, and oil of scorpions, half an ounce each; or a clyster of ordinary oil alone with anise. A larger injection than a pound presses on the kidneys and causes more pain, so it should be avoided, but the quantity may be made up by repeated injections. Apply to the loins oil of scorpions and of sweet and bitter almonds, half an ounce each, with hen's fat, fresh butter, and onion. When the bladder is also full, use a decoction of chamomile, melilot, mallow, marshmallow, helxine, or

units.la: Lib. 5. sanatuenda. Spongia eodem madefacta, & expressa. Sumantur verò saepe iura[?] pinguia, vel unciae octo, aut etiam plures decoctimalvae[?], vel althaeae, cum butyri recentis unc. una, mellis rosati sescuncia. Sumantur etiam oxymeli, syrup. acetat. compositus, syrup. byzantinus acetatus de radicibus, cum duplo aquae bethonicae, aut saxifragiae. Si ventriculus imbecillā vim coërcitricem habet, roboretur litu[?] ex oleo absinthij, méthae, cum galanga, macc, rosis, caryophyllis, ne pituita largior in eo propter imbecillitatem genita, in renes confluat, aut à calculi remedijs trahatur: quae vsta lapidem augeat.
units.tr: Lib. 5. (to be healed). Soak a sponge in the same and wring it out. Let rich broths be taken often, of eight ounces or more, of decocted mallow or marshmallow, with one ounce of fresh butter and six ounces of rose honey. Let oxymel be taken too, compound vinegar syrup, or Byzantine vinegar syrup of roots, with twice as much betony or saxifrage water. If the stomach has weak retentive power, strengthen it with a poultice of oil of wormwood and mint, with galangal, mace, roses, and cloves, lest excess phlegm generated in it through its weakness flow down into the kidneys, or be drawn there by the stone remedies, which, if burned, increase the stone.

units.la: CALCVLI VESICAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: The Cure of Bladder Stones.

units.la: LAPIS in vesica, vt in renibus curandus: sed valentioribus remedijs, quia durior est, & longius ab ore per quod remedia sumuntur, abest: si tamen magnus sit et praedurus: execandus est à lithotomo perito, eoque extracto, vesica hydromelite abluenda. Suffitum aut iniectionem per fistulam argenteam, ex sanguine hirci, vulpis, lupi, & aliorum lapidem frangentium, quidam tentauerunt: sed successu parùm prospero: quòd lapis quibus est in particulas confractus, harum inæqualitate & asperitate, et magnitudine plus molestiæ exhibuerit vrinario meatui, quàm lapis integer vesicæ.
units.tr: A stone in the bladder is treated as one in the kidneys, but with stronger remedies, because it is harder and lies further from the mouth through which remedies are taken. If it is large and very hard, it must be cut out by a skilled lithotomist, and after its extraction the bladder is washed with hydromel. Some have tried a fumigation or an injection through a silver tube, made from the blood of a goat, fox, wolf, and other stone-breaking animals, but with little success: because the stone, broken into pieces, gave the urinary passage more trouble, through the unevenness, roughness, and size of its fragments, than the whole stone gave the bladder.

units.la: STRANGVRIAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF STRANGURY.

units.la: STRANGVRIA curatur auferentibus causam acrimoniæ: quæ si est bilis vrinæ mista, victus ratio sit refrigerans, humectans: vsu lactucæ, portulacæ, bliti, spinacij, attriplicis, buglossi vtriusque, maluæ, bismalvæ, fuga acrium, salsorum, aceti: deinde bilis purgetur mana, cassia, myrobalanis citreis, non autem scammoniatis: eadem purgantia, quarto aut quinto quoque die sumpta, paulatim bilem, vel materias salsas, & nitrosas a partibus vreticis deriuant ad intestina. Idem præstat serum lactis caprini, & lac caprinum. Quia verò idem multam ex se vrinam facit, eamque mitem: sic vrinæ acrimoniâ obtundit. clysteribus quoq; injciendū decoctum malu&, althaę, violarū, nymphaę, salicis cū cassia ad aluum leniendam, & temperandā humorum etiam in vesica acrimoniam. Bibat syrup. violatum, cichorij, cum fero lactis, vel aqua hordei. Si causa est pituita salsa: sumatur frequenter terebinthina lota in aqua rosarum, plantaginis, vel intybi, ad tollendam eius acrimoniam. Hæc enim aluum soluit, et vrinæ morsum mitigat. Si ab excoriatione partiū vreticarum[?], sumat in dies drachmā vnam boliarmenicæ, vel trochiscorum terræ sigillatæ, vel electri cum aqua plantaginis, vel solani. Quòd si vlcus adest, ante vsum prædictorū glutinantium tergendum est fero lactis asinini, vel caprini: decocto se. melonum, & aliorum frig. se. donec pus excerni cesset, aut parcissimum subeat. Si est ob siccatam uesicam, vel absumptam prostratarū humiditatem, quæ feminī[?] viam sternit, alimento pleniore & crasso est opus. Deinde, imò sæpe statim initio, vbi scilicet dolor est vehemens, acrimoniam mordacem vrinæ remittes: vel per vnctuosa, uel sensum tactus partium vreticarum modicè stupefaciendo: vt, syrup. violatus cum aqua lactucæ, portu lacæ, solani, intybi: vel si valentiore opus est, syrupi violati uncia una, syrup. papaueris se muncia cum vncijs tribus decocti se. 4. frig. maiorum vel etiam minorum. Sunt qui se. hyo scyami albi, vel papaueris albi drachmã vnam cum prædictis aquis mane exhibent: his trochisci halicacabi Mesuæ drachma una, sunt efficaciores, quia stupefaciunt, vretici sunt, & vrinæ acrimoniam obtundunt. Decoctum quoque maluæ, violæ, & similium, cum cassia bis die iniectu est efficax: syringe etiam per catheterem breuem in vesicam im misisse lac humanum, caprinum, ouinū, prodest. Nam eius mistio vrinæ acrimoniam frangit: albumen oui agitatu multo fractum donec lentum esse desinat, per se, vel cum papaueris decocto, vel cum lacte. muccago seminis psyllij sex horæ macerati aqua frigida, omnem acrimoniam obtundit, vt etiam dolori magno hæmorrhoidũ mox succurrat, & podagræ calidæ, sed periculum est ne lentæ hæc in meatu vrinario, aut vesica, si eam adi bunt, partium calore tandem siccata, vel ob turent, vel angustent meatum, & malu succedat nouum, priore etiam deterius. Valentius fiet remediu additis caphuræ granis 3. 4. valentissimum addito opij grano vno, vel troch. halicac. script. vno aqua vel decocto ne papaueris soluto. Virgam quoque tenere in lacte calido, vel decocto papaueris albi, inungere ventrem inferiorem, & perinæum oleo salicum, violato, nymphæ, addita pauca camphura. Decoctum foliorum vitis, salicis, malvæ, violæ, infessu, aut fotu ex vesica.
units.tr: Strangury is cured by removing its cause, which is sharpness. If this is bile mixed into the urine, the regimen should be cooling and moistening. Use lettuce, purslane, blite, spinach, orach, both kinds of bugloss, mallow and marsh mallow, and avoid sharp and salty foods and vinegar. Then the bile should be purged with manna, cassia and citrine myrobalans, but not with scammony. The same purgatives, taken every fourth or fifth day, gradually draw the bile, or salty and nitrous matter, away from the urinary parts into the intestines. Whey of goat's milk does the same, and so does goat's milk. Since it also produces much urine of its own, and mild urine, it blunts the sharpness of the urine. Clysters should also be injected, made of a decoction of mallows, marsh mallow, violets, water lily and willow with cassia, to loosen the bowels and temper the sharpness of the humours even in the bladder. Let the patient drink violet syrup and chicory syrup with whey or barley water. If the cause is salty phlegm, terebinth washed in rose water, plantain water or endive water is taken often, to remove its sharpness. For it loosens the bowels and softens the bite of the urine. If the cause is excoriation of the urinary parts, let him take one drachm of Armenian bole daily, or troches of sealed earth, or amber, with plantain or nightshade water. If there is an ulcer, it must be cleansed before the glutinants described above are used, with whey of ass's or goat's milk, or with decoction of melons and other cooling seeds, until the pus stops being discharged or only very little appears. If the cause is a dried-up bladder, or the loss of the moisture that smooths the way for the seed, a fuller and thicker diet is needed. Then, and often straight away at the start, when the pain is severe, you will ease the biting sharpness of the urine, either with oily remedies or by slightly numbing the sense of touch in the urinary parts. Examples are violet syrup with water of lettuce, purslane, nightshade or endive; or, if something stronger is needed, one ounce of violet syrup and one ounce of poppy syrup with three ounces of decoction of the four cold greater seeds, or even the lesser ones. Some give one drachm of white henbane seed or white poppy seed in the morning with the waters just mentioned. More effective than these are troches of Mesue's halicacabum, one drachm, because they numb, act as diuretics and blunt the sharpness of the urine. A decoction of mallow, violet and similar herbs, with cassia, injected twice a day, is also effective. Injecting human, goat's or sheep's milk into the bladder through a short catheter also helps, for its mixture breaks the sharpness of the urine. Egg white, beaten thoroughly until it stops being viscous, helps alone, or with poppy decoction, or with milk. Psyllium seed mucilage, steeped for six hours in cold water, blunts all sharpness, and so it quickly relieves even the great pain of haemorrhoids and of hot gout. But there is a danger that this viscous mixture, if it reaches the urinary passage or the bladder, may dry out in the heat of those parts and then block or narrow the passage, so that a new evil follows, worse than the first. The remedy becomes stronger with 3 or 4 grains of camphor added, and strongest with one grain of opium, or one scruple of halicacabum troches, dissolved in water or poppy decoction. Also hold the penis in warm milk or white poppy decoction, and anoint the lower belly and the perineum with willow, violet and water lily oil, with a little camphor added. A decoction of vine, willow, mallow and violet leaves may be used as an infusion or a fomentation over the bladder.

units.la: MICTVS SANGVINIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF BLOOD IN THE URINE.

units.la: SANGVIS mictu redditur, quum is est quantitate aut qualitate acri, & biliosa, vel aquosa, aut quantitate & qualitate alienus: interdum ab imbecillitate secretis hepatis, renu. Est quando vase in partibus vreticis erosio, calculi attritu lacerato, rupto, lapsu, percussu, vel alio motu violento redditur: sæpe etiam coitu immodico, interdū crisi. Si ob redundantiā fiat, vel criticus est, non supprimatur nisi vacuatione immodica uires deiiciat. Si biliosus est, aut aquosus, sumptis cholagogis, & hydragogis, vel hydroticis auertuntur à partibus vrinarijs hæmateriæ, & à sanguine vacuantur. Si facultas secretrix est imbecilla, illine lubos oleo myrtino, rosc. cydon. cerato Gal. santalino, unguento comitissæ de se. seu crocato flosculo rosarum, quam antheram vulgus vocat: fotu ex balaustiorum, malicorij, gallarum, hypocysthidos decocto in aqua rosar. plantag. ferrata. Sumat etiam syrup. rosatum, myrtinū, cydoniorum, cum aqua solani, rosar. plātag. lactucæ, & drach. vna boli armenicæ, vel troch. electri, vel terræ sigillatæ, vel troch. spodij, cum se. oxalidis à Rasi scriptorum, lactis ouini vnciæ quatuor, sex, mane, cū drachma vna boli armenicæ sumptæ, sunt in id efficacissimæ, & renes valenter roborant, modò ne dormiat, aut exerceatur. Quæ remedia sunt etiam glutinantia, ob id salubria, si vas est apertum casu, vel laceratu, vel alia ratione. Si ob casum tamen est cruentus missus, auerte prius secta basilica dextra. Si pu rulentum est lotium, tergentibus vtendum: deinde glutinantibus prædictis astringentib. Si prætera calidissimum, serù lactis, decoctum hordei saccharatum bibendum & injiciendum: trochisci quoque Rasis liquore ali quo ex prædictis soluti, salubriter in vesicam injiciuntur tunc solum quando ab ea san guis effluit.
units.tr: Blood is passed in the urine when the urine is sharp in quantity or quality, bilious or watery, or otherwise abnormal in quantity or quality. Sometimes this comes from weakness of the secretory organs of the liver and kidneys. Sometimes a vessel in the urinary parts is eroded, or torn, ruptured or injured by the rubbing of a stone, or by a fall, a blow or other violent movement. Often it comes from immoderate intercourse, and sometimes from a crisis. If it arises from excess, or is critical, it should not be suppressed unless the immoderate evacuation weakens the strength. If it is bilious or watery, the haemorrhagic matter is turned away from the urinary parts, and the blood is emptied, by taking cholagogues, hydragogues or diuretics. If the secretory faculty is weak, anoint the loins with myrtle oil, rose oil, quince oil, Galen's cerate, sandalwood ointment, the Countess's ointment, or the saffron-flower ointment of roses, which the common people call anthera. Use a fomentation of a decoction of pomegranate flowers, rind, gall-nuts and hypocist in rose water, plantain water and iron-rust water. Let him also take rose, myrtle and quince syrup with nightshade water, rose and plantain water and lettuce water, together with one drachm of Armenian bole, or troches of amber, or sealed earth, or troches of spodium, with sorrel water as the writers of Rhazes describe. Four or six ounces of ewe's milk in the morning, with one drachm of Armenian bole, are very effective for this and strongly strengthen the kidneys, provided he does not sleep or exercise. These remedies are also glutinant, and so they are wholesome if the vessel has been opened by accident, torn, or in some other way. If the bleeding in the urine follows a fall, first divert it by opening the basilic vein of the right arm. If the urine is purulent, use cleansing remedies, and then the glutinants and astringents mentioned above. If, moreover, the urine is very hot, whey and barley decoction sweetened with sugar should be drunk and injected. Rhazes' troches, dissolved in some liquid of the kinds mentioned above, are also wholesomely injected into the bladder, but only when blood is flowing from it.

units.la: DIABETAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: DIABETES CURE.

units.la: DIABETES, idest transitus, scilicet vrinæ, continuus, aut verius potionis non mutatæ, vt Lœenteria cibi, ab intemperie calida renu cum siti inexpleta: asse ctus rarus: Galeno bis tantum visus, mihi se mel in adulescente cepis largiter, & sæpe vso. Vbi autem verè largior est vrina, sitis si adest, exigua est, et placatu facilis. Puella enim mediolanensis per dies sexaginta singulos, mictu reddidit vrinæ boccalia, seu chopinas sexdesexdecim, cum in dies biberet tantum boccalia circiter tria, magno exepli miraculo: persanata tamen parum corpus conciderat. Si autem inuitis vrina excidat, vt etiam lectum æger permeiat, causa est primùm auferenda: si enim à potu id largiore fit, bibatur parcius: si à potus aut cibi qualitate salsa, acri: vt, esu largo ceparum, alliorum, porrorum: ab his abstineatur: si à frigore externo, calefiat: si ab hepatis imbecillitate, vt in ascite, prius dicta sunt remedia. Si sphincter vesicæ est resolutus mora longa in aqua frigida, vel alio frigidorum contactu, sanetur ea paralysis per calorifica omnia. Si idem est ruptus, vel laceratus vel sectus, vt lapsis ab alto, vulneratis, sectis ob calculum, parientibus ægrè, sæpe accidit: nisi initio sanetur, difficilem habet postea curationem. Si ab hepatis & renum calida intemperie, ea sanetur sumptis & admotis refrigerantibus sæpe dictis. Si à retentrice vesicæ imbecilla, intemperiem eius causam persana contrariis. Thuris etiam scriptulum unum, vel drachma dimidia, cum aqua absinthij, multis est remedio: & spodium, & ex eo, vel balaustijs, vel terra sigillata, trochisci ad drachmam vnam, & puluis glandis assatæ.
units.tr: DIABETES, that is, a passing through, namely of urine, continuous, or more truly of drink passing unchanged, just as lienteria passes food, arising from a hot intemperance of the kidneys, with an unquenchable thirst. The case is rare: Galen saw it only twice. I myself saw it once, in a young man who drank heavily and often. Where the urine is truly excessive, the thirst, if present, is slight and easily quenched. For a girl of Milan passed sixteen bocals or chopines of urine each day over sixty days, although she drank only about three bocals a day, a great marvel. Yet her body, though cured, had wasted a little. If, however, urine escapes against the patient's will, so that the sick person even wets the bed, the cause must first be removed. If it comes from too much drink, let him drink less; if from a salty or sharp quality of drink or food, as from eating a lot of onions, garlic or leeks, let these be avoided; if from external cold, let the body be warmed; if from weakness of the liver, as in ascites, the remedies already described apply. If the sphincter of the bladder has been relaxed by a long stay in cold water or contact with other cold things, the paralysis is cured by all warming remedies. If the sphincter has been ruptured, torn or cut, as often happens to those who fall from a height, to the wounded, to those cut for stone, or to women in difficult labour, it has a difficult cure later unless it is treated at the outset. If it comes from a hot intemperance of the liver and kidneys, it is cured by taking and applying the cooling remedies mentioned often. If it comes from a weak retentive power of the bladder, correct the intemperance that causes it with contrary remedies. Also one scruple of frankincense, or half a drachm, with water of wormwood, is a remedy for many. So too are spodium, and from it, or from balaustines or terra sigillata, troches of one drachm, and powder of roasted acorn.

units.la: LVMBRICORVM CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF WORMS.

units.la: LVMBRICI si imminent, pituitā vacua pane & pauco sinapi: vel, si opus est, medicamento phlegmagogo: & eam gigni prohibe fuga alimentorum, crassorum, lentorum, &c. pituitæ gignendæ aptorum, vt supra in colico affectu, & alibi sæpe diximus. Si verò adsunt, remediorum generibus quinque sanantur.
units.tr: LUMBRICI, if they threaten, are to be purged with a bland, phlegm-free diet with a little mustard, or, if necessary, with a phlegm-expelling medicine. Prevent their generation by avoiding foods that are thick, sluggish, and apt to breed phlegm, as we have often said above in the colic and elsewhere. If they are already present, they are cured by five kinds of remedy.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione parca, calida, sicca, acri, amara: nisi interdum morsus eorum ob famem sæuientium dulcibus sit placandus.
units.tr: 1. DIET: a sparing regimen, warm, dry, sharp and bitter; unless at times their bites, raging from hunger, must be soothed with sweet things.

units.la: 2. NECANTIBVS lumbricos tota sua substantia, & amaris, calidis, siccis ad tertium gradum: vt, omni absinthio, vtroque abrotono, persicorum foliis, & nucleis, lupinis, mentastro, allio, se. brassicæ, apij, radice filicis masculæ, radice graminis: his omnibus vel quibusquibusdam sumptis, iniectis, umbilico admo tis cum aloë, athanasia, felle aliquo, in puellis suillo, ouino, vel alio mitiori in grandibus etiam bouino, additis oleis amaris, absinthij, men-tha.
units.tr: 2. TO KILL the worms in their whole substance, use bitter, warm and dry remedies up to the third degree: such as all wormwood, both kinds of abrotonum, peach leaves and kernels, lupins, mint, garlic, cabbage seed, celery, the root of male fern, and couch-grass root. Take all of these, or some of them, by mouth or as an injection, and apply to the navel with aloes, athanasia, some gall (in girls that of a pig, in sheep, or another milder kind; in adults even that of an ox), adding bitter oils of wormwood and mint.

units.la: 3. ENECATOS expellentibus (ne pu-tridis vaporibus febres & epilepsiam, & alia symptomata saeua excitent) vt, aloë, absinthio, rhabarbaro, agarico, liquore amaro solutis, vel in catapotia formatis: oleo quoque omphacino sumpto saepe, & larga copia, & clystere iniecto, nisi lumbrici sint adhuc vi-ui: nam fuga huius & similium reperent in ventriculum, si rotundi sunt, nisi mista sint dulcia: vt, lac, & similia: ascarides vero mi-nimi ad sedem fere desident sacculo inuoluti, cum quo tandem sunt deturbandi. Lati autem (quos vocant cucurbitinos) intestino caeco saepe affixi: interdum colo, & recto: vix tan-dem magna vi deturbantur, sibi magna ex-crementorum, & velut membranarum il-luuie implexi. Hiera picra. Gal. & ex ea pi-lulae, & quae ex aloë, myrrha, croco communes uocantur: sunt in id efficaces sumptæ, & aliquo oleo, aut syrup. amaro mollitæ, et umbilico admotæ.
units.tr: 3. TO EXPEL the killed worms (lest putrid vapours excite fevers, epilepsy and other savage symptoms), use aloes, wormwood, rhubarb and agaric dissolved in a bitter liquor, or formed into pills; also take oil of unripe olives often and in large quantity, and inject it as an enema, unless the worms are still alive. For the flight of these and similar worms draws them into the stomach if they are round, unless sweet things are mixed in, such as milk and the like. Ascarides, the smallest, settle near the anus, wrapped in a little sac, and with it at last they must be driven out. Broad worms (which they call cucurbitine) are often attached to the blind gut, sometimes to the colon and rectum, and at last are scarcely driven out with great force, entangled in a great deal of excrement and what looks like a filth of membranes. Hiera picra of Galen, and the pills made from aloes, myrrh and saffron, which are commonly called such, are effective for this when taken, softened with some oil or bitter syrup, and applied to the navel.

units.la: 4. LVMBRICOS ad uentriculum ascendere prohibentibus, stypticis, & amaris, & aceto, sumptis, & uentriculo admotis: ut, oleis, cataplasmatibus, unguentis, emplastris.
units.tr: 4. To PREVENT the worms from ascending to the stomach, use astringents, bitter things and vinegar, taken by mouth and applied to the stomach: such as oils, cataplasms, ointments and plasters.

units.la: 5. LVMBRICOS deorsum trahentib. dulcibus, ut lacte iniecto clystere cum melle, nisi febris adest: tunc ius carnium cum saccharo injiciatur. Siaut sint ascarides ad sedem hærentes, balanus ex bombace illito oleis amaris, vel aloë, felle vaccino soluta: vel balanus ex lardo pinguí, cum filo, dum retrahetur, vermes plurimos sibi hærentes, referet. Vsu crebro diutino salsorum, amarorum, acriū, aceti, necantur & expelluntur.
units.tr: 5. To DRAW the worms downwards, use sweet things, such as milk, or an enema of milk with honey, unless fever is present; then broth of meat with sugar should be injected. If the ascarides are sticking to the anus, a suppository of cotton smeared with bitter oils, or with aloes dissolved in ox gall, will bring out many worms clinging to it; or a suppository of fat lard, with a thread, when withdrawn, will bring out many worms sticking to it. By frequent and long use of salty, bitter and sharp things, and of vinegar, they are killed and expelled.

units.la: HAEMORRHOIDON CVRATIO.
units.tr: CURE OF HAEMORRHOIDS

units.la: HAEMORRHOIDVM venarū fluor non ante est stringendus, quàm vacuationis copia vires deijciat, & sanguis pro nigro & crasso, melior iam fluat: à magnis gnis enim morbis feré melancholicis ægrum hæc spontina uacuatio uindicat. Aluus quoque, cassia, aut iure pingui, aut decocto brassicæ est lenienda, ne stercus sua duritie eas lædat. Sistitur aut quatuor auxiliorum genera.
units.tr: The flow from the haemorrhoidal veins must not be checked until the copious evacuation has weakened the strength and the blood now flows thinner and darker, which is better. For this spontaneous evacuation generally frees the patient from serious, mostly melancholic, diseases. The bowels too should be softened with cassia, either in rich broth or in a decoction of cabbage, lest the hard stool injure the veins by its hardness. The flow is checked by four kinds of aid.

units.la: 1. VICTVS ratione frigida astringente: ut, omphac. succo rhois, ros. cydon. & ex his ac similibus syrup. cond.
units.tr: 1. DIET of a cold, astringent kind: such as juice of sumac, rose and quince, and syrups of these and similar things, such as the conserve.

units.la: 2. AVERTENTIBVS: ut secta uena basilica, dextra, uacuatione sanguinis etiam larga: ut etiam cucurbitulis, hypochond. dextro, inter scapulio, humero affixis, frictionibus ligaturis: fotibus brachiorum.
units.tr: 2. TO DIVERT: by opening the basilic vein on the right, with a large evacuation of blood; also by cupping glasses applied to the right hypochondrium between the shoulder blades and the shoulder, by rubbing, bandaging, and fomentations of the arms.

units.la: 3. VENARVM illarum ora contrahentibus & sanguinem crassantibus, & refrigerantibus sumptis & admotis: ut syrup. myrtino, cydoniorum, granatorum cum aquarosarum, solani, plantaginis: ut, saccharo rosato cum boli armenicæ, uel hæmatitæ, uel corallij rubri drachma una horis duabus ante cibum, ut tryphera Phenonis, scrup. scoriæ ferri Rasis. Squamma quoque ferri quater ex aceto cocta & siccata, sumpta à scriptulo vno ad drachmam vnam bis in septimana, ventriculum, hepatque roborat, & humorum malitiam emedat. Vt trochiscis electri, terrae sigillatae, sphodij cum se. oxalidis. Quibus victus etiam narcotico, athanasia Nicolai, aut antidoto Philonis, persica a drachma vna ad scriptula quatuor usurpatur. Foris autem similia admonenda, balaustia, malicorium, galla, rhus, hypocisthis, bolus armenia, sanguis draconis, tragacantha, trita & excepta malo cydonio probe cocto, vel aloe, thus, bolus armenia, sanguis draconis, albumine ovi soluta, pilis leporis, vel tela aranei excepta. Puluis quoque corij usti, vel suberis usti, quorundam secretum remedium, ovi albo exceptus: usti quoque bufonis puluis Nicolo Florentino in id efficax, & usu tutus scribitur: quod venenosa qualitas ex hoc, ut scorpionibus, urendo abigitur. Emplastrum postremo comitissae sedi admotum, & lumbis, est efficacissimum.
units.tr: 3. TO CONTRACT the mouths of those veins, and to thicken and cool the blood, take and apply cooling things: such as syrup of myrtle, quince and pomegranate with rose water, nightshade and plantain; or rose sugar with a drachm of Armenian bole, or haematite, or red coral, taken two hours before food; also Philo's triphera, and a scruple of Rhazes' filings of iron scoria. A scale of iron, calcined four times in vinegar and dried, taken from one scruple up to a drachm twice a week, strengthens the stomach and liver and corrects the malice of the humours. So too the troches of amber, terra sigillata, and sphodium with oxalis seed. With these, the patient also uses a narcotic: Nicolaus' athanasia, or Philo's antidote, or peach-kernel confection, from one drachm up to four scruples. Outwardly, similar things are applied: balaustines, pomegranate rind, gall-nut, sumac, hypocistis, Armenian bole, dragon's blood, tragacanth, rubbed and mixed with well-cooked quince, or aloes, frankincense, Armenian bole, and dragon's blood dissolved in egg white, or applied with rabbit hair or spider's web. Also powder of burnt leather or burnt cork, a secret remedy of some, mixed with egg white; powder of burnt toad too, which Nicolaus of Florence writes is effective and safe in use, since its poisonous quality is driven out by burning, as with scorpions. Lastly, a plaster applied to the seat and loins is most effective.

units.la: 4. SANGVINIS uitium emendantibus, victu tenui, si largior est: siccate si aquo sior:
units.tr: 4. Correcting a fault of the blood: by a thin diet if it is too abundant; drying it out if it is too watery;

units.la: fior:cholagogis, si biliosus est, phlegmagogis, si pituitosus. Si doleant, anodynis saepe diētis: vt, lacte cocto, vitellis ouorum, oesypo, butyro recenti dolor est placandus. Si haemorrhoides sint occultae, & tumore doleat, anodynis placetur, vel sanguis emittatur his apertis per hirudines, aut scalpellum, aut anastomotica post dicenda. Si vero nec tumor est ingens, nec dolor, naturae permitte: nec aperi, nisi tumoris, aut doloris magnitudo compellat: quod saepe cancri, fistulae, & affectus alij difficiles, his partibus per valentia remedia apertis superveniunt. Aluus quoque lubrica est reddenda, vt ante paulo docui, ne stercoris durities dolorifica fluxionem geminet: sanguis quoque malus, si abundet, corrigatur victu idoneo, & caeteris. Auertendus deinde sanguis, vt prius. Dolor leniatur oleo violato, si calor quoq; adest, vel rosato, vel amygdal. dulc. vel lini, vel lumbricorum, millepedarum, scarabeorum cum vitello ouirmi capanis cum lacte & oui vitello cocta, albumine oui tandem adiecto, et adipe gallinae butyro recenti, farina fœnigræci, cum adipe gallinæ, vel anatis, & decocto meliloti: puluis etiã suberis vsti, cũ oleo, vel butyro, vel adipe aliquo: limaces sine testa, tusi cum oleo violato cocti, cum farina se. lini, aut fœnigræci in cataplasma formati, præstantissimum sunt remedium.
units.tr: by cholagogues if it is bilious, and phlegmagogues if it is phlegmatic. If there is pain, soothe it often with anodyne diets: for example, the pain is to be calmed with boiled milk, egg yolks, oesypum and fresh butter. If there are hidden haemorrhoids and they are painful with swelling, soothe them with anodynes, or let blood by opening them with leeches, a lancet or anastomotics, which will be described later. But if the swelling is not great and there is no pain, leave it to nature and do not open them, unless the size of the swelling or pain compels it; for cancers, fistulas and other difficult conditions often follow when these parts are opened with strong remedies. The bowel too must be kept loose, as I taught a little earlier, so that the hardness of the stool does not double the painful flow. Bad blood, if it abounds, is also to be corrected by a suitable diet and the other measures. Then the blood is to be drawn away, as before. The pain is eased with oil of violets if there is heat too, or with rose oil, sweet almond oil, linseed oil, or oil of earthworms, millipedes and beetles; with egg yolk and boiled milk; finally with egg white added, and with hen's fat or fresh butter; with fenugreek meal and hen's or duck's fat, and with a decoction of melilot; also with powdered burnt cork in oil, butter or some other fat; and slugs without shells, crushed and boiled in oil of violets, formed into a poultice with linseed or fenugreek meal, are a most excellent remedy.

units.la: Insessus, aut fotus quoq; saluberrimus ad sedandum dolorem, fiet ex decocto maluæ, althæae, violarũ, florum chamæmeli, meliloti, tapsi, nymphææ, se. lini, fœnigræci, papaueris albi, hyoscyami albi. hæc si non sufficiunt, stupefacientibus tactum dolor prohibēdus: vt, balano ex bombace, cui illitum sit Philonis antidotũ, vel athanasia Nicolai: vel eadem emplastri modo applicentur sedi: vel vnguenti populei vncia vna, oui vitellum, opÿ à drachma vna ad drachmas duas, croci parum, misce, & applica si dolor est vehementissimus. Hæc quoque si non sufficiant, hæmorroidibus apertis, sanguinem emitte doloris causam: aperies autem affricta re aspera: vt, linteo nouo, parietaria, folio ficulno: valentior lentior est pulpa colocynthidos puluerata, ex oleo amygd. amararū admota: nā horis quin que aperit. Idem præstant stercus columbi cū saxifragia, succus cepæ, fel vaccinum, & alia: cyclamini radix, succo aut puluere, & cæ tera acria. Eadem vncta sanguine gallinæ, vel columbi, hirudinibus non venenosis & paratis, affixis, aperiri possunt: quæ si sucto sanguine largo pertinaciter adhuc hæreant, capiti earum insperso cinere mox excidunt: sale autem ipsis imposito, quem suxerunt sanguinem mox reuomunt. Penuria sangui- sugarum, aperi scalpello, sed cum præmeditatione: quia vulnus ægrè glutinatur. Sunt tamen hodie qui scalpellum præponant hirudinibus, ceu tenuem tantum sanguinem trahentibus. Si cui autem recentes adsunt hæmorrhoides: nullo tamē dolore, sed tumore so lo molestæ, nec curentur. Si consueuerint fluere, non comprimantur, præsertim omnes, nisi magna hæmorrhagia sint tunc periculosæ: quæ tamen postea sunt aperiendæ, nisi sponte hiet. Galbani verò drach. duæ triduo sumptæ hæmorrhoidas siccant: & admota puluis sly· by, decoctum ceratij, muria piscium salsorū, & eorundem capita cum pauco caseo salso: anacardi incisi et affricti loco, vel suffitiper infumibulum: dracunculi præterea folia, radix, succus, cortices, cineres, oleum, tota sua substantia idem præstant: vel hæmorrhoides astringantur hippuri, vel filo serico stringantur paulatim magis atque magis. Melancholia vexatis, & renum affectibus hæmorrhoi des superucnientes sunt salubres.
units.tr: A sitz bath or fomentation, also very wholesome for calming the pain, is made from a decoction of mallow, marshmallow, violets, flowers of camomile, melilot, tapsus, water lily, linseed, fenugreek, white poppy and white henbane. If these are not enough, the pain is to be prevented from reaching the part by numbing applications: for example, a suppository of cotton with Philo's antidote or Nicolaus's athanasia spread on it; or the same ointment applied to the seat in the manner of a plaster; or an ounce of poplar ointment, an egg yolk, opium from one to two drachms, a little saffron, mixed together, and applied if the pain is very severe. If these too are not enough, open the haemorrhoids and let out the blood that causes the pain. You will open them by rubbing with a rough thing, such as a new linen cloth, pellitory or fig leaf; the pulp of colocynth, powdered and applied in bitter almond oil, is stronger and opens them within five hours. Dung of pigeons with saxifrage, onion juice, ox gall and other things do the same, as do the root of cyclamen (in juice or powder) and other sharp remedies. Haemorrhoids anointed with hen's or pigeon's blood can be opened by leeches that are not venomous and are prepared and applied; if they stick on stubbornly after sucking much blood, sprinkling their heads with ash will make them drop off at once, and salt put on them makes them vomit up the blood they have sucked. If leeches are lacking, open with a lancet, but with forethought, because the wound heals with difficulty. Yet there are today those who put the lancet before leeches, as drawing only thin blood. If recent haemorrhoids are present without any pain, troubling only with swelling, they are not to be treated. If they are accustomed to flow, they are not to be pressed, especially all of them, unless the haemorrhage is great, when it is dangerous; they are nevertheless to be opened afterwards, unless they open of their own accord. Two drachms of galbanum taken for three days dry up haemorrhoids; and applied: powdered sly-by, decoction of ceratium, brine of salted fish and the heads of the same with a little salted cheese; cut and rubbed anacardium in place of the above, or fumigated through a funnel; the leaves, root, juice, bark, ashes and oil of dracunculus, its whole substance, do the same; or the haemorrhoids are bound with horsetail, or tied with silk thread, tightened little by little more and more.

units.la: ANI PROCIDENTIAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: Treatment of prolapse of the anus

units.la: SEDIS procidentia, si ab intemperie est humida, laxatis musculus sedem releuan-tibus siccabis: si frigida, calfacies: si vtraque calfacies & siccabis: si adsit calor, refrigera bis: puluis ex hypocysthide, acacia, balaustijs, malicorio, rosis, gallis, cortice thuris, scoria ferri: vel ex his vino, si calor abest: aut aquæ hordei si adest, incoctis: fotus vel illitum pòst lotionem vnguentum santalinum, oleum ro-satum, myrteum, cydoniorum, puluere dicto pòst insperso, vel postquam erit aluo deiecta repositu̅:balanus ex bombace prædictus mergatur, illinatur, inspergatur, & clunibus alis & iunctis quiescat. Si sedes procidit, non à violento desidendi, & cohabitæ respirationis conatu, neque ex mora loga in aqua frigida, aut super lapidem, sed ex decubitu pituitæ, ea est coquenda & vacuanda: post in temperies impressa est castiganda. Si à tumore præter naturam, is curandus, appositis cuique tumorum generi, & tempori præsidiȳs: si dolor adest, applicetur decoctum chamæmeli, meliloti, malu æ, althææ, se. lini, fœnigræci.
units.tr: If prolapse of the seat comes from a damp disposition, dry it with astringent muscle-relaxers that lift the seat; if from cold, warm it; if from both, warm and dry it; if there is heat, cool it. Use powder of hypocist, acacia, balaustines, pomegranate rind, roses, galls, frankincense bark and iron scale, or these in wine if there is no heat, or in barley water if there is heat, boiled; as a fomentation or poultice, after washing, sandalwood ointment, rose oil, myrtle oil or quince oil, with the powder mentioned sprinkled on afterwards, or put back once the bowel has been emptied. The cotton suppository described above is to be dipped, smeared and sprinkled, and the buttocks are to rest with the thighs joined together. If the seat has prolapsed not from violent straining at stool or a constrained breath, nor from long standing in cold water or on a stone, but from a downward flow of phlegm, that is to be cooked and evacuated; afterwards the disposition is to be corrected. If it comes from swelling contrary to nature, that is to be treated by applying to each kind of swelling and its stage the appropriate remedies; if there is pain, apply a decoction of camomile, melilot, mallow, marshmallow, linseed and fenugreek.

units.la: VTERI EXITVS CVRATIO.
units.tr: TREATMENT OF PROLAPSE OF THE WOMB

units.la: VTERVS procidit laxatis humore multo ligamentis, vel abscessu, ac vlcere exesis, aut partu inprospero, vel lapsu ab alto ruptis. Causa est (si potest) auferenda, & vterus loco natiuo restituendus, nisi inflatio prohibeat, quàm fotu ex cumino, aniso, baccis lauri, et similibus: hydromeliti, aut vino rubro astringente incoctis dissipabis. mox ne recidat, insperges, pulueribus ftypti-cis, ante scriptis: postea repones. Suffitu etiā rerum graueolentium: vt, pennarum perdi-cis, assæ fœtidæ, castorij & similium, excepto per infundibulum vel cathedram perforatam: sunt qui ouum sub gallina corruptū, fractum, agitatum, lanis illinunt & imponunt vuluæ. Odoret simul iucunda: & docta obstetrix manibus subseruiat, vel instrumen to virgæ virili proximo. Postea clunibus clatis cubet aliquot diebus.
units.tr: The womb prolapses when its ligaments are loosened by much moisture, or are torn by an abscess, an eroding ulcer, a difficult birth, or a fall from a height. The cause, if it can be, is to be removed, and the womb restored to its natural place, unless swelling prevents this. Dissipate the swelling with a fomentation of cumin, anise, bay berries and similar things, boiled in hydromel or astringent red wine. Then, so that it does not slip out again, sprinkle on the styptic powders written above, and afterwards replace the womb. Also fumigate with foul-smelling things, such as feathers of the partridge, asafoetida, castoreum and the like, but through a funnel or a perforated stool. Some smear wool with an egg that has gone bad under a hen, broken and beaten, and place it on the vulva. The smell should at the same time be pleasant, and a skilled midwife should assist with her hands, or with an instrument resembling the male member. Afterwards, with the buttocks raised, she should lie down for some days.

units.la: MENSTRVAE PVRGATIONIS LARGIORIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: TREATMENT OF EXCESSIVE MENSTRUAL FLOW

units.la: MENSIVM fluor immodicus, si est à sanguinis copia, vena interna dextra secetur, & imperetur victus tenuis, & fuga ouorum, carnium, vini, & aliorum sanguinem augentium. Si ob mistā bilem, à cholagogis: vt, myrobalanis citreis vacuetur, et sanguis refrigeretur, & sistatur per astringentia frigida: vt, syrup. granatorum, rosarum, ribes, oxalidis, cum aquis plantaginis, rosarum: portulacæ, oxalidis. Si à serofa pituita tuita largiore sanguini mista, cum myroba- lanis cepulis vacuetur. Si est à lapsu, glutinen tur rupta: si ab vlcere, tergeatur, et glutine- tur, & cicatrice tegatur, vt in mictu sangui nis dictu est. Sanguis quoq; reuellatur secta dextra basilica, cucurbitula magna sub mā- mis affixa, fotu & ligaturis, & frictionib. dolorificis brachiorum: astringentibus quoq; & frigidis simul est sistendus, cogendus, & repellendus: tu sumptis, vt syrup. rosato, myr teo, cydoniorum, granatorū, cum aquis plan taginis, rosarū, solani: additis, trochiscis ter- ræ sigillatæ, vel electri, à script. duobus ad drach. vnam, vel lapide hæmatite, corallio rubro, ferri scoria, tryphera Phenonis: tu im positis sedi, et vteri collo balanis ex bomba- ce, oleo refrigerante, et astringente illitis: vel aqua, vel succo plantaginis, solani, rosarum imbutis, insperso post puluere astringente in sedis procidentia dicto, & mox dicendo. Si à serosa pituita fluunt immodicè, prodest tibias ad genua vsque continere in decocto astringente: vel eodem ventrem inferiorem fouere, aut totum corpus eodem suffire, lumbos pectinemque refrigerantibus, & astrin-gentibus: tum oleis rosato, cydoniorum, myrteo, tum vnguentis ac emplastris, santalino, ex flore rosarum (antheram vulgò vocant) comitissæ: insperso etiam his puluere astringente, ex rosarum foliis, flore, malicorio, balaustijs, gallis, hypocistihide, acacia, bolo armenia, sanguine draconis, & similibus: ex quibus etiam prædictum decoctum faciendum.
units.tr: If the immoderate flow of the menses comes from an abundance of blood, the right internal vein is to be opened, and a thin diet imposed, with avoidance of eggs, meats, wine and other things that increase the blood. If it is due to mixed bile, purge with cholagogues, such as citrine myrobalans, so that the blood is cooled, and check it with cold astringents: for example, syrup of pomegranates, roses, currants and wood sorrel, with waters of plantain and roses, and purslane and wood sorrel. If it comes from serous phlegm mixed in larger quantity with the blood, purge with myrobalans and onions. If it results from a fall and the parts are ruptured, they are to be glued together; if from an ulcer, it is to be cleansed, glued and covered with a scar, as was said under the treatment of bloody urine. The blood is also to be drawn away by opening the right basilic vein and applying a large cupping glass under the breasts, with fomentations, ligatures and painful frictions of the arms. At the same time it must be stopped, checked and repelled with astringent and cold remedies. Take, for instance, syrup of roses, myrtle, quinces and pomegranates, with waters of plantain, roses and nightshade; add troches of sealed earth or amber, from the writers, two scruples to a dram, or haematite stone, red coral, iron scale, or the Tryphera of Phaenon. Then apply to the seat and the neck of the womb pessaries of cotton, smeared with a cooling and astringent oil, or soaked in water or in juice of plantain, nightshade or roses, with astringent powder sprinkled on, as described for prolapse of the seat and mentioned below. If the serous phlegm makes the flow excessive, it helps to bind the legs up to the knees in an astringent decoction, or to foment the lower belly with the same, or to fumigate the whole body with it, cooling and astringing the loins and groin. Then use oils of roses, quinces and myrtle, and ointments and plasters of sandalwood, of rose flower (commonly called anthera), and of comitissa, with astringent powder sprinkled on, made of rose leaves, flowers, pomegranate rind, balaustines, galls, hypocistis, acacia, Armenian bole, dragon's blood and similar things. The aforesaid decoction is also to be made from these.

units.la: In vterum quoque metrenchytâ iniciantur vncijs tres, quatuor succi depurati, vel aquæ plantaginis, cum bolo armenia, sanguine draconis. Si hæc non sufficiant, philonij vel athanasiæ, drach. vna, cum aqua plantaginis sumpta, sanguinem moueri inieptiorem facit, viribus tamen validis adhuc detur, ne imbecillibus calor natiuus extinguatur. Pessos autem causticos tentare non consuluerim, multò minus iniectiones, nisi vlcera essent depascentia, qualia sæpe etiam dysentericis adsunt. Tunc enim leniora tentari possunt: vt pastillus Pasionis, Polyidæ, aqua plantaginis solutus.
units.tr: Into the womb also let three or four ounces of clarified juice or water of plantain be injected in a syringe, with Armenian bole and dragon's blood. If these are not enough, one dram of Philonium or Athanasia, taken with water of plantain, makes the flow of blood less unseemly; but it should still be given to those with strong constitutions, lest in the weak the natural heat be extinguished. I would not advise trying caustic pessaries, much less injections, unless there were eroding ulcers, such as often accompany dysentery too. For then gentler things may be tried, such as Pasion's pastilles or Polyides' pastilles, dissolved in water of plantain.

units.la: MENSTRVAE PVRGATIONIS PROVOCATIO.
units.tr: Provoking the Menstrual Purgation.

units.la: MENSES, si ob sanguinis parsimoniam per se cōstiterint ex inedia, aut victu parco, aut morbo longo, aut alia vacuatione, suppresi proprie non sunt, nec cieri possunt antequam mulier reddita sit habitior: tunc autem & in his quibus alia occasione suppresi sunt, euocantur.
units.tr: If the menses have stopped by themselves through a want of blood, from fasting, a sparing diet, a long illness, or some other evacuation, they are not properly suppressed, and they cannot be provoked until the woman has been restored to a fuller habit. But in those whose menses have been suppressed by some other occasion, they are summoned.

units.la: 1. CAVSAM suppressionis abigentibus, vt obstructionem, aut contractionem, aut compressionem osculorum ex venis & arteriis desinentium in capacitatem vteri. Hæc autem obstructio si à sanguine est multo, secetur vena poplitis, aut malleoli, & victu tenui vtatur, ac multo labore: quæ duo postrema etiam conducunt orificijs à pinguedine multa oppletis: ac etiam viraginibus, & calidis mulieribus: quanquam & his etiam phlebotomia sit salubris. Si à crasso, tenuetur: si à lento incidatur, tergeatur, liquidus fiat: quæ præstant syrupi, byzantinus, duarum aut quinque radicum, hyssopi, cum aquis apij, fœniculi, petroselini: trochisci quoque de rubia, & qui à Rasi scribuntur. Si autem àpituita, ut fere fit, prædictus apparetur: deinde vacuetur agarico, scrup. indo, diaphœnico, roborenturque ventriculus & hepar, ne talem materiam generent.
units.tr: 1. To remove the cause of suppression, one must clear the obstruction, or contraction, or compression of the openings of the veins and arteries that end in the cavity of the womb. If this obstruction comes from much blood, let the vein of the ham or of the ankle be opened, and let her use a thin diet and much exercise. These last two also help openings filled with much fat, and also viragos and hot women, though for these too bloodletting is wholesome.
