If the cause is thick humour, thin it; if it is viscous, cut it, wipe it clean, and make it liquid. Syrups do this well: the Byzantine syrup, the syrup of two or five roots, of hyssop, with waters of celery, fennel and parsley; also troches of madder, and those described by Rhazes. But if the obstruction comes from phlegm, as usually happens, and this is evident, then purge with agaric, a scruple of the Indian drug, and diaphoenicon, and strengthen the stomach and liver, so that they do not generate such matter.

units.la: 2. MENSES prouocantibus, vt syrup. & aquis prædictis: adhæc decocto radicum rusci, asparagi, apij, petroselini, fœnic. addita etiam sabina: et si vis valentius, pulegio, origano, calaminth. cicerib. phaseolis rubris, rubia.
units.tr: 2. To provoke the menses, use the syrups and the aforesaid waters; besides these, a decoction of the roots of butcher's broom, asparagus, celery, parsley and fennel, with savin added; and if you want something stronger, add pennyroyal, wild marjoram, calamint, chickpeas, red kidney beans and madder.

units.la: Datur autem id decoctum mane calidū ab vnc. 5. ad vnc. 6. horis 3. 4. ante cibū. Idem pollet cassia, cinamo. ad drach. 1. & crocus cum prædicto decocto: insessus quoq; ex prædictorum decocto saluberrimus est, si modo in hoc, & prædictis expectes tempus consuetæ purgationis, fotus & sacculi ex ijsdem pectini, lumbis muliebribus admoti: frictiones item partium infernarum: cucurbitulæ coxis internis, vel ad venam poplitis affixæ: sectio eiusdem, aut venæ malleoli. Si autem vasa in vterum desinentia sint clausa, mercurialis curialis herba tusa, linteo inuoluta pesi modo, noctu immittatur, appensa filo: ora enim hac mire aperit: idem potest melanthij farina, et mithridatios antidotus ad drachmam vnam, cum mastiches scriptulo vno: hac enim non solu repellit, sed valentius attrahit, quod apophlegmatisimo probat. Si hac nosuf ficiant, opopanax, galbanum, sagapenu, hammoniacum, euphorbium paucum admota pe Elini, aut pessio immissa, mox prouocant: & cyclamini radix etiasuper ipsam transeunti mulieri, menses prouocare putatur. Quorum acrium vsu multo, si ardor quidam mordax succedat, aqua rosarum, albumen ouii, oleum violatum, & rosatum, lac, & similia, ex panno imponantur collo vteri.
units.tr: This decoction is given warm in the morning, five to six ounces, three or four hours before food. Cassia and cinnamon, one drachm each, and saffron with the said decoction, do the same. A sitz-bath made from the decoction of the aforesaid herbs is also very wholesome, if in this, and in the aforesaid remedies, you await the time of the customary purging. Fomentations and little bags of the same herbs are applied to the pubes and the female loins; likewise rubbing of the lower parts; cupping-glasses on the inner hips, or applied to the vein of the ham; and opening of the same vein, or of the vein of the ankle. If the vessels ending in the womb are closed, mercurial herb, crushed and wrapped in linen to the size of a pessary, is inserted at night, hung by a thread; for this opens the mouth wonderfully. The powder of nigella can do the same, and Mithridates' antidote, one drachm, with a scruple of mastic: for this not only repels but draws more strongly, as the Apophlegmatismus proves. If these do not suffice, opopanax, galbanum, sagapenum, ammoniacum and a little euphorbium, applied at the pubes, or a pessary inserted, soon provoke the menses; and the root of cyclamen, even passed over the woman as she walks, is thought to provoke them. With much use of these sharp remedies, if a biting heat follows, rose water, egg white, violet and rose oil, milk and the like should be applied with a cloth to the neck of the womb.

units.la: SVFFOCATIONIS AB VTERO CVRATIO.
units.tr: Curing of Suffocation from the Womb.

units.la: SVFFOCATIO ab vtero curatur, vapores ab vtero sursum ferri prohibentibus: vt, frictione, ligaturis dolorificis partium infernarum, cucurbitulis coxarum parti interne affixis: vt, secta vena poplitis, vel malleoli, si à suppressis est mensibus hac præfocatio, non autem si est à semine corrupto, ne hac phlebotome id in venas trahatur: debet enim per collum uteri vacuari titillatum digito longo obstetricis illito oleo irino, liliorum, laurino, in quo moschus, ambra, gallia sint dissoluta: vel zebet Arabibus dictum coëundi miram cupiditatem excitare solitum: ut, suffitu uteri per sedem perforatam, vel infundibulum, iucundo: ex gallia moschata, moscho, ambra, cinamomo, caryophyllis, cum myrrha stacte (styracem liquidum vocant) in trochiscos formatis: ut graviter olentibus naso admotis, ut assa fœtida, galbano, sagapeno, castorio carbonibus impositio, pennis, præcipuè perdicum, vtis, corio calceorum, præcipuè vsto in oleum linimox impositio: id enim vapore per os receptō, etiam viperam ex ventriculo per sedem statim fugat. Ne autem postea ex seminis corruptione in id graue symptoma mulier incidat, si nubilis est, viro tradatur: si non vult nubere, aut monialis est, vena sæpe secetur, interdicantur vinum, carnes, oua, & c. sanguinem & semen augentia. Imperentur labor multus, ieiunium: vsus agni, rutæ, dauci, cumini, & cæterorum semen gigni prohibentium, vel genitum absumentium: quale est daucise. drachma vna cum aqua arthemisiæ pota: quibusdam secretum remedium. In nares ore insufflasse, vterum mox deturbat, vice cohibitæ respirationis, quam cohibeat sæpe mulier impendente vteri suffocatu. Metrenchytæ vacui, siphonem collo vteri immisisse, mox internum pulsorium retraxisse, vterum deorsum reuellit.
units.tr: Suffocation from the womb is cured by preventing vapours from rising upward from the womb: for example, by rubbing, by painful bindings of the lower parts, and by cupping-glasses applied to the inner part of the hips. Also by opening the vein of the ham or of the ankle, if this suffocation comes from suppressed menses, but not if it comes from corrupted semen, lest this bloodletting draw it into the veins. For it should be evacuated through the mouth of the womb, by tickling it with a long finger of a midwife anointed with oil of iris, lily or laurel, in which musk, ambergris and galbanum have been dissolved; or by the remedy, said by the Arabs to usually arouse a wonderful desire for intercourse: fumigation of the womb through a perforated seat or funnel, a pleasant one made of galbanum, musk, ambergris, cinnamon and cloves, with myrrh and storax (they call it liquid styrax), formed into troches; applied to the nose in strong-smelling form, such as asafoetida, galbanum, sagapenum and castoreum placed on coals; feathers, especially of partridges; and burnt leather of shoes, especially when burnt and applied as a liniment in oil. For when this vapour is received through the mouth, it at once drives even the viper out of the stomach through the seat. Afterwards, lest the woman fall into this grave symptom again from corrupted semen, if she is marriageable she should be given to a husband; if she does not wish to marry, or is a nun, a vein should often be opened, and wine, meats, eggs and the like, which increase blood and semen, should be forbidden. Hard labour and fasting should be enjoined, and the use of lamb, rue, carrot, cumin, and the other seeds that prevent semen from being generated or consume what has been generated; such as a drachm of carrot seed drunk with water of wormwood, a remedy known to some. Blowing it into the nostrils or mouth soon drives the womb down, in place of the held breath which the woman often holds when the womb threatens suffocation. The metrenchyta: having inserted an empty syringe into the neck of the womb, and then withdrawn the inner piston, draws the womb downward.

units.la: RHAGADON VTERI CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE TREATMENT OF FISSURES OF THE WOMB.

units.la: RHAGADES, rimæ quædam, & fissuræ in muliebribus curantur illitæ œsypo, butyro recenti sine sale vsto, vel oleo resudante ex nuce veteri dum vritur, vel oleo violato, rosato, dusto per mortarium plumbeum pistillo plumbeo, do nec melius habeat crassitudinem.
units.tr: Rhagades, which are small cracks and fissures in women, are treated by applying oesypus, fresh unsalted butter that has been burnt, oil exuding from an old nut as it burns, or violet or rose oil, ground in a leaden mortar with a leaden pestle until it reaches a thicker consistency.

units.la: MOLAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE TREATMENT OF THE MOLE.

units.la: MOLÆ, hoc est caro quædam infor-mis, deturbatur, præsertim priusquā maior euaserit, remediis menses mouentibus. Si vero à flatibus vterus est distentus, pur-gato corpore toto injciantur primum inte-stinis, postea vtero, quæ flatus dissipant, dia-cyminum, dianisum, diagalanga, diadaphni-dum: immittantur quoque pessi illiti succo mercurialis, inspersi melanthio. Si valenti-us vis, cardamomo: si valentissimum galba-no illinantur, et euphorbio inspergantur: in-ungatur peslen oleo nucum, anethino, melle despumato. Fiat insessus ex decosto eorū quæ menses mouere diximus.
units.tr: A mole, that is a certain shapeless flesh, is expelled, especially before it has grown larger, by remedies that move the menses. If, however, the womb is distended by wind, the whole body should first be purged, and then there should be injected into the intestines first, and afterwards into the womb, things that disperse wind: diacyminum, dianisum, diagalanga, diadaphnidum. Pessaries smeared with juice of mercury and sprinkled with melanthium should also be inserted. If you want something stronger, use cardamom; if the strongest, smear with galbanum and sprinkle with euphorbium. Anoint the pessary with nut oil, dill oil, and skimmed honey. Make a sitz bath from a decoction of the things we said move the menses.

units.la: ENTEROCELAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE TREATMENT OF ENTEROCELE.

units.la: ENTEROCELAE ramicis species, in qua intestinum rupto peritonæo dila-bitur in meatum vasorum seminalium, aut etiam inscrotum: curatur primùm repellen-tibus in suam sedem intestinum, deinde con-tinentibus, ne relabatur, & solutum peritonæum glutinantibus. Vt autem tutò citò in dolenter reponatur, flatulenta vitentur, & si flatus lapsum intestinum iam distendunt (quos tumor leuis, transparêş, digiti percussu sonans, vt ascites ostendit) dissipentur fotu cum spongia ex decocto meliloti, chamæmeli, se. cari. fœnic. lini, fœniorœci, anisi, anethi, cymini, & similiû: vel oleo chamæmeli, anethi, amyg. dulc. ricinino, iasmino, leucoÿ, ruta, vel cum vesica prædictis plena fouea tur, vel ex fabis coquendo mollissimis cum aliquo oleo dicto, fiat cataplasma. Si autem stercus insit, clysteribus etiam acribus post mol lientium vsum vacuabimus: dein cruribus elatis, & diductis molliter succutiemus: & si opus adiutrice aliqua manu comprimendo clementer subseruiemus. Retinetur autem subligaculo: & si puer est, & coxas elatiores aliquot dies continet in lecto, vitatq; motus inordinatos, clamore, tussim, sternutam. anhelit. cohibition. omne repletione, à natura vlcus peritonæi glutinatur. In grandioribus autem longum tempus postulat, & remedia præter dictam victus rationem magis exquisita: ut, ceratum de pelle arietis Matth. Gradi, cui simile est emplastrum contra ruptură Nicolai. Sunt qui ferro candenti partem qua descendit intestinum vrendo contrahunt: aliĭ acu & filo advsque cauitatem qua descendunt vasa, carnem pertundunt: ablata acu filum super tessellam corneam vel eburneam astringunt quotidie magis atq; magis, donec totum filo perruperint: carne interim supercrescente in profundo, & meatus partem occupante, ne intestino postea sit via: sed caue ne & vasa cicatrice interna, dura, & eminentiore premas: nam dolorifica sic fuerit, et testem atrophia tabefecerit. Alij sectione fa Eta, execloque teste, vinculo vasorum omnium, & ambientis membranae, aut cauterio meatum contrahunt, & obturant: in qua castratione grandes natu plerique oris primum, deinde corporis reliqui conuulsione tandē moriuntur: pueris alia inde accidunt incommoda non exigua. Ob id hæc curandi forma potius omittenda est.
units.tr: Enterocele is a kind of hernia in which, with the peritoneum ruptured, the intestine slips into the passage of the seminal vessels, or even into the scrotum. It is treated first by pushing the intestine back into its place, then by holding it in so that it does not slip back again, and by gluing together the loosened peritoneum. So that it may be reduced safely, quickly and without pain, flatulent foods are avoided. If winds already distend the fallen intestine (which a slight, transparent swelling that sounds under a finger tap, as in ascites, shows), they are dispersed by fomentation with a sponge soaked in a decoction of melilot, chamomile, caraway, fennel, flaxseed, fenugreek, anise, dill, cumin, and the like; or with oil of chamomile, dill, sweet almond, castor, jasmine, wallflower, or rue; or the part is fomented with a bladder full of the aforesaid things; or a poultice is made by cooking very soft beans with some such oil. If, however, feces are present, we will empty the bowels with enemas, even sharp ones, after using softening agents. Then, with the legs raised and spread apart, we will gently shake the patient; and if need be, with the help of another hand, we will assist by pressing gently. It is kept in place with a truss. If the patient is a boy, he keeps his hips raised in bed for some days and avoids irregular movements, shouting, coughing, sneezing, holding his breath, and any overfilling; by nature the ulcer of the peritoneum is glued together. In adults, however, it takes a long time and remedies more refined than the said diet: such as the plaster made from goat's skin by Matthaeus Gradi, to which the plaster against rupture of Nicolaus is similar. Some contract the part through which the intestine descends by burning it with a red-hot iron. Others pierce the flesh with a needle and thread down to the cavity through which the vessels descend; then, the needle removed, they tighten the thread daily more and more over a horn or ivory tablet, until they have cut through entirely with the thread. Meanwhile flesh grows over in the depth and fills part of the passage, so that the intestine has no way through afterwards; but take care not to press on the vessels with a hard and more prominent internal scar, for that would be painful and would waste the testicle by atrophy. Others, making an incision and removing the testicle, close and obstruct the passage by tying off all the vessels and the surrounding membrane, or by cautery. In this castration most of the elderly die first of convulsions of the mouth and then of the rest of the body, and boys suffer no small other misfortunes from it. For this reason this method of treatment is better omitted.

units.la: Vide Alexandrum benedicti um
units.tr: See Alexander Benedictus.

units.la: EPIPLOOCELAE, HYDROCELAE, CIRSOCELAE CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF EPIPLOOCELE, HYDROCELE AND CIRSOCELE.

units.la: EPIPIPLOOCELE similiter curatur, sed aegrius, uti & hernia sinistra, quàm dextra, quòd in hac caecum intestinum delabi solitum, magno tantum peritonæi hiatu excidit: illæ etiam minimo meatu excidunt.
units.tr: Epiploocele is cured in the same way, but with more difficulty, just as a left hernia is harder to cure than a right one. In the latter the blind gut usually slips down, and it protrudes only through a large gap in the peritoneum. The epiploocele also protrudes through a very small passage.

units.la: Hydrocelæ autem stercore vaccino, & caprarum impositio curetur: id si non sufficiat, filo ad aquarum locum transfixo, paulatim emittantur aquæ, postea vlcus glutinetur, et parti aquas transmittenti: ut hepati, lieni, prospiciatur.
units.tr: Hydroceles, however, are treated by applying cow dung and goat dung. If this is not enough, a thread is passed through the place where the water collects, and the waters are let out gradually. Afterwards the ulcer is closed, and care is taken of the parts through which the waters pass, such as the liver and spleen.

units.la: Cirsocelæ autem post vacuatum phlebotomie, & purgatione melancholicum humorem, sinon cedat ferro candente, cancrorum modo eximantur varices.
units.tr: Cirsoceles, however, after blood has been drawn and the melancholic humour purged, are cut out like cancers, with a red-hot iron, if they do not yield otherwise.

units.la: ARTHRITIDIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF ARTHRITIS.

units.la: Arthritis à calida materia, curatur quinque his remediorum generibus.
units.tr: Arthritis arising from hot matter is cured by five kinds of remedies.

units.la: 1. PHLEBOTOME partis oppositæ, si à sanguine est, aut materia sanguini mista: alioqui clementer purgamus. Repellentibus quoque vtendum: vt oleo rosato.
units.tr: 1. Bleed the opposite part if the matter comes from blood or is mixed with blood; otherwise we purge gently. Repellents should also be used, such as rose oil.

units.la: 2. MATERIAE feruorem remittentibus, frigidis, & astringentibus: vt, syrup. rosato, granatorum, cum dupla aqua plantaginis, rosarum, solani, oxalidis, per dies quatuor, quinque.
units.tr: 2. Remedies that cool the heat of the matter, cold and astringent ones: such as syrup of roses and of pomegranates, with twice the amount of water of plantain, roses, nightshade and sorrel, for four or five days.

units.la: 3. EADEM vacuantibus, vt catapotijs minoribus hermodactylorum à drach. vna ad scriptula quatuor.
units.tr: 3. The same kinds that empty the matter: such as the smaller hermodactyl lozenges, one drachm to four scruples.

units.la: 4. ANODYNIS à quibus incipiendum, et repellentibus: vt, farina hordei, vel casia fistula dissoluta in oleo rosato, vel succo, aut aqua solani, plantaginis. Medulla quoque panis, præcipuè secalini, lacte macerata & parum cocta: additis oui vitellis, et oleo rosato. Si autem dolor est intolerabilis, adde prædictis opij drach. vnam, croci ad penetrationem parum. Si magnus sentitur calor, muccago ex semine psyllij integro extracta, cum aqua rosarum, vel solani, pauco etiam aceto ad penetrationem
units.tr: 4. Anodynes, with which one should begin, and repellents: for example, barley flour, or cassia fistula dissolved in rose oil, or in the juice or water of nightshade or plantain. Also the crumb of bread, especially of rye bread, steeped in milk and lightly cooked, with the yolks of eggs and rose oil added. If the pain is intolerable, add to these one dram of opium and a little saffron, enough to penetrate. If the heat felt is great, mucilage drawn from whole psyllium seed with rose water or nightshade water, with a little vinegar also added to aid penetration, applied as a poultice and changed while it is warm, and this often, is a most excellent remedy. Or rose oil in which earthworms have been boiled may be applied cold.

units.la: Auic. cap. de caísia. nem addito, cataplasmatis modo apposita, et dū calescit mutata, idq; sæpe, est præstantissimum remedium. Vel oleum rosatū, cui lumbrici terræ sint incocti, frigidum applicetur. Si materia fluere desiit, foveatur pars vino rubro austero, cui chamæmelū, melilot. fœnugræc. diuturna nervis roborandis efficacissima herba, sint incocta.
units.tr: Avicenna, chapter on cassia. If the discharge has ceased, the part should be fomented with austere red wine, in which chamomile, melilot and fenugreek have been boiled; an herb very effective for long-term strengthening of the nerves.

units.la: 5. ID quod fluxit dissipatibus: ut, oleo chamæmeli, stercore vaccino, si potes quàm recentissimo & calente. Præcauebis autem sortu partis ex vino nigro austero, cui incocta sint astringentia: ut galla, balaustia, malicorium, addito etiam alumine scissili: abstinebis annis aliquot, vel etiam tota vita à vino præsertim vetere iam malo, si expertis creditur Rasi, Avic. Celso.
units.tr: 5. Things that dissolve what has flowed: for example, chamomile oil and cow dung, if you can get it as fresh and warm as possible. You will prevent a recurrence in the part by means of austere black wine, in which astringent things have been boiled: such as gall nut, pomegranate flower, pomegranate rind, with split alum added as well. You will abstain for some years, or even for the whole of life, from wine, especially old wine already gone bad, if we may trust the experience of Rhazes, Avicenna and Celsus.

units.la: Vitabis coitum, ut Galen. aphorismo: Pueri podagra non laborant ante vsum venereorum.
units.tr: You will avoid intercourse, as Galen says in the aphorism: boys do not suffer from gout before they have used venereal things.

units.la: Tollere nodosam nescit medicina podagrā. Sumātur bis in hebdomada pilulæ miles, ut ex hiera Rufi, quæ materias ad intestina deriuent, ad articulos alioqui fluxuras. Si arthritis est à materia frigida, vt pituita, purga sæpe, mistis etiam cholagogis (quod bilem mistam habere consueuit fluxionis autho-rem) & stypticis, vt vias fluxionis astrin-gant. Quæ omnia præstant pilulæ de hermo-dactylis, addendo calidum aliquid in frigida, aut frigidum in calida: sed initio mitiori-bus vtendum est, ne tenue trahant, cras-sum relinquant. Vino abstinendum, mol-lientia digerentibus miscenda. Curatur quin-que remediorum generibus.
units.tr: Medicine knows not how to remove gout from the knotted joint. Let pills be taken twice a week, such as the hiera of Rufus, which draw the matter down to the intestines and away from the joints, where otherwise it would flow. If the arthritis comes from cold matter, such as phlegm, purge often, mixing in cholagogues (since mixed bile is usually the cause of the flux) and styptics, to constrict the channels of the flux. All these things are provided by pills of hermodactyls, adding something warm to a cold case, or something cold to a warm one. But at first milder remedies should be used, lest they draw off the thin and leave the thick behind. Wine must be avoided, and emollients should be mixed with the digestives. It is cured by five kinds of remedies.

units.la: 1. MATERIAM auertentibus, & cle-menter minuentibus, vt pilularum ex her-modactylis minorum Mesuæ scriptulis duo-bus, rhabarbari scriptulo vno. Vomitus eti-am si facilis est, saluber.
units.tr: 1. Remedies that divert the matter and gently reduce it: such as two scruples of Mesue's smaller hermodactyl pills and one scruple of rhubarb. Vomiting, if it comes easily, is also wholesome.

units.la: 2. MATERIAM coquentibus, & ap-parantibus: primùm melle rosato, deinde sy-rup. stœchados cum aqua bethonicæ, & ab-sinthij. Fugienda autem vretica, nisi exqui-sitè purgato corpore: & neruis noxia: vt ace-ti syrupi, & oxymelitis, oxysaccharis-que que genera.
units.tr: 2. Remedies that concoct and ripen the matter: first rose honey, then syrup of stoechas with water of betony and wormwood. Diuretics should be avoided unless the body has been thoroughly purged, and they are harmful to the nerves: such as vinegar, syrups, oxymel and the kinds of oxysaccharum.

units.la: 3. MATERIAM valenter purgantibus: vt pilularum de hermodactylis maiorum scriptulis quatuor.
units.tr: 3. Those that purge the matter powerfully: such as the greater hermodactyl pills, four scruples.

units.la: 4. DOLOREM sedantibus statim principio adhibendis: vt, oleo chamomeli, oleo lumbricorum, vulpino: cataplasma quoque ex farina foenigraeci, puluere meliloti, & pauco aceti, cassia fistula, cum oleo chamomeli, et melle sufficienti, boum stercus, item vaccae ex ipsa adhuc calens, vel ex oleo chamomeli, vulpino frixum. Muccago se. foenigraeci cum aqua & aceto extracta, adiecto postea melle, multis probatum est efficax remedium si triduo haereat.
units.tr: 4. Sedatives for the pain, to be applied right at the beginning: such as chamomile oil, oil of earthworms, and fox oil. Also a poultice of fenugreek flour, melilot powder, a little vinegar, cassia fistula with chamomile oil and enough honey, cow dung, likewise cow dung still warm from the animal, or fried in chamomile or fox oil. Mucilage of fenugreek extracted with water and vinegar, with honey added afterwards, has been proved by many to be an effective remedy if it stays on for three days.

units.la: 5. RELIQVIAS digerentibus modera te, ne tenui resoluto crassum, lapideam duritiem induat: vt oleo chamomeli, liliorum, vulpino: cataplasma quoque valet ex farina, se. foenigraec. althaeae, lini, floribus chamomeli, meliloti, rad. althaeae. Potest ex ipsdem & rosemarino, salvia, maiorana, abiga, in vino coctis, fieri fotus, balneum, suffitus.
units.tr: 5. Those that digest what remains: be moderate, lest the thick be turned to stony hardness while the thin is dissolved: such as oil of chamomile, of lilies, and fox oil. A poultice of flour is also good, that is, of fenugreek, marshmallow and linseed, with chamomile flowers, melilot and marshmallow root. Fomentations, baths and fumigations can be made from the same, and also from rosemary, sage, marjoram and abiga, boiled in wine.

units.la: ISCHIADIS CVRATIO.
units.tr: THE CURE OF SCIATICA.

units.la: ISCHIAS ijsdem remedijs curatur, præ-terquam quòd repellentia non admittat, sed purgato corpore, ualeter foras ex profun-da cotyle trahentibus: ut, cataplasmate ex stercore columbino indiget. Clysteribus eti-am acribus utendum est.
units.tr: Sciatica is cured with the same remedies, except that it does not admit repellents. But once the body has been purged, strong drawing remedies should be applied, to draw powerfully outward from the deep socket: such as a poultice of pigeon dung. Sharp clysters should also be used.

units.la: MACVLARVM FACIEI PVRGATIO.
units.tr: THE PURGING OF THE SPOTS OF THE FACE.

units.la: FACIEI pustulas, & maculas à san-guine calido, & bilioso nasci solitas, ua-cuato prius corpore, curabis linimento ex li-thargyro auri dealbato maceratione bidui in aceto ter repetita: deinde horis duabus uel tribus sub sole in mortario ducatur, af-fuso ui cissim, & aliquoties aceto puro, & oleo violato, donec crassescat: tunc adde ca-phuræ scriptulum unum, lithargyri unciam unam: mane partem ablue decocto malue, fumariæ, lapathi, violæ nigræ. Eos qui lepro-si facie uidentur, paucis diebus sanat, & ar-dorem uteri à materiæ mordacis transfluxu.
units.tr: Pimples and spots of the face, which usually arise from hot and bilious blood, are cured, after the body has first been evacuated, with an ointment of white litharge of gold, macerated for two days in vinegar and repeated three times. Then it is ground in a mortar for two or three hours in the sun, with vinegar poured on it several times, and with violet oil, until it thickens. Then add one scruple of camphor and one ounce of litharge. In the morning, wash the part with a decoction of mallow, fumitory, sorrel, and black violet. They heal those who seem leprous in the face within a few days, and also the burning of the womb, arising from the flow of biting matter.

units.la: Plura his ex Hippocrate, Galen. aliys huc transcripta nolui: quòd quæ desyderari possunt, partim à me inter docendum, partim à diligenti lectore suffici facilè queant, ne quis primam manum hanc & rudem, parumque digestam farraginem accusét, in auditorum tantùm gratiam foras prodeuntem: vt habeant exercitationis medicæ rudimentum quoddam, non opus absolutum, sed audiendo, absoluendum.
units.tr: I did not want to transcribe here more of these things from Hippocrates, Galen and others, because what may be wanting can easily be supplied partly by me in teaching and partly by a diligent reader. Let no one find fault with this first, rough and rather unpolished heap, which comes out only for the benefit of my hearers, so that they may have a certain rudiment of medical practice: not a finished work, but one to be completed by listening.

units.la: AVTHOR AD LECTOREM de Argumentis trium librorum sequentium.
units.tr: AUTHOR TO THE READER, on the contents of the three following books.

units.la: VT singula quæ in hoc continentur opu sculo facile inueniri possent, in libros tres hanc de victu speculationem partiti sumus.
units.tr: So that the individual matters contained in this little work might be easily found, we have divided this speculation on diet into three books.

units.la: In primo de forma victus loquemur: eius autem anacephalæosin habes in duobus vltimis capitibus.
units.tr: In the first I shall speak of the form of diet; you will find a summary of it in the last two chapters.

units.la: In secundo de quantitate & qualitate victus, & de numero & hora administrationis agemus.
units.tr: In the second we shall deal with the quantity and quality of diet, and with the number and timing of its administration.

units.la: In tertio singulis febribus conuenientem victum inuestigabimus: cui adiecta est victus ratio secundum symptomatum naturam.
units.tr: In the third we shall investigate the diet suitable to each fever, to which is added an account of diet according to the nature of the symptoms.

units.la: DEDICATIO Operis habetur libro 2. Cap.19.
units.tr: The dedication of the work is found in book 2, chapter 19.

units.la: BRVDI LVSITANI DE VI-ctu febricitantium secundum Hippocratem & Galenum, ad Lectorem præfatio.
units.tr: Brudus the Lusitanian, On the Diet of Feverish Patients according to Hippocrates and Galen: a preface to the Reader.

units.la: CUM omnis generis affectus qui homini accidere possunt, uia triplici soluantur, pharmaco, manuali operatione, & debita uictus administratione: partem eam quæ de pharmacis agit quando & qualia exhiberi debeant plurimi Græcorum luculenter tractarunt: disertissime quidem Galenus multis in locis utran-que disseruit: eam uero quæ rectam uictus administrationem docet, calamo ideo dignam nostro iudicauimus, quia qui speculationem generatim tractarunt rationali methodo, cū ad particularia peruentum est, hoc est ad singulas morborū species, deficere uidetur ab eo quod res exigit. Nam & illa animaduersione digna sunt, an ab ijs quæ in uniuersum dicta sunt amplectantur, aut extra sint. Et horum singula diuisione non carent. Qui autem eam in particularibus tractarunt, ut medici recentiores inartificiose quidem & subinde à uera deuiantes methodo, multa tradiderunt, quæ ægrotantibus minus salubria sunt. Rei præterea difficultas medicorum nostri temporis opinionum uarietas, in debita uictus administratione, dictorum Hipp. obscuritas, effecere, ut id quod à perspicua & completa doctrina deest, apponā. Atque eo maxime quod medicæ artis pars quæ uictus rationem docet reliquis duab. potior sit & magis necessaria. Illæ enim morbum & eius causas, hæc corporis facultates præcipue respicit. Reliquæ duæ nisi hæc adsit consistere non ualet. At sola uictus ratione scimus multos à morbis liberatos quotidie: & plures essent profecto, si medici quauis occasione pharmacorum auxilium non implorassent. Quot enim sunt qui solo competenti uictu citra ullum discrimen ab asfectibus liberari possent, qui præter rem pharmacis contunduntur? Iis adde si in quauis illarum error contingat quantum sit exitialis, in acutis præsertim morbis, in quibus noxæ grauiores esse solent: ut scire à Galeno in secundo de ratione uictus scriptum est in hæc uerba: Si enim hominis natura non noueris, metus est ne plus iusto uacues, uel nullo pacto uacuationem moueas aut si moueris, non tamen sufficienter euacues. Quæ omnia magnas in morbis acutis pariunt offensas. Quapropter cum in arte medica ultra artificialem coiecturam, quam Græci tecmarsin dicunt, certitudo alia non sit, caute agendum semper; ad id ubi errores minus discriminis afferunt magis accedendum. Nec in acutis duntaxat morbis maximam uim habet uictus ratio, sed etiam in diuturnis. Quod enim medicaminibus obtinere medicus non potuit, id conuenies uictus temporis longitudine efficit. Cuius argumentum est medicos iis quos incuratos dimittunt, conuenientis uictus obseruare rationem, tanquam ultimum auxilium à quo superfit spes tandem, consulere. Quod autem in acutis admodum sit necessaria hæc speculatio ratio indicat. Nam si minus nutrias naturæ uires admis: sin magis, morbo fomenta ministras, utrunque aut medicus prudens dabit operam ut uitet. Nam ut à Galeno scriptum est in secundo de ratione uictus in morbis acutis, Verum (inquit) si in uentrem absorptus fue rit cibus quod reddat superfluitq;, si alias, multo magis in acutis tollere est difficile. Præterea in eodem, Quod plus est, inquit, exuperatq; noxas inter dum inemendabiles facit. Eodem præterea libro ipse Hipp. neque sane calumniam effugere potest, inquit, qui ægre ualentem ex uasorum inanitione non cognoscit torquetq; diæta, periculum siquidé aliquod affert erratum hoc, sed logé minus quàm alterum & risu dignum magis. Cum hæc igitur spe culatio admodū sit febricitantibus necessaria, magniq; sit momenti in morbis acutis, cernens nostra ætate hanc partem artis à medicis uelut inculta & neglectam, & quosque citra rationalem methodū suum insequi modum, Hipp. dogmata post terga mittentes tanquam inutilia, & quæ ad artis opera adduci non possint: uisum est mihi de ratione uictus librum hunc cõponere, ut in eo mente Hipp. & Gal. aperte ostendamus: & quàm facile sit secun dum eorum doctrinam febricitantibus uictus administrationem debitam disseramus. Singulis posteafebrium speciebus conuenientem uictum per scribemus. Postremò secundum naturam symptomatum uictus formam immutabimus. Vnum ergo prius admonentes ad rem festinabimus, Hippocratis & Galeni dictis fidem dari postulamus, reliquorum uero Græcorum tum Arabum quantam ratio & ueterum auroritas cocesserit. Illud quoque admonere oportet: quod ad modum quem obseruabo in adducendis aliorum medicorum opinionibus, citabo proprijs nominib. eos qui recte sentserint: qui opinione mea à uero deuiauerint innominatos dimittam. Neminem uolo sua defraudare gloria, præcipuè eò quod & ego ipse facile in ijs laudi possum, unde iure mihi fiet, quemadmodum & ego feci. Nam in hoc Hippocratem in libro de arte insequor, qui ita scribit: Malis autem uerbis aliorū inuenta uituperare ars non est.
units.tr: Since every kind of disorder that can befall a human being is treated in three ways, by drugs, by manual operation, and by a proper regulation of diet, most of the Greeks have set out clearly the part that deals with drugs, when and in what kinds they ought to be given. Galen in particular treated both at length in many places. The part that teaches the correct management of diet, however, I have judged worthy of my pen, because those who have written about the theory in general, using a rational method, seem to fall short of what the matter requires once they come to particulars, that is, to the individual species of diseases. Nor do the general statements lack points that deserve attention: whether they are to be embraced or lie outside the particular cases, and each of these divisions has its own difficulties. Those who have treated diet in particulars, the more recent physicians, have indeed offered much, but without skill and often straying from the true method, and much of it is less wholesome for the sick. Moreover, the difficulty of the subject, the variety of opinions among the physicians of our time about the proper management of diet, and the obscurity of Hippocrates' sayings have brought it about that I should supply what is lacking in a clear and complete teaching. This is especially so because the part of the medical art that teaches the regulation of diet is more important than the other two and more necessary. For the others look chiefly to the disease and its causes, while this one looks to the powers of the body, and without it the other two cannot stand. Yet by diet alone we know that many are freed from disease every day, and there would surely be more if physicians had not called on the aid of drugs on every occasion. How many are there who, with a suitable diet alone and without any danger, could be freed from their affections, yet are beaten down with drugs for no good reason? Add to these how deadly an error in either of them can be, especially in acute diseases, in which the harms tend to be more serious. As Galen wrote in the second book of On the Regimen of Diet, in these words: "If you do not know the nature of the man, there is a fear that you may empty him more than is right, or else you will not move the evacuation at all; or if you do move it, you will not evacuate sufficiently." All of these things cause great offences in acute diseases. Therefore, since in the medical art there is no certainty beyond artificial conjecture, which the Greeks call tecmarsis, one must always act with caution and draw closer to where errors bring less danger. Nor does the rule of diet have the greatest force only in acute diseases, but also in chronic ones. For what the physician could not obtain by medicines, the length of time brings about with a suitable diet. The proof of this is that physicians who dismiss patients as incurable turn to the observance of a suitable diet as a last resort, from which hope at length remains. That this speculation is very necessary in acute diseases, reason shows. For if you feed the strength of nature too little, but too much, you supply fuel to the disease; the wise physician will take care to avoid both. As Galen wrote in the second book of On the Regimen of Diet concerning acute diseases: "But truly, if the food has been absorbed into the belly and becomes superfluous, it is difficult to remove it, even in other cases, and much more so in acute ones." Again in the same place: "What is more," he says, "and exceeds the bounds, sometimes makes the harms irremediable." In the same book Hippocrates himself, as he says, cannot escape the charge of calumny: whoever does not recognise, from the emptying of the vessels, a man who is ill with a weak constitution, and torments him with a diet, causes some danger by this error, but of a lesser kind than the other and more worthy of laughter. Since therefore this speculation is very necessary for feverish patients, and of great weight in acute diseases, and since I see that in our age this part of the art is neglected by physicians as uncultivated, and that many follow their own way without a rational method, casting aside the doctrines of Hippocrates as useless and such as cannot be brought into the practice of the art, I have thought it right to compose this book on diet, in which I may openly show the mind of Hippocrates and Galen, and how easily, according to their teaching, we may set out the proper management of diet for feverish patients. I shall write down a diet suited to each of the species of fevers afterwards. Lastly, I shall alter the form of diet according to the nature of the symptoms. So, first admonishing one thing, we shall hasten to the matter: we ask that credence be given to the sayings of Hippocrates and Galen, and of the rest of the Greeks, and of the Arabs, insofar as reason and the authority of the ancients allow. This also I must advise: in the manner I shall follow in citing the opinions of other physicians, I shall name by their own names those who have thought rightly; those whom in my judgment I find to have strayed from the truth I shall leave unnamed. I wish to defraud no one of his glory, especially since I myself can easily be praised in these matters, and so it will be rightly to my credit, as I too have done. For in this I follow Hippocrates in his book On the Art, who writes thus: "It is not the art to censure the discoveries of others with bad words."

units.la: Propositio.
units.tr: Proposition.

units.la: Dionysius medicus & Brudus eius filius interloquutores.
units.tr: Dionysius the physician and his son Brudus, the interlocutors.

units.la: B. Abundè à medicis hodie disceptatū est de epithematum impositione. In re alia non uideo inter medicos citius conuenire ac in debita uictus administratione. Quod argumentum est recta exhibendi uictus rationem aut adeo manifesta esse, ut nullus superfsit dubitationi locus, aut adeo difficilem ut supra omnem sit disputationem. Aut ideo quod ab ijs, quos in uictus exhibitione committunt erroribus parum posse ægrotantes lædi iudicant.
units.tr: B. There has been plenty of dispute among physicians today about the application of poultices. In no other matter do I see physicians agree more quickly than in the proper management of diet. Either the rule for prescribing diet is so plain that there is no room for doubt, or it is so difficult that it lies beyond all discussion; or else it is because they judge that the sick can be harmed little by the errors they commit in prescribing diet.

units.la: D. In utraq; artis medicæ parte, tum quæ de pharmacis, tum ea quæ manuali agit operatione, secundum antiquorum dogmata medici agere conatur. Sola in uictus ratione non aliter quàm si intra portum nauigarent nauticum directorium dimittunt. Cum tamen res aliter habeat. Nam si antiquis aliqua fit adhibeda fides, uni præcipuè Hipp. Scripta quæ posteris reliquit, haud qualescunq;, sed insignes maxime noxas incurrere acutè ægrotantes ab incompetenti uictu, & intempestiue exhibito aperte ostendunt. Quantæ autem huic uires sint, si recte administretur, in roboranda natura, declarat ic iunantium ad quascunq; leuiusculas obeundas actiones formidolosa, imbecillitas.
units.tr: D. In both parts of the medical art, both the one that concerns drugs and the one that works by manual operation, physicians try to act according to the doctrines of the ancients. Only in the rule of diet do they abandon it, as if sailing within harbour they let go the nautical compass. Yet the matter stands otherwise. For if any faith is to be given to the ancients, and above all to Hippocrates, whose writings he left to posterity, which are by no means ordinary, they clearly show that acutely sick patients incur very great harms from an unsuitable diet and one given at the wrong time. And how great the power of diet is, if it is rightly administered, in strengthening nature, is shown by the dread weakness of those who gasp at undertaking even the slightest actions.

units.la: B. Pater optime da quæso ut tecum de hac re sermonem habeam. Nam ocium huic speculationi opportunum rigida præbet hyems. Ardet animus ab ijs quibus nō paucis implicitus est nodis explicari. Scio te annos quadraginta peruigili lectione Græcorum & Arabum uolumina euoluisse, ita ut recentiorum nullum prætermiseris quorum calamus dignus sit nomine. Hoc temporis interuallo incessanter ægrotantiū gemitibus assidens inusitata diligentia præstantissimi apud occidentalissimos hominum medici
units.tr: B. Father, I beg you, allow me to have a discussion with you about this matter. For the rigid winter provides leisure suited to this speculation. My mind burns to be untangled from the knots in which it is caught, not a few. I know that for forty years, with vigilant reading, you have unrolled the volumes of the Greeks and the Arabs, so that you have passed over none of the recent writers whose pen is worthy of the name. Over this stretch of time, sitting constantly by the groans of the sick, with unusual diligence you have been the most distinguished physician among the most western of men.

units.la: dici didnomen es consecutus. Nec me fugit te dicere solitum, ingenuum artificem esse qui sciat quæ cæteri, & quæ cæteros lateant. Hic unus instar multorum est. D. Gaudeo quod in hanc speculationem procliuem studio ardenti te sentiā. Ego uero quod mea dedit scire ætas libenter tibi aperiam. Id enim iam diu decreueram, ut id quod in arte medica longo usu, aut humano generi commodum, aut noxium inueneram, in te ipso ad obliuionem senij, (ut Plato ait) uelut commentarios mihi reponerem. Simul ut mihi ad manus cum morte iam decertanti tertius à patre meo succedas, medico apud principes Hispanorum uiros præclaro. ita ut per te artis medicæ peritia nostræ domui iam familiaris inhabitet. Nam nodus triplex non facile soluitur, ut Hebræorum sapienti placuit.
units.tr: ... you have earned the name. Nor does it escape me that you are accustomed to say that a man is a true craftsman who knows what others know and what others are ignorant of; such a man is equal to many. D. I rejoice that I perceive you inclined to this speculation with an ardent zeal. As for me, I will gladly open to you what my years have let me know. For I had long since decided that what I had found in the medical art by long practice, whether useful to the human race or harmful, I would set down for myself, as commentaries, in you, against the forgetfulness of old age (as Plato says). Likewise, so that when, already struggling with death, I am succeeded by a third from my father, a physician distinguished among the princes and men of Spain, the skill of the medical art may now dwell familiar in our house through you. For a threefold knot is not easily loosed, as the wise man of the Hebrews judged.

units.la: BRVDI LVSITANI DE RATIONE VICTVS IN febribus Liber primus, qui est de forma victus.
units.tr: Brudus the Lusitanian, On the Regimen of Diet in Fevers, Book One, which concerns the form of diet.

units.la: DISCEPTATIO AN CRASSVS VI ctus acutè febricitantibus conueniat, ut medi cus contra methodicos disputans in hoc capite asserit. CAPVT I.
units.tr: A DISPUTATION ON WHETHER A THICK DIET SUITS PATIENTS WITH ACUTE FEVERS, as the physician, arguing against the Methodists, asserts in this chapter. CHAPTER I.

units.la: CIRCA victus administratio‐nem varias esse costat apud medicos opiniões. Fuerűt qui cras‐so semper victu quibuscunque in morbis alendos ægrotátes opinati fuerint, vt olim Romæ Petronas, cuius meminit Galen. in proœmio libri de ratione victus in acu‐tis. Sunt qui semper tenui. Sunt qui in primis ægritudinis diebus magis crasso, deinde magis tenui. Sunt & qui contrà censeant. Cum ijs, qui primum obseruant modű, utpote qui rem attigisse rationibus propriis magis videtur, sermonem habebimus. Et vt disceptatio re‐ctè procedat, præmittere oportet crassi, tenu‐is, et symmetri victus, notiones, vt costet id de quo disputatio est. Est quidem vires augere potens alimentū quod plenum aut crassum vocatur, à Græcis πίωτα ἁδλεά dicitur. Conseruans verò quod symmetrum existit. Quod verò cōminuit tenue, λεπτλὼ πίωτας Græci nuncupant. Has à methodico confessas habere notiones volumus. Insuper & illud, rarò accidere vt robur corporis ægrotantiū mains reddere quā acceperimus, studeamus: imò magna ex parte properandū esse in lōgis morbis vires seruare, in acutis parum debilitatas conseruare. Concessa hæc omnia sunt à Gal. in aphoris. Tenues & exquisiti victus, &c. Ex quibus aperte ostenditur, ægrotantibus symmetrum, tenuem, aut tenuissimum, conuenire victum: eum verò qui crassus dicitur, solum sanis concedendum corporibus, secundum rationalium medicorum dogmata.
units.tr: It is clear that there are various opinions among physicians about how diet should be managed. Some have thought that patients should always be fed a thick diet in every illness, as Petronas did once at Rome, whom Galen mentions in the preface to his book On the Regimen of Diet in Acute Diseases. Some always prescribe a thin diet. Some prescribe a thicker diet in the first days of the illness and a thinner one afterwards. Others hold the opposite view. I shall speak with those who first observe a measure, since they seem to have reached the matter by their own reasoning. So that the dispute may proceed correctly, we must first set out the notions of thick, thin and moderate diet, so that the subject of the dispute is clear. Nourishment that is said to be full or thick is able to increase strength; the Greeks call it πίωτα ἁδλεά [fat, full nourishment]. That which preserves is the moderate kind, which exists as a symmetrical diet. What is thin and sparing, the Greeks call λεπτὰ πίωτα [thin nourishment]. We want the Methodist to admit these notions. In addition, we should aim to keep the strength of the sick, not to make it worse than we found it, since this rarely happens; indeed in long illnesses we must mostly hasten to preserve strength, and in acute ones to keep it from being weakened too much. Galen concedes all this in the Aphorisms: "Thin and exquisite diets, etc." From these points it is plainly shown that a moderate, thin or very thin diet suits the sick, while what is called a thick diet should be given only to healthy bodies, according to the teaching of the rational physicians.

units.la: Eorum verò qui contrà sentiūt nempe qui buscunque in morbis crasso victu, qui vires augeat vtendum esse, rationes audire oportet. In omni morbo ob naturæ robur sequie-nasionem sæpius: ob imbecillitatem verò, in mortis discrimen laborantes devenire. Cibo & potu cum natura vires assumat, talem ic circo ac tantum indulgendū, ut laboratis natu-ram roborare valeat. Id cum crassius solum victus præstet, quibuscunq; in morbis minis-trandum fore. Præterea aut virtus corporis morbo superior est, aut æqualis, aut inferior. Quæ nam vero spes superest tenui aut symme-tro utenti victu, dū natura ab initio morbo est imbecillior, cum horū neuter vires natu-ræ augeat. At posse ex ijs aliquot crasso libe-rari victu, experientia eorum qui pestilen-ti febre detinentur, qua nulla alia exitio-sior est, constat: Cum qua duellum si commit-tat natura, ut plurimum succumbit: ut asse ruit Gal. in expositione illius, Quibuscunque crisis fit: ab ea tamen multos à medicis destitu-tos sanatos esse, quos vulgus ipsa natura edo-ctū, crasso victu nutriuerit. Ita ut nonnulli ra-tionalium medicorū id aduertentes, crasso vi-ctu eos reficere qui pestilentia detinentur iu-beant: Ut Celsus qui vinū calidum ac mera-tius dare iubet, & omnia glutinosa, inter quæ carnem generis eiusdem, Avicenna etiā summus inter Arabes medicus, Qui ex ijs (inquit) viriliter agunt & violenter comedūt, euadunt. Neque id præter rationem est, nam quæ antea inualidæ vires erant, crassi victus ope, firmiores euadunt. Nullos autem tenui aut symmetro posse liberari docet rationalium medicorum sollicitudo, in cognoscēdis ijs morbis qui corporis vires superant, vt ab eis medici illæso honore confestim discedant. Ob quam causam Hippoc. rationalium medicorum princeps, Cognoscere (inquit) oportet, horum affectuum naturas, quantum supra vires sunt corporum. Tenues ergo victus, & qui tenuissimi dicuntur, solum ijs ministrandos morbis fore methodice fatebaris, in quibus natura ab initio morbo superior est. Quod Gal. confessus est, cum de victus forma secundum Hippocratis mentem ageret, nempe vbi tenui, aut tenuissimo vtendum esset, admonet eum victum in ijs duntaxat morbis ministrandum, qui ad salutem terminantur, minime in ijs qui ad mortem.
units.tr: As for those who think the opposite, namely that a thick diet should be used in every illness because it increases strength, we must hear their reasons. In every illness, because of the strength of nature, the sick often recover; but because of weakness, they fall into danger of death. Since nature gains strength from food and drink, the sick should be indulged with such food and in such amounts that they can strengthen nature. Since only a thicker diet does this, it must be given in every illness. Moreover, the strength of the body is either superior to the illness, equal to it, or inferior. What hope is left to one who uses a thin or moderate diet, when nature is weaker than the illness from the start, since neither of these diets increases the strength of nature? But that some are freed from such a condition by a thick diet is shown by the experience of those held by the plague fever, than which no other is more deadly. When nature enters a struggle with it, it usually succumbs, as Galen asserts in his exposition of the passage "In whatever illnesses a crisis occurs." Yet many whom physicians had abandoned have been cured by it, since nature, taught by the common people, nourished them with a thick diet. So some of the rational physicians, noticing this, order that those held by the plague be restored with a thick diet. Celsus, for example, orders warm and rather strong wine, and all glutinous foods, among which is meat of that kind. Avicenna too, the greatest physician among the Arabs, says: "Those who act vigorously and eat greedily, come through." Nor is this against reason, for those whose strength was earlier feeble become firmer by means of a thick diet. But the care of the rational physicians in recognising those illnesses which overpower the strength of the body teaches that none can be freed by a thin or moderate diet, so that physicians may withdraw from them at once with their honour intact. For this reason Hippocrates, the prince of the rational physicians, says: "One must recognise the natures of these affections, how far they are beyond the strength of the bodies." Therefore you admitted, as a Methodist, that thin diets, and those called very thin, should be given only in those illnesses in which nature is superior from the start. Galen too agreed with this when he discussed the form of diet according to Hippocrates' mind. He warns that where a thin or very thin diet must be used, it should be given only in those illnesses which end in health, and by no means in those which end in death.

units.la: In primo prædictionum. Cuius verba ita habent secundum veram ver-
units.tr: In the first book of the Prognostics. Its words run thus in the true version:

units.la: sionem: Non enim distrahere naturam oportet ad aliam nouam coctionem, cum eo tempore humorum morbum efficientium coctio-ni fortiter vacet, & sit paulo post ipsos evi-ctura. Sic a nobis ostensum est in tractatio-ne de crisibus, secundum illos scilicet morbos sermone omni procedente, in quibus omnino diaeta & curatione utimur. Sunt autem illi, in quibus vigorem excipit declinatio. nam in quibus mors post vigorem sequitur, ea solum artis parte quae praedicit utemur, praenuncian-tes quod futurum est, ut absque culpa si-mus futuri euentus. In solis ergo morbis qui ad salutem sunt terminandi tenui, aut tenuis-simo utendum esse victu, aperte supra dicta Gal. verba declarant. Sed dicat methodicus oportet, unde medicus acuto morbo inchoan-te euasurum aegrum certo sciet, ut illi tenuem instituat victum, aut tenuissimum: aut horum neutrum, si moriturum? Cum in arte medi-ca futuri euentus nulla certa habeatur scien-tia, necesse est, ut aliquando eos qui liberandi sunt sunt, praeter medicorum opinionem, crasso alamus victu, & non raro eos qui extremum insperato clausuri sunt diem tenui. Crasso ergo victu medicorum iudicio morituri, sanabuntur: tenui eorundem opinione conualituri, interibunt. Quod fateri cogeris si optimorum medicorum iudicio, quibus non raro praeter opinionem tales euentus accidunt, quicquam certitudinis tribuas. Si necessitatem salutis aut mortis supra dicta Gal. verba supponere dicas, nihili est profecto Hippoc. apud eos qui conualescent necessario aut morientur, et nihil interest si crasso aut tenui hos alas victu comparandae salutis gratia. At si forte methodicus concedat certa scientia nihil haberi, esse tamen in arte medica artificialem coniecturam, quam Graeci τεκμαρσιν dicunt, qua eorum quae sunt aut erunt, cognitio habetur: Hac instructus medicus conjiciens ab initio aegritudinis corporis laborantis virtutem morbo superiorem, aegrum conualiturum spe rabit, tenuemque victum prout morbo acumen contigerit instituet. Quod si inferiorem,
units.tr: "For one must not draw nature to another new concoction, since at that time she is strongly occupied with the concoction of the humours that cause the illness, and shortly will overcome them. So it has been shown by us in the treatise on crises, namely for those illnesses in which we use diet and treatment throughout the whole account. These are the illnesses in which a decline follows the strength. But in those in which death follows the strength, we shall use only that part of the art which foretells, announcing what is to come, so that we may be free of blame for the outcome. In illnesses that must end in health, then, the words of Galen declare plainly that a thin or very thin diet should be used." But the Methodist must say: how will the physician know for certain, when an acute illness is beginning, whether the sick man will recover, so that he may prescribe a thin or very thin diet, or neither, if he is to die? Since in the art of medicine there is no certain science of future events, it is necessary that sometimes we feed with a thick diet, contrary to the physicians' opinion, those who are to be freed, and not seldom feed with a thin one those who were unexpectedly about to close their last day. So by the judgement of physicians, those who are to die with a thick diet will recover; those who are to recover with a thin diet, by the same opinion, will perish. You will be forced to admit this if you grant any certainty to the judgement of the best physicians, to whom such outcomes often happen beyond expectation. If you say that the words of Galen above presuppose the necessity of salvation or death, then the words of Hippocrates are truly nothing to those who necessarily recover or die, and it makes no difference whether they are fed a thick or thin diet for the sake of obtaining health. But if the Methodist perhaps concedes that there is no certain science, yet that in the medical art there is an artificial conjecture, which the Greeks call τεκμαρσιν [tekmarsin, inference from signs], by which knowledge of what is or will be is obtained, then the physician so instructed, conjecturing from the beginning of the illness that the strength of the body suffering is superior to the illness, will hope that the patient will recover, and will prescribe a thin diet as the severity of the illness allows. But if it is inferior,

units.la: moriturum: Quare nec tenuem nec tenuis-simũ huic ministrabit, sola prædiction̄e con-tentus discedet. Attamen cum coniectura-le signum non necessariorum sit, neque im-possibilium aliter habere, non tollet, quod su-pra obiectum est. Præcipuè cum Hippocrat. ipse acutorum morborũ pronunciationes non omnino certas esse nec salutis nec mortis scri-serit. Præterea esto ab initio acuti morbi virtutem superiorem certò conÿcias, tenu-em adhibebis victum methodicè: sed cum ta-lis ob tenuitatem vires minuat, vt supra o-stensum est de mente Gal. fieri posse, vt tenui illo victu moriatur ille, crasso vero seruetur. (Nam si ponas virtutis supra morbum ex-cessum tantillum, vt soli vincendo morbo & eius obsistere incursibus virtus suffici-at: apudque vigorem sola habita morbi ra-tione minori excessu supersit morbo supe-rior quàm sit id quod tenuis victus virium exoluit.) Hunc si tenui victu, qui quantũ ex se est vires exoluat, ab initio alas, putás ne a-pud statum superiorem futurum, an potius in-seriorem? seriorem? Ego quidem non peruenturum ad statum si vltra dies septem prorogetur opinor. At si symmetro victu qui quantum ex se est vires seruat, quo solu in chronicis morbis vtendum fore rationalium medicorum se cta imperat, hunc nutrias, nonne euader? Na ratione symmetri victus nullu patiuntur vires detrimentum. Quod si cibum qui vires naturæ addat ministres multo fortiorem hunc quo vis morbi tempore quam symmetro victu efficies. Sed forsan ad hæc methodicus dixerit, victum tenuem, virtutem etsi imbecilliorem quantumcunque reddat, morbum breuiorem efficere. Nam natura, cibi tenuis coctioni parum incumbens, diutius materiæ morbi vacabit, unde citius fieri coctiones, minusque morbi symptomata et labores naturæ robur exoluentes durare cogin get. Unde etsi magis æger tenui victu exolua tur quam symmetro aut crasso: quia tamen mino ri exoluitur tempore, minus damni natura se ret acuto morbo laborantis, ex tenui victu, quam symmetro aut crasso, si virtutis tenore in statu cum tenui victu conferas, ad eandem cum symmetro aut crasso apud vigorē. Hæc methodicus respondens arbitratur iuxta tenuitatem aut crassitiē victus citius aut tardius futuras coctiones: quare & distantiam status longiorem & breuiorem iuxta cibi crassioris, aut magis tenuis exhibitionem fie ri posse putabit. Cum Gal. lib. de crisib.primo, & in lib.de quatuor morbi temporibus, & in secundo de ratione victus, in expositione illius, Coniecere autem oportet & robur & c.statum esse cum maximè cosiciuntur coctiones ostendat. Quod si ita, vt opinatur, res haberet, grauiter peccasset Galen.rationalis methodi author ab Hippocrate secundus, cū victus formam penes distantiā status sumen dā nobis præcipiat, si pro victus ratione longior & breuior fieri posset. Nam eo modo re ētius esset status distantiam ex forma victus coiicere, quàm contrarium. Sed pone rursus acute febricitantis vires morbo superiores, morbumque ad septimum terminandum, tenui hunc nutries victu qui vires minuit, nempe hydromelite, aut ptisane cremore, aut hu iusmodi tenui sorbitiuncula, septima die, vt- pote quo morbi vigor futurus sit, aegrotante in omnimoda seruabis inedia. Age nunc sanū hominem æquè robustum ac ægrotans erat, simili victu ad septimum seruato, totaque ea die incibatum hominem conuenias vespera- scente die septimo qualem illum fore putas? Quod si prima die miliaria sex pedestri itine- re peragebat citra manifestum incommodu, quot die septima putas posse peragere? Quili- bet sanè mentis compos an tria possit confice re dubitabit. Idem de saltu, cursu, ponderis e- leuatione, in summa in omni conatu multum ab ea deficiet meta, quam prima die attinge- bat. Sed in naturalibus actionibus idem iudi cium. Nam si die septima dimidiū cibi quem ante diem primam facilè digerebat offeras, grauato ventriculo laedetur. Quanto autem vitalis facultas fiet imbecillior declarant lan guidi pulsus integra die ieiunantium. Cum er go sano homini sola illius victus ratione om- nium trium virtutum tam sensibilis accidat imbecillitas, quanto plus læsionis & detrimenti virium ex tali victu ægrotantes ferët arbitraris? Quod si hæsitas, roga huius sectæ principes Hippocratē secundo de ratione victus, & Gal. cum scribunt detrimenta minus sanos quàm ægros afficere. Præterea languentes à repētina victus mutatione lædi magis quàm sanos, sed adhuc eos magis qui acutis infestantur morbis. Item in eodem, permutatio victus si sanis molesta est, languentibus molestior erit. Cum ergo hominem sanum si tenui illo victu ad septimum nutrias, manifestè eius vires minui videmus, multo magis id ægrotanti accidet, ita ut manifesto excessu imbecilliores fiant ex illo victu.
units.tr: "They will die." Therefore he will give this patient neither a thin diet nor the very thinnest, and will leave content with the prediction alone. Yet since a conjectural sign concerns things that are neither necessary nor impossible, it cannot be otherwise, and it does not remove the objection raised above. This is especially so because Hippocrates himself wrote that the prognoses of acute diseases are not wholly certain, either of safety or of death. Moreover, suppose that at the outset you can clearly judge that the strength is superior to an acute disease, and you methodically prescribe a thin diet. But since such a diet diminishes the strength on account of its thinness, it may happen, as was shown above from the mind of Galen, that the patient dies on that thin diet, whereas he would have been preserved on a thick one. (For if you assume that the strength's excess over the disease is so slight that the strength suffices only to overcome the disease and to resist its attacks, and that, while the disease is considered by itself, the superior strength survives with a smaller excess than what the thin diet takes from its powers.) If you feed this patient on a thin diet, which in itself drains the strength, from the outset, do you think he will reach a superior state, or rather an inferior one? I, for my part, think he will not reach a turning point if the disease is prolonged beyond seven days. But if you feed him on a symmetrical diet, which in itself preserves the strength, the very diet the sects of rational physicians prescribe for chronic diseases alone, will he not escape? For under a symmetrical diet the strength suffers no loss. And if you give him food that adds to the powers of nature, you will make him far stronger at the time of the disease than with a symmetrical diet. But perhaps the methodist will reply to this that a thin diet, however much it weakens the strength, shortens the disease. For nature, since it bears less upon digesting thin food, will be free for longer to deal with the matter of the disease, whence the concoctions come more quickly and the symptoms of the disease and the labours that exhaust nature's strength are forced to last less long. So although the patient is more exhausted by a thin diet than by a symmetrical or thick one, nevertheless, because he is exhausted over a shorter time, nature suffers less harm in one suffering from an acute disease from a thin diet than from a symmetrical or thick one, if you compare the level of strength under a thin diet with its level under a symmetrical or thick one, at the same point of vigour. The methodist, replying to this, holds that the concoctions will come sooner or later according to the thinness or thickness of the diet; hence he will think that the duration of the state can be longer or shorter according to whether thicker or thinner food is given. Galen, in the first book of On Crises, in the book On the Four Times of a Disease, and in the second book, On the Regimen of Diet, in its exposition, shows that "one must conjecture that the strength and the state are at their greatest when the concoctions are most in progress." But if matters stood as he thinks, Galen, the second author of the rational method after Hippocrates, would have gravely erred, since he instructs us to take the form of the diet from the duration of the state; if the duration could be made longer or shorter according to the regimen of diet, that would be so. For in that way it would be more certain to infer the duration of the state from the form of the diet than the reverse. But suppose again that the strength of a man with an acute fever is superior to the disease, and that the disease is to end on the seventh day; if you nourish him on a thin diet, which diminishes the strength, namely hydromel, or the broth of barley-gruel, or some such thin little soup, you will keep him, on the seventh day, in complete fasting, as if the vigour of the disease were to be at its height that day. Now then, imagine a healthy man as robust as the patient was, kept on a similar diet up to the seventh day, and suppose you find him, after a whole day of fasting, toward evening on the seventh day: what do you think he will be like? And if on the first day he walked six miles on foot without any obvious discomfort, how many do you think he could cover on the seventh day? Any man in his right mind would doubt whether he could manage three. The same holds for leaping, running, lifting weights; in short, in every effort he will fall well short of the mark he reached on the first day. The same judgement holds for natural functions. For if on the seventh day you offer him half the food that he easily digested before the first day, his stomach, weighed down, will be harmed. How much weaker the vital faculty becomes is shown by the languid pulses of those who fast a full day. Since, therefore, in a healthy man such weakness of all three powers results from the thin diet alone, how much more harm and loss of strength do you think the sick will suffer from such a diet? And if you hesitate, ask the leaders of this sect: Hippocrates in the second book On the Regimen of Diet, and Galen, when they write that such losses affect the healthy less than the sick. Moreover, those who are languid are harmed more than the healthy by a sudden change of diet, but those most harmed are those troubled by acute diseases. Likewise, in the same place: a change of diet that is troublesome to the healthy will be more troublesome to the languid. Therefore, since we see plainly that the strength of a healthy man is diminished if you keep him on that thin diet up to the seventh day, how much more will this happen to a patient, so that they become visibly weaker from that diet.

units.la: Ostensa est causa una insignis diminutionis virium. Sed age morbum et eius symptomata, earum quantum absumant septem dierum interuallo consideremus. Profectò si mens humana ab experientia edocta ut trutina horum admittitur, iudicabit labores acuti morbi vires posse diebus septem insigniter imbecilliores reddere. Una enim die patiens homo ephemeram febrem, die sequenti sensibili- ter imbecillior est, quàm ante febris inua- sionem. A virtutis igitur robore duo sunt, quæ insigniter detrahunt & præter modum absumunt, nempe tenuis victus & morbus. Quod si morbo vires accrescere ad statum vsque iuxta Hipp. sententiam intelligas, Cir ca principia & fines, & c. colliges, non quen cunque excessum naturæ supra morbum, sa- tis esse ad euasionē. Pone exempli causa mor- bum et eius symptomata quartā virium par tem absumpsisse: tenuem victum sextā, mor- bi vires tertiam superaddant, si prima die virtus duplo erat ad morbum excessu superi or, die septima eodem erit imbecillior vna o- ctaua. Quare illa victus ratione morietur il- le cuius virtus prima die erat morbo bis for- tior. Quod si hos respectus nempe quartam, sextam, & tertiam, vt incertos nihil certi ostendere dicas: concedam aliqua ex parte: nam exempli causa adducta sunt, vt manife- stum fiat, plures eorum qui ab initio morbo, erant viribus superiores, posse ex ea victus ratione interire, multoque excessu opus esse ut illo victu quis euadat. At si iis quae à fide dignis medicis & philosophis scripta sunt in reductione effectuum agentium naturalium ad numeros, aliqua fides sit adhibenda, quibus ostendere nituntur ab effectu insensili ad eundem cum manifeste sentitur duplam esse geometricam rationem, minori quàm par erat ratione supra dictos respectus me definisse scies. Maximum ergo malum est eo uti victu, quo plures qui alioquin seruari poterant inter eant. Quod si sermonem ad eos qui à morbi initio pari certant robore, conuertamus: horum nullum intelliges tenui victu posse euadere, ratione monstrante, cum morbi vires ad statum usque validiores fiant, ut ab Hip.scriptum est, corporis autem virtus imbecillior. Qui ergo ab initio pari cum morbo robore certabant paulo post eodem futuros imbecilliores constat. Nisi igitur id quod morbus & eius symptomata virium absumunt, crassi victus ope rependas, mors certa sequetur. Quod si dicat methodicus praeter victum tenuem tenuem esse medicis remedia, quibus morbi causam abscindunt, ut missione sanguinis, et purgatione: ijs siquidem euacuationibus humorem morbum efficientem educunt. Unde & si pari robore ab initio natura cum morbo certet ob causam morbi euacuationem bona acuminis morbi pars tollitur, & multo superior natura redditur, cuius causa euadet infirmus. Sic in Anglia olim Lusitano conti git, laborabat pleuritide, cumque morbo ingrauescente delirare coepisset, omniaque in deterius abiret, tertio facta fuit sanguinis missio, multumque eductum est, confestim omnia mitiora fuere, melior pulsus & urina, cessauit delirium, screauit, sanatus est. Videbatur tamen ante sanguinis missionem virtus morbo inualidior. Sint haec ut vis metho dice, hac tua ratione, ut multoties huiusmodi possis salubres euacuationes moliri, citra magnum virium incommodum: melius tamen egisses si crasso victu qui vires aegrotantis augeat usus esses, quam tenui, a quo vires imbecilliores effectae, plures euacuationes citra magnum vitæ discrimen non ferunt. Insu per si euacuationes pro votis succedant, non oberit ante euacuationem naturam cibo roborasse crassiusculo. Neq; quicquam si idagas postmodum die una interposita lædes. A fœlici nanque euacuatione roborare naturā, ut potentius quod reliquum est coquat et ex pellat, oportet. Quod si econtrà accidat, ut non raro usu venire quotidie cernimus, intempestivas à medicis euacuationes, easdemq; infelices, et cum magno virium ægrotantis incommodo fieri: tenui hos indigere victu indicas qui vires adhuc imbecilliores reddat, an eo magis qui aliquod imbecillæ naturæ solamen afferat, ut eas quas euacuatione dejecit vires medicus cibo roboret? Nec hoc ipsi rationales negabunt, nempe si in euacuatione erratum sit, melius esse crassiori quàm tenui magis usum fuisse victu, nam enuncia tionem à qua illa ostenditur, ut veram admittent, utpote ab Hippocrat. concessam et Galeno, Nempe ægrotâtes ab iis aut quæ ipsi cõmiserint, aut sponte, aut modo quocunq; ac ciderint viderint peccatis, minus laedi, crassiori victu si vsi fuerint, quā tenui. A sanorū experientia ad aegrotātes id deducit Hipp. Sano enim homini si aliquid praeter consuetudinē accidat, vt exempli causa longā pedestri itinere peragat viā, aut venere nimia vsus sit praeter consuetudinē, aut solis aestu diutius passus fuerit, aut alius quicunq; error accidat, magis laedetur si tenui victu ante vsus fuerit quā crassō. Et hoc est quod Hip. dixit, Propterea sanis fallaces sunt valde tenues & exquisitivi ctus quoniam peccata difficilius ferunt. In quo apho. non agit ille de peccato quod in exhibendo victu committitur vtrum maius sit in tenuis exhibitione an crassioris, vt perperam plurimi intelligunt: sed de quibuscunque agit peccatis modo quocunque euenientibus, quae magis eum laedere aegrotantem ait, quam tenuii, quàm crassiori vsus fuerit victu. Et vt certo scias hanc fuisse Hippoc. mentem, non abre fuerit Graecum Galen. contextum adducere qui idem de Hippoc. sentit, cum ita ait, Ἀ μείνωρ δὲ ἡ πρότερα γραφὴ, πρὸ λαμ-
units.tr: The cause of one remarkable diminution of strength has been shown. But come, let us consider the disease and its symptoms, and how much they consume over an interval of seven days. Surely, if the human mind, instructed by experience, is admitted as the balance of these things, it will judge that the labours of an acute disease can make the strength remarkably weaker in seven days. For in one day a patient with an ephemeral fever is noticeably weaker the next day than before the fever set in. Therefore two things from the strength's vigour remarkably detract and consume beyond measure: namely, the thin diet and the disease. But if you understand, as Hippocrates says, that the disease's strength increases up to the state, in the passage "Concerning the beginnings and ends," you will conclude that not every excess of nature over the disease is enough for escape. Suppose, for example, that the disease and its symptoms have consumed a quarter of the strength, the thin diet a sixth, and the disease's strength adds a third more; if on the first day the strength was twice as great as the disease in excess, on the seventh day it will be weaker by one eighth. Therefore the man whose strength on the first day was twice that of the disease will die under that regimen. But if you say that these proportions, a quarter, a sixth and a third, show nothing certain since they are uncertain, I will concede this in part: for they have been adduced by way of example, so that it becomes plain that many who at the outset were superior in strength to the disease can perish under this diet, and that a great excess is needed for anyone to escape by that diet. But if some credence is to be given to what trustworthy physicians and philosophers have written about reducing the effects of natural agents to numbers, by which they strive to show that from an effect too slight to be felt to one plainly felt the ratio is geometric and doubled, you will know that I have defined the above proportions with less than the right ratio. It is therefore a very great evil to use that diet, by which many who could otherwise have been saved perish. But if we turn our speech to those who from the onset of the disease contend with equal strength, you will understand that none of these can escape on a thin diet, as reason demonstrates, since the strength of the disease grows stronger up to the state, as Hippocrates wrote, while the strength of the body grows weaker. Therefore it is plain that those who at the outset contended with the disease on equal strength will soon be weaker still. Unless, therefore, you offset by means of a thick diet what the disease and its symptoms consume of the strength, certain death will follow. But if the methodist says that besides a thin diet physicians have remedies by which they cut off the cause of the disease, such as bloodletting and purging, for by these evacuations they draw off the humour that produces the disease, and so, if nature contends with the disease on equal strength at the start, a good part of the disease's vigour is removed by evacuation because of its cause, and nature becomes much superior, by which the patient escapes; so in England once it happened to a Lusitanian: he suffered from pleurisy, and when the disease grew worse he began to be delirious, and everything went from bad to worse; on the third day bloodletting was performed, and a great deal was drawn off; at once everything became milder, the pulse and urine improved, the delirium ceased, he sweated, and he was cured. Yet before the bloodletting the strength seemed weaker than the disease. Grant that these things are so, as you methodist say, by this your reasoning, that you can often bring about such healthful evacuations without great harm to the strength; you would nevertheless have done better to use a thick diet that increases the strength of the patient, rather than a thin one, after which the strength is weakened, and the many evacuations do not bear without great danger to life. Moreover, if the evacuations succeed as one wishes, it will do no harm to have strengthened nature beforehand with somewhat thicker food. Nor will you harm anything if, after the evacuation, you give a little food one day later. For nature must be strengthened by a successful evacuation, so that it may concoct and expel what remains more powerfully. But if the contrary happens, as we see not seldom happening every day, that the evacuations of physicians are untimely and unsuccessful, and carried out with great harm to the patient's strength: do you say that these patients need a thin diet, which makes their strength weaker still, or rather one that brings some solace to the weakened nature, so that the physician may restore with food the strength that the evacuation has cast down? Nor will the rational physicians themselves deny this, namely that if an error was made in the evacuation, it is better to have used a thicker diet than a thin one; for they will admit as true the statement by which this is shown, as conceded by Hippocrates and Galen: that the sick, whether through their own faults, or by chance, or in whatever way errors befall them, are less harmed if they have used a thicker diet than a thin one. Hippocrates draws this conclusion for the sick from the experience of the healthy. For if something outside custom happens to a healthy man, for instance he travels a long walk on foot, or he indulges in excessive sex contrary to habit, or he has suffered longer in the sun's heat, or any other error occurs, he will be more harmed if he has been accustomed to a thin diet than a thick one. And this is what Hippocrates said: "For this reason very thin and exact diets are deceptive for the healthy, since they bear faults with more difficulty." In this aphorism he is not speaking of the fault committed in prescribing the diet, whether it is greater in giving a thin diet or a thick one, as very many wrongly understand; but he speaks of whatever faults occur in any way, which he says harm the patient more if he has used a thin diet than a thick one.
