And so that you may know for certain that this was Hippocrates' meaning, it will not be out of place to adduce the Greek context of Galen, who holds the same view of Hippocrates, when he says: [ἐλάσσων δὲ ἡ πρότερα γραφή, προλαμβάνει γὰρ καὶ ταύτην, καὶ χρηστότερον ποιεῖ τοῦ ἑτέρου λόγου] "The earlier reading is less; for it also takes this up, and makes the aphorism more useful, as if it taught about every fault, whether committed involuntarily or voluntarily, that befalls the sick, as in the account of the aphorisms; that if any error befalls those who are thus dieted sparingly, it is more dangerous..."

units.la: Βάνει γὰρ καὶ ταύτην, καὶ χρηκώτερον ποιεῖ τοῦ ἑρμ λόγου, ὥσπερ ἁπάσης ἁμαρτίας ἐκδι- δάσκεσθαι τῆς ἀκυσίως τε καὶ ἑκυσίως συμ- πιπτούσης τοῖς νοσοῦσιν, ὡς ἐν τῷ λόγου ἀοῖ- τομ: ὅτι ἂν ἁμάρτημα συμπέσῃ τοῖς λειπῶς οὕτω διαιτωμένοις σφαλερώτερον ᾧ καδί- σατω, παρόσον ἥτε δὶ ὠμιμεῖς ἀρρώστος ἀπὸ τῆς πιαώτης λιαίτης γέγονεν, ἥτε ἐπ' αὐτὴν μεταβασις ἀγθης. μαρτυρεῖ ἡ τῇ πεῖραμένῃ γραφῇ καὶ τὰ πρὸς τῶν ὑγιαινόντων ἐρημία σφαλερᾶς γὰρ ἐπ' αὐτῶν ἔφη τὰς λειπᾶς διαὶ τὰς ὑπάρχειν, ὅτι τὰ ἁμαρτανόμενα χαλεπώ- τερον φέρουσιν, ὅκ ὅτι διά τὸ λειπὸν ᾗ διαίτης ἁμαρτάνειν ἀναγκάζοντες, &c. Hoc est, Me- lior autem est prior scriptura. complectitur enim & hanc, & generaliorem facit sermo- nem, de omni peccato docens uoluntarie aut inuoluntarie cōtingente ægrotantibus: vt ta- lis sit sermo, Quod si peccatum accidat sic te- nuiter diætatis, periculosius illud est, quate- nus virtus imbecillis à tali diæta fuerit, & quatenus transitus ad ipsam insuetus fuerit. Confirmant dictam scripturam quæ de sanis dicta sunt, quibus periculosas tenues dietas existere dicit, quoniam peccata difficilius ferunt. Non quod propter tenuitatem dietæ peccare cogantur. Sentis ne ex vltimis Gal. verbis non agere Hipp. de ijs quæ à tenui victu accidunt peccatis, sed de quibuscunque voluntarie aut inuoluntarie contingentibus, quæ magis lædere asserit eos, qui tenui victu vsi fuerint, quàm qui crassiori: Cúmque non raro accidat ægrotantes ex intempestiuis lædi euacuationibus, id esse agendum & ad id accedendum, unde damna & errores minus discriminis afferant? Id fiet si crassiori victu utemur. Cum autem non solum in euacuationibus, sed in aliis non paucis quotidie ægrotantes delinquât, aut sua sponte, aut assisten tium causa, & non raro ab ipsis delinquatur medicis, accidit iam dictis non parui momenti ratio ostendens crassi victus non spernendam ægrotantibus commoditatem, nempe minus lædi ab erroribus. Quandoquidem peccata euacuationis si cum tenui victu coniungantur, methodo quidem, sed irrationali, ægrotantem in mortem deferunt. Nam vt in proverbio apud Hispanos est, caput cito tondent plures manus. Fateri igitur cogeris methodice cum in euacuatione erratum sit, minus mali ægrotantes passi sunt crassiori, quàm si tenui magis victu vsi fuerint. Quod si pro votis evacuatio succedat, non est quod tenui vtaris. Nam si à naturalibus ad eas quæ ab arte fiunt euacuationibus validum est argumentum, vt tradidit Hippocr. manifestum erit, si quanto maior fuerit expurgatio, tanto magis ad indicationem vsque dare oportet, vt illa scripsit, idem obseruandum fore in ea quam medicus feliciter molitur euacuatione. Quare committendum non est, vt ea fiducia tenui vtaris victu, vt id imbecillitatis quod ex eius vsu natura incurrit, noxij humoris euacuatione rependas. Sed his omissis mentem ad eos qui insuetum nauigant æquor conuerte, eorum turbantur corpora, quorum qui cibo & potui non parcunt minus conturbari certum est. nam facilius & minori cum molestia euomunt, vnde citius ab affectu liberantur. rantur. Qui vero magis abstinent, contrariū eis euenire diligetiores nautæ affirmant. Age experiamur alias causas: pone duos omnia quibus sint paria, ad solis æstū nimis incalescentem, alter tenui victu, alter crassiori vsus sit ab ante hesterna die. vter eorum magis afficietur putas? ego quidem periculum huius rei iam in me ipso faciens sensi minus me solis calore cum crassiori vsus fueram cibo, quàm tenui affectum fuisse. Idem ijs accidit qui alta niue iter peragunt. Quare si quis hæc alta mente revoluat, aperte colliget, verum id esse in cuiuscunque causæ impressione, minus fore obnoxium qui crassiori victu vsus fuerit, multò autem magis qui tenui. Quare cum ita res habeat magnum afferet ægrotantibus crassus victus commodum. Nam cum in morborum consideratione duplex sit medico scopus, alter ad id quod factum est, alter vero ad id quod futurum, id curat medicus quod iam est, id præcauet quod nondum est, hocque est, quod aliis verbis medici dicunt, cum morbus & causa simul coincidūt, curationem mixtam esse, ex ea artis parte, quæ curat, & ex ea quæ præcauet, prophylactice Græcè dicitur. Cum ergo præcipua intentio medici deficiente eo quod vrget, adid sit quod futurum est, danda est opera vt eo disponamus modo ægrotantem, vt minus eius quod futurum est recipiat. Ostendi autem supra crassum victum corpus sic disponere, vt minus quarum vis causarum impressionem percipiat. Quare ægrotantibus omnibus ministrandum est, vt ab eo quod futurum est minus afficiantur. quod si febricitantem con sideres qui tenui victu vsus fuerit, calorem acriorem ad intima corporis penetrantem, morbíque labores molestius ferentem senti-es: contrà qui crassiori, minus à febrili calore molestari, facilius autem symptomata & labores ferre, magis vero morbi & eius causæ impressioni obsistere, validius bonos chymos ne putredinem concipiant manu tenere. Scies signum esse causarum non naturalium actiones minus eos qui crasso vsi fuerint victu premere. Quod si rusticos operarios nau-
units.tr: [Galen's Greek, here rendered in English:] For he also takes up this case, and makes the statement more demanding than the earlier one [Βάνει γὰρ καὶ ταύτην, καὶ χρηκώτερον ποιεῖ τοῦ ἑρμ λόγου], as if it taught about every error, whether voluntary or involuntary, that befalls the sick: so that the sense is this: if a mistake happens to someone who is living on a thin diet, it is more dangerous, insofar as the strength of a weak patient has been reduced by such a diet, and insofar as the transition to it was unaccustomed. The statement is confirmed by what is said of the healthy, for Hippocrates says that thin diets are dangerous for them, because they bear their errors with more difficulty, not because they are compelled to err by the thinness of the diet, etc. That is, the former text is the better, for it includes this case too and makes the statement more general, teaching about every error, voluntary or involuntary, that befalls the sick. Do you see from Galen's last words that Hippocrates is not speaking of the errors that arise from a thin diet, but of whatever errors occur voluntarily or involuntarily, which he asserts harm those who have used a thin diet more than those who have used a thicker one? And since it is not rare for patients to be harmed by untimely evacuations, should we not take care to avoid this, and to approach it in a way that brings less danger of harm and error? That will be done if we use a thicker diet. But since patients err daily not only in evacuations but in many other matters, either of their own accord or at the urging of those attending them, and not rarely the doctors themselves err against them, there is a reason of no small weight, shown by what has been said, for not despising the advantage a thicker diet gives the sick, namely that they are less harmed by errors. For if mistakes in evacuation are combined with a thin diet, the method may be sound, but the reasoning is irrational, and they bring the patient to death. For as the Spanish proverb has it, many hands shave the head quickly. You will therefore have to admit, on the methodical view, that when an error has been made in evacuation, the sick have suffered less harm if they have used a thicker rather than a thinner diet. But if the evacuation succeeds as one wishes, there is no reason to use a thin diet. For if the argument from natural to artificial evacuations is strong, as Hippocrates taught, it will be clear that if the purging is greater, one must give more right up to the point of indication, as he wrote; the same will have to be observed in the evacuation which the physician successfully carries out. Therefore one must not be so confident as to use a thin diet, in order to make up by evacuating the harmful humour for the weakness that nature incurs from its use. But setting these things aside, turn your mind to those who sail on unaccustomed seas: their bodies are disturbed, and it is certain that those who do not spare food and drink are less disturbed. For they vomit more easily and with less distress, and so are sooner freed from the affliction. But experienced sailors assert that those who abstain more suffer the opposite. Come, let us test other causes: take two men who are in all other respects alike, exposed to the sun's heat, which is too intense, one of whom has used a thin diet and the other a thicker one from the day before yesterday. Which of them do you think will be more affected? I myself, making this trial on my own body, have felt that I was affected less by the sun's heat when I had used a thicker food than when I had used a thin one. The same happens to those who travel through deep snow. Therefore, if anyone turns these things over carefully, he will plainly conclude that, whatever the cause that acts upon the body, the one who has used a thicker diet will be less liable to harm, and the one who has used a thin diet much more so. Since this is so, a thicker diet will bring great advantage to the sick. For in considering diseases the physician has a twofold aim: one toward what has already happened, the other toward what is to come. The physician cures what now exists and guards against what does not yet exist; this is what the physicians mean in other words when they say that, since disease and cause coincide, the cure is mixed, consisting partly of the part of the art that cures and partly of the part that guards against, which in Greek is called prophylactic. Since, therefore, the chief aim of the physician, when what presses is set aside, is directed to what is to come, care must be taken to dispose the patient in such a way that he receives less of what is to come. I have shown above that a thicker diet disposes the body so that it perceives less the impact of the causes of harm. Therefore all the sick must be treated so that they are less affected by what is to come. And if you consider a feverish patient who has used a thin diet, you will feel that the hotter heat, penetrating to the inner parts of the body, troubles him more, and that he bears the labours of the disease with more distress; whereas the one who has used a thicker diet is less troubled by the feverish heat, bears the symptoms and labours more easily, and resists the disease and the impact of its cause more strongly, holding the good humours firmly so that they do not conceive putrefaction. You will know that the actions of non-natural causes press less upon those who have used a thicker diet. But if you call to mind rustic labourers, sailors and that kind of people, when they are seized by acute diseases, they do not escape by barley water, nor by oxymel, nor by hydromel, but by strong food and drink; the only difference is that they prepare it in a less refined way, for ease of digestion. You will know this is so, since we see that rustics are not in more danger than townsmen who use a thin diet; indeed rustics are freed more easily and more quickly from diseases.

units.la: 145 tas & id hominum genus in mentem reuo-ces, cum ab acutis corripiuntur morbis, non ptisana, non aqua mulsa, non oxymelite e-uadere, sed valenti cibo & potu, sola ea diffe-rentia quod minus subtili modo parat, ob co-ctionis facilitatem, id ita esse scies, cum ob id periclitari magis rusticos quàm cives non vi-deamus, qui tenui victu vtuntur, quin imò rusticos facilius & citius à morbis liberari.
units.tr: 145 tas and that kind of men, when you call them to mind, when they are seized by acute diseases, do not escape by a tisane, nor by mead-water, nor by oxymel, but by strong food and drink, the only difference being that they prepare it in a less refined way, for the ease of digestion. You will know this is so, since we see that rustics are in no greater danger on this account than townsmen who use a thin diet; indeed rustics are freed from diseases more easily and more quickly.

units.la: Vt Venetijs rusticæ duplici laboranti tertia-na contigit: cui cum accedens medicus aquâ hordei & iusculum pulli frigidis herbis tem-peratum consuleret, illa annuente abiit. Se-quenti die accedens cum nihil eorum quæ ius-serat factum accepisset, ægrè ferens discessit, nihil boni rusticæ futurum sperans, quam duo bus post diebus in domo amici offendit glo-riantem se suo consilio & non medici serua-tam. Sed heus tu methodice, cum virtus ægrotantis nimis imbecillis est, nónne eam cibo & potu roborare conaris, vel in ipso morbi vigore, vt Gal. tradit? An non putas me Aphor. 1. lius crassiori victu corpus antea nutrisse, vt hora maximæ commotionis absque cibo per manere potuisseт:ob id quia natura ad insig- nem deueniente imbecillitatem non facile ci- bo noxa corrigitur. Nisi enim ipsa natura cir ca cibum elaborauerit, cibus per se non con- coquetur aut digeretur, nec vires naturæ mi- nistrabit. nā oportet vt ab ipsa natura prin- cipium sui adiumenti habeatur, quæ cum valde imbecillis est, tantillum non valet ci- bum coquere nec digerere. Quare consultius ageretur craßiori ante corpus victu nutri- re, vt minus in huiusmodi imbecillitates inci dat natura. Dicta sunt nonnullæ rationes ob quas in morbis crasso vti debeamus victu qui vires laborantis augeat, nullamque legitima methodicus ratione ostendet quod tenui qui vires ægrotantis minuat vti oportear. Me- thodicus forsan pro ratione Galenum addu- cit, ita dicentem, Nam si crasso vteremur ci bo, adderemus in morbu. cuius verba sic ha- bent, Nā si eas (vires) tales quales acceperi- mus properemus in istis seruare vel etiā auge re, semper adderemus in morbu. Vnde aperte ostendit ostendit non solum victu crasso sed et symme trosi vtamur augere nos semper morbum. Hæc quidem Verba methodicus pro se citas putat obtinuisse. Et si hoc tibi præstem, vt in hac re Galenum vt iudicem admittam, pos- sem tamen methodice arte tuum in præsenti deuiare telum. Nam male citasti Gal. in eo verbo semper, illud ad sequentem dictionem adderemus referens. Et talem facis sensum, quod si in acutis vires seruare properemus, vel etiam augere, semper adderemus in mor- bum. Cum aliter habeant græca exemplaria, nempe. Εἰ γὰρ ἢ τοι φυλάξαιμεν αὐτῷ οἷαν παρελάβομεν γ' τούτοις ἢ πλεονάξαιμεν καὶ αὐξήσομεν τῷ νόσῳ. hoc est, Si enim seruare ipsam (scilicet virtutem) qualem acceperimus in iis (scilicet acutis) vel augere semper properaremus, addemus in morbum. Vnde non damnat Galen. in acutis simpliciter virium additionem, sed illud maxime ne semper properemus addere eas cibo, innuens in statu, & circa ipsum si cibo vires addere coneris errorem esse. Sed age methodice hæc dimittens volo tecum in hoc duello ea vti animi liberalitate, qua cum Aiace vsum fuisse Hectora, refert Homerus. Crasso victu qui vires augeat ideo vtendum nō esse ais, ne addamus in morbum, vnde quæso hæc fiet additio? an quia cibus in morbi materiam couertitur? aut quia eo tempore interuallo quo natura cibo præparando vacat à morbi coctione cessans causa est vt diutius duret affectus? aut quia affectū maiorem reddimus? aut quia in pricrem causam addimus? ab omnibus hisce modis morbum sumere posse incrementum certum est.
units.tr: As happened at Venice to a rustic woman suffering from a double tertian fever: when the physician who came to her advised barley water and a broth of chicken tempered with cooling herbs, she agreed and he went away. Coming the next day, and finding that nothing he had ordered had been done, he left in irritation, hoping for no good to come to the rustic woman. But two days later he found her in a friend's house, boasting that she had been saved by her own counsel and not by the physician's. But look here, methodist: when the strength of a patient is too weak, do you not try to restore it with food and drink, even at the height of the disease, as Galen teaches? Or do you not think that I, by a thicker diet, had nourished her body beforehand, so that she could remain without food through the hour of greatest disturbance? That is because, when nature has fallen into extreme weakness, the harm is not easily corrected by food. For unless nature itself works upon the food, the food will not of itself be concocted or digested, and will not supply the powers of nature; for the beginning of its help must come from nature itself, and when nature is very weak, it is not strong enough to cook or digest even a little food. Therefore it would be wiser to nourish the body beforehand with a thicker diet, so that nature falls less into such weaknesses. Some reasons have been given why in diseases we ought to use a thicker diet, one that increases the strength of the sufferer, and the methodist will show no legitimate reason why a thin diet, which diminishes the strength of the sick, ought to be used. The methodist perhaps, in support of his view, cites Galen, saying: For if we used a thicker food, we would add to the disease. Whose words are these: For if we hasten to preserve the strength as we received it in these cases, or even to increase it, we would always add to the disease. Hence he plainly shows that not only by a thicker diet but also by a symmetrical one we always increase the disease. The methodist thinks he has won this point with these words. And even if I allow Galen to be judge in this matter, I could still, in the methodist's art, turn aside his weapon in the present case. For you have cited Galen wrongly on the word always, referring it to the following phrase, we would add. And you make the sense: if in acute cases we hasten to preserve the strength, or even to increase it, we would always add to the disease. But the Greek copies read otherwise, namely: Εἰ γὰρ ἢ τοι φυλάξαιμεν αὐτῷ οἷαν παρελάβομεν γ' τούτοις ἢ πλεονάξαιμεν καὶ αὐξήσομεν τῷ νόσῳ. That is: For if we always hasten to keep the strength (namely the virtue) as we received it in these (namely the acute cases), or to increase it, we would add to the disease. Hence Galen does not condemn, in acute cases, the simple addition of strength, but chiefly that we should not always hasten to add it by food, implying that it is an error to try to add strength by food in the state of the disease itself. But come, methodist, setting these things aside, I want you in this duel to use that generosity of mind with which Homer tells that Hector behaved toward Ajax. You say that in order to increase strength we ought not to use a thicker diet, lest we add to the disease. Then I ask: how will this addition happen? Is it because the food is converted into the matter of the disease? Or because, during the interval in which nature is busy preparing the food and ceases from concocting the disease, the cause is that the affection lasts longer? Or because we make the affection greater? Or because we add to the prior cause? It is certain that the disease can increase in all these ways.

units.la: Age nunc an in ratione cibi crassi qui vires augeat aliqua dictarum insit occasionum consideremus. Cibum porro in morbi materiam conuerti duplici de causa contingit, aut quia similis in qualitate, aut substantia: aut quia à natura non commodè apparatur (concoquitur) vnde corruptioni disponitur. non apparatur verò aut ob multitudinem immodicam, aut crassitiem. Proinde fieri potest, vt ægrotantibus cibum offeramus qui vires augeat geat, qui nec qualitate nec substantia humoripeccanti similetur: sed & eius mediocrem exhibere possumus quantitatem, qui quàm minimè difficilis sit coctionis, sed admodum leuis. Verùm ob dictam causam conuincitur Petronas carnes assas acutè ægrotantibus ministrans, quæ cum difficilis sint coctionis, & haud commodè à natura præparentur, causa est vt diutius immorantes in laborantium ventriculis corrumpantur, unde in morbi materiam tandem conuertuntur. Quod ad morbi durationem spectat, necessarium non est, vt quicunque cibus vires ægrotantis augens multū exposcat ad eius coctionem tempus.Nam alica inter crassa ab ipso Gal.conumeratur cibaria, & tamen breui admodum coquitur. Simile habent ova sorbilia, et vinum quod citissimè quidem coquitur, & multum vires iuuat, præcipuè naturales & vitales. Affectum intensiorem efficimus, vt sinocinere aut liene obstructione laborantibus dulcia cibaria ministremus & quæ facilè particulis hæreant: & si liquefacientibus febribus aquam mulsam exhibeamus. Quod autem ne hoc crassum cibum qui vires auge-at comitetur necessario, manifestum est. An postrema participet occasione, tentemus. Priorem dico causam pororum obstructionem, à qua putredo ortum habet, hanc à multitudine humorum intra venas aut ab eorum crassitie aut lentore aut à duobus aut simul ab omnibus prouenire Galen. author est. Cum autem obstructiones sunt, aut suspicio est ne fiant, cauendum fuerit eum cibum qui plethoram efficiat exhibere. Victus autem qui vires auget omnino hoc non caret crimine. nā vires augere nō posset, nisi maior eius pars in sanguinem conuertatur. Ob solam igitur pororum obstructionem crassus victus suspectus esse videtur. Sed cum in omnibus acutis morbis adsint obstructiones, nec dispositio à qua iusta earum detur suspicio, nō est ob id quod singulare est, vniuersale afferendum præceptum, nempe omnibus in acutis tenui esse vtendum victu. Sed age metho dice cum febris acuta cū obstructione adest, quo vteris remedio vt hominem in sanitatẽ vindices? profectò si Gal. in libris de methodo medendi, & in libro de plenitudine consentis, & totirationalium medicorum scholæ, sanguinis missione, nisi quæ prohibeant ad sint, dices. Nam febrem tollere non possies nisi prius obstructionibus liberandis intendas: quorum causa euacuationem molimur, & si plethora non adsit, sola melioris transspiratio nis gratia, vt ab eodem discimus. Nam stante eadem pororum raritate post humoruʰ imminutioñe liberiores fieri inspirationes et expirationes cõtingit. Tu igitur methodice sanguinẽ mittis hac sola de causa vt liberiores fiant transspirationes, ego hac ipsa qua tu, et vt post euacuationem crasso cibo qui vires augeat vti secure et citra læsionẽ possim. Sentis ne pluribus in morbis acutis crasso victu illico citra aliquâ præparationem vtendũ esse: in ijs verò quibus obstructiones coiunguntur quæ morbi materiam fouent aut suspicio est, ne fiant corpus fore præparandum ante crassi victus exhibitionem? Nc hanc præparationem solius huius gratia molior. Nam et tu & rationales quicunque illam tanquam remedium ad sanationem non vulgare ample stimini. Solum vnum est quod inter nos sepa rat, quod vos id agitis vt morbum oppugne tis: ego vero ob idipsum, & vt laborantem naturam citra læsionē roborare possim. An non tibi methodice subijt in mente simile esse illud Hippocratis cum de corporibus athle tarum sermonem faceret? quem Oribasius de omni crasso & obeso intelligendum mo net: Horum igitur (inquit) causa bonam ha bitudinem soluere confert non tarde, vt rur sus principium nutritionis accipiat corpus. Nullam igitur validam perpetuam assigna bis rationem, quod tenui vičtu qui ægrotan tis vires minuat & imbecilliores reddat in acutis vti debeas. Nónne Hippocratis præce ptum est cum aliquod signum proritatorium aut euacuatorium assuerit, vel in hypochon drio, crassiori vičlu vtendum esse. Vbi Gal. communi proritationis nomine comprehen- disse omnia Hippocratem, quæ quo vis modo virtutem
units.tr: Come now, let us consider whether any of the aforementioned occasions lies in the rationale of a thick food that increases strength. Thick food is converted into the matter of disease for two reasons: either because it is similar to the disease in quality or substance, or because it is not properly prepared (digested) by nature, and so is disposed to corruption. It is not properly prepared either because of its excessive quantity or because of its thickness. Accordingly, it is possible for us to offer sick people a food that increases strength and is similar neither in quality nor in substance to the peccant humour. We may also give a moderate amount of it, one that is not difficult to digest but very light. Yet Petronas is refuted for serving roasted meats sharply to the sick. Since these are hard to digest and not well prepared by nature, they remain longer in the stomachs of the sufferers and corrupt, and so are at last converted into the matter of disease. As for the duration of the disease, it is not necessary that every food which increases the strength of the sick should require a long time for its digestion. For Galen counts barley gruel among thick foods, and yet it is digested very quickly. Soft-boiled eggs are similar, and wine, which is digested very quickly indeed and greatly strengthens, especially the natural and vital powers. We make the affection more intense when we give sweet foods, which easily stick to the particles, to those suffering from obstruction of the spleen or liver; and if the fevers are melting, we give them honey water. That this thick food which increases strength need not necessarily accompany such occasions is clear. Let us test whether it shares in the last occasion. I say the first cause is obstruction of the pores, from which putrefaction arises; Galen is the authority that this arises from a multitude of humours within the veins, or from their thickness or viscosity, or from two of these, or from all of them together. But when obstructions exist, or there is suspicion that they will arise, one should take care to give food that produces plethora. Now a diet that increases strength certainly does not lack this fault, for it could not increase strength unless the greater part of it were converted into blood. Therefore a thick diet seems suspect on account of pore obstruction alone. But since obstructions are present in all acute diseases, and there is no disposition from which a just suspicion of them can be given, we should not, on account of what is peculiar, lay down a universal precept, namely that a thin diet must be used in all acute cases. But come, methodically, when an acute fever is accompanied by obstruction, what remedy do you use to restore the man to health? Surely you will say, if Galen in his books on the method of healing, and in his book on plenitude, and the whole school of rational physicians, blood-letting, unless there are things that forbid it. For you cannot remove the fever unless you first aim at clearing the obstructions, for whose sake we bring about evacuation, and, if plethora is not present, solely for the sake of better transpiration, as we learn from the same authors. For while the rarity of the pores remains the same, the inspirations and expirations become freer when the humours are diminished. So you methodically let blood for this single reason, that transpirations may become freer; I, for this same reason as you, and so that after evacuation I may safely and without injury use a thick food that increases strength. Do you think that in many acute diseases one must use a thick diet at once without any preparation? And in those in which obstructions are joined, which foster the matter of disease, or where there is suspicion that they will arise, must the body be prepared before a thick diet is given? I do not undertake this preparation solely for this purpose. For you and all rational physicians praise it not as an ordinary remedy for healing. There is only one thing that separates us: you aim to attack the disease, while I aim at the same thing, and also to strengthen the suffering nature without injury. Did it not occur to you methodically that the saying of Hippocrates is similar, when he spoke about the bodies of athletes? Oribasius warns that it must be understood of every thick and obese person: "For these reasons (he says) it is useful to loosen the good habit not slowly, so that the body may again receive the beginning of nutrition." Therefore you assign no valid and lasting reason why in acute cases you should use a thin diet which diminishes the strength of the sick and makes them weaker. Is not the precept of Hippocrates this: when some sign of irritation or evacuation has appeared, or in the hypochondrium, one must use a thicker diet? Here Galen says that Hippocrates comprehended all things under the common name of irritation, which in any way tend to weaken the strength,

units.la: e ratio uictus. virtutem ad imbecillitatem agunt scribit, ut morsus quem acris humor in intestinis aut ventriculo parit, praeterea vigilia, ira, moeror, lumbrici, helminthes, qui ab intestinis ad ventrem usq; ascendunt, & pruritus cutis & partis alicuius qui nocte oboriatur, et plurima alia quae sub euacuatorio comprehenduntur signo, & sub hypochondrio. Cum ergo omnibus his ob id quod virtutem infirmiorem reddere nata sunt, crassiori victu obstare praeceptum vobis est, id diligenter praecauentibus ne corporis laborantis natura multum imbecillis fiat, consulto tenui victu uti, quo aegrotantium corpora ad insignem ducuntur imbecillitatem praeter rationem esse videtur. Quinimmo nisi mihi certo ostendas commodum quod a tenui victu acute aegrotantibus euenit, maius esse virium infirmarum incommodo, insanam esse temeritatem iudico, eo uti cuius damnum manifestum est, adiumentum vero rationi haud peruium est. Quod si methodicus ad haec: Nihil igitur obstabit quo minus in acutis vinum conceda-
units.tr: On the reason of diet. ...which tend to weaken the strength: such as the bite that a sharp humour produces in the intestines or stomach; besides wakefulness, anger, sorrow, worms, helminths that rise from the intestines up to the stomach, itching of the skin or of some part which arises at night, and very many other things which are comprehended under the sign of evacuation, and under the hypochondrium. Since, therefore, you have the precept that a thicker diet is opposed to all these, because they are by nature apt to make the strength weaker, you should take care, with the aim of preventing the nature of the suffering body from becoming very feeble, not to use a thin diet deliberately; for it seems contrary to reason that the bodies of the sick should be brought to marked weakness. Indeed, unless you show me with certainty an advantage that comes to those acutely sick from a thin diet which is greater than the harm of weakened strength, I judge it mad rashness to use a thing whose harm is manifest while its help cannot be shown by reason. But if the methodist replies to this: "Nothing will therefore prevent us from allowing wine in acute cases,

units.la: {y} ... mus, quod vires insigniter roborat & breui coctionem recipit, nec in morbi materiam aptum est, vt conuertatur, nec affectum auge bit si tenue fuerit & aquosum: sed nec hoc ob structionibus laesionem erit: nam omnes promouere euacuationes asserit Gal. in libris de methodo medendi. Vere quidem, si ægrotans assuetus sit, non est quod interdicatur vinum tenue & aquosum. Nam quam æstimas esse dispositionem methodice cui maxime aduersum sit vinum, forsan febri acuta cum ingenti capitis dolore & mentis laesione, hac constitutione vinum omnino prohibendum esse credideris. In ea ipsa tamen dispositione ante dictum vinum si vestrum concesseris Hippocratem audias, an ne mutabis sententiam & rectius post hac ægrotantibus consules, & saluberrimum esse indicabis, naturæ vires modo quo possis augere præcipue vbi citra effatu di gnu incommodum id efficere possis? Hippocrates igitur ita scribit: Cum vero in huiusmodi morbis fortem capitis grauitatem vel mentis laesionem suspicatus fueris, a vino penitus est abstinenabstinendum, aquamque tunc dare oportet,,, vel unum aquosum flauumque et prorsus inodorum, atque ab ipsius potione aquae exiguum superbibendum. Nam hoc modo unipotentia caput mentemq; minus tentabit. Validum ex dictis Hippocratis sumi potest argumentum, in omni morbi constitutione assueto aegrotanti aquosum unum a rationali medico concedi posse, ut in pleuritide affectu quamuis maxime crudo existente, ut habetur ab eode, ubi ita scribit. Et si morbus siccior, quam ut quispiam existimet fuerit, non multum dare oportet, sed ante sorbitionem vel mulsam vel unum utrum magis auxiliaturum putaueris propinare conuenit. An non percipis ante dictae constitutioni unum & si tenue & aquosum noxa non uacare, cuius causa Hippocrates exiguum aquae superbibendum praecipit: Commodum tamen quod ab eo in corroboranda natura sequitur, maius esse suspicandum ideo esse, quia alioquin non concessisset Hippocrates stantibus forti capitis grauitate, et mentis laesione? Hucusque illius rationes qui crasso semper victu, hoc est, qui vires laborâtis augeat, in quibuscun que morbis vtendum esse opinatur. Qui verò in acutis, tenuem qui vires minuat ministran dũ fore cõtendunt, sic breuiter ratio cinâtur.
units.tr: ...we allow, namely wine, which powerfully strengthens and is quickly digested, and is not apt to be converted into the matter of disease, nor, if it is thin and watery, will it increase the affection; nor will it injure obstructions, for Galen asserts that it promotes all evacuations, in his books on the method of healing." Truly, if the sick person is accustomed to it, there is no reason why thin and watery wine should be forbidden. For you may think that in the methodical disposition to which wine is most opposed, perhaps in acute fever with great headache and impairment of the mind, you should believe that wine must be forbidden altogether in this condition. Yet if you concede wine in that very disposition, would you listen to Hippocrates? Will you not change your opinion, and advise the sick more rightly after this, and declare it most healthful, to increase the strength of nature in whatever way you can, especially when you can do this without any notable harm? Hippocrates therefore writes thus: "When, however, in diseases of this kind you suspect a strong heaviness of the head or impairment of the mind, you must entirely abstain from wine, and it is then right to give water, either one that is watery, yellowish and entirely odourless, and a little water should be drunk after drinking it. For in this way it will affect the head and mind less." A strong argument can be drawn from the sayings of Hippocrates: in any condition of disease, a rational physician may allow the patient who is accustomed to it a watery wine, as in pleurisy, although that affection is very crude; as he has it in the same place, where he writes: "And if the disease is drier than one would think, one should not give much, but before a sorbition or honey water, or whichever you think will help more, it is fitting to offer." Do you not perceive that the aforesaid constitution is not free from harm even with a thin and watery wine, and yet Hippocrates prescribes that a little water be drunk after it? Yet must we not suppose that the benefit which follows from it in strengthening nature is greater, since otherwise Hippocrates would not have allowed it where there is strong heaviness of the head and impairment of the mind? Thus far the reasons of those who think that in all diseases a thick diet, that is, one which increases the strength of the sufferer, must always be used. Those who contend that in acute cases a thin diet which diminishes strength must be given are briefly reasoned thus.

units.la: Quòd tenui uiƈtu alendi sint acutè febrici tantes, iuxta rationalium medicorum sententiam.
units.tr: That those suffering from acute fever must be nourished with a thin diet, according to the opinion of the rational physicians.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: NVNQVID paroxysmo sæuiente inquieto febricitâti, præ igneo calore æ- stuanti, pedes & brachia huc et illuc iactan ti, sitim linguaq́ue aridiratem ægrè ferenti, ci bum offeremus, an paroxysmi inclinationem expectabimus? Nullus profectò qui mentis sit compos ægrotanti paroxysmo ita sæuiente cibum ministrabit. Proinde cum plures sint morbi quos recentiores perperacutos vocât, qui ab initio ad morbi manifestam inclinatio nem similes labores prædictis & plures et ve hementiores afferunt, nec intermissionem ha bent, cibum ne ijs qui vires augere valeat, an an qui minuat ministrabimus? Ego quidem, tantum abesse ut crasso victu qui vires augeat sic laborantem nutriam, ut omnimoda inedia hominem ad morbi inclinationem servare opus esse crediderim: Qua in sententia Hippocratem & Galenum esse certum est. Nec praeter rationem: nam si illud verum est quantumcunque quis saeviente paroxysmo ederit nocumento esse, unde monstrante experientia asseruit Hippocrates, apponere laesionem esse. Quod si in periodica febre in qua errores minus periculi afferunt hoc facere ob timorem laesionis veremur, causatus profecto in peracutis cibum non esse offerendum constat, in quibus certum est citra magnam laesionem ministrari non posse. Nam si in ventrem absorptus fuerit cibus, quod redundat superfluitque, si alias multo magis in acutis tollere est difficile ut scripsit Galen. Praeterea cum inflammatio in aliqua parte excitatur ab humoris affluxu, sive phlegmone aut erysipelas sit, non advertisti nullum cibum quantumcunque levissimum fluxione durate labo
units.tr: Shall we offer food to a feverish patient while the paroxysm is raging, when he is restless, burning with fiery heat, tossing his feet and arms this way and that, and bearing thirst and a parched tongue with difficulty, or shall we wait for the paroxysm to abate? Surely no one of sound mind will give food to a patient whose paroxysm is so violent. Therefore, since there are several diseases which more recent writers call perperacute, which from the beginning bring on labours like those described and more severe ones, with no remission, shall we give food that will strengthen them, or food that will weaken them? I believe that far from nourishing such a sufferer with a thick diet that increases strength, one should keep the man in complete fasting until the disease shows its tendency, provided his strength suffices. It is certain that Hippocrates and Galen held this opinion, and not without reason. For if it is true that whatever a man eats during a raging paroxysm is harmful, as experience showed Hippocrates, then adding to it is injurious. But if in a periodic fever, where errors bring less danger, we fear to do this because of the risk of harm, it is clear that in acute cases food ought not to be offered at all, since it is certain that it cannot be given without great harm. For if food is absorbed into the belly, the excess that overflows is hard to remove, even more so in acute cases, as Galen wrote. Moreover, when inflammation is aroused in some part by an influx of humour, whether it be phlegmon or erysipelas, did you not notice that no food, however light, can be taken by those suffering a durable flux without harm

units.la: 2 lib. de ratione victus in illo, Ciborum autem adiectioi rantes citra lesionem posse sumere? quandoquidem à cibo dolores & fluxus insigniter crescunt. Cumque hæ ita se habeant, nunquam inducar vt rationibus mihi persuadeas ægro tanti cum vel ipsa morbi vehementia, vel ab aliquo dolore nimis molestatur, crassum cibum offerre ex vsu esse. Quinimmo cum Hippocrate sentio in primo de victu acutorum, vbi ita scribit: Postea si dolor vel periculum aliquod comparuerit, sorbitionem dare oportet, neque multam neque crassam, sed post se ptimum vel nonum si validus sit. Vbi igitur morbus statim ab initio maxima affert symptomata, in omnimoda inedia ægrum servare ad morbi inclinationem si virtus sufficiat, rectius esse iudico, quàm cibum offerre qui citra insignem lesionem in tali morbi constitutione exhiberi non potest. In qua sententia video Hippocratem esse, cum ita scribit: Ciborum autem adiectioni intendendum multò minus, subtrahere verò sæpenumero expedit cum æger sufficere posset, donec morbus maturescat. In reliquis ab hac vehementia
units.tr: (2 book of On Diet, in that place) ...taken without harm? For pains and flux grow markedly from food. Since these things are so, I shall never be persuaded by your arguments that it is good practice to offer thick food to a patient when the very violence of the disease, or some pain, troubles him excessively. Indeed, I agree with Hippocrates in the first book of On Acute Diet, where he writes: "Afterwards, if pain or some danger appears, one should give a sorbition, neither much nor thick, but on the seventh or ninth day if the patient is strong." Therefore, where the disease from the start brings the greatest symptoms, I judge it more correct to keep the patient in complete fasting until the disease inclines, if his strength suffices, than to offer food which cannot be given in such a disease without notable harm. In this opinion I see Hippocrates agreeing, when he writes: "Attention should be paid to adding food much less, but withdrawing it is often advantageous when the patient could manage, until the disease matures."

units.la: In secundo de ratione victus. tia degenerantibus morbis tenuem aut tenuissimum concedendum esse victum, tutius que esse in iis ad magis tenuem a iusto aberrando accedere, quam ad crassiorem. Quod valida ratione ostenditur. Pone morbo acuto laborare Socratem. Estne aliquis cibus qui morbo & naturae Socratis et ceteris exactè conueniat? dicatur ille medius. omnia cibaria quae illo tenuiora sunt, haudquaquam conuenient, propter virium diminutionem: quaecunque illo crassiora, incommoda sunt propter morbi additionem. Sed cum acuti morbi ut plurimum iuuenibus aut consistentibus accidant, quorum vires maximè tunc vigent, manifestum est, quod in iis magis urgebit morbus, quàm virtutis imbecillitas.
units.tr: In the second book of On Diet. In the remaining diseases that degenerate from this violence, a thin or very thin diet should be allowed, and it is safer in these to err towards too thin than towards too thick. This is shown by a strong argument. Suppose Socrates is suffering from an acute disease. Is there any food that agrees exactly with the disease, with Socrates' nature and with the rest? Let us call that the middle. All foods thinner than this will by no means agree, because they diminish strength; whatever is thicker is harmful because it adds to the disease. But since acute diseases mostly befall young or middle-aged people, whose strength is then at its height, it is clear that in them the disease will press harder than the weakness of their strength.

units.la: Quod si addere in id quod urget, periculosius est, quàm quod non urget aut minus urget: manifestum est in acutis deterius esse, et magis periculosum, crassiorem cibum offerre, utpote qui in morbum urgentem addit, quàm magis tenuem, qui virtutem, cuius imbecillitas non urget, exoluat.
units.tr: But if adding to what presses is more dangerous than adding to what does not press, or presses less, it is clear that in acute diseases it is worse and more dangerous to offer thicker food, since it adds to the pressing disease, than thinner food, which spares the strength whose weakness is not pressing.

units.la: Quid per crassum, tenuem, exacte tenuem, tenuissimum, & ultimo tenuissimum ui ctum Hippocrates intelligat.
units.tr: What Hippocrates understands by thick, thin, exactly thin, thinnest, and finally the thinnest diet.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: QVID de ijs (diuersis generib. victus) sentiam in præsenti breuiter ostenda, id quod maxime in artis operibus post longa consideration em magis probauerim. Eae-nim est artis vtilitas, inuenire ea quæ ægris conducibiliora sunt. Nunc mihi præbete au-res de ratione victus vobis aliqua dicturo, quæ animos vestros componant. qua quidem in re vnum insequor Hippocratem, cuius scri-pta vltra humanam eruditionem quid præ-stant. huic acceptum fero quæ de victus ra-tione vobis dixero. Sed prius dubitationem soluere expediet. Crassum victum, tenuem, tenuissimum, primus Hippocrates dixit in Aphor. Quid tamen per hæc nomina intelli-gat ex libris de ratione victus elici potest: apertius tamen in libro de Prisca medicina, vbi ita scribit. Qui verò medicinam exco-gitauerunt inuenerunt ue, sententiam opinio-nem ue nem'ue habuerunt quam illi de quibus prius dixeramus. Primum quidem arbitror ex eo- rundem ciborum copia quid sub traxernnt, & pro multis pauca fecerunt & dederunt. Cunque hoc illis satis non videretur: nō enim languentibus hæc æquo modo proderant, sed erant nonnulli, qui sic haberent vti ne exi- guos quidem cibos superare possent: hos itaq; putarunt imbecillioris cuiusdā rei egere: pro- pterea sorbitiones inuenerunt, paulum quid firmioris & robustæ materiæ multa aqua cō miscentes. quod inerat validum mixtione et coctura subtrahebant minuebantque, qui- cunque vero nec sorbitiones poterant supera re, eos ad pocula deducebant: hæcque vsu & copia obseruando, quod modicè ac æquo quo dam modo haberet, nec plusquam oporteret nec minus, nec meracius, nec dilutius, nec se rius, propinabant. Hoc autem probè scire o- portet, quibus sorbitiones in morbis non con ferunt, & considerare. nam cum fecerint fe- bres iritantur & crescunt dolores, clarumq; fit quod propinatur & infertur, morbo quidem nutrimentum & incrementu esse, corpo ri vero tabem, malum & exitium. Quibus autem sic habentibus siccus cibus, panis, placenta, puls, mazáue, et si pusillum datur, de-cuplo magis malu crescit quā si sorbitio, nul-lam aliā ob causam nisi cibi vehementia, quæ ad malum quo quis afficitur non facit. Nam cui sorbere confert, comedere vero minime, hic si plusculum assumat magis afficitur, cu-ius languoris causa huc referatur. Nam quæ valida materia sunt maximè & apertissimè sanum lædunt, nedum languentem. Hucusq; Hippocrates, aut Thessalus eius filius. In qui-bus verbis triplicem designauit victum, nem-pe quæ comeduntur, sorbentur, et bibuntur, nempe crassum tenuem & tenuissimum. In aphorismis quartum addidit, nempe ultimo tenuissimum, quem recte Gal. omnimodam cibi et potus abstinentiam interpretatus est, ut ipse aperte secundo de victu acutorum o-stendit. Ita ut totus victus quadrifariam di-uidatur, nempe in ea quæ comedūtur, sorben-tur, et bibūtur, et in omnimodā cibi et potus abstinenabstinentiam. Verùm si ea quæ sorbentur bifariam partiaris, nempe in crassam & tenuè sorbitionem, habebis differentias omnes in quas Hippocrates victûs partitus est. Verùm quatuor ex ijs sunt, quæ acutè &grotantibus conueniunt, nempe crassa sorbitio, tenuis, poculà, & omnimoda abstinentia, quorû memi nit Hippocrates in libris de ratione victus in acutis. Crassæ quidè sorbitionis in primo, cum de eo victu agit quem hordei substantia præ- stat duplicem ab eo sorbitionem parans, nem pe crassam & tenuem: illam absolutè ptisa- nam, aut totam vocat ptisanam, aut hordea ceam, & est quæ post integrā hordei coctio- nem non colatur. hanc cremorem siue succū ptisanæ nuncupat, et est succus qui post cola- turam remanet. Vt scriptum est à Gal.primo de ratione victus in expositione illius, Talia autem parte plurima prosunt ijs, &c. Ea ergo quæ comeduntur, crassum: sorbitiones crassæ, vt tota ptisana, tenuè: tenuis sorbitio, vt ptisanæ cremor, exactè tenuè: potus, vt meli cratû, tenuissȷ. omnimoda abstinentia vltimo tenuissimum victum constituunt. His omnibus consentire Galenum scito in eo aphorisi Tenues & certe diaetae, ab eo loco nunc sufficit tantum dicere ad finem. Quo in loco Nicolai versio ita habet: Nunc vero tantum dixisse sufficiat, quod in omnibus morbis quibus maximus vigor & iudicatio primis quatuor diebus futura sit, modo natura sit fortior, integra inediam seruare debemus. In quibus vero non ultra primam septimanam protrahuntur, forti existente natura, solo vtendum est melicrato. solus autem et hic ipse victus tenuissimus esset, nō tamen in extremo, &c. Graecus tamen coniextus duo verba addit hoc modo, Νυν δε αρχη των τοσουτων επῶν, ως εφ' ὧν μὲν αὶ νοσημάτων ἢ ἀκμὴ ἢ κρίσις ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ μέλλει γίνεσθαι τεταρτῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἰσχυρᾶς ἀσθενείας, ὧδι ἀσιτίας παντελῶς τούτους φυλάξομεν, ὅπερ ὅταν ἰσχὺς τῶς λεπτότητος διαίτης, &c. hoc est, nunc vero tantum sufficiat dixisse, nempe in quibus morbis vigor & crisis in primis quatuor diebus futura sit, virtute forti existente, in abstinentia omnimoda hos seruabimus. Quod quidem est vltimũ tenuissimi victus. In quibus vero non vltra primam septimanam, forti existẽte virtute, sufficiat melicrato solo vti. Tenuissimus sit hic solus victus, non tamen in vltimo. Ex quibus verbis et ex iis quæ ad finem Aphorismi scribit, aperte ostendit per crassum, tenuem, exacte tenuè, tenuissimum, & vltimo tenuissimum victu, intellexisse se id quod supra diximus. Horum quinque victuum generum meminit Hippocrates in libris de ratione victus in acutis.
units.tr: I shall now briefly show what I think about these kinds of diet, which I have come to prefer most after long consideration of the works of the art. For it is the usefulness of the art to discover what is more suitable for the sick. Now lend me your ears, as I am about to tell you something on the regimen of diet, which may settle your minds. In this matter I follow one author above all, Hippocrates, whose writings surpass human learning. Whatever I shall have told you about the regimen of diet I credit to him. But first it will be useful to resolve a difficulty. Hippocrates first spoke of thick diet, thin diet, and very thin diet in the Aphorisms. What he meant by these names can be gathered from his books on the regimen of diet, but more clearly in the book On Ancient Medicine, where he writes as follows: "Those who first devised medicine, found it, or held an opinion or notion about it, were those of whom we spoke before. First, I think, they reduced the quantity of foods and gave few things in place of many. Since this did not seem sufficient to them, for it did not help the sick equally, and some could not even manage the small amounts, they thought these people needed something of a weaker kind. So they invented gruels, mixing a little of something firmer and more robust with much water. They reduced and lessened what was strong in the material by mixing and boiling. Those who could not even manage gruels they led on to drinks, and by watching their use and quantity they gave what was moderate and even in a certain way, neither more than was right nor less, neither stronger nor weaker, neither thinner nor thicker. But one must know well, and consider, in which diseases gruels do not help. For when they have fevers, the irritation and pains increase, and it is clear that what is given and introduced is nourishment and growth to the disease, but to the body it is wasting, harm and destruction. In those so disposed, dry food, bread, cake, porridge or maza, even if given in small amounts, makes the evil grow ten times more than gruel would, for no other reason than the vehemence of the food, which does not help the disorder by which one is affected. For the one to whom gruel does good but eating does not, if he takes rather more, is affected more, and the cause of his weakness should be referred to this. For strong matter injures the healthy most and most openly, much more the sick." Thus far Hippocrates, or his son Thessalus. In these words he has marked out a threefold diet, namely what is eaten, what is sipped, and what is drunk: thick, thin, and very thin. In the Aphorisms he added a fourth, namely the very thinnest, which Galen rightly interpreted as complete abstinence from food and drink, as he himself clearly shows in the second book On the Diet of Acute Diseases. So the whole diet is divided fourfold: into what is eaten, what is sipped, what is drunk, and complete abstinence from food and drink. If, however, you divide what is sipped in two, namely into thick and thin gruel, you will have all the differences into which Hippocrates divided diet. Now four of these are suited to acute sufferers, namely thick gruel, thin gruel, drinks, and complete abstinence, which Hippocrates mentions in his books On the Regimen in Acute Diseases. Of thick gruel he speaks in the first book, when he treats of the diet which the substance of barley supplies, preparing from it a double gruel, namely thick and thin. He calls the thick one simply ptisan, or the whole ptisan, or barley-gruel, and it is that which is not strained after the whole barley has been cooked. The thin one he calls the cream or juice of the ptisan, and it is the juice which remains after straining. As Galen wrote in his first book On the Regimen of Diet, in his exposition of that passage, "Such things, for the most part, benefit those who..." etc. So what is eaten is thick diet; thick gruels, such as the whole ptisan, are thin diet; thin gruel, such as the cream of the ptisan, is exactly thin diet; drink, such as honeyed water, is very thin diet; and complete abstinence constitutes the very thinnest diet. Know that Galen agrees with all of this in that aphorism, "Thin and certainly diets," from which point it is now enough merely to say to the end. In that place the version of Nicolas reads thus: "Now it is enough to have said only this, that in all diseases in which the greatest vigour and crisis will occur within the first four days, provided the nature is stronger, we must keep the patient wholly without food. In those which are not drawn out beyond the first week, with a strong nature, one must use honeyed water only." But this very diet would be the thinnest, though not the extreme. The Greek text, however, adds two words in this way: "Νυν δε αρχη των τοσουτων επῶν..." that is, "Now let it suffice to have said only so much: in those diseases in which the vigour and crisis will occur in the first four days, the strength of nature being firm, we shall keep these patients in complete abstinence. This is indeed the extreme of the very thin diet. In those in whom the disease does not last beyond the first week, with the strength of nature firm, it is enough to use honeyed water only. This sole diet is the thinnest, but not the extreme." From these words, and from what he writes at the end of the aphorism, he clearly shows that by thick, thin, very thin, the thinnest, and the extreme thinnest diet, he understood what we said above. Hippocrates mentions these five kinds of diet in his books On the Regimen in Acute Diseases. (Hippocrates: see above.)

units.la: Quomodo sint intelligendæ crasi, symmetri & tenuis uictus notiones, quas Galenus primo aphor. asignauit.
units.tr: How the notions of thick, moderate and thin diet, which Galen set out in the first aphorism, are to be understood.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: GALENVS Hippocratica diuisione non contentus, quæ ciborum diuersas formas respicit, eorundem penes virium dispositionem variam, quam cibaria diuersa inducunt, aliam denuo diuisionem superaddit, omnem cibum in crassum, symmetrum, & tenuem dividens. Vires augere valens alimentum, crassum dicens: seruare, symmetrum: minuere tenuem. Quae qualiter sunt intelligenda verba, dicere opus est. Nam si crassi symmetri et tenuis notiones, quas assignauit Gal. respectu virium sanitatis tempore intelligas, nullus utiq; symmeter victus aegrotanti bus daretur. nam satis manifestum est nulli contingere aegrotanti quantumcunq; crassis victa tur cibarijs aeque robustum in aegritudine seruari ac fuerat ante morbi inuasionem. Quod si ad tempus aegritudinis referas, tenuis non datur. nam praeter omnimodam abstinentiam, & aquam frigidam, quem nam assignabis victum qui ex sui ratione vires aegrotantis imminuat? Ego quidem nullum esse victum quantumcunq; tenuem, qui vires, acuto morbo aegrotantis, non augeat existimo. Nam sipti sana dicas, audias Galenum in primo de victu acutorum expositione illius, At si os madefscat, vbi ita de ptisana sentit. Ergo qui probe expurgantur, inquit, his ptisana dare oportet: nō vt virtute modo roboret, verum quoq; &
units.tr: Galen, not content with the Hippocratic division, which concerns the different forms of food, adds a further division based on the varied effects that different foods have on strength, and divides all food into thick (crassum), moderate (symmetrum) and thin (tenue). He says that food which augments strength is thick, food which preserves it is moderate, and food which diminishes it is thin. We must explain how these words are to be understood. For if you take the notions of thick, moderate and thin, which Galen assigned, with respect to strength in health, then no moderate diet would ever be given to the sick. It is quite clear that no one who is ill, however much thick food he takes, keeps the same robustness during sickness as he had before the disease came on. But if you refer them to the time of sickness, no thin diet is given at all. For apart from total abstinence and cold water, what diet will you name that by its nature lessens the strength of the sick? I myself think there is no diet, however thin, that does not increase the strength of someone suffering from an acute disease. For if you say that ptisana is wholesome, hear Galen in the first book of his work on the diet of acute patients, in his exposition of the passage "But if he moistens his mouth", where he thinks thus of ptisana. "Therefore," he says, "ptisana must be given to those who have been properly purged, not only to strengthen their virtue but also to help with the expectoration of moist matter that comes up from the lungs by coughing."

units.la: & his quæ per tusses ex pulmone fiunt humi‑dorum expuitionibus opem ferat. In quo qui dem contextu sic habet Ioannis Vassæi ver‑sio. Sed apertius græcus contextus id quod pro posuimus ostedit. nã propositione affirmatiuã facit, in hunc modu. Dare igitur oportet pro bè expurgatis ptisanam, causa roborandi vir tutem, &c. Audisti ptisanam virtutem ro‑borare posse. Idem de mulsa ab eodem intelli‑ges tertio de ratione victus in expositione il‑lius, Vini autem & mellis &c. Vbi copiosio rem ex mulsa nutritione asserit, quàm ex vi‑no. Idẽ apertius ostendit in expositione illius, Damnata aut propterea, &c. Non ob id er‑go tenuem dixisse victu putandum est, quod ægrotatis vires minuat. Crassi igitur victus, symmetri, et tenuis rationes, ad sanos referen‑dæ sunt, vt crassum eum victu dicas, qui sani corporis vires augere possit. Symmetru, qui eiusdem vires seruare. Tenuem, eum qui sani corporis vires haudquaquam seruare vale‑at. Hunc acute ægrotatibus conuenire scribit. In chronicis vero morbis vires esse seruãdas symmetro victu: hoc est talem esse victum offerendum, qui laborantis cum sanus erat vires seruare posset. Tenuem igitur qui sano Socrati vires seruare non poterat, acuta febre ægrotanti & iam imbecilliori effecto si ministres, easdem augebit. Nam non aliter quàm si in ingenti pyra vt ignem eadem serues magnitudine, certa lignorum multitudine opus est. Quod si eundem augere, maiori. Finge nunc ignem aut ob aquæ effusionem, aut ob quodcunque sit imminutum, minori profecto lignorum congerie seruabis, & augebis. Consimiliter hominum corpora, cum prospera fruuntur valitudine, crasso cibo et multo indigent, vt viriū robur seruetur aut augeatur. Cum ob morbos virtus corporis imbecillis est effecta, subtiliori cibo & eius minori copia & seruari & augeri possunt. Quare mirum non est si à melicrato, vino, oxymelite, & similibus vires acutè ægrotan tium augeantur. Cuius euidens præstant argumentum viatores & operarÿ. Cum integra die à cibo et potu abstinuere, hos vespere vix corporis onus substinere posse. His tunc temporis mellis & aquæ parum si porrigas, alacriores eos ad opus reddes. Hoc ita esse, ostendit Ionathan Saulis Hebræorum regis filius, qui vires resumpsit, id mellis gustans, quod extremæ virgæ inhæsit. Non est igitur, quod acuto morbo laborantis vires melicrato augeri non posse credamus. Cum ergo in artis operibus id verum esse probemus, nempe cibum etsi tenuissimum acutè ægrotantis vires augere posse, nullus vtique tenuis dabitur cibus, sed omnis crassus erit, si crassi & tenuis rationes ad ægritudinis tempus & nō sanitatis referas. Sed non ab re fuerit verba Galeni in præsenti græcè adducere, quandoquidem de ijs contentio est, vt sciatis quantum dictus conueniant. Λεπτὴν δέ, δι' ὀλίγων ἐλλο μάτων, ἢ δι' ὀλιγοφόφων, οἷον περὶ τὸ ὀ τῆς πιοσαωνὸς δὲ χυλὸς, ὃς ἢ ὢ αὐτῆς ἢ δι' δυνά- μεως δὲ καθαίρεσις, ἧς περ γένεα καὶ ζεφο- μέν. ὑδὶ μὲν ὑδ' ὑγιαινόντων ὡς χρὴ τὴν ξῶ μὲν δι' δυνάμεως φυλάττειν ἢ παραιώξειν τὰς ξοφᾶς, ὁ καθαιρῶν, καὶ εἰν ὢ ἢ μὲν ταρεω-
units.tr: In this passage the version of Ioannes Vassaeus reads thus, but the Greek text shows more clearly what we have set out, for it makes the statement affirmative, in this way: "It is therefore necessary to give ptisana to those who have been properly purged, for the sake of strengthening the virtue, etc." You have heard that ptisana can strengthen the virtue. You will understand the same of mulsa from the same author in the third book, on the rationale of diet, in his exposition of the passage "But of wine and honey, etc.", where he asserts that more strength comes from mulsa nourishment than from wine. He shows the same more plainly in his exposition of the passage "Damnata aut propterea, etc." It must not be thought, therefore, that he called a diet thin because it diminishes the strength of the sick. The notions of thick, moderate and thin diet are therefore to be referred to healthy people: thick diet is that which can augment the strength of a healthy body; moderate, that which preserves its strength; thin, that which by no means can preserve the strength of a healthy body. He writes that this last suits acute sufferers. In chronic diseases, however, the strength is to be preserved by a moderate diet, that is, a diet must be offered which can preserve the strength the patient had when he was well. Thus if you give a thin diet, which could not preserve the strength of healthy Socrates, to someone ill with an acute fever who has already become weaker, it will increase that strength. For just as, to keep a great pyre burning at the same size, a certain quantity of wood is needed, and to make it bigger, more is needed. Now imagine that the fire has been diminished, either by pouring water on it or by anything else; you will certainly keep it and increase it with a smaller pile of wood. Similarly, human bodies, while they enjoy good health, need thick food and plenty of it, so that the strength of their powers may be preserved or increased. When through disease the body's vigour has been weakened, it can both be preserved and increased by a thinner food and a smaller quantity of it. It is no wonder, therefore, that the strength of those acutely ill is increased by melicratum, wine, oxymel and similar things. Travellers and labourers give clear evidence of this: when they have abstained from food and drink for a whole day, in the evening they can scarcely bear the burden of the body; if you then give them a little honey and water, you will make them more cheerful for their work. That this is so is shown by Jonathan, son of Saul, king of the Hebrews, who regained his strength by tasting honey which clung to the tip of his rod. It is not, therefore, that we should believe the strength of one suffering from an acute disease cannot be increased by melicratum. Since, then, we prove this to be true in the works of the craft, namely that even the thinnest food can increase the strength of one acutely ill, no food at all would be thin, but all would be thick, if you refer the notions of thick and thin to the time of sickness and not of health. But it will not be out of place to quote here Galen's own words in Greek, since there is dispute about them, so that you may know how well the things said agree with them. "Thin [λεπτὴν] diet is that made of few foods, or of little nourishing foods, such as the juice of ptisana, whose effect is the diminishing of strength, the cause of which is what nourishes us. In healthy people, therefore, it is always necessary to preserve the strength of their power, or to increase it by food, not to diminish it." Then, without finishing the sentence, he adds, linking it to what he had said about healthy people: "And indeed food that augments is thick; that which preserves is moderate; that which diminishes is thin. This one (he says) must always be avoided, that is, in chronic cases; but which of the others the present needs require, that one should be used." In sick people it rarely happens that we can make their strength stronger than we have received it. He said "rarely", excepting the hectic and those worn out by marasmus, whose strength we labour to make stronger every day by a gradual increase of food. In chronic cases we take pains to preserve it, for the most part; in acute cases, to preserve the strength that has been moderately diminished. For if we were always eager to preserve it as we found it in such patients, or to increase it, we would add to the disease. From these words it is gathered that in chronic cases we must take pains to restore, as far as possible, by food and drink, the strength which the disease has taken away; but in acute cases this is not to be done, and it is enough to make good part of the loss of strength by a thin diet, sometimes more and sometimes less, as we judge the strength can bear. This is what he meant by "to preserve what is moderately diminished in acute cases". Therefore the things that are eaten make up a thick diet, because by such a diet the bodies of healthy people are preserved and increased, while broths are thin, for the strength of healthy people cannot be preserved by them if they are used alone. Drinks, the thinnest of all, will cause the greatest loss of strength to healthy bodies if they take nourishment only from them for several days.

units.la: ἐυῦζα ξοφὴ, ἀδ᾽ ἐα, ἢ ἡ φυλάττεσθαι, σύμμετρος: ἢ δὲ καθαίρεσθαι, λεπτὴ. hoc est, Tenuis victus per pauca edulia, vel per ea quae parum nutriunt, quale est ptisanae succus. terminus ipsius, virtutis est imminutio, cuius causa nutrimus. In sanis igitur semper oportet robur virtutis seruare, vel augere alimentis, non minuere. Et statim clausula non finita, ita ait, ijs quae de sanis dixerat sequentia annectens. Et fuerit quidem augens alimentum crassum: seruans vero, symmetrum: immi-nuens, tenue. hoc (inquit) fugere oportet semper, subintellige in chronicis: aliorum vero vtro magis indigeant praesentia, illo vti. In aegrotantibus raro contingit virtutem fortiorem, quam acceperimus efficere. Dixit raro, hecticos & marasmo confectos excipiens, quorum virtutem laboramus singulis diebus robustiorem efficere alimentorum successiuo incremento. Damus operam, vt in pluribus seruare in chronicis: mensuratè quidem imminutam conseruare in acutis. Si enim seruare ipsam qualem acceperimus in ijs, vel augere semper properaremus, adde-mus in morbum. Ex quibus verbis colligi-tur, in chronicis dandam esse operam, vt ci-bo & potu id virium quod à morbo absu-mitur quoad fieri posšit reponamus: in acu-tis verò id non dari, satisque esse si partem detrimenti virium, tenuis victus ope resar-ciamus, modo maiorem, & modo mino-rem, prout nobis virtutem posse sufficere vi sum fuerit. Et hoc est quod dixit, Mensu-ratè quidem imminutam conseruare in acu-tis. Ea ergo quae comeduntur crassum vi-ctum constituunt, ob id quod eo victu sa-norum corpora seruantur, & augentur: sorbitiones verò tenuem. nam vires sano-rum ab ijs seruari non possunt, si eis so-lummodo vtantur. Pocula, tenuissimum, maximum siquidem virium detrimen-tum patientur sana corpora, aliquot diebus ab ijs solummodo ali-moniam suscipi-entia.
units.tr: Tenuis victus per pauca edulia, vel per ea quae parum nutriunt, quale est ptisanae succus. Hoc est: a thin diet is one of few foods, or of foods that nourish little, such as the juice of ptisana. Its aim is the diminishing of strength, whose cause is what nourishes us. In healthy people, therefore, the strength of their vigour must always be preserved or augmented by food, not diminished. And, without finishing the sentence, he adds, linking it to what he had said about healthy people: "And indeed food that augments is thick; that which preserves is moderate; that which diminishes is thin. This one must always be avoided (he says), that is, in chronic cases; but whichever of the others the present needs require, that one should be used." Greek fragment as printed: "ἐυῦζα ξοφὴ, ἀδ᾽ ἐα, ἢ ἡ φυλάττεσθαι, σύμμετρος: ἢ δὲ καθαίρεσθαι, λεπτὴ." (Corrupted in the scan; sense: "the one that augments is thick, the one that is kept is moderate, the one that is purged is thin.") In sick people it rarely happens that we can make their strength greater than we received it. He said "rarely", excepting the hectic and those worn out by marasmus, whose strength we labour to make stronger each day by gradual increase of food. In chronic cases we take pains, for the most part, to preserve it; in acute cases, to keep what has been moderately diminished. For if we always hurried to preserve it as we found it in them, or to increase it, we would add to the disease. From these words it is gathered that in chronic cases we must take pains to restore by food and drink as much as possible of the strength the disease takes away; but in acute cases this is not to be done, and it is enough to make good part of the loss of strength by thin diet, now more and now less, as we judge the strength can suffice. This is what he meant by "to preserve what is moderately diminished in acute cases". Therefore the things that are eaten make up a thick diet, because by that diet the bodies of healthy people are preserved and increased, while broths are thin, since the strength of healthy people cannot be preserved by them if they are used alone. Drinks, the thinnest of all, will cause the greatest loss of strength to healthy bodies if they take their nourishment only from them for several days.

units.la: Locum citat Galeni, è quo ostenditur qua- liter intelligenda fit tenuis uictus ratio: ἢ δὲ λεπτὴ καὶ ἀμεγέθης.
units.tr: He cites a passage of Galen from which it is shown how the notion of thin diet is to be understood: "but the thin and scanty [ἡ δὲ λεπτὴ καὶ ἀμεγέθης]".

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: ALITER tenuis victus ratio intelligitur, prout Galenus exposuit in eo loco, Damnata autem propterea & c. Vbi imbecillitare, & nullo pacto nutrire, & parum nutrire, non idem esse ait. Diminuut (inquit) vires, sanguinis eruptio, deiectio superflua, sudor immodicus, & per accidens cibi abstinentia. hæc verè imbecillitare dicuntur. At quæ nullo pacto nutriunt, vt aqua, ea imbecillitare nec roborare vires quispiam verè dixerit, nisi id per accidens contingat. Tertio sunt loco quæ exiguè nutriunt, & potuissent quidem si quis solis ipsis vsus fuerit, mori, nō equidem quia vires diminuunt, sed quia non sufficienter roborant. Ex his est mulsa. nam si quis diebus quatuor cibo priuatus interire possit, hic mulsæ vsu, non quintâ modo diem, verùm quoque & sextam attinget. Ex ijs elicitur verbis, quod cum in aphorismis dixit detenui
units.tr: In another sense the thin regimen is understood, as Galen explained it in that passage, "Damnata autem propterea" etc. There he says that being weakened, not nourishing at all, and nourishing little are not the same thing. "Loss of blood," he says, "bloody discharge, excessive evacuation, immoderate sweating, and, incidentally, abstinence from food, diminish the strength; these are truly said to weaken." But things that do not nourish at all, such as water, one could not truly say weaken or fail to strengthen the powers, unless this happens incidentally. Third are the things that nourish scantily, which could indeed cause death if someone used only these, not because they diminish the powers, but because they do not sufficiently strengthen them. Mulsum belongs to this group. For if someone can survive four days without food, one who uses mulsum will reach not only the fifth day but also the sixth. From these words it is clear that when in the Aphorisms he spoke of thin food,

units.la: 3. de ratio ne uictus. de tenui loquens victu, H' δὲ λεπτὴν, καθαρὰ-ς: hoc est, Imminuens, tenuis: non quia vere vires imminuat dixit, sed quia non sufficienter roborat. Danda est ergo opera, ut ægrotantis vires cibo tantisper augeamus, quatenus id citra manifestam læsionem fieri possit. Longa didici consideratione, quod postea à Dionysio medico patre meo, viro apud Lusitanos clarissimo accepi, ægrotantibus quibuscunque saluberrimum esse, medicum id agere, ut virtutem, citra morbi aut eius durationis additionem, roboret. Qua de causa inventæ sunt ab antiquis sorbitiones, & pocula, acutis morbis victus idonei, qui sane ægrotantis vires citra noxam augeant, & facile ab imbecillis superentur natura. Quorum uno aut altero prout morbi constitutio est, vtuntur.
units.tr: (Aphorisms, third on the regimen of food.) "Speaking of thin food," [ἡ δὲ λεπτὴ καθαρός]: that is, "diminishing, thin." He did not say it diminishes the powers in truth, but because it does not sufficiently strengthen them. Care must therefore be taken to increase the patient's strength with food for as long as this can be done without manifest harm. I learned from long consideration, and later heard from Dionysius, my father, a physician most renowned among the Lusitanians, that it is most beneficial for all sick people that the physician aim to strengthen their strength without adding to the disease or prolonging it. For this reason the ancients devised sorbitions and drinks, suitable diets for acute diseases, which indeed increase the patient's strength without harm and are easily overcome by weak natures. The physician uses one or another of these, according to the condition of the disease.

units.la: Quod uictus forma robore uirtutis, & à di stantia status sumenda sit: non autem à morbi dispositione uel motu. hic enim tempus tantum uictus indicat, non formam uariat.
units.tr: That the form of the diet should be taken from the strength of the powers and from the distance of the state, and not from the disposition or movement of the disease. For this indicates only the timing of the diet and does not vary its form.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: HIS ita determinatus, methodum de re {H}ello febricitantibus ministrando victu, incipiam breuiori & faciliori quàm possim via tradere. Quinque habet victus debita ad ministratio consideraciones: nempe victus forma, quam Græci διαίτης ξεῦξις vocant, dein de quantitatis, qualitatis, numeri, & horæ. horum singula inuestigäda fore à medico qui victum ægrotantibus conuenientem ministraturus sit.
units.tr: Having been thus determined, I shall set out, by a briefer and easier route than I can manage, the method of providing food to feverish patients. There are five considerations in the proper administration of diet: namely the form of the diet, which the Greeks call [διαίτης ξεῦξις], then its quantity, quality, number, and time. The physician who is to supply suitable food to the sick must investigate each of these separately.

units.la: Victus forma à virtutis robore & statu distantia sumitur, vt scribitur libro Aphorif. Vt si longe fuerit morbi status, symmetro vtemur victu: quod si prope, tenui: tenuissimo vero, si proxime. quòd si iá affuerit, vltimò tenuissimo. Ad hæc virtus corporis consideranda est, an talem victus speciem ferat, quam status distantia præscripserit.
units.tr: The form of the diet is taken from the strength of the powers and the distance from the state, as is written in the book of Aphorisms: if the state of the disease is far off, we shall use a moderate diet; if near, a thin one; and the thinnest if very near; and if it is already present, finally the thinnest. Besides this, the strength of the body must be considered, whether it can bear the kind of diet that the distance of the state has prescribed.

units.la: Verùm in hoc negotio primum quærere oportet, an rectè à distantia status & à virtutis robore, victus formam inquirere oporteat. An potius cū virtute, morbi dispositionem considerandam esse, vt rectè victū ægrotantibus diffinire possimus. Rationales medici qui Hippocratē insequuntur, à virtu tis robore et à distantia status victus formā inuestigandam ideo esse opinantur, quod sola corporis virtus sit, quæ cibo pro sui custodia indiget. Nam ut vitale robur seruemus, ideo cibum ægrotantibus exhibemus: ut scripsit Galenus in expositione illius, Postea si dolor &c. Virtus igitur pro sui custodia eum cibū indicat quo maxime seruari possit. Morbus autem talem diffinit, ut eo ad vigorem solum sufficere possit ægrotas. Nam apud hunc morborum iudicia ad salutem aut mortem fiunt. Eo vsque igitur virtutem seruare cibo oportet. Crassiorem verò exhibere quo vltra durare queat, damno erit. nam morbum augebimus. Nam si morbosam affectionem nullo pacto offenderet alimonia, nos virtuti soli attendentes, ægros ut sanos aleremus. Sed quia sæpius noxam (vti ostendimus) affert, ob id morbi affectionē non tanquā cibi indicatricem, sed tanquam prohibitricem cōtemplamur, ut Galenus prudenter citato loco scripsit. Viri ergo pro sui custodia omnem cibum indicat, què apparare possit. ab hoc morbus omnem abscindit, quo vltra vigorem durare queat ægrotans. Id tunc concedimus, cum eo subtiliori scimus ad statum durare posse. Quare si ad vigorem vsque sufficere posse ægrotantem existimemus solo vi stu per pocula, sorbitiones non dabimus: sed nec ea quæ comeduntur, idque ob morbi rationem, vt scitè ab Hippocrate scriptum est in hæc verba: Postea si dolor quispiam vel periculum comparuerit, sorbitionem dare oportet, neque multam neque crassam: sed post septimum aut nonum, si validus sit. Audis Hippocratem sorbitione supersedere ad septimum aut nonum vsque, cum in eis indicatio nem futuram speramus, vbi ægèr citra sorbitionem eò vsque possit sufficere. In cuius expositione Galenus ita scribit. Cum igitur vir tus ad morbi vsque indicationem sine ptisanæ sorbitione suffecerit, oxymeli & aqua mulsa satis sunt, &c. Ex quibus manifestū est victum eum eligendum fore, quo cū corporis virtus suss.ciat, subtiliori verò sufficerenon posset. An nonne id ab eodem loco citato colligimus, vbi ita ait. At si indicatione septima die citius futurâ speraueris, vt verbi gratia vel quarta vel quinta, ægros sanè multos sufficere citra ptisanæ sorbitionem posse comperies: quod si ad septimam vsque protrahatur, paucos omnino. Qui igitur citra ptisanam sufficere possunt, ijs oxymeli et aquam mulsam exhibere docuit. Qui verò non, ptisanam. Quinimmò si absque cibo & potu ad indicationem vsque durare posse spe remus, omnimodam et inediam consulemus.
units.tr: But in this matter one must first ask whether it is right to seek the form of the diet from the distance of the state and the strength of the powers, or rather whether the disposition of the disease must be considered along with the powers, so that we can rightly determine the diet for the sick. Rational physicians who follow Hippocrates think the form of diet should be investigated from the strength of the powers and the distance of the state, because the strength of the body alone needs food for its preservation. For we give food to the sick in order to preserve their vital strength, as Galen wrote in his exposition of that passage, "Postea si dolor" etc. The strength, then, for its own preservation, indicates the food by which it can best be kept. The disease, however, defines itself in such a way that the patient can be sustained only to the point of vigour. For in this disease the crises lead either to salvation or to death. So far, then, the strength must be preserved with food. To give thicker food by which it could last longer would be harmful, for we would increase the disease.
