For if nourishment in no way offended the diseased condition, we, attending only to the strength, would feed the sick as if they were well. But since it often causes harm (as we have shown), we regard the disposition of the disease not as indicating food but as forbidding it, as Galen wisely wrote in the passage cited. The strength, therefore, for its own preservation, indicates whatever food it can take in; the disease cuts off all food beyond what the patient can endure while keeping their vigour. We allow this when we know the patient can last in the state on a thinner diet. Hence, if we judge that the patient can keep up to the point of vigour on liquid food alone, through drinks, we shall not give sorbitions; nor shall we give solid food, for the reason of the disease, as Hippocrates wisely wrote in these words: "Afterwards, if some pain or danger appears, one should give a sorbition, neither much nor thick, but after the seventh or ninth day, if the patient is strong." You hear Hippocrates delaying sorbition until the seventh or ninth day, when we hope for a crisis in those days, in which the patient can then manage without sorbition. In his exposition Galen writes: "Since, then, the strength suffices up to the indication of the disease without a sorbition of barley-water, oxymel and mulsum water are enough," etc. From these words it is clear that the diet to be chosen is the one with which the strength of the body can cope, but which a thinner diet could not sustain. Do we not gather this from the same passage, where he says: "But if you hope the indication will come earlier than the seventh day, say on the fourth or fifth, you will find that many sick people can get by without a sorbition of barley-water; but if it is put off until the seventh, very few can." So he taught that those who can manage without barley-water should be given oxymel and mulsum water, and those who cannot, barley-water. Indeed, if we hope the patient can last without food and drink until the indication, we shall advise complete fasting.

units.la: Vt ipse Hippocrates aperte monuit secundo eiusdem de ratione victus, vbi ita ait: Cibo-rum autem adiectioni intendendũ multo mi-nus: subtrahere verò omnino sæpenumero expedit, cum æger sufficere posset, donec matu-rescat morbus. Quod Galenus confirmat inhæc verba: Nempe si æger ad morbi vsque vigorem sine cibo sufficere posse videatur, in omni ciborum abstinentia eum & potu so-lo, cum tibi videbitur necessitas, moderaberis. Vocetur autem ille victus quoad statum sufficit ægrotans & eo subtiliori non, medius: hoc subtiliore exhibentibus corporis virtus exoluitur: morbus autem incrementum assumit, eo crassiorem ministrantibus. Quare rationabiliter à distantia status tanquam à termino ad quem vsque ducendus sit æger, victus formam inuestigandam esse rationales opinantur. Nec hoc in arte medica solum didicimus, verum in rebus humanis id licet obseruare.
units.tr: As Hippocrates himself plainly warned in the second book of On Regimen, where he says: "Attention should be paid much less to adding food; but it is often advisable to take it away altogether when the patient could manage, until the disease comes to maturity." Galen confirms this in these words: "Namely, if the patient seems able to last until the strength of the disease without food, you will moderate them by complete abstinence from food, and by drink alone, when you judge it necessary." That diet which suffices for the state is called medium, and not thinner: the patient's strength is spent on the thinner diet, while the disease gains strength when the sick are given thicker food. Hence rational physicians think that the form of the diet is to be sought from the distance of the state, as from the limit to which the patient is to be led. We learn this not only in the medical art but may observe it in human affairs as well.

units.la: Prudens viator quingenta profecturus miliaria, haud nimis festinè equitat: sed moderato ducit equum incessu, & labores diurnos nocturna temperat quiete. Nec solum labori modum imponit, verum & cibo quo equum nutrire oportet, vt eo durare possit. Quod si vnius diei actGurus sit iter, haud necessarium putat quicquam obseruare.
units.tr: A prudent traveller who is about to journey five hundred miles does not ride too hastily; he leads his horse at a measured pace, and tempers the labours of the day with nightly rest. Nor does he impose a limit only on the labour, but also on the food by which the horse must be fed so that it can last. But if the journey is only one day's length, he thinks it unnecessary to observe anything.

units.la: Nónne idem nauigantes obseruare videmus. Nullum quidem sibi parant viaticum, qui à Calesijs in Angliam se recipiunt. Non sic qui à Venetijs Epidaurum Rhagusiorum oppidum proficiscuntur. Iis longe dissimile quod Lusitani indos petituri magnis parant expensis. Ii omnes non ab alio viatici rationem sumunt, quàm ab itineris mora. Cósimiliter in arte medica ægrotantibus victus formam sumendam à distantia status recte quis ratiocinetur. Nam proxime huic adsunt morborum iudicia, alterutrũ exitum minantia.
units.tr: Do we not see sailors doing the same? Those who cross from Calais to England take no provisions at all. Not so those who sail from Venice to Epidaurus, a town of the Ragusans; their provisions differ greatly from those the Portuguese prepare with great expense when setting out for the Indies. All of these take their measure of provisions from nothing but the length of the voyage. Similarly, in the medical art, one may rightly reason that the form of diet for the sick should be taken from the distance of the state. For the crises of the disease, threatening one outcome or the other, are close at hand.

units.la: Sed age, si à distantia status victus formā non quæras, à quo nam altero præter virtutem indicationem sumes? A morbi dispositione forsan ais. Sed cum singulis morborum quatuor adsint dispositiones, quarũ differentiam sensu licet percipere: nempe principium, augmentum, status, & inclinatio: à qua nam harum victus formam sumendam putas?
units.tr: But come, if you do not seek the form of diet from the distance of the state, from what other source besides the strength will you take the indication? From the disposition of the disease, perhaps you will say. But since each disease has four dispositions, whose differences can be perceived by the senses, namely beginning, increase, state and decline, from which of these do you think the form of diet should be taken?

units.la: Proinde cum apud principia & fines omnia sunt imbecilliora, apud statum vehementiora, crassiorem quàm expediat ministrabis si ab illis, aut plus iusto tenuem si ab ijs, indicationem victus sumas. Præterea cum nulla sit morbi dispositio, quæ cibum indicet, sed omnis prohibeat, vt supra ostensum est, cuiq; alio sit alius acutior, & vehementior morbus, non ex æquo omnes pariter prohibebũt, sed vnus magis alio. Cumque virtus eum fem per victu indicet, quo maxime seruari possit, quem nam ab iis duobus, quorum alterum vnum indicat, & id alterum prohibet, elicere possis victum? Finge virtutem pro sui cu stodia victum indicare per ea que comedun-tur: si morbus multum dissuadeat, quid ab eo victu detrahes, quid ue cum parum prohibue-rit? Insuper vnde similes in detractionibus scias aut possis proportiones obseruare, ac in morborum dispositionibus erant. Ceterum no obstiterit, plures esse morbos, qui inaqua liter aegrotantes affligant, ita vt hodie mitius habeant, in crastinum deterius degant: modo absque febre vlla, postmodum magno & estu exagitentur: aliquando dolores labores ue patiantur, quandoque nullo symptomate infestentur: non ob id fieri non posse, vt vna vi ctus forma morbis inaqualiter affligentibus conueniat. Nam & si non eadem ratio in die accessionis, & in die quietiori habenda sit, quo maxime differre oporteat, no victus est, sed tempus quo innoxie cibum offeras. Eande nanque nanque victus formam quam à robore virtutis, & à distantia status sumpsisti, perpetuo ab initio morbi ad statum seruare oportet. Sed tempus obseruare expedit quo innoxie cibum offeras. Nam in paroxysmis subtrahere oportet. apponere enim laxio, vt in aphor. scriptum est. Vnde licet colligere ab vniuersali tempore morbi victus formam, à particulari vero qui singulis accessionibus conueniat, cibationis idoneum tempus suppeditari. Quod manifestius alibi scripsit in haec verba: Tempus autem dandae sorbitionis, tu per initia, tum per omnem morbi decursum. nam si pedes frigidi fuerint non à sorbitione modo, verum quoque et maxime à potu tem perandum. At cum caliditas ad pedes descendit, tunc dare expedit. Idem sub alijs verbis dixit. Cum purgaueris (inquit) sorbitionibus quibusdam vtitor, obseruatis ita febrium accessionibus, vt nunquam cum adsint, neque cum futurae sint exhibeas, sed vel cum cessant vel quieuerunt & maxime à principio recesserunt. Frigentibus ergo pedibus, ne-
units.tr: Therefore, since at the beginnings and the ends everything is weaker, and at the state more vehement, if you take the indication from the first or the last you will prescribe a cruder diet than is expedient, and if from the others a diet too thin. Moreover, since no disposition of the disease indicates food but every one forbids it, as shown above, and since one disease is sharper and more violent than another in each person, they will not all forbid equally, but one more than another. And since the strength indicates the diet by which it can best be preserved, which of those two, one of which indicates and the other forbids, can you deduce the diet from? Suppose the strength indicates diet for its own preservation through the foods that are eaten: if the disease strongly dissuades, what will you subtract from that diet, and what if it forbids only a little? Moreover, how could you know, or be able to observe, in the subtractions proportions like those in the dispositions of the diseases? Nor is it an obstacle that there are many diseases which afflict the sick unevenly, so that today they are milder and tomorrow worse; only without any fever, and afterwards they are racked by great heat; sometimes they cause pains or labours, sometimes they trouble the patient with no symptom. This does not mean that one form of diet cannot suit diseases that afflict unevenly. For although the same account is not to be taken on the day of the attack and on a quieter day, in which respect they chiefly ought to differ, that is not a difference of diet but of the time at which you may offer food harmlessly. For the same form of diet which you have taken from the strength of the virtue and from the distance of the state must be kept constant from the beginning of the disease up to its state. But it is expedient to observe the time at which you may offer food harmlessly. For during the paroxysms one must withdraw food; for to apply it is to relax, as is written in the Aphorisms. Hence from the general time of the disease one may gather the form of diet, and from the particular time that suits each attack a suitable time for feeding is supplied. He wrote this more clearly elsewhere, in these words: "The time for giving sorbitions is both at the beginning and throughout the whole course of the disease. For if the feet are cold, one must abstain not only from sorbitions but especially from drink; but when the heat descends to the feet, then it is expedient to give." He said the same in other words: "When you have purged, use certain sorbitions, observing the attacks of the fevers so that you never give them when they are present or about to come, but when they have ceased or are quiet, and especially at the beginning when they have withdrawn. So when the feet are cold,"

units.la: In 2. de ratione uictus.
units.tr: In the second book On the Regimen.

units.la: 4. de ratione uictus. que potu, neque sorbitiones, neq; aliud quippiam huiusmodi dabis. Sentis in iis duobus locis Hippocratem de particulari victu egisse, ut singulis conuenit accessionibus, vbi nihil à totius victus ratione diuersum docuit, qua tempus cibationis idoneum. Idem intelligendum est dedisse in aphorismis perceptu, cum dixit, In paroxysmis subtrahere oportet, quod confirmat Galenus citans in expositione loci Hippocratis quem supra adduximus quarto de ratione victus. Non igitur eo quod morbi inaequaliter affligant, alio utemur victu quàm virtus & distantia status indicarunt, ut aduersarij opinantur.
units.tr: In the fourth book On the Regimen: "neither drink, nor sorbitions, nor anything else of this kind will you give." You see that in those two passages Hippocrates treated of particular diet, as it suits each attack, and taught nothing different from the general account of diet in respect of the suitable time for feeding. The same must be understood of what he said in the Aphorisms, "In paroxysms one must withdraw," which Galen confirms in his exposition of the Hippocratic passage we cited above, in the fourth book On the Regimen. Therefore it is not because diseases afflict unevenly that we shall use a diet other than the one that strength and the distance of the state have indicated, as our opponents suppose.

units.la: Rationes eorum qui à constitutione morbi, & à robore uirtutis, uictus forma sumendam esse opinantur.
units.tr: The arguments of those who think the form of diet is to be taken from the constitution of the disease and from the strength of the virtue. ## CHAPTER VII.

units.la: CAPVT VII.

VERVM eorum qui contra sentiunt, rationes audire oportet. Haud facile est (aiunt) in arte medica methodum tradere qua id quod est, tale esse dignoscamus, nedum quale illud futurum sit. Difficillima quidem in in omni arte præcognitio est. Quapropter facilius à virtute & morbi dispositione victus formam eliciemus, quàm à distantia status, qui nondum est. Sed quod certius hinc, manifestum erit. Quænam sit ægritudo, & quas habeat causas, & quibus nam comitata sit symptomatibus, quamque perniciosa sint, certius scire potest in arte medica, quàm præsciri. Minus præterea errori obnoxii sunt qui à dispositione morbi cum virtute victus formam inquirunt, quàm qui à distantia sta-tus. Nam considerates quod est, ob mutationes decipi nō possūt, prout accidit iis qui qua-le quicquam erit considerant. Coniciens medicus ab initio morbi, eius acumen, talem fore ad septimum aut nonum æstimat. Hac nixus æstimatione victum inuestigat, quem & nunc et in posterū ad illud usque tempus ægrotanti ministraturus sit. Sed quantum decipi possit aduerte. Quot sunt quæso morbi, qui ultra incrementa periodica, & decrementa inæqualiter moueantur? Ita ut tribus aut primis quatuor diebus ægrotātes grauīter affligant, totidē postea aut plus minus ue citra iudicium intermittant. Deinde iterum increscant & luceant, & ad pristinam vehementiam redeant. Aut si contra mutatio fiat: posset ne in his methodice, viso ab initio morbi acumine, aut segnitie, qualis erit ad quintum aut septimum aut insequentes dies certò coniicere, vt ex hac coniectura distantiam status adipiscaris à qua demum victus formam diffinias? Cunque in eo quod primū praecognoscendum sumpsisti, non parum à veritate aberres, haud leuiter in eo quod vltimum est, in aegrotantem peccabis. Nam parvus error in principio, maximus est in fine.
units.tr: Truly, we must hear the arguments of those who think otherwise. It is not easy (they say) to hand down in the medical art a method by which we may recognise what is as it is, let alone what it will be. Foreknowledge is indeed the most difficult thing in every art. Therefore we shall more easily draw the form of diet from the strength and the disposition of the disease than from the distance of the state, which does not yet exist. But what is more certain will be made clear from this. What the illness is, what causes it has, with what symptoms it is accompanied, and how dangerous they are, one can know more certainly in the medical art than foresee. Moreover, those who inquire into the form of diet from the disposition of the disease together with the strength are less liable to error than those who do so from the distance of the state. For one who considers what is, cannot be deceived by changes, as happens to those who consider what will be. The physician, conjecturing from the beginning of the disease its acuteness, reckons that it will be such at the seventh or ninth day. Relying on this estimate, he works out the diet which he is to give the patient now and afterwards until that time. But consider how much he may be deceived. How many diseases, I ask, move irregularly beyond their periodic increases and decreases? So that for three or the first four days they afflict the sick severely, and for as many days afterwards, or more or less, they remit without judgment; then again they increase and flare up, and return to their former violence. Or if the change happens the other way: could one in such cases, having seen from the beginning of the disease its acuteness or sluggishness, methodically conjecture with certainty what it will be on the fifth or seventh or following days, so that from this conjecture you may obtain the distance of the state, from which at last you define the form of diet? And since in what you first took to be known beforehand you may err not a little from the truth, you will sin no lightly in the last thing, in regard to the patient. For a small error at the beginning is the greatest at the end.

units.la: Quod si in morbis haud contingere huiusmodi mutationes dicas, Hippocratis lib. de morbis vulgaribus revolue, in quibus non paucis hoc accidisse inuenies aegrotantibus. Caeterum de certitudine mittamus sermonem, & aliquantulum perspicacius rem tractemus. Virtutem eum semper victum indicare ais, quo maxime seruari possit. Deinde status distantiam talem diffinire, quo eo vsque suffi-ciat ciat ægrotans, & eo subtiliori non: vocas〈ṡ〉 hunc victum medium, crassiori non vteris, ne in morbum addas: sed nec magis tenui, ne plus iusto virtutem exoluas, & ob id ante statum deficiat. Age methodice laborāti So crati victum quem medium vocas ministres quo ad morbi vigorem posse sufficere æstima sti. Quid per illud verbum sufficere intelligis? An aliud ab eo quod Hippocrates in Apho. intellexit, qui primus illo in hac re vsus est verbo, cum ait: Σωτεκμηρίῳ δὲ χρὴ ἵη τὴν νοσοῦντα ἐξαρκέσει τῇ Διαίτῃ πρὸς τὸ ἀκμὴν τ̄ νόσου. id est, Coniicere oportet laborantem si sufficiat cum victu ad statum ægritudinis. Vbi an perdurare possit tali victu toto intermedio tempore ad statum vsque se intellexisse, ipse statim ostendit, in eo verbo quod sequitur, Καὶ πότερον ἐκεῖνο ἀπαυ- λήσει πρότερον. hoc est, Vtrum ille deficiat prius. Qua etiam significatione verbum illud intellexit Galenus, vt ab expositione licet coniicere. Victum ergo talem ministrare laborāti Socrati intendis, quo perdurare possit roto interim edio tempore ad statum vsque. Quod si id simpliciter intelligas, verbiquesi-gnificationem minime restringens, modo quo-cunque ad statum tali victu perducatur So-crates sat esse putes: quid si adeo imbecillis tui victus ope eò peruenias vt nulli quantum vis mitissimo morbo sit aptus obsistere, nedum morbo maximè apud vigorem sæuiente? An te obtinuisse putabis cum talem victum labo-ranti Socrati longam post meditationem in-ueneris? An hoc est cur palles? Forsan illud verbum ais non fore simpliciter intelligen-dum, sed sufficere ad statum vsque, tunc in-telligis, cum apud vigorem aliquale ægrotan-tis vires robur obtineant. Et si hoc detur, alia vtaris nota oportebit, rem indiuiduā no-bis significante. Nam illud tuum aliquale ni-mis ample patet. nā ea via, omnis crassus vi-ctus Socrati conueniret. Nullumq; damnare posses victu ob crassitiem. Quod si viriūro-bur tantū exposcas, vt morbificas possit de-bellare causas, et morbi incursibus obsistere: ridiculū caput, si hoc quod postulas methodice praestare uiclus posset, nulla esset adeo perniciosa aegritudo, quae non uictus ope medica ri posset. Quod si ita rem habere contendas, scias saltem, hoc tuum latuisse Hippocratem. Sed iis omissis fateberis id saltem, apud morbi vigorem labores & symptomata multo vehementiora fieri, quam ante, ut a uestro scriptum est Galeno, cum dixit de vigore loquens: Μέγισον τῶ νοσήματῶ ὡς γι συμπτωμάτων, hoc est, vigor nihil aliud est, quam maximum morbi, ut in symptomatibus. Putas ergo sat esse qualicunque virium robore eo perducatur aeger, cum tunc maximus sit morbi conflictus? An salubrius fore aegrotanti, si demus operam ut citra morbi additionem, aegrotantem robustiorem quantum possumus ad statum perducamus? Quis hoc damnabit methodice? non tu, si uera & aegrotantibus salubria sequeris dogmata. Cum hoc ita sit, finge Socratem citra sorbitionem ad statum sufficere posse, pocula ei ministrabis, utpote quae minus alimenti praestant. Scis ne eo uictu Socratem sufficienti virium robore ad statum peruenturum? hoc quamuis iuranti tibi vix credam. Sorbitionibus quare non vteris? Nam ijs vsus robustior esset apud vigorem. Forsan ais, quia in morbum addent. Vnde hoc scis quæso? an à distantia status id conijcis, vel potius à morbi dispositione vel acumine? Quod si dicas, cum statum præcognouero, fieri nequit quin morbi dispositione cognoscam. Cedo: sed quod horum prius cognoueris dicas, nam id manifestius & certius scies. Ea enim quæ principiorum vicem obtinent, semper manifesta magis sunt ijs quæ ab eis deducuntur. Cumque à morbi dispositione, status distantiam præcognoscas, morbi dispositionem euidentius cognosces, quàm status distantiam. Quare certius & magis citra errorem à morbi dispositione & acumine conijcies, an sorbitiones laboranti Socrati noceant, quàm si idem à distantia status indicare velis. esset enim tuum non paucis erroribus iudicium obnoxium. Quare cum in inquisitione formæ victus, morbus non tanquam indicans, sed prohibens admittatur, ut rationales omnes fatetur: prohibet autem in quantum victus in morbu, aut in eius auget symptomata: idq; cum a dispositione morbi evidentius dignoscatur, rectius fuerit a virtute & morbi dispositione, victus formam investigare, quam a distantia status. Ad hæc vires corporum & si hora præsenti conjectas, non ob id quales futuræ sint in posterum ab initio recte æstimari possunt. Nam multoties evenit virtutes corporum exolui plusquam æsti marat medicus, aut ob corporis habitu, aut naturam, aut ob morbi aliquod irritatorium symptoma. Quare si ut vitale robur servetur, ideo cibus ægrotantibus exhibetur: hoc vero non semper similiter, sed morbo procedente nonnunquam præter medici opinionem disponatur, fieri non potest ut a distantia status & a virium robore prout est in initio, convenientem victum tum naturæ laborantis per totum morbi decursum ad statum usque, tum morbo ob inæquales mutationes, eliciamus. Sed sint omnia ut vis methodice, scito non satis esse in arte medica, vera dogmata docuisse, nisi in artis operibus vtilia fore ægrotantibus probentur. Vtilitas enim artis non est vera differere, sed remedia inueni re quibus æger sanetur, aut iuuetur. Neque sanitis est, si vera & vtilia tradideris dogmata, sed tradere oportet via adeo perspicua, vt plebi si liceat res innotescat. Sic enim id quod humano generi salubre speramus communissimum faciemus. Quod si ita est, dimittenda fuerint ea dogmata, ad quæ percipienda, aut operibus probanda, difficilis datur via. Quapropter cum præcognitionis status difficilis admodum sit scientia, & ab iis solummodo adepta medicis, qui vires omnium quæ in arte sunt probè didicerint, memoriæ mandauerint, omnique diligentia in artis operibus se exercuerint: paucique cum tales existant, patet dimittendam hanc viam esse, vt quæ a viris duntaxat doctissimis percipi possit. Quare cum facilius & certiori modo res inuestigari possit a morbi dispositione, manifestum est hanc viam eligendam esse in inuestigatione formæ victus.
units.tr: But if you say that such changes do not happen in diseases, turn back to Hippocrates' book On Common Diseases, where you will find that this happened to not a few patients. But let us set aside the question of certainty and treat the matter a little more carefully. You say that the diet to be prescribed is always the one that can best preserve strength. Then you define the distance from the crisis so that the patient can get through to it with that diet, and not with a more subtle one. You call this diet a middle one: you do not use a coarser one, lest it add to the disease, nor a thinner one, lest it wear down strength more than is right and so the patient fail before the crisis. Come, then: tell me methodically what diet you call middle, so that Socrates, who is sick, may be sustained to the height of the disease. What do you understand by the word "sustain"? Is it something other than what Hippocrates meant in the Aphorisms, who was the first to use that word in this matter when he said: "Σὺν τεκμηρίῳ δὲ χρὴ ἰῆσθαι τὸν νοσοῦντα ἐξαρκέσει τῇ διαίτῃ πρὸς τὴν ἀκμὴν τῆς νόσου", that is, one must judge by the signs whether the patient, with his diet, will be sufficient up to the height of the illness? That he understood it to mean whether the patient could endure on such a diet through the whole interval up to the crisis, he shows at once in the words that follow: "Καὶ πότερον ἐκεῖνο ἀπαυλήσει πρότερον", that is, whether the patient will fail first. Galen also understood the word in this sense, as one may infer from his exposition. So you intend to supply Socrates with a diet of such a kind that he can endure on it through the whole interval up to the crisis. But if you understand this simply, without restricting the meaning of the word, and you think it enough that Socrates be brought to the crisis by whatever means, what if you arrive by the help of your diet so feeble that he is able to withstand no disease, however mild, much less one raging at its height? Will you think you have achieved anything when you find such a diet for the sick Socrates after long reflection? Is this why you turn pale? Perhaps you say that the word is not to be understood simply, but to mean sustaining up to the crisis, and you understand it only in the case where the patient's strength keeps some measure of vigour at the height of the disease. Even if this is granted, you will have to use another mark, one that signifies the matter precisely. For your phrase "some measure" is far too wide: in that way every coarse diet would suit Socrates, and you could condemn no diet for its coarseness. But if you demand only so much strength as enables the body to fight off the causes of disease and to resist the attacks of the illness, that is a ridiculous claim: if a diet could accomplish methodically what you ask, there would be no disease so dangerous that it could not be cured by diet. If you maintain that this is how things stand, you should at least know that Hippocrates was unaware of your doctrine. But setting these points aside, you will at least admit that at the height of the disease the labours and symptoms become much more severe than before, as was written against you by Galen when, speaking of the height, he said: "Μέγιστον τοῦ νοσήματος ὡς ἐπὶ συμπτωμάτων", that is, the height is nothing other than the greatest point of the disease, as regards its symptoms. Do you therefore think it enough that the patient be brought to the crisis with any degree of strength, when the conflict with the disease is then at its greatest? Or would it be more wholesome for the patient, if we took care to bring him to the crisis with as much strength as we can, without adding to the disease? Who would condemn this as unmethodical? Not you, if you follow true doctrines that are wholesome for the sick. Since this is so, suppose that Socrates can reach the crisis without gruels: you will give him drinks, since these supply less nourishment. Do you know for certain that on that diet Socrates will reach the crisis with sufficient strength? I would hardly believe this even if you swore to it. Why do you not use gruels? By using them he would be stronger at the height of the disease. Perhaps you say that they would add to the disease. How do you know this, I ask? Do you conjecture it from the distance from the crisis, or rather from the disposition and sharpness of the disease? If you say that, once I know the crisis in advance, I cannot fail to know the disposition of the disease, then tell me which of the two you knew first, for that one you will know more clearly and more certainly. For those things which serve as principles are always more evident than those deduced from them. And since you foreknow the distance from the crisis from the disposition of the disease, you will know the disposition of the disease more clearly than the distance from the crisis. Therefore you will conjecture more surely, and with less error, from the disposition and sharpness of the disease whether gruels will harm Socrates in his illness, than if you wished to judge this from the distance from the crisis; for your judgement would be liable to many errors. Hence, since in the inquiry into the form of diet the disease is admitted not as an indicator but as a prohibitor, as all rational physicians confess, and since it prohibits a diet insofar as the diet increases the disease or its symptoms, and since this is recognised more evidently from the disposition of the disease, it would be better to investigate the form of diet from the strength and disposition of the disease than from the distance from the crisis. Besides, although you conjecture the strength of the bodies in the present hour, one cannot therefore rightly estimate from the beginning what they will be like in the future. For it often happens that the strength of bodies is spent more than the physician reckons, either because of the habit or nature of the body, or because of some symptom of the disease that irritates it. Therefore, if food is given to the sick so that their vital strength may be preserved, yet this is not always done in the same way, and as the disease advances it is sometimes arranged contrary to the physician's expectation, it cannot be that from the distance from the crisis and from the strength of the body as it is at the beginning, we can work out a diet suited both to the nature of the sick person through the whole course of the disease up to the crisis, and to the disease with its uneven changes. But grant that everything is as you wish in method: know that it is not enough in the medical art to have taught true doctrines, unless they are shown to be useful to the sick in the practice of the art. For the usefulness of the art lies not in discussing what is true, but in discovering remedies by which the sick may be cured or relieved. Nor is it enough, if you have handed down true and useful doctrines, to hand them down by a way so plain that they may become known even to the common people, if that is permitted. For in this way we shall make into a most common thing what we hope will be wholesome for the human race. If this is so, those doctrines must be dropped, whose apprehension or proof by practice is by a difficult road. Therefore, since the foreknowledge of the crisis is a very difficult science, and is acquired only by those physicians who have thoroughly learned the powers of all the things that belong to the art, committed them to memory, and exercised themselves in the practice of the art with all diligence; and since such men are few, it is plain that this road must be abandoned, as one that only the most learned men can grasp. Hence, since the matter can be investigated more easily and more certainly from the disposition of the disease, it is evident that this road is to be chosen in the investigation of the form of diet.

units.la: Quod in multis locis Hippoc. secundæ positioni (victum scilicet partim à morbi constitutione, partim à viribus ægri inquirendum esse) consentit in inuestigatione formæ victus.
units.tr: In this, Hippocrates in many places agrees with the second position (namely, that the diet is to be sought partly from the constitution of the disease and partly from the strength of the patient) in the investigation of the form of diet.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: QVAM non esse præter senis mentem accipe paucis, vt qui primus à morbi dispositione & virtutis robore, victus formam inuestigauerit in libro Aphorismorum, vbi ita scribit: Vbi morbus peracutus est, & illico extremos labores habet, extremè tenuissimo victu necessarium est vti. Per labores accessiones & symptomata intellexit quæ morbi dispositiones sunt.
units.tr: Understand briefly that this was not beyond the old man's intention, since he was the first to investigate the form of diet from the disposition of the disease and the strength of the patient, in the Aphorisms, where he writes thus: When a disease is extremely acute and at once has extreme labours, one must use the most extremely thin diet. By "labours" he understood the accessions and symptoms, which are the dispositions of the disease.

units.la: Maxime acuto morbo inediam adhibendam consuluit, quæ extremè tenuissimus est victus. Et infra ait: Vbi verò non, sed convenit crassius reficere, tantum subcodescendere oportet, quantum morbus extremis est mollior. Quibus in verbis apertissimè Hippocrates victu à morbi dispositione seu constitutione inuestigasse videtur. In eo insuper qui sequitur: Cum morbus (inquit) in suo constiterit vigore, tenuissimo victu necessarium est uti. In quo maximum morbi esse in symptomatibus scimus. Eadem in commentariis de ratione victus via, victus formam inuestigat: Ut in primo de pleuritide ages, ita scribit, Postea si dolor quispiam vel periculum comparuerit, sorbitionem dare nec multam neque crassam, sed post septimum aut nonum si validus sit. Idem paulo ante apertius dixit, Vbi autem dolor aliquis vexauerit, oxymeli bibendum dabis. Sentis ex iis duobus locis ex dispositione pleuritidis, victum per pocula ministrandum consuluisse. Sed non solum a morbi dispositione competentem victum investigare docet, sed noxium ab eadem deprehendi Hippocrate, docente eodem commentario, vbi ita scribit: Praeterea si lateris dolor assiduus est, calidisque fomentis nonre mittitur, sputumque non procedit, sed summe glutinosum sit, nisi quis dolorem vel alui subductione vel secta vena, pro vtriusque exigetia soluerit, ptisanam autem ita affectis dederit, praecipitem aget in mortem. Nec illud tanquam tanquā peculiare ptisanæ fore cōcipias. nam omnem sorbitionem, & multo magis ea quæ comeduntur damnauit, stante tali morbi con stitutione seu dispositione. Quod ipse statim monte: Prehendunt (inquit) hæc, non solum si ptisana intempestiuè vtantur, verū et multo magis si quippiam aliud ederint aut bibe- rint, quod ptisana inconuenientius sit. Sed vt non teratur tempus in singulis citandis locis, vnum adducamus, in quo Hippocrates omnes ad rectā victus institutionem scopos collegit, ex quibus post virtutis robur, morbi dispositionem adnumerauit. Coniicere (inquit) oportet & robur, & morbi cuiusque dispositionem: hominis item naturam atque ægrotantis in victu consuetudinem, non cibis solum, verum & in potibus, &c. Sed hoc idē à Galeno audias tertio cōmentario eiusdem libri in expositione illius, Tutius autem longe, &c. Ptisanam (inquit) totā porrigit his qui moderatē habent, (Non qui mitius quie- rusque habent, vt quidam perperam tran- sulit) solum verò cremorem ijs qui deterius
units.tr: He advised that abstinence from food, which is the most extremely thin diet, should be used in a very acute disease. And further on he says: When the disease is not like this, but it is better to restore with thicker food, one should only reduce it as far as the disease is milder than at its extremes. In these words Hippocrates clearly seems to have investigated diet from the disposition or constitution of the disease. In the following passage too: When the disease (he says) has settled into its full vigour, one must use the most thin diet. We know that the greatest part of the disease lies in its symptoms. In the same commentaries on the method of diet, he investigates the form of diet in the same way. In the first book On Pleurisy, he writes as follows: Afterwards, if any pain or danger appears, give a gruel that is neither abundant nor thick, but after the seventh or ninth day if the patient is strong. He said the same a little earlier, more clearly: When some pain troubles, you will give oxymel to drink. From these two passages you understand that he advised giving the diet by way of drinks, from the disposition of the pleurisy. But he teaches not only that a suitable diet must be investigated from the disposition of the disease, but also that a harmful one is detected from the same disposition by Hippocrates, as the same commentary teaches, where he writes thus: Moreover, if the pain in the side is persistent and is not relieved by warm fomentations, and the sputum does not come up but is very sticky, unless one relieves the pain, by reducing the bowels or by opening a vein, according to the need of each, and gives barley-water to those so affected, he will drive them headlong to death. Nor should you think this is peculiar to barley-water, for he condemned every gruel, and much more those things which are eaten, given such a constitution or disposition of the disease. Which he immediately adds: They take hold (he says), not only if they use barley-water at the wrong time, but much more if they eat or drink anything else which is less suitable than barley-water. But so that time is not wasted in citing each passage, let us adduce one, in which Hippocrates gathered together all the aims for the right ordering of diet, from which, after the strength, he counted the disposition of the disease. One must consider (he says) both the strength and the disposition of each disease: likewise the nature of the man and his customary way of life in diet, not only in foods but also in drinks, etc. But you may hear the same from Galen in the third commentary on the same book, in his exposition of the words, "but much safer," etc. He says: He gives barley-water, the whole of it, to those who are moderately well (not to those who are milder and quieter, as some have wrongly translated), but only the gruel to those who are worse off,

units.la: In secundo de ratione victus. dicount. Verùm ijs qui periculosius acutiusq;
units.tr: In the second book On Diet, (in acute diseases) say. But to those who suffer more dangerously and more acutely,

units.la: laborant, potus solos. Ostendimus igitur in ijs quæ dicta sunt, victus formam à morbi dispositione seu constitutione vnà cum virtutis robore, secundum senis mentem inuestigandam esse.
units.tr: are ill, only drinks. We have shown, therefore, from what has been said, that the form of diet must be investigated, according to the mind of the old man, from the disposition or constitution of the disease together with the strength of the patient.

units.la: Non satis esse ad rectâ formæ uictus inuentionem uirtutis robur, & morbi constitutionem considerare: sed ijs præcognitionem statuς adiungendam esse.
units.tr: It is not enough for the discovery of the right form of diet to consider the strength of the patient and the constitution of the disease; the foreknowledge of the state must also be added to these.

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: CHAPTER IX.

units.la: VERVM hæc non satis fuerint ad rectam victus institutionem, nisi ijs distantiæ status præcognitionem adiungas. Et si enim à morbi constitutione, & à virtutis robore victum per pocula conuenientem esse scias in præsenti, non tamen ex his duobus scire posses, citra statuς præcognitionem an cibo illo in posterum ægrotans sufficiat, citra magnum virium incommodum. Nâ si alicuius pedestri itinere quingenta profecturi miliaria robur præsens consideres, et ad vnius diei iter sat esse si hominem pane et melle nutrias, etc. poterit enim eo cibo triginta pertransire ea die miliaria. Quod si reliquū via consideres, crassiori illi opus esse nutrimento iudicabis. Ob id igitur diuinus Hippocrates, postquā morborum dispositionem recensuisset, subintulit: Coniicere autem oportet ægrotantem si sufficiat cum dieta ad statum ægritudinis. Non enim sat esse, vt robur virtutis quale nunc est consideres, et an talem victum hodie citra virium sensibilem læsionem ferat, sed an toto intermedio tempore ad statum vsque ferre possit. Ob id Hippocrates in consideratione virtutis, status meminit. Ꝝ morbi igitur dispositione victus formam primum elicimus. Deinde virtutem laborantis inspicimus. Tertio distantiam status conĭ-cimus. Demum æstimamus an eo victu quem morbi cōstitutio indicauit, virtus ægrotantis ad statum citra magnū virium incōmodum durare possit. Quapropter status distantiam præcognoscere oportet vltra morbi constitutionem, vt rectè ægrotantibus victum diffinire possimus. In qua sententia Galenū esse scito in lib. aphoris. in eo, Paroxysmos et consistentias. Ubi à duobus victus formam inuestigare docet, nempe à virtute & morbi constitutione, in qua morbi dispositionem & status distantiam comprehendit. Cuius verba ita habent: Τὸ μὲν τ' ὅλως διαίτης χῡμα πᾶς σνο σκοπὸς ἐκ βλέπων ἐποιεῖτο, τῇ τε διαίτα μιᾷ τῷ κάμνοντι, καὶ τῶν κατα̈στασιν τῷ νο σήματ’. τὸ γὰρ εἴτε κάτοξυ, εἴτε ὀξὺ, εἴτε χρό νιον ἐσοῖ τὸ νόσημα, καὶ ὁπλωίνα μάλιστα τῇ ἀκμὴν ἐκλήψεις, τῶν κατα̈στασιν ὅσι τ' νοσή ματ’ σκοπῆι. Hoc est, Totius victus formam duos respiciens scopos instituit, ægrotantis nempe virtutem & morbi constitutionem. Illud enim, siue peracutus, siue acutus, siue chronicus morbus erit, & quando maxime in statu consistet, constitutionem morbi est considerare. Unde male quidam vertit hunc locum in hunc modum: Nam si morbus sit peracutus, vel acutus, vel longus, &c. qui verborum sensum corrupit & non transtulit. Ex quibus verbis duo sub constitutionis nomine comprehendisse Hippocratem, nempe morbi acumen, & status distantiam, aperte ostendit Galenus. Verùm unde peracutum & acutum cognoscas & discernas, & eos qui inter hos medium obtinent locum, infrà ostendemus.
units.tr: But these things would not be enough for the right ordering of diet, unless you add to them the foreknowledge of the distance of the state. For even if you know from the constitution of the disease and the strength of the patient that a diet by drinks is suitable at present, you could not know from these two alone, without foreknowledge of the state, whether that food will be sufficient for the sick person in future, without a great inconvenience to his strength. For if you were to consider the present strength of someone who is about to travel five hundred miles on foot, and you judge that it is enough for a single day's journey to feed the man on bread and honey, etc., he will be able to cover thirty miles that day with that food. But if you consider the rest of the journey, you will judge that he needs a heavier nourishment. Therefore for this reason the divine Hippocrates, after he had recounted the dispositions of the diseases, added: One must conjecture whether the patient will be sufficient with the diet for the state of the sickness. For it is not enough to consider the strength of the patient as it now is, and whether it can bear such a diet today without a noticeable injury to its powers, but whether it can bear it up to the state throughout the whole intervening time. For this reason Hippocrates, in considering the strength, mentions the state. Therefore from the disposition of the disease we first derive the form of diet. Then we inspect the strength of the sufferer. Third, we conjecture the distance of the state. Finally we estimate whether the strength of the patient can endure, up to the state, without great harm to its powers, on the diet which the constitution of the disease has indicated. Therefore it is necessary to know the distance of the state beforehand, beyond the constitution of the disease, so that we can rightly define the diet for the sick. You should know that Galen is of this opinion in the book of Aphorisms, in the passage on "paroxysms and states" (consistentias). There he teaches that the form of diet is to be investigated from two things, namely the strength and the constitution of the disease, under which he includes the disposition of the disease and the distance of the state. His words are as follows: Τὸ μὲν τοίνυν ὅλως διαίτης σχῆμα πρὸς δύο σκοπὼ ἐκ βλέπων ἐποιεῖτο, τῇ τε δυνάμει τοῦ κάμνοντος καὶ τῇ τοῦ νοσήματος καταστάσει. τὸ γὰρ εἴτε ὀξύτατον εἴτε ὀξὺ εἴτε χρόνιον ἔσται τὸ νόσημα, καὶ ὁπόταν μάλιστα τῇ ἀκμῇ ἐγκαθίστηται, τὴν τοῦ νοσήματος κατάστασιν σκοπεῖν. That is: He made the whole form of diet look to two aims, namely the strength of the patient and the constitution of the disease. For whether the disease will be most acute, or acute, or chronic, and when it is most firmly settled into its height, one must consider the state of the disease. Hence some have badly translated this passage in this way: For if the disease is peracute, or acute, or long, etc., which corrupts the sense of the words and does not translate them. From these words Galen clearly shows that Hippocrates comprehended two things under the name of constitution, namely the sharpness of the disease and the distance of the state. But how you may recognise and distinguish the peracute and the acute, and those which hold a middle place between these, we will show below.

units.la: Iuxta status distantiā singulis morborū acutorum conuenientem elicere uictus formam docet.
units.tr: He teaches that a form of diet suitable to each of the acute diseases is to be drawn out according to the distance of the state.

units.la: CAPUT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: IIS ita determinatis, morbo peracuto, qui que intra quartum diem terminandus sit, ultimò tenuissimo victu utemur: quem supra omnimodā sumus interpretati abstinentiam. Sic dixit Hippocrates. Vbi peracutus morbus fuerit & statim ultimos labores habet, ultimo tenuissimo victu necessarium est uti. Per morbum qui statim ultimos labores affert, eum intellige qui intra dies quatuor finiri debeat. Et subdit, Vbi verò non, plenio- rem victum adhibebimus. Hoc est ubi morbus ab ultima symptomatum vehementia proximè degenerat, (qualem qui ad septimum terminantur, habent) eo utemur victu, qui inedia proximus est: talis autem est victus per pocula, ut melicratum & similia. Huic tali victum per pocula ministrandum fore consentiente virtute asserit Galenus in expositione illius, Postea si dolor quispiam & c. ubi ita scribit, Si enim validus ad septimum usque diem fuerit, oxymeli & melicratum et aquâ dare satis erit. Per quae ut dixi tunc liberabitur & sanabitur. Idem dixit prima Aphor.
units.tr: Having settled these points, in a very acute disease, which must end within the fourth day, we shall use the thinnest diet of all, which above we have interpreted as total abstinence. Thus Hippocrates said: "When an acute disease is very sharp and at once brings its final crises, it is necessary to use the thinnest diet of all." By a disease that at once brings its final crises, understand one that ought to end within four days. And he adds: "But where it does not, we shall use a fuller diet." This means that where the disease is rapidly passing toward the most violent point of its symptoms (as those do which end on the seventh day), we shall use the diet that comes closest to fasting, and such a diet is given through drinks, such as honeyed water and similar things. Galen, in his exposition of the passage "Afterwards, if some pain..." asserts that a diet of drinks is to be given to this kind of patient, with the same virtue, and there he writes: "For if the patient is strong up to the seventh day, it will be enough to give oxymel and honeyed water and water." By these, as I said, he will then be freed and cured. The same is said in the first Aphorism.

units.la: In quibus vero (inquit) non ultra primam septimanam protrahuntur, forti existente natura solo utendum est melicrato & c. Qui vero morbo simpliciter acuto laborant, cuius terminus ad duas finitur septimanas crassa sorbitione exempli causa, tota ptisana uti debent.
units.tr: He says: "In those who are not carried beyond the first week, while the nature is strong, one must use only honeyed water, etc." But those who suffer from a disease that is simply acute, whose end falls within two weeks, for example, ought to use thick gruel, that is, a full barley drink.

units.la: Qui autem morbo acuto laborantes periculi magis participes fiunt, ad undecimum terminum habituri, tenui sorbitione alendi sunt, ut crem ptisanam. Haec similiter secundum mentem sunt Galeni in libris de ratione victus.
units.tr: Those who suffer from an acute disease and come to be more in danger, since they will reach the eleventh critical day, must be nourished with thin gruel, such as thin barley water. Galen's views in his books On the Method of Diet are similar to these.

units.la: Iis ergo qui peracuto morbo intra primos quatuor dies terminando laborant, omnimo da conuenit inedia. Cum vero eo morbo laborant rät qui ad septimū terminari debeat, pocula. Ex ijs duabus vičtus rationib. quas ab Hippo crate didicimus, manifestū fit, quibus vtraq; sorbitio cōpetat. Nam cū has quatuor vičtus rationes, acute ægrotantibus cōuenire supra ostenderimus, terminusq; acutorū morborū dies xiiij. sit, manifestum fit quod vtraq; sorbitio ijs competet morbis, qui dies xi. et xiiij. terminū habituri sunt. Cūq; ij qui diebus xi. finiendi sunt morbi, grauius affligant, quàm qui xiiij. ijs tenuē exhibenda, qui vero xiiij. crassam fore sorbitionē manifestū est. Morbo rum igitur acutorū intra xiiij. die terminan- dorū, huiusmodi est vičtus ratio à morbi con stitutiōe dissinita. Hæc autē nihil aliud est quā morbi dispositio, terminos morborū dissini- ens. Non immeritò igitur ab huius termini di stantia, vičtus ægrotantibus dissiniendi sunt. Cūnq; quatuor assignentur ab Hippocrate in dies xiiij. quaternarij, qui primam sensibilē differentiam morborum in acumine præstat, quibusque vt plurimū terminari morbi acu- ti solent, singulis suā vičtus speciē dissiniuit. prout morbi ad invicem acumine differunt. Ita vt quatuor qui intra dies xiiij. sunt termi nis, quatuor similiter victus formæ respon- deant.
units.tr: Therefore those who suffer from a very acute disease that must end within the first four days should be given complete abstinence. When those who suffer from a disease that must end on the seventh day are given drinks. From these two rules of diet, which we learned from Hippocrates, it is clear which of the two kinds of gruel is suited to each case. For since we have shown above that these four rules of diet suit acute patients, and the limit of acute diseases is the fourteenth day, it is clear that each kind of gruel suits those diseases which are going to end on the eleventh and fourteenth days. And since diseases which must end on the eleventh day afflict more severely than those ending on the fourteenth, thin gruel is to be given to the former, and it is clear that thick gruel is for those ending on the fourteenth. Therefore the rule of diet for acute diseases which must end within the fourteenth day is determined by the constitution of the disease. This is nothing other than the disposition of the disease, which defines the limits of diseases. Not without reason, then, must diets for patients be determined by the distance of this limit. And since four are assigned by Hippocrates within the fourteen days, the quaternaries, which provide the first perceptible difference of diseases in sharpness, and by which acute diseases usually end, he determined for each one its own kind of diet, according as the diseases differ from one another in sharpness, so that the four that end within the fourteen days correspond to four similar forms of diet.

units.la: An medico liceat quatuor dierum abstinen- tiam febricitatibus aliquado consulere.
units.tr: Whether it is permissible for a physician sometimes to prescribe a four-day abstinence for feverish patients.

units.la: CAPVT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: SVPEREST nunc considerandū qui- bus' nam signis febrium singulas quæ ad quartum, et quæ ad septimum, vndecimum, & quartumdecimum terminum habituræ sint noscamus. Maxime enim conducit in ar- te medica sensu ea discernere, quæ cognita æ- grotantibus salutifera sunt. Deinde de virtu- tis robore sermonem faciemus, vtpote quod non minus indicatiuum est forma victus quàm morbi constitutio, vt infra ostende- mus. Prius tamen vnum quærere oportet, an committendum sit aliquo in morbo ægrotan- tem diebus quatuor omnimoda seruare ine- dia. Res ardua videtur profecto præter assue- tudinem hominem incibatum ad diem quar- tum tum ducere. Nam vt Hippocrates in libro se cundo de ratione victus scribit, oportet disci plinam quae conferat ex sanorum victu face re. In cuius expositione Galenus ita ait, Si fa nis laesionem afferat repentinae victus ad con trapия mutationes, multo maiorem aegrotan- tibus. Ponamus igitur hominem sanum viri bus valentem, aut inualidum, si velis, ab af- sueto victu ad quatuor dierum inediam re- pente mutari: qualem hunc vesperascente die quarta fore aestimas? Profecto si mortuus no fuerit, semimortuus iacebit, collapsis viri- bus, qui an cibo & potu reficipossit, necne, non parum dubito. Cum igitur hoc sano acci dat ex illa repetina mutatione, quid aegrotati maius illo accidere potest nisi ipsa mors ex to tidem dierum inedia? Res plena discrimine vi- detur, aegrotantem sine cibo & potu, ducere vsque ad peracuti morbi inclinationem. Quia ad quartum, quandoque ad quintum, protra hi eius crisis potest, vt Galeno visum est. Praeterea cum morbi quibus inediam consu- limus, maxime acuti sint, & ob id perniciosi, haudquaquam medicus vulgi calumniam effu gere possET, si post quatuor dierum ieiunium moreretur æger. Non quidem ob morbi vim, sed ob inediam mortem subsecutam vulgus clamaret: Vbi insuper hoc ab Hippocrate di dicimus. Et si longiore hæc disceptatio ser monem expostulat, solum tamen eam quæ ad rectam institutionem, & ad ægrotantium commodum spectant attingam, sequens summa rerum fastigia. Non omnem mutatio nem quæ ægrotantibus repente accidit, mole stiore ijs esse quàm sanis costat. Nam id nos sa norū experientia docet, qui prandium præter assuetudinem dimittunt, moleste ferunt. At febre si corripiantur facile eis est prandium assuetum dimittere. In sola igitur dissimilisi-ue disproportionali mutatione peius habent ægrotantes quàm sani. Vt si ab inedia vnius diei aut duorum ad crassa cibaria mutatio fiat, peius habebunt ægrotantes quàm sani. Quod si à crasso victu ad inediam mutatio fiat, gra uius ferent sani, quàm ægrotantes. Ob id quod mutatio dissimilis est. mutatio enim vi ētus Eius ab inedia ad crassa cibaria, ad maius est, quamobrem maiori opus erat viriu robore. Aegrotantes vero dissimiliter mutantur, nempe a maiori viriu robore ad minus, quare molestius ferent. Hoc arbitror sensisse Hippocratem, cum ait, Mutare quidem bene habet nō modicum recte sane transferatur & mutatio. Illo verbo recte quod graece ὀγθῶς dicitur proportionalem intellexit mutationem, quā pluribus ostendit exemplis. hoc idem sed obscure admodum, ut solet, dixit in eo textu qui ita incipit, Τιμωρητέον δὲ τοιοῦδε τὶ μέρος. hoc est, Innuandam partem hanc sermone contrario. In cuius expositione Galenus verbum ὀγθῶς non interpretatus est. Sed dixit Hippocratem nō paucis ostendisse quid per illud adverbium indicare voluisset. Tu ergo breuem habes de mutationibus repentinis sententia, quam arbitror sciptis Hippocratis conuenire. Quod de viriu maximo detrimento ex quatuor dierū inedia dicitur, citra est. Noui Hebraeu sex diebus abstinentem apud Lusitanos, & plures sunt qui trium dierum
units.tr: It remains now to consider by which signs we may recognise which fevers will end on the fourth day, and which on the seventh, eleventh and fourteenth. For it is greatly useful in medical practice to distinguish by the senses those signs which, once known, are salutary for the sick. Then we shall speak of the strength of the powers, since this is no less indicative than the form of diet and the constitution of the disease, as we shall show below. First, however, we must ask whether a sick person may be kept on total fasting for four days in any disease. It certainly seems a hard thing to bring a man to the fourth day without food, contrary to custom. For as Hippocrates writes in the second book of the Regimen, one must make the regimen from the diet of healthy people. In expounding this, Galen says: if a sudden change of diet to opposite habits causes harm to the healthy, it does much greater harm to the sick. Let us suppose, then, a man healthy and vigorous, or weak if you like, is suddenly changed from his usual diet to four days' fasting. What do you think he will be like on the evening of the fourth day? Surely, if he has not died, he will lie half dead, his strength collapsed, and I have considerable doubt whether he could be restored by food and drink. Since this happens to a healthy man from such a sudden change, what greater thing can befall the sick man than death itself from four days without food? It seems a dangerous thing to keep a sick person without food and drink until the onset of a very acute disease, which, as Galen thought, may be protracted to the fourth day, or sometimes to the fifth, as its crisis. Moreover, since the diseases in which we advise fasting are mostly acute and for that reason dangerous, the physician will by no means escape the slander of the common people if the patient dies after a four-day fast. The crowd would cry out that death followed not from the force of the disease but from the fasting. This we have said above, following Hippocrates. And although this discussion calls for a longer treatment, I will touch only on what concerns sound practice and the good of the sick, and I will state the following summary. It is agreed that not every sudden change befalling the sick is more burdensome to them than to the healthy. For the experience of healthy people teaches this, since those who omit their midday meal contrary to custom find it irksome, whereas those who are seized by fever can easily give up their usual dinner. Therefore the sick fare worse than the healthy only in an unlike or disproportionate change. For example, if the change is from a fast of one or two days to coarse food, the sick will fare worse than the healthy. But if the change is from coarse diet to fasting, the healthy will bear it worse than the sick. This is because the change is unlike: the change from fasting to coarse food is a greater one, and so it needed greater strength. The sick, however, change in an unlike way, namely from greater strength to less, and so they will bear it more painfully. I think Hippocrates meant this when he said: "To change is indeed good, provided the change is made not only rightly but also not too much" [ὀρθῶς]. By the word "rightly," which in Greek is orthōs, he understood a proportional change, which he showed by several examples. He said the same thing, though very obscurely, as is his habit, in the passage beginning: "One must indicate a certain part of this by the opposite argument" [Τιμωρητέον δὲ τοιοῦδέ τι μέρος], that is, this part must be hinted at in the contrary manner. In expounding this, Galen did not interpret the word orthōs, but said that Hippocrates had shown in not a few places what he wished that adverb to indicate. So you have a brief opinion about sudden changes, which I think agrees with the writings of Hippocrates. What is said of the greatest loss of strength from four days' fasting is an exaggeration. I know a Hebrew who abstained for six days among the Lusitanians, and there are many who endure a fast of three days, carrying on their affairs without notable inconvenience.

units.la: 2. de victu acutorum.
units.tr: On the diet in acute diseases, book 2.

units.la: Eodē 2. lib. abstinentiam patiuntur, citra insigne incom modum negocia obeuntes sua. Qua in re gens Hebraeorum firmum valet praestare testimo nium, ut quorum plurimi annuatim huius- modi trium dierum abstinentia corporu ab- sumunt libidines. Unde ijs magnitudine mor bi suadente citra vllum discrimen quatuor dierum inediam consulet medicus. Aliys vero propter inassuetudinem nō nisi vrgente mor bi vehementia, & virium imbecillitate id non dissuadente, tum corporis habitu tali ut ob pororum angustiam & cutis spissitudine haud facile corpus effluat, praecipue media hyeme. hac si coniungantur omnia, quatuor diebus hominem omnimoda seruare abstinen tia non vereberis. Aliquo horum deficiente potum dato.
units.tr: In the same second book they endure abstinence, carrying on their business without any notable inconvenience. In this matter the Hebrew people provide a firm testimony, since very many of them every year undergo a three-day fast to subdue the lusts of the body. Hence, where the magnitude of the disease suggests it, the physician may advise a four-day fast without any danger to such people. For others, however, because they are unaccustomed, it is not advisable unless the violence of the disease is pressing and the weakness of their strength does not forbid it; and also when the habit of the body is such that, on account of narrow pores and thick skin, the body does not easily waste away, especially in midwinter. If all these things come together, you will not fear keeping a man on total abstinence for four days. If any of these is lacking, give drink.

units.la: Verum ad hac forsan aliquis insurget. Nam & si hac duo concedantur: nempe cibum quantumcunq; tenuem ijs esse laesioni qui peracuto morbo laborant, ut in superioribus initio huius operis demonstrau mus, & ab inedia quatuor dierum minus ægrotantes laedi quam sanos, non constat ob hac hæc vtrum eorum magis conferat, aut minus lædat, nempe inedia, aut victus tenuissimus. Quod si ab Apho. locum argumentationis sumamus, In paroxysmis subtrahere oportet, &c. dubitationis occasionem dederimus. nam in paroxysmis læsio quæ ex inedia vnius diei prouenit, parua est: quæ verò à cibi oblatione, maior. nā cibus eo tempore sensibili nocumento esse solet. Inedia verò vnius diei cum parum sano noceat, minus ægrotanti nocebit, vt ostensum est. At in peracuto morbo & si cibus non parum lædat, magis fortasse quatuor dierum inedia nocebit. Nam scimus sani corporis robur à quatuor dierum abstinentia prosterni. quapropter cum alia ad id discernendum non detur via, de consuetudine rogare oportet. An vnius aut duorum aut trium dierum inediam sustinuerit. Quòd si se parum fuisse læsum ostendat, audacter eum incibatum ad dies quatuor seruabimus. Præsertim vbi corporis habitus talis fuerit, vt non facile effluat. Quod si ægre ferre vnius diei ieiunium dicat, huic non inediam,
units.tr: But perhaps someone will object to these points. For even if these two things are granted, namely that any food, however light, harms those who suffer from a very acute disease, as we showed at the beginning of this work, and that a four-day fast harms the sick less than the healthy, it is not clear from this which of the two does more good or less harm, namely the fast or the very thin diet. If we take as the ground of argument the aphorism "In paroxysms one ought to withdraw...", it may give occasion for doubt. For in paroxysms the harm that comes from a one-day fast is small, whereas that from offering food is greater, since food at that time is usually felt to be harmful. A one-day fast, while it harms the healthy, will harm the sick less, as has been shown. But in a very acute disease, although food harms not a little, a four-day fast will perhaps harm more. For we know that the strength of a healthy body is overthrown by four days' abstinence. Therefore, since no other way of deciding this is given, we must ask about the patient's custom: whether he has endured a fast of one, two or three days. If he shows that he has been little harmed, we may boldly keep him without food for four days, especially when the habit of his body is such that it does not easily waste away. But if he says that he bears a one-day fast with difficulty, we shall give him not a fast

units.la: { } [small mark at the foot of the text] sed victum per pocula minístrabimus. Quod ad medicum spectat, sciendum in arte medica, neque curatiuam indicationem neque vires ípsius rationem à vulgi opinione sumi. Vnde pius medicus quod de se ipso Galenus scripsit, opinetur æquum est. Nescio, inquit, quo numine inspiratus, aut furore percitus, & famam vulgi contempsi, & solo veritatis studio scientiæque flagraui, nullam honestiorem possessionem esse ratus. Neque hoc extra mentem Hippocratis est, qui ita scribit: Non igitur intempestiue neque fortes vasorum inanitiones moliri conuenit, neque cum morbi vigét aut in summo sunt, quicquam exhibere, &c. Cum morbi vigor nihil aliud sit quàm morbi in symptomatibus summum: vt à Gal. scriptum est, manifestum est peracutum morbum in quo vltima accidunt symptomata statim vigere: ideoque secundum senis mentem ministrandum non esse quicquam. Idem voluit alibi cum dixit: Adiectionì autem ciborum intendendum multo minus, subtrahere verò sæpenumero expedit cum æger sufficere possit donec donec morbus maturescat. In Aphorismo praeterea, Vbi morbus peracutus est, &c. vl timo tenuissimo victu, quem omnimodam su mus interpretati abstinentiam, vtendum es- se monet. Statim extremos habere labores in telligit, cum intra primos dies quatuor sum- mus morbi futurus sit vigor, vt est sententia Galeni.
units.tr: { } [small mark at the foot of the text] but nourishment by drinks. As far as the physician is concerned, it must be understood that in medical art neither the curative indication nor the reasons for the powers are drawn from the opinion of the common people. Hence it is fitting that the devout physician should think as Galen wrote about himself: "I know not by what divine spirit I was inspired, or what frenzy stirred me, but I despised the fame of the crowd and burned only with zeal for truth and knowledge, thinking there was no more honourable possession." Nor is this outside the mind of Hippocrates, who writes thus: "It is therefore not proper to attempt strong evacuations of the vessels at an unseasonable time, nor to administer anything when the disease is vigorous or at its height," and so on. Since the vigour of a disease is nothing other than its height in the symptoms, as Galen has written, it is clear that a very acute disease in which the last symptoms occur is at once vigorous; and therefore, according to the mind of the old man, nothing is to be given. He meant the same elsewhere when he said: "Much less should one attend to the addition of food, but it is often advantageous to withdraw it, since the patient can bear it until the disease ripens." In the aphorism moreover, "Where the disease is very acute," and so on, he advises that the very thinnest diet, which we have interpreted as total abstinence, be used. He understands that they have the greatest labours at once, since the height of the disease will be within the first four days, as is Galen's opinion.

units.la: Virtutis imbecillitas praesens, & quae in po- sterum futura erit, e quibus sit cognoscenda.
units.tr: The present weakness of strength, and that which will be in the future, and how it is to be recognised.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: NEC in ijs solum, qui intra quartum diem terminantur morbis, virtus est inspicienda, sed in alijs quoque qui ad septimum, quos potibus nutriendos supra dixi- mus. Quae si imbecillis in praesenti sit, aut in po sterum ante diem status imbecillem fore spe- ras, non solum poculis hunc, sed tenui sorbi- tione nutries. Primum ex pulsu cognosces. Se cundu ex corporis habitu facile traspirabili, et ex tenui succoru substatia. Qua in re consen tit Galenus in expositione illius: Postea si do- lor quispiam &c. Idem dixit in commento illius: Tenuis et exquisiti victus, &c. Quod si inquit naturæ robori non fidamus, ptisanæ utemur succo. Idem est in aliis iudicium, sem perque proxime crassiorem victum ministra bis cum vitalis facultas eum victum non fert, quem morbi constitutio indicauit. Vitale au tem robur cuius seruandi gratia nutrimus, ex pulsu cognoscendum diximus, quale in præsenti hora est. Quale autem erit in poste rum, ex corporis habitu, nempe aut raro aut denso, & ex dispositione succorum, nempe crassorum aut tenuium, & ex consuetudine, id est an multum & multoties edere sit soli tus, aut modicum & raro. Hæc omnia imo reconde sensibus: nam ægrotantibus salutem & tibi gloriam haudquaquam inanem pa- rient.
units.tr: Strength must be assessed not only in those diseases that end by the fourth day, but also in the others that run to the seventh, which I said above must be nourished with drinks. If strength is weak at present, or if you hope it will be weak before the state of the disease comes on, you should nourish the patient not only with drinks but with thin gruel. You will know this first from the pulse. Second, from the bodily habit, which is easily perspirable, and from the thinness of the humours. In this Galen agrees, in his exposition of that passage: "Afterwards, if some pain..." He said the same in his commentary on it: "Thin and carefully chosen diet, etc. But if," he says, "we do not trust the strength of nature, we shall use barley water as juice." The judgement is the same in other cases: always give a diet a little thicker than the last, when the vital faculty does not bear the diet which the nature of the disease has indicated. We said that the vital strength, for whose preservation we feed the patient, is to be known from the pulse, as it is at the present hour. What it will be later is to be judged from the bodily habit, namely whether it is rare or dense, and from the disposition of the humours, namely whether they are thick or thin, and from custom, that is, whether one is accustomed to eat much and often, or little and rarely. Lay all these things up in your senses, for they will bring health to the sick and no small glory to you.

units.la: Quonam signo discernatur morbus qui ad quartum terminari debeat.
units.tr: By what sign is the disease that ought to end on the fourth day to be distinguished?

units.la: CAPVT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: NVNC quos peracutos qui ad quartū terminētur, et quos acutos qui ad xiiij. & & quos intermedios dixeram, vnde cognoscas audi. Morbum quem Græci καθξύῳ[?] dicunt, nos verò peracutum interpretamur, et qui ad diem quartum finitur per vltima discernes symptomata. Talia autem sunt, cum aliis symptomatibus coniuncta est continua inquietatio. Quod nomen, vt author est Galenus in expositione illius, Si verò nudos habeat pedes, &c. indicat illos cōflictari quo-ius iacentis habitu, nec non alium ex alio mutari. Cuius causam praui humoris copiam in principe parte esse sciendū est. Ob cuius causam breui admodum terminantur ægritudines, in quibus continua adest inquietatio, maligni humoris læsionem principe parte diutius non ferente. Ad hæc scire oportet, vltima non posse dici symptomata si ægrotans vnū decubitus habitum seruet. Significat enim principes partes haud grauiter lædi. Galenus ob ventriculi oris malitiam, aut ob virtutis imbecillitatem inquietationem fieri scribit: Verùm alibi in expositione illius, Interdum autem & cruda tum à capite, &c. ob multitudineum prauorum humorum, quos Graeci ἰχωρας vocant, in ventriculo accidere ait. Verum quamobrem in prædictionibus ἄλνσ μοῦ inquietationem appellet, in libro autem de victu acutorum διαγνώσματα, & aliqua inter vtrunque differentia sit præsentis negotij non est referre. Nunc illud scito inquietationem vnum esse ex signis crisim indicantibus, vt à Galeno scriptum est. Nisi ob ægrotantis teneram naturam accidat, ita vt à mi nimis præ delitijs se vinci ostendat. Inquietatio igitur continua coniunctæ febri morbum ad quartum terminat. Præcipuè si temperatura, ætas, anni tempus, calida fuerint. Hunc peracutum esse morbum dices cum vltimis symptomatibus. Huic si vires constant nihil ministrabis. Quod si hiis non fidas, pocula exhibeto.
units.tr: Now hear how you may tell the very acute diseases, which end on the fourth day, from the acute ones, which end on the fourteenth, and from those I called intermediate. You will distinguish them by the final symptoms. These occur when continual restlessness is joined to the other symptoms. As Galen writes in his exposition of the words "But if he has bare feet, etc.", this name indicates that such patients toss about in their lying posture and keep shifting from one position to another. The cause of this, he says, is an abundance of bad humour in the principal part. For this reason diseases in which continual restlessness is present come to an end very quickly, since the principal part cannot long bear the injury of the malignant humour. Moreover, you must know that final symptoms cannot be said to occur if the patient keeps to one position in bed, for that shows that the principal parts are not seriously harmed. Galen writes that restlessness is caused by the malice of the orifice of the stomach or by weakness of the strength, but elsewhere, in his exposition of "Sometimes, however, also raw matter from the head, etc.", he says that it arises in the stomach from the multitude of bad humours which the Greeks call ichores [ἰχωρας]. Why he calls it alysmos [ἄλνσ μοῦ] in the Prognostics, and whether there is some difference between that and the diagnōsmata in the book on the diet of acute patients, is not to be discussed in the present business. Now know this: restlessness is one of the signs indicating a crisis, as Galen has written, unless it arises from the patient's tender nature, so that he shows himself overcome by too much pampering. Therefore continual restlessness joined to fever brings the disease to an end on the fourth day, especially if the temperament, age and season of the year are hot. You will say that the disease is very acute when these final symptoms are present. If the strength holds firm, you will give nothing to it. But if you do not trust these signs, offer it drinks.

units.la: Acuti morbi quo maximè deprehendātur signo, & quæ nam fit acutarum febrium leuissima, & quem habeat terminum.
units.tr: By what sign acute diseases are best recognised, what is the mildest of acute fevers, and what end it has.

units.la: CAPVT XIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIIII.

units.la: LIBER I. CAP. XIIII.
units.tr: BOOK I, CHAPTER XIIII.

units.la: HIS sic habitis signa percurrere oportet, quibus morborum singulos qui ad septimum, vndecimum, & quartumdecimu terminentur cognoscas. Sed prius dicere qui proprie sint morbi acuti oportebit, & quo maxime deprehendantur signo. quod si omnibus acutis commune sit, manifestum est tale per se acutorum omnium leuissimum morbum efficere. At quod nam tale signum esse dicemus, nam id scire maxime conducit ad intellectum eorum quae ab Hippocrate scripta sunt, in eam artis partem quae victus rationem docet, tum in eam maxime quae praedicit. Hoc profecto sicut & reliqua ab Hippocrate quaerendum: qui in primo de morbis vulgaribus commentario tertio acutissimos et maximos grauissimosq; morbos ac praecaeteris omnib. lethales in continua febre esse scribit. Quo in loco Galenus, Quoquomodo (inquit) febrem continuam accipias, verus est sermo. Acutissimi enim morbi & maximi, et grauissimi in iis fiunt, qui proprie synochi, hoc est continentes, dicuntur febres. Et nihil „ minus in alijs quæ particularibus progrediun„ tur paroxysmis, principia, augmenta, status „ & inclinationes manifestas efficientes, neque „ ad integritatem desinentes, de quibus est sa„ tius hoc loco interpretari. Quoniam synochis „ proprie dictis in ijs contineri contingit, & „ non in synochis has. In quibus verbis aperte nos docet Galenus febris continuitatem acu-tos morbos efficere, & hoc ipsum omnibus quæ acutæ & graves sunt febribus commu-ne esse. Vtpote cum febris continuitas omni-bus coniuncta sit. Cunque continuarum le-uissima sit ea quæ periodice inuadit, princi-pia, augmenta, status, inclinationes apertas efficiens, manifestum est febrem continuam periodicam, primam & leuissimam acuto-rum morborum esse. Cumque acutorum mor-borum terminū intra dies quatuordecim po-suerit Hippocrates, manifestum est febrem continuam periodicam intra dies quatuorde-cim fore terminandam. Morbum igitur qui ad quartumdecimum terminatur, à conti-nuitate febris cognoscēs, vt Galenus scripsit in in expositione illius, secundum eandem rationem in mulieribus. Nec obstiterit esse morbos cum febris continuitate qui ad vigesimū terminentur, unde verisimile non videtur limitem acutorum quartumdecimum esse, sed vigesimum. Vt Galenus tetigit loco proximé citato. Præterea nec te perturbet, acutos morbos esse qui in quadraginta diebus iudicentur, vt Hippocrates docuit in eo, Spirationis facilitatem. Nam & si verum sit febres acutas in viginti, & quadraginta diebus iudicari posse, non tollit quod dictum est ab Hippocrate, acutos morbos in quatuordecim diebus iudicari. Nam cum iudicationum modi quatuor sint, nempe ad salutem, aut ad mortem, ad melius, aut ad peius, vt à Galeno scriptum est in libris de crisibus, manifestum est fieri posse, vt acutus morbus intra quatuordecim ad melius aut ad peius iudicetur: apud vigesimum, aut quadragesimum integra terminatione ad salutem aut ad mortem terminetur. Quare id verum fuerit semper, morbos acutos intra quatuordecim dies aliqua quatuor terminationū iudicari: vt Galenus asseruit in eo, Acuti morbi in quatuor decim diebus iudicantur. Vbiita scribit nullus enim inuentus est vnquā morbus, qui ab initio velociter moueretur, hunc transgredi terminū, quin aliquam ex dictis non acciperet mutationē. De eo igitur nobis termino sermo est, in quo ad salutem aut ad mortem, aut ad melius aut ad peius subitò mutantur ægrotantes. Firmiterq; cū Hippocrate asserimus, febris continuitate intra quatuordecim dies aliquam harū quatuor mutationum ostende re:febremq; continuam periodicam hunc nō transgredi terminum, citra aliquam quatuor iam dictarum mutationum.
units.tr: Having laid down these points, we must now go through the signs by which you may recognise each of the diseases that end on the seventh, eleventh and fourteenth days. But first it will be necessary to say what diseases are properly acute, and by what sign they are chiefly recognised. If this sign is common to all acute diseases, it is clear that such a sign by itself makes the mildest of all acute diseases. What sign we shall call such a sign is something we must say, for knowing this helps greatly to understand what Hippocrates wrote, both in that part of the art which teaches the regimen of life and especially in that which predicts. Hippocrates must be sought here, as in other places, for in the third commentary of his first book of Epidemics he writes that the most acute, greatest and most grievous diseases, and above all others deadly, occur in continued fever. On this passage Galen says: "However you understand continued fever, what he says is true. For the most acute, greatest and most grievous diseases occur in those fevers that are properly called synochus, that is, continuous. And in the others, which proceed by particular paroxysms and produce clear beginnings, increases, states and declines, and do not end in recovery, nothing is less so; of these it is better to interpret elsewhere. Since it happens that in properly so-called synochi they are contained, and not in these." In these words Galen plainly teaches that continuity of fever makes diseases acute, and that this is common to all fevers that are acute and severe, since continuity of fever belongs to them all. And since the mildest of the continuous fevers is the one that attacks periodically, showing clear beginnings, increases, states and declines, it is clear that the first and mildest of the acute diseases is the periodic continuous fever.
