And since Hippocrates set the limit of acute diseases within fourteen days, it is clear that a periodic continuous fever must end within fourteen days. Therefore we shall recognise from the continuity of the fever the disease that ends on the fourteenth day, as Galen wrote in his exposition of that passage, and by the same reasoning in women. Nor should it stand in the way that there are diseases with fever continuity that end on the twentieth day; hence it does not seem likely that the limit of acute diseases is the fourteenth day rather than the twentieth, as Galen touched on in the passage cited just above. Moreover, do not let it trouble you that there are acute diseases which are judged on the fortieth day, as Hippocrates taught in that book, On the Ease of Breathing. For even if it is true that acute fevers can be judged on the twentieth and fortieth days, this does not remove what Hippocrates said, that acute diseases are judged within fourteen days. For since there are four modes of judgement, namely towards safety or towards death, towards improvement or towards worsening, as Galen wrote in his books On Crises, it is clear that an acute disease may be judged within fourteen days as improvement or worsening, and may be brought to a complete ending, to safety or to death, at the twentieth or fortieth day. Therefore, whatever the case, acute diseases are always judged within fourteen days by some of these four terminations; as Galen asserted in that work, Acute Diseases Are Judged in Fourteen Days. There he writes: "For no disease has ever been found which, moving rapidly from the beginning, passes beyond this limit without undergoing some of the said changes." Our discussion, then, concerns that limit at which the sick are suddenly changed, either towards safety or towards death, or towards improvement or worsening. And with Hippocrates we firmly maintain that a continuous fever shows within fourteen days some one of these four changes, and that a periodic continuous fever does not pass this limit without one of the four changes already mentioned.

units.la: E quibus signis morbum ad septimū & ad un decimum terminandum fore sciamus.
units.tr: From which signs we may know that the disease will be terminated on the seventh and on the eleventh day.

units.la: CAPVT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: INTERmedij vero eadem sortiuntur nomina. nam qui ad septimum aut citius terminantur peracutos vocauit Galenus loco iam citato: Qui vero ad vndecimū, acutos, aut exquisitè quisitè acutos: qui ad quartūdecimū, simplici ter acutos dixit. Verū (vt ille ait) superuacua est disceptatio de nomine, modò scias quæ nā sint symptomata, quæ morbū ad septimū, et quæ ad vndecimum terminari faciant. Quod si febris cōtinuitati à primo die dolor capitis adsit, & die quarta magis ingrauescat, ad septimum terminabitur. Sic Hippocrates, Si quibus, inquit, horum cœpit dolor die primo, die quarto premuntur maximè, et quinto, ad septimum soluuntur. Idem asserit eodem libro de acuto aurium dolore in febre continua ac vehementi, quibus si natu minores afficiantur, intra septimum aut morientur aut evadent. Natu tamen maiores, quia minus febre & delirio infestantur, et quia minus acutè do lent ob nervi duritiem, vltra septimum indicantur. Ex ijs verbis Hippocratis, & ex ijs quæ in libris de ratione victus, & in de morbis vulgaribus scripsit, colligimus tria esse symptomata, quæ cum insignem adepta sunt vehementiam et continuitatem, morbū ad septimū terminant: Nempe dolore capitis, vigilia & delirium, si febrem continuam co- mitentur. Vt Melidiæ quæ decubuit iuxta æ- dem Iunonis contigit, de qua Hippocrates in fine primi de morbis vulgaribus agit. Cui ca- put collum & pectus magnopere doluisse cū febre acuta scribit, doloresque omnium ho- rum perpetuos fuisse: quam ait die septimo su- dasse, febremque intermisisse. Vnde apparet iudicatam fuisse, ad melius. Item adolescentu lum qui in mendacium foro decumbebat, igne correptum fuisse scribit Hippocrates in ter- tio de morbis vulgaribus, qui vigilias cum pateretur, aliaque exitialia signa haberet, ad septimum obijt. In cuius expositione Galenus refert hunc adolescentulum omnibus diebus nihil plane dormiuisse. Idem præterea mulie- ri abortione infantis à febre ardente correp- tæ, & vigilias patienti accidit. Nec obsti- terit quod in eodem tertio prædictionum li- bro doloris capitis vehementis meminit, & continui cum febre, de quo iudicium facit cum vigesimum diem transyt. Nam si Galenum in expositione legas, incondite locutum fuisse HippoHippocratem audies. Sed recto ordine Hippocrates sermonem texit in hunc modu. Capitis dolor vehemens & continuus cum febre, si quod ex indicijs extiterit exitiosis, integre lethalis est. Si vero ex ijs quae didicisti de aegro conualituro speres, a principio quidem ad septimum usque sanguinis e naribus fluorem expectato. Procedente vero tempore id etiam eueniet. Unde fieri non potest ut dolor capitis vehemens & continuus cum febre, ultra septimum iudicium differat, quin aut ad salutem, aut ad mortem, aut ad melius, aut ad peius mutationem faciat. Cum vero ultra septimum absque iudicio protrahitur, aut eius vehementiam, aut continuitatem deficere necesse est. Iis fidem praestat versio in octoginta volumina, quae ita habet. Dum autem validus & recens dolor fuerit, sanguinis de naribus eruptionem apud septimum expectato, &c. Ac si dicere velit, post septimum iudicium si protrahatur, ob id esse, quod inualidus dolor erat. Morbi autem qui ad vndecimum iudicantur mediae vehementiae sunt inter eos qui ad septimum terminantur et eos quos simpliciter acutos diximus, qui ad quartumdecimum finiuntur. Propria autem signa quibus discernere eos possis non dantur. Verum per ea quæ diximus symptomata septem dierum terminum ostendentia si die tertio in ceperint, apud quintum vero vehementius molestauerint, morbum discernes ad nonum aut undecimum terminandū. Quod ab Hippocrate didicimus loco iam citato hoc modo: Si quinto inceperit & undecimo magis fluctuauerit, terminum ad quartumdecimū designabit. Sed simul cum ijs temporis constitutionem considerare oportet. Quod si morbo conueniat, fiduciam maiorem habebis, quòd intra præscriptum finietur terminum. Quòd si contrariæ sit qualitatis nempe frigidum & humidum, scito morbum ad vlte riorem protrahendum quaternarium. Huius author est Galenus in expositione illius, Contra arcturū multis facta est indicatio in statu tertio. Simile est prima Apho. vbi æstate dixit morbos breuiare, hyemem producere. Considerate Considerationem etiam temperamenti ægrotantis habitus & regionis non prætermittas vt singulorum morborum terminos artificia lipossis coniectura conjcere. Quod de dolore capitis qui tertio inceperit, & quinto magis fluctuauerit diximus, de vigilia & delirio intelligas oportet. Horum quodlibet si die tertio inceperint, & quinto vehementius affligant, apud vndecimum morbus terminabitur. Verùm quia symptomata quæ acutum, aut peracutum morbum reddunt, cum febri continuæ coniunguntur, à quibus terminum conjciendum supra docuimus, solent diuersimodè in morbis mutari, ita vt noctem vnâ insomnem agat ægrotans, sequenti dormiat: nunc deliret, modò mentis compos videatur: diebus accessionis caput doleat, intermissionis cesset, aut minus torqueatur: quonâ pacto ex iss terminus conjci possit forsan quis dubitabit. Verùm si ea quæ supra diximus, recte quis percipiat, huic dubitationi locum nõ esse intelliget. Nam cũ vigilia cõtinua acutæ febri coniungitur, aut dolor capitis vehemẽs continuus affligit, morbum ad septimum ter-minandum diximus. Quod fi vigiliarum aut doloris delirij�ue continuitas cessent, intelli-ges horum symptωmatum ratione, morbum ⁊ltra septimnm terminandum. Alia obiter symptωmata consules, & febris magnitudi-nem & eius motus ⁊elocitatem,à quibus o-mnibus an ad ⁊ndecimum, aut ad quartum-decimum terminari morbus debeat conici-es. Sat tibi est ad ⁊ictus formam inuenien-dam, quibus nam signis morbos qui ad quar-tum, & qui ad septimum, ⁊ndecimum, & quartumdecimum terminantur cognoscas.
units.tr: Intermediate fevers take the same names. Galen, in the passage already cited, called those that end on the seventh day or sooner "very acute" (peracuti); those that end on the eleventh, "acute" or "exquisitely acute"; and those that end on the fourteenth, "simply acute." But (as he says) a dispute over the name is pointless. It is enough to know which symptoms they are, and which make a disease end on the seventh day and which on the eleventh. If a headache is present from the first day together with a continuous fever, and grows worse on the fourth day, the disease will end on the seventh. So Hippocrates: "If those with these symptoms begin to have pain on the first day, and are most oppressed on the fourth and fifth, they are released on the seventh." In the same book, on acute earache in a continuous and vehement fever, he asserts that if children are affected, they either die or recover within the seventh day. Older patients, however, because they are less troubled by fever and delirium, and because they feel the pain less acutely owing to the hardness of the nerve, are judged beyond the seventh day. From these words of Hippocrates, and from what he wrote in the books On Regimen and On Epidemics, we gather that there are three symptoms which, when they acquire notable vehemence and continuity, bring a disease to an end on the seventh day: namely, headache, vigilance and delirium, if they accompany a continuous fever. Such was the case of the woman of Melidia who lay down near the temple of Juno, of whom Hippocrates speaks at the end of the first book of Epidemics. He writes that she suffered severe pain in the head, neck and chest together with an acute fever, and that these pains were continual in all those parts. He says she sweated on the seventh day and the fever abated. Hence it is clear that she was judged to have changed for the better. Likewise, Hippocrates writes in the third book of Epidemics of a young man who took to his bed in the forum, seized by fever, who suffered sleeplessness and had other deadly signs, and who died on the seventh day. In explaining this, Galen reports that the young man slept not at all on any day. The same happened to a woman who, after a miscarriage, was seized by a burning fever and suffered sleeplessness. Nor is the matter affected by the fact that in the same third book of Prognostics Hippocrates mentions a severe and continuous headache with fever, about which he passes judgment when the twentieth day has passed. For if you read Galen's exposition, you will hear that Hippocrates spoke in a disordered way. But in right order, Hippocrates composes his discourse thus: "Severe and continuous headache with fever, if the signs that appear are deadly, is wholly lethal. But if from what you have learned you may hope for the patient's recovery, from the beginning expect a flow of blood from the nostrils up to the seventh day. As time goes on, this too will happen." Hence a severe and continuous headache with fever cannot defer its judgment beyond the seventh day without producing a change, either to health or to death, or to the better or the worse. When it is protracted beyond the seventh day without judgment, either its vehemence or its continuity must necessarily fail. The Latin version in eighty volumes supports this, which reads: "While the pain is strong and recent, expect a discharge of blood from the nostrils by the seventh day," and so on. It is as if he meant that if judgment is protracted past the seventh day, this is because the pain was weak. Diseases judged on the eleventh day are of middling severity, between those that end on the seventh and those we called simply acute, which end on the fourteenth. But no distinctive signs are given by which you can tell them apart. Nevertheless, by the symptoms we have mentioned, which indicate a seven-day limit, if they begin on the third day and trouble the patient more violently on the fifth, you may judge that the disease will end on the ninth or eleventh. We learned this from Hippocrates in the passage cited: "If it begins on the fifth day and fluctuates more on the eleventh, it marks the end at the fourteenth." But one must consider the constitution of the season at the same time. If it agrees with the disease, you will have greater confidence that it will end within the prescribed limit. But if it is of the contrary quality, namely cold and moist, know that the disease is to be prolonged to the fourteenth. The author of this is Galen, in his exposition of the aphorism, "Against Arcturus many indications were made in the third state." Similar is the first Aphorism, where he says that in summer diseases are shortened and in winter lengthened. Do not neglect the patient's temperament, habit and region either, so that by skilled conjecture you may guess the ends of individual diseases. What we said of a headache beginning on the third day and fluctuating on the fifth, you must understand of sleeplessness and delirium. If either of these begins on the third day and afflicts more severely on the fifth, the disease will end on the eleventh. But since the symptoms which make a disease acute or very acute, from which we taught above that the end is to be conjectured, when joined to a continuous fever, are wont to vary in different ways in diseases, so that the patient one night is sleepless and the next sleeps, now is delirious, now seems in command of his mind, on days of attack the head aches and on days of intermission the pain ceases or is less severe, someone may doubt by what means the end can be conjectured from these. But if one rightly grasps what we have said above, he will see that there is no room for this doubt. For when sleeplessness is joined continuously to acute fever, or a severe continuous headache afflicts, we said the disease ends on the seventh day. But if the continuity of the sleeplessness, the pain or the delirium ceases, you will understand, by reasoning about these symptoms, that the disease ends beyond the seventh day. You will also consult other incidental symptoms, and the magnitude of the fever and the speed of its movement, from all of which you will conjecture whether the disease ought to end on the eleventh or the fourteenth. It is enough for you, in finding the form of the method, to know by what signs you may recognise diseases that end on the fourth, the seventh, the eleventh and the fourteenth.

units.la: Parum referre ad rectam formæ uictus in-uentionem, an terminus diebus inter-medijs accidat.
units.tr: It matters little to the right discovery of the method of diet whether the crisis falls on intermediate days.

units.la: CAPVT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: VERVM ad victus formam inueni-endam parum referre an diebus inter-medijs terminus accidat. Eadem enim victus forma vtéris, cum morbus ad diem nonum, aut ad vndecimum, terminari debeat. Item eodem victu cum ad tertium decimum, aut quartum decimum finiendus sit. Nec hoc praeter senis mentem est, qui eodem victu utitur, nempe poculis, si septimo aut nono terminari morbus debeat, cum dixit, Sed post septimū aut nonum si validus sit. Sentis ex iis verbis Hippocratē eadem victus forma vsum fuisse cum morbus ad septimum, aut ad nonum terminum habiturus esset. Graviter autem errabis, si morbus ad quartum terminandus sit, aegrotantem eo victu nutrias, qui morbis ad duas septimanas finiendis conuenit. Minus autem laedes si eo vtaris quo ad vndecim diebus morbos vtimur. Multo autem minus, si eo qui septem dierum termino conuenit. Porro discernere morbum qui ad quartum terminabitur, ab eo qui ad quartum decimū, aut vndecimū, facillimum est. Non aliter quàm si grauissima symptomata, & febres ardentissimas ab iis discernas, quae mitiores multo sunt febres, et augmenta & decrementa manifesta habent. Et nullum saeuum sortiuntur symptoma. Haec aut ab iis quae morbū intra
units.tr: Indeed, for finding the right form of diet, it matters little whether the crisis falls on the intervening days. For you will use the same diet whether the disease ought to end on the ninth day or on the eleventh. Likewise, with the same diet it may be ended on the thirteenth or the fourteenth day. Nor is this against the mind of the old man, who uses the same diet, namely draughts, if the disease ought to end on the seventh or ninth day, when he said, "But after the seventh or ninth, if the patient is strong." From those words you understand that Hippocrates used the same form of diet when the disease was going to end at the seventh or the ninth term. But you will err badly if you feed a patient, whose disease must end on the fourth day, with the diet that suits diseases ending in two weeks. You will do less harm if you use the diet we use for diseases ending on the eleventh day, and much less if you use the one that suits the seven-day term. Moreover, it is very easy to distinguish a disease that will end on the fourth day from one that ends on the fourteenth or eleventh. It is no different from distinguishing the most severe symptoms and the most burning fevers from those fevers which are much milder and have clear increases and decreases, and which bring no savage symptoms. These, however, are easy for those who have applied their minds to the works of the art to separate from the symptoms that make the disease end within the seventh [day]. [sic]

units.la: {k} ... septimum terminari faciunt symptomatibus, separare, facile ijs est qui in artis operibus mentem excitarunt.
units.tr: {k} ... the symptoms that make it end on the seventh day, to separate, is easy for those who have applied their minds to the works of the art.

units.la: Quaenam febres intra quartum, & quae intra septimum, undecimum & quartumdecimum terminentur.
units.tr: Which fevers end within the fourth day, and which within the seventh, eleventh and fourteenth.

units.la: CAPVT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: SED interim dum vsum in ijs comparas, febres tibi indicabo quibus praedicti termini adaptentur. Vt initiu huius meditationis habeas, causus legitimus hoc est febris ardens, quae à bile impermixta ortu habet, febris praeterea quam synocha recentiores nuncupant, si cum inquietatione coniuncta sit, ad quartum terminabitur. Eadem vero si cum vigiliis, aut capitis dolore, aut delirio, continuus fiant, intra septimum. Febres continuae, quarum in die quietiori symptomata aegrotantem vtcunque molestant, ad vndecimum. Quarum vero apud inclinationem febris symptomata omnino euanescunt, ad quartumdecimum. Haec non sunt praeter senis mentem, ab ijs enim quae dixit in libris de ratione victus, et in de morbis vulgaribus colligere ea licet.
units.tr: But meanwhile, while you are acquiring experience in these matters, I will point out to you the fevers to which the said terms are suited. To give you a starting point for this reflection: a legitimate causus, that is, a burning fever which arises from unmixed bile, and also the fever which the more recent writers call synocha, if it is accompanied by restlessness, will end on the fourth day. Indeed, if these are continuous with sleeplessness, or headache, or delirium, they will end within the seventh. Continuous fevers, whose symptoms trouble the patient in some way on the calmer day, will end on the eleventh. But those fevers in whose decline the symptoms vanish altogether will end on the fourteenth. These things are not against the mind of the old man, for it is permitted to gather them from what he said in the books on the regimen of diet and in the books on common diseases.

units.la: Quibus igitur ardentes febres cum inquietatione fiunt, si robusta sint virtute, & habitu denso, difficulter spirabili, præcipuè si abstinentia longa citra insigne incommodu pati assueti sint, hos in omni seruabis inedia. Si ali quod deficiat, nempe virtus sit imbecillis, aut habitus rarus, facilis resolutionis, aut humores nimium tenues, potibus hunc nutries.
units.tr: For those, therefore, in whom burning fevers occur with restlessness, if they are robust in strength and have a dense, hard-breathing constitution, especially if they are accustomed to bear long abstinence without notable harm, you will keep them on fasting throughout. If something is lacking, namely if their strength is feeble, or their constitution is loose and easily dissolved, or their humours are too thin, you will nourish them with draughts.

units.la: Quòd si febris ardens citra inquietationem sit, & vigilijs torqueat, virtuteque valenti & reliquis vt oportet habentibus, pocula ministrato. Quòd si illorum virtuti non fidas, aut in præsenti aut in posterum, tenuem sorbitionem exhibeto.
units.tr: But if the burning fever is without restlessness and torments with sleeplessness, give draughts to a patient of vigorous strength who otherwise has what is needed. But if you do not trust their strength, either now or in the future, give a thin gruel.

units.la: In febre autem cuius symptomata in die tranquilliori non quiescunt, si cum robore virtutis accidant, tenuem sorbitionem.
units.tr: In a fever, however, whose symptoms do not subside on the calmer day, if they occur along with strength of constitution, give a thin gruel.

units.la: Quod si ob imbecillitatem præsentem aut ob habitum rarum in posterum ægrum non posse sufficere speres, præcipuè si multo sit cibo assuetus, et humores tenues fuerint, crassa sorbitione hunc nutries.
units.tr: But if you expect that the patient will not be able to bear it, either because of present weakness or because of a loose constitution in the future, especially if he is accustomed to much food and his humours have been thin, you will nourish him with a thick gruel.

units.la: Quod si febris continua sit, cuius symptomata in die quietiori omnino euanescunt, crassa sorbitione ales. Quod si imbecillis fuerit virtus, aut habitus, aut tenues humores affuerint, aut multo cibo assuetus sit, præcipue si hyems fuerit, huic comedendum dabis quod facilis sit coctionis: quorum omnium infra latius meminero cum de victus singularum febrium sermonem fecero. Cæterum cum in libris Hippocratis de morbis vulgaribus legamus, plures eorum quos describit ægrotantes ab initio morbo acuto laborare tali symptomatum vehementia, ut videantur intra septimum terminum habituri: rursus que mitiores fiunt citra crisim, aut intermittunt omnino, & cessant aliquot diebus, & rursus redeunt, & vehementer affligunt: horum aliquot ad vigesimum, nonnullos ad quadragesimum, & sexagesimum, & ad octuagesimum absolute fuisse terminatos scribit, quonam victu hos nutrire oporteat forsan quis dubitabit. Dum morbus vehementiam peracuti servat, victum peracuti morbi ministra bis. Cunque mitior est aut intermittit omnino, ab intermissione numeratis duob. diebus victu ei medium exhibebis. Hunc intelligo qui inter duos extremos medius est, quorum alter est victus qui inchoati morbo conueniebat, alter est quem secunda dispositio exigit. Vt exem pli causa si morbus tali incepit vehementia, vt victus per pocula ei conueniat, nunc vero citra crisim mitior factus est, ita vt praesenti remissioni crassa conueniat sorbitio, dum os a remissione dies spectabis absque victus immutatione, ab ijs tenui sorbitione hunc nutrias. Quae media est inter pocula & crassam sorbitionem. Quod si secundum accidat, ad duos similiter dies victum non immutabis. Post vero, crassa sorbitione hominem nutries ad dies septem. Quod si in ijs non redierit morbus, crassiorem cibum huic ministrabis, criticos semper praecauens dies. Horum partem ab Hippocrate didicimus, nempe illud, duos esse expectandos dies absque victus immutatione, nempe parem & imparem, vt in primo de ratione victus in acutis scribitur: ubi ait sed maxime duos ab indicatione dies &c. In cuius expositione Galenus ita scribit, Tutum igitur est etiam si morbus indicatus fuerit, ad duos vsque dies diligentem victus rationem qua æger vsus fuerit seruare. Præteritis autem ab indicatione duobus diebus iam securū est plenius cibare, &c. Cum ergo in iis morbis in quibus iudicium est factum duos obseruare iubeat dies parem & imparem ob timorem accessionum, multo causatius illud obseruandum fore in iis, qui citra iudicium intermiserunt, relinqui discimus monstrante ratione.
units.tr: But if the fever is continuous, and its symptoms altogether vanish on the calmer day, feed him with thick gruel. But if the strength or constitution is feeble, or the humours are thin, or he is accustomed to much food, especially if it is winter, you will give him something easy to digest to eat; I shall mention all of these more fully below, when I have discussed the diet of the individual fevers. Moreover, since we read in Hippocrates' books on common diseases that many of those whom he describes, sick from the outset of an acute disease, suffer symptoms of such violence that they seem likely to end within the seventh term, and then again become milder without a crisis, or stop altogether, and cease for some days, and return again and afflict severely, he writes that some of these ended absolutely at the twentieth day, some at the fortieth, sixtieth, and eightieth. Perhaps someone will doubt on what diet these ought to be fed. While the disease keeps the violence of an acute disease, you will administer the diet of an acute disease. When it becomes milder or stops altogether, you will give a middle diet, counting two days from the intermission, without changing the diet. By middle I mean what lies between the two extremes, of which one is the diet that suited the beginning of the disease, and the other is the one the second condition demands. For example, if the disease began with such violence that a diet of draughts suited it, but now it has become milder without a crisis, so that a thin gruel suits the present remission, then, while you watch the days from the remission without changing the diet, you will nourish him with this thin gruel, which is midway between draughts and thick gruel. But if it happens the other way round, likewise you will not change the diet for two days. After that, you will nourish the man with thick gruel for seven days. But if the disease does not return in those, you will give him more solid food, always taking care of the critical days. We have learned part of this from Hippocrates, namely that two days should be awaited without change of diet, both even and odd, as is written in the first book on the regimen in acute diseases, where he says, "but chiefly two days after the indication," etc. In explaining this, Galen writes thus: "It is therefore safe, even if the disease has been indicated, to keep a careful regimen of diet, which the patient has used, up to two days. But once two days have passed from the indication, it is already safe to feed more fully," etc. Therefore, since in those diseases in which a crisis has occurred he orders two days, even and odd, to be observed because of fear of relapses, we learn, as reason shows, that it must be observed far more carefully in those which have intermitted without a crisis.

units.la: An à statu, uel crise, uel à termino uniuscuiusque morbi, quem à symptomatibus sumendum duximus, uictus ratio sumenda sit.
units.tr: Whether the rule of diet is to be taken from the state, or from the crisis, or from the term of each disease, which we have decided to take from the symptoms.

units.la: CAPVT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: SIC igitur victus formam à duobus inue stigandam dissiniuimus. Nempe à virtutis robore, & à morbi constitutione: in qua duo comprehendimus, nempe morbi dispositionem, an peracutus, an acutus, aut qui medio loco est, & quando ad statum peruenturus sit. Facultatis autem vitalis seruandæ, cuius gratia nutrimus, prout est in hora præsenti senti ex pulsu coꝛciendum robur fuerit. Quale verò erit in posterum, ex habitu denso aut raro, & ex humorum tenuitate aut crassitie & ex assuetudine. Cæterùm per morbi constitutionem seu dispositionem, an peracutus, an acutus, & quando maximè ad statu perventurus sit intelleximus. Ad id cognoscendum, præcepimus quænam symptomata morborum singuli afferant considerare. Vt ex ijs an ad quartum, aut ad septimum, vndecimum, aut ad quartumdecimum morbus terminari debeat sciamus. Ab huius distantia victus formam invenire docuimus. Secundum Hippocratis doctrinam, qui in Apho. secundum quod status prope aut longe est victus formam inuestigandam docet. Status autem distantiam non ex symptomatibus quæ morbos comitantur, sed ex signis coctionis præcognoscere docet Galenus in libris de crisibus.
units.tr: Therefore we have laid down that the form of diet is to be sought from two things: from the strength of the power and from the constitution of the disease. Under these two we include the disposition of the disease, whether it is very acute, acute, or of intermediate course, and when it is about to reach its state. The strength to be kept of the vital faculty, for whose sake we nourish, should be judged from the pulse as it is at the present hour. What it will be in future should be judged from the habit of body, whether dense or lax, from the thinness or thickness of the humours, and from custom. Moreover, through the constitution or disposition of the disease, we have understood whether it is very acute or acute, and when it is most likely to reach its state. To know this, we have taught that one should consider which symptoms each disease brings with it, so that from them we may learn whether the disease ought to end on the fourth, the seventh, the eleventh, or the fourteenth day. We have taught that the form of diet is to be found from the distance of this end. This follows the teaching of Hippocrates, who, in the Aphorisms, teaches that the form of diet is to be investigated according to whether the state is near or far. But Galen, in his books on crises, teaches that the distance of the state is to be known beforehand not from the symptoms that accompany the diseases, but from the signs of concoction.

units.la: Præterea ipse Hippocrates ab eisdem coctionis signis morbu breuem aut longu fore dicit.
units.tr: Moreover, Hippocrates himself says that from these same signs of concoction it will be a brief or a long disease.

units.la: Vt sputu subrubeu si statim appareat, incho-antem abbreuiat. Idé dixit alibi, Nempe quæ ,, citius magisque madescunt, indicationis denunciant celeritatem: Quae verò tardius, minusque, tardiorem significat indicationem. Et alibi coctionem dixit, velocitatem crisis & salutem certam significare. Loca praeterea quae citamus Hippocratis ad cognoscendam termini distantiam, omnia crisim spectant, & non morbi statum. Quod autem haec duo differant, manifestum est. Si ergo à crisis distantia victus formam sumeres, necessum esset, ut quanto propius aegrotans crisis horae accesserit, tanto subtiliorem victum ei ministrares: & quanto longius, crassiorem, ut doctrina est Hippocratis. at huius contrarium inuenimus ab Hippocrate scriptum in in haec verba: Et quanto maior fuerit expurgatio, tanto magis ad crisim vsque dare oportet. Praeterea in textu immediatè quarto loco praecedente, ita ait: Nempe si morbus sicior quàm vt quispiam existimet fuerit, non multum dare oportet, sed ante sorbitionem, vel mulsam vel vinum propinare expedit. Manifestum est ex loco immediatè citato, quod quanto morbus est siccior, hoc est magis crudus, tanto longius à crise distat. Et quanto humidior, hoc est coctionis magis recipit, tanto propius accedit. Vnde ex iis apparet secundum mentem Hippocratis victus formam penes crisis distantiam investigandam non esse. Symptomata vero quorum mentionem fecimus, nempe inquietatio, vigilia, dolor capitis, & delirium, omnia sunt signa crisim indicantia, vt à Galeno scriptum est. Porro institueram iis supersedere quae maiori otio ad eorum exactam speculationem indigent.
units.tr: For example, if reddish sputum appears at once, it shortens the course. He said elsewhere: "Those things which become moist more quickly and more fully announce speed; those which do so more slowly and less fully indicate a slower sign." And elsewhere he said that concoction signifies speed of crisis and certain health. Moreover, the passages of Hippocrates that we cite for knowing the distance of the end all concern the crisis and not the state of the disease. That these two differ is clear. If therefore you took the form of diet from the distance of the crisis, it would follow that the closer the patient came to the hour of crisis, the thinner the diet you should give him, and the farther away it was, the thicker, as is the teaching of Hippocrates. But we find the opposite written by Hippocrates in these words: "And the greater the purgation, the more one ought to give, up to the crisis." Moreover, in the text immediately four places before, he says: "If the disease is drier than anyone would think, one should not give much, but it is useful to offer mulse or wine before the sorbition." It is clear from the passage cited immediately that the drier the disease, that is, the more raw it is, the farther it is from the crisis; and the moister it is, that is, the more it receives concoction, the nearer it comes. Hence it appears from these things that, according to the mind of Hippocrates, the form of diet is not to be sought according to the distance of the crisis. But the symptoms which we have mentioned, namely restlessness, wakefulness, headache, and delirium, are all signs indicating a crisis, as Galen has written. Furthermore, I had intended to pass over those things which need leisure for their exact examination.

units.la: Tempora morborum triplíciter distingui.
units.tr: The periods of diseases are distinguished in three ways.

units.la: CAPVT XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: VERVM ne in hoc soluendo nodo agitandi mentem alicui detur occasio. Hac in re quod intellectus meus capit referam, ne quid speculationi desit, vt obiter studiosos in hanc investigationem prouocemus. Multa quidem in disceptatione inuoluuntur, quae dissimilis sunt rationis & diuersa indigent oratione. Sed vt recta procedat discceptatio, Ciceronis insequar præceptum. Tria sunt quæ in contentionem vocauimus, nem-pe statum, crisim, & terminum morborum quem ex symptomatibus præcognoscendum diximus. Notiones singulorum præmitte-mus, vt sciamus de quo disputare intendi-mus. Statum siue vigorem, qui Græcè ἀκμὴ dicitur, triplicem esse sciendum est: nempe statum quo ad symptomata, & statu quo ad dispositionem, & quo ad coction em mate-riæ. Primum, maximè esse morbi vt in sym-ptomatibus, scripsit Galenus. Quod autem ad-didit præpositionem vt, voluit significare su-perlatiuum non ad morbi dispositionem, sed ad symptomatum magnitudinem referendum, vt ipse apertius scripsit in expositione illius, Circa principia et fines &c. vbi ita scribit: Sym-ptomata omnia circa principia et fines dicit esse imbecilliora, nempe paroxysmos febrium, vigilias & dolores, fastidium et sitim, sicuti ipsas dispositiones in quibus hæc fiunt apud statum necesse est meliores esse, in iis qui ser-uari debent. Ex iis manifestum est secundum Ga-leni leni mentem, illud maximum morbi, non esse ad dispositionem referendum, sed ad symptomatum magnitudinem. Habent praeterea singulae affectionum secundum varias dispositiones, sua tempora, nempe initium, incrementum, statum et declinationem. ut si febris sit, cum primum in vehementiam in anticipatione & durationem addit, augmentum manifestum est: cunctis omnia maximè aucta sunt, status: declinatio cum iam dicta imminuuntur. Hoc colligimus à Galeno multis in locis, tum praecipuè in expositione illius, Paroxysmos & consistentias, &c. Quòd si inflammatio sit, distinguuntur tempora penes tumoris magnitudinis incrementum. Diciturque haec temporum distinctio, quo ad morbi dispositionem, ut ex Galeno licet colligere, cum ait in hunc modum: Ponatur igitur primum principium inquiri, quis negaverit generationem ipsius toto illo tempore esse quo pars sanguinolenta substantia repletur, sive enim propter coincidentiam huiusmodi contigit, sive propter obstructionem omnium vaforum, siue ob circunstantiam quandam tu-morum in poris, siue vs nos docuimus in li-bro de inæquali temperie, & in commenta-rijs de tumoribus præter naturam, abundan-tia sanguinis in particula cōsistit oborta phle-gmone, hoc erit primum tempus in quo im-pletur particula, magnitudini affectus subie-ēta. Quando autem influxus cessauerit, & quod in inflammata particula continetur pu-trefieri inceperit, calor quidam ob putredinē nascitur, & fusio implens propter calorem ob quem spiritus generatur, ob hæc ambo magis quàm antea distenditur, etiam si nihil influat, hoc secundum tempus est augmenti phlegmones. Porrò cum in pus iam vertitur, maximi sanè dolores tunc apprehendunt. Circa enim generationes puris labores & febres magis accidunt quàm facta. Vocatur status affectionis huiusmodi tempus. Si autem in sa-niem versa vel resoluta fuerit, minorem tu-morem & tensionem ostendit, principium in clinationis hoc ipsum est. Distinguuntur etiā tempora penes materiæ coctionem, vt cum cruda est principium sit: cum vero signum incipientis aut debilis coctionis fuerit, principium transisse scies, augmentumque principium sumere: cunque maxime coctio completur, statum esse: cunque completa signum iam appareat statum praeterisse significatur. Haec omnia sunt de mente eius in libris de crisibus & in libro de totius morbi temporibus. Vbi principium dicit esse cruditatem molestantium humorum quando coqui incipiunt: principium finiri, secundum tempus quod incrementum vocatur accedere: quando autem coctio ipsa maxime completur, status tempus esse. Deinceps declinationem, in qua cessare iam magnitudinem symptomatum & abundantiam coctorum scribit. Coincidunt haec aliquando, nempe status quo ad dispositionem & quo ad symptomata, ut in morbo laterali, in quo antequam screare incipiant, maxima tunc vigent symptomata, & inflammationis tumor maximus: cunque screare inceperint, utraque imminuuntur, & tumor & symptomata: ut a Galeno scriptum est in hæc verba: Sæpius autem adinuicè co-augentur et coniunguntur symptomatu ma-gnitudines & dispositiones, & fiunt in ijs phlegmonis, in quibus pus effluit quod iā con-sectum est, vt in vulneribus quibusdam fie-ri consueuit, & in peripneumonijs et in pleu-ritidibus. Quandoque diuersis contingunt temporibus vterque status dispositionis & symptomatum, vt ab eodem sumitur loco citato, vbi ita scribit: Sæpe quidem dispositio ipsa secundum quam infirmatur facilior est, symptomata verò augentur, quemadmodum in inflammatis particulis, vt ipse dixit, Circa generationes saniei dolores, et febres co-incidunt magis quam facta. Hæc ille, in quibus verbis vult, circa saniei generationem augmentum fieri quo ad symptomata, quo tempore dispositionem imminui videtur innuere. Dispositio autem secundum quam ille infirmatur, cum tumor sit præter naturam, hunc apud saniei generationem iam imminui ostendit. cuius contrarium dixisse videtur in libro de Totius morbi temporibus loco iam nobis supra citato, quod tu consídera. Habes ergo ex omnib. ijs, quod penes tria distinguütur tempora morborum, nempe penes morbi, eius causam, & symptomata. Cæterum quomodo huiusmodi tempora in morbis miscean-tur, & quibus in morbis singulæ mixtiones accidant, infra tangemus, quantum ad victus inuentionem opus fuerit. Galenus igitur in libris de Crisibus, & in libro de Totius morbi temporibus penes coctionem & cruditatem materiæ, tempora distinguere videtur: in libro vero Aphorismorum penes symptomatum magnitudinem: in tertio de ratione victus secundum dispositionem.
units.tr: TRULY, lest anyone be given occasion to trouble his mind over the untying of this knot, I shall set out what my understanding grasps on this point, so that nothing is lacking to the speculation, and so that, in passing, I may stir students to this investigation. Indeed, many matters are involved in the dispute which are of unlike nature and need a different style of discourse. But so that the discussion may proceed correctly, I shall follow the precept of Cicero. There are three things which we have brought into the debate, namely the state, the crisis, and the end of diseases, which we said should be known beforehand from the symptoms. We shall first set out the notion of each, so that we know what we intend to dispute. The state or vigour, which in Greek is called the height [ἀκμὴ], must be understood to be threefold: namely the state with respect to the symptoms, the state with respect to the disposition, and the state with respect to the concoction of the matter. Galen wrote first that the state of a disease is greatest in the symptoms. But when he added the preposition in, he meant that the superlative is to be referred not to the disposition of the disease but to the magnitude of the symptoms, as he wrote more plainly in his exposition of the passage On the Beginnings and Ends, where he writes thus: "He says that all the symptoms are weaker about the beginnings and ends, namely the paroxysms of fevers, the sleeplessness and pains, the loss of appetite and thirst; just as the dispositions in which these occur must necessarily be better at the state, in those who ought to be preserved." From this it is clear that, in Galen's mind, that greatest point of the disease is to be referred not to the disposition but to the magnitude of the symptoms. Moreover, each of the affections, according to its various dispositions, has its own times: namely beginning, increase, state, and decline. So if there is a fever, as soon as it has gained strength, an increase is evident in the anticipation and duration of the attacks; at the state all things are at their greatest; in the decline these same things diminish. We gather this from Galen in many places, but especially in his exposition of On Paroxysms and Consistencies, etc. But if there is an inflammation, the times are distinguished by the increase in the size of the swelling. And this distinction of times with respect to the disposition of the disease can be gathered from Galen, when he says in this manner: "Let us therefore first inquire into the beginning. Who would deny that the generation of the disease occupies that whole time in which the part is filled with bloody substance? For whether this comes about through such a coincidence, or through the obstruction of all the vessels, or through some circumstance of tumours in the pores, or, as we have taught in the book On Unequal Temperament and in the commentaries On Tumours Contrary to Nature, the excess of blood settling in a part gives rise to phlegmon; this will be the first time, in which the part is filled, the affection being subject to its magnitude. But when the influx has ceased, and what is contained in the inflamed part begins to putrefy, a certain heat arises from the putrefaction, and the swelling, filling up because of the heat by which spirit is generated, is distended by these two causes more than before, even if nothing flows in; this second time is the increase of the phlegmon. Moreover, when it is now turning into pus, the greatest pains then seize hold. For labours and fevers occur more around the generation of pus than in the deeds themselves. The time of an affection of this kind is called its state. But if it has turned into ichor or dissolved, it shows a smaller swelling and tension, and this itself is the beginning of decline." The times are also distinguished by the concoction of the matter: when it is raw, it is the beginning; but when there appears a sign of an incipient or weak concoction, you will know that the beginning has passed and the increase has begun; and when the concoction is most fully completed, it is the state; and when a sign of completion now appears, this signifies that the state has passed. All these things are according to his mind in the books On Crises and in the book On the Times of the Whole Disease. There he says that the beginning is the raw state of the troublesome humours, when they begin to be concocted; that the beginning ends and the second time, called the increase, arrives; but when the concoction itself is most fully completed, it is the time of the state. Next comes the decline, in which he writes that the magnitude of the symptoms and the abundance of the concocted matter now cease. These sometimes coincide, namely the state with respect to the disposition and with respect to the symptoms, as in pleurisy, in which, before they begin to expectorate, the symptoms are then at their strongest and the swelling of the inflammation is greatest; but when they have begun to expectorate, both diminish, both the swelling and the symptoms. As Galen has written in these words: "More often the magnitudes of the symptoms and the dispositions increase and coincide with each other, and this happens in those phlegmons from which there flows out pus that is already concocted, as usually happens in certain wounds, and in peripneumonias and in pleurisies." Sometimes both states of disposition and of symptoms occur at different times, as is taken from the same place cited above, where he writes thus: "Often indeed the disposition itself, by which one is weakened, is milder, but the symptoms increase, as in inflamed parts; as he himself said, 'Around the generation of pus, pains and fevers coincide more than the deeds.'" These are his words; in which he wishes that, around the generation of pus, the increase takes place with respect to the symptoms, at which time he seems to suggest that the disposition diminishes. The disposition by which he is weakened, since the swelling is contrary to nature, he shows to be already diminishing at the generation of pus; and he seems to have said the opposite in the book On the Times of the Whole Disease, the place already cited by us above; consider that for yourself. You have therefore from all these things that the times of diseases are distinguished in three ways, namely according to the disease, its cause, and its symptoms. As to how such times are mixed in diseases, and in which diseases the individual combinations occur, we shall touch on below, as far as the finding of a regimen requires. Galen therefore, in the books On Crises and On the Times of the Whole Disease, seems to distinguish the times according to the concoction and crudity of the matter; in the book of Aphorisms, however, according to the magnitude of the symptoms; and in the third book On the Method of Regimen, according to the disposition.

units.la: Quotupliciter ab Hipp. crisis accipiatur: & tres esse symptomatum primas causas.
units.tr: How the crisis is understood by Hippocrates in several ways, and that there are three first causes of the symptoms.

units.la: CAPVT XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: CRISIM ὀξύξροπον γὲ νώσῳ μεταβο-λὴ πρὸς ὑγείαν ἢ θάνατον ἐν, hoc est, crisim subito vergentem esse in morbo muta-tionem ad salutem, aut ad mortem, dixit Galenus in libro secundo Aphorismorum. Ve-rum per crisim Hippocrates multoties subitā intellexit morbi solutionem, vt in libro de ra tione victus primo: vbi Galenus in exposi- tione per Crisim dixit, vel perfectam morbi solutionem, vel mutationem eam, quae vsque adeo insignis sit, vt aeger periculum omne eua serit. Accipitur crisis nomen nonnunquam, vt virunque complectatur, nempe subitam mutationem & morbi solutionem. Et est quae praecipue crisis dicitur, quod Galenus scripsit in haec verba: Eas igitur quae cum ma gno & repentino certamine fiunt morborum solutiones, quas praecipue crises nominare di- cebamus, & c. Caeterum haec tria crisis accep tio, in perfectam & in imperfectam diuidi- tur. Primam morbi esse subitam solutionem cum effatu digna excretione, & non modica huic antecedente in aegrotantis corpore per- turbatione. Secundam, cui iam dictis vnu deest, quod non integre a morbo liberat, ita vt crisis perfecta bona, subita sit morbi solu- tio: imperfecta bona subita morbi diminu- tio. Has duas crises, perturbationes in corpo re aegrotantium non modice, & effatu digna excretiones comitantur. Totidem diuisiones in bonas & crises malas efficere licet, nempe perfectam malam ad mortem, eandem vursus imperfectã ad peius. Hæc omnia scito esse secundū mentem Galeni. Crisim igitur prout est subita mutatio ad salutem vel ad mortem fieri, natura separante à bonis mala, & ad excernendū præparante. Rationabiliter igi-tur in tali perturbatione grauiter se habent laborantes, & maximis tunc afficiuntur symptomatibus. Quorū cum tres sint causæ, nempe natura, morbus, vel eius causa, & natura & morbus simul. Quæ morbum insequūtur symptomata παθογνωμονικα, id est symptomata per quæ morbus cognoscitur. hæc increscente morbo augentur, & inclinante imminuuntur. Quæ verò ab ipsa fiunt natura, dicuntur κρίσιμα, hoc est crisis symptomata: Quorum meminit Hippocrates va rijs in locis. quod verò à natura fiant, Galenus docet in expositione illius, Hæc si ab initio non apparuerint, vbi ita scribit. Ergo quoties natura ad excretionem properat, effatul digna in corpore fit permutatio, ob quasymptomata huiusmodi cum manifestissimis coctionis signis apparent. Quæ tertio sunt loco symptomata, pugnã insequuntur naturæ morbificas debellantis causas. Prout verò pugna acerbior est, vehementiora fiunt symptomata. Cunque natura sua maxima vi vltimosq; conatu contra morbum pugnat, maximè et vltima fieri. Ad hoc tertium symptomatum genus reducuntur dolores & febres, quæ circa generationem siunt saniei. Nam hæc à duabus contrarijs generatur causis, nempe à calore naturali coquente, & à præter naturā calore putrefaciente, vt à Galeno scriptum est. Quod si ob sanguinis incensionem, dolores & febres fieri quispiam asserat, cunque perfectè incensum est residuum ipsius saniem fieri, quemadmodum incensis lignis cinerem, ob idque dolores & febres sedari: Cedo, sed si res exactè consideretur, huius incensionis causam non solam humoris putredinem esse, sed pugnam inter naturam coquentem et morbum putrefacientem inueniet: Cunq; altero
units.tr: Galen said in the second book of his Aphorisms that a crisis which comes swiftly is a change in the disease toward health or toward death [ὀξύροπον γε νόσῳ μεταβολὴ πρὸς ὑγίειαν ἢ θάνατον ἐν]: that is, a crisis that quickly turns is a change in the disease to safety or to death. Yet Hippocrates often used "crisis" for a sudden resolution of the disease, as in the first book of the work On the Regimen of Life, where Galen, in his commentary, explains that by crisis he meant either a complete resolution of the disease or a change so marked that the patient escapes all danger. Sometimes the word "crisis" is used to cover both, namely a sudden change and the resolution of the disease. And the crisis properly so called is the one Galen described in these words: "Those resolutions of diseases which come about with a great and sudden struggle, which we were accustomed to call crises above all, and so on." Besides this, the threefold meaning of crisis is divided into perfect and imperfect. The first is a sudden resolution of the disease, with an excretion worthy of note and, before it, no small disturbance in the body of the sick person. The second lacks one of these features, because it does not free the patient from the disease completely: thus a good perfect crisis is a sudden resolution of the disease, and a good imperfect crisis is a sudden diminution of the disease. These two crises are accompanied by no small disturbances in the bodies of the sick and by excretions worthy of note. It is possible to make the same division into good crises and bad crises, namely a perfect bad crisis leading to death, and again an imperfect one leading to something worse. You should know that all this is in accordance with the mind of Galen. Therefore a crisis, insofar as it is a sudden change to health or to death, takes place when nature separates the bad from the good and prepares it for excretion. It is reasonable, then, that the sufferers are in a grave state during such a disturbance, and are then afflicted with the greatest symptoms. Since there are three causes of these, namely nature, the disease or its cause, and nature and disease together, the symptoms that follow the disease, the pathognomonic symptoms [παθογνωμονικά], that is, the symptoms by which the disease is recognised, increase as the disease grows and diminish as it declines. Those symptoms which are produced by nature itself are called critical [κρίσιμα], that is, crisis symptoms. Hippocrates mentions them in various places. That they are produced by nature Galen teaches in his commentary on that passage, "If these do not appear from the beginning," where he writes thus: "Therefore, whenever nature hastens to excretion, a change worthy of note takes place in the body, because of which such symptoms appear together with the clearest signs of concoction." The symptoms that come third follow the struggle of nature against the morbific causes. And the sharper the struggle, the more vehement the symptoms become. And when nature fights against the disease with its greatest force and its final effort, these symptoms also become greatest. To this third kind of symptom belong the pains and fevers that accompany the generation of pus. For pus is generated from two contrary causes, namely from natural heat, which concocts, and from heat contrary to nature, which putrefies, as Galen has written. But if someone asserts that the pains and fevers come from the burning of the blood, so that when it is wholly burned its residue becomes pus, just as ashes come from burned wood, and that the pains and fevers are therefore calmed, then I grant it; yet if the matter is examined exactly, one will find that the cause of this burning is not only the putrefaction of the humour, but the struggle between nature, which concocts, and the disease, which putrefies. And when one of the two conquers, the conflict and the fight cease, and the symptoms also subside.

units.la: In fine primi prædictionũ & 2. Aphor. tero vincente cessat conflictus & pugna, remittuntur etiam symptomata. Remanent autem ea quae saniei acutam qualitatem & particulae tensionem insequuntur. Ob hoc dixit circa generationem saniei dolores & febres accidunt magis quam facta. Non enim ob aliud addidit illud verbum magis quam facta, nisi ut ob naturae pugnam contra morbi materiam prouenire symptomata ostenderet.
units.tr: At the end of the first Prognostic and the second Aphorism: Yet the symptoms that follow the acute quality of the pus and the tension of its particles remain. For this reason he said that the pains and fevers come about during the generation of pus more than the matter itself does. He did not add the words "more than the matter itself" for any other reason than to show that the symptoms arise from nature's struggle against the matter of the disease.

units.la: An non huius validum est argumentum id quod iis contingit qui exitialiter laborant? qui dum natura vires habet ut contra morbum pugnet & eius incursibus obsistat, gravissima ferunt symptomata & labores: Cum quae natura ex certamine vincitur, videntur ab eo tempore minus inquietari, et haud gravissimis conflictari: Ut iis contingit qui obscuris & blandis & contrectabilibus desipientiis laborant. De quibus Hippocrates agit in 1. prorrhetici. Ad hoc itegenus reducuntur ea quae in salubri morbo apud statu fiunt symptomata, et febrium vehementiores paroxysmi, cum manifestiss. coctionis signis. talia ergo sym ptωmata, & febres non ob maiorem mate-riæ putrefactionem fiunt, sed ob maiorem pu-gnam inter naturam & morbū in obtinen-do materiæ apparatu. De ijs alibi latius.
units.tr: Is not the following a strong argument? Those who are dying suffer this: while nature still has the strength to fight against the disease and resist its attacks, they bear the most grievous symptoms and labours; but when nature is conquered in the struggle, from that time they seem to be less troubled and not assailed by the gravest symptoms, as happens to those who suffer from obscure, mild and unnoticed delirium. Hippocrates treats of these in the first book of the Prognostics. To this same kind belong the symptoms that occur in a curable disease during its state, and the more violent paroxysms of fevers, which come with the clearest signs of concoction. Such symptoms and fevers therefore do not arise from a greater putrefaction of the matter, but from a greater struggle between nature and the disease in securing the mass of matter. I have treated these more fully elsewhere.

units.la: De qua status acceptione intelligendus fit aphorismus, Contemplari igitur opor-tet ægrotantem an sufficiat cum uictu ad statum ægritudinis, &c.
units.tr: The aphorism must be understood in this sense of "state": "It is therefore necessary to consider whether the patient, with his diet, is sufficient for the state of the disease," and so on.

units.la: CAPVT XXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: TERMINVM quem supra posuimus victus formæ indicem esse intelligo, il-lum dierū numerū quibus ægrotantis robur morbi acumen, & eius symptωmata ferre posit, citra aliquam quatuor crisium à no-bis supra descriptarū. Vt exempli causa, si quis aliqua continentiū febrium cum vigiliys con-tinuis laboret æstate, iuuenis, calidi tempera-menti: cōiciasque ægrotantē vltra septimum ferre non posse prædicti morbi vehementiā, citra aliquam quatuor crisiū, nempe ad salu-tem, aut mortem, aut ad melius, aut peius, tali ægrotāti dies septem terminū esse victus formam formam indicantem dicimus. Sed de quanâ trium acceptionū status intellexisse Hippocratem asseremus in Aphorismo, cum iubet ægrotantem considerare si sufficiat ad statū usque cum uictu necne. Et primum inquiramus an de statu quo ad materiæ coctionem intelligat. Quod esse rationes negant. nā status quo ad materiæ coctionem in nullo morbo certum nec definitum tempus habet, ut præcognosci possit. Finge Socratem salubri ægrotare febri ut continua tertiana, triplici de causa non dabitur tibi ut præcognoscas, quando potissimum morbus hic in statu quo ad materiæ coctionem erit. Primo ob materiam morbi, si diuersæ substantiæ sit. nam primo, secundo & tertio die in subtiliorem labo rante natura partem, iudicium facies de reliquo consimile: & decipieris in status præcognitione & uictu inueniendo. Secundo ob uires laborantis quæ initio ualidæ erant, procedente autem morbo ob aliquam causam ul tra opinionem imbecilliores fiunt. Vnde grauis committitur error. Nam inter initia &sti-
units.tr: I understand the term I set above, the indicator of the regimen of diet, to be the number of days within which the patient's strength can bear the disease and its symptoms without any of the four crises described by us above. For example, if someone in summer suffers from a continuous fever with constant wakefulness, a young man of hot temperament, and I suppose that he cannot bear the violence of that disease beyond the seventh day without one of the four crises (namely to health, to death, or to better or worse), then we say that seven days is the term for such a patient, indicating the form of diet. But we will argue that Hippocrates, in the Aphorism where he bids the patient consider whether he is sufficient with his diet up to the state or not, meant one of three senses of "state." And first let us inquire whether he means the state with respect to the concoction of the matter. Reasons deny this. For the state with respect to the concoction of the matter has no certain and fixed time in any disease, so that it could be foreknown. Imagine Socrates suffering from a salutary fever, such as a continuous tertian. For three reasons it will not be possible for you to foreknow when this disease will be in its state with respect to the concoction of the matter. First, on account of the matter of the disease, if its substance is diverse. For on the first, second and third days, while nature labours on the finer part, you will judge the rest similarly, and you will be deceived both in foreknowing the state and in finding the diet. Second, on account of the strength of the patient, which at the beginning was robust but, as the disease proceeds, for some cause beyond expectation grows weaker. Whence a grave error is committed: for between the beginning and

units.la: lis mato ægrotantis robore morbi coctionem ad talem dierum numerum coniecisti, frustrabe risque ob naturæ insperatam imbecillitatem.
units.tr: the estimate of the patient's strength you have conjectured the concoction to fall on such a number of days, and you are frustrated by nature's unexpected weakness.

units.la: Tertio tempus quo natura vacat humorem coctioni. Nam si Socrati multum & crassæ substantiæ cibum ut comedat ministres, diutius immorabitur coctio, quàm si sorbitionem crassam offeras. Citius autem si tenui sorbitiuncula, dummodo virtus ab utroque servetur, Socratem alas. Nam cum minus natura in ciborum coctione temporis expendit, in morbi materiam operabitur quod reliquum est. Id maius est si tenuem cibū quàm si crassum exhibeas. Alia prætera accedit ratio, quod crasso victu diutius immorentur cocti nes, eò quod in morbi materiam fiat additio, cunque singulis diebus eius augeatur copia, opus naturæ minus prævalere necessum est.
units.tr: Third, the time during which nature is free for the humour to be concocted. For if you serve Socrates food that is thick and of heavy substance to eat, the concoction will linger longer than if you offer him a thick gruel. But it is quicker if you feed him with a thin little broth, provided his strength is kept up by either. For since nature spends less time on the concoction of food, it will work on the matter of the disease with what remains. This happens more if you give thin food than if you give thick. There is another reason besides: with thick diet the concoctions linger longer, because something is added to the matter of the disease, and since its quantity increases each day, nature's work must necessarily prevail less.

units.la: Tenui autem victu hoc non datur. Cum ergo pro victus forma tempus coctionis immutari possit, qualiter à statu coctionis victus formam recte cöycere possumus? ac si super rem instabilem ædificia firma construere velles.
units.tr: But with thin diet this does not happen. Since therefore the time of concoction can change with the form of diet, how can we rightly judge the form of diet from the state of concoction? It would be like wishing to build firm structures upon an unstable foundation.

units.la: Profecto ridiculum videtur esse quærere, a-per, b, quod quidem immutatur secundum a. dispositionem. Insuper si ita esset, vt de sta-tu quo ad materiæ coctionē intelligeret, in-epte profecto ab Hippocrate dictum esset, Co-templari oportet ægrotantem si sufficiat cum victu ad statū ægritudinis, hoc est ad id tem-poris cum maximè cöplentur coctiones. Ad talem enim statum potestatis victus non est, ægrum ducere. Quantocunque enim crasso nutrias victu ægrotantem, contingret multo-ties vt ad statum eum non perducas. Nā na-tura fortasse morbo inferior est. Quot sunt præterea ægritudines quæ ante coctionem æ-grotantes occidunt? Qualiter igitur sollicitos nos reddit, admonens vt conjiciamus si cum victu sufficiat æger ad statum quo ad coctio-nem, cū eo vsq; ægrotantem durare, virtutis robori, & morbi materiæ dispositioni, tri-buendum sit, & non victui? Alium igitur in illis tetigit statum verbis, ad quem vsque æ-grotante ducere in facultate sit victus. Iis fide præstant quæ ipse alibi dixit, vbi crassiorem victu̅ & copiosiorem ministrat, quanto ma gis morbus ad coctionem festinat, magis ve rò tenuem quanto ab hac longius distat. Iis quidem contrarium in Aphor. dixisset si de statu quod ad coctionem verba eius intelli-gantur. Cæterum dispositionis statum nō teti gisse, ostendere opus non esse arbitror. Cum dispositio per se nullum præbeat iudicium, ni si quatenus actiones laedit: Quæ quidem læsio-nes symptomata dicuntur. Non immeritò igi-tur nec magnus nec paruus morbus dici po-test, si læsionem actionum tollas. Neque enim victu, neque remediorum vllum afferas nisi re-cuperandarū actionum gratia. Nec dispositio ipsa per se noxa, aut periculu̅, nec mortem ægrotanti afferet, nisi interuentu læsarū actio-num. Ad hæc non est medicorū antiquorum vllus qui penes dispositionis status distantia, victus formā inuestigandam pronunciet. De statu igitur symptomatū verba Hippocratis intelligenda fore manifestū est. Iis fidem præ-stant quæcunque Galenus de morbi tempori-bus in Aphorismis secundū mentē Hippocra-tis tis scripsit, nempe statum esse maximum morbi vt in symptomatibus. Præterea in eo, Circa principia & fines omnia imbecilliora: vbi declarat per illud verbum omnia imbecilliora, symptomata esse intelligenda. De principio etiam quod ad symptomata locutus est in Aphorismo, Cocta medicari & mouere non cruda neque in principijs: vbi aperte ostendit, per principium morborum, aliud quam cruditatem humoris intellexisse. Videturque solum tempora distinxisse Hippocrates penes symptomatum magnitudinis incrementum, vbicunque de principio statu ue morborum sermonem facit. Cui opinioni adhærebit quisquis diligenti lectione illius euoluet scripta. Cunque de materia dispositione loquitur, cruda, imperfecte cocta, & coctam dicit, vt de vrinis, sputis, egestionibus. Cum vero principium aut statum scribit, symptomatum meminit. Verum multoties per principium tempus vsque ad tertium & gritudinis diem intelligit, vt constat per Galenum in expositione illius, Si vero in morbo vetere, &c. Significat aliquando principium,
units.tr: Truly it seems absurd to ask whether a, b, which indeed changes according to the a. disposition. Moreover, if it were so, that he meant the state with respect to the concoction of the matter, it would surely have been foolishly said by Hippocrates: one must consider whether the patient is sufficient with diet up to the state of the illness, that is, up to the time when the concoctions are most complete. For the power of diet does not extend to leading the sick man to such a state. However thick the food with which you nourish the patient, it will often happen that you do not bring him to that state, for nature is perhaps inferior to the disease. Moreover, how many illnesses kill patients before concoction? How then does he make us anxious, admonishing us to conjecture whether the sick man is sufficient with diet to the state of concoction, and to keep the patient going so long, when this must be attributed to the robustness of his strength and the disposition of the matter of the disease, and not to diet? He therefore touched on another state in those words, namely the state up to which it is within the power of diet to lead the patient. They are confirmed by what he said elsewhere, where he gives thicker and more abundant food: the more the disease hastens toward concoction, the more thin food is given, and the further it is from that point. In the Aphorism he would have said the opposite if his words were to be understood as referring to concoction. But I think it unnecessary to show that he did not touch on the state of disposition. For disposition in itself yields no judgement, except insofar as it harms the actions; and such harms are called symptoms. Not without reason, therefore, can a disease be called neither great nor small if you remove the harm to the actions. For you bring neither diet nor any remedy except for the sake of restoring the actions. Nor will the disposition itself, in itself, bring harm, danger or death to the patient, except through the intervention of the impaired actions. Besides, there is no ancient physician who, from the distance of the state of disposition, would pronounce on the form of diet to be sought. It is therefore manifest that the words of Hippocrates must be understood of the state of the symptoms. They are confirmed by whatever Galen wrote in the Aphorisms on the times of disease, according to the mind of Hippocrates: namely that the state is the maximum of the disease, as in the symptoms. Moreover, in that passage, "Around the beginnings and the ends all things are weaker," where by the words "all things weaker" he declares that symptoms are to be understood. Also concerning the beginning, which he spoke of in terms of symptoms in the Aphorism, "Cooked things are to be treated and moved, not raw, nor in beginnings," where he clearly shows that by the beginning of diseases he understood something other than the crudity of the humour. And Hippocrates seems to have distinguished the times only by the increase in the magnitude of the symptoms, wherever he speaks of the beginning or state of diseases. Whoever reads his writings diligently will adhere to this opinion. When he speaks of the disposition of the matter, he calls it raw, imperfectly cooked, or cooked, as with urines, sputa and excretions. But when he writes of the beginning or state, he mentions symptoms. Yet often by "beginning" he understands the time up to the third day of the illness, as is clear from Galen in his exposition of that, "But if in an old disease," etc. Sometimes he signifies by the beginning

units.la: primum morbi insultum, quod latitudine caret: cuius meminit Galenus loco citato, & in expositione illius, Paroxysmos & consistentias. Verùm prout est unum ex quatuor morbi temporibus, symptomatum certa magnitudinem significat, prout incrementum potest suscipere. Verùm uno loco videtur per morbi principium illud intellexisse tempus, in quo nondum existunt coctionis notæ, ut apparet in expositione illius, Hæc si ab initio morbi apparebant, &c.
units.tr: the first onset of the disease, which lacks any extent; Galen mentions this in the passage cited and in his exposition of "Paroxysms and consistencies." But as it is one of the four times of the disease, it signifies a certain magnitude of the symptoms, insofar as it can admit increase. In one place, however, he seems by the beginning of the disease to have meant that time in which the signs of concoction do not yet exist, as appears in his exposition of that, "If these appeared from the beginning of the disease," etc.

units.la: Quod in ijs symptomatibus quæ morbum consequuntur, cum ad maximam perueniunt magnitudinem, statum esse intelligere oportet.
units.tr: Concerning those symptoms which follow the disease: when they reach their greatest magnitude, one must understand this to be the state.

units.la: CAPVT XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: CVM igitur ostensum sit per morbi vi gorem, statum quo ad symptomata intellexisse, superest considerare de quonā symptomatum genere maximè sit intelligendum. Quòd nec de ijs quæ accepta feruntur natu-ræ quæ κείσιμα dicuntur, nec de ijs quæ à morbo & natura circa materiæ apparatus pugnanpugnantibus prouenīunt, ab Hippocrate li- cet elicere in expositione illius, Modi autem & constitutiones, &c. vbi morborum modos refert, ab initio vehementißimè incipien tium: quos Hippocrates ab initio florere ait, et vigere, paulatimq; remitti ad iudicationē vsque. Manifestum autem est, ea quæ in morbis ab initio fiunt symptomata, non ob pugnam naturæ cum morbo ob complendā co-ctionem prouenire, aut ob maximos eius conatus cum materiam morbi extra corpus pellere nititur: sed de iis symptomatibus quæ morbum insequuntur, cum ad maximam peruenīunt magnitudinem, statum esse intelligere oportet in doctrina Hippocratis. Cæte rum qua via haberi possit præcognitio maxime eorum magnitudinis considerem̄us oportet.
units.tr: Since it has been shown that the state of a disease, as regards its symptoms, is to be understood from the strength of the disease, it remains to consider of which kind of symptoms this is chiefly to be understood. It cannot be drawn from Hippocrates' exposition (in which he speaks of the modes and constitutions of diseases, etc.) that it concerns either those things which are said to be received from nature and are called [κείσιμα], or those which arise from the disease and nature's struggle against the disordered matter. In that passage he describes diseases whose modes begin most violently at the outset, which he says flourish and grow strong from the beginning and then gradually remit as far as judgement. It is clear, however, that the symptoms which arise in diseases from the start do not come about because nature is struggling with the disease in order to complete concoction, or because of nature's greatest efforts when it tries to expel the matter of the disease from the body. But in Hippocrates' teaching one must understand that the state concerns those symptoms which follow the disease, when they reach their greatest magnitude. We must next consider in what way a prognosis of their magnitude can be obtained.

units.la: Quòd cum duo sint quæ incremento symptomatum finem imponunt, nempe ultimū resistentiæ naturæ, & perfectæ mor bi coctiones: terminum nō à coctione, sed à robore uirtutis & symptomatū magnitudine accipiendum fore ostendit. A quib. ultimū resistētiæ accipitur naturę.
units.tr: Since there are two things which set a limit to the increase of symptoms, namely the final point of nature's resistance and the perfect concoction of the morbid matter, he shows that the term is to be taken not from concoction but from the strength of the virtue and the magnitude of the symptoms. From these the final point of nature's resistance is taken.

units.la: CAPVT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: PROINDE duo sunt, quæ maximè finem magnitudini symptomatum imponunt, vltimum resistentiæ naturæ, & perfectæ morbi materiæ coctiones. Causi siquidem vigiliæ, tanto durabunt tempore, quanto laborantis virtus ferre possit: cum verò vltra non possit, succumbit. Et sic fuit ea hora status quo ad symptomata, ob vltimam resistentiam naturæ. Quandoque increscunt, quousque natura, perfecta morbi coctione crisim faciat. Vltima ergo naturæ resistentia, & morbi coctio, symptomatum incremento fine imponunt. Verùm cū multæ sint ægritudines quæ citra coctionem in abscessus terminentur, vt Hippocrates ait in expositione illius, Qui tenuem crudàque vrinâ diutius mingut, & c. rationi consentaneū non est, vt per coctionis notas, statū quo ad symptomata prænoscamus. Præterea cū in superioribus ostensum sit, tempus completæ coctionis incertum esse ob triplicem causam, æquū non est, ab eo quod in se indefinitum est, victus formâ definire. A robore igitur ægrotantis, & à symptomatum ptomatum
units.tr: Therefore there are two things which chiefly set a limit to the magnitude of the symptoms: the final point of nature's resistance, and the perfect concoction of the morbid matter. For while the symptoms last, they will continue for as long a time as the strength of the sufferer can bear; when it can bear no longer, it gives way. So the hour at which the state as regards symptoms is reached is owing to the final point of nature's resistance. Sometimes the symptoms increase until nature, having perfected the concoction of the disease, brings about a crisis. Thus the final point of nature's resistance and the concoction of the disease set a limit to the increase of the symptoms. But since there are many illnesses which end in abscesses without concoction, as Hippocrates says in his exposition of "He who passes thin and crude urine for a long time," etc., it is not reasonable to foresee the state as regards symptoms by the signs of concoction. Moreover, since it has been shown above that the time of complete concoction is uncertain for a threefold reason, it is not right to define the form of diet by something that is in itself indefinite. We think, therefore, that the state should be conjectured from the strength of the patient and from the magnitude and vehemence of the symptoms, which are...

units.la: 3.prædictionū. ptomatum magnitudine & vehementia, sta-tum conyciendū esse putamus. Exempli gra-tia: Socrate laborante, febre acuta cum viri-um robore, cuius symptomata non cessant, sed continenter capitis dolore, vigilia, & si-ti torquetur, morbi statum ad septimum fo-re diffiniam. Nam ad id temporis, Socratis virtus feret prædicti morbi symptomata. Et non vltra, citra aliquam quatuor crisium, ob quarū singulas symptomatum magnitudo imminuetur. Sis modo mecum, & perpende quàm sit vtilissima huius termini præcogni-tio. Cum sciam Socratis morbū ad septimum vsque statum habiturū, & non vltra, talem victus formā ordinabo vt Socratem ad sep-timum seruare possit. Præterea dabo operā, vt coctiones ad id temporis copleantur, mi-nus naturam cibo impediendo. Hoc enim sci-re magni est momenti, & tempus simul quo compleri oportet. Sic enim artifices cuiuscun-que artis cum aliquod aggrediuntur opus, quod cito compleri oporteat, statim quærūt quid agendum sit, & quāto temporis interuallo. Iuxta quod totum in partes diuidunt opus, in totidemque temporis spacium, itavt in diarias partes operam diuidant. Cunque a-liquid in diuisione erraverint, aut ob quam-cunque aliam causam minus compleuerint, id expeditiori diligentia ante praefinitum ter-minum supplent. Sic profecto in arte medica maxime necessarium est, praecognoscere ter-minum ad quem vsque aegrotatis virtus mor-bi acumen ferre possit. Ad quem terminum dirigendi sunt victus. Talemque praestabis, vt laborantem eo vsque seruare possit. Tum vt spacium sit naturae conficiendi coctiones ad praefinitum terminum. Cunque ex opera na-turae in primis quatuor diebus coniecerit, na-turam posse ad septimum coctiones comple-re, hominem seruandum esse scies: quod si con-trarium eueniat, moriturum in acuta aegritu-dine. Non solum igitur ad victus inuentionem vtilissima est huius termini praecognitio, ve-rum ad partem artis, quae praedicit, validissi-mis est totius praedictionis scientiae nervus. Absque quo nihil certo posses praedicere.
units.tr: ...prognoses. From the magnitude and vehemence of the symptoms and the strength of the patient, we think the state should be conjectured. For example: if Socrates is suffering from an acute fever, with his strength intact, and his symptoms do not cease but he is continually tormented by headache, sleeplessness and thirst, I will define the state of the disease as reaching its seventh day. For up to that time Socrates' strength will bear the symptoms of the said disease, and not beyond, unless some crisis intervenes, by which the magnitude of the symptoms will be lessened. Come with me and consider how most useful is the foreknowledge of this limit. Since I know that Socrates' disease will reach its state at the seventh day and no later, I will arrange such a form of diet that it can keep Socrates until the seventh day. Moreover, I will take care that the concoctions are completed by that time, by not impeding nature with food. For it is of great importance to know this, and at the same time the time by which it must be completed. Thus craftsmen of any art, when they undertake a work that must be finished quickly, immediately ask what is to be done and over what interval of time. According to this they divide the whole work into parts, and into as many portions of time, so that they divide their effort into daily parts. If they have erred in the division, or for whatever other cause have accomplished less, they make it up with more diligent effort before the appointed term. So certainly in the art of medicine it is most necessary to know beforehand the term up to which the patient's strength can bear the sharpness of the disease. To this term the diets are to be directed. And you will provide such a diet that it can keep the sufferer up to that point, and so that there is room for nature to complete the concoctions by the appointed term. And when you have conjectured from nature's work in the first four days that nature can complete the concoctions by the seventh, you will know that the man is to be saved; but if the opposite happens, he will die in the acute illness.
