Therefore the foreknowledge of this term is not only most useful for finding the diet, but it is also the sinew of the whole science of prediction, the part of the art which foretells, and without which you could predict nothing with certainty.

units.la: Quod
units.tr: That

units.la: Quòd primus Hippocrates post asiduas observationes iuxta symptomatum differentias in singulis morbis terminos, hoc est ultimum resistentiae naturae diffiniuit.
units.tr: That Hippocrates first, after assiduous observations according to the differences of symptoms in each disease, defined the term, that is the final point of nature's resistance.

units.la: CAPVT XXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIIII.

units.la: VNDE nam coniecias (inquies) quot dies is qui aegrotat morbi acumen ferre poterit? Diuinus nos docuit Hippocrates inscriptis suis post longas & diligentissimas apud aegrotantes obseruationes id inuestigas, acutas aegritudines in quatuordecim diebus indicari: non quod omnium acutarum crisim in quartadecima die fieri velit, sed crisim acutarum ad vsque quartamdecimam diem protrahi posse. Hunc terminum in acutis signauit. Nō quia eo temporis interuallo coctiones perficere necessum sit naturam: sed quia obseruauit quantumcunque robusti hominis naturam labores acuti morbi vltra dies quatuordecim citra aliquam quatuor crisiu ferre non posse. Ob quam causam crisim hunc terminum vocauit, ac si diceret crisis futurae terminu. Nec hoc praeter mente Galeni est, qui ita in eodem scribit: quòd sit necessarium
units.tr: "How, then, (you will say) can you tell how many days a sick man can bear the severity of a disease? Hippocrates, that divine teacher, has instructed us in his writings, after long and very careful observation of the sick, to look into this: acute diseases are marked out in fourteen days. Not that he wishes the crisis of all acute diseases to occur on the fourteenth day, but that the crises of acute diseases can be deferred as far as the fourteenth day. He marked this limit for acute diseases, not because nature must complete its concoctions in that span of time, but because he observed that however strong a man's nature is, it cannot bear the labours of an acute disease beyond fourteen days without some crisis. For this reason he called it the limit of the crisis, as if to say the limit of the coming crisis. Nor is this contrary to the mind of Galen, who writes in the same place thus: that, because of the size of the diseases and the severity of the symptoms, either the strength is quickly overthrown so that the man dies, or, if the nature makes an effort to expel the humours and overcomes those it has attacked, a good crisis follows; but if it is overcome, a bad one."

units.la: ob morborum magnitudinem, ac symptoma tum vehementiam, vel cito vires prosterni adeo ut homo moriatur, vel si ad excretionē humorum impetum faciat, & quos inuasit exuperet, bonam sequi crisim: si vero exuperetur, malā. Propterea igitur (inquit) est impossibile, ut in longum tempus iudicatio differatur in morbis acutis. Terminum igitur in hisce omnibus Hippocrates posuit duarū septimanarum, tanquam nullus eorum vlterius progrediatur. Verùm ante quartamdecimam diem multi iudicari possunt. In quibus verbis Hippocratis dicto promotus Galenus terminum attigit, quem morbi acumen, & virtutis tolerantia diffiniunt. Quid aliud praterea vult cum in hunc modum scribit? Si ,, quibus (inquit) horū cœpit dolor die primo, ,, die quarto premuntur maximè, & quinto, ,, ad septimum soluuntur. Quid nam aliud intelligit per dicta verba, quā quod dictū est? nempe dolorem capitis vehementem & continuum, naturam vltra septimū citra aliquā quatuor crisium ferre non posse, ut Melidiæ contigisse scribit. Ipse praeterea deterrimas dixit febres ac signis affligentes difficillimis, quarta die aut citius interimere. Quantu autem ad praedictionem iuuet iam dicti termini praecognitio, Hippocrates osiedit in haec verba: Screatio flaua non multo permixta sanguini in pulmonis morbo, si inter initia excernitur, salutaris admodum est: si septimo die, vel tardius, minus secura est. In cuius expositione Galenus ita scribit: Si vero screatio talis persistat qualis ab initio erat ad diem septimum, periculum imminet exolutionis virium antequam morbus coquatur. Ob eam rem minus securum videri dixit pluribus diebus permanere talem screationem. Idem adhuc apertius de vrina cruda, transactis aliquibus morbi diebus, persistente: de qua ita scripsit eodem libro: Si(inquit) multi temporis sit morbus & vrina talis persistat, (sub intellige cruda,) periculum est, quod non possit homo sufficere quousque coquatur vrina. Vides ne ex verbis Hippocratis necessarium esse ad praedictionis scientiam, praecognoscere m
units.tr: Therefore, he says, it is impossible for the judgement in acute diseases to be deferred for a long time. Hippocrates therefore set the limit for all of these as two weeks, as if none of them proceeds further. Yet many can be judged before the fourteenth day. In these words Galen, moved by the saying of Hippocrates, touched upon the limit which define the severity of the disease and the endurance of strength. What else does he mean when he writes in this manner? "If those (he says) who began to feel pain on the first day are most oppressed on the fourth day and the fifth, they are relieved by the seventh." What else does he understand by these words than what has been said? Namely, that a severe and continuous headache cannot be borne by nature beyond the seventh day without some crisis, as he writes happened in the case of Melidia. He also said that the most dangerous fevers, which afflict with the most difficult signs, kill on the fourth day or sooner. But how much the prior knowledge of this limit helps in prognosis, Hippocrates showed in these words: "A yellow sputum not much mixed with blood in a lung disease, if it is expelled at the beginning, is very salutary; if on the seventh day or later, it is less safe." In explaining this, Galen writes thus: "But if such sputum persists, as it was from the beginning, until the seventh day, there is danger of the strength giving way before the disease is concocted. For this reason he said it seemed less safe for such sputum to persist for many days." Even more plainly he says the same about raw urine, when some days of the disease have passed and it persists; of this he wrote thus in the same book: "If the disease lasts a long time and such urine (understand, raw) persists, there is danger that the man will not be able to hold out until the urine is concocted." Do you not see that from the words of Hippocrates it is necessary, for the science of prediction, to know beforehand

units.la: 3. praedictionum. terminu ad quem vsque ferre possit natura la borantis morbum & eius acumen? Et postea ad hunc conferre coctiones, vt quod futurū sit præcognoscamus.
units.tr: 3. of predictions. the limit up to which nature, labouring against the disease, can bear its severity? And afterwards to compare the concoctions with this, so that we may foreknow what is to come.

units.la: Statum à quo uictus formam intuestiganda docuit Hippocrates in aphorismo, Con templari igitur oportet, &c. terminu esse ad quem usque laborantis uirtus morbi acumen citra aliquam quatuor crisium ferre possit.
units.tr: Hippocrates taught that the state from which the form of the regimen is to be examined is set out in the aphorism, "It is therefore necessary to consider," etc.: that the limit is the point up to which the strength of the sufferer can bear the severity of the disease without any of the four crises.

units.la: CAPVT XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: MANIFESTVM igitur ex dictis est, statum de quo locutus est Hippo- crates in Apho.à quo victus formam inuesti gandam diximus, terminum esse ad quem vsque laborantis virtus morbi acumen citra aliquam quatuor crisium ferre possit. Quia vero terminus hic symptomatum incremen- to finem imponit, status ab Hippocrate nun- cupatur. Et quia tempus futura crisis longis- simum complectitur, terminus crisis dicitur. Fiunt apud iam dictu terminu, maxima sym ptomata ob dictam causam, tum ob vltimos naturæ conatus. Potentiæ enim naturales ne cessitatem assumentes, fortius operantur, vt ostensum ostensum est in libris de facultatibus naturali bus. Multoties accidit vt morbi coctiones ad præfinitu̅ compleantur terminu̅, tunc triplici ratione symptomata augentur: nempe ob sla tum symptomatum, tum ob vigentis coctio- nis rationem, tum ob crisim. Simulq; tunc o- mnia tria symptomatum genera coincidere. Hoc in febribus co̅tinuis vsu venire comperi mus. Aliquando co̅tingit vt fiant & co̅ple- antur ante dictum terminu̅ coctiones, et sol- uatur morbus. Accidit’q; hoc ob materiæ mo rigerationem, aut ob victum iusto magis te- nuem. Ad primum spectat modum, quod di- xit, simplicissimas febres, ac signis firmatas securissimis, quarta die aut citius desinere. Secundu̅ attigit in Apho. vbi dixit, Contem plari igitur oportet ægrotante̅, si sufficiat cu̅ victu ad statu̅, et nunquid prius ille deficiat, nec possit cum victu perdurare, vel morbus ante deficiat, atq; obtundatur. De laborantis robore, et morbi acumine, facto iudicio, ter- minu̅ co̅iecimus, ad quẽ vsq; ægrotans morbi acumen citra aliqua̅ quatuor crisium ferre poterat, eò vsque ducere victum posse ægrotantem. Quòd si huic tenuem magis quàm oporteat victum exhibeas, alterum duorum accidet: Aut ægrotantis natura ob tenuitatem cibi alleuiata, diutius morbi causa vacans, citius hoc est ante præfinitu̅ terminum coctiones complebit, & sic morbus soluetur ante statu̅, in quo maxima futura erant symptomata, morbusque obtundetur, quod idem est ac hebetescet, hoc est non perueniet ad vl timam incrementi magnitudinem: Aut eueńiet, vt coctiones complere non potens natu ra, imbecillis facta ob cibi tenuitatem, deficiat ante dictu̅ terminum. Quapropter, cum anceps sit euentus, cauendu̅ est, ne magis tenuem exhibeamus victum eo, qui ægrotantem valeat ad præfinitum terminum ducere. Vocemus hunc victum medium clarioris ser monis gratia. Duo igitur considerare oportet, quisquis tenuiorem victum medio exhibiturus sit, nempe vtrum morbus, an æger prius deficiat. In bene morigeratis morbis, quorum materia paru̅ à naturali symmetria discesserit, credendum est tenui victu morbũ & non virtutem defecturam, vt infra latius ostendemus cum de febre phlegmatica à dulci aut naturali pituita eueniente nobis sermo fuerit. In ijs enim natura ob cibi tenuitatem magis morbo incumbente, futuras coctiones ante praefinitum terminum sperabimus, ob materiæ morigerantiam. At in male morigeratis morbis, quorum materiæ valenti sunt affectæ putredine, tenuiorem victũ medio ministrare caueto. Nam virtus potius quàm morbus ante terminum praefinitum, quem deinceps statum vocabimus, deficiet, materia non cedente. Verum hoc tanquam vniuersale habeto dogma, victum exhibere qui seruare ægrotantem ad statum possit. Hoc tenuiorem non dabis, nisi cum morbum defecturum, & non virtutem ægrotantis, ante statum conieceris, hoc fiet si ante statum coquatur morbus. Hoc est quod Hippocrates dixit, Contemplari igitur oportet ægrotãtem sisufficiat cum victu vsque ad statum, & nunquid prius ille deficiat nec possit cũ victu perdurare, vel morbus ante deficiat et hebe-tescat. Ex dictis licet colligere, morbi statu, & terminu quem morbi acumen et virtutis tolerantia definiunt et crisis terminu idem indicare: & hunc praecognoscendu ex ijs quae morbus affert symptomata, et non ex signis coctionis. Nec id cum dictis Hippocratis pugnat, cu dixit coctione velocitate crisis & signu salutis certu portendere: neque cum scri psit alibi, Quae citius magisque madescunt iudi cationis denunciant celeritatem: neque ijs quae Galenus in tertio de Crisibus scripsit. Aliud enim est crisim ipsam inquirere, et crisis termini. nam crisim utrum bona futura sit, et quando maxime, ex coctionis signis coyicien dam esse opinamur. Quia naturali ordine coctio semper expulsione praecedit. Termin⁹ vero crisis non ex ijs, sed ex morbi vi et virtutis resistentia praecognoscitur. Primu per morbi symptomata, secundu per virtutis robur coniiciemus. Hunc ergo terminu tanqua immobilem et firmu, praecognitione dignu esse, ut ab eo exhibendi victus, & praedictionis scientia sumatur. Quod vtrunq; adipisci potest facilius, coniectura habita huius termini, vt ex dictis manifestu̅ est, et adhuc apertius illi quisquis in lectione Hip. exercitatº fuerit.
units.tr: It is therefore clear from what has been said that the state of which Hippocrates spoke in the aphorism, the one from which we said the form of diet is to be discerned, is the limit up to which the strength of the sufferer can bear the sharpness of the disease without any of the four crises. Since this limit puts an end to the increase of the symptoms, Hippocrates calls it the state. And because the time before a crisis covers a very long period, it is called the limit of the crisis. At this limit the greatest symptoms occur, for the reason stated, partly because of the nature's final efforts. For the natural powers, when they are pressed by necessity, work more vigorously, as was shown in the books On the Natural Faculties. It often happens that the concoctions of the disease are completed by the appointed limit, and then the symptoms are increased in three ways: namely, because of the state of the symptoms, because of the manner of the concoction in progress, and because of the crisis. At the same time all three kinds of symptoms coincide. We have found this to happen in continuous fevers. Sometimes it happens that the concoctions are made and completed before the said limit, and the disease is resolved. This happens either because the matter is well-mannered, or because the diet is too thin. To the first case belongs what he said: that the simplest fevers, confirmed by signs, which are very safe, end on the fourth day or sooner. He touched on the second case in the aphorism where he said: "One must therefore consider whether the patient, with the diet, can last until the state, and whether he gives out first, and cannot endure with the diet, or whether the disease gives out first and is blunted." Having made our judgment about the sufferer's strength and the sharpness of the disease, we have fixed a limit up to which the patient could bear the sharpness of the disease without any of the four crises, and up to that point the patient can be kept on such a diet. But if you give this patient a diet thinner than it should be, one of two things will happen. Either the nature of the patient, relieved by the thinness of the food and so free for longer from the cause of the disease, will complete its concoctions sooner, that is, before the appointed limit, and so the disease will be resolved before the state, in which the greatest symptoms were to occur; and the disease will be blunted, which is the same as becoming dull, that is, it will not reach the final magnitude of its increase. Or it will happen that nature, unable to complete the concoctions, grows feeble because of the thinness of the food and gives out before the said limit. Therefore, since the outcome is uncertain, we must take care not to give a diet thinner than that which can bring the patient to the appointed limit. For the sake of clearer speech, let us call this the middle diet. Whoever is about to give a diet thinner than the middle must therefore consider two things, namely whether the disease or the patient will give out first. In diseases that are well-mannered, whose matter has departed little from natural symmetry, we must believe that the disease, not the strength, will fail under a thin diet, as we shall show more fully below, when we come to speak of the phlegmatic fever arising from sweet or natural phlegm. For in such cases, since nature, owing to the thinness of the food, is more occupied with the disease, we shall hope for the future concoctions before the appointed limit, because of the good manners of the matter. But in diseases that are ill-mannered, whose matter is strongly affected by putrefaction, take care not to administer a thinner middle diet. For the strength, rather than the disease, will fail before the appointed limit, which we shall henceforth call the state, since the matter does not yield. Yet hold this as a universal rule: give a diet that can keep the patient up to the state. You will not give a thinner one unless you have conjectured that the disease, and not the patient's strength, will give out before the state; this will be the case if the disease is concocted before the state. This is what Hippocrates said: "One must therefore consider whether the patient, with the diet, can last until the state, and whether he gives out first and cannot endure with the diet, or whether the disease gives out first and is blunted." From what has been said, one may gather that the state of the disease, and the limit which the sharpness of the disease and the tolerance of the strength determine, and the limit of the crisis, indicate the same thing; and that this must be foreknown from the symptoms which the disease brings, and not from the signs of concoction. Nor does this conflict with what Hippocrates said, that a quick concoction foretells a crisis and a sure sign of health; nor with what he wrote elsewhere, that those things which become moist more quickly and more greatly announce the speed of the judgment; nor with what Galen wrote in the third book On Crises. For it is one thing to inquire into the crisis itself, and another to inquire into the limit of the crisis. For we think that whether the crisis will be good, and when especially, is to be conjectured from the signs of concoction, because in the natural order concoction always precedes expulsion. But the limit of the crisis is not foreknown from these, but from the force of the disease and the resistance of the strength. We shall conjecture the first from the symptoms of the disease, the second from the vigour of the strength. This limit, then, as fixed and firm, is worth foreknowing, so that from it the diets to be given and the science of prediction may be taken. Both of these can be obtained more easily if this limit is conjectured, as is clear from what has been said, and still more plainly by anyone who has been trained in reading Hippocrates.

units.la: Quòd uictus ratio conualituris pariter & morituris adhibenda sit.
units.tr: That the regimen of diet is to be applied equally to those who are going to recover and to those who are going to die.

units.la: CAPVT XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: NEQVE obstiterit, si ab eo quo dixi-mus termino victus formam sumi, co̅ ualituris pariter & morituris victus rationem dissiniret Hippocrates: Cum tamen huius contrarium asserat Galenus, cum ita scribit Aphor. primo: Quorum (inquit) summu̅ vigorem excipit mors, in his ea solum artis parte quæ prædicit vtemur, &c. Neq; igitur curationem, neque victus rationem ijs adhibere consulit qui morituri sunt. Nónne hoc idem sequitur si penes statum quo ad coctiones victum dissinias? quot enim sunt, qui eo tempore quo maximè coctionis opus comple mentu̅ receptu̅ru̅ sit, è vita discedunt? Verum si rem altius consideremus, haudquaquam
units.tr: Nor should it stand in the way, if the form of diet is taken from the term I have mentioned, that Hippocrates defined a diet for those who are going to recover and for those who are going to die alike. Galen asserts the opposite, when he writes in Aphorism 1: "Where death takes the greatest strength" (he says), "in such cases we shall use only that part of the art which foretells, etc." Therefore he advises that neither treatment nor diet be given to those who are about to die. Does not the same follow if you define the diet by reference to the state of the concoctions? For how many die at the very time when the work of concoction is about to reach its completion? But if we consider the matter more deeply, by no means

units.la: profectò sapientissimi viri authoritate dignū videtur esse putare, solum hæc dogmata de ratione victus scripsisse Hippocratem, ad eos quos seruandos esse certò sciamus. Nam cum ars medica nil certi præstare possit, contingit multoties vt felicia promittente medico, moriatur infirmus, & aliquoties sanetur præter medici opinionem. Nonne hæc facilè credibilia sunt? vtpote cum nostra ætate plura horum exempla inter hominum conuentus adducantur, in quibus male audiunt medici. Quare crudelis hominis officio & non medici fungeretur, si artis opem seruandis negaret. Prauam præterea concipiendi de arte medica opinionem hominibus ansam præberemus, cum ij quos sanandos artis remedijs sumpserimus moriantur: quibus verò de eorum salute desperantes nil remedij attulerimus, sponte sanentur. Quare Hippocratis authoritate dignius est putare, hæc dogmata de victus ratione, omnibus tā qui euasuri sint, quàm qui morituri tradidisse ægrotantibus. Atque eo magis quod hæc artis medicæ pars quæ victum docet, medicũ ad quemcunque euentum solet insontem reddere. Non sic ea, quæ de pharmacis agit, aut manualem docet operationem.
units.tr: does it seem, surely, worthy of the authority of so wise a man to suppose that Hippocrates wrote these doctrines about diet only for those whom we know for certain are to be saved. For since the medical art can guarantee nothing certain, it often happens that, although the physician promises favourable results, the sick man dies, and sometimes he recovers beyond the physician's expectation. Are these things not easy to believe? Since in our own age many examples of this are cited in gatherings of men, in which physicians get a bad name. Wherefore it would be the office of a cruel man, not of a physician, if he withheld the help of the art from those to be saved. Moreover, we would give men a reason to form a bad opinion of the medical art, since those whom we have taken in hand to heal by the remedies of the art die, while those whom we, despairing of their health, have given no remedy recover of their own accord. Therefore it is more worthy of Hippocrates' authority to suppose that he handed down these doctrines of the diet to sick people, to all alike, those who are going to escape as well as those who are going to die. And this is all the more so because this part of the medical art which teaches diet usually makes the physician blameless whatever the outcome. It is not so with that part which deals with drugs or teaches manual operation.

units.la: Diximus in iis quæ præcesserunt, à duobus victus formam accipiendā, nempe à morbi constitutione, in qua statvs distantia comprehenditur, & ab ægrotantis robore. Per statum terminum intelleximus, ad quem vsque ægrotantis vires morbi acumen citra aliquā quatuor crisium ferre possint. Principium méque huius termini inuentionis dedisse Hippocratem, nempe, cum per symptomatum differentias, & eorundem vehementias, singulis morbis suum diffinijt terminũ, ad quem vsque increscentibus symptomatibus statũ morbi esse, nisi coctiones præueniant: ob quarum causam morbum solui ante statũ intellexisse Hippocratem diximus. A dicto termino præcognito, victus formam inueniendam esse constat. Vnde si morbus ad quartum terminari debeat, sola abstinentia: si ad septimum, poculis: si ad undecimũ, tenui sorbitione: si ad quartumdecimum crassa, nutriendos esse ægrotantes dicimus. Ab ijs robur laborantium consulendum, an prædicta victus forma ad præfinitum terminum citra magnum viri um detrimentum durare possit. Quod si tenui sorbitione id seruari non posse existimemus, crassam ministrabimus, qua durare possit, eritque hæc ægrotanti medius victus. Tenui autem sorbitione qua æger durare non valet non vtemur, nisi cum senserimus morbū defecturum ante terminum, & non virtutem ægrotantis: idque contingere observatum est in bene morigeratis morbis, quorum materia parum à naturali symmetria discesserit. In male vero morigeratis morbis, quorum materia valenti sunt affectæ putredine, tenuiorem victum ministrare eo, qui ægrotantem ad præfinitum terminum ducat, summè cauendum est.
units.tr: In what has gone before we have said that the form of diet is to be taken from two things, namely from the constitution of the disease, in which the distance of the state is included, and from the strength of the sick person. By the term "state" we have meant the point up to which the patient's strength can bear the severity of the disease, short of one of the four crises. We have said that Hippocrates gave the principle for discovering this term, namely when, by the differences of the symptoms and their vehemence, he defined for each disease its own term, up to which, as the symptoms increase, the disease is in its state unless the concoctions anticipate it; for this reason we have said that Hippocrates understood that a disease is resolved before its state. From the aforesaid term, once known in advance, it is established that the form of diet is to be discovered. Hence, if the disease ought to end at the fourth day, abstinence alone; if at the seventh, drinks; if at the eleventh, thin gruel; if at the fourteenth, we say the sick should be nourished with thick gruel. The strength of those who suffer must be consulted, to see whether the aforesaid form of diet can last up to the set term without great harm to the man. But if we judge that thin gruel cannot be kept up, we shall give thick gruel, which he can endure, and this will be the middle diet for the sick man. Thin gruel, which the patient cannot endure, we shall not use, unless we perceive that the disease will decline before the term and not the patient's strength; and this is observed to happen in well-managed diseases whose matter has departed little from natural balance. But in badly managed diseases, whose matter is affected by strong putrefaction, great care must be taken not to give a thinner diet which would lead the sick man to the set term.

units.la: Quòd duæ aliæ sint morborum constitutiones, quæ victus rationem ualde disimilem à iam dicta exposcant.
units.tr: That there are two other constitutions of diseases, which demand a diet very unlike the one just described.

units.la: CAPVT XXVII. NEQVE
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: NEQVE silentio prætereundum, omnia quæ dicta sunt, in ijs solummodo intelligenda esse morbis, qui posterius statum habituri sint: quique leuiter et summissim incipiunt, subincrescunt verò, & exacerbantur secundum singulos dies, aut alternos, circa crisim verò abundè lucent. In ijs diximus à constitutione morbi, & robore ægrotantis, vna cum status distantia, victus formā inueniendam esse.
units.tr: Nor must it be passed over in silence that all the things said apply only to those diseases which are going to have a later state, and which begin slightly and gently but grow and increase day by day or every other day, and shine out fully around the crisis. In these, as we have said, the form of diet is to be discovered from the constitution of the disease and the strength of the patient, together with the distance of the state.

units.la: Verùm scire oportet, morborum esse duos alios modos, qui diuersam victus rationem indicant, ac longe illi dissimilem quam hucusque tradidimus. Quamobrem animum huc reuocato studiose lector. quæ enim tibi dicenda paro, ad intellectum eorum quæ ab Hippocrate in libris de ratione victus, & in libro Aphorismorum scripta sunt, maximè conducent. Vt aperte sensis mentem percipias in ijs quæ ad victus rationem attinent. Quæ quantam secum in artis opere vtilitatē afferrant, vel tu ipse iudicare poteris. Statu quantum ad symptomata attinet, trib. ægritudinis temporibus haberi posse scito, vt in morbi principio, nempe cum materia cruda est: aliquando posterius, vt cum maxime complentur coctiones. Sunt & morbi qui intermedio tempore vigeant. Huius speculationis primus author Hippocrates fuit, vir sane intellectu maxime philosophico, diligentissimusque scrutator eorum quae humano corpori accidunt. Hic igitur in primo de morbis vulgaribus tertio commentario ita scribit: Εἰσὶ δὲ χρόνοι καὶ καταστάσεις καὶ παροξυσμοὶ τῶν πυρετῶν, ὁμοίως ξωεχέων, ἀλλεινόντων, αὐτίκα γὰρ σωεχὴς δίηρ, ἰοσιρ ἀρχόμεν᾽ ἀυδὲι καὶ ἀκμάζει μάλιστα, καὶ ἀ- νάγει ὧδι ᾽ρ χαλεπώτερον, ποῦ δὲ κρίσιν καὶ ἅμα κρίσει ἀχλεπύνετ̣ ... Ὅσι δὲ οἶσιν ἀρχεταί μαλακῶς καὶ ἀνωδρυχίᾳ, ἐπαναδιδοῖ δὲ καὶ παροξύνεται καθ᾽ ἡμέραν ἑκάστην· ποῦ δὲ κρίσιν καὶ ἅμα κρίσει ἄλις ἐξελαμψεν. ἐσὶ δ᾽ οἶσιν ἀρχόμεν πρωΐως ἐπισιδοῖ ἡ παροξύνεται, ἡ μέχρι τινὸς ἀκμάζας, πάλιν ὑφίνει μέχρι κρίσεως καὶ ποῦ κρίσιν. ξυμπίπτει δὲ ταῦτα καὶ γίνεται ὧδε πάντες πυρετοὶ καὶ ὧδε πάντες πανὺς νοσήματος. Hoc est, secundū veram versionem: sunt modi, & constitutiones, et paroxysmi cuiuslibet harum febrium, similiter continuarum, intermittentiū. Nempe continua quædam incipiens floret, & viget maximè, & ad difficilius ducit, circa crisim vero & simul in crisi imminuitur. Est quæ incipiat leuiter & summissim, subincrescit vero & exacerbatur secundum singulos dies, circa crisim verò, & simul in crisi abundè lucet. Sunt quæ incipiūt leuiter, augentur vero & exacerbantur, & ad certum augescentes terminū rursus remittunt ad crisim usque & circa crisim. Accidunt hæc & fiunt in omni febre, & in omni morbo. Hæc sunt Hippocratis verba, quæ ob id maximè expositione digna esse duxi, propter id quod statim subiungit, Oportet (inquit) ex horū consideratione offerre victum. Triplicem in iis verbis designauit Hippocrates modum, aut tres differentias, quæ contingere possunt singulis morbis & febribus. Aliquando symptomata quæ morbum sequuntur, statim ab initio molestant, & grauiter torquent ægro tantem, augentur & increscunt & difficiliora fiunt, citra crisim vero et simul in crisi imminuuntur, hoc est cum morbi materia fere cocta est, aut perfecte cocta, quo maxime in tempore crisis fieri solet. Hoc accidit in pleuritide, & peripneumonia, & in omni inflammatione quæ in iis corporis partibus fit, quæ ad motum a natura ordinata sunt. Hæc inquâ a naturali motu magis perturbantur, ob multitudinem materiæ & eius cruditatem. Quapropter huiusmodi partes cum inflammationibus corripiuntur, inter initia, materia cruda existente, graviora patiuntur laborantes symptomata, & periculosiora, quàm cum morbus coctionem recipit. In omni præterea febre secundum accessiones aut exacerbationes inuadente, cum à multa ortum habeat materia, aut nimis crassa, deteriora fiunt morbi principia. Cuius signum est illud quod Galenus tertio libro de Crisibus cap. 9. scripsit: nempe in principiis accessionum contingere mori ægrotantes ob multitudinem materiæ, & ob eius crassitiem, aut inflammationis magnitudinem. Scis enim mortem semper in deteriori parte paroxysmi fieri. Cum igitur ob dictas causas grauiora fiant accessionum principia particularia, manifestum est, eadem ratione totius morbi vniuersale principium fore deterius. Cunque in pleuritide, aut peripneumonia, morbus coqui incipit, minus grauat inflammatio membra spiritus, tum quia coctione leuior fit, tu quia materia per halitum & per screatum imminuitur. Quae causa sunt imminutionis symptomatum, & dolorum, vt scribit Hippocrates, Dolores, in quit, pleuriticorum confestim sponte desinunt, vbi aliquid effatu dignum tum expui, tum expurgari coeperit. In febribus similiter quae ratione multitudinis, aut crassitiei, deteriora fiunt principia, cum coctionis vestigium in materia conspicitur, & multitudo imminui incipit, & crassities materiae attenuari. Vt à Galeno in libro de Totius morbi temporibus scriptum est.
units.tr: But one must know that there are two other kinds of diseases which indicate a different rule of diet, and quite unlike the one we have set out so far. Therefore, reader, call your mind back to this with care; for what I am preparing to tell you will contribute greatly to understanding those things Hippocrates wrote in his books on diet and in the book of Aphorisms, so that you may clearly perceive his mind in the matters that concern the rule of diet. How useful these things are in the work of the art you may judge for yourself. As for the state, so far as the symptoms are concerned, you should know that it can be found at three times of the illness: at the beginning of the disease, when the matter is still raw; sometimes later, when the concoctions are at their fullest; and there are diseases which are at their height in the intervening time. The first author of this observation was Hippocrates, a man of most philosophical understanding and a most diligent investigator of what happens to the human body. Therefore in the third commentary of the first book of Epidemics he writes thus: [Εἰσὶ δὲ χρόνοι καὶ καταστάσεις καὶ παροξυσμοὶ τῶν πυρετῶν, ὁμοίως συνεχέων, ἀπολειπόντων]. That is, according to the true version: there are periods, states and paroxysms of fevers, likewise of continuous and intermittent fevers. For there is one continuous fever which begins and is at its height and at its worst, and which goes towards the more severe; but around the crisis and at the same time in the crisis it abates [Ἔστι δὲ οἷσιν ἀρχεται μαλακῶς καὶ ἀνωδυνίῃ, ἐπαναδιδοῖ δὲ καὶ παροξύνεται καθ᾽ ἡμέραν ἑκάστην]. There is one which begins gently and without pain, but grows and is exacerbated every single day, and around the crisis and at the same time in the crisis it shines out fully. There are some which begin gently, but grow and are exacerbated, and, growing to a certain fixed term, again remit up to the crisis and around the crisis. These things happen and come about in every fever and in every disease. These are the words of Hippocrates, which I have judged especially worthy of explanation for this reason: that he immediately adds, "It is necessary (he says) to offer diet in accordance with the consideration of these." In these words Hippocrates has marked out a threefold mode, or three differences, which can occur in each disease and fever. Sometimes the symptoms which follow the disease at once trouble and grievously torment the sick man from the beginning, grow and increase and become more difficult, without a crisis; but at the crisis, and at the same time in the crisis, they diminish, that is, when the matter of the disease is nearly cooked or perfectly cooked, which usually happens at the very time of the crisis. This happens in pleurisy, in peripneumonia, and in every inflammation which occurs in those parts of the body that are ordained by nature for movement. These parts, I say, are more disturbed by the natural motion because of the multitude of matter and its rawness. Therefore when such parts are seized by inflammations, at the beginning, while the matter is still raw, those who suffer endure more severe and more dangerous symptoms than when the disease receives concoction. Moreover, in every fever which attacks according to paroxysms or exacerbations, when it arises from a large or overly thick matter, the beginnings of the disease become worse. A sign of this is what Galen wrote in the third book of On Crises, chapter 9: namely that at the beginnings of the paroxysms it happens that the sick die because of the multitude of matter, and because of its thickness, or the size of the inflammation. For you know that death always occurs in the worse part of the paroxysm. Since, then, for the reasons mentioned, the particular beginnings of the paroxysms become more grave, it is clear that by the same reasoning the universal beginning of the whole disease will be worse. And when in pleurisy or peripneumonia the disease begins to be concocted, the inflammation burdens the organs of breath less, partly because it becomes lighter through concoction, partly because the matter is diminished through breath and through spitting. These are the causes of the lessening of the symptoms and pains; as Hippocrates writes: "The pains of pleuritics, he says, cease at once of their own accord, when something worthy of mention begins to be both expectorated and purged." Similarly in fevers which become worse at the beginning because of the multitude or thickness of the matter, when a trace of concoction is seen in the matter, and the multitude begins to diminish, and the thickness of the matter to be attenuated. As is written by Galen in the book On the Times of the Whole Disease.

units.la: Aliquando symptomata in initijs morborum debilia sunt & parua, augenturque indies et exacerbantur, circa crisim vero & in crisi abunde elucent, hoc est eo tempore quo maxime complentur coctiones, in maxima sunt vehementia. Fiunt q; tunc temporis grauissima symptomata, ob duplice causam, ob materiae putredinem, & ob maximu certamen naturae cum morbo circa materiae dispositionem. Ad hunc modum reducitur quod dixit, Circa generationem puris dolores & febres accidunt magis quam facto. accidit hoc in omni inflammatione, quae ad suppurationem peruentura sit, cuius materia multitudine, & qualitate, mediae sit dispositionis, ut in phlegmone euenit cum ad suppurationem peruenit, grauiora tunc accidunt symptomata cu maxime complentur coctiones & fit sanies, quam anteactis morbi temporibus. In febribus similiter quarum materia ad vnam criticam seruatur expulsionem, vt in continuis tunc grauiora fiunt symptomata cum maxime complentur coctiones. In summa vt iteru repetam, in omni morbo, in omni febre, vbi materia multitudine, aut crassitie, aut acri qualitate, &agrotantis naturam grauiter molestat, inter initia grauiora fiunt symptomata. Et prout morbus coctione recipit, ita mitiora fiunt. Hoc modo plures febrium phlegmaticarum et tertianarum & quartanarum, multo magis quintanarum, inter mitia grauius affligunt, & periculosiores sunt. Prima tim hoc accidit thoracis morbis ob partium motum. Cum autem morbi a materia mitiori ortum habent, vt est sanguis, dulcis pituita, naturalis melancholia, tum qui ex bile et pituita miscentur adinuicem humores, circa morbi initia omnia mediocriter se habent. Procedente morbo augentur symptomata, tum ob qualitatem putredinalem magis auctam, tum ob maiorem pugnam inter naturam & morbum: ita vt circa crisim & simul in crisi maxima fiant ob dictas causas: tum vltimo ob ea quae crisis subitam mutationem insequuntur symptomata. Vnde fit, vt omnia tria genera symptomatum in vnum tempus coincidant. Nempe quae a morbo, & quæ à natura, & quæ ab utroque simul proveniunt. De hoc igitur statu in quo tria symptomatum genera coincidunt, intelligendus est Aphorismus hic, Quando morbus in suo vigore consliterit, tum victu tenuissimo necessarium est uti. Ob id dixit Hippocrates, Circa crisim & simul in crisi abundè elucet. Qualem porrò victum in morbis qui huiusmodi statum sortiuntur ministrare debeamus, in superioribus diximus.
units.tr: Sometimes symptoms are weak and slight at the beginning of diseases, and they increase daily and grow worse. Around the crisis, and in the crisis itself, they stand out abundantly; that is, at the time when the concoctions are most complete, they are at their greatest violence. The most grievous symptoms then occur, for two reasons: because of the putrefaction of the matter, and because of the greatest struggle between nature and the disease over the disposition of the matter. To this manner belongs what he said: "Pains and fevers occur more around the formation of pus than before it." This happens in every inflammation that is going to come to suppuration, whose matter is of intermediate disposition in quantity and quality, as happens in phlegmon when it comes to suppuration. Then more severe symptoms occur, when the concoctions are most complete and pus is formed, than in the earlier times of the disease. Likewise in fevers whose matter is directed to a single critical expulsion, as in continued fevers, the symptoms then become more severe when the concoctions are most complete. In short, to repeat again: in every disease and every fever, where the matter by its quantity, or thickness, or sharp quality grievously troubles the nature of the sufferer, the symptoms are more severe at the beginning. As the disease yields to concoction, so the symptoms become milder. In this way, more of the phlegmatic fevers, tertians and quartans, and much more the quintans, afflict more grievously at the beginning than in the milder stages, and they are more dangerous. Chiefly this happens in diseases of the chest, because of the movement of the parts. But when diseases arise from a milder matter, such as blood, sweet phlegm, or natural melancholy, or from humours mixed of bile and phlegm, then at the beginning of the disease everything is moderate. As the disease proceeds, the symptoms increase, both because the putrid quality is more augmented and because of the greater fight between nature and the disease. So they become greatest around the crisis and in the crisis itself, for the reasons stated, and finally because of the sudden change that follows the crisis. Hence it happens that all three kinds of symptoms coincide at one time: those that come from the disease, those that come from nature, and those that come from both together. It is of this state, in which the three kinds of symptoms coincide, that this aphorism must be understood: "When the disease has settled into its full vigour, it is necessary to use the thinnest diet." For this reason Hippocrates said: "Around the crisis, and in the crisis itself, it stands out abundantly." What kind of diet we ought to provide in diseases that take on this state, we have said in what precedes.

units.la: Quandoque contingit ut intermedio tempore graviora accidant symptomata commotionis humorum causa, hæc sæpius in augmento morborum fieri contingit, quàm in principio, in quo immoti perstant in propriis locis humores: & quàm in statu, utpote iam ferè facta separatione. Quæ ergo à vi morbi commotio fit, in augmento magis accidit, in quo adhuc prayi humores cum bonis mixti sunt. At quæ à natura fit commotio non similiter est. nam facta coctione natura ut molestos expellat humores, commotionem in corpore excitat.
units.tr: Sometimes it happens that in the intervening time more severe symptoms occur because of a disturbance of the humours. This happens more often in the increase of diseases than at the beginning, when the humours remain fixed in their own places, and than in the state, since separation has by then nearly been made. So the disturbance that comes from the force of the disease occurs more in the increase, when the bad humours are still mixed with the good. But the disturbance that comes from nature is not similar: for when concoction has been made, nature, in order to expel the troublesome humours, stirs up a disturbance in the body.

units.la: Secundum igitur hanc triplicem considerationem, tionem, nempe an status quo ad symptomata, inter morbi initia, materia adhuc cruda existente eueniat, aut cum maximè complentur coctiones, aut intermedio tempore, inquirendos victus fore laborantibus salubres constat. Quare à triplici status consideratione, triplex victus elicienda est ratio. Alia enim habenda est, cum morbus inter initia status habet. Alia cum eo tempore quo maximè complentur coctiones. Et denum alia cum interme dio tempore viget. Longè enim differunt victus qui horum singulis conueniunt. Horum trium modorum consideratonem ad victu̅ maxime necessariam, primus Hippocrates tradidit. Primi modi meminit in libris de ratione victus, vbi sub exemplo pleuritidis & peripneumoniæ de omnibus qui à principio florent, & statim vigent morbis, ad crisim vel mitiores fiunt, agit.
units.tr: According to this threefold consideration, namely whether the state, as regards symptoms, falls between the beginnings of the disease while the matter is still crude, or when the concoctions are most complete, or in the intervening time, it is clear that the diets suitable for the sufferers must be sought. Hence a threefold rule of diet is to be drawn from the threefold consideration of the state. One kind must be held when the disease has its state among the beginnings; another when it is at the time when the concoctions are most complete; and finally another when it flourishes in the intervening time. For the diets suited to each of these differ greatly. Hippocrates first taught the consideration of these three modes, which is most necessary for diet. He mentions the first mode in the books On the Regimen, where, using the example of pleurisy and peripneumonia, he treats of all diseases that flourish and are vigorous from the start, which become milder at the crisis or otherwise.

units.la: In morbis iis qui ab initio statim florét & uigét, non à distantia status, sed à coctione morbi victus rationem sumendam esse ostendit.
units.tr: In those diseases which flourish and are vigorous from the start, he shows that the rule of diet is to be taken not from the distance of the state, but from the concoction of the disease. ## Chapter XXVIII.

units.la: CAPVT XXVIII.

IN ijs igitur morbis, victus forma non à distantia status, vt supra diximus, sed à co-ctione morbi sumenda est: ita vt cum mor-bus crudus omnino est, tenui aut tenuissimo vti vi&tu oporteat. Cū autem coquitur plus concedendum, et iuxta maiorem coctionem, magis ministrandum. Primū ostendit Hip-pocrates cum dixit, Si morbus siccior quàm vt quispiam existimet fuerit, non multū da-re oportet, sed ante sorbitionem vel mulsam vel vinum, vtrum magis auxiliaturum pu-taueris propinare conuenit. Manifestum au-tem tibi est ex ijs quæ supradicta sunt, pocula, victum tenuissimū constituere. Secun-dum ostendit in ijs quæ sequūtur verbis, vbi ita ait: At si os madescat, & quæ à pulmone expuuntur talia sunt qualia esse oportet, sorbitionis quantitatem vt dicā summatim au-gere conuenit. Nempe quæ citius magisque madescunt iudicationis denunciant celerita-tem. Tertiū similiter ostendit cum statim scribit, & quanto fuerit expurgatio maior, tanto magis ad iudicationē vsq; dare oportet.
units.tr: In these diseases, therefore, the form of diet is to be taken not from the distance of the state, as we said above, but from the concoction of the disease. So when the disease is entirely crude, one must use a thin or very thin diet. When it is being concocted, more is to be allowed, and more given in proportion to the greater concoction. Hippocrates first shows this when he says: "If the disease is drier than anyone would think, one should not give much; but before sorbition, it is fitting to give either mulsum or wine, whichever you think will help more." It is clear to you from what has been said above that drinks make up the thinnest diet. Secondly he shows it in the words that follow, where he says: "But if the mouth moistens, and what is spat up from the lungs is of the right kind, it is fitting to increase the quantity of sorbition, to speak briefly." For what moistens more quickly and more fully announces speed of judgment. Thirdly he likewise shows it when he immediately writes: "And the greater the purgation, the more one must give, up to the judgment."

units.la: Neque id praeter rationem est. nam in huiusmodi morbis qui ab initio vigent, graviora inter initia accidunt symptomata, ob materiae cruditatem, aut multitudinem, aut acrem qualitatem. utrunque autem coctione cum evanescat, ut supra ostendimus de mente Galeni in libro de Totius morbi temporibus, fit, ut a coctione materiae, victus formam & quantitatem mutandas fore nemo non arbitretur. Id quod ipse Hippocrates ostendit sta-tim, ac si formae victus mutationis rationem reddat: Dolores siquidem (inquit) pleuriticorum confestim sponte desinunt, ubi aliquid effatu dignum tum expui, tum expurgari coeperit. nempe & purgationes longe perfectiores existunt, minusque purulenti ita fiunt, quam si quis aliter cibaret. In omni ergo morbo in quo procedens coctio symptomata mitiora reddit, ab ea victus ratio sumenda est.
units.tr: Nor is this beside reason. For in such diseases as flourish from the start, more severe symptoms occur at the beginning because of the crudity of the matter, or its quantity, or its sharp quality. Since both diminish with concoction, as we showed above from Galen's mind in the book On the Times of the Whole Disease, no one would fail to think that the form and quantity of diet must be changed according to the concoction of the matter. Hippocrates himself shows this at once, when he gives the reason for changing the form of diet: "For the pains of pleuritics (he says) at once cease of themselves, when something worth mention has begun both to be expectorated and to be purged." Indeed, the purgations also become much more perfect and less purulent than if someone fed otherwise. In every disease, then, in which advancing concoction makes the symptoms milder, the rule of diet is to be taken from it.

units.la: Item victus forma et quantitas ad maius mutandae sunt: ita ut toto eo tempore quo materia cruda est, una victus forma nempe tenui aut tenuissima alendus sit aeger. Cunque in materia coctionis manifestum signum appareat crassior victus exhibendus est. Secundi au tem modi meminit in Apho. vbi docet victū inuestigandum secundum statūs distantiam, & morbi constitutionem, de quo diffuse in su perioribus dictum est. Hac igitur de causa Hippocrates in libris de ratione victus, co ctionis meminit ad victus formam inuenien dam. Meminit & quandoq; statūs, vt in Ap-horismorum lib. obscure nimis praedictos mo dos attinges, vt scopos ad victus inuentionē. Quod manifeste apparet ex iis quae Galenus scripsit, omnia quae ab Hippocrate dicta erat de ratione victus repetens sub compendio, vbi ita scribit: Meminit quoq; et coctionis morbi saepe, non parum scopum vniuersi victus, & quae in ipso fiunt mutationum hunc facien s. Pari modo & de morbi vigore quippiam di xit, ad quem respiciens neque tanquā ad ab iectissimum in victus ratione scopum, alimo niam ministrat. Haec quidē scripsit Galenus de coctionis scopo, nō ostendes in quibus mor bis ad victū inueniendū respicere ea debea mus.
units.tr: Likewise the form and quantity of diet are to be changed to a greater extent, so that for the whole time in which the matter is crude, the sufferer must be fed with one form of diet, namely thin or very thin. And when a manifest sign of concoction appears in the matter, a thicker diet is to be given. He mentions the second mode in the Aphorisms, where he teaches that diet is to be sought according to the distance of the state and the constitution of the disease, which was discussed at length above. For this reason Hippocrates, in the books On the Regimen, mentions concoction as the means of finding the form of diet. He also sometimes mentions the state, as in the Aphorisms book, where he touches too obscurely on the aforesaid modes, as targets for discovering diet. This clearly appears from what Galen wrote, summarising all that Hippocrates had said about the regimen, where he writes thus: "He often mentions also the concoction of the disease, which makes the target of the whole diet and of the changes that occur in it, no small one. In the same way he has said something also about the vigour of the disease, looking to which, as to the most important target in the rule of diet, one nourishes." Galen wrote this about the target of concoction, but did not show in which diseases we ought to look to these things in finding diet.

units.la: In fine ter tij de ra tione ui ctus. mus, & in quibus morbi statum. Hæc igitur omnia & singula diligenter in morbis aduertere oportet. Et has tres morborum differentias aut modos, in singulis morbis à natura et habitu nostro fieri posse cogitandum, vt pru dentissimè tetigit Hippocrates in eo: Neque enim horum video, ita expertos medicos, &c. Quapropter consideranda est ægrotantis natura, & habitus. nam picrocholorum natura talis est vt febrium initia deteriora efficiat. Qui etiam natura frigidi sunt, exilium ve narum, crasso habitu, pingui abdomine. Præterea corporis nostri partes vt septũ, pulmo, et guttur similiter habet. Biliosi mediocri qui cuq; sunt, & sanguinei, et hepar, hæc magis propè crisim exacuūt. Hoc est profectò quod Hippocrates loco citato dixit, Quæcunq; no stra natura et habit9 singulis in morbis fabre faciat, affect9, et species omnigenas (nosse oportet) quæ cognita salutē & mortè ignorata ferant. Sed forsan quis dubitabit, quā ob causam in Aphorismorum libro, in quo vniuersalia victus dogmata collegit, secundæ morborum dispositionis qui inter initia vigent non meminit, vt in ijs suam victus rationem doceret. Quinimmo quicunque scripta Hippocratis peruigili & non tumultuaria lectione euoluerit, sex de victus ratione Aphorismos consequenter scriptos inueniet.
units.tr: At the end of the third book on the regimen of diet, and on the states of the disease. All these things, singly and together, must be carefully noted in diseases. We should also reflect that in each disease these three differences or modes can arise from our nature and habit, as Hippocrates wisely touched upon when he said: "For I see that physicians are not so experienced in these matters," etc. Therefore the patient's nature and habit must be considered. For the bilious (picrocholi) by nature make the beginnings of fevers worse. Those who are naturally cold, with thin frames, a thick habit and a fat belly, likewise have the septum, lungs and throat as weak parts of the body. Those who are moderately bilious, and the sanguine, sharpen the liver; these bring on the crisis more quickly. This is indeed what Hippocrates meant in the passage cited, when he said: "Whatever our nature and habit makes of each disease, and all the affections and kinds (it is necessary to know), which, when known, bring salvation and, when unknown, death." But perhaps someone will ask why, in the book of Aphorisms, in which he gathered the general rules of diet, he does not mention the second disposition of diseases which prevail at the beginning, so that he might teach the regimen of diet for them. Indeed, whoever reads the writings of Hippocrates with a vigilant and not a hasty reading will find six aphorisms on the regimen of diet written in sequence.

units.la: Ab ijs septimus sic habet: Quibuscunque qui dem igitur statim status est tenuiter dietare conuenit. Quibuscunque status postea, ad illud & ante illud parum auferendum, prius vero vberius reficiendum, vt sufficiat aegrotans. Cum attente legeris eos qui hunc praedunt Aphorismos de victus ratione inuenies breuitate sermonis Hippocratis, & eiusdem sententiarum grauitatem septimu Aphorismu tanquam superfluum non admittere, si de ijs quae dixerat intelligatur. Praeterea si de ijs morbis ageret qui ob vltimos labores statim vigent & crisim habent, tenuissimo eos victu, vt antea dixerat, & non tenui scripsisset indigere. Alium igitur tetigit statum, qui ita vehemens non sit, quem plurimi morborum inter initia obtinent, quiq durat donec nec materia morbi cruda est. Nam cum sym ptomata quæ inter morbi initia fiunt, ob so- lam materiæ multitudinem, aut crassitiè, aut humoris acrem qualitatem efficiunt, & nō ob cōmotionem naturæ ad expulsionem pa- rantis molestantes humores, neque ob maxi- mam pugnā naturæ coquentis cū morbo pu- trefaciente, vt eo fit maximè tempore, quo complentur coctiones, fieri nequit vt sint ve- hementissima & vltima, prout ijs contingit morbis qui tunc viget, cum duo aut tria sym ptomatum genera coincidunt. Verùm quia in morbis ijs qui inter initia vigent, quibus- dam vehementiora contingunt symptomata & periculosiora, ita vt eorū ratione tenuissi- mus victus adhibendus esset, quibusdam ve- rò minus vehementia & periculosa, ita vt tenuis victus ijs conueniens esset, prudentissi- mè Hippocrates ijs morbis tenuem victum ministrandum docuit in Aphorismis cū ait, Quibuscunque igitur slatim vigor est tenui- ter diƈtare conuenit: quibus verò posterius debet consistere, in ipso consistendi tempore, & parum ante illud cibus subtrahendus. Prius vero vberius reficiendum, vt aeger sufficiat. Quibus verbis de eo morborum statu agit, qui in eo maxime fit tempore quo conficiuntur coctiones. Duos ergo praedictos modos tetigit morborum Hippocrates in dicto Apho. a quibus victus rationem inuestigare docuit, breuissime quidem vt solet. Cum ergo symptomata periculosa et vehementia inter initia fiunt, vt in angina, & pleuritide morosa, tenuissimo victu dum materia cruda est vtemur, prout ipse monuit in libro de ratione victus. Quod si aliter eueniant tenui victu vti sat erit. Nam cum talia symptomata eo vsq; durent quo ad coctionem materia recipiat, idq; non vna die sed multis fortassis fiat, consulte non ageretur, si tenuissimo victu to to eo vteremur tempore, quo materia cruda permanet. Repentinas praeterea mutationes detestatur Hippocrates sub iis verbis: Nec repente quicquam huc, vel illuc, mutare in toto negocio licet. Quapropter homine hesterna die, solido cibo vso, omnimodam inediam hodie iniungere, conueniens non est, vbi corporis dispositio maximo interuallo à naturali nō discesserit symmetria. quod in solis per acutis & vltimis accidit morbis. In ijs ratio nabile est vt victus similiter maxime distet ab eo, quo bona vsus est valitudine. Ob id prudenter dixit senex, Mutare quidem bene habet, si recte transferatur.
units.tr: The seventh of these reads thus: "For those who are at once at the height of their illness, it is proper to diet thinly. For those whose height comes later, it is necessary to take away a little before and during it, but first to feed more richly, so that the patient may hold up." When you read attentively those who precede this aphorism on the regimen of diet, you will find, from the brevity of Hippocrates' language and the weight of his sentences, that the seventh aphorism, if it is understood as referring to what he had said, is not to be admitted as superfluous. Moreover, if he were speaking of those diseases which at once reach their height because of the final labours and have a crisis, he would have written that they need the most slender diet, as he had said before, and not a thin one. He therefore touched on another state, one that is not so violent, which most diseases hold at their beginning, and which lasts until the matter of the disease is not yet raw. For when the symptoms that arise at the beginning of a disease are caused solely by the quantity of the matter, or by its thickness, or by the sharp quality of the humour, and not by a disturbance of nature driving out the humours that trouble it, nor by the greatest struggle of nature concocting against the putrefying disease, which happens most of all at the time when the concoctions are completed, then they cannot be most violent and final, as happens in diseases that are at their height when two or three kinds of symptoms coincide. But since in those diseases which prevail at the beginning, some symptoms are more violent and dangerous, so that for them the most slender diet should be used, while others are less violent and dangerous, so that a thin diet suits them, Hippocrates most wisely taught in the Aphorisms that the most slender diet is to be given in the former cases when he says: "For those who are at once at the height, it is proper to diet thinly; but those whose height should come later, in the very time of their standing still, and a little before it, food should be withdrawn, but first they should be fed more richly, so that the patient may hold up." In these words he treats of that state of the disease which occurs chiefly at the time when the concoctions are completed. Hippocrates therefore touched upon the two modes of disease mentioned in that aphorism, from which he taught us to seek the regimen of diet, very briefly, as is his custom. Therefore, when dangerous and violent symptoms arise at the beginning, as in quinsy and in the lingering pleurisy, we shall use the most slender diet while the matter is still raw, as he himself advised in the book on the regimen of diet. But if they occur otherwise, it will be enough to use a thin diet. For since such symptoms last until the matter is received into concoction, and this happens not in one day but perhaps in many, it would be imprudent to use the most slender diet for the whole time that the raw matter remains. Hippocrates also condemns sudden changes in these words: "Nor is it permitted to change anything suddenly, either this way or that, in the whole business." Therefore, when a man has eaten solid food the day before, it is not fitting to impose complete starvation today, where the disposition of the body has not departed far from its natural symmetry, which happens only in the acute and final diseases. In these cases it is reasonable that the diet should likewise differ most from that which he used in good health. Hence the old man wisely said: "To change is indeed good, if it is done rightly."

units.la: Quotupliciter uirtus urgeat: & signa per quae uirtutem maxime, multum & parum urgentem dignoscere posimus.
units.tr: How many ways the strength (virtus) presses; and the signs by which we can recognise a strength pressing most, much, and little.

units.la: CAPVT XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: CAETERVM quia nō facile est cuilibet ea quae dicta sunt percipere, neque percepta ad opus deducere, omnes de statu, quas hucusque percurrimus speculationes, ad indicationem unam in maximum studiosorum commodu reduximus. Scimus enim hominum mentem paucis satiari. Quapropter omnia quae hucusque de victus forma diximus, secundum mentem Hippocratis faciliori, magisque compendiosa via trademus. Paruo siquidem pondere gaudet Hylas. Totum ergo huc studiose lectior animum renocato.
units.tr: Since it is not easy for everyone to grasp what has been said, or to put what has been grasped into practice, I have reduced all the considerations about the state of the body that we have gone through so far to one guiding indication, for the greatest benefit of students. For we know that the human mind is satisfied with few things. Therefore I shall set out everything we have said so far about the regimen of diet, according to the mind of Hippocrates, by an easier and more concise route. "For Hylas delights in a small weight." So let the reader carefully recall the whole of this to mind.

units.la: Scire aut oportet, virtutem & morbum aliquando non, & quandoque parū, nonnun quam multū aut quammaximè vrgere. Horum singula cognoscere medicum oportet, hoc modo.
units.tr: It must be known that strength and disease sometimes do not press, sometimes press slightly, sometimes press considerably, or press most of all. The physician must know each of these in the following way.

units.la: Virtus tunc maximè vrget, cū prope syn copen est: quod ex pulsu, & facie certissimè deprehendere poteris. Multum vrget, cū ægrotans ijs perturbatur symptomatibus, quæ syncopen solent inducere. Talia sunt ventris crebra deiectio corpus absumens, sanguinis fluor immodicus, incessantes sudores.
units.tr: Strength presses most of all when the patient is close to syncope, which you can determine most surely from the pulse and the face. It presses considerably when the patient is disturbed by those symptoms that are wont to bring on syncope. Such are frequent evacuation of the bowels that wastes the body, an immoderate flow of blood, and unceasing sweats.

units.la: Multū præterea tunc dicimus vrgere virtutem, cum in ijs quæ à voluntate fiunt actionibus multum deficere ægrotans videtur. Sed diligenter considerare oportet, cum ab ijs iudicium imbecillitatis naturæ simus facturi, ne ob morbi acumen in huiusmodi imbecillitates deueniant laborantes, & non ob venarum inanitionem: Quod à rationalium medicorum principe Hippocrate scriptum est in hæc hæc verba: Ingens siquidem malum est, si ob laborem, morbiqué acumen, imbecillitato, porrexerit quis potum vel sorbitionem copiosiorem, vel esculentum, imbecillitate eam ex vasorum inanitione contigisse arbitratus. Neque sanè calumniam effugere potest, qui ægrè valentem ex vasorū inanitione, non cognoscit, torquetque dicta. Diligenter ergo ob seruare oportet, naturæ imbecillitates, an ob inanitionem venarum sensibilem, aut sensui occultam, aut ob morbi acumen eueniant.
units.tr: Furthermore, we say that strength presses considerably when the patient seems to fail greatly in those actions that proceed from the will. But we must consider carefully, since from these we are going to judge the weakness of the nature, lest the patients become weak from the sharpness of the disease and not from emptying of the veins. Hippocrates, the prince of rational physicians, wrote the following words on this: The following words: "It is a great evil if, on account of the labour and the sharpness of the disease, someone gives a more copious drink or spoonful of food, supposing the weakness to have come from emptying of the vessels. Nor can he who does not recognise the weakness of the sick man as coming from emptying of the vessels, and twists what has been said, escape the charge of calumny." Therefore we must carefully observe whether the weaknesses of the nature arise from an emptying of the veins that is perceptible to the senses, or hidden from them, or from the sharpness of the disease.

units.la: Cum ob venarum inanitionem sensu perceptam, aut occultâ, imbecillitates fiunt, multum tunc virtutem urgere putandum est: non ita vero ob morbi acumen. Utrunque autem discernere à nullo alio quàm à pulsu certius possis. Non ex eius magnitudine, utraque enim dispositio, paruum efficit pulsum: verum ex distensione & contractione, id percipiliecet. Pulsus siquidem eorum qui ob morbi acumen imbecillitantur, parum distenduntur, quasi puncto digitum feriant, festineque contrahuntur, ac si intro surripiantur. Eorum vero qui ob inanitionem venarum inualidi fiunt, longe aliter habent, ita vt quiuis illud dignoscere possit, si in cognitione pulsuum mediocriter sit exercitatus. Aut enim æquales faciunt contractionibus distentiones, aut has quidem maiores. Hoc quidem magni facere oportet. Nam non solum ad victus inuentionem, verùm ad eam artis partem, quæ morbos curat maximè valet.
units.tr: When weaknesses come about from an emptying of the veins, whether perceived by the senses or hidden, strength must be thought to press considerably; but not so when they come from the sharpness of the disease. You can distinguish the two most certainly by nothing other than the pulse. Not by its size, for either condition makes the pulse small; but it can be perceived by its distension and contraction. For the pulse of those who become weak from the sharpness of the disease is little distended, striking the finger as if with a point, and is contracted quickly, as if it were snatched inward. But in those who become feeble from emptying of the veins, it is quite otherwise, so that anyone may recognise it if he is moderately practised in knowing pulses. For either the distensions equal the contractions, or the distensions are the greater. This is worth much attention. For it is of great value not only for the discovery of diet, but for that part of the art which cures diseases.

units.la: Parum virtus vrget, aut ratione ætatis, vt cum puerulus, aut senex infirmantur: aut cum corpora rara, & tenuium succorum, febribus corripiuntur. Vbi præterea irritantia adsunt symptomata, vt pruritus ingens, tenesmos, morsus quem acris humor in ventri culo aut intestinis parit: vigilia, ira intus co-pressa, mœror, et similia quæ communi pro-ritationis nomine comprehenduntur, vt in expositione illius de mutatione, Quæ in hæc vel illa, &c.
units.tr: Strength presses slightly either by reason of age, as when a little child or an old man falls ill, or when bodies that are loose and have thin humours are seized by fevers. Moreover, where irritating symptoms are present, such as intense itching, tenesmus, the gnawing that a sharp humour produces in the stomach or intestines, wakefulness, anger held in check inwardly, sadness, and similar things that are comprehended under the common name of irritation, as explained in the discussion of that aphorism, "Those things which in this or that...," etc.

units.la: Quotupliciter morbus urgeat.
units.tr: How many ways disease presses.

units.la: CAPVT XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER 30.

units.la: MAXIME vrgere morbũ dicimus cum vltimos affert labores. Hos esse intelliges cum symptomatibus coniuncta est inquietatio, & angustia.
units.tr: We say that a disease presses most when it brings the most severe troubles. You will understand these to be present when restlessness and distress are joined to the symptoms.

units.la: Tunc multum vrget, cum aliquod affert sæuum symptoma, vt cõtinuas vigilias, aut perpetuum soporem, aut cõma, aut fortem capitis dolorem cõtinuũ, aut difficilem anhelitũ, delirium, aut cum vrina suppriminitur, aut alius nimis cietur.
units.tr: It presses hard when it brings some grievous symptom, such as continual sleeplessness, perpetual drowsiness, coma, a strong and continuous headache, difficult breathing, or delirium; or when the urine is suppressed; or when some other part is excessively disturbed.

units.la: Parum vrget, vt cum sitim patitur, aut cibos valde fastidit, aut si præter modum astricta sit aluus. Aut cum ea successiuis temporibus patitur symptomata, quæ morbum multũ vrgentem reddere diximus.
units.tr: It presses little when the patient suffers thirst, or greatly loathes food, or when the bowels are constipated beyond measure. Or when, at successive times, he suffers those symptoms which we said make a disease press strongly.

units.la: Quando igitur maximè vrget virtus, id exhibendum fore præcipimus, quo maximè laborantis natura seruari possit, quamuis illud morbus prohibeat. Nam virtutis maximè vrgentis indicatio, eam quæ à morbo suppeditatur, obscurat indicationẽ, quanquã morbus maximè tunc vrgeat. Nónne hoc à Galeno rationalium medicorum summo concessum est? in Aphorismis, nempe vbi ita scri-bit: Quo circa aliquando in ipso morbi vigo-re, vbi symptoma aliquod interuenerit robur naturæ dissoluens, nutrire cogimur. Sciendū præterea has victus formas sibi proximas es-se, nempe quæ comeduntur, sorbentur, & bi-buntur, & inediam, ita vt inter has aliam intermediam victus formam inuenire neque as. Præterea, virtus pro sui custodia illū ma-xime cibum indicat, quem coquere, & digé-rere & (vt oportet) apparare posset. Quo fit vt cum virtus multum imbecillis est, victū per ea quæ comeduntur non indicet, quando-quidem difficilioris coctionis est, sed sorbitio-nes aut potus. Morbus præterea maxime vr-gens ex sui ratione omnem cibum prohibet. Manifesta hæc omnia sunt & à rationali-bus concessa medicis, præcipuè Hippocrate & Galeno.
units.tr: Therefore, when the strength presses most, we direct that the remedy be given which can best preserve the nature of the sufferer, even though the disease forbids it. For the indication of the strength, which presses most, obscures the indication that comes from the disease, although the disease presses most at that time. Has this not been conceded by Galen, the chief of the rational physicians, in the Aphorisms, where he writes thus: "Wherefore sometimes, in the very vigour of the disease, when some symptom has come upon us which dissolves the strength of nature, we are compelled to nourish." Furthermore, you should know that these forms of nourishment are close to one another, namely what is eaten, what is sipped, and what is drunk, and fasting; so that you cannot find any other intermediate form of diet between these. Moreover, for its own preservation the strength indicates above all that food which it can concoct, digest and prepare (as it ought). Hence it comes about that when the strength is very feeble, it does not indicate a diet of things that are eaten, since these are harder to concoct, but broths or drinks. Furthermore, a disease that presses most, by its very nature, forbids all food. All these things are plain and have been conceded by rational physicians, especially Hippocrates and Galen.

units.la: Ponamus igitur primum, maxime morbo vrgente, non vrgere ægrotantis virtutem, quæ nam victus forma huic conueniet? Sola inquam inedia. Nam virtus non dissuadet id quod morbus maximè vrgens indicauit. Tan diuque hæc victus forma seruanda est, quâ- diu virtus & morbus ita habuerint. Se- cundum, quòd si idem virtutis robur cũ mor bo multum vrgente coniungatur, victu̅ per pocula exhibebimus. Nam si à vehementis- simo morbo aut maximè vrgente ad proxi- mam differentiam, quæ sensu percipi possit, descendas, quem alium quàm valde acutum morbum, aut multum vrgentem intelliges? Quòd si consimiliter ab inedia ad victu̅, qui eidem tenuitate sit proximus, ascendas, quæ alium quàm per pocula victum, magis tenuè inuenias? cum ergo morbo maximè vrgen- te inediam solam ministremus, virtute non dissuadente: manifestum est, quòd cum mor- bus proximè à vehementissimo degenerat, victum inediæ proximū ministrandum fore. Nec ad id rectè inueniendum opus est similes seruare proportiones, inter victus, ac inter morbos. Ars enim medica, res nō prout à na- tura sunt considerat, sed vt sensum immu- tant. Cum ergo à morbo maximè vrgente morbus multum vrgens, & inedia victus per pocula proximè abesse sensu percipiatur, rectè colligitur victui per pocula morbo multum vrgenti, virtute non dissuadente, convenire. Simili ratione colliges, virtute similiter habente, & morbo parum vrgente, sorbitiones exhibendas esse. Verùm cum inter symptomata, quæ morbum multum vrgentè reddunt, & ea quæ parum, medio sint loco symptomata sensu perceptibilia, quæ manifestè ab alijs discerni possint, non immeritò inter morbos parum & multum vrgentes, medïæ vehementiæ morbus collocabitur. Diximus autem supra fortem capitis dolorem continuum, delirium, difficilem anhelitum, vigilias perpetuas, aut soporem, comata, vrinæ suppressionē, & similia, cū vnà permanent, vehementia symptomata esse quæ morbum multum vrgentē efficiant. Hæc eadem si successiuis fiant temporibus, ita vt modo sint, in crastinum omnino euanescant, morbum parum vrgentem constituunt. Quod si hæc eadem cum à sua desistunt vehementia nō omnino nino euanescere intelligas, sed solum remitti, medij acuminis morbum constituent, & me diocriter vrgentem. Cum ergo morbo multum vrgente, nihilque vrgente virtute pocu la exhibenda fore ostenderimus, fit, vt si ab huius vehementia, proximè morbus degene ret, differentia sensu perceptibili, morbus quem nunc diximus, medij acuminis succe dat. A poculis similiter si abscedas ad proxi mè crassiore tenues esse sorbitiones, indican te sensu, comperies. Ostensum igitur tertio est cum virtus similiter habet, & mediocriter morbus vrget, sorbitiones fore ministrandas tenues. Tum quarto, cum parum vrget crassas. Simili ratione quinto, cū mor bus omnino non vrget, virtute similiter habente, victū exhibendum fore per ea quæ co meduntur. Ponamus rursus sexto, quod virtus parum, & morbus maximè vrgeant, quem nam alium huic ministrabis victum, quàm pocula, si rectè ea quæ dicta sunt perce pisti nam ab eo quod primo ostendimus, simili vi deduci potest. Septimo, stante eadem morbi vehementia, virtus si multum vrgeat, tenues sorbitiones constat ministrandas. Sciendum autem plures horum qui ita habent interire. Octauo, morbo multum vrgente, virtus si parum vrgeat, tenues dandæ sunt sorbitiones: quod simili modo ab eo quod secundo ostendimus loco, manifestum est.
units.tr: Let us then first suppose that, while the disease presses most, the strength of the patient does not press. What form of diet will suit this? Only fasting, I say. For the strength does not dissuade what the disease, pressing most, has indicated. This form of diet must be kept for as long as the strength and the disease remain in that state. Second, if the same strength of the body is joined with a disease pressing hard, we shall give nourishment by drinks. For if you descend from the most violent disease, or the one pressing most, to the nearest difference that can be perceived by the senses, what other than a very acute disease, or one pressing hard, will you understand it to be? And if you ascend similarly from fasting to a diet which is nearest to it in thinness, what will you find thinner than a diet of drinks? Since, then, we give only fasting to a disease pressing most, when the strength does not dissuade, it is clear that when the disease falls away from the most violent state to the nearest degree, the diet nearest to fasting must be given. Nor, to find this correctly, is it necessary to keep similar proportions between diets and diseases. For the medical art considers things not as they are in nature, but as they affect the senses. Since, then, from a disease pressing most to a disease pressing hard, and from fasting to a diet of drinks, the difference is perceived by the senses as nearly absent, it is rightly inferred that a diet of drinks suits a disease pressing hard, when the strength does not dissuade. By a similar reasoning you will conclude that when the strength is similarly placed and the disease presses little, sips are to be given. But since, between the symptoms which make a disease press hard and those which make it press little, there lie in the middle symptoms perceptible to the senses which can be clearly distinguished from the others, a disease of middle intensity will rightly be placed between the diseases that press little and those that press hard. We said above that a strong and continuous headache, delirium, difficult breathing, perpetual sleeplessness or drowsiness, coma, suppression of urine, and the like, when they remain together, are the violent symptoms that make a disease press hard. If these same symptoms occur at successive times, so that they are present now and wholly vanish by the next day, they constitute a disease that presses little. But if you understand that these same symptoms, when they abate from their violence, do not vanish altogether but are only remitted, they will constitute a disease of middle sharpness, pressing moderately. Since, then, we have shown that when the disease presses hard and the strength presses not at all, drinks must be given, it follows that if the disease falls away from its violence to the next degree, perceptible to the senses, the disease we have just described succeeds to the middle sharpness. Likewise, if you withdraw from drinks to the next thicker thing, you will find by the senses that broths are thinner. Third, therefore, it has been shown that when the strength is similarly placed and the disease presses moderately, thin broths are to be given. Fourth, when it presses little, thick broths. By a similar reasoning, fifth, when the disease does not press at all and the strength is similarly placed, the diet is to be given from things that are eaten. Let us suppose again, sixth, that the strength presses little and the disease presses most: what other diet will you give this than drinks, if you have rightly grasped what has been said? For this can be deduced by the same force from what we first showed. Seventh, with the same violence of disease, if the strength presses hard, it is agreed that thin broths are to be given. But it should be noted that many who are in this state die. Eighth, when the disease presses hard and the strength presses little, thin broths are to be given; which is plain in a similar way from what we showed in the second place.

units.la: Nono, virtute multū vrgente, stante eadem morbi vehementia, crassæ. Decimo, morbo mediocriter vrgente, virtus parum si vrgeat, crassas quoque ministrandas fore sorbitiones. Vndecimo, quod si multum vrgeat virtus, stante eadem morbi vehementia, quæ comeduntur, si ea coquere laborantis natura possit. Cum enim virtus multum vrget, non solum tunc morbus tenuem victum indicat, sed virtutis imbecillitas tanquā secunda causa tenuitatis accedit. Duodecimo, cū morbus & virtus parum vrgent, victus per eas quæ comeduntur, exhibendus est: Quod ex iis quæ quarto ostendimus loco perspicuum est. Tertiodecimo, morbo parū vrgente, virtus si multum vrgeat, ea quæ comeduntur.
units.tr: Ninth, when the strength presses hard, with the same violence of disease, thick broths.
