Tenth, when the disease presses moderately and the strength presses little, thick broths also are to be given. Eleventh, if the strength presses hard, with the same violence of disease, things that are eaten, provided the nature of the sufferer can concoct them. For when the strength presses hard, not only does the disease then indicate a thin diet, but the weakness of the strength is added as a second cause of thinness. Twelfth, when both the disease and the strength press little, a diet of things that are eaten is to be given; which is clear from what we showed in the fourth place. Thirteenth, when the disease presses little and the strength presses hard, things that are eaten.

units.la: Tabella, qua facilè quiuis in singulis morbis conuenientem uictus formam inuenire possit.
units.tr: A table, by which anyone can easily find the suitable form of diet in each disease.

units.la: CAPVT XXXI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: Cæterum nosse oportet, eorum quæ comedun-tur multiplicem esse differentiam, ita ut hæc difficilis sint coctionis, facilis illa. Virtute igi-tur multum imbecilli existente, si victum per ea quæ comeduntur exhibeamus, danda est opera, ut ea quæ lenioris sint coctionis, mi-nistremus. Finge igitur hominem continua febre laborare, quæ singulis alternis diebus fortior euadit, ita ut & capitis dolorem et vigilias accessionis die patiatur: die vero in-termissionis omnino cessent: Laborans ipse adolescens, gracili habitu, calida & sicca temperatura sit, tenuium succorum, qui ci-tra læsionem una die abstinere non possit. Mor-bum ex notarum concursu parum urgere sci-to. Similiter & virtutem obrarum habitu. nam huiusmodi hominum compages facile à morbificis causis soluuntur. Morbum igitur sub signo, d, virtutem vero in, g, inuenias.
units.tr: Moreover, one must know that among the things that are eaten there is a manifold difference, so that some are hard to digest and others easy. Therefore, when strength is very weak, if we provide diet by means of things that are eaten, care must be taken to supply those of gentler digestion. Suppose, then, a man suffering from a continuous fever, which grows stronger on alternate days, so that he endures headache and wakefulness on the day of the paroxysm, while on the day of remission these cease altogether. The sufferer himself is a young man, of slight build, warm and dry in temperament, with thin humours, who cannot go one day without food without harm. Know that the disease presses only slightly, judging from the concurrence of signs. Likewise, the strength is judged from the habit of body, for such men's frames are easily loosened by morbific causes. Therefore look for the disease under the sign d, and the strength under g.

units.la: Sed singulas nostræ tabellæ partes secundū senis sententiā esse ostendamus. Morbus ma-ximè vrgens omnimodam exposcit inediam, virtute non dissuadente, quod ostendit in A-phorismo quem supra citauimus: Vbi igitur peracutus morbus est, & statim vltimos la-bores habet, extremo tenuissimo victu ne-cessarium est uti. Quem alium rationabilius maxime vrgere morbum dixeris, quam eum qui vltimos affert labores? cui extremo tenuessimum victum conuenire ait, quem supra cum Galeno omnimodam sumus inedia interpretati. Idem apertius scripsit commentario secundo de ratione victus, vbi ait: Nec cum morbi vigent feruoremque habent cibu dare. Secundum, morbo multu vrgente, pocula ministranda constat, quod in primo de victu acutorum scripsit in eo: Postea si dolor vel periculum aliquod comparuerit, sorbitio nem dare oportet, nec multam, nec crassam, sed post septimu, aut nonu si validus sit. Vbi per id verbum si validus sit, virtutis nihil vrgentis indicatione addidit. Idem paulo ante apertius dixit, vbi dolor aliquis vexauerit, oxymeli bibendum dabis. Manifestum est per hos dolores, no esse eos intelligendos, qui secundum accessiones ægrotantes torquent, sed de iis qui assidui sunt, & ab inflammatio nibus ortum habent, qui morbum vrgentem reddunt: vt manifestum iis est, qui in libris de ratione victus exercitati sunt. Sed ne rem pus teratur in singulis locis citandis, comodi us fuerit ita rem ostendisse, vt facile cui vis sit, reliqua ab ijs quae dicta sunt colligere. Ostensum est secundum Hippocratis mentem, morbo maxime vrgenti, inedia, multu vero vrgeti, pocula competere. Cum ergo ab eode praeceptu sit tantu fore condescendendu versus craßiorem victu, quantum morbus mol lior fuerit vltimis: morbo igitur mediocriter vrgente, craßiorem competere victu quam multum vrgenti, cunq; vterque morbus, & qui multum, & qui mediocriter vrget, sibi proximi sint vicinitate, manifestum est tenues huic sorbitiones exhibendas fore secundum Hippocratis mente. Nam post pocula, craßior proxime victus tenuis sorbitio est. Parum vero vrgenti craßas, non vrgenti vero ea quae comeduntur. Quapropter eos qui morbo nõ vrgente laborant, si sorbitionibus aut poculis nutrire velis, non leuiter peccabis. Quod a sene aperte scriptu est, in eo Aph. qui incipit, Victus tenuis atq; exquisitus, in morbis quidem chronicis semper, et in acutis quibus non conuenit, fallax. Manifestum est morbos quos chronicos vocat, symptomata non adducere quorum ratione morbus vrget: sed nec febris continuitatem chronicum morbum admittere. Nam hæc eadem continuitas febris morbum acutum constituit, vt author est Hippocrates & Gal. in lib. prædictionum. Tenuem ergo victum, quem suprà (secundum Hippocratis sententiam in lib. de prisca medicina) sorbitiones crassas interpretati sumus, vt ex quisitè tenuem victum sorbitiones tenues, morbo chronico tanquam non vrgenti non cõpete re manifestum est. Hucusque ostendimus, secundum senis sententiam qui conueniant victus ijs quos maxime, multum, mediocriter, parumq;, et nihil, vrgent morbi. Verum in ijs virtutis tanquam non urgentis scopum nõ adduximus: Diximusque cum uirtus parum urgere incipiat, proxime cras̄iorem uictum, eo quem morbi dispositio indicauit exhibendum. Quod si multum uictum qui secundo loco est, fore ministrandum: Ita ut cum uirtus multum, & morbus maximè urgent, tenues sorbitiones competant. Quod asseruit Hippocrates in tertio cõ mentario libri de ratione victus, cum de col- liquantibus febribus sermonem facit, in hunc modum. Deiectiones (inquit) huiusmodi ha- bent quidem, & alias, quae graues sunt, offen sas. neque enim hypochondriorum extinguunt ardorem, sed excitant, inquietationem & membrorum iactationem faciunt: intestina eti am sedem & exulcerant. Quibus verbis Hip- pocrates morbum maximè vrgentem depin xit, virtutem ob maleficas deiectiones mul tum vrgere. Sed audi quae statim scribit: Qui ergo in morbis huiusmodi, relictis sorbitioni- bus, mulsa potius alterius vice vtetur, is vt multa feliciter consequetur, sic ei nequaquam praeter animi sententiam succedet multa. Sed quasnam an tenues aut crassas intellexerit Galenus in expositione recte in hunc modum expressit: Nempe in solis (inquit) qui colliquę faciunt morbis, vel in quibus hominum vir- tus ad morbi vsque iudicationem sufficere non possit, ad ptisanæ cremore perueniemus. Cremorem ptisanæ, tenuem esse sorbitionem supra diximus. Rursus ponamus morbum & virtutem multum vrgere, crassam sorbitionem ijs conuenientem victu esse diximus: Quod similiter secundum senis sententiam esse ostendimus, qui ita scribit: Quibus (inquit) per febres aluus liquida est, & mens turbatur, horumque multi floccos vellunt, naresque fodiunt, & parum quidem interrogatis respondent, sed ex se nihil quod compositum sit dicunt, & c. Et statim ita scribit: His igitur ita habentibus, si venter liquidus fuerit, absumensque & contabefaciens, sorbitiones crassiores frigidiores, exhibendae sunt. Percepisti ne, ex signis morbum et virtutem multum vrgentes descripsisse, crassasque sorbitiones tali concursu ministrasse?
units.tr: But let us show that the individual parts of our table are in accordance with the old man's opinion. A disease pressing most demands complete fasting, strength not dissuading, as he shows in the aphorism which we cited above: "Where, therefore, the disease is very acute and at once has its final pains, it is necessary to use the most attenuated diet at the extreme." What other disease could you more reasonably call one pressing most than one which brings the final pains? To such a disease he says the most attenuated diet at the extreme is suited, which above, with Galen, we interpreted as complete fasting. He wrote the same more openly in the second commentary on the regimen of diet, where he says: "Nor should food be given while the diseases are vigorous and have heat." Second, with the disease pressing much, it is agreed that drinks are to be administered, as he wrote in the first book on the diet of acute diseases, in these words: "Afterwards, if pain or some danger appears, one should give gruel, neither much nor thick, but after the seventh or ninth day if the patient is strong." Where he added the words "if he is strong," he made an indication of strength not pressing. A little before, he said more openly: "Where some pain has troubled, you will give oxymel to drink." It is clear that by these pains are not to be understood those which torment the sick according to the paroxysms, but those which are constant and arise from inflammations, and which make the disease press; as is plain to those practised in the books on the regimen of diet. But lest time be wasted on citing each passage in turn, it would be more convenient to have shown the matter in such a way that anyone may easily gather the rest from what has been said. It has been shown, according to the mind of Hippocrates, that fasting suits a disease pressing most, and drinks suit one pressing much. Since by the same precept one must descend to a thicker diet only as far as the disease is milder at its end, a thicker diet suits a disease pressing moderately than one pressing much; and since both the disease which presses much and that which presses moderately are closely neighbouring, it is clear that thin gruels are to be given in this case according to the mind of Hippocrates. For after drinks, the next thicker diet is thin gruel. But for a disease pressing slightly, thick gruels; for one not pressing, things that are eaten. Therefore, if you wish to nourish those who suffer from a disease that does not press with gruels or drinks, you will not err slightly. This is plainly written by the old man in the aphorism beginning: "A thin and exquisite diet is always deceptive in chronic diseases, and in acute ones to which it is not suited." It is clear that the diseases he calls chronic do not bring symptoms by reason of which the disease presses; nor does a continuous fever admit a chronic disease. For this same continuity of fever constitutes an acute disease, as Hippocrates and Galen are the authors in the book of prognostics. Therefore it is clear that a thin diet, which above (according to Hippocrates' opinion in the book On Ancient Medicine) we interpreted as thick gruels, namely that an exquisitely thin diet, thin gruels, is not suited to a chronic disease as if it were not pressing. So far we have shown, according to the old man's opinion, which diets suit those diseases that press most, much, moderately, slightly, and not at all. But in these we have not included the aim of strength as not pressing; and we said that when strength begins to press slightly, the thicker diet nearest to that which the disposition of the disease indicated must be given. But if the second diet is to be administered for strength pressing much, then when strength presses much and the disease most, thin gruels are suitable. Hippocrates asserted this in the third commentary on the book On the Regimen, when he discusses colliquative fevers, in this manner: "Evacuations of this kind," he says, "have other things too which are heavy and offensive; for they neither extinguish the heat of the hypochondria but excite it, cause restlessness and tossing of the limbs, and they also ulcerate the seat of the intestines." By these words Hippocrates depicted a disease pressing most, with strength pressing much because of the harmful evacuations. But hear what he writes next: "Therefore whoever in diseases of this kind, leaving aside gruels, uses mulsum instead, will succeed happily in many things; but in no way will many things succeed for him beyond the intention of the mind." But what Galen, in his exposition, rightly expressed as to whether he meant thin or thick: "Namely, in those diseases alone which cause colliquation, or in which the strength of men cannot suffice up to the judgement of the disease, we come to the broth of barley." We said above that the broth of barley is a thin gruel. Again, let us suppose that disease and strength both press much; we said that a thick gruel suits such a diet. This we have likewise shown according to the old man's opinion, who writes thus: "In those (he says) whose bowels are liquid through fevers, and whose mind is troubled, and many of whom pick at flocks and dig at the nostrils, and answer little when questioned but say nothing coherent of themselves, etc." And immediately he writes: "These things being so, if the belly is liquid and wasting and consuming, thicker and colder gruels are to be given." Have you perceived that from these signs he described disease and strength both pressing much, and that he administered thick gruels to such a concurrence?

units.la: Sed abunde de victus forma dictum est.
units.tr: But enough has been said about the form of diet.

units.la: BRVDI LVSITANI DE VICTV FEBRICITANTIVM LIBER SECVNDVS, qui est de quantitate & qualitate uictus, & de numero & hora administrationis eius.
units.tr: The Second Book of Brudus the Lusitanian on the Diet of Feverish Patients, which is concerning the quantity and quality of diet, and concerning the number and hour of its administration.

units.la: A quibus quantitas uictus sumatur. CAPVT I.
units.tr: From what the quantity of food is taken. CHAPTER I.

units.la: NVNC de quantitate uictus, tempestiuum est agere. Nisi enim potus, aut sorbitionis quantitatem nouerimus, aut naturam minus iusto exhibentes laedimus, aut morbum si plus ministrauimus, augebimus. Victus quantitatis, à consuetudine & morbi constitutione, indicatio sumitur. Consuetudo eam uictus quantitatem designat, quam aegrotans solidioris cibi bona ingerebat valitudine. Sunt enim qui multum noraces sunt cum sanitate fruuntur, ijs multum sorbitionis tionis, aut potus concedendum est, parum ijs qui parce utuntur. Hoc nos docuit Hippocra- tes in hæc uerba: Verùm inter initia, neq; multam, neq; crassam admodum dare oportet, sed quantum ob consuetudinem, & ne multa uasorum inanitio fiat. Morbi proinde constitutio ab ea quam consuetudo indicauit quantitate detrahit. Vt si uictus quantitatem laborantis naturam ferre non posse coieceris, aut ob temporis breuitatem ad sequentem accessionem, aut ob morbi molestationem, aut quia sorbitionibus æger usus non est, ab ea quâ no bis quantitate consuetudo indicauit, detrahemus. Subtractionis autem modus erit, ut nō multa fiat uasorum inanitio. Consuetudo igitur maximam designat quantitatem, quam inter initia morbi offeremus. Vt si Socrati laboranti, uictus formâ tenues sorbitiones esse diffinieris, tantū eorū offeres inter initia quantum solidiori cibo bona utebatur ualitudine. Proinde prout morbus, & eius symptomata aucta fuerint, ita ab ea quam consuetudo indicauit quantitate detrahendum est. Vt si manifesto incremento morbi symptomata aut ęta fuerint penes vehementiam & duratio nem, sensibiliter ab ea victus quantitate quā primis obtulimus diebus minuemus. Nec hoc præter senis mentem est, loco citato, vbi ita scribit: Postea si dolor quispiam, vel periculum comparuerit, sorbitionem dare oportet, lum comparuerit, sorbitionem dare oportet, nec multam, nec crassam &c. Rationi præterea consentaneum videtur, vt eo minus ex hibeatur tempore quo laborans magis morbo molestatur, quā cum mediocriter habet. In initio cum ægrotantes vtcunque moderatius habeant, tantum exhibendum, quantū consuetudo indicauerit. Apud statum verò quia morbi symptomata in maxima sunt vehementia, nihil esse exhibendū, ab eodē didicimus. Intermedio verò tempore mediocrem ministrabimus quantitatem, sed cum non ex æquo singulis diebus, aut alternis, nec morbus, nec eius symptomata augeantur, non iu xta dierum numerum à principio, quantitatem minuendam, sed prout morbus & symptomata increscunt. Ex ijs tamen ad exactā victus victus quantitatem te posse peruenire haud-quaquam speres. Nam quantum a quantitate quam consuetudo indicauit, demere oportet, ob morbi & symptomatum incrementum, exacte nõscimus. Ob id igitur prudentissimus Hippocrates ciborum adiectionem intendendum multo minus ait, &c. In cui usexpositione Galenus ita scribit: Adscripsit in quantitate ipsa ad id quod minus est, procedendum esse magis, quàm ad id quod exuperat, vbi quis a iusto modo abscedit. Nempe quod plus est exuperatque, noxas interdum inemendabiles facit: verùm quod minus est, facile emendatur. Nempe si virtus elabi videatur cibi exiguum ministrare posse sumus. Verùm si in ventrem absorptus fuerit cibus, quod redundat superfluitque, si alias multo magis in acutis tollere est difficile. In quibus verbis aperte ostendit cum ab exacta errandum sit quantitate, melius esse, ad id quod minus est accedere. Nam error hic minus laesionis afferet.
units.tr: NOW it is time to discuss the quantity of food. For unless we know the quantity of the drink or gruel, we either harm the patient by giving less than is right, or, if we give too much, we make the disease worse. The indication for the quantity of food is taken from the habit of the patient and the constitution of the disease. Habit shows the quantity of food which the patient, when in good health, used to take of more solid nourishment. For there are some who eat a great deal when they are well; these must be allowed more gruel or drink, and those who eat sparingly, less. Hippocrates taught us this in these words: "But at the beginning, one should give neither much nor very thick food, but as much as the habit requires, and so that there is no great emptying of the vessels." The constitution of the disease therefore takes away from the quantity which habit indicated. For if you judge that the patient's strength cannot bear the quantity which habit indicated, either because of the shortness of time before the next paroxysm, or because of the troublesomeness of the disease, or because the patient is not accustomed to gruel, you will subtract from that quantity which habit has shown us. The manner of subtraction will be that no great emptying of the vessels occurs. Habit, then, indicates the greatest quantity which we shall offer at the beginning of the disease. So if you have decided that Socrates, who is ill with a fever, should have thin gruel as his diet, you will offer him at the start only as much as he took when he was in good health with more solid food. Accordingly, as the disease and its symptoms increase, so the quantity must be reduced from that which habit indicated. So if, with a clear increase of the disease, the symptoms have become more severe and longer lasting, we shall diminish noticeably the quantity of food which we offered on the first days. Nor is this against the mind of the old man, in the passage cited, where he writes: "Afterwards, if some pain or danger appears, one must give gruel, neither much nor thick, etc." Moreover, it seems consonant with reason that less should be given at the time when the patient is more troubled by the disease than when he is moderately affected. At the beginning, when the patients are in a fairly moderate state, as much should be given as habit indicates. But at the height of the disease, when its symptoms are at their most violent, we learned from the same man that nothing should be given. In the intervening time we shall give a moderate quantity, but not equally on each day or on alternate days; and if neither the disease nor its symptoms increase, the quantity is not to be reduced according to the number of days from the beginning, but as the disease and symptoms increase. Yet you must not hope to arrive at the exact quantity of food from these things, for we do not know exactly how much must be subtracted from the quantity which habit indicated, on account of the increase of the disease and its symptoms. For this reason, therefore, the most prudent Hippocrates says that the addition of food should be attended to much less, etc. Galen, expounding this passage, writes: "He has added that in the quantity itself one should proceed more toward what is less than toward what is excessive, when one departs from the right measure. For what is in excess does sometimes produce harms that cannot be remedied, but what is less is easily corrected. Indeed, if strength seems to be slipping away, we can give a small amount of food; but if food has been absorbed into the belly, what overflows and is superfluous is difficult to remove, especially in acute cases." In these words he clearly shows that, since one must err from the exact quantity, it is better to move toward what is less. For this error will cause less injury.

units.la: An melius sit ad id quod magis est accede-re, quàm ad minus, ubi à iusto modo sit abscedendum.
units.tr: Whether it is better to move toward what is greater than toward what is less, when one must depart from the right measure.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: AT alicui forsan contrarium videbitur. Nam id certum est grauioribus ægrotantes offensis affici, cum propè statum erra tum sit, quàm si in morborum principijs quip-piam delinquatur. Vt ab Hippocrate & Ga leno scriptum est, illo loco, Hoc autem verius efficaciusque, &c. Cunque inter initia minus quàm iustum est offerimus, sic agentes virtutem imbecilliorem reddemus, ita vt apud morbi statum, omnimodam sustinere inediam non possit. Quare cibum tunc tem-poris offerre cogemur, quod multo grauius est, quàm si inter initia vberius ægrum re-ficeremus. Nec putandum est fieri posse, vt minus inter initia quàm iustum est exhi-bentibus, virtus ad statum peruenire possit, tanto virium robore, vt totum vigoris tem pus omnimoda transfire queat inedia. Nam si id possit, non minus quàm quod iustum est exhibuisti, sed quod mediocre & conueniens erat.
units.tr: BUT perhaps it will seem otherwise to someone. For it is certain that patients who are weighed down by more serious offences are affected when the disease is nearly at its height, more than if some fault is committed at the beginning of the diseases. As is written by Hippocrates and Galen in that passage, "But this is truer and more effective," etc. And when at the beginning we offer less than is right, in this way we make the strength weaker, so that at the height of the disease it cannot endure total fasting. Therefore we shall be forced to offer food at that time, which is much more serious than if at the beginning we had restored the patient more fully. Nor should one think that it can happen that, when less than is right is given at the beginning, the strength can reach the height of the disease with such robustness that it can get through the whole period of vigour without any fasting. For if it could, you have given not less than what is right, but what was moderate and suitable.

units.la: 2. de ratione uictus in acutis. erat. Praeterea Hippocrates ipse pare confessus est errore esse, postquam enim de forma victus sermone fecisset, de quantitate agens, ita scribit: Praeterea (inquit) non minor est error, nec minus homine laedit, si quis det, propinet ue, minus, tardius ue, quam satis est, et expediat. Pars enim famis, & inediae, plurimum in homines natura, & valentem facere, & infirmum, ac perimere potest. Multa etiam alia mala illis non similia ex plenitudine proficiscuntur, quae non minus etiam gravia & periculosa sunt. Vere ita res habet, graviorem esse errorem, qui in id quod magis urget addit. Cunque morbus ob eius vehementiam magis urget, potiorem praebet indicationem, unde minus laedemus minus exhibentes, magis vero plus ministrantes. Nam sic in id, quod magis urget addimus. Quod si de virtute, ob eius imbecillitatem magis simus soliciti, cauendum esse constat errorem eum, quo virtus imbecillior reddatur, quare tunc temporis ad id quod magis est accedimus, dumodo quatitas pro virtute sit. Morbis autem acutis cum ut plurimum capiantur iuuenes, aut consi-stentes, quorum vires valida sunt, minimeque in longum morbus protrahatur: magis vrge re morbum, quam virtutis imbecillitatem, rationabile est. Quare ad id quod minus est accedemus, magis verentes, ne plus exhibentes in id quod magis vrget addamus. Recte igitur Hippocrates dixit, ciborum adiectioni intendendum multo minus, magis nos solicitos esse oportere, de morbi acumine, quam virtute docet, praecipue in morbis iis qui breui terminantur. In quibus saepenumero omni no subtrahere expedit, cum aeger sufficere possit, donec morbus maturescat. At in libro de prisca medicina, universalem faciens sermonem, vtrunque errorem grauem esse dixit, ac si aeque vrgentes virtutem & morbum sin xisset. Neque ratio quicquam eorum quae diximus tollit: nam errorem quem prima exhibitione committimus, minus exhibentes, non apud statum corrigimus, sed secunda, aut tertia oblatione emedamus. Quod quia ad opus apprime vtile erit, explicabimus. Socrati febre continua laboranti, sorbitionem dare decreueris, in primis modum, quo in bona valitudine, cibo & potu vtebatur, inquires, iuxta quem sorbitionis quantitatem diffinies. A qua postea iuxta morbi incrementu detrahes. Talemque (eamq;) offeres primu quantitatem, vt commode apparare (cocoquere) possit, citra additionem vehementia aut durationis accessionis febrilis. Quod si ab eo cibo quem primo exhibuisti nullu horu sequatur, aegrotansq; plus ferre posset, aut voluisset, paru addes sequenti oblatione, quia quod minus est exhibuisti. Et ita id quod minus est facile emendatur. Quod si plus exhiberemus quam aegrotantis natura citra lasionem ferre posset, noxam emendari ita facile non est. Errorem quidem hunc hac sequuntur incommoda, nempe grauitas hypochondriorum, frequentia anhelitus, febriles incensiones, sitis, capitis dolores, &c. Hac omnia in morbis acutis eueniunt ex immodica cibi quantitate, & ex intempestiua eius oblatione, vt ab Hippocrate scriptum est in libris de ratione victus. Nulla ergo alia melior mensura dari potest, qua victus quantitatem diffiniamus, quàm sensus ægrotantis, qui magis & minus indicat citra errorem. Prima autem oblatio-ne, ut ab ea iudicium capiamus in posterum, minus quàm consuetudo indicat offerri melius esse diximus. Nec hoc est præter senis mentē, qui in eodem de prisca medicina libro, ita ait:
units.tr: 2. On the regimen in acute diseases. Besides, Hippocrates himself has openly confessed that it is an error; for after he had spoken of the form of diet, treating of the quantity he writes: "Moreover (he says), it is no smaller an error, and it harms a man no less, if someone gives, or lets him drink, less or later than is enough and expedient. For a part of hunger and fasting can by nature destroy men, making them strong or weak, and can kill them. Many other evils, not similar to these, arise from fullness, which are no less grave and dangerous." Truly the matter stands thus: the error is more serious when it adds to what presses harder. And when the disease, because of its violence, presses harder, it offers the stronger indication; so we shall do less harm by giving less, but more harm by giving more, for thus we add to what presses harder. But if we are more anxious about the strength, because of its weakness, it is established that we must avoid the error by which the strength is made weaker; therefore at that time we move toward what is greater, provided the quantity is suited to the strength. But in acute diseases, since they are for the most part seized on young men, or men of settled age, whose powers are sound, and since the disease is least drawn out over a long time, it is reasonable to be more concerned about the disease than about the weakness of the strength. Therefore we shall move toward what is less, being more fearful lest by giving more we add to what presses harder. Rightly, then, did Hippocrates say that the addition of food should be attended to much less; he teaches that we ought to be more anxious about the sharpness of the disease than about the strength, especially in those diseases which end in a short time. In these cases it is often expedient to subtract entirely, since the patient can get along until the disease comes to its crisis. But in the book On Ancient Medicine, making a general statement, he said that both errors are serious, as though he had considered strength and disease to be equally pressing. Nor does reason remove any of the things we have said; for the error which we commit by giving less at the first offering we do not correct at the height, but by the second or third offering we remedy it. Because this will be especially useful for the work, we shall explain it. If you have decided to give gruel to Socrates, who is suffering from continuous fever, you will first inquire into the manner of diet by which he used to eat and drink when in good health, and according to that you will define the quantity of gruel; from this you will afterwards subtract according to the increase of the disease. And you will offer first such a quantity that it can be conveniently prepared and digested, without addition in the violence or duration of the febrile paroxysm. But if none of these things follows from the food which you first gave, and the patient could bear or would have wished more, you will add a little at the next offering, since you gave less. And so what is less is easily corrected. But if we gave more than the patient's nature could bear without injury, the harm is not so easily repaired. This error is followed by these discomforts: heaviness of the hypochondria, frequent breathing, feverish burnings, thirst, headaches, etc. All these happen in acute diseases from an immoderate quantity of food and from an untimely offering of it, as Hippocrates wrote in the books On Regimen. No better measure can therefore be given by which to define the quantity of food than the sense of the patient, which indicates more or less without error. But with the first offering, so that from it we may form a judgement for the future, we have said that it is better to offer less than habit indicates. Nor is this against the mind of the old man, who in the same book On Ancient Medicine says:

units.la: Præterea varia multo magis est, ac maioris diligētiæ eget hæc res. mensuram enim cuius-dam animo considerare oportet. Mensuram dico non quæ pondere, numeróue ullo cōstet, quā si quis respiciat quod expediat, exactum ue sit, possit cognoscere. Nihil enim aliud inuenires quàm corporis sensum. Quam ob rem tam exactè rem nouisse uti parū utrinque er-ret quis difficillimū est. Tametsi hunc ego me dicū valdè laudo, qui paululū in iis rebus ab-erret peccet ne. Quod autem exactum & ve-ro proximum est, raro admodū scire et vide-re est. Siquidem plurimi medici in iis mihi si-miles esse videntur, prauis nauium rectori-bus. Nam cum illi in tranquillitate regendo peccant, errant ue eorum error non patet. Cum autem eos magnus ventus, atq; aduersa tempestas deprehendit, liquido iam & aperte cunctis hominibus qui in ea sunt patet, per eorum ignorantiam & errorem peccatu̅ nauem nisi succurratur perditum iri. Sic mali & plurimi medici, cum homines qui nihil graue & periculosum habent curantur, si quis in ijs maxime peccet, erret ue, nihil admodum graue & periculosum admittat. Nam multo plura & saepius leuiuscula hominibus mala fiunt, quam grauia & periculosa. In quibus si peccet errent ue, rudibus & ignaris non patet. Cum autem magnum & vehementem fallacemque morbum nanciscuntur, tunc eorum error, & peccatum, arsque cunctis patet.
units.tr: Moreover, this matter is far more varied and needs much greater care. For one must consider the measure in the mind of the physician. I do not mean a measure that is fixed by any weight or number, by which anyone who looks to what is expedient could know whether it is exact or not. For you would find nothing other than the sense of the body. Therefore it is very difficult for anyone to know the matter so precisely that he errs in neither direction at all. Even so, I highly praise the man who errs only slightly in such things. But to hit what is exact and very close to the truth is rarely something one can know and see. Indeed, most physicians seem to me like bad pilots of ships. When they make mistakes in steering in calm weather, their error is not apparent. But when a great wind and adverse storm catches them, it becomes clear to everyone on board that the ship will be lost through their ignorance and error unless help is given. So too with many physicians: when they treat people who have nothing serious or dangerous, if they go most wrong in these cases, or err, they commit nothing very serious or dangerous. For far more numerous and frequent are the trivial ailments that befall people than the grave and dangerous ones. If they sin or err in these, the mistake is not apparent to the untrained and ignorant. But when they encounter a great and violent and deceptive disease, then their error, their fault and their skill are all plain to everyone.

units.la: An forma uictus seruanda sit à morbi initio ad statum usque, & quantitas mutanda an econtra.
units.tr: Whether the form of diet is to be kept from the beginning of the disease until its state, and whether the quantity is to be changed, or the reverse.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: SED forsan quis obiiciet, ex iis quae dicta sunt apparare, vna victus forma, nutrie dos esse ægrotantes, à morbi initio ad statum vsque incedendo: quantitatem autem secundum morbi incrementum mutandam. Inter initia, iuxta consuetudinem, victus quantitatem, mensurandam, increscente verò sensibiliter morbo, minuendam. At videtur magis ex vsu fore ægrotantibus, si semper quantitatem seruemus quam consuetudo indicat, formam verò mutemus. Vt si inter initia morbi, crassa sorbitione ægrotantem alere nobis visum fuerit, increscente morbo tenuem offeramus, ea qua vsus est quantitate. Naturam siquidem semper gaudere consuetis, asseruit Galenus ex auctoritate Hippocratis. Praeterea hoc idem in Aphorismis sentire videtur, cum ait, Ἐμπροσθεν δὲ ἀπιωτέρως σιαυταχῳ, ὡς αὐ ἐξαρκεῖσι ὁ νοσέων. hoc est, Ante verò vberius reficiendum, vt sufficiat ægrotans, per illud verbum ἀπιωτέρως σιαυτῶν nō quantitatem, sed victus formam intellexit. Praeterea in loco quem citasti, non magis quantitatem mutandam esse docet, quàm formā, cum ait. Neque multā, neque crassam dare oportet. Sicut
units.tr: But perhaps someone will object, from what has been said, that one form of diet should be kept for the sick from the beginning of the disease until its height, and that only the quantity should be changed as the disease grows. At the start, by custom, the quantity of food is to be measured, and when the disease sensibly increases, it is to be reduced. Yet it seems more useful to the sick if we always keep the quantity that custom indicates and change the form instead. For example, if at the beginning of the illness we have thought fit to nourish the patient with thick gruel, then as the disease increases we should offer thin gruel in the same quantity he was used to. Galen asserts, on the authority of Hippocrates, that nature always delights in what is customary. Moreover, Hippocrates seems to hold the same view in the Aphorisms, when he says: [Ἐμπροσθεν δὲ ἀφθονωτέρως σιτευτέον, ὡς ἂν ἐξαρκῇ τῷ νοσέοντι], that is, "Before this, one should feed more generously, so that the patient is sufficiently nourished." By the phrase "more generously" he meant not the quantity but the form of the diet. Furthermore, in the passage you cited, he teaches that the quantity is not to be changed any more than the form, when he says: "One must give neither much nor thick food."

units.la: 8. de methodo mendi.
units.tr: 8. de methodo medendi.

units.la: 1. de victu acutorum. Sicut enim multitudo ad quantitatem attinet: sic crassities & tenuitas formam victus respiciunt. Verùm vbi ut quicquam asseras deest recta ratio, dicta insequere antiquissimi viri Hippocratis, qui multorum sapientum vnus instar est: à quo didicimus victus formam morbi initio adstatum non permutandam esse. Sed quo in loco forsan quæres. Ex libro de victu acutorum secundo, cum de permutationibus agit colliges. Apertius tamen à Galeno duobus in locis, nempe in expositione illius, Conijcere autem oportet robur & morbi, &c. vbi ita scribit, Nempe summa quam adstruit est, nõ permutandam esse victus speciem, priusquam signa coctionis manifesta sint. Id autem fiet, si quot die bus ad vigorem morbus venturus sit, præco gnoueris. In quibus verbis manifestè ostendit à morbi initio ad status introitu vna victus forma nutriendos esse ægrotantes. Alia verò toto eo tempore quo durat status ad perfectā morbi solutionem. Demum alia per totū convalescentiæ tempus ad sanitatis habitum. In singulis ergo harum quatuor conditionū, non faciendæ sunt insignes victuum permutationes de vna victus forma in aliam, priusquā ad aliam conditionem peruentum sit. Idem prætereā in eodem secundo, ita scribit in expositione illius, Interdum aut et cruda, &c. Vniuersa hæc contingere ÿs ait, qui perperā cibati sunt à medicis, quicunque primis diebus exoluentes laborantes, sanè circa tertiū, vel quartum, vel quintum, vel sextum, repente ad edulia permutauerūt, nondū morbi vigore peracto: quasi peracto, conuenienter eos permutasse victū dicat. Quod igitur dicebat quod permutare quidem oportet victum sanorū in morbis, non quidem vt forte euenit illud agendum, iam puto manifestū ex dictis esse. Existētē enim constitutione corporis vna cum sanitas adesl: altera à morbi principio vsque ad statum, alia ad perfectam solutionem, & post hanc alia quæ convalescentiæ tempus ad vsque sanitatis habitum occupat. In nulla harum quatuor constitutionum facere oportet magnas victus mutamutationes, antequam in aliam constitutionis speciem perveniantur. Qui igitur aegros morborum exordiis in omni ciborum abstinentia servant, si ad vigore usque talem victus speciem servare possent, nemo eos culpauerit. Quod si facere non possunt, &c. Idem dixit in eodem in expositione illius, De mutatione quae in hac vel illa fit, plurima sum locutus, &c. Rursus sermonem totum in summa unam coegit Hippocrates: In iis qui similiter habent victu haudquaquam permutare praecipies: verum in iis qui ex sanitate ad morbu transeunt, permutare quidem, non tamen ut caeteri permutant. Deinde compendio quodam victus scopum in acutis morbis declarauit. Siquidem morbus maturuerit transeundu ad cremorem ptisanae praecipit: Si adhuc crudus fuerit non transeundum, nisi ob aliquod symptoma. Haec sunt loca ex quibus colligo in constitutione una, prout est a morbi initio, ad statum usque, non permutandam esse victus speciem. Quod si iam dictis illud Hippocratis adiungas, Nō igitur intepestiuae neque fortes vasorum inanitiones moliri, neque cum morbi vigent, cibum dare, neque repente huc, vel illuc, in toto negocio quicquam mutare licet, manifestum erit quod si eadem victus forma, & eadem quantitate, per morbi initium & incrementum vtere-mur, apud statum vero cibum omnino prohi beremus, ægrotantes ex repentina victus mu tatione læderemus. Item rationi consonũ est, vt cum paroxysmorum incrementa, & lon giores durationes minus temporis quiescere laborantes permittunt, magis tenui victu nu triendos fore. Cunque victus species secundũ antiquorũ mentem mutanda non sit, durante eadem morbi constitutione, reliquum est, vt quantitates imminuamus, prout morbus incrementum accepit. Id etiam ab Hippocra te licet colligere in primo de victu acutorũ, nam stante eadem morbi constitutione, cum alimoniam addere intendit, & virtutem ro-borare, victus formam seruat immutatam, quantitatem augendam præcipit. Vt in eo, ⁂ At si os madescat, et quæ à pulmone expuun turtur talia sint qualia esse oportet, sorbitionis quantitatem, vt summatim dicā augere conuenit. Et infra statim, Et quanto maior fuerit expurgatio, tanto magis ad indicationem vsque dare oportet. Econtrario igitur à morbi initio per totum incrementum adstatum, cum minus nutrire ægrotantem intendamus, victus specie manente, quantitatem imminuemus, prout morbus manifesta habuerit incrementa. Minusque naturam huiusmodi laedi posse mutatione, quàm si formam victus immutaremus cogitabimus. Consuetudo enim magis formam victus & eius qualitatem respicit, quàm quantitatem. Et ob id difficilius fert natura, si assuetam victus formam, & qualitatem immutes, si verò ab assueta detrahas quantitate, non adeo. Ob id stante eadem morbi constitutione, vt minor fiat mutatio, quantitas mutanda est, forma autem victus seruanda. Nec praetereundum est, aetatem, regionem, coindicatrices quantitatis esse, praeterea numeri multiplicationis prohibitione. Haec enim maiorem indicant quantitatem. Vt si puero multoties edere assueto propter morbu toties ministrare cibu non possimus, quod a numero deest, id quantitate ipsa sup-plebimus. Vt scite a Galeno scriptum est in expositione illius, Quibus semel, aut bis &c. vbi ita scribit: Si vero accessiones no permiserint, neq; alimenti offerendi occasiones fuerint multae, raro plura dabimus. Vnde quida male hunc vertit locum, in hunc modu, Neque multi alimeti offerendi occasiones fuerint. Hyems multu exhibendu esse indicat: consimiliter et regio frigida. Sed haec ad imminuendam victus quantitate, qua consuetudo indicat, vires habent: minime ad augendam. Ab ijs ergo victus quantitas diminienda est.
units.tr: 1. de victu acutorum. For just as multitude relates to quantity, so thickness and thinness relate to the form of diet. But when right reason fails you in any assertion, follow the sayings of the most ancient man, Hippocrates, who is equal to many wise men together, and from whom we have learned that the form of diet is not to be changed from the beginning of the disease until its height. But you will perhaps ask in what place. You will gather it from the second book of the work On the Diet in Acute Diseases, where he treats of changes. More plainly, however, Galen says so in two places, namely in his exposition of the passage beginning "But one must consider the strength of the disease," etc., where he writes: "The sum of what he asserts is that the kind of diet must not be changed before the signs of concoction are manifest. This will happen if you have foreseen on how many days the disease will come to its vigour." In these words he clearly shows that from the beginning of the disease until the onset of its height, the patients are to be nourished with one form of diet; another during the whole time the height lasts, until the complete resolution of the disease; and finally another throughout the whole period of convalescence until the state of health. In each of these four conditions, therefore, no striking changes of diet from one form to another are to be made before the patient has reached the next condition. Likewise, in the same second book, in his exposition of that passage, Galen writes: Sometimes also raw, etc. He says all these things happen to those who have been fed badly by physicians, who, while the patients were discharging in the first days, suddenly switched to solid foods around the third, fourth, fifth or sixth day, before the vigour of the disease was over, as if he were saying that they had changed the diet appropriately once the disease was over. So what he said, that one ought indeed to change the diet of the healthy in diseases, but not in the way that happens by chance, I think is now clear from what has been said. For when the state of the body exists, health is present; the first state is from the beginning of the disease to its height, another to complete resolution, and after this another which occupies the time of convalescence up to the state of health. In none of these four states should great changes of diet be made before passing into another kind of state. Therefore, if physicians keep the sick at the beginning of their diseases on complete abstinence from all food, no one could blame them, provided they could keep such a form of diet until the vigour of the disease. But if they cannot do so, etc. He said the same thing in the same book, in his exposition of that passage: "I have spoken at length about the change that occurs in this or that case," etc. Again, Hippocrates gathered the whole discourse into one summary: "In those who are alike, you will by no means advise a change of diet; but in those who pass from health to disease, a change should indeed be made, yet not as others make it." Then, in a kind of brief summary, he set out the aim of diet in acute diseases: if the disease has ripened, he advises a move to the gruel of barley-water; if it is still raw, one should not move on, unless because of some symptom. These are the passages from which I gather that, in a single constitution, from the beginning of the disease up to its height, the kind of diet is not to be changed. And if you add to these things that saying of Hippocrates, "Therefore it is not allowed to attempt untimely or strong evacuations of the vessels, nor to give food when the disease is at its height, nor to change anything suddenly, this way or that, in the whole business," it will be clear that if we used the same form and the same quantity of diet through the beginning and increase of the disease, but withheld food altogether at its height, we would harm the patients by a sudden change of diet. It is also consistent with reason that, since the increases of the paroxysms and their longer durations do not allow the sufferers much rest, they should be nourished on a lighter diet. And since the form of diet, according to the mind of the ancients, is not to be changed while the same constitution of the disease lasts, it remains that we diminish the quantities as the disease gains in strength. Hippocrates also allows this to be inferred in the first book On the Diet in Acute Diseases; for while the same constitution of the disease persists, when he intends to add nourishment and to strengthen the vital powers, he keeps the form of diet unchanged and orders the quantity to be increased. As in that passage: "But if the mouth grows moist and what is brought up from the lungs is of the proper kind, it is fitting, to put it briefly, to increase the quantity of gruel." And directly after: "And the greater the discharge, the more one must give, up to the point indicated." Conversely, therefore, from the beginning of the disease through its whole increase up to its height, since we intend to nourish the patient less, while the kind of diet remains the same, we shall diminish the quantity as the disease shows clear increases. And we shall consider that such a nature can be harmed less by a change of quantity than if we changed the form of diet. For custom regards the form of diet and its quality more than its quantity; and for that reason nature bears it less well if you alter the accustomed form and quality, but not so much if you take away from the accustomed quantity. Therefore, while the same constitution of the disease continues, the quantity is to be changed, so that the change is smaller, but the form of diet is to be kept. Nor must we pass over the fact that age, region and the number of meals are indicators of quantity, besides the prohibition on frequent feeding. For these indicate a larger quantity. For example, if a boy accustomed to eat many times a day cannot be given food so often because of the disease, what is lacking in number we shall make up in quantity. As Galen wrote well in his exposition of the passage beginning "To those who once or twice," where he says: "But if the attacks do not permit it, and there are not many occasions for offering food, we shall give more rarely, but more at a time." Hence some translate this passage badly, as follows: "Nor are there many occasions for offering food." Winter indicates that much should be given, and likewise a cold region. But these considerations have force for diminishing the quantity of diet that custom indicates, and hardly any for increasing it. Therefore the quantity of diet is to be diminished from these considerations.

units.la: A quibus numerus oblationis cibi sumatur.
units.tr: From what the number of offerings of food is to be taken.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: SED easdem numerus habet considerationes. nam a consuetudine in primis, & a morbi dispositione oblationis numerum scito sumendum esse: vt scriptum est ab Hippocrate in haec verba: Qui enim bis cibari sunt soliti, his ptisanam dare oportet: quibus se mel, semel quidem primo die detur, &c. hoc numero quem consuetudo indicat, qua à morbo sumitur indicatio detrahit. Nam prin cipia, & incrementa, & status accessionu, aliquando numerum oblationis consuetu seruare prohibent. Virtus autem corporis plerunque super addit, cum imbecilles sunt: aut cum eum ministramus cibum, qui parum nu triat, & volumus ut roboretur natura, nu merum tunc cibationis addimus, si per morbum liceat. Vt si febre continua labores is qui multo cibo bona utebatur valitudine, vi- sumus nobis sit huic ptisanam exhibere ob aliquas causas, cum vltra eam quantitatem quam consuetudo praestitit exhibere non lice at vice vna, numerum oblationis addere stude bimus, ob id quod hic multo indiget nutrime to, parum & alimenti ptisana suppeditat. Hoc videtur intellexisse Hippocrates eodem primo libro, in haec verba: Quibus semel, semel quidem primo die detur: deinde sensim, pau- latim, si fieri potest, ijs quoque detur, si quid putas adjiciendum. Infirmum igitur toties nu-triemus quoties consuetudo indicauerit, nisi aut facultas crebrius, aut morbus rarius in-dicauerint. Consuetudo igitur primam quan-titatem siue maximam, & primum nume-rum, penes quem aliquando rarius, quando-que crebrius, ægrotantibus cibum ministra-re dicimus, proponit. Huic aut virtus addit, aut morbus minuit. Scite ergo Hippocrates in Aphorismis dixit: Quibus semel aut bis, aut plura, dandum est aliquid tempori, ætati & consuetudini. neque igitur quantitas vi-ctus, nec oblationis numerus inueniri posset, si à consuetudine indicationem tollas.
units.tr: But the same number has its own considerations. First, one must know that the number of feedings is to be taken from custom and from the disposition of the disease, as Hippocrates wrote in these words: "For those who are accustomed to be fed twice, one must give them ptisan; to those who have been fed once, give it once on the first day, etc." The number that custom indicates is reduced by the indication drawn from the disease. For the beginnings, the increases and the states of the paroxysms sometimes forbid keeping the customary number of feedings. Yet the strength of the body often adds to it, when the patients are feeble, or when we give a food that yields little nourishment and we want the nature to be strengthened; then, if the disease allows, we add to the number of feedings. For example, if someone who was used to a great deal of food and enjoyed good health is struck by a continuous fever, and for some reason we are obliged to give him ptisan, but may not give more than the amount custom has allowed at one feeding, we aim to add to the number of feedings, because such a man needs much nourishment and the ptisan supplies little nutriment. Hippocrates seems to have understood this in the same first book, in these words: "For those to whom [something is given] once, give it once on the first day; then, gradually and little by little, if it can be done, give it to them as well, if you think something should be added." Therefore we shall feed the sick as often as custom has indicated, unless ability has indicated more often, or the disease less often. Custom, then, sets out the first quantity, or the largest, and the first number, according to which we say that food is given to the sick sometimes more rarely, sometimes more often. Strength adds to this, or disease diminishes it. Hippocrates rightly said in the Aphorisms: "For those who [are fed] once or twice, or more, something must be given in accordance with the season, the age and the custom." Thus neither the quantity of food nor the number of feedings could be determined if you removed the indication from custom.

units.la: A quibus sumatur qualis uictus febricitan-tibus sit exhibendus.
units.tr: From whom the quality of the diet to be given to the feverish is to be taken.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: QVALITATEM cibi multa indi-cant, nempe morbus, natura ægrotan-tis, ætas, consuetudo, regio, anni tempus, & cœli status. In morbi appellatione, morbum & eius causam intellige. Natura ægrotantis, ætas, & consuetudo similia semper indicant. Cœli status, regio, et anni tempus, si temperata sint, similiter autem intemperata, contraria indicant, qualitate victum. Vt si calida imodera te sint, victum frigidum exposcunt. Quod si temperata fuerint, victum medium indicat. Non sic profecto laborantis temperatura, ætas, & consuetudo. Semper enim hæc similia siue commoderata sint, aut non, indicant.
units.tr: Many things indicate the quality of food: namely the disease, the nature of the patient, age, custom, region, season of the year, and the state of the sky. By the name of the disease, understand both the disease and its cause. The nature of the patient, age and custom always indicate similar things. The state of the sky, the region and the season of the year, if they are temperate, indicate similar things, but if they are intemperate, they indicate opposite things, as to the quality of the diet. For example, if they are hot and immoderate, they call for a cold diet; if they are temperate, they indicate a middle diet. But the temperament of the sufferer, his age and his custom do not behave in this way. For these always indicate similar things, whether they are moderate or not.

units.la: Cùmque ea iam dicta in vnum consentiunt cum morbo, eum esse exhibendum victum constat qui qualite insigni morbo aduersetur, vtpote omnibus indicationibus id dictatibus: cum vero contraria indicant, à potioribus sumendam esse indicationem qualitatis victus. Vt si morbus frigidum & humidum indicet, cætera vero omnia calidum & siccum, ambigui tas, vtique pugnaque indicationum inter se oritur. Quo casu magnopere opus est, tum numerum indicationum tum earum magnitudinem simul conferas. Quippe quæ à febre sumitur, ea reliquis quando omnes contrarium faciendum perscribunt, numero quidem inferior est, magnitudine tamen quæ ex dignitate potestate spectatur, vtiq; superior est: potissimum, si longè à natura recessit. Prout quidem febris est, plus cæteris omnibus solicitos nos habet. Et quia præterquâ quod febris est, etiâ magnitudo illi notabilis accessit, iccirco contrarias indicationes inducit atque obumbrat. Sin febris parua fuerit, fas est reliquas omnes vna coniunctas cum ea conferri atque expendi. Ac siquidem pares videntur, neque febris indicatio præferetur, sic vt humectandum & refrigerandū sit: neque eti am reliquorum, sic vt calfaciendum & sic-candū sit. Immo media victus ratio, vbi ita se corpus habet, eligenda erit. Sin altera indi catio exuperet, tantum recessisse à tempera-to & medio victu par est, quantum ea quæ pollent sua contraria superant. Ergo exerci-tatum & natura prudentem esse medicum conueniet, quo cuiusq; indicationis potestate diligenter considerata, omnibusque inter se collatis vnam idonei victus summam quæ la boranti sit commoda comparet, Hactenus Galenus, cum de qualitate victus inuestigan da sermonem facit.
units.tr: When the things already mentioned agree together with the disease, it is established that the diet to be given is the one which is strongly opposed in quality to the disease, since all the indications prescribe this. But when they indicate opposite things, the indication of the quality of the diet must be taken from the stronger ones. For example, if the disease indicates cold and moist, while all the other things indicate hot and dry, there arises uncertainty and conflict between the indications. In this case it is very necessary to compare both the number of the indications and their magnitude together. For the indication taken from the fever, although it is inferior in number when all the others prescribe the opposite, is nevertheless superior in magnitude, which is judged by its dignity and power, especially if it has departed far from nature. Indeed, to the extent that it is a fever, it troubles us more than all the others. And because, besides being a fever, it has also acquired a notable magnitude, it therefore brings in opposing indications and overshadows them. But if the fever is slight, it is right to compare all the remaining indications together with it and weigh them. And if they seem equal, the indication of the fever will not be preferred, so that one should moisten and cool; nor will that of the rest be preferred, so that one should warm and dry. Rather, the middle course of diet is to be chosen when the body is in such a state. But if one indication outweighs the other, the diet must depart from the temperate and middle course only as far as the things that have the greater power exceed their opposites. Therefore it is fitting that the physician be experienced and prudent by nature, so that, having carefully considered the power of each indication and compared them all with one another, he may arrange the one suitable summary of diet that is convenient for the sufferer. So far Galen, when he makes his discourse on investigating the quality of diet.

units.la: Sed non deerit qui in hunc modū dictis Galeni opponat, haudquaquam sperans hac methodo qualitatis victus scientiam se inuenire posse. Ponamus vt ipse proposuit omnia indicantia, victum suadere calidum & siccum: febris vero leuiuscula tertiana sit, victū qualitate frigidum & humidum indicans. Coniungantur, vt ille ait, omnes indicationes, et cum febre eas conferamus, & expendamus an pares sint morbo aut impares. Vnde nam hoc mihi notum erit rogabit quis. Nam nec id se scire ait, nec unde sciat. Multo adhuc minus, si alterum exuperet, quantum vtique alterum excedat. Praeterea cum indicationes regionis, temporis anni, coeli status, ad inuicem dissentiunt, vtrum eorum superare debeat.
units.tr: But there will not be lacking someone who will raise objections to Galen's words in this manner, by no means hoping that he can discover the knowledge of the quality of diet by this method. Let us suppose, as Galen himself proposed, that all the indications suggest a hot and dry diet, but that the fever is a slight tertian, indicating by its quality a cold and moist diet. Let all the indications, as he says, be joined together, and let us compare them with the fever and weigh whether they are equal or unequal to the disease. Someone will ask: "How will this be known to me?" For he says that he does not know it, nor how he might know it. Much less, if one of them exceeds, how far it exceeds the other. Moreover, when the indications of region, season of the year and state of the sky disagree with one another, how is one to know which of them ought to prevail?

units.la: Proprium insuper aegrotantis temperamentum, si forte consuetudini obuiauerit, quomodo quis similes qualitate victus ministrare possit? Oportuisset methodum tradere qua vires horum singulorum nosci possent.
units.tr: Furthermore, if the sufferer's own temperament happens to conflict with custom, how can anyone administer a diet similar in quality? It would have been necessary to hand down a method by which the powers of each of these could be known.

units.la: Nos igitur pro virili tentabimus in commodum studiosorum, viam ostendere, qua faci le qualitem victus inuenire possimus, ab iis quæ ab Hippocrate & Galeno didicimus, initium hinc sumentes, consuetudinis indica-tionem potestate digniorem esse quam propij temperamenti et ætatis. Nam si quispiam sit siccus temperamento, ætate consistens, humi do assuetus victu, siccum eis dabis, ratione temperamenti & ætatis. An consuetudinem magis seruabis? Quod si hæsitas, Hippocratem roga, qui ita scribit: Cibos quibus vti consueuerunt, facile ferunt, temetsi natura haud quaquam boni fuerint, similiter & potus. Cibos vero quibus vti nō consueuerunt, & si mali non fuerint, molestè ferunt, consimili modo & potus. In quorum expositione Galenus ita ait, consuetudo maxime potest, repentinaque ab ea digressio corpora non parum offendit. Ipse idem loco supra citato ita scribit: A consuetudine (inquit) semper est indicatio similium, quoad scilicet ægrotant homines: ab ætate, natura, regione, anni tem pore, statu cœli, vbi temperata sunt, similiū semper præsidiorum est indicatio, siue valeant homines siue ægrotant. Contra ab intem peratis, anni tempore, statu cœli, et regione, contrariorum est indicatio. Cæterum ab æta te, natura, subintellige intemperatis, non absolutè, sed cū consuetudine. Audisti Galenum dicentem, naturam ægrotantis & ætatem cum intemperata sunt, nihil absolutè indicare, sed cum cōsuetudine. Duo igitur hæc, ægrotantis naturam, & ætatem, cum intem perata sunt, ad vnius consuetudinis indicationem reducimus. Prætera regio, & anni tempus, ad cœli statum si res exactè consideretur, reducibilia sunt. Nam nec regio, nec anni tempus, quicquam agent, nisi per immu tationem aëris nos continentis dispositionis aut si mauis temperiei, quam cœli statū medici vocant. Quod si ad huius assertionē Hip pocratis aut Galeni testimonium optas, prout sunt plures studiosorū nostra tempestate, apud quos paruum habent rationes locū, plu rimum authoritates: Tantũ iuuat alieno Marte ditescere: Galenum audi, qui in libro nono de methodo medendi ita scribit: Voco (inquit) cœli statum ipsam ambientis nos aëris tempe riem, sub qua & anni tempus, & regio com prehenduntur, quando horum quoq; utrun- que ex ambientis temperie indicationem mu- tuatur. Ex dictis manifestum est, omnes in- dicationes qualitatis victus, ad tres reduci posse: nempe morbum, consuetudinem, & aë ris temperiem.
units.tr: We, therefore, will try, as far as we are able, to show the studious a way by which we can easily find the quality of diet, starting from what we have learned from Hippocrates and Galen, namely that the indication of custom is more powerful than that of one's own temperament and age. For if someone is dry by temperament, of settled age, but accustomed to a moist diet, you will give him a dry one, on account of his temperament and age. Or will you rather keep to custom? If you hesitate, ask Hippocrates, who writes thus: "Foods to which they are accustomed they bear easily, even if by nature they are not at all good; likewise drinks. But foods to which they are not accustomed, even if they are not bad, they bear with difficulty; likewise drinks." In explaining this, Galen says: "Custom is most powerful, and a sudden departure from it harms the bodies not a little." The same writer, in the passage cited above, writes thus: "From custom (he says) there is always an indication of similar things, namely as far as sick people are concerned; from age, nature, region, season of the year and state of the sky, where they are temperate, there is always an indication of similar remedies, whether men are healthy or sick. On the contrary, from intemperate season of the year, state of the sky and region, there is an indication of contrary things." Moreover, understand that from age and nature, when they are intemperate, the indication is not absolute but is joined with custom. You have heard Galen saying that the nature of the sufferer and his age, when they are intemperate, indicate nothing absolutely, but only together with custom. Therefore we reduce these two, the nature of the sufferer and his age, when they are intemperate, to the indication of custom alone. Besides, region and season of the year, if the matter is considered exactly, can be reduced to the state of the sky. For neither region nor season of the year can do anything, except through the change in the air surrounding us, or, if you prefer, in the temperature of the disposition, which physicians call the state of the sky. But if you desire the testimony of Hippocrates or Galen for this assertion, since many students in our time, among whom the reasons have little place, rely very much on authorities, then: "It is so pleasant to grow rich at another's expense." Hear Galen, who in the ninth book of the Method of Healing writes thus: "I call (he says) the state of the sky the temperature of the air surrounding us, under which both the season of the year and the region are included, since each of these also takes its indication from the temperature of the surrounding air." From what has been said it is clear that all the indications of the quality of diet can be reduced to three: namely the disease, custom, and the temperature of the air.

units.la: An uictus affectū & eius causam respicere debeat.
units.tr: Whether diet ought to regard the affection and its cause. ## CHAPTER VI.

units.la: CAPVT VI.

CAETERVM cum morbum in asse ctum & in eius causam diuiserimus, inquirendum est, an victus qualitas utrun- que nempe affectum & causam respicere de beat, an solū eorum alterum: & sunt in libris Hippocratis nonnulla loca utrunq; asserentia. Nam affectū, aphorismus ille, Humidæ diæ- tæ, & c. ostendit. Quodq; et causam respicere debeat, ipse idem in lib. 1. de ratione victus, de ptisana sermonem faciens ostendit, ita scribes: Si quid ablui eget probè abluit, nō astringit. hæc omnia causam respicere manifestum est. Ratio tamen aliud dictat. nam cum duo sint quæ in medici cōsideratione ʃubeant, nempe corpus febricitans, & humores putridi: ita duo sunt instrumenta, illorū gratia, quorum altero corpus seruamus, & altero putridos humores extra pellimus. Victus quidē corpus respicit, & id quod ab eo effluxū est, tum si ratione morbi corpus intemperatū est, id cōtrarijs emendat qualitatibus, paulatim id agens. Respicere humores medicaminū est, vt crassos extenuent, lentos detergeant, putridos expellant. Victus igitur munus est id quod à patiente particula affluxū est instaurare, & id quod alteratū est reducere. Hæc solum euenire corporis partibus simplicibus possunt. Verum ad illud quod dixit Hippocrates, Si quid ablui eget, probè abluit, ipse statim illo verbo si quid ablui eget, respondet, id tanquā non necessariū euenire innuens: quod Galenus asserit cum air: Si quid ablui egeat, ))
units.tr: Since we have divided disease into the affection and its cause, we must inquire whether the quality of diet ought to regard both, namely the affection and the cause, or only one of them. Some passages in the books of Hippocrates assert each view. That aphorism, "Moist diets...", etc., shows that diet regards the affection. That it ought to regard the cause, he himself shows in book 1 of On the Regimen of Diet, where, speaking of ptisan, he writes: "If something needs washing out, it washes it out well; it does not constipate." It is clear that all these things regard the cause. Reason, however, dictates otherwise. For since two things come under the physician's consideration, namely the feverish body and the putrid humours, there are accordingly two instruments: by one we preserve the body, and by the other we expel the putrid humours. Diet indeed regards the body and what has flowed away from it; then, if the body is intemperate because of the disease, diet corrects it by contrary qualities, doing so gradually. It is the business of medicines to regard the humours: to thin the thick, cleanse the viscid, and expel the putrid. Therefore the office of diet is to restore what has flowed away from the patient and to bring back what has been altered. These things can happen only to the simple parts of the body. But as to what Hippocrates said, "If something needs washing out, it washes it out well," he himself answers with the very phrase "if something needs washing out," hinting that this does not happen as a necessity. Galen asserts this too, when he says: "If something needs washing out,"

units.la: quasi non omnibus acutis morbis probè ab-luente edulio utamur. Nempe cætera omnia quæ de ptisana dicuntur bona, morbis omni-no prosunt acutis: sed abluendi bonitas qui-bus ventrem subduci volumus, ubi cibus in via moratur est idonea. Probè igitur abluere febrili affectioni neque tanquam contrariũ, neque tanquam familiare auxilium unum utile existit, sed bene tanquam symptoma-tis alicuius emendatorium correctoriumque.
units.tr: as if we did not always use a washing food in acute diseases. Indeed, all the other things said about ptisan are good and benefit acute diseases altogether; but the washing quality, by which we wish the bowels to be loosened, is suitable only where the food lingers in the passage. To wash out well is therefore useful neither as a contrary remedy nor as a familiar help for a feverish affection, but only as a corrective and amender of some symptom.

units.la: Mentem adhibe ad illud verbum: febrili affectioni, ac si velit, victum, febrilem affectionem, & non causam, respicere oportere. Quod si accidat ut victus utrique adversetur, & affectui, & causæ, ob id rejiciendus non est. Cum ergo victus id solum quod à corpore exolutum est reponere, aut id quod alteratum à morbo est, reducere debeat, manifestum est cibis astringentibus utendum nõ esse, nisi cum morbus ad eam corpus alterarit dispositionem, à qua aut ventris fluxus, aut uteri, aut alterius momentaneæ partis, aut symptomatici sudores robur virtutis exoluentes, oluentes, aut animi deliquium, proueniant. Alioquin non est quod corpus moderatè habens in raritate & densitate cibo astringen te obstruas. Proinde cum aëris nos continen tis temperies nihil indicet, nisi prout nostrum afficit corpus, tantumque indicationis sortia tur, quantū corpus ab illo mutatur, manife-stum etiam est, indicationem continentis nos aëris ab ea sumendam esse immutatione qua nostra afficit corpora. Consimiliter de morbosa sentiendum est affectione. nam tantum indicabit quantum corpus à naturali muta-uerit symmetria, licet febris in sua causa ma gna esse videatur. Parumq; si corpus à pro-prio amouerit temperamento, parum indica bit iuxta recessus magnitudinem. Duo igitur indicantia, nempe aëris nos continentis tem-peries, & ægritudinalis affectio, ad corpus reducuntur affectum. Neque vlli mirum id videri debet, quod ambientis indicationem ad præsentem corporis affectum reducamus. Nam iure id mirum videri non debet, quod rationi peruium est. Pone affectum & ambientem vtrunque calidum & siccum. Corpus vtique affectum tale est, nō solū propter morbosam affectionem, sed ob ambientis calidi & sicci operationem. Vtriusque igitur operatio affectum corporis præsentem produxêre. At pone ambientem frigidum et humidum affectioni contrarium, corpus profectò affectum, nō tale est ob solam morbosam affectionem, ob quam magis tale esset, sed ob ambientis etiam qualitatem affectioni contrariam, eius vim refringentem. Neque quæ dicta sunt præter mentem Galeni esse putes. Ille enim in libris de methodo medendi, ambientis indicationem ad præsentem affectum quem morbum nominat reducit. Cum ex tribus indicantibus quorum tertium ambiens erat, duo collegit indicantia. Ad duas igitur indicationes in vniuersum omnes quæ victus qualitatem indicant reduximus: nempe corpus affectum et consuetudinē. Ab ijs igitur qualitas victus quærenda est. Verum cū hæc cōsideratio medicæ artis parti, quæ morbos curat subiaceat, necessum est recessus corporis ris à naturali temperamento scire, ut contra rium applicantes qualitate victum, ad sym- metriã particulam reducamus. Recessus ve- rò nisi naturale nouerimus temperamentum alia scirivia non potest. Quapropter alia præ ter duas indicatione naturali, nempe tempe- rie opus est. Quibus autem notis hæc inueniri posset medico considerandum est. Proinde cũ omnibus in vnum collatis temperamentorũ signis, coniectura, & non scientia assequa- mur, ab vna cõsuetudine id certius sciri pos- se cum Galeno afferimus: quì ita scribit: Nos certè, quibus cura fuit, inquirendi illud, inue- nimus quod per plures cognitu difficiles no- tas cuiusque membri temperamentum conie- ctura potius quàm scientia inuenitur. Si igi- tur notis multis & paruis aliqua certior ap- paruerit, nónne abiectis illis, hanc pro omni bus arripiemus? nemo id arbitror qui mentis compos est, negabit. Atqui si omnes tempe- ramentorum notas in vnum colligas, hæc lon gissimè absunt, ut parem ei quam consuetu- do præstat fidem faciant.
units.tr: Take note of that phrase "for a feverish affection." It is as if he wished diet to regard the feverish affection, not the cause. But if it happens that diet is opposed to both the affection and the cause, it is not for that reason to be rejected. Since diet ought only to restore what has been drained from the body, or to bring back what has been altered by disease, it is clear that astringent foods are not to be used, except when the disease has altered the body into that disposition from which either a flux of the belly, or of the womb, or of some other momentary part, or symptomatic sweats, which dissolve the strength of the vital power, or a faintness of spirit, arise. Otherwise there is no reason to block up a body that is moderately balanced in its looseness and density with an astringent food. Accordingly, since the temperature of the air surrounding us indicates nothing except insofar as it affects our body, and has only as much indicative force as the body is changed by it, it is also clear that the indication of the surrounding air must be taken from the change by which it affects our bodies. The same must be thought of the morbid affection. For it will indicate only as much as it has changed the body from its natural symmetry, even though the fever may seem great in its cause; and if it has moved the body only a little from its proper temperament, it will indicate little in proportion to the size of the departure. Therefore the two indications, namely the temperature of the air that surrounds us and the sickly affection, are both referred to the present state of the body. Nor should it seem at all surprising that we refer the indication of the surrounding air to the body's present affection. For that ought not to seem surprising which is open to reason. Suppose the affection and the surrounding air are both hot and dry. The body, clearly, is affected in such a way not only by the morbid affection but also by the operation of the hot and dry surrounding air. Thus the operation of both has produced the body's present affection. But suppose the surrounding air is cold and moist, contrary to the affection; then the body, affected in this way, is certainly not so disposed by the morbid affection alone (by which it would be more so), but also by the surrounding quality contrary to the affection, which blunts its force. Nor should you think these things are said apart from the mind of Galen. For in his books On the Method of Healing he refers the indication of the surrounding air to the present affection, which he calls the disease. Out of three indications, of which the third was the surrounding air, he gathered two. Therefore we have referred all the indications that show the quality of diet, in general, to two: namely the affected body and the custom. From these, then, the quality of diet is to be sought. But since this consideration belongs to that part of the medical art which deals with curing diseases, it is necessary to know the departure of the body from its natural temperament, so that by applying a diet of contrary quality we may bring the body back to its proper symmetry. But unless we know the natural temperament, the departure cannot be known by any other means. Therefore, besides the two indications, a third, namely the temperament, is needed. What signs will make this discoverable is for the physician to consider. Accordingly, even when all the signs of temperaments are gathered together into one, we attain it by conjecture, not by knowledge; so we affirm with Galen that it can be known more certainly from custom alone. He writes thus: "We, indeed, who have taken care to investigate this, have found that the temperament of each member is discovered by conjecture rather than by knowledge, through many signs of each member that are hard to recognise. If, then, from many small signs some more certain one has appeared, shall we not, setting the others aside, seize upon that one for everything? No one who is in his right mind, I think, will deny it. Yet if you gather all the signs of the temperaments into one, these are so far from making a belief equal to that which custom provides."

units.la: An uictus opponi debeat intemperiei simi li gradu contrariæ qualitatis.
units.tr: Whether diet ought to be opposed to an intemperature by a contrary quality of similar degree.

units.la: CAPVT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: VERVM quia in cognoscendo ægro-tantis à proprio temperamento recessum, duplex datur consideratio: Nempe generatim scire versus quam qualitatem corpus altera tum sit: secundò quantitate illius declinatio-nis: hæc non valde speculationi huic de ratio-ne victus necessaria est. Nam particulæ intemperiem semel à suo contrario auertere in ratione ciborum non est, sed medicaminum. Sat enim est si cibus paulatim bono tempo-ris interuallo id agat, id autem contrario re-misso effici potest. Quamobrem, & si cor-pus à naturali abscesserit symmetria per duos gradus versus calorem, necessarium nō est, nec (vt opinor) commodum, frigidū huic totidem gradibus victum offerre. id enim ci bi natura egrederetur. hæc est vt à naturali calido patiatur, parum autem in id agat, vt cibo medicinali vsu venit. Quapropter satis sit frigidum in primo victum offeramus. Hic enim cibi munus adimplebit, facultatem vero medicaminis temporis interuallo crebriori vsu præstabit. Vnde fit, vt cum cibis ea mi scere quæ valentibus sint prædicta qualitatibus cauendum sit. Id solum ergo scire conuenit ad quod extremum alteratum sit corpus: an versus calidum & siccum, an frigidum & humidum, & an parum, aut multum a naturali symmetria recesserit, quod haud difficulter inuenies, si considerationem de consuetudine habeas in iis quæ vsus est bona valitudine citra noxam, & ex iis quibus vsus lædebatur. Ex iis enim temperamentum corporis, certius alia quacunque nota cognosces, vt prudentissime Galenus citato libro dixit. Videtur, inquit, non sicut alia quædam exiguam, leuemque, sed plane maximam, maximeque principalem potestatem habere consuetudo, vt quæ singulorum corporum naturam ostendat. Et statim inquit, Sane ipsi via rationeque ab ea procedentes, fatemur nos partium affectu inuenire. Deinde ex illo rursus ad faciendorum indicationem venire. In hocque pars hæc, quæ de victus qualitate agit, ab ea medicæ artis parte, quæ singularum, aut simplicium partium morbos curat differt, quod hæc quantitatem recessus à naturali temperie nosse desiderat, ut æquali contraria gradu applicet remedia. Illa vero solum quærit versus quam qualitatem intemperatum sit corpus, & an multum, an parum recesserit.
units.tr: Now, since in recognising the disease there are two considerations of the departure from the patient's own temperament: first, to know generally in which direction, that is, towards which quality, the body has been altered; secondly, the degree of that deviation. The second is not especially necessary for this discussion of the rationale of diet. For it is not the business of food, but of medicines, to turn a temperament away from its contrary once and for all.
