It is enough if food does this gradually over a good interval of time, and this can be achieved by relaxing the contrary. Therefore, even if the body has departed from its natural symmetry by two degrees towards heat, it is not necessary, nor (in my opinion) advisable, to offer a cold diet of the same number of degrees. For that would take the food beyond its own nature. This is what happens with the medicinal use of food: it is to suffer from the natural heat only a little, and to act upon it only a little. Hence it is enough to offer a cold diet of the first degree. For here the food will fulfil the function of food, while its medicinal power will be supplied by more frequent use over shorter intervals. Hence it follows that when mixing foods one must take care not to combine things that possess qualities strong enough to affect the healthy. It is therefore necessary to know only towards which extreme the body has been altered: whether towards hot and dry, or cold and moist; and whether it has departed a little or a great deal from its natural symmetry. This you will discover without much difficulty, if you take account of what the patient habitually ate in good health without harm, and of what harmed him. For from these you will learn the temperament of the body more certainly than from any other sign, as the very wise Galen said in the book cited: "Custom, he says, seems to have not a small or slight power, but a plainly very great and most principal power, since it reveals the nature of each individual body." And presently he says: "Indeed, we admit that we discover the condition of the parts by the methods and reasoning that proceed from it, and then from that again come to the indication of what is to be done." And in this respect this part, which treats of the quality of diet, differs from that part of the medical art which cures the diseases of individual or simple parts, in that the latter needs to know the degree of departure from the natural temperament, so that it may apply remedies of equal contrary degree. The former, however, seeks only towards which quality the body has been disordered, and whether it has departed much or little.

units.la: Qualitatem uictus à tribus sumi.
units.tr: The quality of diet is to be taken from three things.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: ATribus igitur qualitas victus sumitur: à naturali temperamento, & ab affectione, & à consuetudine: cunque hæc in unum consentiant, quod simul indicauerint statim exhibendum. At contraria indicare solum affectum & consuetudinem posse. Nam naturale temperamentu semper cu affectu in indicatione qualitatis victus consentit. Na affectus indicat sui ablatione, per quam ad temperamentu pristinu ægrotas reducitur. Huic indicationi naturalis ægrotatis teperies semper consentit. Duo sunt igitur quæ contraria indica repossunt, nempe affectus et consuetudo. Vt si affectus calidus & siccus humidũ exposcat victũ, consuetudo verò prohibeat (nã calidis et siccis assuetus erat cibis) in hac indicationis cõtrarietate inquirendũ est, an calidis & siccis assuetus sit, ob id quod male ex frigidorũ vsu, aut quia melius calidis et siccis quã à frigidis et humidis haberet, aut à frigidis & humidis nihil incõmodi percipiens. Si primũ contingat, eo esse vtendũ victu, qui tempera tus sit, aut id mixtis adinuicem contrariarũ qualitatũ alimẽtis conficiendũ. Si quidẽ dum sanus erat calidis & siccis opus ei erat cibariis, vt inculpatè viueret: febre correptũ, calidum & siccum iam effectum, frigidis & humidis lædes, aut nunc, aut cũ febris abierit. Nã id præstitit affectus quod calidis et siccis cibariis quærebat. Quapropter si tunc iustè ea quæ calfaciebant & exiccabant amplectebatur, non est cur nunc caliditatem et siccitatem affectus, frigidis & humidis euer tas, nisi multum exuperent. Quod si contingat, victu medio vtendum est quo excessus securissimè reprimetur. Quod si secundum evenìat, dandum est aliquid consuetudini, minus tamen quàm in prædicto, eo vtendo victu qui refrigerare & humectare moderatè valeat. Liberalius id agere licet si tertium contingat, parui consuetudinem illam faciendo. Ad tria igitur omnes reduximus indicationes, cum regio & tempus anni non agant, ni si status cœli interuentu. Hic autem nihil indicat ex se, sed in quantum corpus afficit. In vno igitur affectu corporis, regionis, anni temporis, status cœli, & morbi, temperamenti ægrotantis, ætatisque vires siue actiones, potestate sunt: & id quod tandem ab eorum actionibus, & reactionibus, & alterius supra alterum exuperantia superest, in vno affecto corpore conspicitur. Non est igitur quod medicus in æstimandis horum cum contraria indicant viribus, mentem inaniter agitet. Idenim quod ab exactissima consideratione elici posset, corpus affectum indicat. Diximusque ætatem ad proprium reducitemperamentū, cuius ope scimus an parū, aut multum, à naturali recesserit corpus symmetria. Ad opus præstat id commodi, ut sciamus quando maxime finem alteranti victui imponemus. Cæterum in indicatione qualitatis victus cum affectu consentit. Nam si quis sitiam sit calidus natura, calidiorque ob ægritudinem euaserit, affectus indicat, ut id caliditatis quod superexcreuit abscindatur. Idem proprium indicat temperamentum. Et non calidum potestate victum, ob id quod ante natura calidus erat. Sola igitur illius gratia corporis temperatura à medico inuestiganda est, ut an parum an multum, à naturali recesserit corpus symmetria, & quando maxime alteranti victui finem imponemus sciamus. Sola igitur consuetudo est quæ aliquando dissentit affectui. Tuncque diuisionem illam quam supra triplicem fecimus inquirere ab ægrotante, & ab iis qui hominem multo ante nouerunt oportet. At cum omnes tres in vnum consentiunt, cum humidus natura, & humido victui assuetus, febre corripitur, audacter frigido & humido victu vtemur. Nónne hæc sunt senis verba? Humidi victus omnibus febricitantibus conueniunt, maximè pueris, et alijs sic assuetis refici. Sunt tamen febres quæ non humidum, sed siccum indicant victum, de quibus infra nobis sermo erit vbi mentem Hippocratis in dicto Aphorismo ostendemus. Nunc ad reliqua properemus.
units.tr: The quality of the diet is therefore taken from three things: from the natural temperament, from the disease (affectio), and from habit. When these agree, what they jointly indicate must be given at once. When they conflict, the disease and habit alone can indicate. For the natural temperament always agrees with the disease in indicating the quality of the diet. The disease indicates by its removal, by which the patient is brought back to his former temperament, and the natural temperature of the sick person always agrees with this indication. There are therefore two things that can indicate in opposite ways, namely the disease and habit. Suppose the disease is hot and dry and calls for a moist diet, while habit forbids it, since the patient was accustomed to hot and dry foods. In this conflict of indications one must inquire whether the patient is used to hot and dry food, either because he has been harmed by eating cold food, or because he has fared better on hot and dry food than on cold and moist, or because he has noticed no inconvenience from cold and moist food. If the first holds, he should use the diet that is temperate, or prepare it by mixing foods of contrary qualities. For while he was healthy he needed hot and dry food in order to live without harm. If he is seized by fever, and has already become hot and dry, he will be harmed by cold and moist food, either now or when the fever has gone. For the disease is doing what he previously sought from hot and dry food. Therefore, if at that time he rightly took what warmed and dried him, there is no reason now to be concerned about the heat and dryness of the disease, unless they greatly exceed the norm, in which case he should be given a middle diet, by which the excess will be most safely checked. If the second holds, something must be granted to habit, though less than in the previous case, by using a diet that can cool and moisten moderately. It is permissible to do this more generously if the third holds, making only a small concession to habit. Thus we have reduced all indications to three, since region and season of the year act only through the state of the sky. But this in itself indicates nothing, except insofar as it affects the body. In the single affected body, therefore, the powers or actions of the region, the season of the year, the state of the sky, the disease, the temperament of the patient and his age are present, and what finally remains from their actions, reactions and the excess of one over another is seen in that one affected body. There is no reason, then, for the physician to trouble his mind in vain in weighing the forces of these things when they indicate opposite courses. For what could be drawn from the most exact consideration indicates the affected body. We have also said that age is reduced to the proper temperament, by which we know whether the body has departed from its natural symmetry a little or a great deal. This is useful, so that we may know when we should most of all impose an end to the alternating diet. Otherwise, in the indication of the quality of the diet, the natural temperament agrees with the disease. For if someone is naturally hot, and has become hotter through sickness, the disease indicates that the excess of heat should be cut away, and the proper temperament indicates the same. Nor does the physician order a warm diet merely because the patient was naturally warm before. Therefore only the temperature of that body is to be investigated by the physician, so that we may know whether the body has departed from its natural symmetry a little or a great deal, and when we should most of all end the alternating diet. Thus habit alone is what sometimes disagrees with the disease. Then the division which we made above into three must be inquired into from the patient and from those who knew the man well before. But when all three agree, as when a man who is naturally moist and accustomed to a moist diet is seized by fever, we use a cold and moist diet boldly. Are these not the words of the old man? "A moist diet suits all febrile patients, especially children, and others who are accustomed to be restored by it." Yet there are fevers which indicate not a moist but a dry diet, about which we shall speak below, when we show the mind of Hippocrates in the said Aphorism. Now let us hasten on to the rest.

units.la: Vnde sumantur indicationes quando exhibendus sit febricitantibus.
units.tr: Whence the indications are drawn when food should be given to febrile patients.

units.la: CAPVT IX.
units.tr: Chapter IX.

units.la: ADuobus sumitur quando exhibere cibum debeamus, à facultate, & à morbo non prohibente. Prohibet ab initijs paroxysmorum aut exacerbationum ad manifestam inclinationem. Iis enim temporibus natiuo calore ad thoracem collecto, vt morbi causam vincat, cibus dandus non est, quanquã corpus iam iam indigere videatur quod cum Galeno asserimus primo de ratione victus in acutis. Opportunum igitur exhibendi victus tempus fuerit, cũ caliditas ad pedes descenderit, viscera iam deserens, vt ab Hippocrate scriptum est. Verũ si facultas nimis langueat,
units.tr: Two things determine when we ought to offer food: the strength (faculty) and a disease that does not forbid it. Food is forbidden from the onset of the paroxysms or exacerbations until a clear tendency toward the decline appears. At those times the natural heat is gathered about the chest to overcome the cause of the disease, so food is not to be given, although the body may seem already to need it. We affirm this with Galen, in the first book On the Method of Diet, on acute diseases. The opportune time for giving food will therefore be when the heat has descended to the feet, leaving the inner organs, as Hippocrates wrote. But if the strength is too weak

units.la: n fine pri ni de ra- ione uigueat, ita vt imbecillitas eius maximè vrge- at, indiscretè quolibet tempore nutriemus æ-grũ. Et in statu totius morbi, vt scripsit Gal. in apho. Cunq; in declinatione accessionis da re expedit, nõ ea statim victũ forma, quâ æ-grotâti definieris exhibebis, sed magis tenuë, vt si sorbitionibus ægrotantem alere decreueris, satis sit si potiunculâ, inchoante inclinatione, ministraueris. Postmodum aut febre cessante, aut omnino remittente, sorbitionẽ exhibeto, quem modum vidi à peritis medicis obseruari in Italia. Quibus enim ægrotantibus sorbitionem ex pane & iure pulli, quâ panatellã vocant, ministrare decernunt, hos primo in inclinatione febris tenui pulli iure nutriũt. Ac postmodũ cessante febre, aut manifestè remittente, sorbitionẽ exhibent. Hoc ut arbitror sensit Hippoc. cũ in fine primi de ratione victus immediatè dixisset, Cũ calor ,, ad pedes descederit, tunc dare expedit, subiun ,, git statim. Vtere primũ et maximè cremore, ,, postea ptisana, secundũ perscriptas cõiecturas ,, exactè speculatus. Quæ quidem verba, & ,, si Galenus ad victum vniuersalem referat, de particulari cibatione eadem posse recte in telligi asserimus. Vt talem faciant sensum, quod si sorbitionibus ægrotantem nutrire de beamus, melius esse inclinante febre à tenui sorbitione, vt cremore ptisanæ incipere. Ne ab vnius diei inedia ad crassiusculum cibum mutatione subita, lædatur ægrotantis natu- ra. Quod autem scribit, secundum perscri- ptas coniecturas, hunc sensum habet. Qui- buscunque coniectura habita de morbi con- stitutione & ægrotantis robore, dandam fo- re sorbitionē decreueris, hanc non in initijs, neque incrementis accessionum exhibeto, sed in declinatione. In qua commodius ages si pri mum cremore vsus fueris, deinde ptisana.
units.tr: (as the end of the first book On the Method of Diet says, it should be vigorous), so that its weakness especially presses, we shall feed the sick person indiscriminately at any time. And throughout the whole course of the disease, as Galen wrote in the Aphorisms: when it is expedient to give food in the decline of the paroxysm, you will not immediately give the form of diet you had decided on for the patient, but a thinner one. So if you decide to nourish the patient with sorbitions (thin broths), it is enough to give a little drink as the decline begins. Afterwards, when the fever has ceased or entirely remitted, give the sorbition. I have seen this method observed by skilled physicians in Italy. For those patients for whom they decide to prepare a sorbition of bread and chicken broth, which they call panatella, they first nourish them with thin chicken broth in the decline of the fever. Then, when the fever has ceased or clearly remitted, they give the sorbition. I think Hippocrates meant this when, at the end of the first book On the Method of Diet, he had just said: "When the heat has descended to the feet, then it is expedient to give food," and immediately adds: "Use first and chiefly gruel, afterwards ptisan, having carefully observed the written conjectures." If Galen refers these words to the general diet, we affirm that they can rightly be understood of particular feeding as well, so that they make this sense: if we decide to nourish the febrile patient with sorbitions, it is better, when the fever is declining, to begin with a thin sorbition such as the gruel of ptisan, so that the patient's nature is not harmed by a sudden change from one day's fasting to a rather thick food. As for what he writes, "according to the written conjectures," it has this sense: whatever conjecture you have formed about the constitution of the disease and the strength of the patient, and have decided that a sorbition is to be given, give it not at the beginning or the increase of the paroxysms but in the decline. In this you will act more conveniently if you use gruel first and then ptisan.

units.la: Cæterum in continentibus febribus quæ vnicam à principio ad finem accessionem ha bent, nutriendi idoneum tempus, à consuetu- dine, & à facili toleratione accipitur. Vt si in aurora facilius æger malum tolerat, eodēq; tempore cibari solitus est, commodissime ea hora cibum ægrotanti ministrabimus. Hoc discimus
units.tr: But in continued fevers, which have a single paroxysm from beginning to end, the suitable time for feeding is taken from custom and from easy tolerance. So if the patient tolerates the illness more easily in the morning, and is accustomed to eat at that same time, we will most conveniently give food to the patient at that hour. We learn this from Galen

units.la: discimus à Galeno vndecimo de methodo in hæc verba: Tempus verò nutriëdi, quod quidem ad reliquas spectat febres quæ ex putredine oriuntur, in progressu sermonis dicemus. Quæ verò vnicam à principio suo adsi-nem habent accessionem (de his nanque præsens sermo est) in his facilis toleratio, & consuetudo, spectari debebunt: Quando cibus illis eo tempore est offerendus, quo facilius quàm in cæteris morbum tolerant: eoque potissimum diei tempore quo prius cibari sunt sueti. Etenim facillimè cibum ferent si ex his considerationibus assument, Hucusque Galenus.
units.tr: in the eleventh book On the Method, in these words: "The time for feeding, which relates to the other fevers arising from putrefaction, we shall discuss in the course of our discourse. But in those fevers that have a single paroxysm from their onset (for it is of these that the present discourse treats), easy tolerance and custom are to be considered. Food is to be offered at the time when they bear the disease more easily than at other times, and especially at that time of day when they were accustomed to eat before. For they will bear food most easily if they take it with these considerations in mind." Thus far Galen.

units.la: Cæterùm scire oportet quod aliquando consuetudo & facilis toleratio, in indicatione temporis dissentiunt: vt si is qui ægrotat eorum sit, qui semel cibum solent capere occumbente sole. Morbum verò facilius toleret æger initio diei. Pugna inter indicantia oritur, quo casu indicatio à facili toleratione prævalet ei quæ à consuetudine. nec præter rationem. nam si bis aut ter cibum bona valitudine capere assueto ægrotanti, propter febriles accessiones, semel ministramus, ob timorem ne cibus intempestiuè exhibitus aut in vehementiam febrilem, aut in eius addat durationem, vt in superioribus ostendimus: multo causatius in synochis, quæ acutiores multò sunt, febribus, prohibendus est ea hora cibus, qua plus læde re potest: eaque maximè ministrandus, cum ab eo corporis natura capiet commodius vsum, minusque prompte in morbi causam transibit. Quod si facilior toleratio manifesta non detur, à sola consuetudine in continentibus febribus tempus nutriendi idoneum sumendum est.
units.tr: But one must know that sometimes custom and easy tolerance disagree in indicating the time: for example, if the patient is one of those who are accustomed to take food only at sunset, but bears the disease more easily early in the day. A conflict between the indications arises, and in such a case the indication from easy tolerance prevails over that from custom, and not without reason. For if we give food once, rather than twice or thrice as the patient was accustomed to take it in good health, because of the febrile paroxysms, for fear that food given at an unseasonable time may either increase the violence of the fever or prolong it, as we showed above; then, much more so in synochal fevers, which are far more acute, food must be withheld at the hour when it can do the most harm. It is to be given especially when the nature of the body will take it more usefully and it will less readily pass into the cause of the disease. But if an easier tolerance is not clearly apparent, the suitable time for feeding in continued fevers is to be taken from custom alone.

units.la: Porrò aptissimũ in febribus quæ intermittunt & repetunt, tempus est, cum vti dictum est, exhalare iam cœperit febrilis calor, huius quoq; opportuno tempore ex duplici coniectato respectu, nempe summo præcedentis accessionis vigore, & futuræ principio. Ad hæc nam spectantes, operam dabimus, vt quàm longissimè ab vtroque nutriamus.
units.tr: Moreover, in fevers that intermit and recur, the most suitable time is, as has been said, when the febrile heat has begun to subside. This too must be judged at an opportune time, from a twofold consideration: namely, the height of the preceding paroxysm and the onset of the next. Looking to both, we shall take care to feed the patient as far as possible from each.

units.la: Ergo si spatium quod inter summũ prioris accessionis vigorem, & sequentis principi-um um interuenit, satis sit amplum, facile est ido neum tempus inuenire. sin exiguu id fuerit, alterum facias necesse est, ut aut ægrum admodu adhuc calentem nutrias, aut sequentis accessionis inuasione iamia affutura. At sum mi vigoris & accessionis principij moram sic consideres censeo. In summo vigore notabis an citra magnitudinem febrilis caloris sic cus sit & squalens, an citra siccitate vrens. Priorem nanque humectante victu madefacere quamprimum oportet. In secundo dum plurimu caloris se remittat, manere. In principij vero accessionis mora æstimabis, an corporis extrema perfrigeret, & magnam sanguinis revocationem ad interiora corporis faciat, an omnino corpus non premat. Quippe secundum hoc, ceu facile contemnes. In prio re distinguas oportet. Nam si absque phlegmone, aut succorum redundantia, motus ad interiora in accessionibus pollet, nihil offendes paulo ante cibans. Sin vel phlegmone, vel redundantia subsit, cauenda est ante accessionē cibatio, ceu res maxime noxia.
units.tr: So if the interval between the height of the previous paroxysm and the onset of the next is long enough, it is easy to find a suitable time. But if it is short, you must do otherwise: either feed the patient while still very hot, or when the next paroxysm is already about to attack. I think you should consider the interval between the height of vigour and the onset of the paroxysm as follows. At the height, note whether the patient is dry and parched without great febrile heat, or burning with dryness. The first must be moistened as soon as possible with moistening food; in the second, wait while the heat is largely remitting. In the interval before the onset of the paroxysm, judge whether the extremities of the body grow cold and draw a great quantity of blood inward, or whether the body is not oppressed at all. Indeed, according to this you will easily decide. In the first case you must make a distinction. For if, without phlegmon or excess of humours, the movement to the interior is strong in the paroxysms, you will do no harm by feeding a little beforehand. But if either phlegmon or excess of humours is present, feeding before the paroxysm must be avoided as most harmful.

units.la: Hæc quidem Galenus scripsit de tempore, quando opportunè in febribus æger cibetur, cum exiguum fuerit tempus, quod inter summum prioris accessionis vigorem, & sequentis principiũ interuenit. Vt si ponamus à summo vigore ad sequentem accessionem trium horarum spatium esse, an prima cibare febri citantem hora, commodius sit quàm secunda, hinc maximè disces. Cibum ideo febricitantibus exhibemus vt eo virtutem seruemus, cauentes quo ad fieri possit ne in vehementiam morbi aut eius durationem addamus. Virtus ab eo cibo vsum capit quem coquit & apparat. Melius autem apparabit, cum à febrili labore quietior fuerit laborantis natura.
units.tr: Galen wrote these things about the time when it is opportune to feed the patient in fevers, when the interval between the height of the previous paroxysm and the onset of the next is short. So, for example, if we suppose the space from the height of vigour to the next paroxysm to be three hours, you will learn chiefly from this whether it is more convenient to feed the febrile patient in the first hour rather than the second. We give food to febrile patients so that by it we preserve their strength, taking care, as far as possible, not to add to the violence of the disease or to its duration. Strength draws its use from the food that it digests and prepares; but it will prepare it better when the patient's nature is quieter from the labour of the fever.

units.la: Verùm facultas naturalis quæ cibum coquit, quietior est in paroxysmi inclinatione, quàm in initio accessionis, vt ab ipso Galeno secundo Aphor. scriptum est in hac verba. In vigore eo quod iam coquit superfluum euacuare. Tum propter alia & quia animalis facultas omnino instatu laborat, licet maximè secundum illud tempus vitalis
units.tr: But the natural faculty that digests food is quieter in the decline of the paroxysm than at its onset, as Galen himself wrote in the second Aphorism in these words: "In the vigour of the disease it is expelling the superfluity that it already digests." Besides, for other reasons, and because the animal faculty labours altogether in this state, although at that time especially the vital

units.la: & & naturalis fortes persistant. Ab initio igi-tur paroxysmi naturalis facultas quæ conco-quit maximè adstatum vsque fatigatur, ab statu verò inclinationem versus, fortis, vt il-le ait, permanet. Quare hac ratione commo-dius est inchoante inclinatione cibum exhi-bere quàm propè accessionem. His adde ci-bum si quando eum in ventriculo sequens ac cessio offendat corrumpi, vt in pluribus cer-tum esse. Paucis verò omnino quibus inchoante inclinatione exhibetur illud accidere. Quare siue in iocineris phlegmone aut ven-triculi, aut pulmonis, siue ephemera, aut pu-trida febre quauis natura, & habitu, salu-brius est parum post vigorem cibare quàm modicum ante sequentem accessionem. Hoc in singulis morbis naturis & habitibus osten-dere haud magnum negocium est. Verum id studioso lectori dimittere commodius erit.
units.tr: and natural faculties remain strong. Therefore at the beginning of the paroxysm the natural faculty that digests is most worn out throughout the state, but from the state toward the decline it remains strong, as he says. For this reason it is more convenient to give food at the onset of the decline than shortly before the next paroxysm. Add to this that if the following paroxysm finds food in the stomach, it is certain to be corrupted in most cases; but this happens to few of those to whom food is given at the onset of the decline. So whether in inflammation of the liver, stomach or lungs, or in ephemeral or putrid fever of any kind, whatever the nature and habit, it is healthier to feed a little after the height than a little before the next paroxysm. To show this for each disease, nature and habit is no great task, but it will be more convenient to leave that to the studious reader.

units.la: Sat nobis est, qui Hippocratis dogmata inse-quimur, eius sententiæ stare in primo de ra-tione vidtus vbi scripsit: Nam si pedes frigi-di fuerint, non à sorbitione modo, verū quoq̈ & maximè à potu temperandum. Item quar to eiusdem, cum dixit: Frigentibus ergo pe- dibus neque potum, neque sorbitionem, ne- que aliud quippiam huiusmodi dabis, sed ma- ximum existimato si id tantisper obserua- ueris, donec valde incaluerint, deinde ita quod confert exhibe. Frigiditas siquidem pe- dum parte plurima febris accessura signum exi- stit, quo tempore siquid porrigas maximè, prorsus peccabis, nempe morbum non parum augebis. At verò cum febris desierit, contrario modo pedes reliquo corpore calidiores sunt. Idem infra, Nempe cum pedes frigidi fuerint, venter de necessitate calet fastiditque ci- bum, intenditur hypochondrium, iactatur propter internam turbationem corpus, mens fixa non est, dolet æger, lancinatur, vellica- turque, vomere affectat, & si mala vomue rit dolet. Ergo cum calor ad pedes descende- rit, curritque vrina, & si non sudet, omnia cessant, quo tempore sorbitionem dare expe- dit, nam alias pernitiosa existit, Hæc quidem Hippoc. scripsit incommoda euenire ijs qui in initijs initiis accessionum cibatur. Sit igitur a nobis in præsenti definitum, quod cum ob brevitatem temporis a vigore præcedente ad sequentem accessionem, alterum duorum sequi sit necesse, aut ægrum adhuc calentem nutriamus, aut sequentis accessionis invasione tam iam affuturam: consultius esse primum, ut sanum magis eligere, in omni morbo, in omni natura, & in omni habitu. In qua sententia Hippocratem esse certum est libro de ratione victus, in eo loco qui ita incipit: Cum autem purgaueris sorbitionibus quibusdam utitor.
units.tr: It is enough for us, who follow the doctrines of Hippocrates, to stand by his opinion in the first book of the Regimen, where he writes: "For if the feet are cold, one must moderate not only sipping but above all drinking. Likewise in the fourth book of the same work, when he says: 'Therefore, when the feet are cold, you will give neither drink, nor sipping, nor anything else of the kind, but you should judge it most important to observe this for a while, until they have grown quite warm, and then give what is suitable. For coldness of the feet is for the most part a sign that a fever is about to come, and if at that time you offer anything at all, you will certainly err, since you will greatly increase the disease. But when the fever has ceased, the feet are warmer than the rest of the body.' Again below: 'Indeed, when the feet are cold, the belly is necessarily hot and loathes food, the hypochondrium is tense, the body is tossed about by inner disturbance, the mind is not steady, the patient is distressed, suffers stabbing pains and cramps, is inclined to vomit, and if he vomits he is distressed. Therefore, when the heat has descended to the feet, and the urine flows, and if he does not sweat, all these symptoms cease; at that time it is expedient to give sipping, for otherwise it is harmful.' These are the things Hippocrates wrote about the inconveniences that befall those who are fed in the beginnings of the paroxysms." So let it be settled by us here: since, because of the shortness of time between the height of one paroxysm and the onset of the next, one of two things must follow, either we feed the patient while he is still hot, or we take up the next paroxysm when it is already at hand, it is better to choose the former, namely to keep the patient well fed, in every disease, every constitution and every habit. Hippocrates is certainly of this opinion in the book On Regimen, in the passage that begins: "But when you have purged, use certain sippings."

units.la: Caeterum cum spatium quod inter summum prioris accessionis vigore & sequentis principium interuenit, adeo amplum fuerit, ut satis sit ad binas cibi oblationes, offeremus, semel quidem resoluta omnino priori accessione, iterumque sequenti nondum incipienti. Temporis autem inter secundam oblationem & sequentem accessionem quidam quatuor horas sat esse putarunt. Idque forsan ex Galeni octauo de methodo sumunt, vbi asserit abunde esse si tres æquinoctiales horæ quatuor ne inter balneum, accessionisq; tempus interponan-tur. à balneo enim semper ægrotantibus cibũ ministrabat. Verùm in præsenti citra dispu-tationem, non satis esse, si tres quatuor ue ho-ræ inter cibũ & sequentem accessionem in-tersint arbitror. Nam intra limites disposi-tionis ad futuram accessionem, naturam a-lió intentam ciborum coctioni segniter atque imbecilliter vacare putandum est. Quæ cau-sa est vt diutius eo tempore cibus in ventri-culis laborantium immoretur. Quapropter iis qui ab humore putrido à febre detinetur, si quando ante accessionem cibum sint captu-ri, septem horarum interuallum ad sequentis accessionis initium, necessarium esse, vt ci-bus in ventriculis eorum decenter coquatur, & ad inferiores partes descendat, iuxta sen-tentiam Haly medici arbitramur. Nec Ga-lenus huic contrarius est opinioni. Nam si ea quæ parum vltra eum quem citarunt locum scripsit, legant, ita dicentem audient: Tempe stium (inquit) est vt iam ad ea quæ post bal-neum adhibentur accedamus. Sunt autem ea minimè multa. Nam præter aquam quæ pa- rum apÿ incoctum in se habuerit, nihil his est offerendum. Licet quod inter balneum et suspectas horas spacium erit, trium fore ho- rarum coniçiamus, Hæc quidem Galenus. Et vt apertum fiat ob angustiam temporis ad sequentem accessionem, febricitantem nõ cibasse, audias quid is statim subiungat: Si ve rò (inquit) circa vesperam, aut duabus ho- ris citius accessio inuadat, tum lauisse mane liceat, tum cibasse, &c. Audisti Galenum eum cuius accessio ad vesperam futura est, mane cibasse. quod nostrorum medicorum im peritiam, aut insanam temeritatem arguit, qui sat esse si tres quatuor'ue horas à cibo ad accessionem interponant arbitrantur. Sed re liqua proposita prosequamur.
units.tr: Moreover, when the interval between the peak of the earlier paroxysm and the beginning of the next is so long that there is time enough for two offerings of food, we shall offer food twice: once when the earlier paroxysm has been wholly resolved, and again while the next has not yet begun. Some have thought that four hours is enough between the second offering and the next paroxysm, and perhaps they take this from Galen's eighth book On the Method of Healing, where he asserts that three equinoctial hours, or four, are sufficient to be interposed between the bath and the time of the paroxysm; for he always gave food to the sick after the bath. But in the present matter, without dispute, I judge that it is not enough if three or four hours lie between food and the next paroxysm. For within the limits of the disposition towards the coming paroxysm, nature, intent on something else, must be supposed to be sluggish and feeble in digesting food. This is why food remains longer in the stomachs of those who are ill. Therefore, for those who are held by a fever from putrid humour, if they are about to take food before the paroxysm, we judge, in accordance with the opinion of the physician Haly, that an interval of seven hours before the onset of the next paroxysm is necessary, so that the food may be properly digested in their stomachs and descend to the lower parts. Nor is Galen contrary to this opinion. For if they read what he wrote a little beyond the passage they cite, they will hear him speaking thus: "It is now time (he says) to come to the things that are given after the bath. Yet these are by no means many. For besides water, which has in itself been little cooked, nothing is to be offered at this time. Although, as to the interval between the bath and the suspected hours, we may conjecture that there will be three hours." So Galen. And so that it may be clear that, because of the shortness of time before the next paroxysm, he did not feed the febrile patient, hear what he immediately adds: "But if (he says) the paroxysm attacks around evening, or two hours earlier, then it is allowed to bathe in the morning and to eat, etc." You have heard that Galen, whose paroxysm is to come in the evening, ate in the morning. This proves the inexperience or the insane rashness of our physicians, who think it enough if they interpose three or four hours between food and the paroxysm. But let us set aside these matters and proceed with what remains to be proposed.

units.la: Porrò corpora quæ calida & sicca sunt na tura, gracili habitu, & si parum ante accessionem cibentur, minimè lædentur. Quinimmò Galenus refert plures eorum à febre libe- rasse, quibus in ipso horrore cibum exhibuit. Illud tamen intelligere oportet, cum ob retentionem mordentis halitus febricitant. Tunc enim cibo conuenienti, corpore humectiori reddito, acrium excrementorum minor copia monetur: sed & cutis mollior redditur. Vnde fit vt ij qui inchoante horrore per cutem corporis ab acri excremento mordentes feruntur fumi, cibi & potus dulci halitu mitiores reddantur, vnde ob dictas causas febrilem nõ concipiunt calorẽ. Ob id igitur Galenus cibum ijs durante horrore cocedit, minimè aut cum iam calorem febrilem patiuntur. His tamen si, quando febre à putrido humore laborat, cibũ in accessionibus exhibeamus ea fiducia, vt eos à febre liberemus, non leuiter in eorũ damnũ errabimus. Minus tamen ij quàm qui alio sunt habitu lædentur.
units.tr: Furthermore, bodies that are by nature hot and dry, of a slender habit, will by no means be harmed if they are fed a little before the paroxysm. Indeed Galen reports that many of those to whom he gave food during the very chill were freed from the fever. Yet one must understand that this holds when they are febrile because of the retention of a biting vapour. For then, when suitable food is given, the body is made moister, and a smaller quantity of sharp excrement is produced; and the skin also becomes softer. Hence it comes about that those who, at the onset of the chill, are attacked by the biting fumes of a sharp excrement through the skin of the body, are made milder by the sweet vapour of food and drink, and for the reasons mentioned they do not conceive a febrile heat. Therefore Galen allowed food during the chill, and never when they already suffer febrile heat. Yet if, when the fever arises from a putrid humour, we give food during the paroxysms with the confidence of freeing them from the fever, we shall not be mistaken to their considerable harm. Still, these patients will be harmed less than those of another habit.

units.la: Sed hæc de tempore nutriendi febricitâtes opportuno, satis sint dicta. Resumentes igitur ea quæ hucusque diximus quod reliquum est prosequemur. Formam victus quam Græci διαιτα vocant, à morbi constitutione, & ægrotantis robore sumendam esse diximus: Scopumque totius huius cõsiderationis esse, an ijs quæ comeduntur aut ijs quæ sorbentur, aut bibuntur ægrotantem nutrire, an omnimoda cibi & potus abstinentia uti debeamus. Hoc est formam victus quærere: quà inuenta, quantitatem determinabimus, à consuetudine primo, deinde à morbi cõstitutione. In initio tantũ esse exhibendum, quantum in dicat cõsuetudo diximus. Deinde ut symptomata increscunt, ita minuere, ita ut in vigore, & paruũ ante ipsum, nihil sit exhibendũ. Deinde ostendimus secundũ Hippocratẽ et Galenũ vnica victus forma à principio ad statũ vsq; & paruũ ante ipsum nutriendos esse ægrotantes: Non ut aliqui senserunt crassiori victu in principio, quàm in augmento, & in hoc quàm propè statum, hanc crassitiem maiorem aut minorem, non ad quantitatem solum, sed ad formam victus referentes. Unde cibarijs vtuntur & forma & substantia longè dissimilibus stante eadem morbi constitutione. Cum quibus disceptare hac de re breuitati consulens præterminto. Solum lectores admonitos esse velim: qui si Hippocratis libros diligenter euoluant, vnica victus forma, ægrotátes alere ab initio acuti morbi ad statum vsque addiscent. Porrò iam dicta de ea morborum differentia fore intelligenda di ctum est, qui ab initio leuiter incipiunt, & summissim increscunt, & exacerbantur ad iudicationem vsque in qua abundè elucent. Verùm in morbis ijs qui ab initio florent, & vigent maximè, & ad difficilius increscunt, iuxta verò crisim imminuuntur, aliam fore diximus victus obseruandam rationem, nem pe a robore virtutis & a coctione morbi vi ctus formam sumendam esse: ita vt cum mor bi cruditas affuerit, tenuiter ægrotantes nu- trire oporteat. Cunque coctio in materia ap- paruerit, formam victus mutandam esse ad crassiorem, quantitatemque augendam. Di- ximusque in omnibus morbis in quibus pro- cedens coctio symptomata imminuit, hanc victus rationem seruanda esse. Cæterum nu- merum diximus a robore virtutis, & a mor- bi constitutione, & a consuetudine sumi. Hæc primum oblationum numerum indicat, a quo à quo morbus detrahit, aut virtutis imbecil litas addit. Si ergo quis recte quæ dicta sunt in singulis victus scopis percipiat, quatuor esse vniuersi victus indicantia rationem col liget: Nempe virium robur, morbum ægro- tantis temperamentum, & consuetudinem. Tot enim & non plura in iis quæ diximus nu merauimus. Hancque indicantium victus ra tionem summam, secundũ mentem senis esse scito in libro secundo de ratione victus, vbi ita scribit: Conijcere autem oportet robur, et morbi cuiusque modum, hominis item natu- ram, atque ægrotantis in victu consuetudi nem, non in cibis solum, verùm quoque & in potibus.
units.tr: But enough has been said about the right time for feeding feverish patients. Resuming, then, the things we have said so far, we shall go on to what remains. We have said that the form of diet, which the Greeks call diaita [διαιτα], is to be taken from the constitution of the disease and the strength of the patient; and that the aim of this whole consideration is whether we ought to nourish the patient with what is eaten, or with what is sipped or drunk, or whether we ought to use a total abstinence from food and drink. This is to seek the form of diet; once it is found, we shall determine the quantity, first from custom, then from the constitution of the disease. We have said that at the beginning only as much should be given as custom indicates. Then, as the symptoms increase, so it must be diminished, so that at the height, and a little before it, nothing is to be given. Next we have shown, following Hippocrates and Galen, that by a single form of diet the sick are to be nourished from the beginning until the state of the disease, and a little before it; not, as some have thought, with a coarser diet at the beginning than in the increase, and in the increase closer to the state, referring this greater or lesser coarseness not only to quantity but to the form of diet. Hence they use food differing greatly in form and substance while the constitution of the disease remains the same. I pass over disputation on this matter, out of regard for brevity. I only wish the readers to be reminded: if they diligently turn over the books of Hippocrates, they will learn that one single form of diet is to be used in nourishing the sick from the beginning of an acute disease until its state. Moreover, what we have said already about that difference of diseases must be understood as applying to those that begin mildly, increase gradually, and grow worse up to the judgement, in which they are plainly evident. But in those diseases that flourish and are most vigorous from the beginning, and increase more difficultly, and diminish towards the crisis, we have said that another method of diet must be observed, namely that the form of diet is to be taken from the strength of the powers and from the concoction of the disease: so that when the disease is still crude, the sick must be nourished sparingly; and when concoction has appeared in the matter, the form of diet must be changed to a coarser one and the quantity increased. We have said that in all diseases in which the progressing concoction diminishes the symptoms, this method of diet is to be kept. Further, we have said that the number of offerings is taken from the strength of the powers, from the constitution of the disease, and from custom. This indicates the number of offerings first, from which the disease subtracts, or to which the weakness of the powers adds. If, then, anyone rightly grasps what has been said about each aim of diet, he will gather that there are four indications for the whole of diet: namely, the strength of the powers, the constitution of the sick person's temperament, and custom. For we have counted these four in what we have said, and not more. And you should know that this summary of indications, according to the mind of the old physician, is set out in the second book On Regimen, where he writes thus: "One must conjecture the strength, and the manner of each disease, likewise the nature of the man, and the custom of the sick person in diet, not only in foods but also in drinks."

units.la: Eorum quę de ptisana Hippocrates scripsit nonnulla esse aliis cibariis communia, & aliqua ptisanæ peculiaria.
units.tr: Of the things Hippocrates wrote about ptisan, some are common to it and other foods, and some are peculiar to ptisan. ## Chapter X.

units.la: CAPVT X.

DIVINVS igitur Hippocrates in libris de ratione victus, de sorbitionibus & poculis solum egit, tanquã hæ solũ acutis morbis conueniant victus formæ. De ptisana scripsit, utpote quæ leuissima omniū aliarū sorbitio est, & acutis maximè conueniens: vt ostendat, quòd cum in exhibitione huius comitatur error, non paruas inde fieri in acu tis noxas, grauiores multo fore si aliys vta- mur cibis. Primū ipse ostendit ijs verbis: Lu- bricissima est, sitim maximè arcet, facillimè coquitur, infirmissima existit si optimè co- ⁠cta fuerit, quibus omnibus est opus. Secun- dum, ijs verbis ostendit, si lateris dolor assi- duus est, calidisque fomentis non remittitur, sputumque non procedit, ptisanā aut ita asse- ctis dederit, præcipitem aget in mortē. Quod autem ijs similia accidant eis qui aliys cibis vtantur, ipse statim ostendit. Prehendunt au- tem (inquit) hæc, non solum si ptisana intem- pestiue vtātur, verū & multo magis si quip- piam aliud quàm ptisana inconuenientius e- dant, aut bibant. Sunt igitur nonnulla quæ scripsit Hippocrates de ptisana iudicia cum aliys cibariys communia, quædā peculiaria ipsi ptisanæ. Communia hæc sunt: Cū morbus à principio floret & viget; vt pleuritis et peripneu monia, vitanda est ptisanæ sorbitio, & multo magis quæ ex aliis cibarijs fit, maximè ea quæ eduntur, affectu existente crudo, sunt enim causa suffocationis & mortis. Sed tunc temporis potus humectantes exhibere conuenit. Cunque morbus coctionem iam recipit, & sputa procedunt, sorbitionem dare licet, & eius quantitas prout morbus magis maturescit augenda est. Præterea symptomate quocunque superueniente aut periculo, sicut tunc ptisanæ sorbitionem suspectam esse dixit, ita & omnem alium cibum qui solidior sit ea. Insuper & illud commune est, nempe tempus exhibitioni opportunum, cum caliditas ad pedes descenderit. Præterea incipiendū esse inclinante febre à magis tenui cibo ægrotantes alere. Demum illud, nempe post purgationem medicaminis sorbitione esse ministrandam quæ consueta sit minor.
units.tr: Hippocrates, then, was divinely inspired. In his books on the regimen of diet he treated only of gruels and drinks, as if these alone suited the regimen of acute diseases. He wrote about ptisan because it is the lightest of all gruels and is especially suited to acute illness, so that he might show that when its administration is accompanied by error, no small harm follows in acute cases, and much graver harm if we use other foods. First, he shows this himself in these words: "It is very slippery, it best quenches thirst, it is most easily digested, and it is least harmful if it is very well cooked; all of which are needed." Second, he shows in these words that if the pain in the side is constant and is not relieved by warm fomentations, and the sputum does not come up, giving ptisan to such patients will drive them headlong to death. He shows at once that things similar to this happen to those who use other foods. "These things" (he says) "befall not only if they take ptisan at the wrong time, but much more if they eat or drink anything else than ptisan, which is less suitable." So there are some judgements Hippocrates made about ptisan that are common to it and other foods, and some peculiar to ptisan itself. The common ones are these. When a disease is at its height and in full vigour, as in pleurisy and peripneumony, the sipping of ptisan is to be avoided, and much more so that made from other foods, especially those that are eaten, while the crudity is present; for these cause suffocation and death. At that time, however, it is fitting to give moistening drinks. When the disease now admits of concoction and sputa come up, it is permitted to give a gruel, and its quantity is to be increased as the disease matures more. Further, if any symptom or danger supervenes, just as he said that the sipping of ptisan was then to be suspected, so also is any other food that is more solid than it. Moreover, this too is common: the proper time for administration is when the heat has descended to the feet. Furthermore, as the fever declines, patients should begin to be nourished with a thinner food. Lastly, after the purgation by a medicine, a gruel which is usually small should be administered.

units.la: Peculiaria sunt hæc: Vt ptisana optime apparetur. Nam nisi quis quantum deest contulerit, vt ptisanæ sorbitio sufficienter paretur, crebrius sane detrimentum afferet. Deinde illud: Quibus enim cibus statim inclusus, si quis non vacuato eo sorbitionem dederit, dolorem si adesset adaugebit, & si non adesset protinus inducet frequentiorque reddetur spiritus, quod malum est. nam pulmonem exiccat. Praeterea & illud: Vbi autem quis medicamentum ebibit, ptisanam protinus sorbendam dato, nec insigniter minore quam consuetum est quantitate. Praeterea & illud: nisi propter pharmaciam aut clysterem ab usu ptisanae desistendum sit: Galeno addit, aut propter sanguinis missionem. Haec omnia soli competunt ptisanae, minime aliis cibariis.
units.tr: These are peculiar to ptisan: that ptisan be prepared very well. For unless one adds what is lacking, so that a sufficient gruel of ptisan is made, it will surely do harm more often. Next, that: "For if, when the food has been taken in and not yet evacuated, someone gives a gruel, it will increase the pain if there is pain, and if there is none it will at once induce it, and the breathing will become more frequent, which is bad, for it dries the lung." Also this: "When someone has drunk a medicine, give ptisan at once to be sipped, and not in a quantity markedly smaller than is customary." Also this: "unless on account of a drug or an enema the use of ptisan must be stopped," to which Galen adds: "or on account of bloodletting." All these apply to ptisan alone, and in no way to other foods.

units.la: Vbi mulsa, ubi oxymelite utendum sit.
units.tr: Where honeyed wine (mulsa) and where oxymel is to be used.

units.la: CAPVT XI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XI.

units.la: IN solis iis morbis mulsa utendum est, in quibus praeacuminis vehementia morbus peracutus fuerit. Aut ob aliquem dolorem, aut si periculum instat. In summa morbis iis quibus supra sorbitiones prohibuimus, indigentes eo quod pulmonem humectet, & sputum tum mediocriter educat, & tusses mitiget, aut eo quod vrinas abunde cieat, aut biliosa deiiciat excrementa, mulsam eligimus. Macerationem cauentes in iis qui natura calida et sicca sunt, amara bilis hominibus, picrocholi Græce dicuntur. Iis vero quibus tumefacta sunt viscera ob scirrhum, aut ob phlegmonem, immoderato calore biliescit. Scirrhus enim impedimento est, ne citò adrenes & viscera transeat. Vnde longa mora in bilem similiter vertitur. Picrocholis igitur dilutior exhibenda est, vt citius penetret. Iis si mili modo ministrato, in quibus pulmonem magis lenire cupimus & sputum magis educere. Meracior verò potentius biliosa deiicit excrementa, magis tamen suspecta iis est qui calida sunt natura. Spumosa siquidem iis & plusquam conuenit biliosa efficit excrementa, in bilem flauam transiens. Vnde aduersissimam liquefacientibus febribus esse mulsam scripsit Galenus in tertio de ratione victus.
units.tr: Mulsa is to be used only in those diseases in which the illness is very acute, with the violence of the sharp stage. Either because of some pain, or if danger threatens. In short, in those diseases for which we forbade sorbitions above, when the lung needs moistening, moderate expulsion of sputum, the easing of coughs, or abundant evacuation of urine or of bilious excrements, we choose mulsa. Taking care to avoid maceration in those who are hot and dry by nature, bitter bile in men is called picrochole in Greek. In those whose viscera are swollen from a scirrhus or from a phlegmon, the bile turns to excess heat. For a scirrhus is an obstacle, so that the matter does not pass quickly through the reins and the viscera; hence a long delay turns it similarly into bile. A more dilute mulsa is therefore to be given to picrochole patients, so that it penetrates more quickly. In those for whom we wish to soothe the lung more and draw out sputum more, the mulsa should be given in this mild way. A stronger mulsa, however, expels bilious excrements more powerfully, yet it is more suspect for those who are hot by nature. For it produces frothy and more than appropriate bilious excrements, passing into yellow bile. Hence Galen wrote in the third book of On the Regimen of Life that mulsa is most harmful in fevers that melt the humours.

units.la: Oxymelite in iis vtemur morbis in quibus sorbitionibus supersedemus. Tunc maximè, cum sputum crassum & glutinosum educere volumus, aut sitim sedare, flatum discutere, et vrinas movere. Proinde oxymeli quod val de acre est, ad crassa sputa & vehementer glutinosa vim habet. Verùm si huiusmodi sputa non secat aut educit, non solum non confert, verùm & detrimentũ affert. Nam exic cans, ea magis reddit crassa & glutinosa. Aut ergo quod valde acre oxymeli est prodesse rit, crassa si secuerit sputa, et ea eduxerit: aut idsi non præstet, abundè nocebit. Quapropter recte Hippocrates dixit nihil mediocriter efficere, in iis quæ non facilè educuntur sputis. Iccirco ægritudinis morigerationẽ aut malignitatem considerandam esse ait, ut scia mus quibus exhibitum secabit sputa, & quibus non. Iis igitur qui graviter habent, et virium imbecillitate laborant, non propinabis. Quod si ob virium robur de eo bene sperare is, dabis paulatim & tepidum. Oxymelitis nocumenta sunt hæc, quod partem intestini imam reddit humectiorem, & ramenta facit. Unde imbecilla habetibus intestina exhibendum. bendum non est. Est aliquando in acutis mor-bis vt ramēta intestini praua ob id sint, quod flatum non modo foras prodire vetant, verū quoque reuerti faciant. Et ob hæc vires fran-gunt, extremaq; infrigidant. Qui autem non sorbitionibus sed potione sola vtuntur, ijs nō semper oxymelite vti expedit, ob intestino-rum abrafionem, eò præcipuè quod stercore vidua sint. Cū igitur sputa quæ in bronchijs pulmonis continentur, vel glutinosa vel ad modum crassa sunt, mulsaqué sitim inferat, solo est vtendum oxymelite. Quare vt longo vsu non noceat, aquæ mulsæ tantum aceti mi-scendum est, vt duntaxat sentiri possit. Et ita simul ad lentum ignem coquere oportet. Hoc enim pacto ad nocendū infirmius erit. Sed abundè à nobis de victus ratione secun-dum mentem Hippocratis hucusque dictum sit.
units.tr: We use oxymel in those diseases in which we forgo sorbitions. Especially when we wish to draw out thick and viscous sputum, or to quench thirst, dispel wind, and move the urine. Therefore oxymel that is very sharp has force against thick and very viscous sputa. But if it does not cut or draw out such sputa, it not only does no good but also does harm, for by drying them it makes them thicker and more viscous. So either a very sharp oxymel will help, if it cuts the thick sputa and draws them out, or, if it does not, it will do great harm. Hence Hippocrates rightly said that nothing done halfway succeeds in those matters which are not easily brought out by sputum. For this reason he says that the patient's disposition or the malignity of the disease must be considered, so that we may know to whom it will cut the sputa and to whom not. Therefore you will not give it to those who are gravely ill and suffer from feebleness of strength. But if, because of the robustness of their strength, you may hope well of it, you will give it gradually and lukewarm. The harms of oxymel are these: it makes the lowest part of the intestine more moist and produces fragments. Therefore it must not be given to those who have weak intestines. Sometimes in acute diseases the fragments of the intestine are harmful because they not only forbid the wind to go out but also cause it to turn back. And for these reasons they break the strength and chill the extremities. Those, however, who use not sorbitions but drink alone, it is not always useful for them to use oxymel, because of the abrasion of the intestines, especially since they are deprived of stool. Therefore, when the sputa contained in the bronchi of the lung are either viscous or thick, and mulsa would bring on thirst, oxymel alone must be used. So that it does not harm with long use, only enough vinegar should be mixed into the mulsa water for it to be just perceptible. And so it must be boiled together over a slow fire. For in this way it will be less able to harm. But enough has been said so far, following the mind of Hippocrates, about the regimen of diet.

units.la: A quibus ratio potus qui ægrotantibus mi-nistrandus sit sumatur.
units.tr: From what sources the rule of drink to be given to the sick is to be taken.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: SED tempestiuum est, vt de potu sermo-nem faciamus, qui febricitantibus conue-niat. Hunc, omnia quæ supra ostendere vi-ctum diximus, indicant: nempe virtutis ro-bur, morbi dispositio, ægrotantis natura, & consuetudo: Vt nos docuit Hippocrates in se-cundo de ratione victus, in hæc verba: Προ-σεμμαχετικα δὲ καὶ ἡ ἰσχὺς καὶ ὁ ὁρόπ[?]Φ τ' ν[?]ο-μάχτ[?] ἑκάστ[?], καὶ ἡ φύσις [?] τὸ τ' αὐθεω-πος καὶ τὸ ἐθος [?] τ' διαίτης τὸ πάμνοντ[?], ὁ μόνον σιτίων ἀλλὰ καὶ ποτῶν. Hoc est, Con-ijcienda sunt & robur, & modus cuiusque morbi, hominisque naturæ, & consuetudi-nis laborantis in victu, non in cibis solum ve-rum quoq; in potibus. Quibus in verbis quo-tuor esse quæ potum indicant aperte docuit.
units.tr: But it is now timely to speak of drink, which is suitable for the feverish. All the things we said above show this regimen: namely the strength of the power, the disposition of the disease, the nature of the patient, and habit. As Hippocrates taught us in the second book of On the Regimen, in these words: Conjectural factors are the strength, the manner of each disease, the nature of the man, and the habit of the patient's regimen, not only in foods but also in drinks. [Προσεμμαχετικὰ δὲ καὶ ἡ ἰσχύς, καὶ ὁ τοῦ ἑκάστου νοσήματος τρόπος, καὶ ἡ φύσις τοῦ ἀνθρώπου καὶ τὸ ἔθος τῆς διαίτης τοῦ πάσχοντος, οὐ μόνον σιτίων ἀλλὰ καὶ ποτῶν.] In these words he clearly taught that there are four things which indicate drink.

units.la: Cæterum si eorum quæ supra in de qualitate victus diximus meminEris, tria sat esse ad po-tus indicationem intelliges. Nam laborantis natura vt illic ostendimus, non nisi interuen-tu consuetudinis indicat. Nam ægrotanti fri-gidæ naturæ, potui aquæ assueto, aquam non vinum ministrabimus, sumpta à consuetudi-ne ne indicatione, & non à laborantis natura. Neque rursus homini calidæ naturæ ægrotan ti, aquam in potu dabimus, qui perpetuo vi- no assueuerit. Hæc ex Galeni octauo de me- thodo colligimus de calidis naturis & siccis loquente in hunc modum: Si quis vero (in- quit) non assueuit scilicet frigidæ, huic per fe- brem dare non inceperim, nisi pristina plane sanitate prius reddita. Indicatio igitur à con- suetudine, eam obumbrat, quæ à natura la- borantis sumitur indicatione, durante mor- bo. Nec id mirum videri debet, nam maximâ vim habet consuetudo, repentinaque ab ea digressio corpora non parum offendit, vt à Galeno scriptum est secundo de ratione vi- ctus. Tria igitur sunt quæ potum indicant, nempe virtutis robur, morbus, & consuetu do. Virtus cum valet, consuetudini in indica- tione potus consentit, eum maximè potū in- dicans quem consuetudo. Cum vero imbecil- lis est, quandoque dissentit, vnde fit vt ægro- tanti frigidæ assueto, modicum vini quo eius roboretur natura concedamus. Cuius argumentum est, pluribus, dulce Bacchi venenum, primam labijs admouendi occasionem dedisse ægritudines. Morbus cum magnus est, & vehemens consuetudinis indicatione obscurat. Na laboranti acuta febre vino assueto, eum ministrabimus maximè potum quem ægritudo indicauerit, virtute nequaquam dissuadente, vt ex Galeni nono de methodo colligitur cum de continentium febrium curatione agit: vbi frigidæ potum post coctiones exhibet, à consuetudine nullam sumens indicationem: vbi in hunc modum scribit: Cum ergo coctionis humorum in iis notas videris, de quibus dictum abundè in libris de crisi est, audacter frigida dabis. Et subiungit statim, Quod si etiam frigidæ assuetus æger sit, magna cum fiducia frigidam exhibebis, &c. Ac si velit id quod eodem libro scripsit in hæc verba: Siquidem cùm sæpe iam viderimus nõpaucos ex iis qui febribus ardentibus premerentur, cùm iam mediocriter concocti humores essent, statim ex frigidæ potione à febre liberatos, quamvis ei potioni parum assueti fuissent:
units.tr: Moreover, if you remember what we said above about the quality of the regimen, you will understand that three things are enough to indicate drink. For the nature of the patient, as we showed there, indicates only through the intervention of habit. For to a patient of cold nature who is used to water, we will give water, not wine, taking the indication from habit rather than from the patient's nature. Nor again will we give water to a patient of hot nature who has been accustomed to wine all the time. We gather this from Galen's eighth book On the Method, speaking of hot and dry natures in this way: "But if someone," he says, "is not accustomed to cold things, I would not begin to give him cold drink during a fever, unless his former health has first been fully restored." So the indication from habit overshadows that which is taken from the patient's nature while the disease lasts. Nor ought this to seem strange, for habit has the greatest power, and a sudden departure from it offends the body not a little, as Galen wrote in the second book of On the Regimen. There are therefore three things which indicate drink: namely the strength of the power, the disease, and habit. When the strength is sound, it agrees with habit in the indication of drink, indicating especially the drink to which habit is accustomed. When it is weak, it sometimes disagrees, whence it comes about that for a patient accustomed to cold drink we allow a modest amount of wine by which his nature may be strengthened. The evidence for this is that for many people sweet poison of Bacchus gave the first occasion for sicknesses by touching the lips. When the disease is great and violent, it obscures the indication from habit. For to a patient in acute fever who is accustomed to wine, we will give chiefly the drink which the illness indicates, the strength by no means dissuading, as is gathered from Galen's ninth book On the Method, when he treats of the cure of continual fevers, where he gives cold drink after the concoctions, taking no indication from habit; there he writes in this way: "When therefore you see the signs of concoction of the humours in those cases of which we have spoken fully in the books on crisis, you will boldly give cold things." And he immediately adds: "But if the patient is also accustomed to cold things, you will give cold drink with great confidence, etc." And it is as if he wished to express what he wrote in the same book in these words: "For since we have often seen not a few of those who were oppressed by burning fevers, when their humours were already moderately concocted, freed from fever at once by a drink of cold water, although they were little accustomed to that drink:"

units.la: ɔɔ marks: pointers in the margin, each beside a line of the lower part, not text. sent: multò arbitror magis in iis qui assuevê-runt vtilitatem fore, citra noxam vllam spe rabimus. Vnde non ob id quod aquæ assuetus non sit, ab ea desistendum est, nisi cum aliquod effatu dignum incommodum naturæ ab eius occursu timemus. Ob id apposui, virtute nequaquam dissuadente. Idem ab eodem vndecimo libro de methodo medendi colligi potest, cum in febribus continuis, absolute citra consuetudinis consideratione, vinum prohibet, & frigidam exhibendam consulit. Imbecilli verò morbo existente, diuersumque ab eo, quem consuetudo indicauit potum exposcente, quæ à consuetudine sumitur prævalebit indicatio. Vt manifestum est ex eo quod Galenus octauo de methodo scripsit. Qui cum vinum vtilius esse quàm aquam dixisset, ad cötiones, & vrinæ, ac sudorum prouocationem, statim subiungit: Ego igitur censeo eius generis naturas, et dum valet, huiusmodi potione, scilicet aqua magnopere iuuari, nec in diaria febre iis quibus in vsu fuit eam circundo. Si quis verò non assuevit huic per febrem dare non inceperim, nisi pristina pla- nè sanitate prius reddita. Oslensum igitur est quod cum morbus & consuetudo diuersos potus indicat, si morbo magnitudo accesserit, huius indicationem obscurare eam quæ à consuetudine sumitur. Quod si morbo nulla effatu digna accesserit magnitudo, aut vehementia, scito indicationem à consuetudine tunc prævalere. Cæterū de robore virtutis & morbi magnitudine supra abundè dictum est, cū de victus forma sermonem fecimus. Sciendū præterea, quod cum virtus ob imbecillitatē urget, eum semper indicat potum, quo maximè roborari possit. Qua de causa roboratem potum nuncupamus, quem causa roborandæ virtutis ægrotantibus cōcedimus. Tale in primis vinum est, quod omnium maximè corporis vires naturales & vitales roborat. Morbus eum indicat potum, qui morbo aut eius causæ qualitate contrarius sit. Ob id curantem potum eum dicimus, quem morbus ipse indicat. Est autem talis, acutis & vehementibus febribus, aqua: ut ex Galeno in tertio de de ratione victus (licet sub aliis verbis) colligitur, cū ita scribit: Quando igitur (inquit) bibi idonea est aqua? cum scilicet potu solo æger nutritus fuerit, nullo pacto accepto ptisanæ cremore. Tunc enim in potionum aliarum medio, aquā tempestiue quis ingesserit, & præsertim cum siticulosus æger fuerit. Per illa verba, potu solo nutritus fuerit, intelligit, ab aliquo ægrotantem acutorum morbo rum affici, cuius causa solo victu per pocula nutriatur. Ac si velit quibuscunque acuto morbo laborantibus, aquam conuenienter in potum exhiberi. Aqua igitur in primis, potus curans in acutis affectibus est. Vires tamen corporis minime roborat, vt ab eodem loco citato scriptum est cum ait: Quod autem (inquit) non alat antea dictum est, quo fit vt facultatem vitalem roborare non possit, &c. Ab aqua simplici consequenter est ea in qua virtus alicuius rei per decoctionem transmissa est: vt aqua ex decoctione hordei, aut liquiritiæ, aut prunorum, &c. Et sunt tot numero quot sunt res quæ simul cū aquæ decoquipossunt. Est & vinum in aliquibus morbis potus curans. Vt ex Galeno in libris de methodo medendi apparet, & ex Hippocrate tertio de ratione victus, Consuetudinem vero eum cui æger assueuerit potūindicare diximus, qua de causa consuetum potum eū dicimus, quem consuetudo indicat. Qui vnus e tribus est potus, quibus vbique terrarū viuntur homines, nempe aqua, vino, ceruisia. Lu sitani aquæ potu delectantur, Galli & Itali vino, Germani et Angli cernisia. Cæteri potus roborans multiplex est. Nempe vinū potens, quod vinosum Hippocrates nūcupauit, id tale est quod in aliquo vehementissimū est. Est & huius contrariū, quod aquosum ob id medici nuncuparunt, quòd aquæ maximè in omnibus simile exỉstit, nempe tenuitate, colore, & odoris carentia, et nō manifesta calefactione. Iis omnibus cōsentit Galenus tertio de ratione victus in initio. Porrò inter hæc multa esse quæ mediæ naturæ sunt vina comperies. Non clarioris sermonis gratia, tria inter iam dicta, media locauimus. Vnum quod vehevehementissimo proximum est. Aliud quod aquoso. Tertium quod medium obtinet locu. Primu ex duobus maxime dignoscere oportet: nempe ut in mixtione vinum aquam manifeste euincat: Item ut in eo aliquod sit vehementia vestigium. Secundum contraria qualitate dignosces: nempe ut in eo aqua euincat & imbecilliter calfaciat. Ex iis duobus medium intelliges, nempe in quo neutrum sensibiliter euincat, & nullum in eo vehementia vestigium appareat. Nos quo facilius res percipiatur, singulis horum nomina imponemus. Vinum vehementissimum, vinosum nuncupamus. Eius contrarium aquosum. Huic proximum imbecille. Eius oppositum potens. Et medium inter haec. Scire oportet has vinorum species reperiri posse in simplici vinorum natura. Nam quod fuluum colore est, vehementissimum est. Huius contrarium est, quod imbecillitate, colore, tenuitate substantiae, odoris carentia, et occulta calfactione, aquae similimum est. Huic proximum, vinum album tenue, sine odore, imbecilli calfactione: Cuiusmodi sunt vina alba tenuia inodora quæ in aliquibus Italiæ locis proueniunt. Proximum vino so est vinum colore rubeum, crassum, odorum, cum vehementia calfaciens, cuiusmodi sunt quæ Hispania profert. Medium, colore subrubeo est, splendidum, mediocris substantiæ, inodorum, manifeste citra aliquam vehementiam calfaciès: cuiusmodi sunt vina quæ ex Gallia deferuntur. Posset quisque imitari has naturas, potenti vino aquam pro ratione cuiusque immiscens. Ita ut aquosum efficias, si aquæ portioni tantùmodo id vini misceas, ut modica fiat in eo vini repræsentatio. Id enim discimus à Galeno in tertio de ratione victus in acutis, qui vinum sic temperauit multa aquæ commixtione, cuius verba ita habent: Cum igitur (inquit) seni cuidam ægrotanti quotidie vinum aquosum exhibe-rem, quidam ex huiusmodi medicis præsens, me vini minimum, aquæ instillantem con-templatus risit, ægrumque vinum non bibere, sed duntaxat videre dixit: non sane intelligens, mixtionis vini quod gratia voluptatis datur datur ad aquam aliam esse symmetriam, & aliam esse eius quod ad opem ferendam mini-stratur. Nam vini omnino minimū veluti ex citationem quandam quæ ad distributionem aquam trahat permiscemus: ut duntaxat a-quæ tollamus sinceritatem, non autem aquā vinum faciamus. Sunt autem plerique ex sa-nis qui vinum aqua dilutum bibant, sed in iis aquam gustatu ipso euincere non oportet. In ægris vero ut modica sit vini repræsentatio. Sic de oxymelite paulo ante dicebat aquosum laudans, &c. Hucusque Galenus: quibus in verbis modum mixtionis aquæ cum vino ad aquosum vinum efficiendum aperte docuit.
units.tr: Yet I think the benefit will be much greater for those who are accustomed to it, and we shall hope for it without any harm. Therefore one should not give up on water merely because the patient is not used to it, unless we fear some serious harm to the strength from its contact. I have added this, since reason does not advise against it. The same can be gathered from the eleventh book of Galen's On the Method of Healing, where in continued fevers he forbids wine and recommends cold water absolutely, without regard to habit. But when the illness is feeble and the indication for a drink different from what habit demands, the indication drawn from habit will prevail, as is clear from what Galen wrote in the eighth book of On the Method. After saying that wine is more useful than water for promoting urine and sweat, he immediately adds: "I therefore judge that such natures, while they are healthy, are greatly helped by this kind of drink, namely water, and I do not exclude from it in a daily fever those who are accustomed to it. If anyone has not been accustomed to it, I shall not begin to give it in fever until health has first been fully restored." It is therefore shown that when the illness and habit indicate different drinks, if the illness acquires a serious severity, the indication of habit is overridden. But if no severity or vehemence worth mentioning attends the illness, know that the indication of habit then prevails. Concerning the strength of the power and the magnitude of the illness, enough has been said above, when we discussed the form of diet. Moreover, one should know that when the power is urged by weakness, it always indicates that drink by which it can be most strengthened. For this reason we call the drink that restores strength the strengthening drink, which we give to the sick for the sake of restoring strength. Above all, wine is of this kind, since it strengthens most of all the natural and vital powers of the body. The illness indicates the drink that is contrary to the illness or to the quality of its cause, and for this reason we call the drink the illness itself indicates the curing drink. Such a drink, in acute and violent fevers, is water, as is gathered from Galen in the third book of On the Regimen of Diet (though in other words), when he writes: "When, then, is water suitable to drink?" Namely, when the patient has been nourished by drink alone, with no barley-water gruel taken at all. For then, in the midst of other drinks, one may pour in water at the right time, especially when the patient is thirsty. By the words "nourished by drink alone" he means that the patient is affected by some acute illness, and for that reason is nourished by drink alone. It is as if he wished water to be suitably given as a drink to all who labour under an acute illness. Water, therefore, is above all the curing drink in acute affections. Yet it does not strengthen the powers of the body at all, as is written in the same passage cited, where he says: "But that it does not nourish has been said before, so that it cannot strengthen the vital faculty, etc." Next to plain water is that in which the virtue of some substance has been passed over by decoction, as water from a decoction of barley, or of liquorice, or of prunes, etc. There are as many of these as there are substances that can be boiled together with water. Wine too, in some illnesses, is a curing drink, as appears from Galen in the books On the Method of Healing and from Hippocrates in the third book of On the Regimen of Diet. We have said that the drink to which the patient has become accustomed indicates a customary drink, and for this reason we call the customary drink the one that habit indicates. This is one of the three drinks which men everywhere use: namely water, wine, and beer. The Lusitanians delight in water, the French and Italians in wine, the Germans and English in beer. The strengthening drink is of many kinds. There is the potent wine, which Hippocrates called "vinous," being that which is most vehement in some respect. There is also its opposite, which physicians have called "watery," because it most resembles water in all respects: in thinness, colour, lack of smell, and absence of manifest warming. Galen agrees with all this at the beginning of the third book of On the Regimen of Diet. Moreover, you will find among these that many wines are of intermediate nature. For the sake of clearer speech, I have placed three of the aforementioned kinds in the middle: one nearest to the most vehement, another nearest to the watery, and a third which holds the middle place. The first must be recognised by two things most of all: namely, that in the mixture the wine clearly overcomes the water, and that some trace of vehemence is in it. The second you will recognise by its contrary quality: namely, that in it the water overcomes and warms only feebly. From these two you will understand the middle, namely that in which neither perceptibly overcomes, and in which no trace of vehemence appears. So that the matter may be grasped more easily, I shall give a name to each of these. The most vehement wine we call "vinous"; its contrary is "watery"; that nearest to it is "weak"; its opposite is "potent"; and the middle between these is the "moderate." One should know that these kinds of wine can be found in the simple nature of wines. For what is tawny in colour is most vehement; its contrary is what, in weakness, colour, thinness of substance, lack of smell, and hidden warming, is most like water. Nearest to this is thin white wine, without smell, with a weak warming: such are the thin white wines without smell that grow in some parts of Italy. Nearest to the potent wine is wine that is red in colour, thick, fragrant, and warming with vehemence; such are the wines that Spain produces. The moderate is of a slightly reddish colour, bright, of middling substance, without smell, and warming plainly without any vehemence; such are the wines brought from France. Anyone could imitate these natures, mixing water with potent wine in proportion to each. Thus you will make a watery wine if you mix into the portion of water only so much wine that a slight impression of wine remains in it. For we learn this from Galen in the third book of On the Regimen of Diet in acute cases, who so tempered the wine with much admixture of water. His words are these: "When I was giving an old patient wine that was watery every day, a certain physician of this kind who was present, seeing me pour in a very small amount of wine, laughed and said that the sick man was not drinking wine but merely looking at it, not understanding that the proportion of wine mixed for pleasure is one thing, and that of wine supplied to bring help is another. For we mix in altogether a very small amount of wine, as if to draw in a certain quickening that spreads through the water, so that we take away only the purity of the water and do not make wine out of water. Indeed, many of the healthy drink wine diluted with water, but in them one should not make the water prevail by its taste. In the sick, however, there should be a slight impression of wine. So also earlier, in praising the oxymel, he said it was watery," etc. Thus far Galen, in whose words he clearly taught the manner of mixing water with wine so as to make watery wine.

units.la: Talem in mixtione seruare iubens symmetri-am, ut modica sit vini in gustatu ipso repræ-sentatio. Imbecille efficies si tantum aquæ iniycias ut vinum imbecilliter calfaciat. Sed ut exactius rem assequi possis, vinum super aquam infundere expediet; id subinde labijs admoneto ut cum primum ad metam imbe-cillis calfactionis deuenerit mixtio, vini non amplius infundas. Simili ratione vinū quod moderatū diximus efficies, tandiu vinum a- quæ immiscendo, donec neutrum duorū euin cat. Posset quinis his alia media inserere, na- turasq; eorum penes aliquod triū sensuum ob ieƈtum dissinire. Sed hæc sufficere omnibus tam ijs qui acuto, quam ijs qui hebeti sunt sen su, arbitramur. Eo præcipuè quod reliquæ quæcunq; inter has sunt potus differētiæ haud facilè à sensu discernuntur.
units.tr: Ordering that such a proportion be kept in the mixture, so that there is a slight impression of wine in the taste itself, you will make a weak wine if you pour in only so much water that the wine warms only feebly. But so that you may achieve the matter more exactly, it will be useful to pour the wine over the water, and from time to time to warn with your lips that as soon as the mixture has reached the limit of feeble warming, you should pour in no more wine. In the same way you will make the wine we called moderate, adding wine to water until neither of the two overcomes. One could insert other intermediate kinds among these, and define their natures by the sense of one of the three senses through the taste. But we think these are enough for all, both for those with a keen sense and for those with a dull one. Especially since all the other differences of drink that lie between these are hardly ever distinguished by the sense.

units.la: Potus similiter quo communiter Angli vtuntur multiplex est: nempe vehemens me dius & imbecillior. Discrimen inter hos pe- nes vehementiam, & imbecillitatem, cal- faƈtionem, & refrigerationem, & penes substantiæ crassitiem & tenuitatē habetur. Apud Anglos triplex semper paratur potus, nempe aquosus, quem simplicem cernisiā di- cunt: medius, quē trihapeninam: potens, quē duplam cernisiam nuncupant. simplex eus- dem effeƈtus præstat quos vinum aquosum. Aperit siquidem, refrigerat, & distributio- nem adimuat. Nec decipiatur aliquis credens ob eius amaritudinem calfacere. partes enim quæ cernisiam amaram reddunt, pauca admodum sunt, si ad reliquas conferas, quæ in ipsa refrigerant. Quod colligere ex ratione lupulorum poteris ad aquæ & hordei portiones. Citò prætereà amaritudo à cernisia evanescit, reliquarum verò partium facultas tandiu permanet donec in aliam transmutetur substantiam.
