Potens cernisia quam duplicem dicunt, potenter calefacit, & aliquid habet vehementiæ, ut potens vinū. Trihapenina mediæ naturæ est, manifestè calfacit, in nullo tamen vehemens est. Posset quis duos alios potus efficere mediæ naturæ inter hos, & totidem in cernisia differentias ac in vini natura faceremus. Ut si simplicis cernisiæ duos cyathos vni triahapeninæ misceas, medium potum inter duos efficies. Quod si simplicis cernisiæ vnum, mediæ vnum, duplicis vnum, simul misceas, medium potum inter mediam & duplicē efficies. Vocemus hos quinque cernisiæ potus eisdem nominibus quibus in vinorum naturis vsi sumus. Simplicem aquosum, proximū quem ex mixtione duorum cõfecimus, imbecillem, deinde medium, & huic proximum potentem, omnium postremum vehementem. Simili ratione totidẽ posses efficere differentias, illius potus quo molliores Anglorum vtuntur. (Allam vulgari sermone appellant) sunt qui ceruisiã per u, hũc latine dicant. Potus est vltra modum inflatiuus, nullam ex eo febricitantes vtilita tem capiunt. Neque enim refrigerat, neque aperit, neque vllam promouet euacuationẽ: sed nec sitim sedat. Corruptioni praeterea aptissimus est potus, & vicinos ad similem affectum disponit chymos. Eius insuper substantia nimis prompta est, vt in flatuosos sol uatur halitus. Qua de causa capiti & neruis incommodus est. Materia insuper obstructionum est, vnde iocineri & lieni inimicus est. In summa amicus potus nemini nisi vene ri. Ab ijs tamen qui eo vsi sunt bona valitudine, dimittendus per aegritudinem non est, vt supra ostendimus. Potus quem curantem diximus, nullas tales recipit differentias. Nam cum morbo aut eius causæ contrarius sit, fieri non potest, vt per intensionem alicuius qualitatis aut remissionem vllas praestet differentias. Oppositio siquidem omnis latitudine caret. Caeterum meminisse oportet virtutem in maxime, multum, & parum, & nihil vrgentem, supra nos explicasse. In totidem que morbum partitiones vna plus diuisisse. Nempe in maxime, multum, mediocriter, parum, & nihil vrgentem. Signis q in vtriusque sectionibus vsi sumus, quibus cuiusfacile erit, si non admodum crassa sit natura, cum virtus & morbus maxime, an multum, an parum, an nihil vrgeant, discernere. Ponamus igitur primum a consuetudine nihil indicari, hoc est nulla sit is qui laborat astrictus consuetudine in potibus, vt si aquae, vino, & cernisix si velis assuetus sit: (vt consuere gentis Lusitanae profugi, qui in Anglia, & Flandria sedem habuere.) Huic si virtus corporis sit imbecillis, eum indicabit potum quo maxime seruari possit, si morbus non prohibeat. Talis potus vini est quem virtutis imbecillitas indicat. Sed quod nam eligemus nondum constat: an aquosum, an imbecille an medium. Verum id natura corporis indicabit, ijs siquidem qui calido & sicco sunt temperamento, gracili habitu, imbecille vinum convenit. Iis vero qui frigida sunt natura, crasso habitu, pingui abdomine tardi, potens, aut vinosum. Quicunque atrabiliosi & media inter hos naturae sunt, medium. In sanis igitur corporibus nulli potui assuetis, cum aliqua imbecillitate laborant, ab ea solummodo indicatio potus in genere sumi tur, a naturali vero temperamento species. Quod si nulla imbecillitate eorum virtutes vrgeant, a sola corporis naturali temperie, potus indicatio est sumenda. Ut in sexto de morbis vulgaribus sive Hippocrates sive Thessalus eius filius tradidit, calidis naturis refrigerationem, aquae potionem, tunc quietem, consulens. Et hinc licet colligere ijs qui calida & sicca sunt natura cum robore virium, aqua uti commodius esse quam vino. Verum quicunque calidi & sicci sunt temperamenti, imbecilli natura, salubrius ijs esse aquoso vino in potu vti quàm aqua. Quia enim aquo sum est, calidæ naturæ cõuenit. Vt verò vini facultate habet, imbecillitati subuenit. Vnde manifestũ est, quòd ij qui calida & sicca sunt natura, gracili habitu, tenuium succorum, ob id quod citò eorum corpora in halitum sol uuntur, & imbecilliores exinde fiunt, vino aquoso per sanitatem cõmodissimè vtantur. Hoc Galenus asseruit octauo de methodo, cũ ait: Vinũ ipse conscius es, me omnibus huius- modi naturis concedere, sed quod tum aspe- ctu tum viribus sit aquosum. Id enim ad o- mnia vtilius est quàm aqua, vtpote quod cõ coctionem iuuet, et Vrinas ac sudores prouo cet. Ostensum igitur est quod seclusa indicatio ne à cõsuetudine, sanis corporibus imbecillib. genus potus à dispositione virtutis sumendũ esse, speciem verò à naturali temperamento. Vbi verò virtutis imbecillitas nihil indi- cet, prout contingit inculpatis naturis, quas semper, nisi cum à morbo detinentur, robu- stæ comitantur vires, à sola naturali tempe- rie & genus potus, & species sumuntur. Vnde fit vt corporibus calidis robustis aqua per sanitatem vti, & non vino salubre sit. Anglis & Germanis qui simili valent viri um robore, & simili sunt temperatura, & quicunque ijs borealiores sunt, cum prospe ra fruuntur valitudine, trihapeninam cerni siam, quæ media inter simplicem potum & duplicem est, magis conuenire arbitramur. Simplici potu, nisi æstate feruente non vta tur. Vinum ijs nisi medicinæ gratia incommo dum est. Nam ob frigidam continentis intem periem, tum ob excrementosa cibaria, tum ob faculentos potus, crassa in horum ven triculis aggregantur excrementa de genere pituitæ, quæ longa mora vitiosam qualitatẽ acquirunt. Iis vinum potens si exhibeas, vi tiosos humores ad iecur & venas secum de fert. Quare ob eorum crassitiem in angustis iocineris meatibus detenti, vias obstruunt. Quæ causa est vt coctionem sanguinis pertur bent, & depravent, iocinere ab eis vitium contrahente. Quod si imbecilla ijs vina mini stres, alterum duorum efficies, aut vitiosos chymos chymos ventriculo magis impinges, aut cru dos hos magis reddes. Huiusmodi siquidem vi na astrictionis aut acetosi aliquid habent. Ve rum medicinæ gratia, modicum vini ad se cundas mensas vt coctionem ventriculi ad iuuet, & cibariorum incoctorum à sole cru ditatem emendet suo moderato calore, his sa lubre est. Quapropter ijs media vina quæ ni hil vehementiæ habeant commoda sunt.
units.tr: Similarly, the drink that the English commonly use is of several kinds, namely strong, medium and weaker. The difference between these lies in strength and weakness, in heating and cooling, and in the thickness and thinness of the substance. Among the English there are always three kinds of drink prepared: the watery one, which they call simple cernisia; the medium, which they call trihapenina; and the strong one, which they call double cernisia. Simple cernisia produces the same effects as watery wine: it opens, cools and diminishes distribution. Let no one be deceived into thinking it heats because of its bitterness, for the parts that make cernisia bitter are very few compared with the rest, which cool. You may gather this from the proportion of hops to water and barley. Moreover, the bitterness quickly fades from the cernisia, but the power of the other parts lasts until they are changed into another substance. Potent cernisia, which they call double, heats strongly and has some of the vehemence of strong wine. Trihapenina is of a middle nature: it clearly heats, yet is in no way vehement. One could make two other drinks of intermediate nature between these, and as many differences in cernisia as we made in the nature of wine. For example, if you mix two measures of simple cernisia with one of trihapenina, you will make a medium drink between the two. But if you mix one of simple, one of medium and one of double together, you will make a drink between the medium and the double. Let us call these five kinds of cernisia by the same names we used for the kinds of wine: the simple and watery; next to it the one made from the mixture of two, the weak; then the medium, and next to it the strong; and last of all the vehement. In the same way you could make as many differences in that drink which the gentler English use, which they call ale (allam in the vulgar tongue). Some write it with a u, calling it in Latin cerusia. This drink is excessively inflating, and feverish people derive no usefulness from it. For it neither cools, nor opens, nor promotes any evacuation; nor does it quench thirst. Moreover, it is most liable to corruption, and it disposes the humours nearby to a similar affection. Its substance is also too readily dissolved, so that it dissolves into flatulent vapours. For this reason it is harmful to the head and nerves. Moreover, it is a material of obstructions, whence it is hostile to the liver and spleen. In sum, this drink is a friend to no one except Venus. Yet it should not be discarded by those who use it and enjoy good health, as long as they are not ill, as we showed above. The drink which we said is used for curing admits no such differences. For since it is contrary to the disease or its cause, it cannot be that by an increase or decrease of some quality it offers any differences. For opposition admits of no degrees. Moreover, we must remember that we have explained above the virtue that presses to the greatest, much, little and no degree; and we divided the disease in the same number of parts, namely that which presses to the greatest, much, moderately, little and none. By the signs we used in both divisions, it will be easy, if the nature is not too gross, to distinguish whether the virtue and the disease press to the greatest, much, little or nothing. Let us suppose, then, that first nothing is indicated by custom, that is, the sick person is not bound by habit in his drinks, as when he is accustomed to water, wine and cernisia alike (as the Portuguese exiles, who have settled in England and Flanders, are wont to be). If the strength of his body is weak, this will indicate the drink by which he can best be preserved, if the disease does not forbid it. Such a drink of wine is the one that the weakness of the strength indicates. But which one we shall choose is not yet settled: whether the watery, the weak or the medium. Yet the nature of the body will show this; for to those of hot and dry temperament, of slender habit, the weak wine suits. But to those who are cold in nature, of thick habit, fat in the belly and slow, the strong or vinous one. Whoever are melancholic and of a nature between these, the medium. Therefore in healthy bodies not accustomed to any drink, when they suffer some weakness, the indication of the drink is taken in general from that weakness alone, but the kind from the natural temperament. But if their strengths press with no weakness, the indication of the drink is to be taken from the natural temperature of the body alone. As Hippocrates, or his son Thessalus, taught in the sixth book of the Epidemics, advising cooling, water-drinking and then rest for hot natures. And from this one may gather that for those of hot and dry nature, with strength of powers, water is more suitable to use than wine. But whoever are of hot and dry temperament and weak nature will do better to drink watery wine than water. For inasmuch as it is watery, it suits a hot nature; and inasmuch as it has the power of wine, it helps the weakness. Whence it is evident that those of hot and dry nature, of slender habit and thin humours, since their bodies are quickly dissolved into vapour and thereby grow weaker, use watery wine most conveniently for health. Galen asserted this in the eighth book of the Method, when he said: You yourself are aware that I grant to all natures of this kind wine, but such as is watery both in appearance and in strength. For this is more useful than water in every respect, since it aids concoction and promotes urine and sweat. It has been shown, therefore, that, setting aside indication from custom, for healthy bodies that are weak the kind of drink is to be taken from the disposition of the strength, but the species from the natural temperament. Hence it comes about that for hot, robust bodies, to use water in health is not wholesome, rather than wine. We judge that trihapenina cernisia, which is intermediate between the simple drink and the double, suits the English and Germans who are of similar robustness of men, of similar temperature, and whoever live further north than they, when they enjoy good health. They use the simple drink only when the summer is fierce. Wine is inconvenient for them unless for medicinal purposes. For on account of the cold intemperature of their stomachs, and on account of excrementitious food and thick drinks, gross excrements of the phlegmatic kind collect in their stomachs, which by long delay acquire a vicious quality. If you give them strong wine, it carries the vicious humours with it to the liver and veins. Therefore, being held back by their thickness in the narrow passages of the liver, they block the ways. This is the cause that disturbs and corrupts the concoction of the blood, the liver contracting the fault from them. But if you administer weak wines to them, you will do one of two things: either you will drive the vicious humours more into the stomach, or you will make them crude. For wines of this kind have something astringent or sour. But for medicinal purposes, a moderate amount of wine with the second course, to aid the concoction of the stomach and correct the crudity of food imperfectly cooked by the sun with its moderate warmth, is wholesome for them. Therefore for them medium wines, which have no vehemence, are convenient.

units.la: Cæterum cum consuetudo suam præstat in dicatione, virtute sani corporis robusta exi stente, considerandum est, an proprium cor poris temperamentum, eundem potum quem consuetudo, indicet, an alium. Quod si eunde citra aliam considerationem exhibendu eum esse potum scito, quem simul consuetudo & temperamentum indicarunt. Quod si alium, pugna fit inter duo indicantia. Quapropter ætas inter hæc dirimet. Nam si homo citra an num quadragesimum quintum sit, tempera mento consentit: si vltra, consuetudini. Om nis siquidem mutatio magno virium robore indiget, quod raro in ijs qui vltra quadragesimumquintũ annum sunt, reperitur. In omni siquidem mutatione duo adsunt labores, nem pe rei consuetæ dimissio, & ad insuetā trans-missio. Vt ergo quæ ab ÿs eueniunt incommo-da, quis effugiat, & vt spes sit quæ futura sunt corrigantur damna, certo virium robo-re opus est, quod raro in ÿs qui vltra annum quadragesimũquintum sunt, reperitur. Vnde prouerbium apud Hispanos est, Qui cõsuetu-dinem dimiserunt prope mortem accesserũt. Neq; immerito: nam mors & consuetudo è regione habitant. Nõ possis consuetudinis e-gredi limites, quin patentes mortis fores in-spicias. Quapropter senibus, consuetis foueri melius est.
units.tr: Moreover, since custom has its own claim in the choice of drink, when vigour of body is robust, it must be considered whether the individual temperament indicates the same drink that custom does, or a different one. If it indicates the same, you may know that this is the drink to be given, without any further consideration, which custom and temperament both indicate together. If it indicates a different one, there is a conflict between two indications. Age therefore settles the matter between them. For if a man is under forty-five, he agrees with his temperament; if over, with his custom. Every change indeed requires great strength of powers, which is rarely found in those who are over the age of forty-five years. For every change involves two efforts: the abandonment of what is customary, and the passage to what is unaccustomed. So, that someone may escape the discomforts that arise from these, and that there may be hope of correcting the losses that lie ahead, a firm store of strength is needed, which is rarely found in those who are over forty-five. Hence the Spanish proverb: those who have given up their customs have come near to death. Nor undeservedly, for death and custom dwell in the same region. You cannot go beyond the limits of custom without looking upon the open gates of death. Therefore it is better for the old to be cherished in their accustomed ways.

units.la: Sed de sanorum potu satis hæc dicta sunt. Hoc enim negocium ad speculationẽ de tuen-da valitudine spectat, quare illic quod reli-quum est quære. Nos adægrotantes sermonẽ conuertamus. Positis duobus potum indi-cantibus nempe virtute & morbo, à con-suetudine nulla sumpta indicatione, si virtus maximè vrgeat, eum esse exhibendũ potum quo maximè laborantis natura seruari possit, neglecta omnino indicatione quæ à morbo sumitur, supra ostendimus de mente Galeni cũ de victus forma nobis sermo erat. Quod si multũ vterq; vrgeat et virtus & morbus, dissentiant q; in indicatione potus, prævalebit à virtute indicatio, nõ tamẽ neglecta illa quæ à morbo sumitur. Sic Hippocrates in quarto de ratione victus, Quibus per febres aluus liquida est, et mẽs turbatur, horũq; multi floc cos vellunt, naresq; fodiunt, et parũ quidem interrogatis respondent, sed ex se nihil quod compositũ est dicunt, talia ijs melancholica esse arbitror. His igitur ita habentibus si ven ter liquidus fuerit, absumensq; & contabe faciens, sorbitiones frigidiores, crassioresque exhibendas esse puto. Potusq; qui sistant, vinosioresque, vel etiam astringentiores. Quibus verbis descripsisse & virtutem, et morbum multum vrgentes, ex ijs quæ in superioribus diximus manifestum est. Vinum tamẽ, non obstante delirio cõcessit in prædicta constitutione causa virtutis multum vrgentis. Appositi, qui sistant, ob aliquid liquidæ symptoma. Vinosioresque, ob imbecillitatis rationem: non equidem vinosum ijs concedit vinum, qui huiusmodi delirio laborant, sed aquoso vinosius. Postremo enim de aquoso vino sermonem fecerat, cum dixit in tertio, Cæterum vino albo tenui paucifero & inodoro, &c. Cum ergo vinosiores potus scribit, ad aquosum conferre opinandum est, & eo maximè quod a-quosum vinum in simili delirio concesserat, libro tertio in expositione illius, Cum verò in huiusmodi morbis, &c. Imbecille igitur vinum quod aquosum proxime subsequitur ad vinosum versus, intellexisse arbitror. Sed quodidem rubrum esse oportet, inde manifestum est, quod in huiusmodi vinorum natura adstrictio reperitur. Ex ijs igitur duobus locis, & ex ijs quæ supra in initio huius speculationis diximus, licet colligere quantum sit aduersantibus indicationibus à prævalente detrahendum. Sed ut omnibus inuestigationis modus pateat, tabellam apponemus, ijs inserientem in quibus virtus & morbus potum indicant à consuetudine nulla sumpta indica-tione. Peracuto igitur morbo multumque vr-genti, aquam in potu exhibendam esse, virtu-te robusta existente, supra ostendimus in ini-tio huius meditationis. Quod si virtus parum ob imbecillitatem vrgeat, aquosum vinum ministrandum est. Quare picrocholis quam-uis acuta febre laborantibus aquosum vinū propinabimus, ob id quod horum, virtutes semper parum vrgeant. Nam horum corpo-rum substantia facile à leui occasione effluit, ob raritatem pororum, & succorum tenui-tatem, & calidam eorum naturam. Sic Ga-lenus octauo de methodo dixit. Vinum verò ipse conscius es, omnibus me huiusmodi natu-ris cōcedere, sed quod aquosum tū aspectu tū viribus sit. Id enim ad omnia vtilius est quā aqua: vtpote quod et coctionem iuuet, et vri-nas ac sudores prouocet. Constat autem & Hippoc. non in diarijs modò febribus, verùm etiam in acutis, ex iis quae de acutarum vi-ctu prodit, vinum dare, &c. Ex quibus ver-bis manifestum est aquosum vinum in acutis cocedendum picrocholis esse, ob futuræ eorum imbecillitatis timorem. Causatius igitur vbi virtus corporis ob præsentem imbecillitatem parum vrgeat, aquosum vinum ministrandum est. Hoc dico quod in omnibus quàm maximè sit aquæ simile. Hoc efficies modici vini multa cum aqua permixtione. Modus sit, vt modica sit vini repræsentatio, vt legimus Galenum fecisse, qui minimum vini multa aqua commiscens id ægrotanti seni exhibuit, riden te alio medico qui forte tunc aderat. Semperque cum vinum aquosum dixero, tale intelligo, in quo aqua qualitate & viribus multum in mixtione superat, vinum vero in gustatu modicè solummodo præsentetur. Quod si virtus multum vrgeat, stante eadem morbi vehementia, aquoso vinosius exhibere oportet.
units.tr: But enough has been said about the drink of the healthy. For this matter belongs to the study of preserving health, so look for the rest there. Let us turn our discourse to the sick. When two indications for drink are present, namely vigour and disease, with no indication taken from custom, if vigour presses most strongly, the drink to be given is the one by which the nature of the sufferer can best be preserved, the indication taken from the disease being wholly disregarded. We showed this above, according to the mind of Galen, when we were discussing the form of diet. But if both vigour and disease press strongly and differ in their indication for drink, the indication from vigour will prevail, yet without neglecting that which is taken from the disease. Thus Hippocrates in the fourth book of the Regimen: "Those in whom the bowels are liquid through fevers, and the mind is disturbed, and many of them pick at the wool, and dig at the nostrils, and answer little when questioned, yet say nothing coherent of themselves, such I judge to be melancholic." If these people, then, have liquid bowels, which waste and consume them, I think cooler and thicker gruels should be given, and drinks that check the flux, more wine-like, or even more astringent. In these words he has described both vigour and disease pressing strongly, as is clear from what we said above. Yet wine was allowed in that condition, despite the delirium, because the cause of the strongly pressing vigour was present. The astringent drinks were added because of some symptom of liquid flux. "More wine-like" was said because of the weakness of the powers. Not indeed that he grants unmixed wine to those who suffer such delirium, but wine that is more wine-like than watery. Finally, he had spoken of watery wine when he said in the third book: "But for thin white wine, sparing in body and without smell," and so on. When, therefore, he writes of more wine-like drinks, it must be taken that he means one closer to watery wine, especially since he had allowed watery wine in a similar delirium in the third book, in the exposition of that passage: "But when in diseases of this kind..." I think, therefore, that by "weak wine" he meant the wine that comes next after watery wine and tends toward wine. But that it must be red is clear from the fact that astringency is found in the nature of such wines. From these two passages, and from what we said above at the beginning of this study, one may gather how much must be subtracted from the prevailing indication when the indications conflict. But so that the method of the whole inquiry may be open, we shall set out a table, including those cases in which vigour and disease indicate the drink, with no indication taken from custom. In an acute disease that is very severe, we showed above at the beginning of this meditation that water should be given to drink when vigour is robust. If vigour presses only weakly because of feebleness, watery wine must be administered. Hence to those suffering from bilious fevers, though acute, we shall give watery wine, because their powers always press only weakly. For the substance of these bodies easily dissolves from a slight occasion, because of the rarity of their pores, the thinness of their juices, and their hot nature. Thus Galen said in the eighth book of the Method. You yourself know that I grant wine to all such natures, but wine that is watery both in appearance and in strength, for this is more useful in every respect than water, since it both aids digestion and provokes urine and sweat. It is also established that Hippocrates, not only in ephemeral fevers but also in acute ones, from what he gives on the diet of acute cases, prescribes wine, and so on. From these words it is clear that watery wine should be granted in acute cases to bilious patients, because of the fear of future weakness. Therefore, wherever the strength of the body, because of present feebleness, presses only weakly, watery wine must be given. I mean wine that in everything is as much like water as possible. You will achieve this by mixing a little wine with much water. The measure should be that the wine is only a slight tincture, as we read that Galen did, who, mixing a very small amount of wine with much water, gave it to an old sick man, while another physician who happened to be present laughed. And whenever I say watery wine, I mean such wine as in mixture is far superior to the wine in quality and strength, the wine being perceptible in taste only slightly. But if vigour presses strongly, while the severity of the disease remains the same, it is right to give wine that is more wine-like than watery.

units.la: Tale imbecille fuerit, in quo aqua in mixtione superat, vini tamen in gustatu ipso manifestè qualitas percipiatur, vt dulcor, si dulcedo astrictio, si austerum, &c. Hoc imbecille supra vocauimus. Sic Hippocrates loco iam citato, vinosiores potus ijs administrare iubet, het, quorū virtutes multum ob imbecillitatem vrgeant. Signum, quòd sic habeant, est fluxus ventris cōtabefaciens absumensque. Quod si morbus parum vrgeat, virtute multum vrgente, mediū potū exhibebimus. Talem dicimus in quo neutrū sensibiliter in mixtione vincit. Quod si omnino nō vrgeat morbus, virtute similiter habente, eū quo maximē seruari possit virtus, ministrabimus. Hūc potum quādiu virtus et morbus similiter habuerint, non mutabimus. At cum duorum alterum in aliud variauerit, pro ratione mutationis, potum ministrabimus. Sic supra cum de victus forma ageremus iuxta mutationē indicantium, victus formam immutauimus. Nec enim in ea sum opinione, vt credam, ab initio morbi posse medicum, victum & potum cōjcere, qui aegrotanti per totum morbi decursum exacte coueniat. Dementia est putare posse hominem eò cognitionis peruenire. Sed de ijs abundè in superioribus diximus. Verum nunc haec ad tabellam reduximus, vt facilius habeantur. Per potum curantem eum intelligo, qui morbo aut eius causæ sit qualitate contrarius. Aquosum roborantem cum, qui ex roborante & curante mixtus est potus. Sed similem in eo rationem habet ad curantem roborans, ac vinum ad aquam in vino aquoso. Imbecilliter roborans est, in quo hic ad potum curantem similem seruat symmetriam, ac vinum ad aquam in vino imbecilli. Reliquorum similis est ratio.
units.tr: A drink of the weak kind is one in which the water is superior in the mixture, yet the quality of the wine is clearly perceived in its taste itself, such as sweetness, if it is sweet, or astringency, if it is austere, and so on. We have called this the weak drink above. Thus Hippocrates, in the passage already cited, orders more wine-like drinks to be given to those whose powers press strongly because of feebleness. The sign that they are so disposed is a flux of the bowels that wastes and consumes. But if the disease presses only weakly while vigour presses strongly, we shall give a middle drink. We call that one in which neither element clearly prevails in the mixture. But if the disease does not press at all, and vigour is in the same state, we shall administer that drink by which vigour can best be preserved. We shall not change this drink as long as vigour and disease remain in the same condition. But when one of the two has varied into the other, we shall administer a drink according to the manner of the change. Thus above, when we were treating the form of diet, we changed the form of diet according to the change in the indications. For I am not of the opinion that the physician can, from the beginning of the disease, conjecture a diet and drink that will fit the sufferer exactly throughout the whole course of the illness. It is madness to think a man can reach such knowledge. But we have said enough about these matters above. Now, however, we have reduced these points to a table, so that they may be grasped more easily. By a curing drink I mean one that is contrary in quality to the disease or its cause. A strengthening-and-curing drink is one mixed of a strengthening and a curing drink. But it has the same relation to the curing drink as the strengthening drink has to water in watery wine. A weakly strengthening drink is one in which it keeps the same proportion to the curing drink as wine keeps to water in weak wine. The rest follow the same reasoning.

units.la: Vt si ponas Socratem morbo parum ꝑgen-te laborare, ac virtus eius multum ꝑgeat, potum ei potenter roborantem dabimus. Vt si aquam decoctionis feminis fœniculi Socra-ti potum curantem diffinieris, hunc vino mi-scebis tali symmetria, vt vinum in mixtione manifeste superet. Cæterum tempestiuum est vt de iis faciamus sermonem, in quibus assuetudinem tanquam indicatricem contem-plamur, seclusa in primis ea quæ robore viri-um sumitur indicatione. Deinde omnia tria simul in indicationem potus conuocabimus.
units.tr: If you suppose Socrates is suffering from a disease that only mildly weakens him, while his strength is greatly reduced, we will give him a strongly restorative drink. If you define the curative drink for Socrates as the water of a decoction of fennel seed, you will mix it with wine in such proportion that the wine clearly predominates in the mixture. But it is now appropriate to discuss those cases in which we take habit as the indicator, setting aside first the indication drawn from the strength of the forces. Then we will bring all three together into the indication of a drink.

units.la: Nunc quæ in superioribus de consuetudine dixim-us, in mente reuocare oportet. Nem-pe consuetudinem in maximam, et minorem dividi. Maximam dicimus, vt cum vni dun= taxat potui quis insueuerit, vt Galli vino, Anglorum nonnulli cernisiæ, Lusitanorum plurimi aquæ. Minorem, cū quis vino insue-uit, quia eo bonæ valitudini consulit, citra aliquod incommodum alio non (forte legen-dum, alio etiam vtens) vtens potu. Eisdē modis dicitur id quod insuetum est. Ad hæc sci-re oportet quod cum morbus & consuetudo consentiunt, ministrandum eum esse potum, quem indicant citra aliam considerationem: Vt laboranti acuta febre Lusitano cum vi-rium robore aquæ potui assueto, aquam hor-dei quam morbus & consuetudo indicarunt, citra contentionem ministrabimus. Quod si pugna in indicatione fuerit, quod viribus su-perius est, in indicatione prævalet. Nempe morbus si multum aut quàm maximè vrge-at. Aut consuetudo, si morbus parum aut ni-hil vrgeat. Sic Galenus octavo de methodo:
units.tr: Now we should recall what we said above about habit. Namely, habit is divided into greatest and lesser. We call it greatest when someone has become accustomed to only one drink, as the French to wine, some English to beer, and most Portuguese to water. Lesser, when someone is accustomed to wine because he thereby looks after his health, and uses another drink too without any inconvenience (perhaps we should read "alio etiam utens"). In the same ways, that which is unaccustomed is so described. Further, we must know that when disease and habit agree, the drink that both indicate is to be given without any other consideration. For example, to a Portuguese suffering from an acute fever, who is accustomed to water and whose strength is intact, we will give barley water, which both the disease and the habit indicate, without contention. But if there is a conflict in the indication, what is superior in strength prevails in the indication. Namely, the disease prevails if it presses hard or most urgently, or habit prevails if the disease presses little or not at all. Thus Galen in the eighth book of the Method:

units.la: „ Si quis verò (inquit) frigidæ non adsueuit, huic per febrem dare non inceperim nisi pri-stina plane sanitate prius reddita. Rursus po-namus hominem acuta febre laborantem vi no assuetū, aquaque nunquam fuisse vsum, quem huic ministrabimus potum, morbo aquam indicante, consuetudine fortiter dissuadente? Morbus quidem in indicatione ob id quod multum vrget praevalebit, consuetudine tamen non neglecta. Quinimmo aliquid ei indulgendum est iuxta sententiam Hippocratis in Apho. Id praestabimus si in dicta constitutione potum aquosum consuetū, hoc est, vinum aquosum ministremus. Sic olim Dionysio patri meo contigit. Laborabat acuto morbo Gallus, cunque de consuetudine quaereret, dixit se aquā fuisse nunquam vsum nisi ad manus ablutionem. Quapropter homine a morbo liberauit, consuetudinem in indicationem potus admittens. Licet ergo morbus multum vrgeat, consuetudini dandum est aliquid, hoc est neque totum neque maximum.
units.tr: "If, however," he says, "someone is not accustomed to cold water, I would not begin to give it to him during a fever unless his health had first been fully restored. Again, suppose a man suffering from an acute fever who has never used wine but has always used water. What drink will we give him, when the disease indicates water and habit strongly advises against it? The disease will prevail in the indication, because it presses hard, yet habit must not be neglected. Indeed, something must be granted to him according to the saying of Hippocrates in the Aphorisms. We will do this if, in the said condition, we give him the watery drink he is used to, that is, watered wine. So once it happened to my father Dionysius: a Gaul was suffering from an acute disease, and when he was asked about his habits he said that he had never used water except for washing his hands. Therefore he freed the man from the disease, admitting habit into the indication of the drink. So although the disease presses hard, something must be given to habit, that is, neither the whole nor the greatest part."

units.la: Neque obstiterit quod Aphorismus solum de numero oblationum agat. nam verus est sermo etiam in indicatione potus: vt ab eodem didicimus secundo de ratione victus loco supra à nobis citato, vbi consuetudinis ad indicationem potus meminit. Sed quod in tali morbi constitutione non sit plus concedendum consuetudini, hinc manifestum est. Hippocrates in tertio de ratione victus ita scribit: Cū vero in huiusmodi morbis fortem capitis grauitatem vel mentis læsionem suspicatus fueris, à vino penitus est abstinendum. Aquamque tunc dare oportet, velvinum aquosum, flauum mq, & prorsus inodorū, &c. In quibus verbis multum vrgentem morbū depingit. Cunque morbus ita habuerit, à vino penitus abstinendum esse iubet, aquamq; tunc dare consulit. Et subiungit statim, Vel vinum aquosum prorsus inodorum. Cunque non eadem sit aquæ & vini aquosi natura, opinandum est aquam vel vinum aquosum non ideo dixisse, ac si vellet citra discrimen vllum vtrouis æque nos vti posse. Quod ex ijs quæ statim sequuntur verbis manifestum est, cum dixit: Atque ab ipsius potione aquæ exiguum superbibendum est. nam hoc modo vini potentia caput minus tentabit. Cum ergo vinum aquosum alterius sit naturæ quàm aquæ aqua, ab eisdem indicantibus utrunque indicari non potest. Cunque tria sint quae potu indicent, nempe morbus, virtus, & consuetudo, stanteque eadem morbi constitutione utrunque consuluerit potum, necesse est, aut virium robur, aut consuetudinem, mutationem accepisse. Proinde cum observemus in scriptis suis Hippocratem ea semper recensere signa quae vires laborantis imbecilles esse often dunt, cum ab imbecilli virtute capturus est indicationem, fit manifestum, quod cum scribit, aut vinum aquosum, iis ministrandum iis bet, qui vino per sanitatem perpetuo sunt usi, minime aqua. Iis fidem praestat, quod quarto volumine scripsit, in simili morbi constitutione, imbecillitatis virium causas apponens, cum dixit: His ita habentibus, si venter liquidus fuerit, absumens, & contabefaciens, &c. In qua quidem morbi constitutione potus vinosiores, ut diximus, ratione imbecillitatis virium administrare consulit.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that the Aphorism deals only with the number of feedings, for the saying is true also for the indication of a drink, as we have learned from the same author in the second book of the Regimen, cited above by us, where he mentions habit in relation to the indication of a drink. That in such a condition of disease more should not be conceded to habit is clear from this. Hippocrates in the third book of the Regimen writes thus: "When, however, in diseases of this kind you suspect a strong heaviness of the head or an impairment of the mind, you must abstain entirely from wine, and then it is advisable to give water, or watery wine, yellowish and entirely without smell, etc." In these words he depicts a disease that presses hard. And when the disease is of this kind, he bids us abstain entirely from wine and advises giving water then. And he immediately adds: "or watery wine entirely without smell." Since the nature of water and of watery wine is not the same, we must suppose that he did not say "water or watery wine" as though he wished us to be able to use either equally, without any difference. This is clear from what follows immediately: "And a small amount must be drunk over the drinking of water itself, for in this way the power of the wine will affect the head less." Therefore, since watery wine is of a different nature from aqua water, both cannot be indicated by the same indicants. Since there are three things that indicate a drink, namely disease, strength, and habit, and since with the same condition of disease he advises either drink, it is necessary that either the strength of the forces or the habit has changed. Accordingly, since we observe that in his writings Hippocrates always lists those signs which show that the strength of the patient is weak, when he is going to take the indication from weakness of strength, it becomes clear that when he writes "either watery wine," it is to be given to those who have always used wine for health, and by no means water. He confirms this in the fourth volume, where in a similar condition of disease he sets out the causes of weakness of the forces, when he says: "When these things are so, if the belly is loose, wasting and consuming, etc." In such a condition of disease he advises giving drinks that are more wine-like, as we have said, on account of the weakness of the forces.

Secundo, causa imbecillitatis virtutis, vt cū dixit, His ita habētibus si venter liquidus fuerit corpus absumens &c. Tertio, ratione consuetudinis. Hoc est quod Galenus oīauo de methodo dixit: Constat aut et Hippocrate nō in diarijs modo febribus, verū etiā in acutis, ex ijs quæ de acutarū victu prodit, vinū dare &c. Ostensum igitur est, quod cum consuetudo morbi multum vrgentis indicationi dissentit, cum esse exhibendum potum, in quo minimum sit consueti, multum verò curātis: Hunc dicimus aquosum consuetum, vt vinum aquosum ijs qui vino sunt assueti. Quòd si Anglo cernisiæ potui assueto acuta febris accidat, modicum cernisiæ ei assuetæ multa aqua hordei miscebimus, & ei ministrabimus.
units.tr: 1. On the regimen of diet. By reason of the disease, as when he said: "Whether you think mead or wine would be more helpful." Secondly, by reason of the weakness of strength, as when he said: "With these things so, if the belly is liquid, consuming the body, etc." Thirdly, by reason of custom. This is what Galen said in the eighth book of the Method: "It is established that Hippocrates gave wine not only in continued fevers but also in acute ones, from what he hands down about the diet of acute patients, etc." It has therefore been shown that when the custom of a very urgent disease conflicts with the indication, the drink to be given should contain as little as possible of what the patient is used to, and as much as possible of what the cure requires. We call this a watered customary drink, such as watered wine for those accustomed to wine. But if an acute fever attacks a man accustomed to English beer (cervisia), we will mix a small amount of his customary beer with a great deal of barley water and give it to him.

units.tr: 4. Of the same. 3. Of the same. We have said so far about cold drink that it is to be understood when the drink is taken for the pleasure of drinking, not for the sake of cooling, when it is given once, in full, after the concoctions of the disease. Above, in the places we cited, we showed from Galen that no indication for giving it should be drawn from custom. It must also be noted that what we have said so far about custom is to be understood of the greatest and chief custom. But the custom which we called the lesser sometimes has no force in the indication: for example, we will give acute fever patients water to drink, though they do not use it because of its coldness and the bloating it causes, yielding nothing to their custom. For the faults they have contracted from water are corrected by the immoderate heat of the acute fever. But if the discomforts of an unaccustomed drink cannot be corrected by the disease, the lesser custom has force in the indication of drink, though inferior to the former. Yet it rarely happens that the harms of the drink given by the one treating are not corrected by the contrary qualities of the disease.

Iis vero qui secun-da valitudine medio potu cernisiæ vtuntur trihapeninam bijram dicunt, cu à febre cor-ripiuntur simplici cernisiæ potu vti commodum est. Diximus siquidem hunc potum refrigerare, & meatus aperire. Quare qui ipso per febres vtuntur, trimestrem, defecatum, & quàm maximè simplicem quærant, qui-que ex aqua fluente confectus sit. Hunc quidem in acutis febribus commodiorem ijs esse arbitror quàm aquam. Quod si iam dictorum aliquod defit, cu aqua hordei hunc ministrare oportebit. units.tr: It remains that, when all three indicators come together to indicate the drink, we turn to discourse. One must know that when the weakness of strength, the severity of the disease and custom all bear on the choice of drink, it usually happens that two of the indicators agree on one drink. So you will draw a suitable drink from the other of the two tables, in this way. One must ask from that table the drink which suits the stronger of the two agreeing indicators, and add to it, or take away from it, the indication of the third. For example, let a Frenchman be suffering from an acute fever, with his strength much pressed by weakness. In such a condition all three indicators concur: strength, disease and custom. Two of them agree on one drink, namely strength and custom; disease disagrees with both. So, seeking a drink that suits strength and disease, both strongly urgent, you will find in the first table a drink that strengthens weakly; this is weak wine. To this you will add according to the indication of custom. Therefore, in such a condition, we will give the Frenchman, who is seized by acute fever, a drink that strengthens weakly but is stronger, that is, a drink a little more wine-like than the weak one. Again, let a Portuguese labour under an acute fever, and be accustomed to drink water, and let his strength be much pressed by weakness. Whenever custom and disease agree on one drink, seek a drink suited to disease and strength, both strongly urgent. You will discover in the first table one that strengthens weakly, from which you will remove the indication of custom. Therefore, for a Portuguese labouring in this way, we will give a drink weaker than one that strengthens weakly, such as a weak wine that is more watery. We have said, then, that when all three indicators concur for the choice of drink, two usually agree on one drink, whether a Portuguese, a Spaniard, a Frenchman, an Italian or an Asian falls ill. This is especially so because all of them use one of two drinks, namely wine or water. By the name of water I mean those waters in which seeds, herbs or roots have been steeped, such as barley water, maidenhair water, liquorice water and so on. For those who are accustomed to water-drinking, barley water cannot be called an unaccustomed drink, even if they have never used it. Thus it often happens to the English, to those who live in Flanders and upper Germany, and to the Scots, when they fall ill, that all the indicators disagree in choosing a drink. Indeed, whenever an Englishman accustomed to the beer called cernisia is seized by an acute illness with weakness of strength, a struggle arises among all the indicators. For the disease demands water as a curing drink, strength demands wine as strengthening, and custom demands cernisia as the customary drink. Therefore in such a meeting either all three drinks must be mixed according to the ratio of the indicators, or a small amount of wine should be given separately, once or twice or as often as it is useful for strengthening nature, and then, whenever needed, we will give a drink mixed from plain cernisia and water, in the proportion that corresponds both to the disease and to custom. I do not approve the first method, because wine and cernisia do not agree well together; much less so if they mix wine with what they call ale. For such a drink is made from things that readily turn sour in the stomachs of healthy people and spoil, let alone in those who suffer from acute fever. So I think the second method should be followed: we divide the drink for such sufferers into two parts. With one part we will indulge the weakness of strength and the disease, with the other the disease and custom. I have said that wine strengthens, but it is very inconvenient in acute fever. Therefore we will mix the wine with a decoction of barley and maidenhair, or of polytrichum, according to the ratio of the first table. We add the capillary herb so that it is boiled together with the barley, so that it keeps the barley from corrupting and so that it does not turn sour when mixed with wine. Next we will compose, if we mix cernisia, customary for the patient, with barley water, according to the ratio of the second table. For barley water agrees best with the drink of either cernisia. Therefore the mixture made from these is most suitable to the nature of an Englishman labouring under acute disease. This precept must be carefully observed by those who in good health choose the cernisia that they call ale in common speech. For when they are seized by an acute disease, cernisia is the most unsuitable drink. It is not the time then to change to another plan, for, as we learned from Galen, a sudden departure from custom offends bodies not a little. I also mentioned above a patient for whom water was, as he said, a suitable drink, but because of unaccustomedness he did not give it during fever. Since, then, cernisia is the most unsuitable drink for those with acute fever, whoever has used it constantly in good health will act rightly if he drinks cernisia mixed with much barley water. For those in poor health who drink the middle kind of cernisia, which they call trihapenina bijra, when they are seized by fever it is convenient to drink plain cernisia. For I have said that this drink cools and opens the passages. So those who use it during fevers should seek one that is three months old, settled, and as simple as possible, made from running water. I think this is more convenient in acute fevers than water. But if any of the aforesaid is lacking, it will be necessary to give this with barley water. We have said enough about the indications of drink.

units.la: Quòd Lusitani medici & Hispani methodũ Hippocratis in administratione uictus non insequantur.
units.tr: That the Lusitanian and Spanish physicians do not follow the method of Hippocrates in the administration of diet.

units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: EXperiamur an medici Lusitani in artis operibus methodum Hippocratis de ratione victus insequantur: narremusq; quam victus rationem in febricitantibus, dictam Lusitani vocant, observent. Si quis febre corripiatur, moto statim ventre inferiori per clysterium, iure lentium aut cocta borragine cucurbitaue & similibus ad sextam diem ducitur: qua purgante pharmaco adhibito pulli gallinacei iure & carnibus alitur. In reliquum tempus hunc observant victum, paroxysmorum aut exacerbationum diem cauentes ad morbi solutionem usque. Tenui magis victu primis aegritudinis diebus vtuntur stante virium robore. A purgatione autem quâ ut plurimum die sexta, aut octaua exercent, crassiori victu, nempe capi aut pulli gallinacei carnibus, febricitantes nutriunt. Id agunt, vbi nullum symptoma occurrat, a praedicto ordine eos perturbans. Hunc modum Lusitani & Hispanorum bona pars insequuntur. Sed vt ostendamus quantum a re & ratione & a mente simul Hippocratis alieni sint, operæprecium erit eorum audire rationes, et fundamenta, quibus innituntur, vt his destructis sponte eorum labatur opinio. Ferunt nostra tempestate hominum corpora ob delicias, Venerem, et ob inordinatum victum, su perfluis abundare. Facile enim his de causis accrescere ventriculo, intestinis, iocineri, et venis, excrementa. Communes vocant materias. Has, vtpote propriam morbi effectricem causam fouentes, prius soluendas esse iudicat. Quæ in inferiori sunt ventre clysterio, quæ vero in ventriculo, & venis, tum subtili victu, tum pharmaco deiciente, quod non solum communes, sed & propriæ morbi materiam respiciat. Aiunt huiusmodi purgatio ne quam minoratiuam nuncupant, laborantes minus periclitari, imminuta quantitate propriæ materiæ, cuius multitudinem ob iam dictas causas suspicantur. Hippocrati etiam hanc euacuationem quæ inter initia morbi exercent, acceptam ferunt in Apho. Inchoantibus morbis. & Galenum citant dicta Hippocratis exponentem in hæc verba: Ad hoc ,, ut citius fiant coctiones, melius in principio ,, euacuare, ut materiam minorem redactam, ,, facilius natura coquere possit. Die autem sexta iudicantes naturam iam sibi separasse ex communibus materijs bonum, prauumque expulsioni apparasse, pharmacum ministrat ut naturam minus grauata celebris dies critica offendat, (inueniat.) A purgatione uires naturæ roborare conantur, quam langue resuspicantur ob clysteria, pharmacum & tenuem uictum. Quare sorbitionem ex iure pullo gallinaceo, & carnes eiusdem febricitanti apud sextam (die sexto) ministrant. Ut apud uigorem uires habeat natura, quibus morbo fiat superior. Sed usum sorbitionis a-pud diem pharmaci, approbant ex Hippocra ,, te dicente: Cum autem purgaueris, sorbitio- ,, nibus quibusdam utitor, obseruatis ita febri- ,, um accessionibus ut nunquam, &c.
units.tr: Let us test whether the Portuguese physicians, in their practice, follow Hippocrates' method of regulating diet. I will describe the diet which the Portuguese call the diet for feverish patients, and how they observe it. If someone is seized by fever, the lower belly is first loosened by an enema, and the patient is kept for six days on broth of lentils, or on boiled borage or gourd, and similar foods. On the sixth day a purgative medicine is given, and afterwards the patient is nourished with chicken broth and chicken flesh. For the rest of the time they keep to this diet, taking care on the days of the paroxysms or exacerbations until the disease resolves. In the first days of the illness they use a thinner diet, while the strength of the body holds. After the purgation, which they usually carry out on the sixth or eighth day, they feed the feverish patient with a richer diet, namely the flesh of capons or chickens. They do this whenever no symptom arises to disturb this order. Most of the Portuguese and Spanish physicians follow this method. But to show how far it is from reason, from sound judgement, and at the same time from the mind of Hippocrates, it will be worth hearing their arguments and the foundations on which they rest, so that once these are overthrown their opinion will fall of its own accord. They claim that in our day human bodies abound in superfluities because of luxury, sexual indulgence and disordered diet. For from these causes excrement easily accumulates in the stomach, the intestines, the liver and the veins. They call these the common matters. These, since they nourish the morbid cause proper to the disease, they judge must be dissolved first. What lies in the lower belly is to be removed by the enema; what lies in the stomach and the veins is to be removed both by a thin diet and by a purgative medicine, which affects not only the common matter but also the matter proper to the disease. They say that patients suffer less danger from this purgation, which they call minorative, since the quantity of the proper matter, which they suspect is multiplied for the causes already mentioned, is diminished. They also say that Hippocrates received this evacuation, which they carry out at the beginning of the disease, in the Aphorism Inchoantibus morbis, and they cite Galen expounding Hippocrates' words as follows: "So that concoctions may come more quickly, it is better to evacuate at the beginning, so that nature, having reduced the matter to a smaller amount, may more easily digest it." On the sixth day, judging that nature has already separated from the common matters what is good and what is bad and has prepared the bad for expulsion, they administer the purgative so that the critical day, which is famous, may find nature less burdened. After the purgation they try to strengthen the powers of nature, which they fear have been weakened by the enemas, the medicine and the thin diet. Therefore they give the feverish patient, on the sixth day, a broth of chicken and its flesh, so that nature may have strength by which it may overcome the disease. They approve the use of broth on the day of the medicine from Hippocrates, who says: "When you have purged, use certain broths, observing the attacks of the fever so that never, etc."

units.la: Contra eosdem, Minoratiuam euacuationem quæ per pharmacum fit non semper administrandam in initijs febrium putridarum.
units.tr: Against the same: the minorative evacuation which is made by medicine should not always be given at the beginning of putrid fevers.

units.la: CAPVT XIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIIII.

units.la: SED vt ostendamus quantum à ratione hæc via deuiat, oportebit vt primum de minoratiua quam dicũt euacuatione parum disseramus, (nã hanc suspicor præcipuã huius vitium occasionem esse,) hinc sumpto initio. Quamlibet artem cõstrui, tum ex ijs quæ in vniuersum dicuntur, tum ex ijs quæ in partem, quæ sunt excepta ab ijs quæ generatim dicuntur, non est dubium. In singulis præterea artibus duo contingunt errores: alter, cũ ea quæ in vniuersum dicũtur, in partem quis accipiat: alter, cum ea quæ in partem, in vniuersum esse dicta accipiantur. Grauior quidem error hic priore est, summeque vitandus in arte medica, in qua crudele professo erra re est. Concocta medicari & mouere, non cruda neque in principijs, &c. Vniuersale hoc dogma aut si mauis præceptum tres habet exceptiones. Quarum singulæ secundum partem dicuntur: Nempe nisi sint furiosa. Item in acutis passionibus raro & in principijs pharmacijs vti. Præterea inchoantibus morbis, &c. Horum singula ab vniuersali præcepto excepta esse ex eo intelliges, quòd dixit, nisi sint furiosa. Item in eo, In acutis, passionibus raro. Præterea in eo, Si quid videtur. Cunq; singulos quos sanandos sumis, initio moueas pharmaco, innixus Aphorismo, Inchoantibus morbis, nonne sententiam vniuersalem facis, cum eam Hippocrates, particularem fecerit, in eo quod dixit, Si quid videtur. At tibi forsan id semper faciendū videtur. Cu tamen mens Hippocratis si quis rē ex actè consideret fuerit, in tribus affectib. non oportere coctionem humoris adeius euacuationem spectare. Nempe aut cum motu inordinato, aut qualitate, aut quantitate, aliquod vitæ discrimen afferunt. Primum intellexit, cum dixit, nisi sint furiosa, per corpus inordinato motu vagantes humores ab ignobili ne ad nobilem & principem partem ferantur, timor est. Aliquando contingit humore mor bum efficientem adeo quantitate exuperare, vt merito timeat medicus, ne coctrix facultas sit coquendo aut expultrix expellendo. Consulte aget medicus aut venæsectione, aut purgante
units.tr: But so that we may show how far this method departs from reason, it will first be necessary to say a little about what they call the diminishing evacuation (for I suspect this is the chief cause of its fault), starting from this point. That any art is constructed both from what is said in general and from what is said in particular, excepted from what is said generally, there is no doubt. Moreover, two errors occur in each art: one, when what is said in general is taken as said in particular; the other, when what is said in particular is taken as said in general. The latter error is indeed graver than the former, and is most to be avoided in the medical art, in which it is a cruel error for a practitioner. "To treat with concocted matter, and to move it, not raw, nor at the beginnings," and so on. This universal dogma, or precept if you prefer, has three exceptions. Each of these is stated with respect to a part: namely, "unless they are furious"; likewise, "in acute diseases, rarely"; and "in the beginnings, to use drugs"; besides, "in incipient diseases," and so on. You will understand that each of these is excepted from the universal precept from the fact that he said "unless they are furious," and likewise in "in acute diseases, rarely," and besides in "if anything seems." When, leaning on the aphorism "in incipient diseases," you move each of the patients you undertake to cure with a drug at the outset, do you not make a universal statement, when Hippocrates made it particular in what he said, "if anything seems"? But perhaps it always seems to you that this must be done. Yet if one considers the matter exactly, Hippocrates' intention was that in three kinds of affection one should not look to the concoction of the humour for its evacuation. Namely, they bring some danger to life either by disordered motion, or by quality, or by quantity. He understood the first when he said "unless they are furious": there is a fear that humours wandering through the body in disordered motion may be carried from an ignoble part to a noble and principal part. Sometimes it happens that the humour causing the disease so exceeds in quantity that the physician rightly fears lest the concocting faculty be unable to concoct, or the expelling faculty to expel. The physician will act prudently, by bloodletting or by a purgative, whichever he judges will help more, to diminish the quantity of humour at the beginning.

units.la: — (no further printed notes on this page) purgante pharmaco, vtro magis auxiliatu- ro putauerit, humoris quantitatem inter ini- tia imminuere. Antequam quæ à pharmaco euenire solet cōmotio, læsioni sit magnæ. Ma- gis eo læsit tempore, quo iam colore putredi- nali & actione naturæ humores agitantur. Fit enim ut ob agitationem boni cū prauis si- mul educantur. Cōmotio insuper pharmaciin augmento morbi causa est additionis potius quàm diminutionis prauorū humorū. Id ma- nifestū quilibet existimabit, si opus naturæ in telligat esse coctione media separare bonos à prauis: & qualitatis putridi humoris esse cō tactu afficere quibuscunque obuiauerit, eos præcipuè qui à naturali calido haud cōmodè reguntur. Quod si ijs addas, naturæ vires im- becilliores reddi ex pharmaco intempestiuè exhibito, cuius proprium est, multum boni & prauiexiguum euacuare, intelliges quan- tum mali sit, perpetuò pharmacum sexta die exhibere: ni facilè conieceris, humorem quantitate adeo exuperantem esse, vt ti- meas ne vires naturæ superet. Quod si id iudicas, non sexta die sed ab initio morbo inchoante evacuare expedit. Quod vero citat dictum Galeni, nempe ad hoc ut citius fiant coctiones melius in principio evacuare, perperam de pharmacia intelligendum fore contendunt. Nam per evacuationem, venae sectionem intelligit. Hanc in principiis morborum adhibendam esse ait, ut materiam minorem factam, facilius natura coquere possit. Quod ipse ostendit in expositione Apho. Vbi cibus praeter naturam intrat, vbi ita scribit: ὁ τὶ ϳ νένωσιν μὲν ἀπλῶς ἀωδε λέγειν ὁ ἱπποκράτης ὅταν ὁμοτίμως ἅπαντες χυμοὶ κενῶνται· κἀδἀεσιν δὲ, ὅταν οἱ μοχθηροὶ κατὰ ποιότητα, μεμνῆσθαι χρή. Id est, Quod autem evacuationem simpliciter consueuit Hippocrates appellare cum humores omnes aequaliter evacuantur, purgationem autem quando mali sunt secundum qualitatem, meminisse oportet. Et infra, declarans quomodo maxime humores omnes aequaliter evacuantur. Evacuatio (inquit) omnium humorum aequaliter quae exquisitissima est, fit per venae sectionem. Vnde ex ijs manifestum est per verbum κε- νώσεως euacuationem omnium humorum æqua- liter, quæ per venæ sectionem fit, intelligen- dum esse, & non eam quæ per pharmacum fit, quam Hippocrates & Galenus κάθαρ- σιν nuncupare consueuerunt, & nō κένωσιν. Sed eundem vndecimo de methodo medendi audi, eadem quæ hic de vacuatione in princi- piis morborum retulit, de venæ sectione di- centem. Cum enim de vacuatione in febribus quæ à putrido humore ortum habent ageret: Saluberrimum, inquit, non solum in conti-,, nuis, verùm in omnibus quas putrescens ac-,, cendit humor, venam incidere. Leuata enim,, natura ab eo quod velut sarcina premitur, quod reliquum est potentius coquet & ex- pellet. Verbum igitur mouere quod in Aph. Inchoantibus morbis, est, de venæ sectione maximè intelligendum est. Aliquando verò de purgatione vt scriptum est à Galeno in expositione, cum ait, Si quid videtur moue-,, re, sunt autem hæc maximè, venæ sectio, ali,, quando verò purgatio. Vnde ex ijs colligi,,
units.tr: ...whichever of the two, venesection or a purgative drug, he thought would help more, to reduce the quantity of humour at the start. Before the disturbance that usually follows a drug occurs, it does harm. It does more harm at the time when the humours are already stirred up by a putrid colour and the action of nature. For it happens that, because of the agitation, good humours are drawn out together with bad ones. Moreover, the agitation caused by the drug is a cause of the disease's increase by the addition, rather than the diminution, of the bad humours. Anyone will judge this clear if he understands that the work of nature is to separate good from bad by intermediate concoction, and that a putrid humour, by its quality, affects by contact whatever it meets, especially those parts that the natural heat does not govern well. If you add to this that the strength of nature is made weaker by a drug given at the wrong time, whose property is to evacuate much good and very little bad, you will understand how great an evil it is to give a purgative on the sixth day every time. Unless you can easily conjecture that the humour so exceeds in quantity that you fear it may overcome the strength of nature. But if you judge this, it is expedient to evacuate not on the sixth day but from the beginning, while the disease is starting. As for the saying of Galen that they cite, namely that it is better to evacuate at the beginning so that the concoctions come about more quickly, they contend that it must be understood of drugs wrongly. For by evacuation he means venesection. He says it is to be applied at the beginnings of diseases, so that, with the matter made smaller, nature can concoct it more easily. He himself shows this in his commentary on the Aphorism "Where food enters contrary to nature", where he writes thus: ὁ τὶ ϳ νένωσιν μὲν ἀπλῶς ἀωδε λέγειν ὁ ἱπποκράτης ὅταν ὁμοτίμως ἅπαντες χυμοὶ κενῶνται· κἀδἀεσιν δὲ, ὅταν οἱ μοχθηροὶ κατὰ ποιότητα, μεμνῆσθαι χρή. That is: one should remember that Hippocrates is accustomed to call evacuation simply the case when all the humours are evacuated equally, but purgation when they are bad in quality. And below, explaining how all the humours are most equally evacuated, he says: "The evacuation of all the humours equally, which is the most exquisite, is made by venesection." From these words it is clear that by the word κενώσεως [kenōseōs, evacuation] one must understand the evacuation of all humours equally, which is made by venesection, and not that which is made by a drug, which Hippocrates and Galen were accustomed to call κάθαρσιν [katharsin, purgation], and not κένωσιν [kenōsin, evacuation]. But hear the same man in the eleventh book of his Method of Healing, speaking of venesection in the same terms that he used here of evacuation at the beginnings of diseases. For when he was dealing with evacuation in fevers that arise from a putrid humour, he said: "It is most healthful to open a vein not only in continual fevers but in all those that a putrefying humour kindles. For when nature is relieved of that which presses it like a burden, what remains it will concoct and expel more powerfully." Therefore the word "to move" in the Aphorism "In diseases beginning..." is to be understood chiefly of venesection. Sometimes, however, it refers to purgation, as Galen wrote in the commentary, when he says: "If anything seems to move, these are chiefly venesection, and sometimes purgation." Whence it may be gathered that venesection is to be practised more often than purgation in beginning diseases.

units.la: [the marks ,, at line ends are printed quotation marks, not notes] licet, sæpius exercendam esse venæ sectionem inchoantibus morbis, quàm purgationem. At ij contrarium agunt purgatione, quibuscunque in morbis perpetuò inter initia adhibent, venæ sectionem aliquando. Sed in acutis saltem errorem esse fatebuntur. Nam raro in acutis passionib. expedit in principijs pharmacijs vti. Quòd si die sexta, aut octaua transactum principium in acutis esse dicant, cedo. Sed cum status iam inslet, graviori noxa naturam afficient vt supra ostendimus. Ob id enim dixit inchoantibus morbis. In acutis vero quantum periculosæ sint purgationes tum ob medicaminis qualitatem, tum ob commotionem, declarat Galenus quarto de ratione victus in expositione illius, Verusi ad hæc nō aperiatur. Tum non minus ob errores qui perpetuò in huiusmodi purgationibus committuntur, quos magnas in acutis parere offensas ex Galeno supra ostendimus. At venæ sectio minus errori obnoxia est. Quinimmo nec circa eius occasionem nec quantitate errabit doctus et diligens medicus sanguini missionì sioni assistens, sola ex pulsu facta coniectu-ra. Qua in re Dionysius medicus pater me-us facile omnes sui temporis medicos supera-uit, perspicuo ex pulsu putridu sanguinem di-gnoscens. Quod quam medico possibile sit sen-su assequi, & ad opera deducere, testabun-tur Angli qui mea vsi sunt arte, de quo alibi nobis sermo erit. In acutis ergo morbis raro pharmacijs vtendum est, nec in eorum princi-pijs.nam commune in ijs praeceptum Hippocra
units.tr: It is allowed that bloodletting should be practised more often than purging in the early stages of diseases. Those who think otherwise purge, and they often resort to bloodletting at the beginning of diseases of every kind. But they will admit that this is an error at least in acute cases. Seldom in acute illnesses is it advantageous to use medicines at the beginning. If they say that the beginning in acute cases has passed by the sixth or eighth day, I grant it. But once the state of the disease has set in, they will harm nature more gravely, as we showed above. That is why he said "in the beginning of diseases." How dangerous purgatives are in acute cases, both because of the quality of the medicine and because of the disturbance they cause, Galen explains in the fourth book of On the Regimen of Acute Diseases, in his commentary on the passage beginning "To Verus..." (not to be opened here). Nor are they less dangerous because of the errors that are constantly made in such purgings, which, as we showed above from Galen, cause great offences in acute cases. Venesection, however, is less open to error. Indeed, neither in judging when to bleed nor in how much will a learned and careful physician go wrong when he attends a bloodletting, provided he makes his judgement from the pulse alone. In this matter my father, the physician Dionysius, easily surpassed all the physicians of his time, recognising putrid blood clearly from the pulse. How possible it is for a physician to grasp this by the senses and put it into practice is attested by the English who used my art, of which we shall speak elsewhere. In acute diseases, then, medicines are seldom to be used, and not at their beginning. For the common precept in these cases is that of Hippocrates: to open a vein, the only indication taken being the magnitude of the disease.

units.la: tis est venam incidere, sola indicatione sum-pta a magnitudine morbi. Quare Apho. In a-cutis passionibus raro, exceptio est duorum com-munium praeceptorum, nempe illius quod no-bis tradidit quarto de ratione victus, ubi scri-bit: In acutis morbis sanguinem detrahes si vehemens morbus videatur, &c. Et praece-pti, Concocta medicari. Prout enim inter ini-tia acuti morbi pharmacum ministramus, com-munem frangimus regulam, Concocta medi-cari. Vt vero venae sectione non vtimur, con-tra praeceptum de mittendo sanguine in acutis agim. Ob quam causam dixit, et hoc pri bene diudicantes facere. Hoc est an pharmacum magis competat phlebotomo, quod quidem valde necessarium & acuto morbo maximè conueniens dixerat. Sed quando liceat in acutis pharmacum exhibere alibi ostendemus. Dixit ergo in acutis passionibus raro, & in principijs pharmacys vti, ac si velit dicere, In acutis raro purgante medicamento vtimur, quia vt plurimum sanguinem in ijs mittere maximè necessarium est. Quapropter discernere oportet, an pharmaco vti magis commodo possis, quàm sanguinis missione. Cum ergo hoc ita se habeat, fieri non potest vt perpetuò id quod sexta aut octaua die pharmacum adhibent, rectè & secundum rationem ministret. Vere ita res habet, quod non paucos absque vlla purgatione sanauerim, & multo plures quibus nec quarta, sexta, nec octaua, pharmacum purgans exhibui, sed in morbi inclinatione, natura incompletam crisim faciente. In continuis febribus raro quantum memini occasionem inueni ex hibendi pharmacum inter morbi initia, nedum dum apud incrementum. Febris enim continua est, quæ proprie & maxime acuta est ægritudo, vt tradidit Hippocrates. Ostensum igitur est purgationem non esse ex vsu quæ perpetuò quibuscunque in morbis die sexta aut octaua fit: quare & victum qui purgationem consequitur. Quod autem de communibus dictum est materijs, non iusta occasio est à recta deuiandi. Quod si multitudine earum nec clysteribus nec syrupis digerentibus absumi posse iudicat medicus, quod rarum est, potiunculâ caßiæ ex oxymelite initio dare expedit: aut eiusdem tres bolos deuorandos ei qui potionem fastidiat. A quibus quinque oxymelitis aut syrupi quem acetosum vocant cochlearia deglutire commodè erit. Sic enim bilem & pituitam leniendo educit. Nec erit impedimento quo minus rectâ victus rationem ab initio ad vigorem vsque instituas. Sed mihi admirari sæpe contingit, quod nostro sæculo infelici omine communes materiæ antiquis temporibus non visæ, com paruêre: aut si erat, nô tanti certè habebatur.
units.tr: Hence the aphorism: "In acute illnesses, seldom," is an exception to two common precepts, namely the one he gave us in the fourth book of On the Regimen, where he writes: "In acute diseases you will draw blood if the disease seems violent," etc., and the precept, "Treat after concoction." For when we administer a medicine at the beginning of an acute disease, we break the common rule, "Treat after concoction." And when we do not use venesection, we act against the precept about letting blood in acute diseases. For this reason he said "and this, if they judge well, is to act at the beginning." That is, whether a medicine is more suitable for the phlebotomist, which he had said was very necessary and best suited to an acute disease. But when it is permissible to give a medicine in acute cases we shall show elsewhere. He said, therefore, "in acute illnesses, seldom," and "to use medicines at the beginning," as if he meant: "In acute cases we seldom use a purgative medicine, because for the most part it is especially necessary to let blood in them. So one must judge whether you can use a medicine more suitably than bloodletting." Since this is so, it cannot be that a medicine given on the sixth or eighth day is always rightly and rationally administered. Indeed, it is true that I have cured not a few without any purging, and many more to whom I gave no purgative on the fourth, sixth or eighth day, but when the disease was declining and nature was making an incomplete crisis. In continued fevers, as far as I remember, I have rarely found occasion to give a medicine during the beginning of the illness, let alone during its increase. For a continued fever is that which is properly and most acutely a sickness, as Hippocrates taught. It is shown, therefore, that purging, which is always done on the sixth or eighth day in whatever diseases, is not in use; and so is the diet that follows purging. What has been said about common matters is not a just reason for departing from the right course. But if the physician judges that, because of their number, they cannot be disposed of either by enemas or by digestive syrups, which is rare, it is useful at the start to give a little draught of cassia in oxymel; or three boluses of it to be swallowed by one who dislikes the draught. Of these, a spoonful or five of oxymel, or of the syrup which they call acetous, may conveniently be swallowed. For thus he draws off bile and phlegm by softening them. Nor will it be a hindrance to your keeping the right regimen from the beginning until strength returns. But I often wonder that in our unhappy age common matters, not seen in ancient times, have appeared; or if they were there, they were not held in such esteem.

units.la: {1} I. de morbis vulg. Adhuc contra eosdem, Quòd qui inter initia morborum tenui magis victu utuntur: cumq; prope statum peruentum est, solidiori, in damnum aegrotantium graviter peccant.
units.tr: {1} Book 1 of On Common Diseases. Again against the same people: those who use a thinner diet at the beginning of diseases, and a more solid one when they have nearly reached the crisis, sin gravely to the harm of the sick.

units.la: CAPVT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: SED ad reliqua proposíti sermonem convertamus. Primis quinque aut sex diebus febricitantes tenui magis victu alere, deinde cum morbus prope vigorem est solidiori cibo pascere, omnino praeter rationem est. Minus siquidem natura cibo impedienda est, cum morbi vi stimulata, circa morbi materiae coctionem impensius vacat, ut scitè à Galeno scriptum est. Prudens igitur medicus ad cibórum coctionem, naturam tunc temporis ab opere non distrahet: quinimmò ab ijs quos ante ministrabat cibis subtrahet, ut cibus quacunque leui naturae actione transmutetur. Quod si crassior esset natura alio intenta corrumperetur, aut certè laboranti naturae superadderet laborem. Omnis insuper mutatio disproportionalis si repente fiat, sanis molesta est, quare multo magis aegrotantibus, vt supra ostendimus de mente Hippocratis. Cum ergo virtus laborantis die sexta, aut octaua imbecillior sit, quàm erat in initio, minus cibi feret tunc temporis natura. Quare ut recte mutatio fiat, mutare cibum pro ratione ad magis tenue oportet. Quod si alter, dispro portionalis fiet mutatio, non parum natura ag grauans. Ipsa enim (natura) à magis robusta, prout erat initio, ad magis imbecillem, prout est sexta, aut octaua die acuti morbi, muta tionem habuit. Ratio autem victus contra rio, nempe à magis tenui ad crassiorem muta ta est. Quapropter nullo pacto credendum est, natura posse ex huiusce modi victus ratione iuuari. Insuper mutationes insignes in cibo ab initio morbi ad statum usque faciendas non esse supra ostendimus: Pessimam omnium & magis grauantem naturā, quæ à tenui victu ad crassum repente fit. Ad hæc Hippocrates commentario secundo de ratione victus aperte damnat eam victus rationem qua primis ægritudinibus dieb. inaniuntur ægrotātes, deinde ad sorbitiones, antequam morbo iudicetur » transeunt:cuius verba ita habent: Melius si-» quidem esse dico, vt protinus à morbi initio » sorbere incipias, quàm inanitis euacuatisque » venis, vel die tertio, vel quarto, vel quinto, » velsexto, velseptimo, si ante hoc tempus mor-» bus haudquaquam iudicatus fuerit, sorbitio » nem inchoare. Praeterea ipse eodem libro in expositione illius, Hoc autem verius effica-» ciusque ita scribit: Sed sanè deterius aget, qui » omnibus ijs diebus vasa ante exinaniuerit, et »sequentibus quibusdam diebus ita pauerit pri » usquam morbus maturus reddatur. Nempe »hoc pacto mortem plurimis liquido affert, ni » si morbus omnino beneficus fuerit. Quæ ve-» rò in principio committuntur delicta ea non » similiter domantibus reniuntur, sed facilius » domari possunt. In quibus verbis aperte no-bis ostendit maximum periculum esse in acu-to morbo primis quinque aut sex diebus te-nui victu aegrotantis venas inanire, postmo-dum morbo adhuc non maturo ad ea quæ co-meduntur transfire. Ipse praeterea eam muta-tionem damnauit, qua ad sorbitionem tran-situs situs sit à magis tenui victu, cum ait: De mutatione quæ in hac vel illa sit, plurima sum lo cutus quod re vera hæc nouisse commodissimum sit, cū ad omnia tum ad id de quo nunc agitur. Nam in morbis acutis ex vasorū inanitione ad sorbitiones transitur. Transeundū quidem præcipio ego sed sorbitionibus haud quaquam vtendum, prius quàm morbus ad maturitatem perductus fuerit, aut signū aliquod aliud apparuerit, &c. Vides ad sorbitiones transeundum non esse à magis tenui victu antequam morbus maturuerit, nedum à iure lentium aut à cocta cucurbita ad capi aut pullæ gallinaceæ carnes. Quæ crassum victum constituunt huiusmodi se habent victus, quos febricitantibus ministrant occidentalissimi medici: qui quantum ab eo quod febricitantibus conuenit, aberrent, & à vera Hippocratis mente satis ostensum est.
units.tr: But let us turn our discussion to the rest of our subject. To feed feverish patients with a thinner diet during the first five or six days, and then, when the disease is near its height, to feed them with more solid food, is altogether against reason. Nature is less to be hindered by food when it is roused by the force of the disease and is more intent on concocting the morbid matter, as Galen has rightly written. A prudent physician therefore will not draw nature away from its work of digesting food at that time; rather, he will withdraw from the foods he was giving before, so that the food may be changed by whatever slight action of nature is available. But if the nature were coarser, it would be corrupted when it is occupied elsewhere, or at least it would add labour to a nature already labouring. Moreover, every disproportionate change, if it happens suddenly, is troublesome even to the healthy, and so much more to the sick, as we showed above concerning the mind of Hippocrates. Since, therefore, the strength of the sufferer on the sixth or eighth day is weaker than it was at the beginning, nature will then bear less food. So for the change to be made rightly, the diet must be changed in proportion to a thinner one. But if it is otherwise, the change will be disproportionate and will burden nature not a little. For nature has undergone a change from a stronger state, as it was at the beginning, to a weaker one, as it is on the sixth or eighth day of an acute disease. Yet the regimen of diet has been changed in the opposite direction, namely from a thinner to a coarser one. Therefore on no account should it be believed that nature can be helped by a regimen of this kind. Furthermore, we have shown above that marked changes in diet are not to be made from the beginning of the disease up to its height; the worst and most burdensome of all is the change that suddenly goes from a thin diet to a thick one.
