Hippocrates, moreover, in the second commentary on the regimen of diet, openly condemns that regimen by which patients are emptied in the first days of the illness and then move on to broths before the disease is judged; his words are these: "I say it is better that you begin to take broth right from the beginning of the disease than to begin broth after the veins have been emptied and evacuated, whether on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth or seventh day, if the disease has by no means been judged before that time." Besides, in the same book, in his exposition of that passage, he writes more truly and effectively thus: "But certainly he will act worse who has first emptied the vessels on all those days, and then in the following days has fed the patient in such a way before the disease has ripened. For in this way he brings death to most people, unless the disease is entirely beneficial. But the errors committed at the beginning are not overcome in the same way, but can be overcome more easily." In these words he clearly shows us that there is the greatest danger in an acute disease if, during the first five or six days, the veins of a patient on a thin diet are emptied, and afterwards, while the disease is still not ripe, he passes on to the foods that are eaten. He also condemned that change by which the transition is made to broth from a thinner diet, when he says: "I have spoken at length about the change that is made in this or that case, since knowing these things is really most useful, both in all matters and in the point we are now discussing. For in acute diseases the transition is made from emptying the vessels to broths. I do indeed advise that the transition be made, but broths must by no means be used before the disease has been brought to ripeness or some other sign has appeared, etc." You see that one must not pass to broths from a thinner diet before the disease has ripened, much less from barley-water or boiled gourd to the flesh of a capon or a young hen. These kinds of food, which make up a thick diet, are what the most western physicians give to feverish patients; how far they stray from what suits feverish patients, and from the true mind of Hippocrates, has been sufficiently shown.

units.la: Victus rationem quam medici Angli obser uant præceptis artis medicæ magis consentire.
units.tr: The regimen of diet that English physicians observe agrees more with the precepts of the medical art.

units.la: CAPVT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: MAGIS Anglorum medicorum vi-ctus ratio præceptis artis medicæ con-sentit: vnica siquidem victus forma febrici-tantes ab initio ad morbi solutionem nutri-unt. Ius pullæ hoc modo parant. Ante diem mactant quam crassam elegerunt. Deinde hordeo præparato, prunis, passulis, buglossa, endiuia, violis, & huiusmodi herbis, co-quunt plus satis, ita vt ius spissum reddatur. Hac sorbitiuncula non solum febricitantes, sed eos qui aliis detinentur affectibus nutri-unt. Hunc victum à morbi initio ad manife-stam vsque inclinationem ministrant: & an-tiquorum regulas maiori se cura obseruare ostendunt. Tum quia vnica victus forma à morbi initio ad statum vsque procedunt ci-tra permutationem insignem: tum quia sic agentes læsionem quæ ex victus formæ muta-tione ægrotantibus euenire solet, effugiunt. Secundum ex libro secundo de ratione vi-ctus colligunt. Primum ex Galeno eodem li-bro in expositione illius, Interdum aut et cru-da, etc. Vbi ita scribit, Vniuersa (inquit) hæc contincontingere his ait, qui perperam cibati sunt ab medicis, qui primis diebus exiccatos ægros die tertio, vel quarto, vel quinto, vel sexto, repente ad edulia non peracto morbi vigore permutauerunt. Quasi peracto morbi vigore conuenienter eos victum permutaturos fuisse dicat. Quod aut dicebat, Permutare quidem sanorum victum in morbis, neque tamen temere id agendum, iam patere ex dictis arbitror. Nempe cum una quidem corporis conditio sani sit: altera quæ à morbi initio ad statum vsque extenditur: mox & tertia, quæ ad perfectam morbi solutionem sese prorogat: deinde & quarta, quæ totius convalescentiæ tempus ad vsque sanitatis habitum occupat: in nulla harum quatuor conditionum permutationem victus insignem facere oportet, nisi prius in alteram conditionis speciem peruentum sit.
units.tr: The regimen of diet of the English physicians agrees more closely with the precepts of the medical art: for they nourish feverish patients from the beginning until the resolution of the disease with a single form of diet. They prepare the broth of a hen in this way: they slaughter the hen before the day on which they have chosen it to be fat. Then, with prepared barley, prunes, raisins, bugloss, endive, violets and herbs of this kind, they boil it more than enough, so that the broth is made thick. With this little broth they nourish not only the feverish but also those held by other affections. They give this diet from the beginning of the disease up to the clear decline, and they show that they observe the rules of the ancients with greater care. They proceed up to the state of the disease with a single form of diet, without any marked change; and in this way they avoid the harm that usually comes to the sick from a change in the form of diet. They gather the second point from the second book on the regimen of diet. The first is from Galen, in the same book, in his exposition of that passage, "Sometimes also raw...", where he writes: "All these things (he says) continue to happen to those who have been fed wrongly by physicians, who in the first days dried out the sick and then, on the third, fourth, fifth or sixth day, suddenly changed them to foods before the vigour of the disease was completed." As if he were saying that they would have changed the diet appropriately once the vigour of the disease was complete. That it is right to change the diet of healthy people in diseases, but not to do so rashly, I think is now plain from what has been said. Indeed, since the condition of a healthy body is one, and the second condition extends from the beginning of the disease up to its height, then the third, which prolongs itself to the complete solution of the disease, and then a fourth, which occupies the whole time of convalescence up to the state of health, one must make no marked change of diet in any of these four conditions, unless the body has first reached the next kind of condition.

units.la: Anglis ægrotantibus non esse tenuem victum offerendum, sumpta indicatione à consuetudine, regione, & cœli temperie.
units.tr: That English sick people should not be offered a thin diet, the indication being taken from custom, region and the temperature of the climate.

units.la: CAPVT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: SED quo magis antiquorum dogmata in sequi eo modo conantur, eo grauius Anglos lædunt ægrotantes, eorum vires exoluen tes. Angli animo & corpore vigent, cibi & potus multũ & crebro ingerere assueti. Assuetudini autem cum aliquid concedendum nos doceat Hippocrates, colligitur non esse dictam victus rationem quibuscunque in febribus certam, sed nimis tenuem, sumpta indicatione ab assuetudine, regione, et cœli tem perie. Corpora siquidem quæ multo & crasso vtuntur victu in prospera valitudine, simplici sorbitiuncula alere, tribus morbi tempo ribus, haud iustum est. Nam verendum est ne corporis vires labantur ob defectum. Nec obstiterit quod supra in inuestigatione formæ victus consuetudinis nõ meminimus. Nã & si vere formam victus consuetudo non per se indicet, interuentu tamen virtutis indicare videtur. Nam crasso victu assueti, tenui si aliquot diebus vtantur, imbecilles fiũt. Quapropter supra cum de virtutis robore quæreremus, cõsuetudinis mentionẽ fecimus.
units.tr: BUT the more they try to follow the doctrines of the ancients, the more gravely they harm English patients by wearing down their strength. The English are vigorous in mind and body, and are accustomed to take food and drink in large quantities and often. Since Hippocrates teaches that some concession must be made to habit, it follows that a single fixed rule of diet cannot be set for all fevers, and that a diet that is too thin is wrong, when the indication is taken from habit, region and the temperature of the sky. For it is not right to nourish with a simple little broth, through the three periods of a disease, bodies that in good health are used to a copious and thick diet. For one must fear that the strength of the body will fail for want of food. Nor would it be an objection that above, in our investigation of the form of diet, we did not mention habit. For even if habit does not in itself indicate the form of diet, it seems to indicate it through its effect on strength. For those accustomed to a thick diet become weak if they live on a thin one for some days. That is why, when above we were inquiring into the strength of vigour, we mentioned habit.

units.la: Ita vt eorum virtutes qui multo & crasso victu in prospera vsi sunt valetudine, ob id parum vrgere ac si imbecilles sint, posueri-mus. Regio praeterea ad quinquagesimū quar-tum gradum versus boream vergens cū fri-gida valde sit, calidum innatum intra viscera colligens fortius reddit. Vnde crassiores in-digent alimento, tum ob hoc, tum vt frigori continentis validius obsistat. Quod autē à fri-gida regione similis sumatur indicatio ac à frigido tempore, ex eo fit manifestum, quia vires validas similiter efficit, & consimiles in corpore humano creat humores. Sed hy-berno tempore multa quidem propter robur virium & raro danda sunt, vt scriptum est à Galeno in expositione Apho. Quibus semel aut bis. Consimiliter igitur iis qui frigidam re-gionem incolunt, plus cibi quàm morbi natu-ra exposcat, ministrandum. Illud regioni & consuetudini concedentibus medicis. Gaude-re enim semper naturam consuetis dixit Ga-lenus octauo de Methodo ex authoritate Hip-pocratis. Sunt praeterea quàm plurimæ acu= tarum ægritudinum quæ adeò tenuem victū non ferant. Præter acutas febres, quas tropicas appellitant medici, quibus non competit. sunt & quæ die vndecima, et tertiadecima, & quartadecima terminantur, quibus perscriptus victus non est ex vsu, non Italo, nō Hispano, si aliqua supra dictarum febrium specie laboret, cum vterque eorum parcius secunda valetudine viuat. Quod si febre ponas esse ex ijs quæ longiorem habeant terminum, rectè profectò colligetur Anglos ægrotantes à tenui victu graviter lædi. Ea siquidem impense grauis noxa non est, qua morbus vires assumit, sed quæ vires, quibus natura morbum oppugnat, adimit.
units.tr: So we set down that the strength of those who in good health have lived on a copious and thick diet is not, for that reason, to be counted as weak. Moreover, the region that lies at the fifty-fourth degree towards the north is very cold, and by gathering the innate heat within the viscera it makes it stronger. Hence people of a stouter build need more nourishment, both for this reason and so that they may resist the cold of the continent more vigorously. That an indication is taken from a cold region in the same way as from a cold season is clear from the fact that it likewise produces strong powers and creates similar humours in the human body. But in winter many things must be given, because of the strength of the powers, and seldom, as Galen wrote in his exposition of the Aphorisms: "To those [who eat] once or twice..." Likewise, then, those who live in a cold region must be given more food than the nature of the disease requires, the physicians conceding this to the region and to habit. For Galen said in the eighth book of the Method, on the authority of Hippocrates, that nature always rejoices in what it is used to. Moreover, there are very many acute illnesses that do not bear so thin a diet. Apart from the acute fevers that physicians call tropical, to which it does not suit, there are also those that end on the eleventh, thirteenth and fourteenth day, for which the diet prescribed is not suitable, neither the Italian nor the Spanish, if the patient suffers from any of the kinds of fever mentioned above, since each of these people lives more sparingly in good health. But if you suppose the fever is one of those that have a longer course, it will rightly be concluded that English patients are gravely harmed by a thin diet. For that is not a serious harm which takes away the strength by which the disease gains ground, but that which takes away the strength by which nature fights the disease.

units.la: Anglos uitiosis aut semicorruptis humoribus abundare, non crudis.
units.tr: That the English abound in vitiated or half-corrupted humours, not in raw ones.

units.la: CAPVT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: SED non deerit fortasse errandi occasio, Anglos bona valetudine inordinato aut vti victu, ventresq; eorum ob id crudis humoribus redundare. Hos cum ægrotant tenui victu absumi oportere iudicant. Fouent enim (inquiunt) propriam morbi effectricem causam. Sed res aliter habet ut existimo. Ventres Anglorum non crudis sed prauis aut semicorruptis humoribus abundare opinor. Quod si crudos eos dicas, quos natura non euincit cedo, appellationem non moror. sed eo modo quo Hippocrates solet cruda nuncupare excrementa, nempe flauam bilem & reliqua quæ corpus alere non valent. Eos prauos esse dico, qui post coctricis facultatis actionem nutritioni permanent inepti, cōsimilem à natura mutationem recipientes ac excrementa. Eos ineptos nutritioni esse signum est, quod ieiunium haud facile ferant. quorum enim ventres crudis abundant humoribus nutritioni aptis facile ieiunŭ ferunt, siue assueti sint multum, aut parum ingerere, ut scitè scripsit Hippocrates in hæc verba: Nō assuetam (inquit) cibi abstinentiā facilius omnino ferunt, qui parte superiori pituitosi sunt. Quo fit ut si semel die, cibo vtantur, facilius etiā ferant. Ratione} assignans Galenus ad hunc
units.tr: But perhaps there will not be lacking an occasion for error: the English, being in good health, may eat in a disorderly way or use a diet that is wrong for them, and their stomachs are therefore overflowing with raw humours. When they fall ill, they judge that they must be wasted by a thin diet, for they nourish (they say) the very cause that produces the disease. But I think the matter stands otherwise. I hold that the stomachs of the English abound not with raw humours but with bad or half-corrupted ones. But if you call them raw, I do not object to the name, provided it is used in the way Hippocrates usually calls excrements raw, namely yellow bile and the other humours that cannot nourish the body. I say they are bad: those which, after the action of the concocting faculty, remain unfit for nutrition, having undergone a change from nature like that of excrement. That they are unfit for nutrition is shown by the fact that they cannot easily bear fasting. For those whose stomachs abound with raw humours fit for nutrition bear fasting easily, whether they are accustomed to eat much or little, as Hippocrates wisely wrote in these words: "Those who are phlegmatic in the upper part bear abstinence from food to which they are not accustomed far more easily. So it comes about that if they take food once a day, they bear it more easily still." Galen, giving the reason, writes in this manner:

units.la: {y} 2 modum scribit: Pituita verò temporis processu coquitur, sanguisque efficitur. Unde facilius ieiunium ob pituitam in sanguinem conuersionem ferunt, id longa docente experientia. Argumento ergo dialectico, quod à negatione consequentis dicunt, perspicuo apparet, eorum qui ieiunium difficulter ferant ventres carere humoribus aptis ut nutriant. Vnde manifestum fit humores quibus eorum ventres abundant, alimoniae aptos non esse. Ratio verè rem ita esse ostendit. Etsi autem hæc sola sit satis ut de re certa habeatur scientia, alia tamen adducemus obiter signa ut pusillanimes ad rem percipiendam confortemus.
units.tr: "But phlegm is cooked with the passage of time, and becomes blood. Hence they bear fasting more easily, because phlegm is converted into blood, as long experience teaches." Thus by a dialectical argument, which they call one from the denial of the consequent, it clearly appears that those who bear fasting with difficulty lack humours apt to nourish them. Hence it becomes manifest that the humours with which their stomachs abound are not suited to nourishment. Reason shows that the thing is so. Although this alone is enough to hold the matter as certain knowledge, we will nonetheless add, in passing, other signs to encourage the timid to grasp the matter.

units.la: Cum humores in ventriculo contenti, laudabiles sunt, halitus qui ab iis ad caput feruntur humidi sunt nulliusque prauæ qualitatis participant. Cunque per poros capitis & faciei effluunt, nulla in transitu particulas extranea afficiunt qualitate. Cum verò prauî fuerint, & ventriculo qui insederint, necesse est partes eas quæ ab eo per consensum affici solent, similiter afficiantur. Facies igitur halitus à ventriculo ascendentis qualitatem haud obscurè indicat. Corpora igitur Anglo rum si circunspicias pulchra esse videbis, alba & læui cute eorum membra obduci. Faciem verò eorum, quorum ventriculi crudo- rum humorum congerie grauantur, obscura rubedine, pustulis conspersam, lacera multis in locis cute intueberis. Simile igitur aliquo videns faciem, crudisque humoribus grauatri eius ventriculum, quem iandiu conqueren tem audias, nónne recte colliges coniectura habita ex facie eius, humores prauâ nactos esse qualitatem longa in ventriculo mora, halitusq; inde ascendentes, faciem inficere? Ut enim id calido iocineri quis tribuat, sanguinem biliosum efficienti talemq; ad corporis particulas mitteti, fieri nequit. Nam cum materia quæ totum nutrit corpus, à naturali mutata est symmetria, necesse est ut singulæ corporis particulæ lædantur cum facie. Quod si adhuc insistas. Sanguine biliosum aut magis natura excalfactum, facilius ad superiora vergere, cedo. Sed fieri nequit temporis longitudine ad totum corpus qui vitium permeet. Id præterea senibus crebrius accidere, quàm iuuenibus videmus, quibus minus causa est quod biliosum generent sanguinem. Ventres tamen eorum crudis abundare humoribus non extra rationem est. Verum est quod quibuscunque talis facies futura erit humorum in ventriculo congestorum occasione, immoderato opus est calore, tum ut humores corruptioni disponat, tum ut ab eis fumosos educat halitus, qui faciem maculent. Senibus igitur immoderato vini vsu immoderatum calorem intra viscera excitante, talis generatur facies & non ratione calidi incineris. Quibuscunq; igitur talis affectus accidit materiam à ventriculo praua qualitatis suppeditari, calorem verò efficiente vel ab incinere vel ab ipso ventriculo ascitiū certū est. His fidem præstant, cibos et potus quibus vtuntur, aptissimos esse vt in ventriculo corrumpantur. Vino & ceruisia, quam aliâ vulgari sermone dicunt, ad vnam mensam vtuntur. Potus enim ceruisiæ, cum flatuosus natura sit, vini consortio magis inflatiuus reddi-tur, ita vt caput magis impleat & feriat. Bu tyro praeterea salsis cum piscibus vescuntur. Ita fit vt aduersantibus ciborum & potuū dissimilibus qualitatibus, tota mixtio corru ptioni fiat obnoxia. Ratione igitur quispiam asseret, eos nō crudis solū, sed et vitiosis abun dare humoribus, minime ad nutritione aptis.
units.tr: When the humours contained in the stomach are wholesome, the vapours that rise from them to the head are moist and share in no bad quality. As they pass out through the pores of the head and face, they do not affect the particles they pass through with any foreign quality. But when the humours are bad and have settled in the stomach, the parts that are usually affected by it through sympathy must be affected in the same way. The face therefore clearly indicates the quality of the vapours rising from the stomach. If you look at the bodies of the English, you will see that they are fair, with white and smooth skin covering their limbs. But the faces of those whose stomachs are burdened with a mass of raw humours you will see marked with a dark redness, sprinkled with pustules, and with skin torn in many places. Seeing a face like this, and hearing a man who has long complained that his stomach is weighed down with raw humours, will you not rightly conclude from the appearance of his face that the humours have acquired a bad quality from a long stay in the stomach, and that the vapours rising from them infect the face? For it cannot be attributed to the warm liver, which produces bilious blood and sends such blood to the parts of the body. For when the matter that nourishes the whole body has been changed from its natural balance, it is necessary that each part of the body be harmed, including the face. But if you still insist that blood which is bilious, or heated more by nature, tends more easily upwards, I answer that this cannot affect the whole body in the time available. Moreover, we see that this happens more often to the old than to the young, who have less cause to generate bilious blood. Yet it is not unreasonable that their stomachs abound with raw humours. It is true that whoever is to have such a face, from the occasion of humours gathered in the stomach, needs an immoderate heat, both to dispose the humours to corruption and to draw from them smoky vapours that stain the face. Therefore in the old, immoderate use of wine, which excites immoderate heat within the viscera, produces such a face, and not because of the heat of the liver. Whoever suffers such a condition, it is certain that the matter is supplied by the stomach with a bad quality, and that the heat comes either from the liver or from the stomach itself. What confirms this is that the foods and drinks they use are very apt to corrupt in the stomach. They drink wine and ale, which others in the vernacular call beer, at the same table. For beer, being flatulent by nature, is made even more inflating when mixed with wine, so that it fills and strikes the head more. Moreover, they feed on salted fish with butter. So it happens that, with the foods and drinks having contrary qualities, the whole mixture becomes liable to corruption. By reason, then, someone may assert that they abound not only in raw humours but in vicious ones, quite unfit for nutrition.

units.la: Aegrotantibus Anglis tenuem uictū ob id ministrare, ut redundantes in eorū uen-triculis humores absumant, errore esse.
units.tr: To give thin diet to the English when they are ill, for the reason that it consumes the humours overflowing in their stomachs, is an error.

units.la: CAPVT XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: AVDI quo rem deducam. Aegrotanti bus Anglis tenuem victum ministra-re medicos, ob id quod eorum ventres crudis redundent humoribus, quos ita absumi spe-rant, errorem esse arbitror. Victum tenue mi nistras, vt humores in ventriculo redundan tes absumas? At ij cum a propria mutati na tura, prauamque nacti qualitatem, nutrire non valeat, vt ostendimus, fit, vt prauos hu mores morbum efficientes natura (alioquin multum temporis ventriculi coctioni impendere assueta) ad expulsionis opus parante, alter naturæ hostis insurgat, ipsam multitudine & praua qualitate & ob sedis nobilitatem grauiter perturbans, præter id quod pro pria morbi effectrice causa laboris patitur. Quod si naturam duplicis hostis incursu gravatam, viriumque robore indigentem, accedens medicus contra consuetudinem agens, tenuem victum offerat, sponteq; reddat imbecilliorem, nonne merito non medicus sanas sed occidens, non adiutor naturæ sed ægritudinis dicetur? Sed ut nulla aduersario superstit spes, constituamus hominem ex corruptione humorum ægrotantem, cum robore virium, (Corruptos humores eos dico qui à natura propria migrantes nutrire nō valent: quales Anglorum esse supponimus, qui diu ventriculo insederunt, ) sumpta solummodo ab ijs indicatione, parum an multum, raro aut crebro huic cibum offeres? Medicus Anglus modicum iuris pullæ gallinaceæ conuenientibus herbis decenter temperati bis aut ter in die
units.tr: Listen while I make my point. I think it is an error for physicians to give sick Englishmen a thin diet, on the ground that their stomachs abound with crude humours which they hope will be consumed in this way. Are you prescribing a thin diet so that the humours abounding in the stomach will be used up? But these humours, once changed from their proper nature and having acquired a corrupt quality, cannot nourish, as we have shown. So it happens that while nature, which is accustomed to spend much time on digesting the stomach's contents, prepares for the work of expelling the bad humours that cause the disease, another enemy of nature rises up. By their quantity and bad quality, and by the nobility of the seat they occupy, they grievously disturb nature, over and above the labour it already suffers from the disease's own cause. If a physician comes to a nature weighed down by the attack of a double enemy and in need of strength, and, acting against custom, offers a thin diet which makes it weaker of its own accord, will he not rightly be called not a physician but a killer, not a helper of nature but of the sickness? But so that our opponent has no hope left, let us suppose a man sick from a corruption of humours, but with his powers of strength intact. (By corrupt humours I mean those which, departing from their proper nature, cannot nourish. Such, we suppose, are the humours of the English, who have long settled in the stomach.) Taking his indication from these alone, would you offer this man food rarely or often, little or much? The English physician gives a small amount of chicken broth, suitably seasoned with appropriate herbs, twice or three times a day.

units.la: Hostis: inimicus. die ministrabit: aut quam dicunt hyposetalam: aut analberi, aliud sorbitionis genus, quæ parùm alimenti præstant. Quid si Galenum audias contrarium dicentem, nónne deinceps mutabis sententiam, & Anglos in posterum ægrotantes crassiori victu ales? Ille igitur in expositione Apho. Quibus semel aut bis, ita scribit: Εἰ δὲ μιᾶ φιλίας ἢ ἀφθορᾶς ἢ δια-μὶς ἐρρωμένῃ τύχοι, καὶ πολλὰ καὶ πολλάκις σιτία τοῖς οὕτω κάμνουσι δώσομεν, ὡς αὖ καὶ τ' ἀσθενείας, ἀσομένης πολλῶν, ἡ ἢ διὰ- μεως κρατεῖν αὐτῶν δυναμένης. Hoc est, Si cũ indigentia aut corruptione facultas robu- sta fuerit, & multa & multoties cibaria it͛ laborantibus dabimus, vtpote multa exigen te dispositione & facultate illa vincere po- tente. Sentis ne dispositionem quæ ex humo- rum corruptione accidit, non modicum cibū̃ indicare. Sed eundem in eodem audi dicente. Si facultas (inquit) laborantis imbecillis fue- rit, & ea quæ in corpore est dispositio ex cor ruptione sit vel indigentia, paucum alimen- tihis, & sæpius dabimus. Parum quidem, quia semel totam multitudinem alimenti substinere non potest facultas debilis. Sæpius autem quoniam multis indiget dispositio. indi-gentia siquidem adiectione indiget, corruptiovero epicrasi. Hos enim qui cum virium im becillitate corruptione humorum laborant, docet Galenus curare in libris de methodo medendi, paulisper noxios humores vacuan do, & decenti victu laudabiliores semper ap ponendo. Curationem hanc per epicrasim fieri nuncupat. Quod si cum virium robore, & corruptione humorum, hominem crebro mul-tum cibi & potus assuetum ingerere, ponas: præter hæc, in regione frigida, qualis est An glia, iudicas ne hunc exiguo & tenui victu alendum fore, an multo & crasso, indicatio-nibus tribus in id consentientibus, nempe corruptione humorum, consuetudine, & regione? Ego quidem multum ijs & crebro exhibendum esse arbitror. Nisi obstent paroxysmorum aut exacerbationum inuasiones. Quod si contingat, rarius multum ijs ministrare oportet. Nec hoc præter mentem Galeni est, qui in expositione dicti Apho. ita scribit, Si vero accessiones non permiserint, nec multi alimenti offerendi occasiones praestiterint, ra ro plura exhibebimus. Sic quidam translu- lit: aliter tamen habet Graecum exemplar, nempe: Μηδὲ πολλὰς ἡ ἔοφης ἡμῖν καιρὸς παρεχόντως, ὀλιγάκις ἀλώσομεν τὰ πολλά. hoc est, Neque plures ad cibum offerendum occasiones habentes raro plura dabimus. Ea vere ita res habet. Nam accessiones non solent plura cibationi opportuna tempora praestare, praecipue si longae sint. Velim quisquis haec legerit sibi persuadeat, me haec scribere non ut in medicos Anglos invehar, sed ut veritatem omnibus aperiens, simul & Anglis amorem quo eos hucusque prosequor ostendam. Daboque operam ut absens, calamo efficiam, quod praesens apud vos praestabam.
units.tr: Hostis: the enemy. He administers each day, or what they call hyposetala, or analberi, another kind of broth, which give little nourishment. What if you heard Galen saying the opposite? Would you not then change your opinion and feed sick Englishmen a richer diet from now on? In his exposition of the aphorism "To those who have it once or twice," he writes thus: "If, however, the faculty happens to be strong, we shall give much food and often to those who are so affected, since the disease, when it is great, needs that much and that often to overcome it" [Εἰ δὲ μιᾶ φιλίας ἢ ἀφθορᾶς ἢ διαμὶς ἐρρωμένῃ τύχοι, καὶ πολλὰ καὶ πολλάκις σιτία τοῖς οὕτω κάμνουσι δώσομεν, ὡς αὖ καὶ τ' ἀσθενείας, ἀσομένης πολλῶν, ἡ ἢ διαμεως κρατεῖν αὐτῶν δυναμένης]. That is: "If the faculty is robust in spite of want or corruption, we shall give much food and often to the sufferers, since the disposition, which needs much, is able to overcome it by that faculty." Do you see that the disposition arising from a corruption of humours does not call for a small amount of food? But hear him again, saying in the same place: "If the faculty of the sufferer is weak, and the disposition in the body arises from corruption or want, we shall give a little food, and more often." A little, indeed, because a weak faculty cannot sustain the whole quantity of food at once; but more often, because the disposition needs much. For want needs addition, while corruption needs epicrasis. Galen teaches that those who suffer from weakness of powers together with corruption of humours should be cured, in his books On the Method of Healing, by gently purging the harmful humours and always applying more wholesome food in a suitable diet. He calls this cure by epicrasis. But if you posit a man with strength of powers and corruption of humours, who is accustomed to eat and drink much and often, and in addition he lives in a cold region such as England, do you judge that he must be fed on a scanty and thin diet, or on a large and rich one, since three indications agree on this: the corruption of humours, custom, and region? I myself think he should be given much, and often. Unless the onsets of paroxysms or exacerbations stand in the way. If that happens, it is necessary to give much less often. Nor is this beyond Galen's meaning, who, in his exposition of the said aphorism, writes thus: "If the accessions do not allow it, and the occasions do not offer us the chance of giving much food, we shall give more rarely." So someone has translated it, but the Greek copy reads otherwise, namely: "Neither having many occasions for offering food, we shall give more things rarely" [Μηδὲ πολλὰς ἡ ἔοφης ἡμῖν καιρὸς παρεχόντως, ὀλιγάκις ἀλώσομεν τὰ πολλά]. That is: "Having neither many occasions for offering food, we shall give much rarely." And indeed the matter is so, for attacks do not usually afford many opportune times for feeding, especially if they are long. I would wish that whoever reads this may be persuaded that I write these things not to inveigh against English physicians, but to reveal the truth to everyone, and at the same time to show the English the affection with which I have so far regarded them. And I will take care that, though absent, I accomplish with my pen what I used to do in person among you.

units.la: Clarissime vir Thomas Aldae totius Anglia cancellarie dignissime vnicum Anglorum decus, Ioannes Bakeri primitiarum cancellarie humanissime, in paternarum legum peritia prudentissime, rectissimobilis trutina, uobis hæc commentaria de victus ratione confcri psi, vestra gratia tueamini. Scio non deerunt detractores. Speculatio tamen cum homini- bus exvsu maximè sit, si vestra gratia apud Anglos commendetur, erit vt ad hominum manus libellus veniat, legatur, quod reliquū est speculationis vtilitas præstabit. Hoc quic quid est vobis dicare decreui, vt beneficiorū animum meum nunquā immemorem osten- dam vobis, in quibus virtutū singulare exem plar situm esse scio. Beatam rempublicam in qua ad honores tales euehuntur viri. Sed bea tissimam si vos ad magistratus culmen eue- ctos, diu superstites foueat.
units.tr: Most distinguished man Thomas Aldae, most worthy chancellor of all England, the single glory of the English; John Bakeri, most courteous first-fruits of the chancellery, most prudent in the knowledge of the laws of our fathers, most upright balance of the nobility: I have composed these commentaries on the regulation of diet for you; may you protect them by your favour. I know there will be detractors. Yet since speculation is above all of use to men in practice, if it is commended among the English by your favour, the little book will come into people's hands and be read, and the usefulness of the speculation will do the rest. I have decided to dedicate this to you, whatever it is, so that I may show you that my mind is never unmindful of your kindnesses, in which I know a singular example of virtues is set. Happy is the commonwealth in which men of such stature are raised to honours. But most happy will it be if, raised to the summit of the magistracy, you are cherished for a long time while you survive.

units.la: Sed ad reliqua propositi redeo. Obiiciet no bis Anglus medicus illud Hippocratis, Non pura corpora quantumcunque nutries magis lædes: qualiter ergo eos qui ex corruptiõe hu morum laborant adiectione indigere asseri- mus? Praui humores aliquando in ventricu li capacitate continentur, & quandoq; inter eorum tunicas: & eorum aliqui crassi & len ti sunt, aut tenues: quandoque quiescētes ventriculo inhærent, aut mouentur intra eius ca-pacitatem. Hippocrati sermo de iis est humo-ribus, qui in spatio ventriculi, aut in viis per quas commeat cibus, continentur: qui in præ-dictis locis tumultuantes praua qualitate ci-bum nuper aducnientem corrumpunt. Vnde fit vt cibo talia non corroborentur corpora. Nobis verò de iis, qui intra ventriculi tuni-cas crassitie & lentore pigri cōtinentur, ser-mo est. Quorum causa non est quod corpus non nutriatur. Sed aliter dicamus. Posito virium robore in duobus æquali, & paribus cæteris, eorum alter corruptione humorum laboret, alter ex multitudine eorum qui lau-dabiles sunt. Cui nam eorum plus cibi conce-das. Ego quidem sentio cum Galeno, corpus humorum laudabilium multitudine graua-tum, multum inuari inedia, aut modico cibo: alterum verò ex his deteriorem fieri. Nam corruptorum humorum praua qualitas na-turæ vires dissoluit. Quare inediam si his aut tenuem victum iniungas, multum profecto imbecilliorem reddes. Quia tamen euenire potest, ut ob prauam humorum qualitatem ci bus corrumpatur, præsertim cum in vijs cibi fuerit, adhibere purgationem consulit, ante quam reficienti victu conualescentium corpora nutriamus Hippocrates: et causam reddens quare corpora eorū qui cibum assumpse runt non corroborentur, ait, quod eorū corpora nō pura sint, vacuationeque indigeant, vt corpus sumpto cibo corroboretur. Nobis verò in præsenti de ijs sermo est, qui intra ventriculum diu inhærentes nutritioni corporis non obstant: Quod ex eo manifestū est, quoniam non obstante humore ventriculi, ex cibo & potu inuantur. Quod argumentū est, aut humores intra tunicas vētriculi esse, cibum aduenientem non tangentes (cui adhæreo sententiæ) aut si capacitate ventriculi sint, ob eorum pigram crassitiem & lentorem haudquaquam posse aduenientem cibum multum inficere. Corruptio igitur humorum non indicat inanitionem, vt arbitratus est Oribasius in expositione Aph. corpora non pura & c. sed potius cibi adiectionem, vt manifestè à Galeno scriptũ est in fine dicti Apho. Quibus semel aut bis. Autumno verò (inquit) morbi qui ex corruptione fiunt assi-milantur. Quapropter qui eo febricitant tempore continua optimi indigent adiectione, et si vires valide fuerint sæpe & multa: si ve-rò imbecilles pauca & sæpius afferemus. An glis igitur cum humores ÿ qui ventriculis eo-rum inhærent et crassi sint & lenti, aut in-ter ambas ventris tunicas collecti, aut certè quiescentes, non est quod tenuis victus minì-stretur. Quinimmò danda est opera, ut cum huiusmodi corpora febre detinentur, aut alio morbo, vires eorum quoad fieri possit serue-mus. Ut natura multitudinem humorum ma-nuteneat. Si enim ob imbecillitatem imbecil-liter eis dominetur, facilè in eis febrilis con-cipitur calor, ob pravam eorum qualitatem. Unde fit ut præter propriam morbi materi-am, aliam denuò morbificam causam suppe-ditet ventriculus, prima multo tenaciorem & sæuiorem. Cautè ergo cum ijs agendum molliterque tractanda sunt huiusmodi corpora, & crassiori victu quàm pro morbi ra tione sunt alenda. Euacuatio etiam talis adhi benda his est, vt propriam morbi materiam solum respiciat, incommodis ijs qui in ven-triculo commorantur humoribus. Hos enim securius bona valitudine tractabit medicus.
units.tr: But I return to the rest of my purpose. The English physician will object to me that saying of Hippocrates: "You will harm pure bodies more, however much you nourish them." Why then do we say that those who suffer from a corruption of humours need addition? Bad humours are sometimes contained within the capacity of the stomach, and sometimes between its coats; some of them are thick and sluggish, or thin; sometimes they lie fixed in the stomach, sometimes they move within its capacity. The saying of Hippocrates concerns those humours which are contained in the space of the stomach, or in the passages through which food travels; humours which, stirring up tumult in those places with their bad quality, corrupt the food that has lately arrived. Hence bodies are not strengthened by food of this kind. But our discussion concerns those humours which lie sluggish within the coats of the stomach through thickness and viscidity, and which do not hinder the nourishment of the body. The reason is not that the body is not nourished. But let us put it differently. Granting equal strength of powers in two men, and other things being equal, let one of them suffer from a corruption of humours and the other from a multitude of those that are laudable. To which of them would you give more food? I, for my part, agree with Galen that a body burdened by a multitude of laudable humours is greatly helped by fasting or a small diet; but the other becomes worse from these. For the bad quality of corrupt humours dissolves the powers of nature. Hence if you enjoin fasting or a thin diet on these men, you will certainly make them much weaker. Yet because it can happen that food is corrupted by the bad quality of the humours, especially when it is in the passages, Hippocrates advises employing purgation before we nourish the bodies of convalescents with a restoring diet; and giving the reason why the bodies of those who have taken food are not strengthened, he says that their bodies are not pure and need evacuation, so that the body may be strengthened by the food taken. But in the present case our discussion concerns those who, lying long in the stomach, do not hinder the nutrition of the body. This is clear from the fact that, despite the humour of the stomach, they are helped by food and drink. This argues either that the humours lie between the coats of the stomach without touching the food that arrives (to which opinion I adhere), or, if they are in the capacity of the stomach, that because of their sluggish thickness and viscidity they cannot greatly contaminate the food that arrives. Therefore the corruption of humours does not indicate emptying, as Oribasius thought in his commentary on the aphorism "bodies not pure, etc.," but rather an addition of food, as Galen clearly wrote at the end of the aforementioned aphorism, "For those who are sick once or twice." "In autumn (he says) the diseases that arise from corruption are similar." Wherefore those who run a fever at that time need a continual and very good addition; if their powers are strong, often and much; but if they are weak, we shall offer few things and more often. So for the English, when the humours that lie in their stomachs are thick and sluggish, or collected between the two coats of the belly, or at any rate quiescent, there is no reason for a thin diet to be administered. Rather, care must be taken that when bodies of this kind are held by fever or another disease, we preserve their strength as far as can be done, so that nature maintains the multitude of humours. For if from weakness it weakly dominates them, a febrile heat is easily conceived in them because of their bad quality. Hence it comes about that the stomach, besides the proper matter of the disease, supplies another disease-causing cause, far more tenacious and fiercer than the first. Such bodies must therefore be handled with caution and gently, and nourished with a richer diet than the course of the disease requires. Evacuation too should be applied to them in such a way that it looks only to the proper matter of the disease, and not to the inconveniences of the humours that linger in the stomach. For the physician will treat these more safely in good health.

units.la: Hoc meo discrimine didici, crassiori victu huiusmodi corpora alere, & leuiusculis pur-gationibus subducere, in quorum ventriculis multitudo frigidorum humorum diu conge-sta est: semper diligenter præcauens ne qui in ventriculo sunt humores morbosam affectio-nem concipiant. Tribus ergo indicationibus in crasso victu consentientibus, iudicas An-glum exiguo & magis tenui victu, posito morbi acumine æquali nutriendũ, quàm His-spanum aut Italum? Ego quidem arbitror crassiori & ampliori cibo Anglos indigere, scioque optimos quosque medicos probatu-ros sententiam meam. Nam nullam mihi le-gitimam reddes rationem ob quam causam magis tenui cibo, & eius minori copia ægro tantes Anglos nutrias, posito æquali morbi acumine, quàm Hispani medici ægrotantes Hispanos, aut Itali Italos, qui alioquin magis tenui indigerent, tum ob calidam regionem, tum maximè ob id quod parcius secunda viuunt valetudine. Manifestum igitur est hunc victum Anglis virium esse detrimentum & labefactationem maximam. Nec illa iusta errandi occasio est, ob fugiendâ mutationem in victu, febricitantium robur simplici iure multis diebus absumere. Profectò grauior error est, quo naturæ vires exoluimus, quàm quo morbo fomenta ministramus æque vrgentibus virtute & morbo.
units.tr: From my own experience I have learned to feed bodies of this kind with a thicker diet, and to draw them off with mild purgings, in whose stomachs a multitude of cold humours has long been gathered; always taking careful precaution that the humours in the stomach do not take on a morbid condition. So, with the three indications agreeing in favour of a thick diet, do you judge that an Englishman, with the sharpness of the disease equal, should be nourished on a small and more slender diet than a Spaniard or an Italian? I for my part think the English need a thicker and more ample food, and I know that all the best physicians will approve my opinion. For you will give me no legitimate reason why, with the sharpness of the disease equal, you should nourish sick Englishmen on a more slender diet and in smaller quantity than Spanish physicians nourish sick Spaniards, or Italian physicians sick Italians, who otherwise would need a more slender diet, both because of the hot climate and above all because they live more sparingly in good health. It is therefore evident that this diet is a great detriment and weakening of strength for the English. Nor is it a just occasion for error, in order to avoid a change in diet, to use up the strength of feverish patients for many days on plain broth. Indeed it is a graver error by which we dissipate the powers of nature than that by which we administer remedies to the disease when both virtue and disease are equally pressing.

units.la: Nec omnem damnauit Hippocrates mutationem quæ in victus ratione apud ægrotantes fit, sed solum repentinam & disproportionalem, vt in superioribus dictum est. At tenui igitur victu ægrotantes Angli grauiter læduntur: cuius argumentum est sudores qui non raro his, per febres circa caput & collum accidunt. Quorum causa præcipua, virium est imbecillitas & non morbi acumen. Nam & huiusmodi sudores in acuta ægritudine & in mitiori contingere solent: vt ab Hippocrate scriptum est cum de sudoribus qui circa caput & vultum & ceruicem fiunt, loquitur, quos in acuta ægritudine & mitiori posse contingere ait. Imbecillitas virtutis ergo est quæ præcipuè hos operatur sudores, & non morbi acumen. Anglis igitur hos crebrius per morbos accidere, quàm sibi vicinis Gallis, Hispanis, aut Italis, à duabus causis, nempe ob victus tenuitatem, & eò quod cubiculis aërem velut carcere occludunt, euenire putandum est. Tenui siquidem victu citò labuntur corpora multo cibo assueta.
units.tr: Nor did Hippocrates condemn every change that is made in the diet of the sick, but only a sudden and disproportionate one, as was said above. But the English who are sick on a slender diet are grievously harmed: the proof of this is the sweats which not rarely occur in fevers around the head and neck. The chief cause of these is weakness of strength, and not the sharpness of the disease. For sweats of this kind are wont to occur both in acute illness and in a milder one, as Hippocrates wrote when he spoke of the sweats that occur about the head, face and neck, which he says can occur in acute illness and in a milder one. It is therefore the weakness of strength that chiefly produces these sweats, and not the sharpness of the disease. That these occur more often in the English during illnesses than in their neighbours the French, Spanish or Italians, we must think arises from two causes, namely the slenderness of their diet, and because they shut out the air in their bedchambers as if in a prison. For bodies accustomed to much food quickly fail on a slender diet.

units.la: BRVDI LVSITANI DE VICTV FEBRICITANTIVM AD ANGLOS, LIBER TERTIUS: qui singulis febribus conuenientem victum inuestigat, deinde victus rationem secundum symptomatum naturā præscribit.
units.tr: THE BOOK OF BRUDUS THE LUSITANIAN ON THE DIET OF FEVER-SUFFERERS, ADDRESSED TO THE ENGLISH, BOOK THREE: which seeks out the suitable diet for each fever and then prescribes the regimen of diet according to the nature of the symptoms.

units.la: Causo legitimo quis uictus competat.
units.tr: Which diet is suitable for which cause.

units.la: CAPVT I.
units.tr: CHAPTER I.

units.la: ED Tempestiuū est vt de victu agamus qui singulis febribus conueniat. Exemplis siquidem manuducere lectorem oportet, vt facilis fiat sermo. Causus cum a biliosò ortum habet humore, si cum robore virium adsit & æger talis sit habitu vt non facilè exoluatur, potu nutriatur, vt dictum est. Hordeum mediocris ætatis, plenum, album, exutumque ab vtroque cortice coquito in aquæ fontis, quæ aut coctione aut lōga mora resi-dentiam fecerit. Sitque hordei pars vna, aquæ partes viginti. Bulliat tandiu vt infletur hordeum & rumpatur. Colatu propina cum opus fuerit. Hic potus erit ægrotantis viclus. Quod si sitim non sedat: præparato eundem potum, & hora vna antequam ab igne amoueas recentes violas mediocris magnitudinis insimul coquito, à colatura parum zucari misceto. Eligito pruna quorum sapor medius sit inter dulcem & acetosum, ita vt nulla participent adstrictione. Coquantur quoque in aqua quæ prius per se ante ebullierit, sitque prunorum pars vna, quæ partes duodecim, coquantur tandiu vt pruna tumescentia rum pantur. In eadem testa qua cocta sunt potum seruato. Dato cum modico zucari vbi oportet. Aquam per se coquito ad tertias, cumque subsidentiam fecerit, ad aliudque vas colatam effuderis, syrupi acetosi imbecillioris partem vnam, aquæ partes quindecim misce to ad lentum ignem, spumam auferendo, tandiu vt permisceantur adinuicem. Quia vero non omnibus vna placet mixtio, consulto ægrotantis palato prædictum syrupum magis aut
units.tr: It is now the right time to discuss the diet suited to each fever. For examples must guide the reader, so that the discussion becomes easy to follow. When a causus arises from a bilious humour, and the patient still has strength and is of such a habit that he is not easily worn out, he is to be nourished with drink, as has been said. Boil barley of medium age, full, white, and stripped of both husks, in spring water that has been left to settle either by boiling or by long standing. Use one part barley to twenty parts water. Let it boil until the barley swells and bursts. Strain it and give it to drink when needed. This drink will be the patient's diet. But if it does not quench his thirst, prepare the same drink, and an hour before you take it off the fire, boil fresh violets of medium size in it together, and add a little sugar to the strained liquor. Choose plums whose flavour lies midway between sweet and sour, so that they have no astringency. Let them also be boiled in water that has first been boiled by itself, using one part plums to twelve parts water, and boil them until the plums swell and burst. Keep the drink in the same pot in which it was cooked. Give it with a little sugar where appropriate. Boil the water by itself down to two-thirds, and when it has settled, pour it off strained into another vessel. Mix one part of a fairly weak sour syrup with fifteen parts of this water over a slow fire, skimming off the foam, until they are thoroughly blended. But since one mixture does not please everyone, consult the patient's palate and adjust the aforesaid syrup to be more

units.la: Aqua hordei cū uirtute uiolarum.
units.tr: Barley water with the virtue of violets.

units.la: Decoctū prunorū.
units.tr: Decoction of plums.

units.la: Potus acetosus.
units.tr: Sour drink.

units.la: aut minus acrem efficito, plus aut minus aquæ miscens. Idem cum syrupo violarum effi cies, si tibi commodum videbitur aut aliys.
units.tr: or less sharp, adding more or less water. You will make the same with syrup of violets, if it seems convenient to you or to others.

units.la: Quod si de viribus ægrotantis non fidas, ut solo potu perdurare possit ad crisis horâ, aut et si in præsenti vires consistent, nihilomi nus times futuram imbecillitatem, aut quia homo raro habitu est, aut consuetus alioquin multum ingerere, horum utrique talem exhibebis victum. Aquam hordei, ut suprà, parato, tandiuque hordeum coquito ut rumpa tur, linteo raro hordeum suscipito, fortiterque exprimito, ita ut totam hordei medullâ exire facias, hanc multa aqua hordei misceto ut tenuis fiat sorbitio, et cum pauco zucaro exhibeto. Syrupi acetosi acris (acidi) si tantum misceas, ut aliquid acetosi habeat iam dicta sorbitio, faciasque ut modicum bulliat, optimum cibum huic febri efficies. Idem cum prunis efficere possis. Mica panis mediocris ætatis à furfure synceri ad parvulas partes radito, in aquam infundito frigidam, digitisque confricato, terque aquam innouato, deinde coquito in aqua hordei violacea, cunque vtrunque permixtum fuerit, infunde succigra natorum acetosorum & zucari singulorum tantum vt aegrotantis palato placeat, iterū coquito vt misceantur, fac valdè tenuem sorbitionem multa aqua panem diluens, quam ijs dabis, quorum virtutes ob imbecillitatem parum vrgent. Hippocrates de curatione huius febris agens, aquæ mulsæ coctæ et aquo sæ, quantū æger voluerit, concedit: hocq; potu ægrotantem ad crisis horā ducit. quod manifestum est ex eo quod in hunc modum scribit: Et sorbitiones (inquit) nisi dies indicatorij transierint non dabis. Subaudies cum Galeno, si virtus ægrotantis robusta esse videatur. Zucarum vsum melius præstat. Efficacio rem tamen virtutem mel habet. Zucarū vtpote temperatius ad causi curationem magis probandum. Antiquorum ætas eo carebat, & si saccharum tunc non deesset.
units.tr: But if you do not trust the patient's strength to hold out on drink alone until the crisis hour, or if, although his strength is sound at present, you still fear future weakness, either because the man is of a spare habit or because he is accustomed to eating a great deal, you will prescribe a diet of the following kind for either case. Prepare barley water as above, and boil the barley until it bursts. Strain the barley through a loose linen cloth and press it firmly, so that all the marrow of the barley comes out. Mix this with a large quantity of barley water, so that it becomes a thin gruel, and give it with a little sugar. If you add enough sour syrup (acid) that the aforesaid gruel has some sourness, and bring it to a gentle boil, you will have made an excellent food for this fever. You can do the same with plums. Take a crumb of medium-aged bread, free of bran, and scrape it into small pieces. Pour it into cold water, rub it with your fingers, and change the water three times. Then boil it in violet barley water, and when the two are mixed, add the juice of sour fruits and a little sugar, just enough to please the patient's palate. Boil again so that they mix, and make a very thin gruel by dissolving the bread in plenty of water. Give this to those whose strength is little pressed because of weakness. Hippocrates, when treating the cure of this fever, permits barley water boiled and strained, as much as the patient wishes, and by this drink he leads the patient to the crisis hour. This is clear from what he writes in this way: "And you will not give gruels (he says) until the critical days have passed." You must understand, with Galen, that this applies if the patient's strength seems robust. Sugar is the better choice for use. Honey, however, has greater efficacy and virtue. Sugar, being the milder, is more to be commended for the cure of causus. The age of the ancients lacked it, although sugar was not then unavailable.

units.la: Causo notho seu spurio conueniens ui ctus qui sit.
units.tr: What diet suits a notho, or spurious, causus.

units.la: CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: QVOD si causus à materia pituitosa salsa fuerit, crassiori victu alendi sunt aegrotantes, nempe sorbitione tenui. Potus non erit ijs victus idoneus. Quare sorbitionibus in hunc modum, veteris, si virium adfuerit robur, habitusque talis sit ut non facile corpus effluat, parceque sit assuetus viuere secunda valitudine. Sorbitionem ex hordei medulla cum syrupo acetoso, eo quo supra dictum est modo, praeparato. Acrem ptisanae sorbitionem appellauimus, administra vbi oportet. Eam insuper sorbitionem quam ex mica panis ter loti scripsimus, acetosam panatellam diximus, praeparabis, addito loco succi granatorum syrupo acetoso acri: hunc dico qui plus aceti recipit. Hunc victui intellige ijs conuenire qui maligno cau so non laborant. Discernitur cum malignus est, ex assidua extremorum frigiditate, de ijs infra agemus. Iis ergo qui causo a pituita sal sa laborant, sorbitionem dato ex hordeo aut pane modo praedicto bona syrupi acetosi quā titate iniecta, ita vt palato effatu dignam offerat repræsentationem. Quod si facultas imbecillis fuerit, aut futuræ imbecillitatis suspicionem præstet corporis habitus, aut consuetudo, aut si alvus ab initio liquida fuerit corpus absumens (hoc enim symptomate solo posito, virtutem multum urgere supra diximus) talis commodus fuerit victus. Pullum gallinaceum qui matrem insequitur pinguem coquito ad lentum ignem recenti testa, prunorum & hordei præparati quantum singulorum manu capi possit, aquam sufficientem infundito, mali deinde granati acidi grana quantum manu capere possis proijce media hora antequam pullum ab igne moveas. Sunt qui tandiu pullum ad ignem coquunt donec hordeum rumpatur. Huius decocti portionem servato ut ægrotanti exhibeas, cum tibi opportunum videbitur, ex residuo decocto cum pane in aqua frigida ter infuso sorbitionem facito. Dato quando oportet ei cui alvus liquida fuerit. Cæterum scire oportet causam cum a salsa pituita generatur, si cum alvo ab initio perturbata fiat vires naturæ multum absumere. Quapropter victu crassiori eos in digere qui huiusmodi causo laborant, praesertim si habitu sint raro & assueti multū edere. Natura siquidem huiusmodi causo laborantis symptomatum prauitate, & humoris contumaci resistentia coctrici facultati repugnantis, exoluitur.
units.tr: BECAUSE if the causus arises from salty phlegm, patients must be nourished with a thicker diet, namely thin gruel. Drink is not a suitable diet for them. Therefore, with gruels of this kind, provided the strength is firm and the habit of body is such that the body does not waste easily, and the patient is accustomed to live on a moderate diet, make the gruel from barley marrow with sour syrup, prepared in the way described above. We have called this the sharp ptisan gruel; administer it where appropriate. Moreover, the gruel that we described above as made from bread washed three times, we called acidic panatella; you will prepare it by adding a little juice of pomegranates, with sharp sour syrup. I mean the kind that takes more vinegar. Understand that this diet suits those who do not suffer from a malignant cause. Whether the cause is malignant is discerned from constant coldness of the extremities, which we shall discuss below. For those, then, who suffer from a causus of salty phlegm, give a gruel of barley or bread prepared as described, with a good measure of sour syrup added, so that it presents a dish worthy of the palate. But if the patient's strength is weak, or the habit of the body or his custom gives suspicion of future weakness, or if the bowels were loose from the start, consuming the body (for, as we said above, when this symptom alone is present, it strongly presses on the strength), then the following diet will be suitable. Cook a fat chick that follows its mother, in a fresh pot, over a slow fire, with as much prepared plums and barley as can be held in each hand, and pour in enough water. Then throw in as many grains of sour pomegranate as you can hold in your hand, half an hour before you move the chick from the fire. Some cook the chick over the fire until the barley bursts. Keep a portion of this decoction to give the patient when you judge it fitting, and from the rest of the decoction, with bread steeped three times in cold water, make a gruel. Give it when it is needed, to one whose bowels are loose. Moreover, one must know that when the causus is generated from salty phlegm, if the bowels are disturbed from the start, it consumes the strength of nature greatly. Therefore, put those who suffer from this kind of causus on a thicker diet, especially if they are of a spare habit and accustomed to eating much. For nature, when afflicted by the malignity of the symptoms of such a causus, and by the stubborn resistance of the humour opposing the concocting faculty, is dissolved.

units.la: Quid Hippocrates per attractorias intelligat sorbitiones.
units.tr: What Hippocrates means by attractive gruels.

units.la: CAPVT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: HIPPOCRATES iubet attractori bus exhiberi sorbitiones. Sed quid sibi velit per illud verbum attractorias, dicere non facile est. Praecipuè cum Galenus, verbum absque interpretatione reliquerit. Graece ita habetur, Ὑποφύματα ἐπιταχσικὰ δίδω. Hoc est sorbitiones superattractorias. ἐπιταχσικὰ composita dictio est à praepositione ἐπί, cuius officium est dictionis significato aliquando aliquid addere: ut Hippocrati infra, Ἡ ἀλλαπαγὼ ἐοντι ἀκῶς & ἐπιγρήντς, hoc est causus superueniat. Aliquando idem valet quod apud Latinos In, ut cum idem ait τὸ ἐξωθὲν πνεῦμα ἐπάγειν, hoc est exteriorem spiritum inducere. Vult Hippocrates ut sorbitiones attrahentipharmaco misceamus. Pharmacum enim sorbitione mixtum, melius nuncupare non potuit, nomen ab utroque simplici compositum efficies, nempe sorbitiones attractorias. Quod autem antiquioribus consuetum fuerit medicis, in sorbitionibus pharmaca miscere, manifestum est ei qui antiquorum scripta evolverit. Ipse etiam Galenus in phlegmones iocinoris curatione, cortice elleboriin ptisana, mercuriali, & filicula utitur. Idque non vulgare praeceptum est in vehementi febre aut maligna: Nempe cum purgatio admodum sit necessaria, timeatque medicus inualidis aegrotantis viribus, consulte aget ut cum pharmaco uti velit, id simul cum sorbitione aegrotanti offerat. Sic enim pharmacum minus commouebit, minusque calfaciet & exicCabit, quae omnia in vehementi febre aut maligna ne fiant, diligenter obseruandum est. Pharmacum praeterea ita exhibitum vires naturae minus nus exoluit. In maligna febre aut pestilenti optimus fuerit exhibendi pharmaci modus, quo nullus alius certior, minoriq; humani ge neris damno. Id ita esse intelliges si Galeni sen tentiæ sis memor, in expositione Aphorismi Quibuscunque crisis fit, vbi plures iudicatio nes ad bonum terminari vidisse ait. Nouimus »» (inquit) ipse plures esse ex ægrotis sanatos »» quàm mortuos, nisi pestilens sit constitutio. »» In iudicatione autem natura tristantes chy- mos ad expulsionem commouet. In qua qui- dem commotione natura solet in pluribus vi Ætrix exire, nisi cũ pestilens morbus fuerit. Cauendum ergo, quæ humorem pestilentem pura pharmaca commoueant, offerre. Ab vtroque enim & à pestilenti humore & à pharmaco ægrotantis robur absumitur. Quod si pharmacum cum sorbitione misce- as, ab vtriusque ictu naturam magis serua- bis, eique simul materiam vnde sibi arma mi nistret suppeditabis. Prudentissimè igitur Hip pocrates in maligni causi curatione sorbitio nes attractorias ministrare iubet. Quod autem in causi curatione pharmacum purgans aliquando exhibere oporteat, ipsemet docuit eodem libro in haec verba: Si liquidam aluum habenti causas superueniat, si tibi videatur purgatio necessaria, intra dies tres non purgabis, sed quarto. Sermonis consequentia huc me adduxit, ut de administrandi pharmacimodo dissererem. alibi enim de pharmacorum administrandorum methodo latius agemus, vbi quale, quantum, quando, & quibus exhiberi debeat pharmacum, inuestigabimus.
units.tr: HIPPOCRATES orders sorbitions to be given to the attractives. But it is not easy to say what he means by the word attractorias, especially since Galen left the word without explanation. In Greek the passage reads "Ὑποφύματα ἐπιταχσικὰ δίδω" [Ὑποφύματα ἐπιταχσικὰ δίδω], that is, I give superattractive sorbitions. The word ἐπιταχσικὰ is a compound of the preposition ἐπί, whose office is sometimes to add something to the meaning of the word, as Hippocrates says later, "Ἡ ἀλλαπαγὼ ἐοντι ἀκῶς & ἐπιγρήντς" [Ἡ ἀλλαπαγὼ ἐοντι ἀκῶς & ἐπιγρήντς], that is, if a cause supervene. Sometimes it has the same force as In in Latin, as when he says "τὸ ἐξωθὲν πνεῦμα ἐπάγειν" [τὸ ἐξωθὲν πνεῦμα ἐπάγειν], that is, to induce the external spirit. Hippocrates wants us to mix an attractive medicine into the sorbitions. For he could not have named a mixture of a medicine with a sorbition better, and you will form the name from both simple words, namely attractive sorbitions. That it was customary for the older physicians to mix medicines into sorbitions is plain to anyone who has read through the writings of the ancients. Galen himself, in treating inflammation of the liver, uses hellebore bark in barley-water, with mercurial and fern. And this is no common precept in a violent or malignant fever. Since purgation is very necessary, and the physician fears for the weakened strength of the patient, he will act wisely if he wishes to use a medicine and offers it to the patient together with a sorbition. For in this way the medicine will disturb less, heat and dry less, and all these things must be carefully guarded against in a violent or malignant fever. Moreover, a medicine given in this way uses up the strength of nature less. In a malignant or pestilential fever the best method of giving a medicine is one than which none is surer, and which does least harm to the human race. You will understand that this is so if you remember Galen's opinion, in his exposition of the aphorism "Quibuscunque crisis fit," where he says he has seen more judgements end well. "We know," he says, "that more of the sick are cured than die, unless the constitution is pestilential." In judgement, nature stirs the offending humours toward expulsion. In that stirring, nature usually, in most cases, comes out as a victor, unless the disease is pestilential. Therefore one must take care not to offer medicines that stir a pestilential humour in its pure state. For the strength of the patient is consumed by both the pestilential humour and the medicine. But if you mix the medicine with a sorbition, you will protect nature better from the blow of each, and you will supply at the same time the material from which it may furnish itself with weapons. Hippocrates, therefore, most wisely orders that attractive sorbitions be administered in the treatment of a malignant cause. That in treating a cause it is sometimes right to give a purgative medicine, he himself taught in the same book in these words: "If a cause supervenes on one who has a loose bowel, and purgation seems necessary to you, you shall not purge within three days, but on the fourth." The sequence of my discourse has led me to speak of the manner of administering the medicine. For we shall treat more fully of the method of administering medicines elsewhere, where we shall inquire what, how much, when, and to whom a medicine ought to be given.

units.la: Victus quos recentiores medici tradidêre, causo non conuenire ostendit.
units.tr: The diets which recent physicians have handed down, he shows, do not suit the cause.

units.la: CAPVT IIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER IIII.

units.la: NVNC ad sermonē reuertamur. E nostris medicis nonnulli medullam cucumeris, citrulli: alij lactucam, portulacam: alij lac amygdalarum, aliqui scariolam cum aceto, aut agresta, vel succo berberorum, aut acetositate citri, vtrisque causo concedunt. Sed quantum astringentia aduersa sunt legitimo timo causo:tantum frigida potentia, notho. Quod ex hoc maximè intelliges. Legitimus causus fluxu sanguinis aut sudore soluitur, vt ab Hippocrate discimus: Quæ autem potentia nimis frigida sunt, tum ea quæ astrin-gunt, vtrique obstat terminationi. Quod no tho seu non vero causo non conueniat ea quæ potentia valde sunt frigida, ratione manifestum fit. Humor siquidem huius febris difficilis coctionis est, idque maximè ob id quod frigida glutinosa & crassa pituita sit, quæ hac febre generat. Quapropter abscessu solet hæc febris terminari, vt à Galeno scriptum est. Quare omnia quæ potentia frigida valde sunt huic febri incommoda esse quinis percipiat: Quod Rasis in hæc verba asseruit: Et pone (in quit) in cibarijs (scilicet in non pura) res calefacientes & subtiliantes. Quid igitur prudens lector de illo sentis, qui camphorâ cum aquarosarum dissoluens, laboranti causo exhibet? At quæ astringunt nisi symptomatis gratia exhibita, vtrunque causum perniciosum aut dyscritum efficiunt. De causi vtraq; specie satis sint dicta. Qui uictus synochis febribus competat.
units.tr: Now let us return to our discussion. Some of our physicians allow the marrow of cucumber or melon to patients with causus, others lettuce and purslane, others almond milk, some endive with vinegar, or verjuice, or barberry juice, or the sourness of citron; they allow these for both kinds of causus. But just as astringents are harmful to the legitimate causus, so cold potency is harmful to the spurious one. You will understand this most clearly from the following. The legitimate causus is resolved by a flow of blood or by sweat, as we learn from Hippocrates. Things of excessively cold power, and especially astringent ones, hinder the termination of both kinds. That foods of very cold power are unsuitable for a spurious or false causus is plain from reasoning. For the humour of this difficult fever is hard to concoct, chiefly because it is a cold, glutinous and thick phlegm, which this fever generates. Therefore this fever usually ends in an abscess, as Galen has written. Hence all things of very cold power are seen to be unsuitable for this fever. Rhazes asserted this in these words: "And put (he says) into the foods (namely the non-pure ones) heating and thinning things." What then, prudent reader, do you think of the man who dissolves camphor in rosewater and gives it to a patient with causus? But astringents, unless given for the sake of a symptom, make either kind of causus pernicious or dyscritical. Enough has been said about both kinds of causus. Now let us consider which diet suits synochus fevers.

units.la: CAPVT V.
units.tr: CHAPTER V.

units.la: VTriusque synochi victus forma, similis est ei, quam causo conuenire diximus. Cum enim vterque synochus febris sit nullas habens intermissiones, indicat aegrotantem potu fore nutriendum. Et quia haec febris raro accidit cum imbecilli facultate, aut calido & sicco temperamento, neq; habitu raro, ob id solum in hac febre de consuetudine quaeremus. Quem ergo aegrotante par ce viuere in bona valitudine scieris, solo potu tu nutrire oportet. Aquam igitur hordei ut suprà paratõ, cuius accipito partes decem, syrupi acetosi acrioris partem vnam, misceto simul ad lentum ignem, dato vbi oportet. Bonu est hordeum à primo solum exuere cortice. nã ab vtroq; exutum, magis humectat & minus absterget.
units.tr: The form of diet for either synochus is similar to that which we said suits causus. For since each synochus is a fever without any intermissions, it indicates that the patient must be nourished by drink alone. And because this fever rarely occurs with weak faculties, or with a hot and dry temperament, nor with a lean habit, we shall inquire into custom only in this fever. Therefore, whoever you know to be living sparingly in good health must be nourished with drink alone. Take barley water prepared as above, ten parts of it, and one part of sharp acetous syrup; mix together over a slow fire and give when needed. It is good to strip the barley of its first husk only, for barley stripped of both moistens more and wipes away less.

units.la: Ad synochu absq; putredine. Antequam aquã hordei ab igne amoueris hora vna mali granati acidi grana secundum quantitatem hordei proiicito, zucari purissimi quantum satis, coquito spumam auferendo, ad lentum ignem exhibeto ægrotanti quando oportuerit. Commodissimus huic febri est potus.
units.tr: For synochus without putrefaction. An hour before you take the barley water off the fire, throw in the grains of a sour pomegranate in proportion to the amount of barley, with as much of the purest sugar as is enough. Boil, skimming off the foam, and give it to the patient over a slow fire when it is needed. This drink is most suitable for this fever.

units.la: Ad putrescentem synochum.
units.tr: For putrescent synochus.

units.la: Hordeum ablato uno cortice coquito in aqua ut dictū est, antequā ab igne amoueas hora una, polytrichi aut capillorum veneris non vetustioris uno mense, acetosæ herbæ, proïcito singulorum quantū manu capi possit. Transfacta hora, remoue herbas quas filo collegeris & proïcito syrupi acetosi acrioris quantum vi debitur, dato vbi oportet, postquā ad lentum ignem probè mixta fuerint. Obseruandū tamen est, ante missionē sanguinis, aut ventris subductionē, aut clysterū bono temporis interuallo exhibendam non esse aquā hordei ut discimus ab Hippocrate. Non prætermittendū est, synochū à putredine paulo solidiorem exigere victū. Nam dispositio ex corruptione humorum, indicat ciborum adiectionē, ut supra ostendimus de mente Galeni in expositione illius, Quibus semel aut bis. Natura insuper citius labitur à febre & à putredine simul innadentibus quàm ex sola febre. Sorbitiunculam igitur tenuem ex hordeo aut pa ne parato in hunc modum: Aquam hordei cū polytricho & acetosa coctam parato, in eius portione dissolue micam panis per horam in aqua endiuiæ infusi. Coquito ad lentum ignē, cunque permixta fuerint infunde syrupi acetosi acrioris quantum in gustatu aperte sentiatur, iterum modicum coquito miscendo. Potus sit aqua hordei cum malo granato acido coĉta, in synocho absque putredine: in eo verò qui cum putredine est, aqua hordei cū polytricho & acetosa cocta.
units.tr: Boil barley with one husk removed in water as said above. An hour before you take it off the fire, add a handful of each of polytrichum or of maidenhair (not more than a month old) and of sorrel, as much as can be held in the hand. When the hour has passed, remove the herbs you have gathered with a thread, and add as much sharp acetous syrup as the strength requires. Give it when needed, after it has been well mixed over a slow fire. It must be noted, however, that barley water should not be given before bloodletting, or purging of the bowels, or enemas, for a good interval of time, as we learn from Hippocrates. It must not be omitted that synochus with putrefaction requires a somewhat more solid diet. For the condition arising from corrupt humours indicates the addition of food, as we showed above, following Galen's meaning in the exposition of the aphorism "Those who once or twice..." Moreover, nature falls away more quickly from a fever and putrefaction floating together than from fever alone. Therefore prepare a thin little gruel of barley or bread in this way: prepare barley water boiled with polytrichum and sorrel, and in a portion of it dissolve a crumb of bread that has been soaked for an hour in endive water. Boil over a slow fire, and when they are well mixed, add sharp acetous syrup to the extent that its taste is clearly perceived, and boil again briefly, stirring. The drink for synochus without putrefaction should be barley water boiled with sour pomegranate; for that which is accompanied by putrefaction, barley water boiled with polytrichum and sorrel.

units.la: Inconuenientes esse uictus synochis quos recentiores medici tradunt.
units.tr: That the diets which recent physicians hand down for synochus are unsuitable.

units.la: CAPVT VI.
units.tr: CHAPTER VI.

units.la: NOSTRI iuniores medici, cibos ex cucurbitis, spinachis, lactucis, portulacæ virgulis, citrulli medulla coficiunt. Hos victus in continentibus febribus reprobandos fore, vna ratione ante ostendi. Hæ quidē febres cum valdè acutæ sint, natura eas diu ferre ferre non potest, cito enim fit crisis qua aut natura vincit, aut vincitur, vt scripsit Galenus primo ad Glauconem. Summa ergo diligentia curare medicus debet, ne aut humores aut corporis vias ad crisim indisponat.
units.tr: Our younger physicians prepare foods from gourds, spinach, lettuce, shoots of purslane, and the pulp of melons. I have already shown, on one principle, that these diets should be rejected in continuous fevers. Since these fevers are very acute, nature cannot bear them for long, for a crisis comes quickly, in which nature either wins or is overcome, as Galen wrote in the first book to Glaucon. The physician must therefore take the greatest care not to disorder the humours or the bodily passages before the crisis.

units.la: Victus autem ex frigidis herbis potius effice re hoc valent, quàm humoris igneam qualitatem refringere, aut sitim aegrotantis sedare, quæ alioquin magna aquæ frigidæ quantitate vno hausta ebibita vix sedatur. In continentibus igitur febribus verendum est ne victus ex huiusmodi valde refrigerantibus herbis aut mortem aut prauam crisim inducant, ad fluxum sanguinis e naribus, & ad sudores corpus laborantis, & humores simul indisponendo. Est qui iuiubas, & lentes cum aceto & cum granatis & sumachijs concedat quando intentio esset ingrossare sanguinem, aut quando natura esset nimis mollis. Et subdit, Et si sit aliquod horum per quæ constrictio timeatur, scilicet ne ventre strin gat, frangatur eius constrictio cum siracost, & prunis, & cibetur tunc cum cibo facto
units.tr: Diets made of cold herbs are better suited to producing this effect than to blunting the fiery quality of the humour or quenching the thirst of the sick, which is hardly quenched even when a large quantity of cold water is swallowed at one draught. In continuous fevers, then, one must fear that diets of such strongly cooling herbs may bring on death or a bad crisis, by disordering the body and the humours together, causing a flow of blood from the nose and sweats in the suffering body. Some allow jujubes and lentils with vinegar, and with pomegranates and sumac, when the aim is to thicken the blood, or when the nature is too soft. And he adds: "And if there is any of these things that might cause constriction, namely that it might bind the belly, let its constriction be broken with quince and plums, and then let him be fed with food made of gourd and sorrel."

units.la: Aa de cucurbita, & herba acetosa. Et conuenit olus frigidum factum de acetosa, endiuia, & lactuca. Sed forsan quis contra hæc obiiciet. Quod nam magnæ dignitatis commodum in continenti febre ex sanguinis ingrossatione sequitur, ut eius gratia sumach condimentis miscere ausus fuerit in synocha febre? Videtur tamen duplici de causa id concessisse, nempe aut ingrossationis, aut symptomatis gratia, ut cum aluus liquida præter modum fuerit. An symptomatis occasione concedi debeat, prætermitto. At ingrossandi sanguinis gratia, haud quaquam recte esse opinor. Nā prudentis medici non videtur esse, influxione quæ à toto, aut ab aliqua parte in aliā fit, biliosum sanguinem crassiorem reddere cum ijs, quæ valide astringunt, ne superfluum humorem fluentem in parte aliqua maioris fortasse momenti detineamus. Aut ne id quod in parte affecta est, magis impingamus. In synocha verò febre sanguis feruens in altum tumet, more aquæ ebullientis in olla. Huius feruorem igne non remoto compesces, si igneam igneam qualitatem ab aqua remittas.id effi-cies aut aqua frigida iniecta, aut si os testæ discooperias ut aëris refrigerium capiat. Sic in febre synocha aut potu aquæ frigidæ efferentem humorem compescere oportet: aut conandum est, ut per corporis poros ebullientes chymi libere transpirare possint. Hæc enim via ad salutem certior est. Nam febris remissio ex efferuentium humorum transpiratione fit. Quæ duplici arte fieri potest, nempe cum aut pori totius aperiuntur, aut humores æqualiter minuuntur, ut à Galeno discimus octauo & nono de methodo medendi. Astringentia autem ex quibus unum viribus valens rhus est, quæ recentiores sumach appellant, tantum abest ut perspirationes liberas efficiant, ut eas prohibeant corpora constringendo. Nam è triplici causa prohibitæ transpirationis, una, cōstrictio corporū est. Ex iis igitur manifestum est, rhoëm & cætera astringentia nimis esse cōtinuis febrib. infesta, eo quod transpirationes quæ remissionis febris sunt causa prohibeant. Symptomatis gratia uti possumus iis quae potetia mediocria sunt. Frigidae potus exhiberi potest utrique synocho, sed signum coctionis in eo qui cum putredine est observare oportet. Exhibitio tamen frigidae uno haustu, disputationis nostrae egre ditur limites. non enim ut potus, sed ut medicinalis potio offertur.
units.tr: And a cold dish made of sorrel, endive and lettuce agrees with him. But perhaps someone will object to these things: what great advantage follows in a continuous fever from thickening the blood, that for its sake someone has dared to mix sumac into the seasonings in a synochus fever? Yet it seems that this was allowed for one of two reasons, either for thickening or for the sake of a symptom, as when the bowel is more liquid than usual. Whether it ought to be allowed for the sake of a symptom, I pass over. But for the sake of thickening the blood, I think it is by no means right.
