For it does not seem to be the mark of a prudent physician to make bilious blood thicker with things that bind strongly, by means of an influx that comes from the whole body or from one part into another, lest we detain a superfluous flowing humour in some part of perhaps greater importance, or lest we press further upon what is already affected. In a synochus fever, moreover, the seething blood swells upward, like boiling water in a pot. You will restrain its heat, without removing the fire, if you take away the fiery quality from the water, which you will do either by pouring in cold water or by uncovering the mouth of the pot so that it may take the cooling of the air. So in a synochus fever one must restrain the rising humour either by a drink of cold water, or one must strive to let the boiling humours pass freely through the pores of the body. For this way is the surer path to health. For the remission of the fever comes from the transpiration of the effervescent humours. This can be done in two ways: either when the pores of the whole body are opened, or when the humours are equally diminished, as we learn from Galen in the eighth and ninth books on the method of healing. Astringent things, of which one of the most powerful is rhus, which the more recent writers call sumac, are so far from making transpiration free that they prevent it by constricting the bodies. For of the three causes of prevented transpiration, one is the constriction of the bodies. From these things it is clear that rhus and the other astringents are very harmful in continuous fevers, because they prevent the transpirations which are the cause of the remission of the fever. For the sake of a symptom we may use those things which are of moderate power. A drink of cold water may be given to both synochus patients, but in the one who has putrefaction one must observe the sign of concoction. Yet giving cold water in a single draught goes beyond the limits of our discussion, for it is offered not as a drink but as a medicinal potion.

units.la: Victum tertianae continuae conuenientem inquirit.
units.tr: He inquires into the diet suitable for continuous tertian fever.

units.la: CAPUT VII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VII.

units.la: FEBRIS tertiana continua dupliciter intermittit, aut intermissione quiescunt symptomata, aut solum remittuntur. Sitque primum continua tertiana, in cuius remissione non omnino quiescunt symptomata. Haec sunt capitis dolor, vigilia, sitis magna, delirium, graviter ferre morbum & reliqua. Facultate robusta existente, habitu tali ut non facile corpus in halitus digeratur, si aeger consuetus sit parce viuere, acriptisanae sorbitione ut itor, eo quo supra parauimus modo. Febricitanti panis offam infusi in aqua endiuiae & & succo granati acidi, simulque decem, aut duodecim pruna in aqua tantum percoêta, modico zucari superaspersó superexhibeto.
units.tr: FEVER of the continuous tertian kind intermits in two ways: either the symptoms cease entirely during the intermission, or they are only remitted. Let us take first the continuous tertian, in whose remission the symptoms do not wholly cease. These are headache, wakefulness, great thirst, delirium, bearing the disease with difficulty, and the rest. If the patient has a robust constitution, a habit such that the body is not easily dissipated into vapours, and is accustomed to live sparingly, let him take a barley-water as described above. Give the feverish patient a morsel of bread soaked in water of endive and juice of sour pomegranate, and at the same time ten or twelve plums boiled only in water, with a little sugar sprinkled over, given afterwards.

units.la: Prætereapruno rum acetosorum ad dulcorem accedentium quantum manu capi possit, borraginis recentis à vermibus non tactæ ea dem mensura, hepaticæ quam lichena Dioscorides appellat (Lusitani hepatega, Angli liueruurth) bis tantum, hordei ab utroque cortice exuti, ter(tantum) mundato diligenter à terrestri excremento herbas, coquitoque omnia cum pullis duobus teneræ ætatis crassis admodum, tandiu vt hordeum rumpatur, dato vbi oportet. Conuenientissimus hic cibus fuerit ad omnes febres quæ à putrescente bile ortum habent. Febrilem calorem reprimit qui in iocinere est, facultatem coëtricem iuuat. Quod si facultas imbecillis fuerit, aut habitus rarus, aut multo cibo æger assuetus, crassiorem sorbitionem hordeo expresso multoties in prædictum ius efficito. Aut medulla panis infusi in aqua endiuiæ in idem pulli decoctum dissoluta, sorbitionem conficies magis nutrientem.
units.tr: Besides this, let there be given a quantity of sour plums, approaching sweetness, that can be held in the hand; the same measure of fresh borage not touched by worms; the same of liverwort, which Dioscorides calls lichen (the Portuguese call it hepatega, the English liverwort), only two of these; barley husked of both coverings, three times, after the herbs have been carefully cleansed of earthy filth; and boil all together with two chickens of tender age, quite fat, until the barley bursts, and give it when it is needed. This food will be most suitable for all fevers that arise from putrescent bile. It checks the febrile heat that is in the liver and helps the retentive faculty. But if the strength is feeble, or the habit is lean, or the patient is accustomed to much food, make a thicker drink by pressing barley repeatedly into the aforesaid broth. Or you will make a more nourishing drink by dissolving bread soaked in water of endive into the broth of the same chicken.

units.la: Quod si in intermissionibus quiescunt omnino symptomata, virtute robusta existente, et habitu dura & resolutionis, assuetus q; sit par ce viuere, altera duarum sorbitionum pulli dicto modo temperati febricitantem alito. Panemque in aqua endiuiæ & succo granato rum infusum superexhibeto. Quod si facultas debilis, aut habitus rarus facilis resolutionis, aut multum edere assuetus sit, febricitantem altera sorbitionum iam dictarum, & pulli extremitatibus alito, pane similiter infuso. Quod si febris continua nulla quidem aut parua afferat symptomata, virtute, habitu, & assuetudine, vt supra habentibus si mili victu hominem nutries.
units.tr: But if in the intermissions the symptoms wholly cease, and the strength is robust, the habit firm and not easily dissolved, and the patient is accustomed to live sparingly, feed the feverish patient with one of the two drinks made of chicken seasoned in the said manner. And give bread soaked in water of endive and juice of pomegranates, as an addition. But if the strength is weak, or the habit is lean and easily dissolved, or the patient is accustomed to eat much, feed the feverish patient with one of the drinks already mentioned, and with the extremities of a chicken, with bread similarly soaked. But if a continuous fever brings little or no symptoms, feed the person with a moderate diet, for those who have strength, habit and custom as above.

units.la: Quod si virtus imbecillis fuerit, aut reliquis crassiorem victu indicantibus, pulli eti am carnes febricitati ministrato. In tertiana igitur continua quae debilia affert symptomata virtute robusta existente, habitu & assuetudine vt supra habentibus, sorbitione vtere in hunc modum. Hordei ab vno cortice tice exuti man.tres, capillorum veneris, cy- marum lupulorum, passulárum enucleata-rum, ana, quantū manu capi possit, coquan-tur simul cū pulla crassa quæ nuper matrem reliquerit, hora vna antequam ab igne amo ueas, immitte aceti albi quantum satis sit, vt acetum gustatuisse offerat, huius partem ser-uato vt bibat inclinante febre, sorbitionem ex reliquo cum pane conficito.
units.tr: But if the strength is weak, or if the other circumstances indicate a thicker diet, give the feverish patient the chicken also, and meat. In continuous tertian fever, then, which brings weak symptoms, where the strength is robust and the habit and custom are as above, use a drink in this manner. Take three handfuls of barley husked of one covering, of maidenhair, of hop shoots, and of stoned raisins, each as much as can be held in the hand; let them be boiled together with a thick chicken that has only just left its mother; one hour before you take it off the fire, add enough white vinegar that the taste of vinegar is just perceptible; keep part of this for the patient to drink when the fever declines, and make the drink from the rest with bread.

units.la: Quod si virtus imbecillis fuerit, aut habi-tus & consuetudo similiter indicent, extre-mitates pullæ quæ teneræ sunt magis, inuali-do ægrotanti exhibeto. Huic victus conueni-ens forma, per ea quæ comeduntur est. Sem-perq; à tenui iure incipiendum est, deinde tem-poris interuallo sorbitionem ministrato.
units.tr: But if the strength is weak, or the habit and custom similarly indicate it, give the feeble patient the tender extremities of the chicken. A suitable form of diet for him is according to what is eaten. And one must always begin with a thin broth, and then after an interval of time give the thicker drink.

units.la: Contingit aliquando febre iam inclinante iterum à quodam inflammante calore febrici-tantes rursus molestari. Quod duplici de cau-sa contingit, aut quia intempestiue eis oblatus est cibus, aut cum in vi-ētu erratum est.
units.tr: It sometimes happens that, when the fever is already declining, the feverish patients are again troubled by a burning heat that inflames them. This happens for one of two reasons: either food was offered to them at an unseasonable time, or an error was made in the diet.

units.la: Contra exhibentes assa gallorum hepata in feb. cont. Item cibum ex refrigerantibus herbis ante morbi coctionem in continuis febribus non conuenire.
units.tr: Against those who give roasted livers of fowls in continuous fevers. Likewise, a diet of cooling herbs is not suitable in continuous fevers before the morbid matter has been concocted.

units.la: CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: SVNT qui assa gallinaceorum hepata post sorbitiones laborantibus febre continua exhibent, quod minime probo. Nam cibus longum in laborantium ventriculis immoratur. Quod non parua occasio est vt ob id corrum patur. Praeterea hepar assum inter cibos exiccantes numerandum est, quapropter febrici tanti non conuenit: cuius argumentum est sitis quam excitat.
units.tr: There are some who give roasted chicken livers after broths to those suffering from a continuous fever, which I by no means approve. For food lingers a long time in the stomachs of the sick, and this is no small occasion for it to spoil there. Moreover, roast liver must be counted among the drying foods, so it does not suit a fever of this kind. The proof is the thirst it provokes.

units.la: Eos qui in continuis febribus, lactucis, et huiusmodi refrigerantibus herbis vtuntur, ante morbi iudicationem, supra ostendimus in damnum aegrotantium errare.
units.tr: We have shown above that those who, in continuous fevers, use lettuce and similar cooling herbs before the crisis of the disease, err to the harm of the sick.

units.la: Sed non erit ab re, recensere victum quo vtitur quidam e nostris recentioribus. nam ex hoc aliquod capiet lector commodum. In die remissionis febricitantem pulla alterata (vt ille ait) nutrit, ante vero exacerbationem et in infebris inclinatione farre & lactucis, qui valde dissident ab inuicem victus, & qualitate & substantia. Nutrimentum insuper quod ex pulla habetur multum est, paruum vero quod lactucæ præstant. Aquosum nanque sanguinem generant excrementis abundantem, quapropter cum insignis sit inter eos differentia, magna fiet vtique mutatio cum ab vno ad alium transitus fiat. Stante autem eadem morbi conditione mutationem in victu faciendam non esse supra ostendimus de mente Hippocratis, vbi Galenum citauimus dicentem à morbi principio ad statum vsque eadem victus specie alendum esse febricitan tem. Quo in loco cautum medicum reddit, vt (tuc) insignes mutationes caueat. Nonne melius esse iudicas si pulla ægrotantem alere illi mens erat, vt ante exacerbationem & infe bris inclinatione, sorbitione ex pullæ decocto vteretur? Multo siquidem magis inter se con ueniunt pulla, & sorbitio ex eius decocto, quàm pulla cum lactuca & farre. facilioris præterea sorbitio coctionis est. Quod si cibũ minus nutriente se velle exhibere dicat, pullam quare exhibuerit die tranquilliori rogabit quis, quae multo magis nutrit quam eius sorbitio. No enim prudentis medici est, aegro tantem vice vna implere, vt cum vice alia parum exhibuerit satisfaciat. Multo salubrius aegrotanti esset, id in partes secare, vt natura nullo ex mutatione afficiatur grauamine. Si ergo pulla recte in die tranquillo exhibetur, facta ex ea sorbitio modo quem diximus salubrior erit profecto aegrotanti ante exacerbationem, quam far & lactucae. Multo praeterea commodius fuerit inclinante febre ius pullae dicto modo confectum exhibere, deinde temporis interuallo sorbitione vti, quam far & lactucas in cibum ministrare. Oportet ergo non solum simili forma victus, sed simili substantiae cibarijs febricitantem quoadpossis, stante eadem morbi conditione nutrias.
units.tr: But it will not be out of place to review the diet used by one of our more recent writers, for the reader will gain some benefit from it. On a day of remission he nourishes the feverish patient with a pulla altered (as he calls it), but before the exacerbation and during the decline of the fever with spelt and lettuce, two diets that differ greatly from each other both in quality and in substance. Moreover, the nourishment supplied by the pulla is considerable, while that supplied by lettuce is slight, since lettuce produces watery blood abounding in excrements. So, because the difference between them is so marked, the change will certainly be great when the transition is made from one to the other. But while the condition of the disease remains the same, we have shown above, following the mind of Hippocrates, where we cited Galen saying that a feverish patient should be fed with the same kind of diet from the beginning of the disease up to its height, that a change in diet must not be made. In that passage he warns the physician to avoid marked changes at that time. Do you not judge it better, if the pulla was his intention for feeding the patient, that he should use, before the exacerbation and during the decline of the fever, a broth made from the decoction of the pulla? For the pulla and a broth made from its decoction agree with each other much more closely than the pulla with lettuce and spelt. Moreover, a broth is easier to digest. But if he says he wished to give a food of less nourishment, someone will ask why he gave the pulla on a calmer day, since it nourishes much more than its broth. For it is not the mark of a wise physician to fill the patient at one time so that he is satisfied by giving little at another. It would be much more wholesome for the patient to divide it into portions, so that nature is not burdened by any change. If therefore the pulla is rightly given on a calm day, a broth made from it in the manner we have described will certainly be more wholesome for the patient before the exacerbation than spelt and lettuce. Moreover, it will be much more convenient, when the fever is declining, to give the broth of the pulla prepared in the way described, and then, after an interval of time, to use a broth rather than to serve spelt and lettuce as food. It is therefore necessary to nourish the feverish patient, as far as possible, not only with a similar form of diet but also with similar substance of food, while the condition of the disease remains the same.

units.la: Quis uictus continuae a phlegmate conueniat.
units.tr: What diet suits continuous fever arising from phlegm.

units.la: CAPVT IX. FEBRIS
units.tr: CHAPTER IX. FEVER

units.la: FEBRIS continua à pituita ortum habens si cū virtute robusta fuerit, habitu et assuetudine vt supra habentibus, hunc victum exposcit. Hordei ab vno cortice exuti quantū manu capi possit, passularum enuclea tarum & petroselini tantū, thymi parte me diam, coquito simul cum pulla crassa modicum, antequam ab igne amoueas immittito capillorum veneris recentis aut polytrichi man. vnū. Ligato simul herbas, coctasque abstrahe. Proicito aceti albi quantum satis vt in gustatu repræsentetur. Denuò coquito quousque permisceatur. Fac sorbitionem ex pane, vtere et iure si videbitur. Ex pullæ carnibus hora quietiori dato febricitanti quod tenerrimum sit.
units.tr: A continuous fever arising from phlegm, if it is accompanied by robust strength, calls for this diet in those who have the constitution and habit described above: take barley, peeled of its outer husk, as much as can be held in the hand; a moderate amount of raisins with the seeds removed, and of parsley as much; half a handful of thyme. Boil these together with a little thick pulla. Before you remove it from the fire, add one handful of fresh maidenhair or polytrichum. Tie the herbs together, and take them out once they are cooked. Add white vinegar in such quantity that its taste is perceptible on the palate. Boil again until it is well mixed. Make a broth with bread, and use the meat too if you think fit. Give the feverish patient the most tender meat of the pulla at a quieter hour.

units.la: Meminisse oportet in continuis febribus vbi suspicio est de pororū obstructione, ante totius euacuationem incommoda esse quæcunque aperiunt & incidunt.
units.tr: In continuous fevers, where there is suspicion of an obstruction of the pores, one must remember that before the whole evacuation, any remedies that open or cut through are harmful.

units.la: Cicerū facilis coctionis man. vnū infundito in modicum aquæ endiuiæ, testam tota no cte in calido cinere seruato. Mane in aqua è fonte sufficienti bulliant, adiectis hordei ab uno cortice exuti man. tribus, passularum enucleatarum manip. uno, cortice radicis ci chorij uno. coquantur insimul cum pulla, et antequam ab igne amoueas, petroselini man. semis addito, & parum aceti, fac sorbitionem ut supra. Extremitates pullae aegrotati dato.
units.tr: Pour a handful of easily cooked chickpeas into a small quantity of endive water, and keep them overnight in warm ashes. In the morning let them boil in water from a sufficient spring, adding three handfuls of barley peeled of its outer husk, one handful of raisins with the seeds removed, and one piece of the root of coriander. Let them cook together with the pulla, and before you remove it from the fire add half a handful of parsley and a little vinegar. Make a broth as above. Give the patient the extremities of the pulla.

units.la: Quod si imbecillis aeger fuerit, permitte ei fasianum edere, optima siquidem ijs caro est. Bonum est ut cibum assumpturus aeger, syrupi acetosi acrioris cochlearia duo, mellis rosati colati unum, mixta ante sorbeat. Aquam decoctam cum hordeo & semine foeniculi bibant. Verum de potu abunde dictum est.
units.tr: But if the patient is weak, allow him to eat pheasant, for its flesh is the best for such people. It is good for the patient, before taking his food, to drink, mixed together, two spoonfuls of sharp sour syrup and one spoonful of strained rose honey. Let them drink water boiled with barley and fennel seed. But enough has been said about drink.

units.la: Phlegmatica febris quem exposcat uictum.
units.tr: What diet a phlegmatic fever requires.

units.la: CAPVT X.
units.tr: CHAPTER X.

units.la: IN febre phlegmatica, quam Arabes latiçam dicunt aut latentem, humidi natiui multum exoluitur, cibum ideo multi nutrimenti dare oportet. Corpus humiditate madefaciente & laxante affectum est ab humore frigido & humido, sed ob putredinem calido calido effecto. Vnde non aliter ab hac febre corpus, quàm pars aliqua ab occursu aquæ ebullientis afficitur. Vnde ebullientem hanc febrem nonnulli dixere. Cibum cōuenientem ÿs qui hac detinentur febre actu frigidum et siccum esse oportet, potentia autem humidu. Hoc autem est, vt humiditatem madefacien tem exiccet, & vt corpus ab humido innato exolutum reficere valeat, et vt laxa mem bra induret. Hoc autem difficile est in simpli cibus inuenire. Quapropter sorbitionem ÿs ita parabis. Phasianum iuuenem aut perdice{a} aut hœdum (hæc enim ex carnibus optimæ ÿs sunt) coquito cum radicibus cichorÿ, petroselini, passulis, tenerrimis lupulorum cymis, & corticibus citri, cauliculis altilis cardui, quem Hispani cardo vulgariter appellant, quo vbique locorum ad finem mensævtimur, simul coquantur ex iure, fac sorbitionem cum pane. Dictam herbam quam nonnulli scolymon, esse à Dioscoride appellatam opinantur, cum capo aut pulla si simul coquas, si phasioni aut perdicis copia non detur idoneum illis parabis cibum. Carduus humi-ditatem madefacientem, laxantem maxime remouet. Membrum laxum indurat, idque ci-tra humidi natiui absumptionem. Ad hac a-perit, & vrinam prouocat, & in altum pe-netrat, quod ad huius febris sanationem ex-petendum est. Humor siquidem ad minimas est corporis particulas dispersus. Vnde crassam vrinam copiosamque & sudorem duo esse huius febris remedia ratione quis arbi-trabitur. Tres ergo simul coquens caulicu-los, cardui sorbitionem facito, quam febrici-tanti ministrabis vbi oportet. Ex carnibus id quod maxime tenerum sit, & facile ab aegrotante coqui possit, exhibeto. Nec prae-termittendum, solam hanc febrem ex hu-moralibus indigere victu qui maxime vir-tutem corporis augere possit: more hectica febris cui valde similatur. In illa enim cali-ditas praeter naturam totum iam occupans, naturalis similitudinem acquisiut. Sic hu-more huius febris per totum ad minimas vs-que partes dispersos more naturalis humidi-tatis, tatis, natura eius coctionem, separationem aut expulsione non curat. Sed eum ob mixtionem ad minima cū naturali humiditate seruat. Vnde hos nec euacuatione ventris, aut fluxu sanguinis sanatos videmus. Quinimmo si spote aut a medico imperito aluus moueatur, peiores reddūtur. Quod si aliquandiu manet, euacuato bono simul cum malo separatione non facta, moriuntur. Quapropter scopus cu rationis in ijs fuerit, eos more hectici nutrire. Oportet enim totum id quod in ijs de humiditatibus est superfluis, sensim absumere, ciboque salubriores inducere, qualitatesq; humoris quibus corpus affectum est, cotrarijs successiue euertere. Et quia huius febris cura tio a victu vt diximus maxime dependet, libet sermonem longiorem facere.
units.tr: In phlegmatic fever, which the Arabs call latent or hidden, a great deal of the natural moisture is dissolved away, so one ought to give food of much nourishment. The body is affected by a moistening and relaxing humour that is cold and moist, but because of putrefaction it has been made hot. Hence the body is affected by this fever no differently than some part is affected by the contact of boiling water, and for this reason some have called it the boiling fever. The food suited to those held by this fever should be actually cold and dry, but moist in potential. This is so that it may dry up what moistens, restore the body that has been loosened by the loss of its natural moisture, and harden the slack limbs. It is difficult, however, to find such food among simple foods. Therefore you will prepare a broth for them as follows. Boil a young pheasant or a partridge or a kid (for these are the best of meats) with roots of chicory and parsley, raisins, the tenderest hop shoots, and citron peel, and with the stalks of cultivated cardoon, which the Spanish commonly call cardo and which we use everywhere at the end of a meal. Let them be cooked together in the broth, and make a sop with bread. If you cook together the herb that some believe Dioscorides called scolymus, with a capon or a hen, you will prepare a suitable food for them if there is no plenty of pheasant or partridge. Cardoon removes what moistens and loosens most strongly. It hardens a slack member, and does so without consuming the natural moisture. Besides this, it opens, provokes urine, and penetrates deeply, which is what must be sought for curing this fever. For the humour is dispersed through the smallest particles of the body. Hence, as reason suggests, thick and copious urine and sweat are the two remedies for this fever. So, boiling three stalks together, make a broth of cardoon, which you will give to the feverish patient when needed. Give them the meat that is most tender and that the patient can digest easily. It must not be overlooked that this fever alone requires a diet of humours that can especially increase the strength of the body, in the manner of hectic fever, to which it is very similar. For in hectic fever heat, unnaturally occupying the whole body, takes on the likeness of the natural. Thus the humour of this fever, dispersed throughout the body into the smallest parts in the manner of natural moisture, nature does not seek to concoct, separate, or expel. Rather, because of the mixture, it keeps the humour in the smallest parts together with the natural moisture. Hence we see these patients are not cured by purging the bowels or by a flow of blood. Indeed, if the bowels move of their own accord or by an unskilled physician, they become worse. If this lasts for some time, they die, since the good is evacuated along with the bad without any separation having been made. Therefore, the aim of reason in such cases must be to nourish them in the manner of a hectic patient. For it is necessary to consume gradually all the superfluous moisture in them, to bring in foods that are more wholesome, and gradually to overturn by contraries the qualities of the humour by which the body is affected. And because the cure of this fever depends above all on diet, as we have said, it is worth making a somewhat longer discourse.

units.la: Iis qui cum imbecillitate virium hac febre detinentur hunc ministrato cibum.
units.tr: For those who are held by this fever together with weakness of strength, give this food.

units.la: Perdicis secundum complementū assa succum ad aequales portiones cum vino albo decoctionis radicum plantaginis misceto, febricitanti ieiuno stomacho exhibeto. Fac ut modicum sudet. Idem e phasiano efficere possis. Quòd si carnes perdicis aut phasiani digerere non valeat, ipsarum succus postquam completè assa fuerint diligenter per linteum expressus, cum pane ministretur aut cum modico vini albi misceatur & propinetur. Sed diligenter observare oportet, ut vinū sit maximè imbecille quod ijs propinaueris, nam aliàs non parua ijs læsioni erit.
units.tr: Take the breast of a fully roasted partridge, mix its juice in equal portions with white wine and a decoction of plantain roots, and give it to the feverish patient on an empty stomach. Make them sweat a little. You can do the same with a pheasant. But if the patient cannot digest the flesh of a partridge or pheasant, let the juice of the completely roasted birds be carefully pressed through a linen cloth and given with bread, or mixed with a little white wine and offered to drink. But care must be taken that the wine you give them is very weak, for otherwise it will do them no small harm.

units.la: Nec silentio prætereundum est, ijs qui ita laborant commodo esse in edulijs sorbitionibus ue, præsertim ijs qui assueti sunt, allium ut simul bulliat, immittere. Nam prærogatiuam habet in roborando naturales facultates, corrigendoque damna quæ in ijs à duarū qualitatum immoderantia fiunt, nempe à frigore & humiditate. Putridi insuper humoris, cum per totum spargitur corpus, vitiā corrigit. Habet etiā præter hæc facultatem quā à centro ad circumferentiam pellit. Tria hæc quæ allium habere diximus ex Dioscoride licet colligere, qui de eo ita scribit: Potum cum origani decocto pediculos, & lendes enecat.
units.tr: Nor must it be passed over in silence that for those who suffer in this way it is advantageous to put garlic into their foods or broths, especially for those who are accustomed to it, so that it boils along with them. For it has an excellence in strengthening the natural faculties, and in correcting the damage done to them by the excess of two qualities, namely cold and moisture. Moreover, when putrid humour is spread through the whole body, it corrects the faults. Besides these things it also has a faculty by which it drives from the centre to the circumference. We may gather these three properties that we said garlic has from Dioscorides, who writes of it thus: drunk with a decoction of marjoram, it kills lice and nits.

units.la: ß ß ß Marks in the text beside the last lines. enecat. Praeterea, Magnae & alijs vtilitates contra aquarum mutationes. Demum in fine dixit, Vtile hydropicis, ad quem quidem morbum haec febris corpus non parum disponit. Veruntamen propter calorem & eius acrimoniam modicum in sorbitionibus miscendum est. Macerare tamen prius oportebat in succo herbae acetosae.
units.tr: ß ß ß Marks in the text beside the last lines. enecat. Besides, Magnus and others [note] on its usefulness against changes of water. Finally, at the end he said: useful for dropsical patients, to which disease this fever disposes the body not a little. Nevertheless, because of its heat and sharpness, it must be mixed into the broths only in small amount. It was, however, first necessary to steep it in the juice of sorrel.

units.la: Potus ijs conueniens sit vinum album pau ciferum defecatum clarum, cuius sumito partes duas, succi granatorum medij saporis partis vnius semis, aquae in qua decocta est capillaris herba recens aut polytrichum, vnā misceтo. Conuenientissimus huiusmodi ijs potus fuerit. Nec praetermittendum est Indicae radicis decoctum maximo ijs fore remedio. Cuius si detur copia, vnciam vnam in lupinares, sed multo subtiliores formulas scissam, in decem libris aquae in qua nocte ante eam macerauerиc coquito. Sequenti die ad lentum igne ad medias ebullire permittito. Propinato in aurora quantum vno haustu bibere possit calidum, sed aegrotantis corpus prius fricare linteo aspero oportet. Apotu vestimentis cooperiatur & sudet quantū pro virium ratione. Cubiculum vbi ægrotans iacet, perpetuo calidum vndique clausum seruare oportet. Nullus alter potus melius sudores ciet. Partes insuper ab humore assiduo laxas roborat, indurat, sed iis qui iam sunt imbecilles caute exhibendus est, quia plus iusto exiccat. Qua re iis qui imbecilliter habent non inutile fuerit, succi granatorum medii saporis partem vnam miscere tribus decoĉti, simulque propinare. Summa diligentia obseruandum est ne iis aluus liquida fiat, quin potius huius contrarium, nempe astrictam aluum efficere conamur iis quæ poros cutis aperiunt, & sudores mouent.
units.tr: A suitable drink for them is clear, clarified white wine of light body, of which take two parts, with one and a half parts of juice of pomegranates of medium flavour, and mix them with water in which maidenhair fern fresh or polytrichum has been boiled. Such a drink will be most suitable for them. Nor must it be overlooked that a decoction of Indian root will be of the greatest help to them. If a supply of it is available, boil one ounce of it, cut into slices like lupine seeds but much thinner, in ten pounds of water in which it has been steeped overnight. On the following day, let it boil over a slow fire down to half. Give the patient at dawn as much warm as he can drink in one draught, but first the patient's body must be rubbed with a rough linen cloth. After drinking, let him be covered with clothes and sweat as much as his strength allows. The room where the sick person lies must always be kept warm and closed on all sides. No other drink stirs up sweats better. It also strengthens and hardens the parts that are constantly loosened by moisture, but it must be given cautiously to those who are already weak, because it dries too much. Therefore, for those who are weak it will not be unhelpful to mix one part of juice of pomegranates of medium flavour with three parts of the decoction, and to give them both together. Great care must be taken that their bowels do not become loose; rather, we try to produce the opposite, namely a constipated bowel, with those things that open the pores of the skin and stir up sweats.

units.la: Tertianæ conuenientem uiĉtum inuestigat primum exquisitæ, deinde alijs eius differentijs.
units.tr: For tertian fever, first seek out the suitable diet in its most exact form, and then according to its other differences.

units.la: CAPVT XI.
units.tr: Chapter XI.

units.la: TERTIANA simplex pura hunc exigit vicțu. Paretur crassa sorbitio ex hepatica altero duorum modorum quos supra traditradidimus. Ius dato vt bibat in febris inclinatione, ex reliquo fac sorbitionem, qua vti tor ante aduentum paroxysmi & cessante febre. Carnibus in die tranquillo vescatur.
units.tr: A simple pure tertian fever requires this diet. Prepare a thick gruel from liver by one of the two methods we gave above. Give broth to drink at the onset of the fever, and from the remainder make a gruel, which the patient may take before the paroxysm comes and when the fever has subsided. On a quiet day he may eat meat.

units.la: Pullam cum cucurbita & prunis & vua acerba coquito, fac vt supra.
units.tr: Boil a chicken with gourd, plums and sour grapes, and prepare it as above.

units.la: Panem album trium dierum in subtiles par- tes planas diuidito, & in aquam endiuiæ infundito, acidumque succum aranty desuper exprimito. Zucarum deinde radito, tantum vt dulcor & acetositas manifeste ingustatu sentiantur. Pane in hunc modum vtatur die tranquillo bis aut ter, & in maxima inclinatione paroxysmi ante sorbitionem. Magna huic cibo vis est, in refringendo biliosi humoris acuitatem. Ventriculi praeterea & iocineris immoderatum ardorem extinguit. Robur eis addit. Plures à tertianis liberari iuuenes & adultiores aetate hoc cibo vidi, absque pharmaco, aut alia potione. Oportet tamen diligenter aduertere ne adsit pororum obstructio, aut condensatio, aut corporum constrictio. Quapropter in continuis febribus à bile ortum habentibus in quibus de pororum apertione soliciti sumus, ante totius euacuationem exhibendus non est. A venæ sectione in continuis febribus secure exhibebitur.
units.tr: Cut three-day-old white bread into thin flat pieces, steep them in endive water, and squeeze orange juice over them. Then grate sugar on top, just enough that sweetness and sourness can clearly be tasted. On a quiet day the patient should eat this bread two or three times, and at the height of the paroxysm, before the gruel. This food has great power to check the sharpness of bilious humour. It also quenches the excessive heat of the stomach and liver, and it strengthens them. I have seen many young people and adults older than that freed from tertian fever by this food alone, without medicine or any other drink. Care must nonetheless be taken that there is no obstruction or thickening of the pores, or constriction of the body. Therefore it should not be given before the whole body has been evacuated in continued fevers that arise from bile, where we are anxious to open the pores. In continued fevers, it may safely be given after bloodletting.

units.la: Duplex tertiana tenui eo magis victu indiget, quantum in ea minus quiescit natura. Sorbitione cucurbitæ aut hepaticæ vtere. A carnibus, nisi sit imbecillis ægrotans, temperandum est. Aut nisi multo sit cibo assuetus. Potus vtriq; febri conueniens aqua hordei est.
units.tr: A double tertian needs a thinner diet, the more so as nature rests less in it. Use a gruel of gourd or liver. Meat should be restricted unless the patient is weak, or unless he is accustomed to a heavy diet. For drink, barley water suits both kinds of fever.

units.la: Tertiana simplex non pura ab humore bilioso cum crasso phlegmate mixto ortum habens, quem recentiores choleram vitellinam dicunt, hunc exposcit victum. Thymi, petroselini, passularum enucleatarum, singulorum man. vnu hordei ab vno cortice exuti tres, coquito cum capo aut pulla gallinacea. herbas iam coctas extrahito, immittitoque aceti albi quantum satis. Parum coquito denuo quousque permixta sint. Dato vt bibat incli nante febre. Ex residuo fac sorbitionem: qua vti poterit cessante febre & ante aduentum paroxysmi. Horis septem ante accessionem, carnibus vesci poterit in die quietis.
units.tr: A simple tertian that is not pure, arising from bilious humour mixed with thick phlegm, which recent writers call yolk-coloured bile, calls for this diet. Boil three of each: thyme, parsley, stoned raisins, and one handful of barley hulled of its outer skin, in a capon or chicken broth. Take out the herbs once they are cooked, and add white vinegar as much as is enough. Boil briefly again until they are well mixed. Give it to drink while the fever is abating. From the remainder make a gruel, which the patient may take when the fever has subsided and before the paroxysm comes. Seven hours before the attack he may eat meat on a day of rest.

units.la: Piscmiculos saxatiles in aqua coquito, cum satureia, thymo, sale, & aceto, & modico purissimi olei. Facilis coctionis cibus est. Ventriculi appetentiam excitat, quæ in hac febre plurimum expetenda sunt.
units.tr: Boil rock-dwelling mussels in water with savory, thyme, salt and vinegar, and a little very pure oil. It is an easily digested food. It stimulates the appetite of the stomach, which is much to be desired in this fever.

units.la: Olei purissimi ex immatura oliua, partem vnam, aceti albi duas permisceto. Panem infundito, febricitanti exhibeto. Quod si olei immaturi copia non detur, Hispano vtere. Mixtio ex oleo & aceto cum humana maxime conuenit natura. Quandoquidem ex contrariis vtriusque qualitatibus constat. Miscentur enim calidum, frigidum, humidum et siccum. Ventriculum roborat: Hepar & lienem. Distributionem adiuuat. Coctionem et appetentiam excitat. Aperit, incidit, humectat, refrigerat. Quod si piperis grosso modo contusi parum addas, frigido ventriculo pituitoso conferet: quod euenire in hac febre multoties solet. Fa- lem merito quis mixtionem dixerit, & febri a pituita, a bile et ab atra bile conuenit. Quod si oleo & aceto parum aqua misceas sitim sedabit.
units.tr: Mix one part of very pure oil from unripe olives with two parts of white vinegar. Steep bread in it and give it to the feverish patient. But if unripe oil cannot be had, use Spanish oil. The mixture of oil and vinegar agrees especially well with human nature, since it consists of the opposite qualities of each: for hot, cold, moist and dry are mixed together. It strengthens the stomach, the liver and the spleen. It aids distribution. It stimulates digestion and appetite. It opens, cuts, moistens and cools. If you add a little pepper, coarsely crushed, it will benefit a cold, phlegmatic stomach, which often happens in this fever. One may rightly call this mixture a kind of salve, and it suits a fever arising from phlegm, from bile and from black bile. If you mix in a little water with the oil and vinegar, it will quench thirst.

units.la: Alid, Alexandri herbæ cauliculos, laueris super aquas crescentis, foliorum raphani, violarum, borraginis, lactucæ, singulorum man. vnu coquito in aqua quousque percocta sint. Herbas exprimito quantum possis, cultelloque ad minimas partes incidito, addito olei purissimi salis & oxymelitis acris singulorum quantum sit satis. Cum pane vtitor. Mundificat cibus hic ventrem, vtrancque euacuationem promouet.
units.tr: Another: boil the stalks of Alexanders, gathered from the water-growing kind, with leaves of radish, violet, borage and lettuce, one handful of each, in water until they are thoroughly cooked. Squeeze out the herbs as far as you can, cut them with a knife into very small pieces, and add pure oil, salt and sharp oxymel, each as much as is enough. The patient should eat it with bread. This food cleanses the stomach and promotes evacuation in both directions.

units.la: Quod si post expressionem herbarum & eandem incisionem cum pinguitudine iuris capi aut pullæ herbas coquas, adiecto oxymelite, magis nutrientem cibum efficies.
units.tr: But if, after squeezing out the herbs and chopping them in the same way, you boil them in the fatty broth of a capon or chicken and add oxymel, you will make a more nourishing food.

units.la: Quod si bilis permixta tenui humiditati aquosæ fuerit, febrisque fiat ex cholera citrina, vtere sorbitione ex cucurbita: aut crassa sorbitione ex hepatica, adiecto malo granato acido hora vna antequam abigne amoveas. Dato ius in febris inclinatione, ex residuo fac sorbitionem. Vtere & pane infrigidante, modico cinamomi adiecto si opus fuerit. fuerit. Lentes Hispanas coquito in aqua cum petroselino, coriandro viridi, oleo, sale & aceto, & modico croci. Vtere decocto cū pane. Cibus hic frigidus & aliqualiter exiccans est. Hispanis multum in vsu est. Febricitantibus quibuscunque sorbitionem ex lentibus exhibent, exceptis quartana laborantibus. Quos etsi nulla ob id laude dignos esse existimem, ita eos non absque erroris crimine, qui lentes omni prohibent aegrotanti: id ex Galeno afferentes qui eas cibum hominum non esse dixerit, cum de pleuritide aegeret in qua lentes prohibuit. Sed relicta pleuritide, febricitanti febre tertiana à cholera citrina certè cōuenient, si febris effectricem causam & qualitatem in partibus derelictam consideres. Cholera citrina humor calidus & tenuis substantiæ est, maxime omnium humorum penetrans. Ius lentium contrarias operatur qualitates: nam refrigerandi et inspissandi vim habet. Cholera insuper citrina eam in quā incidit partem, totā sua acuta penetratione macerat. Ius lentium non solum partem cogit vt minus prompte penetratio- ni fiat peruia, verum id quod humidum est tollit æquali sua siccitate. Iis præterea qui ex hac febre immoderatè sudant, & non ob id alleuiantur, non parum cibus ex lentibus con fert. Quod si adhuc lentes aciem oculorum ob- tundere, & ægrè concoqui, & somnia tu- multuosa excitare ex Dioscoride afferas, hæc omnia lentibus non earum decocto tribuit. Hæc damna in Hispana lente non percipi- mus. Stomachum male habere ex ea scripsit Dioscorides: Hispana vero lens ventriculum roborat & minimè inflat. Lens Italia maior & candidior est, minor verò Hispana colo re ad rubeum vergente nec tumultuosa exci tat somnia, vt de ea proditum est. Et si quid vitiosæ qualitatis Hispanam habere conten das, à viridi coriandro castigatur. Vbicunq; ergo humores corporis inspissare, aut corpo- ris particulas cogere citra calfactione mens est, ius Hispanæ lentis in cibis recte porrigi- tur. Quod si id cum petroselino, coriandro vi ridi, oleo, aceto, sale & croco parauerit, conficies cibum ad iam dicta couenientissimum in passiuis qualitatibus temperatum, in actiuis ad frigiditatem declinantem.
units.tr: But if bile is mixed with thin watery moisture, and the fever arises from yellow bile, use a gruel of gourd, or a thick gruel of liver with pomegranate juice added, an hour before you remove it from the fire. Give broth at the abating of the fever, and from the remainder make a gruel. Also use cooling bread, with a little cinnamon added if needed. Boil Spanish lentils in water with parsley, green coriander, oil, salt, vinegar and a little saffron. Use the decoction with bread. This food is cold and somewhat drying. It is much in use among the Spanish. They give a gruel of lentils to all feverish patients, except those suffering from quartan fever. I think they deserve no praise for this, yet those who forbid lentils to every sick person are not free of the fault of error either. They cite Galen, who said that lentils are not human food, when he was treating pleurisy, in which he forbade lentils. But setting pleurisy aside, lentils will certainly suit a feverish patient with tertian fever arising from yellow bile, if you consider the efficient cause of the fever and the quality left in the parts. Yellow bile is a hot and thin humour, the most penetrating of all the humours. The broth of lentils works the opposite qualities: for it has the power to cool and to thicken. Moreover, yellow bile by its sharp penetration wears down the whole part into which it falls. The broth of lentils not only compels the part so that it becomes less readily open to penetration, but by its equal dryness it removes what is moist. Furthermore, for those who sweat excessively in this fever and are not relieved by it, food of lentils contributes not a little. But if you say, following Dioscorides, that lentils dull the sight of the eyes, are digested with difficulty, and stir up disturbed dreams, all these faults should be attributed not to the decoction of lentils but to lentils themselves. We do not notice these faults in Spanish lentils. Dioscorides wrote that lentils upset the stomach, but Spanish lentils strengthen the stomach and do not cause flatulence at all. The Italian lentil is larger and whiter, while the smaller Spanish lentil, tending to a reddish colour, does not stir up disturbed dreams, as has been reported of it. And if you think the Spanish lentil has some harmful quality, it is corrected by green coriander. Wherever the intention is to thicken the humours of the body, or to compress the particles of the body without heating them, the broth of Spanish lentils is rightly offered among foods. If you prepare it with parsley, green coriander, oil, vinegar, salt and saffron, you will make a food most suitable for the aforesaid purposes, tempered in its passive qualities and inclining to coldness in its active ones.

units.la: Pedes vituli anteriores duos, aut arietis omnes in aqua plus satis coquito: radicum plantaginis, cichorij, petroselini, singulorum manip. vnius tertiam, hepaticæ, hordei ab vno cortice exuti, prunorum & passularum singulorum vnum, addito mali granati acidi tres, ius dato vbi oportet, ex reliquo facsorbitionem. Quod si post coctionem pedum, an tequam malum granatum iniicias, herbas abstrahas, ius colans, tertiam sui partem succi acidi mali granati immittas, pane & zucaro simul coquas, quousque permixta sint, cibum ijs valde idoneum & plurimis aliis aegrotantium parabis. Quem vt couenientissimum memoria dignum ducito. Nam multum nutrit, corpus refrigerat, & humectat, particulas cogit, tenues humores inspissat, bilis feruorem reprimit, ventriculum, et iecur roborat, sitim sedat.
units.tr: Boil two front calves' feet, or all of a ram's, in water more than enough. Take a third of a handful each of plantain root, chicory root and parsley root; one of each of hepatic (liverwort), barley hulled of its outer skin, plums and raisins; add three of sour pomegranate. Give the broth where it is needed, and from the remainder make a gruel. But if after the feet are boiled, and before you add the pomegranate, you take out the herbs, strain the broth, add a third of its part of sour pomegranate juice, and boil it together with bread and sugar until they are well mixed, you will prepare a food very suitable for these and for many other sick people. Regard it as worthy of remembrance as most suitable. For it nourishes much, cools and moistens the body, compresses the particles, thickens thin humours, checks the heat of bile, strengthens the stomach and liver, and quenches thirst.

units.la: Disceptatio an rectè consuluerint Arabes medici, in tertiana pura à cibis in quibus est caro abstinendum esse.
units.tr: A dispute whether the Arab physicians rightly advised that in pure tertian fever one should abstain from foods containing meat.

units.la: CAPVT XII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XII.

units.la: EX Arabibus medicis sunt qui in tertia pura à cibis in quibus est caro abstinendum esse dixerunt. Alius, Rectum est (inquit) vt in potu ei detur sicut sorbitio hordei, & etiam ei simile, nisi natura iam fuerit lenificata. Dixit alius, Si in vltimo diei erit tempus accessionis, non erit incongruum in diei principio aquam hordei propinare ad subtilitatem declinantem. Dixit vnus e nostris, Intellexerunt praedicti regulariter operando: nā coactè aliquando cibamus ante accessionem, & in ipsa. Dixit infra hic idem vir, Aqua tamen carnis in ijs febribus prohibenda est quantum possibile fuerit. Si autem coactè eam exhibere debeamus, ab ea carne in frusta parua redacta, & aquis infrigidantibus abluta, sublimiter, & cum aquis infrigidatibus tribuatur. Sed operæpre cium studioso lectori erit examinare, an dicti medici rationabiliter vereantur carnes, ne-dum dum aliū paruarū, exhibere vsq; ad inclina- tionem vniuersalem febris. Et siquidem has in die accessionis prohibent, recte agere ita consulentes arbitror. Quod si nec in die quie- tis vtendū eis asserant, audire quibus innitun tur rationibus oportet. Tertianam puram ex Hippocrate asserūt intra septem periodos in- dicari, hos dies tredecim cōtinere, terminum vero acutarum quatuordecim esse. Omnia au tem morbo intra quatuordecim dies iudican do, tenuis victus exhiberi debet, vt supra o- stensum est. Carnes igitur nullæ dandæ sunt, quia tenuis victus limites transcendunt. Præ terea in ea febre bilis vtpote nimium acris, membra plus iusto calfacere solet, exiccare & corrodere. His vero symptomatibus ven triculum & iecur plus affici, eorumq; actio nes imbecillores ob id fieri certū est. Iis ergo de causis victu facilis coctionis, quiq; contra ria sit qualitatis, nutrire eos oportet. Carnes vero ob id quod non facilè coquantur, & qualitate humori contraria non vigeant, sed media, à ventriculo, & iecinere male parantur. Vnde fit vt ad humoris morbum efficientis naturam, bona earum pars conuertatur. Danda igitur sunt quæ facillimæ sint coctionis, & quæ humori qualitatibus contrarijs vigeat. Hæc non in carnibus, sed in herbis, fructibus, seminibus, inuenire est. Vt in lactuca, endiuia, portulaca, cucurbita, malo granato, arantio, hordeo, prunis & si milibus.
units.tr: Among the Arab physicians there are some who have said that in pure tertian fever one must abstain from meat-based foods. One says: "It is right (he says) to give the patient, to drink, something like barley gruel, and similar things, unless nature has already been softened." Another said: "If the time of the paroxysm falls at the end of the day, it will not be out of place to give barley water early in the day, as the disease declines toward its finer stage." One of our own writers said: "The aforementioned men understood this as the general rule, since we sometimes feed patients by force before the paroxysm and during it." The same man said further below: "Meat broth, however, is to be avoided in these fevers as far as possible. But if we must give it by force, then the meat should be cut into small pieces, washed in cooling waters, and given raised up and with cooling waters." But it will be a matter of careful work for the studious reader to examine whether the said physicians reasonably fear meats, not to mention small pieces of them, given up to the general decline of the fever. If they forbid these on the day of the paroxysm, I think they advise rightly. But if they say they must not be used even on the day of rest, one must hear the reasons on which they rest. They assert from Hippocrates that pure tertian fever is determined within seven periods, that these days contain thirteen, and that the limit of acute illnesses is fourteen. Now, since in an illness judged within fourteen days a thin diet ought to be given, as has been shown above, no meats are therefore to be given, because they go beyond the limits of a thin diet. Moreover, in this fever the bile, being excessively sharp, tends to heat the limbs more than is proper, to dry them and to corrode them. With these symptoms the stomach and liver are plainly more affected, and it is certain that their actions are weakened for this reason. For these reasons, therefore, one must nourish the patient with food that is easy to digest and of an opposite quality to the humour. Meats, however, because they are not easily cooked and are not strong in a quality opposed to the humour but are mild, are poorly prepared by the stomach and liver. Hence it happens that a good part of them is turned into the nature of the humour that causes the disease. Things that are very easy to digest and strong in qualities contrary to the humour must therefore be given. These are found not in meats but in herbs, fruits, seeds: for example in lettuce, endive, purslane, gourd, pomegranate, orange, barley, plums and the like.

units.la: Has & similes non contemnendas rationes assignabunt, qui in tertiana pura die quietis à carnibus quibuscunque ægrotantes prohibent. Sed nos qui in supradictis gallinaceum vnum aut duos parari iussimus cum hordeo, violis, endiuia, hepatica, prunis, adiecto succo mali granati acidi: consuluimusq; vt hoc iure in febris inclinatione febricitans veretur, positoque temporis interuallo sorbitione ex pane in aqua endiuia hora vna infusio: in die verò quietis præterius & sorbitionem pulli carnibus vescerétur. Et arbitramur sic iubentes, rectè ægrotantibus consulere. Nullum equidem aliu salubriorem quis victum victum inueniat, quique magis naturam roboret, & corpus ad suam temperiem efficacius, morbifica qualitate euersa reducat.
units.tr: Those who forbid patients with pure tertian fever any kind of meat on the day of rest will give these and similar reasons, and they are not to be despised. But we, in the passage above, ordered one or two hens to be prepared with barley, violets, endive, liverwort, plums, and sour pomegranate juice added; and we advised that the febrile patient use this broth as the fever declines, and after a set interval, a sop of bread in endive water for one hour; but on the day of rest, besides, he should eat the chicken broth and meat. And we think that in so directing we give sound advice to the sick. Indeed, no one could find a more wholesome diet, one that strengthens nature more and restores the body more effectively to its proper temperament, once the morbid quality has been overturned.

units.la: Quod ita ostendimus. In tertiana pura duplex corporis siccitas aduenit, altera positiua (vt dicunt) qua bilis natura sicca corpus afficit, altera ex consumptione humiditatis naturalis à sanguine ortum habentis. Vtrique siccitati subuenire tenetur medicus. Sed secunda citius occurrere medicum posse, iure pulli refrigerantibus herbis temperato & sorbitione ex eodem, quàm herbaceo quocunque cibo inde manifestum est, quod in sanguinem bona illius cibi pars vertatur, minima ex oleribus & fructibus. Quod si mente concipias, corporis quamuis minimæ particulæ concessam esse facultatem, qua conueniens trahat & molestum eiciat, intelliges ius pulli aut eius sorbitionem quia humanæ naturæ magis familiaris est, multo magis humectare exteriores corporis & interiores particulas. Adde quod cibus ex herbis & oleribus cum minimè ad sanguinem laudabilem conuertatur, iecinoris gibbũ transsmeans ad vri-nam demittitur, aut in halitum euanescit. Vnde minimum est id quod conuersum in san-guinem humeƈtare singulas corporis parti-culas possit. Quare si vtrique velimus obsta-re siccitati, non cibum ex herbis solum, aut fruƈtibus, exhibebimus, sed cum ijs simul mi-scebimus quæ bonum præbeant alimentũ, in-digenti naturæ opem ferentes. Per hoc enim herbarum facultates efficacius operabũtur, cum ad minimas ita corporis particulas defe-rantur. Quàm autem facilis coƈtionis sint ius pulli, aut eius sorbitio, costat. Ad hæc, in in-clinatione paroxysmi & ante accessionem, ex infrigidantibus herbis & cibis alendos ob id non esse febricitantes opinor, quod illa fe-brilem caliditatem intropellant, hi expulsio-nem naturæ retardent. Quo in tempore infri-gidantia & corpus constringentia ministran-da non sunt: sed potius quæ à centro ad cir-cuñ ferentiam educant, Vt naturæ opus immite-mur regulariter agentis. Hoc discimus à Ga-leno oƈtauo de Meth. qui à balneo ægrotanti ante accessionem aquam in qua apiu incoctu erat ministrauit. In die quietis pulli carnes exhibentes nihil peccabimus. Nam a paroxysmo praeterito & ab instante intersunt horae decem & octo, quibus corporis natura a labore praeterito iam quiesces, vires resumpsit, vt pullum tenellum satis coctum coquere & parare possit. Superestque idem temporis interuallum, ad initium instantis paroxysmi. Quo tempore verendum non est, ne paroxismis cibum adhuc incoctu offendat. Quanto enim citius anticipatio fit, tanto & citius febris finit in tertiana exquisita. Adde quod cibi ex herbis & fructibus promptissimi sunt vt putredinem efferuentis humoris concipiant. Quapropter recte a medicis prohibentur in febribus horarij fructus. Aliae rationes satis efficaces adduci possunt, ad id ostendendum. Hæc tamen sano intellectui satis sunt. Hunc dico, qui vero statim assentit, falsaque (etsi magis appareant) arguit minime applaudens. Quod autem de numero dierum quibus iudicatur tertiana dictum est, nihil obstat iis quæ diximus. Formam enim victus à constitutione morbi & robore ægrotantis sumendam esse ostendimus: diximusque eum cuius virtus parum ob imbecillitatem vrgeat, crassiori victu quàm morbi dispositio exposcat alendum esse. Ostendimus insuper iis qui raro sunt habitu & humores tenues habent, & natura sunt calida & sicca, ob id quod eorum corporū citò resoluuntur virtutes, crassiorem cibum ministrandum esse. Vnde manifestum est medicos qui in tertiana pura tenui victu febricitantes utraque die nutriunt, in marasmum eos qui gracili habitu & natura calida & sicca sunt, deducere. Aut si alio sint temperamento, ex pura notham tertianam administratione frigidarum herbarum & olerum efficere. Quorum utrunque bonus medicus summa cauere debet diligentia, nempe ut ne morbum periculosiorem aut diuturnio rem efficiat. Quod si sitis vexetur ægrotans, multò sanè commodius fuerit si frigidam propines (si ea vsus fuerit) quæ multo magis sitim sedabit, quàm cibus ex refrigerantibus herbis.
units.tr: We show this as follows. In pure tertian fever a twofold dryness of the body comes on: one positive (as they call it), by which the dry nature of bile affects the body; the other arising from the consumption of natural moisture derived from the blood. The physician is bound to meet both dryness. But that the physician can more quickly meet the second, by the right of broth tempered with cooling herbs and by a sop made from the same, than by any herbaceous food, is evident from this: that a good part of such food is turned into blood, but only a small part of vegetables and fruits. If you grasp in your mind that even the smallest particles of the body have been granted a faculty by which they draw in what is suitable and expel what is troublesome, you will understand that broth, or its sop, since it is much more familiar to human nature, moistens the outer and inner particles of the body far more. Add that food from herbs and vegetables, since it is scarcely turned into good blood, passes through the gall-bladder of the liver and is sent down to the urine, or vanishes into vapour. Hence very little of it, once turned into blood, can moisten the individual particles of the body. Therefore, if we wish to resist the dryness in both ways, we shall give food not from herbs or fruits alone, but shall mix with them things that supply good nourishment, bringing help to a nature in need. For by this means the powers of the herbs will work more effectively, when they are carried to the smallest particles of the body in this way. How easy to digest broth, or its sop, is, is clear. Besides, in the decline of the paroxysm and before the attack, I believe that febrile patients should not be fed with cooling herbs and foods, because these repel the febrile heat, while those retard the expulsion of nature. At that time cooling and binding things must not be given; rather those that draw from the centre to the circumference, so that we may assist the work of nature acting in its regular course. We learn this from Galen, in the eighth book of the Method, who gave a patient, after the bath and before the attack, water in which dill had been boiled. On the day of rest, we shall commit no error in giving the flesh and broth of a chicken. For between the past paroxysm and the one at hand there are eighteen hours, in which the nature of the body, now rested from the past labour, has regained its strength, so that it can digest and prepare a young chicken that has been cooked enough. The same interval of time remains up to the beginning of the coming paroxysm. At that time there is no need to fear that the food, not yet digested, will harm the paroxysm. For the sooner the anticipation occurs, the sooner the fever ends in a well-marked tertian. Add that foods from herbs and fruits are very quick to be taken up so as to undergo putrefaction in a boiling humour. For this reason physicians rightly forbid fruits in hourly fevers. Other reasons, quite persuasive, can be brought forward to show this. These, however, are enough for a sound understanding. I mean the one who assents at once, and who, not applauding, argues against what is false, however plausible it may appear. As for what has been said about the number of days by which tertian fever is judged, it does not stand in the way of what we have said. For we have shown that the form of diet must be taken from the condition of the illness and the strength of the patient; and we have said that one whose strength is little pressed by weakness must be fed with a thicker diet than the disposition of the illness requires. We have further shown that for those who are of spare habit and have thin humours, and who are by nature hot and dry, a thicker food must be given, because the powers of their bodies are quickly dissolved. Hence it is clear that physicians who feed febrile patients with a thin diet on both days in pure tertian fever lead to emaciation those who are of slender habit and hot and dry by nature. Or if they are of another temperament, they bring about a spurious tertian from a pure one by the administration of cold herbs and vegetables. A good physician must take the greatest care to avoid either of these, namely, that he should not make the disease more dangerous or more long-lasting. But if the patient is troubled by thirst, it will certainly be much more convenient to give him cold water (if he is accustomed to it), which will allay thirst far more than food from cooling herbs.

units.la: Sed non ab re fuerit in præsenti adducere quas nugas nobiscum agat vnus è nostris medicus: qui cū nos cautos in tertiana pura sim plici, ijs verbis reddidisset: Aqua (inquit) car nis ijs febribus prohibenda est quantum pos- sibile fuerit. Si autē eam coactè exhibere de- beamus, ab ea carne in frusta parua redacta, et aquis infrigidantibus abluta, sublimetur, & cum aquis refrigidantibus tribuatur.
units.tr: But it will not be out of place here to bring up the nonsense that one of our own physicians puts forward; for when he had, in those words, rendered us cautious about pure simple tertian fever: Meat broth (he says) is to be avoided in these fevers as far as possible. But if we must give it by force, then the meat should be cut into small pieces, washed in cooling waters, raised up, and given with cooling waters.

units.la: Post hæc cum de victu continuæ cholericæ agat, inquit: Ipsa enim egret subtiliori regimi- ne & frigidiori quàm sua compar interpolla ta. Ipse tamen in curatione vnius qui febre continua tertiana laborabat, cöplexione cho lerica, ætatis quadraginta annorum macro corpore, mense Septembri, cum capitis dolo-re, & magna siti, delirabatque per accessio-nes, hunc post lenitiuum ex manna singulis diebus intermissionis pulla nutriuit. Forsan aliquis in secunda intermissione pulsum ma-gis debito prostratum inuenisse eum dicet. Ob idq; pullā ei dedisse. Quā tamen ea de causa nō concessisse, arguit id quod in alio scribit febricitante in quo nihil tale inuenit in pulsu si gnum, de quo ita scribit. Iuuenis erat choleri cæ complexionis, febre continua tertiana laborabat, cui pullam paruam alteratam cum lactuca superasperso succo arantij exhibui. Quid nam de eo sentiendum est, qui cum tenui magis victu alendos esse qui continua febre laborant, quàm qui sua compare interpollata, scribat: in interpollata ab aqua carnis abstinere iubens, in quantū possibile fuerit, in continua tamen sua compare carnes pullæ febricitanti ministrare audet, nullo interueniēte symptomate quod vires deiecerit? Turpe profecto est honesto viro contrarium ei quod dixerit agere. Vnum scriptis posteris mandare, aliud operibus exercere. Necesse enim est aut altero aut virobiq; falsus deprehendatur. Sed melius fuerit in hac re Galenū in libro de febribus ad Glauconem vt iudicē admittere, an à carnibus auis abstineat nec ne, sed de ijs hactenus. Nō enim id ago vt medicos dicos carpam: quod si voluissem, ampla nobis dabatur area, quae charta longiore exponsceret. Ob id dedita opera authorum nomina praetermisi, qui de hac re aliter senserunt. Quod si quis hoc mihi vitio vertat, cedo sententiam quiuis ut voluerit, & mihi quae a tergo mantica est, ut suspendam aequum est cadant, aduncos quoscunque nasos. Mihi ipsi viuere, & more meo agere decreui. Popularem auram & vulgi famam veritatis studio scientiaeque postponens, ratus cum Galeno hac nullam esse honestiorem nec diuinio-rem possessionem.
units.tr: After this, when he treats of the diet for continued choleric fever, he says: "For that fever requires a more delicate and cooler regimen than its intermittent counterpart." Yet in treating a man suffering from continued tertian fever, of choleric complexion, forty years old, with a lean body, in September, with headache, great thirst, and delirium during the paroxysms, he fed him on chicken broth each day during the intermission, after a laxative of manna. Perhaps someone will say that in the second intermission he found the pulse more depressed than it should be, and so gave him broth. But that he did not allow this for that reason is shown by what he writes of another patient with fever, in whom he found no such sign in the pulse, and of whom he writes thus: "He was a young man of choleric complexion, suffering from continued tertian fever, to whom I gave a small broth, altered with lettuce and sprinkled with orange juice." What are we to think of a man who writes that those suffering from continued fever must be nourished on a thinner diet than those with intermittent fever, and who, while in the intermittent fever bidding them abstain from meat broth as far as possible, dares to give chicken broth to a feverish patient in his continued fever, with no intervening symptom that had weakened their strength? It is truly shameful for an honest man to do the opposite of what he says he does. To commit one thing to writing for posterity and to practise another is shameful. For one of the two must be found false, or both. But it would be better in this matter to let Galen, in his book On Fevers to Glaucon, be the judge whether he refrains from birds' flesh or not. But enough on these points. For I do not intend to carp at physicians; if I had wished to, a wide field would have been open to us, which would need a longer sheet of paper. For this reason I have deliberately omitted the names of those authors who have thought otherwise on this matter. And if anyone takes this amiss in me, I leave everyone free to judge as he pleases, and it is right that those who turn up their noses at whatever they like should fall, and that I should hang the wallet that is at my back. I have resolved to live for myself and to act in my own way, putting popular opinion and the talk of the crowd behind the pursuit of truth and knowledge, thinking with Galen that there is no more honourable or more divine possession than this.

units.la: Febri a pituita dulci & salsa quis uictus conueniat.
units.tr: For fever arising from sweet and salty phlegm, what diet is suitable.

units.la: CAPVT XIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: FEBRIS quae a pituita dulci ortum habet, talem exigit victum. Coquito phasianum aut capum aut pullam ijs quae sequuntur. Petroselini, thymi, endiuiae amarae, singulorum manus semis. acetosae manu. vnum, berberorum tantundem, salis parum. antequam ab igne amoueas immitte capillorum veneris aut polytrichi manu. vnu. bulliant quousque
units.tr: A FEVER that arises from sweet phlegm requires a diet such as this. Cook a pheasant, or a capon, or a chicken with the following: parsley, thyme, bitter endive, half a handful of each; one handful of sorrel; barberries, the same amount; a little salt. Before you remove it from the fire, add one handful of maidenhair or polytrichum. Let it boil until

units.la: Sorbitio berberorum permixta sint, da ubi oportet. Cicerum infusorum in aqua tepida per totā noctem manentes, petroselini, thymi, hordei, ana man. unum. radices tres cichorij coquito cum pulla crassa, adiecto aceto, vt supradictum est. Aceti albi partes tres, olei purissimi oliuarum immaturi partes duas, zucari aut mellis partem vnam, his madente vtatur pane. Mirabile est ad omnes febres quae à pituita oriuntur habent. Ventriculum roborat, appetentiam excitat, omnes praeterea naturales actiones adiuuat. Nec praetermittendum his vtile fore, ante cibū oxymelitis cochlearia duo, mellis rosati colati vnum, singulis diebus deglutire ante cibum. Nam plurimum confert stomachum mundificans, & praeparans ad ciborum rectam coctionem.
units.tr: the barberries are mixed in the gruel; serve it when needed. Chickpeas steeped in lukewarm water through the whole night, one handful each of parsley, thyme and barley, three roots of chicory: cook these with a thick chicken broth, adding vinegar as said above. Three parts white vinegar, two parts of the purest oil of unripe olives, one part sugar or honey: let the patient use these with moistened bread. It is wonderful for all fevers that arise from phlegm. It strengthens the stomach, stimulates the appetite, and moreover aids all the natural functions. Nor should it be omitted that it will be useful to swallow two spoonfuls of oxymel and one of strained rose honey before food, each day. For it greatly helps by cleansing the stomach and preparing it for the proper digestion of food.

units.la: A pituita salsa febricitantibus sorbitionē parato, in qua sit duarum sorbitionum facultas, nempe hepaticae & petroselini absque aceto. Caput arietis post decentem eius praeparationem cum hordeo, violis, petroselino, hepatica, pulegio, thymo, passulis, prunis, radicibus cibus cichorÿ, et petroselini coquito. Fac ut crebrò decoctum febricitans sorbeat. Optimum ijs huiusmodi decoctum fuerit, quod nutrit, abluit, & pituitæ salsæ malitiam corrigit. Bonum est ut ij ante cibum zucari offam devorent, parumque aquæ ex hordeo et fœniculo dulci coctæ superbibant.
units.tr: For those with fever from salty phlegm, prepare a gruel which has the virtues of two gruels, namely that of liverwort and that of parsley, without vinegar. After its proper preparation, cook a ram's head with barley, violets, parsley, liverwort, pennyroyal, thyme, raisins, plums, and the roots of chicory and parsley. See that the feverish patient drinks this decoction often. The best decoction for such people is the one which nourishes, cleanses, and corrects the malice of the salty phlegm. It is good that they eat a lump of sugar before food, and drink a little water boiled with barley and sweet fennel.

units.la: Qui à pituita acida laborant, raro febricitant. Nam pauci omnino fumi à re acida eleuantur. Quare ad eos qui à pituita crassa & lenta febricitant sermonem convertere commodius erit. His talem ministrabis victum. Pullam crassam aut capum coquito cum thymo, hordeo, passulis, ut singulorum manip. unum, pulegij duos sumas, bulliant simul ut supra, modico sale ius parato & sorbitionē.
units.tr: Those who suffer from sour phlegm seldom have fever, for few fevers at all are raised from a sour cause. Therefore it will be more fitting to turn our discourse to those who fever from thick and viscous phlegm. For these you will prescribe such a diet. Cook a thick chicken or capon with thyme, barley, raisins, one handful of each, and take two handfuls of pennyroyal; let them boil together as above, and prepare a broth with a little salt, and a gruel.

units.la: Item paretur sorbitio ex furfure quam infra trademus cum de obstructione nobis sermo fuerit, quæ valenter incidit, aperit, & abstergit. Capparibus, ciceribus, radicibus, utpote nimium aperientibus, in principio nō utemur, cum obstructionis suspicio est. Præstat enim ijs quæ abstergunt & leniter inci-
units.tr: Likewise prepare a gruel from bran, which we shall set out below when we speak of obstruction, which cuts, opens and cleanses vigorously. We shall not use capers, chickpeas, or roots at the beginning, since they open too strongly, when there is a suspicion of obstruction. For it is better to mix with the food those things which cleanse and cut gently

units.la: Sorbitio ex pulegio. dunt cum cibis miscere, ut pulegium thymū & id genus alia.
units.tr: Gruel of pennyroyal: thyme and the like.

units.la: Crassiorem victum exposcere tertiana quā quotidianam, contra recentiores medicos.
units.tr: That a tertian fever requires a thicker diet than a quotidian one, contrary to the more recent physicians.

units.la: CAPVT XIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIIII.

units.la: SED qualis victus febri quæ à pituita orQ tum habet conueniat hucusque dictum est. Inuestigare tamen oportet, an verum sit quod nonnulli ex nostris medicis asserunt, crassiorem victum exposcere hanc quàm tertianam simplicem: rationem ad id sumentes longiorem hanc febrem esse quàm tertianam: cunque crassities victus & eius contrarium, à distantia status sumenda sint, fit, ut morbi qui breuius finiantur magis tenuem, qui verò tardius, crassiorem victum exposcant. Præterea labores et symptomata maiora seu vehementiora, cibū magis quàm remissiora prohibere. Iis & similibus adducuntur rationibus ut phlegmatica febre crassiori victu laborantes alant, quàm tertiana. Sed eos à via recta deuiare existimo triplici ratione, duabus ab ipsa febre, tertia à morbi vtraq ytraque causa, coniuncta & antecedente. Et ut apertius res percipiatur, ponamus duos temperatura, ætate, habitu, & reliquis con similes, alterum phlegmatica, alterum chole rica febre laborare. Positis ceteris paribus præter febres & causas vtrasque earundem. Victus vt in superioribus ostensum est, à vir tute sumitur morbo non prohibente: Vnum- que diximus alimoniæ scopum esse, virtutis custodiam, vt à Galeno primo de ratione vi ētus scriptum est in fine. Vbi igitur virtus magis exoluitur, plus alimoniæ requiritur, vt feruetur: quàm vbi minus, fi per mor- bum liceat. At in tertiana febre plus ex- olui corporis virtutem quàm in febre phle- gmatica manifestum est, experientia id o- ftendente. Plus igitur in illa ministrandum est fi per morbum liceat. At licet, nam vna integra die et nocte sunt à morbo liberi ægro tantes, & placidè quiescunt. At in phlegma tica febre contrarium accidit, ita vt neque tanta fiat exolutio, neque tantum per mor- bum liceat. Corripiuntur enim à febre omni die: & non raro prima adhuc non euanescen te, proxima subintrat. Aut parum est id quo quiescunt temporis & id quantumcunq; est, absque motione aliqua intrinseca non est, incipiente ad instantem paroxysmum dispone-re. Vnde fit vt necessum sit febricitantem alere priore febre adhuc non soluta: aut si id spectes, intra limites dispositionis ad futurū paroxysmum nutrias. Cunque hoc vt deteri-us caueant prudentes medici, reliquum est vt primum sit eligendum. At febre adhuc nō euanescente, minus cibi & tenuioris dan dum esse supra ostendimus de mente Hippo-cratis: plus & crassioris, cum corpus ab ea liberum est. Vnde fit vt magis tenui victu in phlegmatica vtendum sit, crassiori vero in cholerica. Ad hæc si humorem pituitosum vlteriori coctione in sanguinem conuerti & nutrire posse intelligas, magis assentes opinio ni huic. Nam in corporibus quæ ab hac detinentur febre, abundant pituitosis excremen tis ventriculus, intestina, & meseraicæ: Quæ resolutioni vtriusque causæ antecedentis & coniunctæ obstant. Hæc nullo alio melius quàm subtili victu consumes, vt rectè senserit, qui vsque ad septimum subtili victu hos transfigere præcepit. Quod si antecedentem spectes causam, propter inæqualitatem substantiæ pituitosæ & qualitatis eius diuersitatem, multo plus habet hic natura quod separet, coquat, & conuertat, quàm in cholerica, in qua propter causas contrarias æqualiter putredo concipitur. Ex iis igitur manifestum est magis tenui victu alendos esse qui à pituita, quàm qui à bile febricitant. Iis adde ob multitudinem materiæ quæ vt plurimum in hac febre coincidit, cibū non parum obstare eius subtiliationi, incisioni, & consumptioni. In febre verò cholerica quantum ad biliosi humoris synceri dispositionem attinet, non solum cibum non lædere, verùm & iuuare, et ad reprimendam humoris acredinem, & ad inducendam humori nimis tenui crassitiem debitam. Assenties verum esse quod opinamur, si audias quæ aduersarius de victu agès qui quotidiana febre laboranti conueniat, scribat, citans Hippocratem quarto de ratione victus dicentem, Custodire patientem febrem hyemalem in fame oportet. Per hyemalem febrem eam intelligit, quæ fit à phlegmaticis humoribus similibus naturæ hyemis. Hæc ille. Quod si ita est, ut ille Hippocratem intelligit. Subtilior victus in phlegmatica, quàm in tertiana exhibendus est. In tertiana enim non custodimus ægrum in fame. Sed re vera Hippocrates aliter quàm ille contra se perperam opinatur, intellexit. Nam Hippocrati non de omni febre hyemali sermo est, sed de illa quæ prava affert symptomata: ut patet ex iis quæ dixit, Lingua aspera redditur, prehendunt animi defectiones. Hunc iubet symptomatum non febris ratione ægrum in fame seruare. Hæc ipsemet sentit, cum dicit, Huic tametsi febris remitti consueuerit, in eo tamen qui per famem fit cruciatu conseruare ægrum oportet. Neque per famem solum inediam intelligas, sed victum qui solis adhibetur potibus. Nam λιμοκτονία vel abstinentiam omnimodam significat, vel eam saltem quæ in potibus solis fit victus rationė: vt Galenus citato loco scripsit. Ā manu igi-tur aduersarij oblatam nobis palmam renui-mus, malumus quam victrici manu decerpsi-mus. Ad rationem quam adducit pro se ad-uersarius de distantia & propinquitate sta-tus, iam supra diximus. Sciendumque non o-mni febre instituendam victus rationem pe-nes status distantiam, sed solum in ijs quæ aut continuitate aut symptomatum causa pe-riculum intra dies aliquot vitæ afferunt. At tertiana, & præcipuè exquisita, citra peri-culum est, vt ab Hippocrate in primo cōmen tario de morbis vulgaribus accipimus. Quan-to autem ab hac degenerat, mixtione phle-gmatis cum biliosō humore non absque peri-culo aliquo febris est. Nam quotidiana, siue ea nocturna, siue diurna sit, eo non vacat, vt ab eodem discimus. Quapropter ratione peri-culi quod in phlegmatica febre est, tenui ma-gis victu eos, qui ea detinentur, alere oportet: vt in superioribus adduximus de mente Hip-pocratis in eo, Quod si dolor aliquis vel periculum aliquod comparuerit. Quod si in hac re Galenum vt iudicem quis admittat, scio aduersarium non obtenturum. Nam legimus eum auium carnes, oua, & pisces petrosos, gallorum testiculos, & similia concedere ei qui tertiana febre laborat. Verùm in primo ad Glauconem de quotidiana agens, victum incisuum administrare iubet. Talem minus nutrire quàm prædicta manifestum est.
units.tr: So far I have said what diet suits a fever that arises from phlegm. We must nonetheless examine whether it is true, as some of our own physicians assert, that a tertian fever calls for a coarser diet than a simple tertian. They base this on the argument that this fever lasts longer than a tertian. Since coarseness and fineness of diet are to be judged from the distance of the state, it follows that diseases which end more quickly call for a finer diet, and those which end more slowly call for a coarser one. Moreover, greater or more violent labours and symptoms forbid food more than milder ones do.
