By such arguments and others like them they are led to think that patients with a phlegmatic fever should be fed with a coarser diet than those with a tertian. But I hold that they go astray from the right path for three reasons: two arising from the fever itself, and a third from the cause of the disease, both the conjoined and the antecedent cause. To make the matter clearer, let us suppose two people alike in temperament, age, habit and the rest, one suffering from a phlegmatic fever and the other from a choleric fever. Everything else being equal, apart from the fevers and their respective causes. As I showed above, diet is taken from strength, provided the disease does not forbid it. We also said that the aim of nourishment is the preservation of strength, as Galen writes at the end of the first book of On the Method of Nourishment. Where strength is more depleted, more nourishment is needed to keep it up than where it is less depleted, if the disease allows. Now it is plain, and experience shows it, that in a tertian fever the strength of the body is depleted more than in a phlegmatic fever. More must therefore be given in the former, if the disease allows. And it does allow, for patients are free from the disease for one whole day and night, and rest quietly. In a phlegmatic fever the opposite happens: the depletion is not so great, and the disease does not allow as much. For they are seized by fever every day, and often before the first has faded, the next comes on. Or the time in which they rest is short, and however long it is, it is not free of some inner motion, since it is spent preparing for the approaching paroxysm. Hence it is necessary to feed the feverish patient while the earlier fever is still unresolved, or, if you look at it that way, to nourish him within the limits of the arrangement for the coming paroxysm. Since prudent physicians take care to avoid the worse outcome, what remains is that the milder option must be chosen. While the fever has not yet faded, less food and a thinner diet must be given, as we have shown above according to the mind of Hippocrates; more and coarser food when the body is free of it. So it follows that a thinner diet should be used in a phlegmatic fever, and a coarser one in a choleric fever. Besides, if you understand that the phlegmatic humour can be further concocted and turned into blood and nourish the body, you will agree more readily with this opinion. For in bodies held by this fever the stomach, intestines and mesenteric vessels abound with phlegmatic excrements, and these hinder the resolution of both the antecedent and the conjoined cause. Nothing consumes these better than a subtle diet, as he rightly judged who ordered that these be carried through to the seventh day on a subtle diet. If you look at the antecedent cause, because of the unequal substance of the phlegmatic humour and the diversity of its quality, nature here has much more to separate, concoct and convert than in a choleric fever, where putrefaction arises equally because of the opposite causes. From these things it is clear that those who are feverish from phlegm must be fed with a thinner diet than those feverish from bile. Add to this that, because of the quantity of matter which for the most part coincides in this fever, food is no small obstacle to its attenuation, division and consumption. In a choleric fever, however, as far as the disposition of pure bilious humour is concerned, food not only does no harm but actually helps, both to restrain the sharpness of the humour and to give the overly thin humour its proper thickness. You will agree that what we hold is true if you hear what our opponent writes about the diet suitable for a patient with a quotidian fever, citing Hippocrates in the fourth book of On the Regimen, who says: "A patient with a winter fever must be kept in hunger." By a winter fever he means one that arises from phlegmatic humours, like the nature of winter. So far he. If that is so, as he understands Hippocrates, a subtler diet should be given in a phlegmatic fever than in a tertian. For we do not keep a tertian patient in hunger. But in truth Hippocrates meant something other than what our opponent wrongly supposes against himself. For Hippocrates was not speaking of every winter fever, but of the one that brings bad symptoms, as is clear from what he said: "the tongue becomes rough, and fainting of the spirits seizes them." He orders that the patient be kept in hunger on account of these symptoms, not on account of the fever. He himself feels this when he says: "Although the fever is usually remitted in such a case, nevertheless the patient must be preserved from the torment caused by hunger." Nor should you understand by hunger only total fasting, but also a diet which consists only of drinks. For λιμοκτονία [limoktonia] means either complete abstinence, or at least a regimen that consists only of drinks, as Galen wrote in the passage cited. Therefore we decline the palm offered to us by our opponent; we would rather not take it than take it by a victor's hand. As for the argument from the distance and nearness of the state which our opponent brings forward in his favour, we have already spoken of it above. It should be known that a diet is not to be instituted according to the distance of the state in every fever, but only in those which, either by continuity or because of their symptoms, put life in danger within a few days. A tertian, especially a pure one, is free of danger, as we learn from Hippocrates in the first commentary on Epidemics. But the further it degenerates from this, through a mixture of phlegm with bilious humour, the more the fever involves some danger. For a quotidian fever, whether it is nocturnal or diurnal, is not free of this, as we learn from the same author. Therefore, because of the danger present in a phlegmatic fever, those held by it must be nourished with a thinner diet, as we have adduced above according to the mind of Hippocrates in the words: "But if some pain or some danger should appear." If anyone admits Galen as judge in this matter, I know our opponent will not win. For we read that he allows the flesh of birds, eggs, rocky fish, cocks' testicles and similar things to one suffering a tertian fever. But in the first book To Glaucon, dealing with the quotidian, he orders a diet of thin foods to be given. It is plain that such a diet nourishes less than those mentioned.

units.la: Ex ijs aliquis recte colliget, in tertiana nô pura, vbi bili pituita est admixta, subtiliore victum competere quàm in ea quæ exquisita est. Qua in sententia Galenus est eodem libro, vbi de victu per cibum & potum agens, inquit: In non certis tertianis prohibere oportet magis, inquantum possibile est, ita vt neque ægritudinem augeamus, neq; prosternamus patientis virtutem tempori ampliori affligendam. Id præterea ab eo percipimus cum in huiusmodi non certis tertianis singulis alternis diebus febricitantes solummodo alere iubet. Quod in pura tertiana non cõsuluit. Quod ergo tenui magis victu qui à febre a febre phlegmatica, quàm qui à tertiana detinentur indigeant satis ostensum est.
units.tr: From these things someone may rightly gather that in a tertian which is not pure, where phlegm is mixed with bile, a subtler diet is appropriate than in one that is pure. Galen agrees with this view in the same book, where, speaking of diet by food and drink, he says: "In tertians that are not certain, one must forbid as much as possible, so that we neither increase the illness nor cast down the patient's strength, which must be worn down over a longer time." We further gather from him that when, in such uncertain tertians, he orders the feverish to be fed only on alternate days, he did not give this advice for a pure tertian. Therefore it has been sufficiently shown that those held by a phlegmatic fever need a thinner diet than those held by a tertian.

units.la: An in febre phlegmatica procedendum sit tenui uictu ad septimum usque, ut arbitrati sunt antiquiores Arabum.
units.tr: Whether in a phlegmatic fever one should proceed with a thin diet until the seventh day, as the older Arabs thought.

units.la: CAPVT XV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XV.

units.la: SED operæpretium erit via speculationis inquirere quæ nam victus forma in quotidianis competat. Nam inter recentiores medicos non conuenit in hac re. Aliqui antiquiores insequentes tenui victu alere febricitantes vsque ad septimū iubent. Ab hoc ingrossare victum præcipiunt vt virtus resiciatur idque gradatim. Cunq; ad ingrossationem debitam augmento peruentum sit, subtiliori victu tuntur vsque ad statum. Alius non solum primis septem diebus, sed per totum ad declinationem vsque iubet, dicens: Non oportet vt comedat pullas, neque coturnices: subintelligit quidam neque alias carnes donec quiescat febris ab acuitate sua & violentia. Alius dixit, Neq; subtilibus aut subtiliter diaetetur, ne virtus infirmi deficiedo molestetur. De iis qui subtilem amant victum, quidam aquam hordei ad tres dies consuluit. Qui post hunc se cuti sunt medici, per tres totum principium morbi intelligunt. Quidam ex Arabibus non spernendus author consulit ut per hebdomadam regatur aeger ex aceto & oleo rosarum, zucaro, menta, & oleribus, radice ficlæ et si milibus. Ab alio tamen ex Arabibus antiquiore medico hanc habuit opinionem, dicen-
units.tr: But it will be worth the effort to inquire, by way of speculation, what form of diet is fitting in daily practice. For the more recent physicians do not agree on this point. Some of the older writers, following on, direct that feverish patients be nourished with a thin diet until the seventh day. After this they advise thickening the diet, so that strength may be restored, and this gradually. When the thickening has reached the due increase, they return to a more subtle diet until the state [of the fever]. Another directs that this be done not only for the first seven days but throughout the whole course, until the decline, saying: It is not right to give chicks or quails; one must understand, nor other meats, until the fever has abated from its sharpness and violence. Another said: Neither should they be fed on subtle foods, nor on a subtle regimen, lest the strength of the sick person fail and be harmed. Among those who favour a subtle diet, one advised barley water for three days. The physicians who followed after him reckon the whole beginning of the disease as three days. One of the Arabs, a writer not to be despised, advises that the patient be kept for a week on vinegar and rose oil, sugar, mint and herbs, the root of ficaria, and the like. Yet another of the Arabs, an older physician, held this opinion, saying:

units.la: te: In febre phlegmatica subtilia regime usq; ad septimu diem. Et si vides eam diminutam
units.tr: "In phlegmatic fever, a subtle regimen until the seventh day. And if you see it diminished

units.la: diminutione multa, procede hac via. Si vero
units.tr: by a great diminution, proceed in this way. But if

units.la: non vides eam minui, ingrossa regimen secun-
units.tr: you do not see it lessen, thicken the regimen according to what seems best to you,

units.la: dum quod tibi videbitur, quoniam inuetera-
units.tr: since it will grow inveterate, and there is doubt about the failure of strength."

units.la: bitur, et est dubium de casu virtutis. Sunt & plures qui diuersa sentiunt, sed longu esset omnium percurrere opiniones. Sed ante quam in hanc messem nostram immittamus falce. Dicere necessariu duco, unde tanta inter medicos discordia in victus exhibitione in hac febre orta sit, ut a communi ratione quae chronicae febri qualis victus competat ostendit, dit, discedant. Causa est vt supra tetigimus communis materiæ abundantia, eugetiens vt plurimum in hac febre: Quæ vtriusque causæ, antecedentis & coniunctæ, præparationem, consumptionēq; remoratur. Hanc esse in ventriculo, intestinis, meseraicis: & in sanguinem conuerti posse si cõtagium corruptionis non acceperit certum est. Hæc propter eius lentorem & tenacē adhærentiam nõ potest clystere aut vllo alio medicamento incisiuo citra commotionem & læsionem melius erat dicari quàm subtili victu. Nam tenui victu non solum hanc putant consumere, sed et antecedentis materiæ bonam partem, naturæ alimentum sumente conuerso crudo humore in sanguinem. Nam vt supra tetigimus, putredo in phlegmate inæqualiter concipitur, propter partium substantiæ diuersitatem, vnde natura multum habet quod separet. Vt ergo medici experiantur phlegmatis putrescentis dispositionem, nempe aptum sit vt actione naturæ ad bonũ reduci possit, nec ne, subtili victu febricitantes regunt ad septimum vsque. Considerantq; tunc virtutis dispositionem multum aut parum aut nihil sit imbecilliorfacta. quod si parum aut nihil imbecillitatis incurrerit, & cum hoc materiam morbi dispositiones naturales recepisse medicus coniecerit, sciet humorem aptum nutrication, actionique naturæ cedentem, & hac via procedendum esse ad sanationem vsque. At si contrarium eueniat, a subtili victu cessandum, naturamq; crassiori reficiendam, vt vires assumat contra malum et fortem hostem. Signum siquidem est, putredine humorem vasta correptum esse: quapropter ineptum nutricationi esse, contumaciscq; resistentiæ. Vtraque ergo de causa crassiori victu iudicant alendum febricitantem. Quod si quod medio loco est eueniat, vt virtus imbecilla fuerit, humor autem dispositionem naturæ receperit, paulo crassiori victu febricitantem ales, vt natura roboretur: sed minus crasso quàm in prædicto. Etsi & alia causa huius controuersiæ. Febrem hanc chronicam ex sui natura esse, & non absque periculo. culo, vt Græci & Arabes medicitestantur. Quia longa est, crassum victum exposcit. ob periculum verò quod affert, ob paroxysmorum quotidianam invasionem, & eorum longitudinem, & oris ventriculi laesionem ad nauseam disponentem, tenuem. Vbi enim aliquod vitæ periculum imminet attenuandum esse victum nos docuit Hippocrates primo de ratione victus, & primo de morbis vulgaribus. Cum ergo hæc ita se habeant, nō ex æquo hæc victus difficultas in omni phlegmatis specie accidet. Nā in acetoso, minus quàm in dulci, & quàm in naturali: at in vitreo ad huc acetoso minus. In salso adhuc multo minus. Nam in omnibus præter naturalem & dulcem pituitæ speciebus materiæ communis multitudo non coiungitur. Nutricationi præterea parum aptæ sunt. Quo fit vt in iis præter rationem sit subtili victu per septem dies uti. Præsertim in ea quæ à pituita salsa ortum habet. Tum in ea summatim, in qua materiæ communes pituitosæ in ventriculis, intestinis & vijs ductuum existentes, ineptæ sunt nutrication, ob prauam earum dispositionem: quarum in huius operis initio mentionem fecimus. In quibus non parum læduntur febricitantes ex subtili victu per hebdomadam.
units.tr: There are also many who hold different views, but it would be too long to run through all the opinions. But before we put the sickle to this our harvest, I think it necessary to say whence such great discord among physicians about the giving of diet in this fever has arisen, and to show what diet suits chronic fever by common reasoning, and why they depart from it. The cause is, as we touched on above, the abundance of common matter, which generally abounds in this fever, and which delays the preparation and consumption of both kinds of cause, the antecedent and the conjoined. It is certain that this matter lies in the stomach, the intestines and the mesenteric vessels, and that it can be turned into blood if it has not taken on the contagion of corruption. Because of its viscosity and tenacious adherence, it cannot be dislodged by a clyster or any other incisive medicine without disturbance and injury; it would be better to be treated with a thickening diet than with a subtle one. For by a subtle diet they think not only that this matter is consumed, but also a good part of the antecedent matter, since nature takes its nourishment by converting the crude humour into blood. For, as we touched on above, putrefaction is conceived unevenly in phlegm, on account of the diversity of the substance of its parts, so that nature has much to separate out. Therefore, in order that physicians may test the disposition of putrescent phlegm, whether it is apt to be brought by nature's action to good, or not, they keep feverish patients on a subtle diet until the seventh day. And they then consider whether the strength has been weakened much, or little, or not at all. If little or no weakening has occurred, and the physician has concluded with this that the morbid matter has received natural dispositions, he will know that the humour is apt for nourishment and yields to nature's action, and that one must proceed in this way to the cure. But if the contrary happens, one must cease the subtle diet and restore nature with a thicker one, so that it may gain strength against the disease and a strong enemy. For it is a sign that the humour has been seized by putrefaction over a wide area, and therefore is unfit for nourishment and obstinate in resistance. On either ground, then, they judge that a feverish patient should be fed a thicker diet. But if the middle case occurs, namely that the strength is feeble while the humour has received the disposition of nature, feed the feverish patient with a somewhat thicker diet, so that nature may be strengthened, but less thick than in the aforesaid case. There is also another cause of this controversy. This chronic fever is by its nature not without danger, as the Greeks and Arabs testify. Because it is long, it calls for a thick diet; but because of the danger it brings, on account of the daily onset of the paroxysms and their length, and the injury to the mouth of the stomach which disposes to nausea, it calls for a thin one. For where some danger to life threatens, Hippocrates taught us that the diet must be made thin, in the first book of the Regimen and in the first book of the Epidemics. Since these things stand thus, this difficulty of diet will not arise equally in every kind of phlegm. For in the acid kind it is less than in the sweet, and than in the natural; in the glassy and still acid kind it is less; in the salt kind, much less still. For in all species of phlegm except the natural and the sweet, the mass of common matter is not joined together. Moreover, they are scarcely apt for nourishment. Hence it comes about that, in these cases, to use a subtle diet for seven days is against reason, especially in the kind that arises from salt phlegm. Then, in general, in that kind in which the common phlegmy matter, existing in the stomachs, intestines and the passages of the ducts, is unfit for nourishment on account of its bad disposition, of which we made mention at the beginning of this work, feverish patients are not little harmed by a subtle diet for a week.

units.la: In summa in omni febre logæ terminationis, cum materia nutricationi est inepta ex absti-nentia, aut subtili victu, febricitantes graui-ter læduntur. Ea siquidē grauis noxa non est qua morbus vires assumit, sed qua corporis virtus exoluitur, morbi dispositione nihil aut parum in melius addente. Id enim manifestū est. nam si hominem qui sic afficiatur, sola inedia per aliquot dies serues, multo eum imbecilliorem reddes, humore pituitoso parum in melius addente. Crassus enim humor & frigidus natura longo indiget tempore, vt co-ctionem recipiat: præcipue cum longe à pro-pria natura est. Quare citius virtutem corporis in deterius subtili victu adduces, quàm morbum in melius. Cum ergo hæc ita se habeant, grauemque noxam febricitantes incurrere ostenderimus à subtili victu, cū humor nutricationi ineptus est, nisi perpetuo aliquo signo aut signis id discernere valea-mus, dementis profecto est aliquid agere alicuius commodi gratia, sub periculo maioris damni. Quod si citra virium dispendiu adipisci posse alia via speres, qua materias communes absumas, & antecedentes, si opus fuerit, non ne illam amplectendam esse merito quis existimabit, quapropter cum signum certum firmum non habeamus, quo a prima die discernamus humoris dispositionem, an ad nutritionem sit aptus nec ne, multo melius est & aegrotantibus salubrius, communi via & regia circa victus rationem procedere, citra aliquod virium incommodum, quam aegrotantem per discriminum compendia ducere. Adde quod si hoc detur ut a primo die humoris natura cognoscas aptam esse nutritioni, si materiae communis adest abundantia, & hanc quoque subtili victu consumere speres, prius pu-tredo in antecedentis materiae altum penetrabit, quam natura communem absoluerit. Longe melius profecto est, clystere quae in inferiori continentur vetere evacuare, lenitiuo manna aut floris cassiæ cū oxymelite aut melle quæ in superiori sunt. Hoc si semel aut bis vsus fue ris cum victu vt oportet incisiuo, intra dies tres materias communes absumes, licet earū abundantia detur: Et interim materiam antecedentem non penitus neglexisti. Horum si quidem lenitiorum quæ acutior pars est ad iecur venas, & renes festinat, ad materiāq́ antecedentem cui obuias non parum iuuat. Quibus ij qui subtili victu suos nutriunt febricitantes vti non possunt. Nam ieiunantes non oportet laborare. Quod si communes nō adsint materiæ, antecedentis autem bonam nutrire posse partem conieceris, optimū esse iudico subtilem victum administrare. Vipote quo natura plus temporis in opere impendit, antecedentemq́ue ob id materiam citius apparabit, bonum separans & sibi accipiens, prauum ad expulsionem præparans. In subtili præterea victu incisiuas qualitates et abstergentes inuenias, quibus in magis nutriente victu similes non reperies. Sed difficilis admodum est coniectura dispositionis humorum morum qui iam putredinem conceperunt, an sint ad nutritionem apti, néc ne, nisi id experientia ostendente discamus. Qua in re nō ex pectandum esse septenarium duco, sed melius ita agere: Cum ex signis pituitam naturalem aut dulcem esse, putredinemque non profundè infixam in materia conieceris (quod ex febris vehementia, longitudine, & ipsius inceptione & finitione, praeterea ex symptomatibus & ex colore faciei, & aliis percipies:) parato statim clysterium ad hunc modu: Centaureai minorem, chamaemelu, hyssopum, maluas, hordeum excorticatum, contusum, in aqua & oleo communi ad æquas partes, bulliant quousque consumpta sit aqua, olei residentis vncias decem accipito, adipis anatis aut capi, & mellis, singulorum vncias tres, salis parum, quantum possit substineat. Ab excretione dato oxymelitis vnciam vnam, mellis rosati colati vnam & semis, aquæ de coctionis seminis fœniculi dulcis duas & semis, misce, dato bis eadem die. Sequenti auro ra floris cassiæ aut mannæ vnciam vnam et semis, dissoluta in aqua decoctionis seminis fœniculi dulcis, thymi & hyssopi, oxymelitis vncias duas dato hora quietiori diei secunda. Quod si bibere potione renuerit, fac tres bolos cum zinziber & zucaro, quæ postquam deglutierit, sorbeat oxymelitis cochlearia septem. Cunque hæc peregeris ægrum symmetro victu seruato eo modo quo supra dixi mus. Hoc est crassa sorbitione ex decocto pulte & ex carnibus eius. Die tertio syrupū bis dato, & similem victu exhibeto. Quarto die clysterium ministrato & simili victu febrici tantem alito.
units.tr: In sum, in every fever of long course, when the matter is unfit for nourishment, feverish patients are gravely harmed by abstinence or a subtle diet. For that grave injury is not one by which the disease gains strength, but one by which the strength of the body is worn away, the disposition of the disease adding little or nothing for the better. This is clear. For if you keep a man so affected on fasting alone for some days, you will make him much weaker, while the phlegmy humour gains little or nothing for the better. For a thick and cold humour by its nature needs a long time to receive concoction, especially when it is far from its own nature. Therefore you will sooner bring the strength of the body to a worse state by a subtle diet than the disease to a better one. Since these things stand thus, and we have shown that feverish patients incur grave harm from a subtle diet when the humour is unfit for nourishment, unless we can distinguish this by some constant sign or signs, it is surely madness to do something for the sake of some advantage at the risk of greater loss. But if you hope to attain by another way, without loss of strength, the consumption of the common and antecedent matter, if need be, who would not rightly think that this way ought to be embraced? Therefore, since we have no certain and firm sign by which we may discern from the first day the disposition of the humour, whether it is apt for nourishment or not, it is far better, and more wholesome for the sick, to proceed by the common and royal way in regulating the diet, without any inconvenience to the strength, than to lead the sick person by the shortcuts of danger. Add that if it be granted that from the first day you can know that the nature of the humour is apt for nourishment, and if there is an abundance of common matter, and you hope to consume this too by a subtle diet, the putrefaction of the antecedent matter will first penetrate deeply before nature has finished with the common matter. It is certainly far better to empty by a clyster what lies in the lower parts, with the old [clyster], and in the upper parts with a mild purgative of manna or cassia flower with oxymel or honey. If you use this once or twice, along with a diet suitably incisive, within three days you will consume the common matter, however great its abundance is given to be; and meanwhile you will not have wholly neglected the antecedent matter. For of these milder remedies, the more active part hastens to the liver, the veins and the kidneys, and it greatly helps against the antecedent matter, which it meets. Those who feed their feverish patients on a subtle diet cannot use these remedies, for one must not labour the fasting. But if common matter is not present, and you suppose that the antecedent matter, or a good part of it, can be nourished, I judge it best to administer a subtle diet. For nature spends more time on the work by this means, and so the antecedent matter will be prepared more quickly, separating the good and taking it to itself, and preparing the bad for expulsion. Moreover, in a subtle diet you will find incisive and detergent qualities, which you will not find in a diet that is more nourishing. But it is very difficult to conjecture the disposition of humours that have already conceived putrefaction, whether they are apt for nourishment or not, unless we learn this from experience showing it. In this matter I think we should not wait for the seven days, but do better to act thus: when from the signs you have conjectured that the phlegm is natural or sweet, and that the putrefaction is not deeply fixed in the matter (which you will perceive from the violence and length of the fever, from its beginning and ending, besides from the symptoms, the colour of the face, and other signs), immediately prepare a clyster in this manner: lesser centaury, chamomile, hyssop, mallows, barley husked and crushed, boiled in water and common oil in equal parts until the water is consumed. Take ten ounces of the remaining oil, and three ounces each of duck or capon fat and honey, with a little salt, as much as it can bear. After the evacuation, give one ounce of oxymel, one and a half ounces of strained rose honey, and two and a half ounces of water from a decoction of sweet fennel seed; mix, and give twice the same day. On the following morning, give one ounce and a half of cassia flower or manna, dissolved in the decoction of sweet fennel seed, thyme and hyssop, with two ounces of oxymel, at the quieter hour of the second day. But if he refuses to drink the potion, make three boluses with ginger and sugar, and after he has swallowed these, let him sip seven spoonfuls of oxymel. When you have done these things, keep the sick person on a thick diet in the way I said above; that is, thick sops of broth, and the flesh of the same. On the third day give the syrup twice, and give a similar diet. On the fourth day administer the clyster and feed the feverish patient on a similar diet.

units.la: Verum à quarto die ad septimum hoc victu ægrotantem nutrias: Cicerum electorum man. tres, ordei duos, infundito in aqua tepida per totam noctem in testa recenti, proiiceq; aci. albi tantū vt aqua acetosa redda tur. In crastinū olei purissimi antiqui quantum satis misceto, petroselini, thymi, singulorum man. vnum, salis parum, coquito ad lentum ignem. Vtere decocto ter in die, et cū pane sorbitiunculam facito. Propinabisq; ante cibum mellis rosati colati cochlearia duo, oxymelitis vnŭ vt supra diximus. Hoc victu vtitor ad septimŭ vsq;. Quo temporis interuallo nec purgáte medicamento, nec clysteri vteris. Die octauo & vires infirmi et ægritudinis dispositionē cōtemplare. Si nullam differentiam inueneris sensibilem ad vndecimum ita transi. Quod si tunc ægrotantis vires tusparum fuerit imbecillior, morbi autem dispositio in melius plus addiderit, perge hac victus ratione. Si aliter eueniat, crassiori vtitor victu. Et quia bona hominum pars vnum duntaxat victum per dies aliquot ferre non possunt, sunt & qui cicera odio habent, cibum alium apponemus huic proposito maxime idoneum, quo vti possunt qui tenui victu in hac febre per dies aliquot procedendŭ esse iudicant. Petrosełini, berberorum, singulorum man. vnum, coquito in aqua modicâ quantitatis &c. in qua duo ova bullire tandiu sinito, vt satis dura reddantur, fac colatură cuius accipito partes tres, olei purissimi vnius semis, aceti vnă, zuçari vnă, cum pane fiat sorbitio ad lentum ignem. De subti li igitur victu qui ad dies septem ab antiquis Arabum medicis obseruatur satis sint dicta.
units.tr: But from the fourth day to the seventh, nourish the patient on this diet. Take three handfuls of selected chickpeas and two of barley, and soak them in warm water all night in a fresh earthen pot, then add enough white vinegar to make the water sour. The next day add as much of the purest old olive oil as is needed, one handful each of parsley and thyme, and a little salt, and boil it over a slow fire. Give the decoction three times a day and make a little sop with bread. Before food, give two spoonfuls of strained rose honey and one of oxymel, as we said above. Keep to this diet until the seventh day, and during this interval use neither a purgative medicine nor an enema. On the eighth day, consider the patient's strength and the state of the disease. If you find no noticeable change, pass on to the eleventh day in the same way. But if by then the patient's strength has become somewhat weaker while the disease has improved more, continue with this diet. If it turns out otherwise, use a thicker diet. And since many people cannot tolerate one diet for several days, and some hate chickpeas, we will give another food, very suitable for this purpose, which those may use who judge that a thin diet must be continued for some days in this fever. Take one handful each of parsley and barberries and boil them in a moderate quantity of water, in which two eggs are left to boil until they are quite hard. Make a strained liquor and take three parts of it, one and a half parts of purest oil, one part of vinegar and one part of sugar, and make a sop with bread over a slow fire. So much has been said about the thin diet which the ancient Arab physicians observe for seven days.

units.la: Febri quartanæ quis uictus competat.
units.tr: For quartan fever, what diet is suitable.

units.la: CAPVT XVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVI.

units.la: SED qualis victus ijs qui à quartana destinentur febre conueniat, iam percurramus. Hæc à triplici humore ortu habet, nempe ab atra bile quam sanguinis secem rectè quidam nuncuparunt. Et vt plurimum fit, nulla alia precedente febre. Fit etiam à bilis croceæ & à pituitæ incensione, & hæ duæ species quartanam notham seu non puram efficiunt, succesu aliarum febrium, scilicet tertianæ & quotidianæ. Fit etiam ex sanguinis adustione. Verum ex incensione melancholiæ naturalis atram bilem posse fieri certum est, sed quod ab ea generetur febris quartana non recipimus. De hoc alias differendi aptior dabitur locus.
units.tr: But let us now run through what diet suits those who are destined for quartan fever. This fever arises from three humours, namely from black bile, which some have rightly called the dregs of the blood. It usually arises with no preceding fever. It also arises from the burning of yellow bile and of phlegm, and these two kinds make the quartan fever spurious or not pure, as it follows other fevers, namely tertian and quotidian. It also arises from the burning of blood. It is certain that black bile can be produced from the burning of natural melancholy, but we do not accept that a quartan fever is generated from it. We will have a more suitable place to discuss this elsewhere.

units.la: Nunc quem victu singulæ species exigant dicamus. Iis qui à naturali melancholia febricitant, bricitant, hanc ministrato sorbitionem: Pulegij, scolopendrij, hepaticæ, passularum enucleatarum singulorum man. unum, coquito cum pulla crassa, parum antequam ab igne amoueas, immitte florum borraginis mā. unū. Coquantur simul, quousque sint permixta, croci modico adiecto, ius dato febricitanti. Ex reliquo fac sorbitionem.
units.tr: Now let us say what diet each kind requires. For those who are feverish from natural melancholy, give this broth: of pennyroyal, hart's tongue, liverwort and stoned raisins, one handful of each; boil them with thick broth, and a little before you remove it from the fire, add one handful of borage flowers. Let them boil together until they are well mixed, add a little saffron, and give the broth to the feverish patient. From the remainder make a thin broth.

units.la: Iis qui intemperie frigida & sicca labo- rant, conuenit pulegij, chamæmeli, scolopen drij, hepaticæ, singulorum man. unum, passu larum enucleatarum unum, coquito cum ca po, aut pulla crassa, adiectis floribus borragi nis, fac ut supra. Cuncq; omnia perco�considerata erunt, decoctum colato, cuius accipe libras tres, me dullæ cruris vituli libræ vnius semis, bulliant ad lentum ignem quousque permisceantur.
units.tr: For those who suffer from a cold and dry intemperament, pennyroyal, chamomile, hart's tongue and liverwort, one handful of each, and one handful of stoned raisins, are suitable. Boil them with broth of capon or thick broth, add the borage flowers, and proceed as above. When everything has been boiled through, strain the decoction, and take three pounds of it with one and a half pounds of marrow from a calf's shin. Let them simmer over a slow fire until they are well mixed.

units.la: Dato ut sorbeat bis in die aut ter. quod si iuuenibus aut alijs natura calidis cibum similem parare velis, loto chamæmeli vtere vio lis, cū pullis duobus, reliqua exerce ut supra.
units.tr: Give it to be sipped twice or three times a day. But if you wish to prepare a similar food for young people or others who are naturally hot, use the washed chamomile in the same way, with two young chickens, and prepare the rest as above.

units.la: Aceti albi libram vnam & semis, passularum enucleatarū man. unum, pulegij, chamæmeli, conquassatorum ana man. vnum et semis, infunde in acetum per diem & noctè, deinde parum coquito & colato. Hoc acetum dicatur pulegij.
units.tr: Take one and a half pounds of white vinegar, one handful of stoned raisins, and one handful and a half each of pennyroyal, chamomile and crushed (herbs). Infuse them in the vinegar for a day and a night, then boil briefly and strain. This vinegar is called pennyroyal vinegar.

units.la: Huius accipe partem vnam, olei amygdalarum dulcium receter extracti partes tres, zucari albi partes duas, coquito in dupilciua se quousque permixta fuerint, dato cochleario quinque vt sorbeat ter in die. Quod si caput arietis coquas cum pulegio, chamæmelo, passulis, scolopēdrio, quod aliâs ceterach Arabes nuncupant, efficies ius & sorbitionem satis conuenientem ad siccum affectum. In Anglia expertum est mixtionem vini & lactis his prodesse facta distillatione. Calidâ et humidam aquam ex ijs fore ratio demonstrat. Qua sanari posse eos qui frigida & sicca intemperie laborant verisimile est, si parum abscesserint à naturali temperie.
units.tr: Take one part of this, three parts of oil of sweet almonds properly extracted, and two parts of white sugar. Boil them in a double vessel until they are well mixed, and give five spoonfuls to be sipped three times a day. If you boil a ram's head with pennyroyal, chamomile, raisins, hart's tongue (which the Arabs otherwise call ceterach), you will make a broth and a thin soup well suited to a dry condition. In England it has been found helpful to mix wine and milk for these, with distillation carried out. Reason shows that the water from these will be warm and moist. It is likely that those who suffer from a cold and dry intemperament can be cured by it, if they have departed only slightly from natural temperament.

units.la: Quod si quartana à bili adusta ortum habeat, hoc victu vtere. Si inuenis fit.
units.tr: But if the quartan fever arises from burnt bile, use this diet. If it is for a young person.

units.la: Accipe hordei excorticati ab vtroq; corti ce man. vnū & semis, violarum recentium, hepaticæ, hepatica, chamaemeli, singulorum man. unum, coquito cum duobus pullis crassis quantum satis, deinde parum antea quàm ab igne amoveas, addito florum violarum man. tres, colato accipitoque huius decocti libras tres, medullae cruris vituli libræ vnius semis, coquantur omnia simul donec permisceantur, dato vt ter in die sorbeat.
units.tr: Take one and a half handfuls of barley hulled from both husks, one handful each of fresh violets, liverwort, and chamomile. Boil them with two thick chickens as much as is enough; then, a little before you remove it from the fire, add three handfuls of violet flowers. Strain, and take three pounds of this decoction with one and a half pounds of marrow from a calf's shin. Let all of them boil together until they are mixed. Give it to be sipped three times a day.

units.la: Sorbitio quoque ex pedibus vituli decoctis cum hordeo, violis, hepatica, pulegio, scolopendrio aut polytricho, passulis, croco, valde utilis est iis qui à bile adusta febricitant, cum coquuntur donec tenerrimi reddantur.
units.tr: A thin broth made from boiled calf's feet with barley, violets, liverwort, pennyroyal, hart's tongue or polytrichum, raisins and saffron is also very useful for those who are feverish from burnt bile, when it is boiled until the feet become very tender.

units.la: Aquæ decoctionis florum violarum, aut borraginis libram vnam, amygdalarum dulcium, & nucleorum persicorum singulorum vncias tres, excorticentur & triturentur diligenter, & exprimito in decoctum toties donec aqua albescat, butyri recentis multoties loti vncias tres, zucari albi quantum satis sit, cinamomi parum, bulliant ad lentum ignem donec permixta sint.
units.tr: One pound of water in which violet or borage flowers have been boiled; three ounces each of sweet almonds and peach kernels, peeled and carefully crushed, and pressed into the decoction again and again until the water turns white; three ounces of fresh butter washed many times; as much white sugar as is enough; a little cinnamon. Let them simmer over a slow fire until they are mixed.

units.la: Lactucas quoque crudas ex melle offeres iis, ut cum libuerit devorent. Iis ante cibum dato syrupi violarum purissimi vncias tres, vinum album dilutum ex aqua decoctionis polypodii recentis, superbibant.
units.tr: Offer them also raw lettuces in honey, so that they may eat them whenever they like. Before food, give them three ounces of the purest syrup of violets, and let them drink afterwards white wine diluted with the water of a decoction of fresh polypody.

units.la: Iis qui quartana ex phlegmate adusto laborant sorbitionem parato, ex pulla crassa cum chamaemelo, pulegio, thymo, passulis, satureia, postquam herbas iam coctas abstulerris, axungiae ab anate recenter extractae, aut capisti illius copia non detur, immitte vncias tres, longi piperis grosso modo contriti grana tria, bulliant simul adiecto croci modico. Ius propina vbi oportet, ex residuo fac sorbitionem.
units.tr: For those who suffer from quartan fever from burnt phlegm, prepare a broth from thick chicken broth with chamomile, pennyroyal, thyme, raisins and savory. After you have removed the herbs once they are cooked, add three ounces of goose fat freshly extracted, or, if that is not available, of capon fat, and three grains of long pepper coarsely crushed. Boil them together, adding a little saffron. Give the broth to drink when it is needed, and make a thin broth from the remainder.

units.la: Sorbitionem praeterea ex furfure cum chamaemelo, pulegio et melle administrato. Quam in fine huius libri cum de obstructione nobis sermo fuerit trademus.
units.tr: Moreover, a thin broth of bran with chamomile, pennyroyal and honey is to be given. I will set it down at the end of this book, when we come to discuss obstruction.

units.la: Pinguis arietis ceruicem, satureia, chamaemelo, pulegio, tribusque allijs integris ciceribus & sale coquito, cunque herbas abstraxeris, addito adipis anatis, aut capi recentis partem quintam, croci parum fac vt supra.
units.tr: Take the neck of a fat ram, savory, chamomile, pennyroyal, and three other whole chickpeas, and boil them with salt. When you have removed the herbs, add a fifth part of duck fat or fresh capon, and a little saffron, and proceed as above.

units.la: Capum pinguissimum cum chamæmeli tribus man.coquito, & cum sale & croco fac vt bulliat sufficienter, consulito ægrotanti ut bis aut ter in die magnum sorbeat haustum calidum. Commodissima his sorbitio hæc est, ad alios vsus etiam vtilis. Ante cibum ijs da to mellis violacei cochlearia quinque.
units.tr: Boil a very fat capon with three handfuls of chamomile, and with salt and saffron make it boil sufficiently. Advise the patient to take a large warm draught of it to sip twice or three times a day. This broth is most convenient for these patients, and is also useful for other purposes. Before food, give them five spoonfuls of violet honey.

units.la: Iis qui quartana ab adußione sanguinis la borant, hunc administrabis victum. Hepati cæ man.tres, hordei ab vno cortice exuti, ca pillorum veneris recentis, prunorum, singu lorum man. vnum, passularum enucleatarū vnum, eupatorij quod aliâs agrimonia à Dio scoride dicitur, foliorum pentaphylli singulo rum vnum & semis, coquito simul cū duo bus pinguissimis pullis, aut iuuene capo, fac vt supra. Ante cibum sorbeat syrupi violarū cochlearia tria, syrupi borraginis cochlearia duo simul mixta.
units.tr: For those who suffer from quartan fever from burning of the blood, you will prescribe this diet. Three handfuls of liverwort, barley peeled of one husk, one handful each of fresh maidenhair, and of plums; one and a half handfuls of stoned raisins; one and a half handfuls of eupatorium, which Dioscorides calls agrimony; and of cinquefoil leaves one and a half handfuls each. Boil these together with two very fat young chickens or a young capon, and proceed as above. Before food let the patient sip three spoonfuls of syrup of violets and two spoonfuls of syrup of borage mixed together.

units.la: Qua specie quartanæ tenui sit utendum ui ctu ad uigesimum usque diem.
units.tr: In which kind of quartan fever the thin diet is to be used, up to the twentieth day.

units.la: CAPVT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: INTER medicos circa victum qui quar-tanæ cõpetit nõ satis conuenit. sunt qui ma-gis crasso in initio quàm in augmento, et hic quàm in statu vtendum esse contendant, con-tinuarum febriū rationem, ad omnia febri-um genera cõmunem facientes. Sunt qui con-tra censeant, nempe in principio magis tenui et crassiori semper ad statum nutriendos esse ægrotantes, in eo autem tenuius multò reficiendum esse. Sunt & alij mediæ opinionis, qui à principio ad aliquot dies tenuiter febrici-tantes reficiunt, deinde crassiorem exhibent victum, multoties quartanas febres in prin-cipio curatas esse tenui victu dicentes. Si e-nim febris parum sit duratura, & crassum victum in principio humoris resolutionem prohibentem ministraueris, longiorem eam efficies. Quodsi longa futura sit, parum no-cebis aut nihil, si tenui victu quo virtus non absumatur per dies aliquot vtaris. Qui ita sentiunt pullorum carnes ad vigesimā diem prohibent.
units.tr: Among physicians there is no great agreement about the diet suited to quartan fever. Some hold that a thicker diet should be given at the beginning rather than during the increase, and during the increase rather than in the height of the fever, thus treating it by the method common to all continued fevers. Others think the opposite: that at the beginning the sick should always be nourished with a thinner diet, becoming thicker up to the height of the fever, but that during the height they should be restored with a much thinner diet. Others take a middle view: they nourish the patient with a thin diet for some days from the beginning, and then give a thicker diet, often saying that quartan fevers are cured at the start by a thin diet. For if the fever is unlikely to last long, and you administer a thick diet at the beginning, which hinders the resolution of the humour, you will make it longer. But if it is to be long, you will do little or no harm if you use a thin diet for some days, by which the strength is not wasted. Those who think this way forbid the flesh of young chickens until the twentieth day.

units.la: Ego autem quid sentiam citra disputatio-nis nis contentionem dicam. In quartanis quæ aliarum febrium successu fiunt, locum non esse huic dubitationi arbitror. Nō est enim quod virtutem multum defatigatam à præcedente febre, & aduentu alterius, iam languescentem, tenui victu exoluas, ad certamen eam denuò impellens. Neque si detur ut tenui victu laborantem ad vigesimum diem serues, & morbi materiam absumas, ob id hominē à febre liberabis. Nam in quartanis febribus quæ post alias succedunt, solent ab intemperie aliqua, viscera molestari, quæ morbum fouet, & durationis eius præcipua est causa. Hac enim stante in vasis, iocinere, aut liene, continua fit humoris regeneratio. In quartana igitur febre quæ successu alicuius alterius facta est, præcipuus sanandi hominis scopus est, ut viscera ad pristinam reducamus temperiem. Cæterùm alterantia medicamina cibis immiscere melius esse supra ostendimus, quàm si nuda exhibeamus, ut cō sueuere triuiales nostri temporis medici, quo rū nisi quis syrupos, apozemata, distillationum aquas, electuaria, purgatia medicamen ta exhibeat, si nihil bono medico dignum e- gisse putat. Et hinc fit ut ex reiteratione mul tiplici illa fastidientibus infirmis, in ventri- culo non recte ad actum reducatur, quae cau sa est ut infeliciter operentur. Quapropter non solum non prodesse tunc temporis, sed nocere certum est, cum multoties propter il la cibos fastidiant infirmi, & imbecilliores ideo reddantur. Quicunque igitur medicam artem ita exercent, necesse est ut multoties ægrotantes lædant, præsertim si corporibus imbecillibus & à longis ægritudinibus tabe- factis obuient. Qui vero Hippocratem sequu tur, & eius in primo de morbis vulgaribus acquiescunt consilio, dicentis: In hoc te exer ceto ut saltem si non possis ne quid noceas, longe melius esse existimabunt ut huiusmodi corporibus non tenuem victum, non medi- camina alterantia, si nuda offerantur, sed iis quae nutriunt, & bonum generant chymu, ea miscere, quae paulatim valeant morbificas partium intemperies euertere. At in febre quartana quartana quæ repente incipit, subtilem vi-ctum vtpote qui facilioris coctionis sit, ad dies viginti qui septem continet quartanæ pe-riodos; probo: Hunc dico, pullorum inscula, sorbitiones, eo quo supra parauimus modo.
units.tr: I shall state my own view, without the heat of dispute. In quartan fevers that arise after other fevers, I think this question has no place. There is no reason to starve a strength already greatly worn down by the previous fever, and now growing faint with the onset of another, and so drive it into a new contest. Nor, if you keep a patient on a thin diet up to the twentieth day and use up the matter of the disease, will you free the man from fever on that account. For in quartan fevers which follow others, the viscera are usually troubled by some intemperance, which nourishes the disease and is the principal cause of its duration. For while this persists in the vessels, the liver or spleen, the humour is continually regenerated. Therefore, in a quartan fever which has arisen after some other fever, the chief aim in healing the man is to bring the viscera back to their former temperament. Moreover, I have shown above that it is better to mix alterative medicines with foods than to give them plain, as our common physicians of this age are accustomed to do, who, unless they give syrups, apozems, distilled waters, electuaries, and purgative medicines, think they have done nothing worthy of a good physician. And hence it happens that, from this repeated multiplicity of remedies, which the sick find distasteful, the stomach does not properly perform its action, and this is the reason why they work unhappily. Therefore it is certain that these remedies not only do no good at that time but do harm, since the sick often loathe food on account of them and are thereby made weaker. Whoever practises the medical art in this way must necessarily often injure the sick, especially if they encounter weak bodies wasted by long illnesses. But those who follow Hippocrates, and obey his counsel in the first book of the Epidemics, saying: "In this exercise yourself so that, if you cannot do good, at least you do no harm," will judge it far better that for such bodies one should not give a thin diet or alterative medicines offered plain, but should mix them with things that nourish and generate good chyle, which will gradually overcome the morbid intemperaments of the parts. But in a quartan fever that comes on suddenly, I approve a subtle diet, as being easier to digest, for twenty days, which contain seven periods of the quartan. I mean this: the soft flesh of young chickens, broths, and soups, prepared in the manner we set out above.

units.la: Rationem inquirit quare diuersis cibarijs prauæ substantiæ aliquando sanentur ij qui quartana febre laborant, occasiones que singulorum remediorum signis docet cognoscere.
units.tr: He inquires why sick people suffering from quartan fever are sometimes cured by various foods of poor substance, and teaches how to recognise the occasions for each remedy from its signs.

units.la: CAPVT XVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: SED cum quartana febre compertum sit cibaria diuersa prauæ substantiæ, liberare multoties eos qui hac febre laborant: Ita vt alios, virides ficus, aut vuas nocturno rore madentes, alios carnes porcinas ad satietatem comedentes, sanatos esse sciamus, & plurima alia id genus. Ad medicum arbitror attinere, si horum non nesciat rationes, vt ijs quando occasio affuerit vti sciat. Prætereà quantum medico dedecoris est, si eo per plures dies & menses varijs remedijs abuso, & nihil proficiente accedens rusticus salsuginem offerens sanet ægrotum medicum & eius artem irridens: tantum ei gloriæ est ea non nescire quæ multoties admirabili vi homines repente ab antiquis liberant ægritudinibus. In febre igitur quartana rationem reddere conabimur. Quamobrem diversa cibaria quæ prauæ substantiæ sunt, aliquoties quartanam soluant. Secundo illud aliquoties, signis manifestis describemus, ut cum occasio affuerit eā arripere diligens possit medicus. Paroxysmorum causa, motus est humoris putrescentis, cui naturæ expulsio coniuncta est. Putridi humoris est, quodam putredinali irritamento naturam stimulare. Facultatis vero expultricis, humorem certis periodis irritantem, meliori quo possit modo, depellere. Contingit autem ut cum per sensiles repente excrementorum copia feratur partes, horrorem, rigorem, aut frigus excitari. Motus ergo ille quo dammodo medius est inter naturalem, quia natura sola naturaliter operante fit (ut cum post coëtricis facultatis actionem agit) in naturalem, quia sola causa præternaturalis fit, vt cum mouetur furiosus humor. Nec igitur à sola natura fit paroxysmus: nec à solo humoris irritatiõis motu, periodicæ febres contingunt. Vterq; enim motus & naturæ et humoris cõcurrunt, in paroxysmo, vt perdo ẽte à Petro Aponensi peritissimo medico scriptum est, in hæc verba. Quantum (inquit) ad naturam particularem comparando, inquantum scilicet motus humorum ex actione virtutis dependet, tempora periodorum in morbis nõ sunt determinata, nec vnius modi, vt possimus dicere quod morbus factus ex cholera habeat motu̅ de tertio in tertium, & de phlegmate in die, et ex melancholia in quartum, immò respectu cuiuslibet humoris hæc tempora sunt, & possunt esse diuersa. Ita vt aliquando periodice morbus factus ex vno humore eueniat secundum dies, aliquando secundū menses, vel annos. Quod ideo cõtingit, quia virtus expulsiua suam operatur actionem quocunque tempore superfluũ ei occurrit, irritans eam per sui lesionem ad actum expulsionis, & quia tale superfluum potest diversis temporibus occurrere, cum eius generatio dependeat à causis diversis, nunc vno tempore occurrentibus, nunc alio & alio, iccirco tempus periodici motus non est vnum, sed diversum. Similiter & aggregatio superfluitatis quæ dependet ex defectu virtutis digestiuæ non habet tempus præcise determinatum, sed diversum secundum diversitatem eorum quæ occurrunt intrinsecus & extrinsecus, Hæc ille. Interceptio ergo paroxysmorum dupliciter contingere potest, aut ratione expultricis facultatis, aut ratione superflui aggregati. primum adhuc dupliciter, aut quia non stimulatur, facto sensu hebetio ri, aut ob fortem animi motionem expultricem ab opere suo perturbantem. Ad primum modum reducuntur medicamenta ea, quæ virtutes habent narcoticorum, vt theriaca, athanasia, philonium Romanum, quæ sanare quartanas febres experientia comperium est. Id etiam discimus ex Galeno ijs diversis locis vtente, ad sanationem febris quartanæ.
units.tr: But since it has been found in quartan fever that various foods of poor substance often free those who suffer from this fever, so that we know some have been cured by eating green figs or grapes moistened with night dew, others by eating pork to their fill, and many other things of this kind, I think it belongs to the physician, if he does not ignore the reasons for these things, to know how to use them when the occasion arises. Besides, how great a disgrace it is for a physician, if after many days and months of abusing various remedies with no result, a countryman comes along and cures the sick man by offering salted meat, mocking the physician and his art! It brings him as much glory not to be ignorant of those things which often, by a remarkable power, suddenly free men from old diseases. In quartan fever, then, we shall try to give the reason. Therefore various foods of poor substance sometimes dissolve the quartan. Second, we shall describe in clear signs that these occur sometimes, so that the diligent physician may seize the opportunity when it arises. The cause of the paroxysms is a movement of putrid humour, to which the expulsion of nature is joined. It belongs to a putrid humour to stimulate nature by a certain putrefying irritant; and it belongs to the expulsive faculty to drive out, in the best way it can, the humour that irritates at fixed periods. It happens that when a quantity of excrement is suddenly carried to the sensible parts, a shivering, a rigor, or a chill is excited. That movement is therefore in some measure midway between natural and unnatural: natural, because it is brought about by nature working alone (as when it acts after the action of the constrictive faculty), and unnatural, because it is caused only by a non-natural cause, as when a furious humour is set in motion. Thus the paroxysm is not produced by nature alone, nor do periodic fevers arise from the movement of the irritating humour alone. For both movements, of nature and of the humour, concur in the paroxysm, as has been written in these words by Peter of Abano, a most skilled physician: "As far as the particular nature is concerned (he says), insofar as the movement of the humours depends on the action of the power, the times of the periods in diseases are not determined, nor of one kind, so that we can say that a disease arising from choler has its movement from the third day to the third, and from phlegm on the day, and from melancholy on the fourth; indeed these times are with respect to each humour, and may be different. So that sometimes a disease arising from one humour occurs periodically every few days, sometimes every few months or years. This happens because the expulsive power performs its action at whatever time a superfluity occurs to it, irritating it by its injury to the act of expulsion; and because such a superfluity can occur at different times, since its generation depends on causes which sometimes occur at one time and sometimes at another, the time of the periodic movement is not one but varied. Likewise the accumulation of superfluity, which depends on a defect of the digestive power, does not have a precisely determined time, but a varied one according to the variety of things that occur within and without." So far he. The interruption of paroxysms can therefore happen in two ways: either by reason of the expulsive faculty, or by reason of the accumulated superfluity. The first happens in two ways again: either because the faculty is not stimulated, its sense having become dulled, or because of a strong emotion of the mind that disturbs its work of expulsion. To the first kind belong those remedies which have the powers of narcotics, such as theriac, athanasia, and the Roman philonium, which experience has shown to cure quartan fevers. We learn this also from Galen, who uses them in various places for curing quartan fever.

units.la: Ad secundū reducitur quod ab aliquibus dictum ob vehementem lætitiam plures quartanam euasisse febrem, sensoria facultate munere suo non fungente. Ob quamlibet prædictarum causarum virtus expultrix non irrita, expulsionis opus non aggreditur. Non facta expulsione interrūpitur paroxysmus, vt supra habitum est. Ratione superflui dupliciter, aut quia non aggregatur, aut si aggregatur euacuatur. Primo modo adhuc dupliciter, aut ob vigorem virtutis coctricis, aut ob defectum causæ aggregatricis. Et hoc adhuc dupliciter, aut vt efficiens, aut vt materia. Hoc modo alimus febricitantem febre quartana cibarijs, quæ suapte natura in melancholiam facile conuerti non possunt. Talia sunt cibaria calida & humida, non quæcunque, sed quæ non facile in melancholiam conuertantur, vt pulla gallinacea, capus, arietis caro. Sunt alia quæ calida & humida sunt & longè absunt, vt in melancholiā conuerti possint, talia sunt olea matura, præcipuè amygdalarum, sesamæ, axungiæ anatis,
units.tr: To the second belongs what some have said, that many have escaped quartan fever through a violent joy, the sensory faculty not performing its function. Whatever the cause of these, if the expulsive power is not roused, it does not undertake the work of expulsion. If expulsion does not take place, the paroxysm is interrupted, as has been said above. By reason of the superfluity, again, it happens in two ways: either it does not accumulate, or if it accumulates, it is evacuated. In the first case there are again two possibilities: either from the strength of the concocting faculty, or from a lack of the cause that gathers it; and this again in two ways, either as efficient cause or as matter. In this way we nourish the patient with quartan fever with foods which by their own nature cannot easily be turned into melancholy. Such are warm and moist foods, not all of them, but those that are not easily turned into melancholy, such as young hen, chicory, and mutton. There are others which are warm and moist and are far from being able to turn into melancholy, such as ripe olives, especially of almonds, sesame, duck fat, dried figs, and the like. All such warm and moist foods, which yield with difficulty to the melancholic nature, if they are easily overcome by the constrictive faculty, cure quartan fevers in both ways, namely by removing the efficient cause and the matter.

units.la: Ec 3 ficus aridæ, & similia. Omnia ergo huiusmo di cibaria calida & humida difficulter melancholicæ naturæ cedentia, si cum hoc à coËtrice facultate facilè vincantur, vtroq; modo quartanas febres sanant, nempe efficientis causæ & materiæ ablatione. Id est quia melancholici humoris intemperiem, aggregatri cem scilicet causam, contraria qualitate enertunt. Et quia vt materia inepta melācho lico humori, cessare faciunt atrabiliarÿ humoris regenerationē. Ad has duas causas reducuntur cibaria à nobis supra scripta, quæ quartana laborantibus administrari iusimus. Hoc modo oleū amygdalarum dulcium cum croco, aceto pauco bibitum, sanat quartanas. Hac de causa destillatione vini & lactis plures quartanam euasisse compertum est in Anglia. Tunc ob fortitudinem coctricis facultatis ægrotantes euadunt quartanā, cum maior pars humoris qui ad paroxysmū aggregatur, suppeditatur, à cibis & potibus quibus quotidie laborans vtitur. Cunque hoc conieceris facultatem roborare coctricem, quarquartanæ remedium esse scias. Roboratur du pliciter, aut absolutè, aut respectu alicuius ci bi, & potus. Pro comperto est ea quæ nimis delectant, & placent, melius à coctrice co qui, ab attractrice trahi, à retentrice retine ri, vberiusq; multo nutrire, & minus super fluì ab ijs quàm ab alio implacido accrescere. Hoc modo cibum quem auidissimè febrici tans appetat quartanam posse sanare expe rientia compertum est. Quod si præter hoc quod magno appetatur affectu supra dicta habe at, quæ ad defectum aggregatricis causæ face re diximus, adhuc certius quartanam eradi care posse sperabimus. Hac de causa plurî mos carnis porcinæ vsu, à quartana libera tos fuisse compertum est. Quia enim nimis ap petitur, recte coquitur in ventriculo, iocine re, & venis. quare parum ex ea superflui col ligitur, sed & intemperiem obiter siccà quæ humoris atrabiliarij velut scaturiesfons est, mire corrigit. Soluere igitur quartanam car nem porcinam aliquando posse, ex dictis ma nifestum est.
units.tr: Dried figs, and the like. All such warm and moist foods, which yield with difficulty to the melancholic nature, cure quartan fevers in both ways, namely by removing the efficient cause and the matter, provided they are readily overcome by the concocting faculty. That is, they weaken by their contrary quality the intemperance of the melancholic humour, which is the aggregating cause. And they make the matter unfit for the melancholic humour, so that the regeneration of black bile ceases. The foods written above, which we ordered to be given to those suffering from quartan fever, are reduced to these two causes. In this way oil of sweet almonds with saffron, drunk with a little vinegar, cures quartan fevers. For this reason, the distillation of wine and milk is known to have freed many from quartan fever in England. Patients then escape the quartan through the strength of the concocting faculty, when the greater part of the humour that gathers for the paroxysm is supplied from the foods and drinks they use every day. And when you conjecture that the concocting faculty is strengthened, know that this is a remedy for quartan fever. It is strengthened in two ways, either absolutely or with respect to some food and drink. It is established that things which delight and please too much are better concocted by the concocting faculty, drawn by the attractive faculty, retained by the retentive faculty, and nourish far more abundantly, and produce less superfluous matter than other, less agreeable things. In this way experience has shown that the food which the feverish person craves most eagerly can cure quartan fever. But if, besides being craved with great desire, the food also has the qualities said above, which we said serve to remedy a deficiency in the aggregating cause, we may hope to eradicate the quartan more certainly. For this reason many have been freed from quartan fever by eating pork. Since it is craved so much, it is well cooked in the stomach, liver and veins, so little superfluous matter is gathered from it; and it marvellously corrects the somewhat dry intemperance which is like the fountain from which the atrabilious humour wells up. Thus it is clear from what has been said that pork can sometimes resolve a quartan.

units.la: Quæ absolutè roborant cœlricem facul-tatem, quartanā soluere possunt. Vinum ante omnia, præcipuè odoriferum, id habet vt valenter naturales roborat actiones, vnde ebrietatem posse curare febrem quartanam tum hac de causa, tum sensu facto hebetiori haud dubium est. Curantur similiter quartanæ febres ex superflui aggregati euacuatione. Hoc modo medicamenta melancholiam educentia, vt polypodium, epithymum, senam, corticē, ellebori, sanare quartanas pro comperto est. Hanc partem solū sibi nostræ tempestatis medici reseruarunt, reliquas omittentes, ac si non esset præter illam via alia, qua à quartana liberentur homines. Hoc modo qui vuas maturas nocturno rore madentes ad sanitatem ingerunt, & ficus magnas tempestiua maturitate cadentes, à quartanis febribus liberantur. Hi enim & similes fructus aliquando immodice cient. Cum igitur perceperis ex cibis aut potibus humoris maiorem partem qui paroxysmum efficit suppeditari, dandi ea quæ placent tunc occasio est.
units.tr: Those things which absolutely strengthen the concocting faculty can resolve quartan fever. Wine above all, especially scented wine, has the power to strengthen the natural actions vigorously; hence it is certain that drunkenness can cure quartan fever, both for this reason and because the sense is made duller. Quartan fevers are likewise cured by the evacuation of the superfluous aggregated matter. In this way medicines that expel melancholy, such as polypody, epithymum, senna, the bark, and hellebore, are known to cure quartan fevers. The physicians of our own time have reserved this part to themselves alone, neglecting the others, as if there were no other way besides that by which men are freed from quartan fever. In this way those who take ripe grapes moistened with night dew for their health, and large figs falling at their proper ripeness, are freed from quartan fevers. For these and similar fruits sometimes move the bowels immoderately. Therefore, when you have perceived that the greater part of the humour which produces the paroxysm is supplied from foods or drinks, then is the occasion to give what pleases.

units.la: Illud autem ijs signis percipies. Primo subtiliori te vtente victu per aliquot dies, si immi-nuatur febris magnitudo & vehementia. Secundo, cibo id experieris, qui difficulter in melancholiam conuertatur, aut minimum habeat melancholicæ naturæ. Si enim hoc cibo te vtente per dies aliquot, imminuatur paroxysmus, adhuc certiori coniectura innitêris, à cibis & potibus humoris maiorem partem ad paroxysmum suppeditari. Hoc idê est acsi dicas, si iuxta ciborum quantitatem et qualitatẽ quibus laboras vtitur ita variêt paroxysmi, coniectura assequeris, exhibendi ea quæ ægro tanti placent occasionem adesse. Quare diligenter inquirito quem nam ex cibis febricitans ardenter appetat. Si ex ijs fuerit qui qualitate atræ bili contrarius est, & tali substantia, vt difficulter in melancholiam conuertatur, laboranti porrige hora consueta, quæ ab initio venturi paroxysmi duodecim horis ad minus distet. Comedat pro appetentia citra saturitatem. Quod si cibus quem appetierit melancholicæ naturæ sit, aut in melancholiam facile conuertatur, considerare tu opus est signa coctionis: quæ si sint, dato, eo quo diximus modo: quod si non, modicum illius febricitanti abnegare nolli, sciens non- nulla fieri & plura posse, citra rationem ho- mini manifestam. Parum insuper deterior ci- bus si delectabilis, &c. Quæ facultate expul- tricem respiciunt, tunc sunt administranda cum nimis vigilanti sensoriæ facultati præci- puam continuationis paroxysmorum dederis causam. Tunc aut his quæ aliquâ habent nar- cotici virtutem, aut forti & repentina ali- qua motione, sensum ægrotantis oportet hebe- tescere, animum alio trahendo. Illud percipi- es si primo quænam sint corpora acuti sensus cognoscas. Hæc aliquando iusto quæruntur, quandoq; iniusto. Cum initia paroxysmorum grauiter ferunt, rigore, frigore, vehemen- ter quatiuntur, molestantur, ipsam autem febrem paruam, magnitudine, duratione, ve- hementia intelligas. Scito sensoriam in ijs fa- cultatem parumper obdormire remedium esse. Sunt tales ij qui acerrima sunt præditi imaginatione, ita vt multoties cogitantes ride- ant, facies mutent, oculos manus ue moueat. Iis paruæ occasioni, imaginatio coniuncta, multoties paroxysmum efficit. Quare hos ta les curabis si eorum mentes alio trahas, vt mihi in Anglia contigit.
units.tr: Now you will perceive this by the following signs. First, if, while you use a more delicate diet for some days, the size and violence of the fever diminish. Second, you will test the food that is less readily turned into melancholy, or has the least melancholic nature. For if, while you use this food for some days, the paroxysm diminishes, you may rely on the still more certain conjecture that the greater part of the humour that supplies the paroxysm comes from foods and drinks. This is the same as if you were to say: if the paroxysms vary in step with the quantity and quality of the foods you live on, you will conjecture that the occasion for giving what pleases the patient is at hand. Therefore carefully inquire which of the foods the feverish person craves eagerly. If it is one of those that is contrary in quality to black bile and of such a substance that it is turned into melancholy with difficulty, offer it to the sufferer at the usual hour, which should be at least twelve hours before the onset of the coming paroxysm. Let him eat for appetite, short of satiety. But if the food he craves is of a melancholic nature, or readily turns into melancholy, you must consider the signs of concoction. If these are present, give it in the way we have described; if not, do not refuse the feverish person a little of it, knowing that some things can be done, and more can be done, without any manifest reason. Moreover, a somewhat worse food, if it is pleasant, etc. Those things which affect the expelling faculty must be administered when you have given the principal cause of the continuation of the paroxysms to a sense that is too watchful. Then the patient's sense must be made duller, either by things that have some narcotic power or by some strong and sudden motion, drawing the mind elsewhere. You will perceive this if you first learn which bodies are of acute sense. These are sometimes sought rightly, sometimes wrongly. When at the onset of the paroxysms they bear it heavily, shaken violently by shivering and cold, and you understand that the fever itself is slight in size, duration and violence, know that it is a remedy to lull the sensory faculty a little. Such are those who are endowed with a very sharp imagination, so that while thinking they often laugh, change countenance, or move their eyes or hands. In these, a slight occasion joined to the imagination often produces a paroxysm. Therefore you will cure such people if you draw their minds elsewhere, as happened to me in England.

units.la: § Historia tertianarij curati fallacia quadam, qui imaginationis vi propemodum perierat.
units.tr: A story of a tertian patient, cured by a certain trick, who had nearly perished through the force of his imagination.

units.la: Erat iuuenis habitu gracili, sicco tempera mento, laborans tertiana: cunq; post aliquot dies abire Sondinum decreuissem (nam in ru re erat) ei dicturus accessi, quæ me discedente agere deberet. Cunque finem sermoni imposuissem, tu (inquit) discedis quia me moritu rum certò coniicis. Cunque iureiurando contrarium ostendissem, repente in lecto sedens, vestem et calceos petiuit. Quid inquam cum istis agere vis? Surgere, inquit, an me meis pedibus sustinere valeam, quod si hoc detur abij. Cunque surgens in fenestram, quæ in vi rides campos latè patentes prospectum habebat, concessisset, intuens, animi deliquio captus est. Cunque in lectum portaretur, parumque requieuisset, lachrymis obortis: Domine (inquit) Brude nonne tibi dixi quia morior. Cunque vxorem, clientes & amicos conuocasset, omnibus astantibus dixit: Scitis amici morior, medicus abire vult, vt me morientem non videat. Cunque ei obiecissem, Quid (inquam) mihi dabis, si te ab hoc morbo liberum reddam. Repente miro animi affectu commotus, Pete (inquit) non minus dabo quam postulabis. Cunque peterem dedita opera aliquot aureos: Parum (inquit) pertysti, allato scrinio numerauit pecunias. Quia (inquam) statim soluisti liberalis viri functus officio, non te relinquam prius, quam ad rus concedas & perdices & phasianos aliquot ex tua venatione mecum in domum portem. Hoc audito clamauit, Sanus sum. Cunq; aperte perspexissem hominem acri praditum imaginatione, vt qui modo mortuum se esse putabat, nunc se sanum fateatur, pectore hac versans, modum quo hominem a tertiana liberarem inueni. Die sequenti cum febris hora ra decima eum inuasura esset, nocte ante habito cum vxore & clientibus consilio: iussi vt omnes fenestræ ad horam nonam aperirentur (aperiebantur enim ante sextam) tresque horas hero suffurarentur. Cunque hoc ita decretum esset, mane omnes ex consulto non intrarunt in cubiculum. Cunque vxorem hora octaua vocasset, Quota inquit hora est? illa quintam dicens, dormireque eum iubens abiit. Hora transacta clientem vocans, cum ab eo accepisset horam esse sextam, quiete egit, post horam quam septimam existimabat, accessi. Cunque in sermonibus horā traxissemus, Precor inquam domine Culpepare duas horas quæ ante paroxysmum supersunt ad aleam teramus. Cunque annuisset, lusimus hora vna. Cunque vxor eius rem risu dissimulare non posset, rem omnem homini pandimus. Meridiemque iam esse, duasque horas post paroxysmi tempus, & ita sanatus est.
units.tr: There was a young man of slender build and dry temperament, suffering from a tertian fever. When I had decided to leave Sondinum after some days (for I was in the country) I went to him to tell him what he should do in my absence. When I had ended my talk, he said: "You are leaving because you are certain that I am going to die." When I had shown him on oath that this was not so, he suddenly sat up in bed and asked for his clothes and shoes. "What," I said, "do you intend to do with them?" "Get up," he said, "and see whether I can stand on my own feet; if I can, I will go." Then, rising and going to the window, which looked out over the wide open fields of the countryside, he stood gazing out and was seized by a faint of the spirits. When he had been carried back to bed and had rested a little, with tears streaming down his face he said: "Master Brude, did I not tell you that I am dying?" After he had called together his wife, his dependants and his friends, he said to all who stood by: "You know, friends, that I am dying; the doctor wants to leave so as not to see me die." When I objected to him, "What," I said, "will you give me if I free you from this illness?" he, suddenly moved by a strange emotion of spirit, said: "Ask; I will give you no less than you demand." When I deliberately asked for a few gold coins, he said: "You have asked for too little," and, bringing a casket, he counted out the money. "Since," I said, "you have at once paid me, and have discharged the duty of a generous man, I will not leave you until you go into the country and bring me some partridges and pheasants from your hunting, to carry home with me." On hearing this he cried out, "I am well!" When I had clearly perceived that the man was endowed with a keen imagination, since he who a moment before thought himself dead now confessed himself well, I turned the matter over in my mind and discovered a way of freeing him from the tertian. On the following day, when the fever was going to attack him at the tenth hour, I had, on the night before, taken counsel with his wife and dependants, and I ordered that all the windows should be opened at the ninth hour (for they had been opened before the sixth) and that they should steal away three hours from him. When this had been decided, in the morning they all purposely did not enter the bedroom. When at the eighth hour he called his wife, he asked, "What hour is it?" She, saying it was the fifth hour, told him to sleep and went away. When an hour had passed, he called a servant and, having learned from him that it was the sixth hour, he grew quiet. I went to him after the hour which he thought was the seventh. When we had spent an hour in conversation, I said, "I beg you, Master Culpeper, let us spend the two hours that remain before the paroxysm at dice." When he agreed, we played for one hour. Then his wife could not hide the matter with laughter, and we disclosed the whole business to the man. It was now midday, and two hours had passed beyond the time of the paroxysm, and so he was cured.

units.la: Superesst nunc occasionem designare qua adhibitis iis quæ aluum cient, curetur quartana. Et si à medicis plurimis sciamus signis esse ostensam, nihilominus quia id communi bus non proprijs egere signis, in praesenti tan tummodo libare non ab re erit, ut copleamus sermonem, commune illud medici obseruantes praeceptu, nempe, Concocta medicari & mo uere nō cruda, & c. Item, Inchoantibus mor bis, & c. pharmaco educente vtuntur. Nec itaq; ob id quod morbus statim non curatur, male egisse censebitur. Nam non omnis eua cuatio quae ab arte fit, ideo fit vt illico & agro tans sanetur. Neque etiam euacuationes quae à natura regulariter operante fiunt, hoc ob tinent, sed aut sanant, aut alleuiant, aut in praesenti, aut in posterum. Sic sat est si quae ab arte recte fiunt euacuationes sanent aut alleuient. Occasionem medici signis designa runt, qua pharmaca educentia adhibita al terum duorum efficiunt. Et est cum adest mor bi coctio. Tunc enim euacuatio adhibita vt plurimum illico sanat, aut alleuiat. Praete rea cum materia nimis multa est, euacuatio adhibita alleuiat in posterum. At occasio nem signis designare qua euacuatio adhibita illico sanet, difficile admodum est. Adhuc dif-ficilius eam sensu assequi, vtpote nimis præ-cipitem. At plures scimus qui longas febres passi, medicorum opem inanem diu experti, à rustico filiculam aut ricini semen aut quod uis aliud ministrate repente liberati sunt. In-deque arbitratur vulgus illa pharmaca lon-ge ab iis quibus medici vtuntur abesse, & ea vt sacra veneratur, ignorans quanti sit occasio ad sanationem momenti. Hanc na-ctum medicus secure operari, cito sanare posse certum est, minimo humani corporis damno. Morituris nullius occasionem esse. Adhi-bendi ea quæ aluum cient in quartana aut ali-a longa febre occasionem, in principio mor-bi aut inclinatione quærere oportet. Iis duo-bus temporibus intemperies non est, quæ fe-brem ad longum foveat. Verum quandoq; in-temperies febres præcedit. Oportet ergo vt si-gnis propriis singulas quas in corpore vna-quæq; febris generat intemperies cognoscas. Cum has omnino abesse scies, humorem au-tem collectum in loco vno ex hypostasi laudabili, conijcies occasionem adesse phar-macum offerendi. Fructus autem qui medi-camenti educentis vim habent, plus prodesse quia citra abominationem assumuntur, quin immo appetuntur vt plurimum.
