Quapropter recte in ventriculo ad actum reducuntur, et per totum distribuuntur corpus. Unde quaedam naturali & consueta naturae corporis actione, suum opus agunt. Quare multo commodius id quod noxium est educunt. Contrarium euenit ijs quae cum violentia operantur pharmacis, naturae corporis vim inferentibus, quadam praeternaturali commotione, bonum simul cum malo educentibus. In ea autem commotione noxij contactu bonu posse affici certum est: ac inde fomentum darireci diuae. Quare habita occasione ijs quae citra commotionem educunt vtere.
units.tr: It remains now to point out the occasion on which a quartan fever is cured by the use of agents that purge the bowels. Although many physicians have shown by signs that this is so, nevertheless, since it needs general rather than particular signs, it will not be out of place here to add, in order to complete the discussion, that common precept which physicians observe: "Medicate what is concocted, and do not move what is raw," and so on. Likewise: "When diseases are beginning," and so on, they use a purgative drug to draw the morbid matter out. Therefore one should not be thought to have acted badly because the disease is not cured at once. For not every evacuation made by art brings about recovery of the sick person at once. Nor do evacuations that are made regularly by nature operating have this effect, but they either cure or relieve, either now or in the future. Thus it is enough if evacuations rightly made by art either cure or relieve. Physicians have pointed out by signs the occasion on which purgative drugs, when used, bring about one of two things. And this occasion is when the disease is concocted. For then an evacuation, when applied, usually cures or relieves at once. Moreover, when the matter is too abundant, an evacuation applied relieves in the future. But to point out by signs the occasion on which an evacuation applied would cure at once is very difficult. It is even more difficult to grasp it by the senses, since it is too fleeting. Yet we know many who, having suffered long fevers and having tried the useless help of physicians for a long time, were suddenly freed by a country person who gave them a little wild-carrot root, or castor seed, or whatever else. From this the common people judge that those remedies are far removed from those which physicians use, and they venerate them as sacred, not knowing how great a part the occasion plays in healing. It is certain that a physician who has seized this occasion can operate safely and cure quickly, with the least harm to the human body. There is no occasion for those who are about to die. The occasion for applying purgatives in a quartan or other long fever must be sought at the beginning of the disease or in its decline. At these two times there is no intemperance which would keep the fever going for a long time. But sometimes intemperance precedes the fever. It is therefore necessary that you know by specific signs the intemperance which each fever produces in the body. When you know that these are wholly absent, and that the humour has collected in one place from a laudable deposit, you will judge that the occasion for offering the drug is present. Moreover, the fruits which have the power of a purging medicine benefit more because they are taken without loathing; indeed they are generally desired. Therefore they are rightly brought into action in the stomach and distributed throughout the whole body, and thence by a natural and customary action of the body's nature they perform their work. Hence they expel what is harmful much more conveniently. The opposite happens with those drugs which act with violence, doing violence to the power of the body's nature, by a preternatural commotion expelling the good together with the bad. It is certain that in that commotion the good can be affected by contact with the harmful, and from this a fuel is supplied to the disease. Therefore, when the occasion offers, use those things which expel without commotion.

units.la: Pestilenti febri conuenientem uictum inuestigat.
units.tr: He seeks a diet suitable for pestilential fever.

units.la: CAPVT XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: MALITIA morbi quam Graeci κακοήθεια vocant, dupliciter dicitur, aut actionis, aut resistentiæ ratione. Primo modo malignum dicimus morbum, cum violenta actione substantiam spiritus qui naturæ vnicum est instrumentū exoluit, aut sanguinem ad eorum generationem indisponit. Aut quia pertinaci resistentia vires coquentis facultatis obtundit. Primum malignitatis modum tetigit Galenus in expositione illius, Et refrigerata extrema. Secundum, quarto de methodo medendi, aliquod vlcus cacoëthes, hoc est malæ morigerationis vocans. Pestilentes febres primo modo maligna sunt. Vtroque autem modo febris quæ à carbunculi inflammatione originem habet. Pestilens febris non eam quam reliquæ acutæ febres victus rationem exposcit. Causa est quia tenuem victum in illis, ob id maxime ministramus, vt natura coctioni materiæ morbi fortiter vacet. At in pestilenti febre id diligenter curamus, vt duellum inter naturam & pestilentē humorem caueamus. Nam vt plurimum ex tali certamine natura vincitur, vt scite à Galeno scriptum est in Aphorismis
units.tr: Malignancy of disease, which the Greeks call κακοήθεια [kakoētheia], is spoken of in two ways, either with respect to the action of the disease or with respect to its resistance. In the first sense we call a disease malignant when, by its violent action, it dissolves the substance of the spirit, which is the sole instrument of nature, or makes the blood unfit for generating spirit. In the second sense, it is malignant when, by its stubborn resistance, it weakens the powers of the concocting faculty. Galen touched on the first kind of malignancy in his commentary on the aphorism "And the extremities being chilled." He touched on the second in the fourth book of the Method of Healing, where he calls a certain ulcer cacoëthes, that is, of bad disposition. Pestilential fevers are malignant in the first sense. Fever arising from inflammation of a carbuncle is malignant in both senses. A pestilential fever does not require the same regimen of diet as other acute fevers. The reason is this: in those other fevers we chiefly give a thin diet so that nature may vigorously be free to concoct the matter of the disease. But in a pestilential fever we take great care to avoid a struggle between nature and the pestilential humour. For, as Galen wrote well in the Aphorisms, nature is for the most part overcome in such a contest. He says: "We know that more people are saved by crises than die, unless the constitution is pestilential, etc."

units.la: Ff cum dixit. Nouimus plures ex crisibus sanatos quàm mortuos, nisi pestilens fuerit constitutio &c. Cum ergo hoc itase habeat, cessat in pestilenti febre vna tenuis victus causa. Quinimmo cum hæc febris substantiam spiritus fortiter exoluat, & materiam ad eorum generationem indisponat, oportet vt diligentia omni, prudens medicus & cibo & potu competentibus, materiam generationis spiritus suppeditet. Et quia ab antiquis medicis ostensum est spiritus vnicum esse ad omnes actiones instrumentum, cunque in nullo etsi acutissimo morbo tanta fiat spiritus consumptio ac in pestilenti febre, rectè quis colliget eo cibo vtendum esse qui facillimæ sit coctionis. At huiusmodi cibaria tali sunt substantia, vt prompte huc et illuc mutentur, ita vt rationabiliter verendu sit ne à pestilenti corrumpantur prius contagio, quàm à naturali calido vincantur. Crassa verò cibaria exhibenda nõ sunt, quia à naturali eorũ calido vt pote lãguido vinci nõ possunt. Quæ causa est vt non solum spiritus materiã non ministret, verùm verum & in pestilentem causam addant. Cum necesse sit alterum duorum eis dominari. Quae facillimae coctionis sunt & mediocriter nutriunt vt oua, & carnium succus, fugienda esse videntur. nam promptius à pestilentis contagij vi, quàm à natura vincentur. Difficile igitur nimirum est conuenientem cibū in pestilenti febre reperire. Talem dico qui materiam spiritus abundè suppeditet, facillimae sit coctionis, difficulterque pestilenti cedat contagio. In simplicibus haec inuenire raro admodum est: Quare in iis quae adinuicem miscentur, quod conueniat reperire tentandum est. Iis quidem quae spiritus multitudinē creant, & facilis coctionis sunt, ea miscere quae pestilenti contagio obsistant, oportet. Ea autem sunt, quae natura sunt sicca, & in altum corporis cita penetratione se mergunt exiccantem facultatem toti communicantia. Quod si praeter haec à terguo (videtur locus corruptus) astrictoria polleant vi, qua corporis vias compescant, quodcunq; id sit, pestilenti contagio obstare recte dicetur. Salin primis habere locum vsus ostenditur, quo corpora incorrupta ad longum tempus serua mus. In eo igitur iam dicta percipimus nem- pe exiccationem, penetrationem, & astri- ctionem. Secundum locum habent omnia a- cetosa, ex quibus acetum in primis se offert, deinde succus arantij, & succus maligrana ti acidi. Ab ijs amara, sed quia calida sunt, minus conueniunt. Oua recentia facillime sunt coctionis, & ad generationem spiritus materiam praebent. Ne ergo in pestilente ma teriam conuertantur, ea hoc modo exhibere expediet. Ouum recens integrum immittito in aquam frigidam mixtam cum aceto, ibiq; esse sinito tribus horis, tandem ouum rumpi- to, et album extra mittito, succo arantij aut aceto albo capacitatem impleto, salis tantum addito, vt mediocriter salsum efficias, coqui- to supra cinerem calidum, miscetoque donec crassum reddatur. Vtere eodem cum succo mali citrei loco arantij aut aceti. Item perdi- cis carnosae aut phasiani aut iuuenis columbae viscera effodito, camque sale condito, ita vt perdicem mediocriter salitam efficias, eam sic esse finito die vna in æstate, aut duabus in hyeme. Postmodum in eam mali citrei frusta immittito, & petroselini folia, vt quod inane in perdice est impleatur, eamque ad ignem lentum coquito. Cunque humor intrinsecus extra erumpat, et perdix tota humecta fiat, super eam sal vndique inspergito. Cumque mediocriter assafuerit, humorem qui ab ea deor sum destillauerit digito excipito, experireque an salsus sit: quod si non, adhuc iterum sal inspergito, vt tandem succus mediocriter salsus reddatur. Tandiu ad ignem perdicem esse finito quousque humor exiccetur, postea ab igne amoueto, perdicemque in parua frusta secato, & in linteum demittito, duobusque in contrarium retorquentibus pro viribus totus eius succus extrahatur, quem ægrotanti ministrato. Multum quidem nutrit, spiritus substantiam auget, ventriculum roborat, et pestilenti infectioni valde obsistit. Idem è capo aut pulla gallinacea si illorum non detur copia efficere possis, et aliys motanis passerib.
units.tr: Since this is so, the one reason for a thin diet ceases in a pestilential fever. Indeed, since this fever strongly dissolves the substance of the spirit and makes the matter for generating spirit unfit, the prudent physician must, with all diligence, supply that matter by suitable food and drink. And since the ancient physicians showed that spirit is the one instrument for all actions, and since in no disease, however acute, is there such a consumption of spirit as in a pestilential fever, one may rightly conclude that food should be used which is very easy to concoct. But such foods are of a substance that changes readily hither and thither, so that there is reasonable fear they may be corrupted by the pestilential contagion before they are overcome by the natural heat. Heavy foods, on the other hand, should not be given, because being sluggish they cannot be overcome by their natural heat. The result is that they not only fail to supply matter for the spirit but actually add to the pestilential cause, since one of the two must necessarily dominate them. Foods that are very easy to concoct and give moderate nourishment, such as eggs and the juice of meats, seem therefore to be avoided, for they will be overcome more readily by the force of the pestilential contagion than by nature. It is therefore certainly difficult to find a suitable food in a pestilential fever. I call suitable one that abundantly supplies matter for spirit, is very easy to concoct, and yields with difficulty to the pestilential contagion. Among simple foods such a thing is very rarely found; therefore we must try to find what is suitable among those mixed together. Certainly, among those that create a quantity of spirit and are easy to concoct, we must mix those that resist the pestilential contagion. These are foods that are dry by nature and, by rapid penetration into the depths of the body, sink in, imparting their drying power to the whole. If, in addition to these, from behind, they possess an astringent power by which they check the passages of the body, whatever that may be, they will rightly be said to resist the pestilential contagion. Salt, in the first place, is shown to have this use, by which we keep bodies uncorrupted for a long time. In it, then, we perceive the things just mentioned: drying, penetration, and astriction. In second place are all acid foods, among which vinegar presents itself first, then the juice of the bitter orange, and the juice of the sour pomegranate. Bitter foods are less suitable, because they are hot. Fresh eggs are very easy to concoct and provide matter for generating spirit. So that they may not be turned into pestilential matter, it will be useful to give them in the following way. Put a whole fresh egg into cold water mixed with vinegar, and leave it there for three hours. Then break the egg and put out the white. Fill a vessel with juice of bitter orange or white vinegar, add only enough salt to make it moderately salty, and cook it over a warm ash fire, stirring until it becomes thick. Use the same mixture with juice of citron or lemon in place of the orange or vinegar. Likewise, take the entrails of a fleshy partridge, or a pheasant, or a young pigeon, and season it with salt, so that you make the partridge moderately salted. Let it stand thus for one day in summer, or two in winter. Afterwards put into it pieces of citron and leaves of parsley, so that the empty space in the partridge is filled, and cook it over a slow fire. When moisture breaks out from within and the partridge becomes wholly wet, sprinkle salt over it on all sides. When it has roasted moderately, catch with your finger the liquid that has dripped down from it, and test whether it is salty. If not, sprinkle salt on it again, until at last the juice is moderately salty. Keep the partridge on the fire until the liquid dries up. Afterwards remove it from the fire, cut the partridge into small pieces, put them into a linen cloth, and, twisting the two ends in opposite directions with all your strength, squeeze out all its juice, which you give to the sick person. It nourishes greatly, increases the substance of the spirit, strengthens the stomach, and strongly resists pestilential infection. The same may be done with a chicken or a young hen, if you cannot obtain these, and with other small birds.

units.la: Neque aliquis admiretur, nos & ouum et succos ex carnibus salsa ex consulto efficere. Cum enim obijciens animo voluat, pestilentem febrem naturales priuatim actiones corrumpere, nempe cordis, iocineris, & ventri culi(vt ex vomitu, fluxu ventris, vrinis rubeis conturbatis, & ex inordinato pulsu, ostenditur)pestilentemque infectionem citius ijs partibus quae humidiores sunt communicari(humiditas enim pestilentis contagij fomentum est)haud quaquam praeter rationem esse ea quae diximus existimabit. Quinimmo ab ipsa rerum natura in id ducimur. Eas siquidem corporis partes quae pestilenti contagio affectae sunt, scimus praeter naturam humectas esse, actionesque earum ob id resolui. Quare vel cibaria ipsa natura sicca esse oportet, aut si talia propter duram coctionem non conueniant, salte cibis ea quae exicare valeant sunt miscenda. Sal autem vt diximus omnium est efficacissimum aduersus omnem corruptelam, maximeque humano generi familiare. Quare salsa omnia huic febri conuenire rationalis methodus docet. Neque ob id quod sitim generant reicienda sunt, quinimmo hoc nomine amplectenda. Nam saluberrimum est in hac febre sitire, duplici ratione, & signi & causæ. Indicat enim actionem sensoriæ facultatis oris ventri culi incolumē esse. Sitiens præterea frigida delectatur. Potum autem aquæ frigidæ ijs salubrem esse communis medicorum schola fatetur. Sed non deerunt qui salsa ijs damnent, tanquam febri & eius causæ incommoda. Nam salsa febri non sunt contraria. Potius enim frigida & humida. Nam omnem febrem calidam & siccam esse intemperiem, medici asserunt. Putridus præterea humor nō salsus, sed ijs quæ per aluum, aut vrinam, aut sudores educere possunt extra corpus pellitur. Sed si quis accuratius cuiusque humoralis febris remedia consideret, inueniet, medicum vtraque artis medicæ parte vti, tum ea quæ curat, tum ea quæ præcauet. Frigidam offerens medicus, febrem præsentem curat. Exhibens pharmacum, futuram præcauet.
units.tr: Let no one wonder that we deliberately make eggs and juices from salted meats. For when someone considers in his mind that a pestilential fever corrupts the natural actions of the heart, the liver, and the stomach in particular (as is shown by vomiting, diarrhoea, disturbed red urine, and irregular pulse), and that pestilential infection is passed more quickly to those parts that are more moist (for moisture is the fuel of pestilential contagion), he will judge that what we have said is by no means against reason. Indeed, we are led to it by the very nature of things. We know that those parts of the body affected by pestilential contagion are unnaturally moist, and that their actions are therefore loosened. Hence the foods themselves ought to be dry by nature, or, if such foods are not suitable because of their difficult concoction, then foods that can dry out should be mixed with them. Now salt, as we have said, is the most effective of all things against every corruption, and it is especially familiar to the human race. Therefore reasoned method teaches that all salted things are suited to this fever. Nor should they be rejected because they produce thirst; rather, on this account they should be embraced. For it is most healthful to be thirsty in this fever, for two reasons, both as a sign and as a cause. It indicates that the sensory faculty of the mouth and stomach is intact. Moreover, the thirsty person takes pleasure in cold things. The common school of physicians admits that cold water is wholesome for such people. But there will not be lacking those who condemn salted things for these patients, as harmful to the fever and its cause. For salted things are not opposed to fever; rather they are cold and moist. Physicians assert that every hot and dry fever is an intemperance. Moreover, putrid humour is not salted, but is expelled from the body by those means that can draw it out through the bowels, the urine, or the sweats. But if anyone considers more carefully the remedies for each humoral fever, he will find that the physician uses both parts of the medical art: that which cures and that which prevents. By offering a cooling remedy, the physician cures the present fever; by administering a medicine, he forestalls the future one.

units.la: Vomitum, sudores, vrinas euocans, humore putridum febrem efficientem extra corpus pellit. Poros autem corporis aperiens, aut abundantiam euacuatione minuens, perspirationes liberas efficit. Exindeque praecauet ne vlterius putredinalis affectio graßetur, & sanos corruptela ne afficiat humores. Hoc autem est causam corruptionis tollere. Hocque est vltimum ad quod rationali deuenimus methodo. Idque primum quod opere exequimur. Nempe cum aliquis intra corpus putridus humor sit, febrem efficiens, vt qui sani sunt ne eius contagio afficiantur, humores in primis curare oportet. Si igitur in omni hu morali febre id agere tenemur, multo profecto causatius in pestilenti, quae efficacissima vi quibus obuiat afficit, id in primis nos agere iustum est. Quare non solum iis quae perspirationes liberas efficiunt, nec potionibus & medicamentis quae intro assumuntur (quod alias in aliis febribus ob imbecillem putridi humoris vim fecisse sat est) sed & cibis id tentandum efficere, vt pro virili corruptio-ni niexitialiter grassanti obstemus. At salsa (ut diximus) primum habent locum, vt experientia & ratio ostendunt. Melius si quidem res salsis quàm acetosis seruantur. Efficatius sale quàm aceto. Neq; ideo quod febrilem calorem acuunt, ab eorum vsu cessandum est. Nam prudentis est inter damna minus eligere. Insuper præceptum est nobis à Galeno, in complicatis affectibus, ad id quod vicem causæ habet, aut magis vrget, præcipuam indicationem habendam esse. Quapropter vtraque ratione pestilenti contagio prius obstare debemus: tanquam ei quod magis vrget, & febris futuræ vicem habeat causæ. Medici præterea cibos exiccantes ministrare iubent: vt acetum, & multa quæ potestate astringunt: Vt succus granatorum, arantij, acetosæ herbæ, & similia, quæ omnia humoris corrupti excretioni obstant. Corruptionē grassantem, magis quàm febrem & eius causam respicientes. Ad hæc in pestilenti febre diligenter prospiciendum est ventriculo, vt id quod assumit æger retinere possit, alioquin neq; virtuti opitulari, neque morbo occurre re possimus. Quare eò me hæc adduxit ratio, ut mihi persuasum sit, salitos piscesiis fore ex usu, si sint ex iis qui facile coquatur. Hos si- quidem ventriculum valde exiccare, robora re, appetentiam excitare, sitim immodera- tam inducere, subuersum ventriculu et nau- seantem componere certum est. Cum hæc scri ptis mandarem, mihi relatum est, chirurgum senem in Anglia solitum esse piscibus salitis quos herinches Angli vocant, pestilentia la borantes fœliciter nutrire. Quorum si copia non detur, eorum loco ex paruorum piscium genere utitor, quod sal & fumum melius re- cipiat. Cæterùm oportebit ab usu salitorum piscium ægrotantem admonere, ut à potu hora una abstineat. Postmodum frigidam quantum hauflu bibere possit dato. Vsus hu iusmodi piscium aduersus humiditatem te- nuem corruptam in ventriculo efficacissi- mus est. Quantum autem huiusmodi salitipi sces ventriculum roborent, & nauseantem reprimant, & appetentiam excitent, odor eorum declarat, quo non parū ventriculi appetentia elicitur. Qui ergo ijs assentit rationibus, eis vtatur assis infusis in aceto aut in succo acetosæ herbæ. Carnibus aut sale condi tis quibus borealior Hispaniæ pars vtitur, obid quia duræ sunt coctionis vti consilium non est. Earum tamen succo cum decenter assæ sunt vti melius erit. Spiritus abundè carnium succus generat & ventriculum roborat. Proinde id summo opere cauendum est, ne eundem cibum toties offeramus vt eum fastidiat æger. Quare oportet medicum diuersa cibaria mente concipere, vt eorum singulis vtatur cum opportunum fuerit.
units.tr: Bringing on vomiting, sweating and urine, one drives out of the body the putrid humour that causes the fever. Opening the pores of the body, or reducing the excess by evacuation, one makes perspiration free. From this one guards against the putrefactive affection spreading further and keeps corruption from infecting the healthy humours. This indeed is to remove the cause of corruption, and it is the last thing we reach by rational method and the first thing we carry out in practice. For when some putrid humour is within the body, causing fever, the humours must first be treated so that those who are well are not infected by its contagion. If we are bound to do this in every humoral fever, it is surely much more right that in the plague, which strikes with the most effective force, we should do this first. Therefore not only by those things which make perspiration free, nor by drinks and medicines taken internally (which in other fevers, because the power of the putrid humour is weak, is enough to do), but also by food we must try to resist, as far as we can, the corruption that spreads destructively. But salted things (as we said) have first place, as experience and reason show. Things are indeed better preserved with salt than with acid things, and more effectively with salt than with vinegar. Nor, because they increase febrile heat, should their use be abandoned. For it is the mark of a wise person to choose the lesser of two harms. Moreover, Galen has taught us that in complicated affections the principal indication is to be taken from that which stands in the place of a cause or presses harder. Therefore on both counts we must first resist the pestilential contagion: as that which presses harder, and which stands in the place of the cause of the fever to come. Physicians also order drying foods to be given, such as vinegar and many things that are astringent in power, such as juice of pomegranates, orange, sorrel and similar things, all of which obstruct the excretion of the corrupt humour. In this they look more to the spreading corruption than to the fever and its cause. Besides, in pestilential fever care must be taken diligently of the stomach, so that what the patient takes in can be retained; otherwise we can neither aid his strength nor meet the disease. Hence reason has led me to be persuaded that salted fish will be of use, if they are of the kind that cook easily. For it is certain that these greatly dry the stomach, strengthen it, excite appetite, induce immoderate thirst, and settle a upset and nauseated stomach. When I was committing these things to writing, I was told that an old surgeon in England used to feed, with success, those labouring with plague on salted fish, which the English call herrings. If a supply of these is not available, use instead some small fish, which takes salt and smoke better. But it will be necessary to warn the patient who is eating salted fish to abstain from drink for one hour, and afterwards to give cold water to drink as much as he can. The use of this kind of fish is most effective against thin, corrupted moisture in the stomach. How much such salted fish strengthen the stomach, check nausea and excite appetite, their smell declares, since it draws out no small appetite in the stomach. Whoever therefore assents to these reasons, let him use them roasted and steeped in vinegar or in juice of sorrel. Meats salted or cured, which the more northern part of Spain uses, are not advised, because they are hard to digest; yet it will be better to use their juice when they have been roasted properly. The juice of meat generates plenty of spirits and strengthens the stomach. Therefore this must be guarded against with great care: we must not offer the same food so often that the patient loathes it. Hence the physician must devise varied foods, so that he uses each of them when it is opportune.

units.la: Dulcia omnia & vnctuosa & quæ calida sunt & humida diligenter cauenda sunt. Lentes cum multo aceto, & sale, croco, & petroselino coctæ, vt supra diximus, conueniunt. Granata acida cum voluerit laboranti dato. Soleas conditas salsamento salubriter ijs ministrato: quas ita parabis. Lauato & sale eas conspergito, & oleo coquito, postmodum eas refrigerari sinito, eas tandem in acetum acerrimum infundito. Et frusta mali citrei & limonij & folia lauri proÿcito, quantum earum copia poposcerit. Iis ad diem tertium vtere. Carnes ad hunc modum quæ sub renibus sunt vitulæ sale conspergito & in acetum acre cum origano & mali citrei aut limonÿ segmentis & allÿs infundito. Ad diem quintum percoctarum ad ignem succis vtere vt supra dictum est. Quod si æger carnes huiusmodi edere appetierit parum dato, & cultello minutatim incidito. Simili modo perdices, phasianos, & montanos passeres condire possis.
units.tr: Sweet, oily, and whatever is hot and moist must be carefully avoided. Lentils cooked with much vinegar, salt, saffron and parsley, as we said above, are suitable. Give sour pomegranates to the sufferer when he wishes. Give him soles preserved in brine, which is healthful; prepare them thus. Wash them, sprinkle them with salt, and cook them in oil; afterwards let them cool, and then steep them in very sharp vinegar. Add pieces of citron and lemon and bay leaves, as much as their quantity calls for. Use them for three days. Sprinkle calves' kidney meat with salt and steep it in sharp vinegar with oregano, segments of citron or lemon, and garlic. Use it after five days, cooked, with juices as said above. If the patient wants to eat such meats, give a little and cut them up finely with a small knife. In the same way you can pickle partridges, pheasants and mountain sparrows.

units.la: Quòd allia conueniant in pestilenti consti tutione gratia præseruationis & curationis.
units.tr: That garlic is suitable in a pestilential constitution, for the sake of prevention and cure.

units.la: CAPVT XX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XX.

units.la: EST quidem vnus è nostris qui cum de cibis & potibus ageret qui præseruant ab epidemia, dixit: Non auscultetur opinio illorum qui dicunt allium valere, quia falsa est. quia generat (inquit) fumositatem & su percalpercalfaciendo adiuuat ebullitionem & sanguinem adurit, ex quo adusto generantur apostemata mortifera. Sed non ab re fuerit an allia in pestilentia conueniant gratia præservationis inuestigare. Et postmodum an in cibis miscenda sint gratia curationis. Primum illud quærendum an præseruādus ijs assuetus sit in bona valitudine. quod si sic, haud dubio dimittenda non sunt. Nam imprudentis fuerit hominis consuetudinem in pestilenti constitutione demittere. Nam eius demissionem efficacissimam causam esse à peritissimis medicis ostensum est. Ægrotandi autem occasionem dare in pestilentiali constitutione stultissimum est. Quod si ex ijs fuerit qui alijs aliquoties vtatur, & quandoque non (vt saepe accidit) neque capitis grauitatem, nec præter solitum se calidiorem ab eorum vsu sentiat, huic profecto ad præseruationem pestilentis contagij allia administranda fore, prout cis aliâs vsus est, censeo, præsertim si hyems sit. Hoc vt ostendamus, experientiam aliorum in medium adducere non ab re erit.
units.tr: There is indeed one of our own people who, when discussing foods and drinks that protect against epidemic, said: "Let not the opinion of those be heeded who say garlic is good, for it is false, because it generates (he says) fumes and, by over-heating, helps the boiling and burns the blood, and from this burnt blood deadly abscesses are generated. But it will not be out of place to inquire whether garlic should be used during pestilence for the sake of prevention, and afterwards whether it should be mixed into foods for the sake of cure. First, it must be asked whether the person to be protected is accustomed to it while in good health. If so, it should certainly not be discontinued, for it would be the act of a foolish man to give up a habit during a pestilential season. Indeed, the most learned physicians have shown that giving it up is a very effective cause of illness, and to offer an occasion for sickness during a pestilential season is the height of folly. But if he is one who uses it now and then, and who (as often happens) feels neither heaviness of the head nor more heat than usual from its use, I judge that garlic should be given to him for protection against the pestilential contagion just as he has used it before, especially if it is winter. To show this, it will not be out of place to bring forward the experience of others.

units.la: Messores æstate feruente incalescëte solepost meridiem allia cũpane vorant, vt minus ab æstu offendantur, & in sudores eorum minus soluantur corpora. Nam alliÿ vi continentis æstui fortius obsistunt, quàm ÿ qui eis vsi nõ fuerint. Adde quod ab externo frigore idem corpora tuetur, & ei minus obnoxia ea reddit. Hos effectus allium sola vt agat qua litate fieri nonpotest. Nam in symbolizantibus facilior est transitus. Necesse est ergo hoc inesse allio ob id, quia calidum roborat naturale: quo fit vt corpori validius dominetur. Ita vt ab externa causa quæcunque sit difficilius vincatur. Fieri quidem nequit, vt exterior occasio in corpus humanum suam imprimat actionem, calido naturali valido existente. Quod cum ita sit, quis negabit pro pestiferi contagiï aut cuiusuis impressionis præseruatione, ea fore omni diligentia quærenda auxilia, quæ natiuum calidum roborare queant? Cunque hoc insit allijs, recte ministrari ijs qui citra læsionem eis vescuntur, quilibet sanæ mentis concedet. Iis autem qui allijs vsi non sunt, pestilenti constitutione incipere eis assuescere, an rectum sit, apud me decretum non est. Nam calidis temperatu ris et ijs qui gracili sunt habitu, præterea pue ris, & imbecillibus, in summa ijs quorum facile digeruntur corpora, crediderim allijs in pestilenti constitutione primo vti incommodum fore. Qui autem crasso sunt habitu, aut frigido temperamento, & difficulter in halitus soluuntur, præsertim si hyems sit, eos arbitror ex vsu aliorum votum consecuturos. Iis adde allium à crapula & ebrietate optimè præseruare, vt ab Hippocrate & Galeno scriptum est. Quantum autem crapula & ebrietas corpora ad quælibet impressionem externam suscipiendā disponant, declarant malæ habitudines quæ ijs exinde nascuntur. Qui ergo inordinato vtuntur victu in pestilenti commorantes aëre, allium vorare sanum esse censeo. Quod si ijs addas illud Dioscoridis dicentis, magnæ & allio vtilitates cōtra aquarum mutationes, non solum via præservationis, sed gratia curationis concedenda esse allia recte colliges. Huic fortasse assenties opinioni, in mentem si revocés, hanc febrem adeò perniciosam esse, vt nostrorum medicorum quidam dixerit, remedia in hac febre cū temeritate esse sumenda, aliusque curationē Deo committat. Cunque medicamentis vtentes medici omnia etsi temerariē tentare non verecantur: cur nobis idem non licebit, qui cibis tentamus, minorique damno humani corporis si aliter eueniat, rem tractamus? Quod si eo tentemus quod longa experientia scimus naturale roborare calidum, appetentiā ventriculi excitare, coctiones & reliquas naturales actiones acuere, cibumque corrumpi non sinere, quæ omnia in allio scimus esse, horumque omnium contrarium corpora patiā pestilenti febre, nonne ob iam dicta allium cum cibis ei qui pestilenti febre laborat citra temeritatem miscere nos iudicabis? Quod si allium ventriculum exiccare vt de eo scripsit Dioscorides consideres, in pestilentiali verò febre humiditatem prauam esse in ventriculo à qua omnes eius actiones corrumpuntur, puntur, præsertim qua cibus coquitur, & ea qua retinetur, has omnes vtilitates ob id nihili faciendas esse rectum esse existimabis, quod allium plus iusto calfacit? Ego sane ob id ab aliorum vsu non desisterem, sciens minus mali pati laborantes à caliditatis, quàm à pestilentis putredinis additione. Si enim contra aquarum mutationes magnæ sunt allio vtilitates, ob id quod naturale calidum robo rat, hac ipsa de causa & contra mutationes aëris pestilentes valere haud dubium est. Naturale siquidem calidum cum potens est, humido naturali validius dominatur, extranea rumq; causarum impressioni fortius obsistit. Caliditas etiam allij in terrestri parte nō est, vt caliditas rei amaræ, sed in parte aquosa quæ statim in halitus soluitur, ab internis ad partes externas statim migrans: Quod in pestilenti febre non parum conducit, vt aliàs demonstrabimus. Neq; te dictum Hippocratis turbet, allium flatum parere, caliditateq; in thorace & capitis grauitatem & cibi fa stidium facere. Nam contraria efficere, asserit Galenus ipsa experientia edoctus. Quin immo ait capitis soluere grauitatem si post euacuationem detur. Omnibus igitur pestilenti febre laborantibus allij virtutem in cibis miscendam vt saluberrimum consulo. Vt exiccatione sua, naturaleque calidum roborando, corruptioni exitialiter grassanti obstet. Et vt videlicet quod corruptum est, aut per vias vrinæ, aut suo violento motu ad circunferentiales partes detrudat. Et non minus symptomatum ventriculi gratia, nempe vomitus, & ciborum abominationis. Caeterum scire oportet, omnibus nec similiter, nec quantitatem eandem fore exhibendam. Sed cuilibet pro consuetudine & vehementia febrilis caloris, pro ætate, temperatura, & anni tempore.
units.tr: Reapers, when the summer heat is fierce and they grow warm after midday, eat garlic with their bread so that they are less troubled by the heat and their bodies are less dissolved in sweats. For garlic, by its power, resists the heat of the season more strongly than those who have not used it. Add that it protects the same bodies from outside cold and makes them less liable to it. Garlic cannot produce these effects by its quality alone, since transmission is easier in things that are alike. It must therefore be that garlic has this power because it strengthens natural heat, by which it gains greater mastery over the body, so that any outside cause is more difficultly overcome. Indeed, an external influence cannot impress its action upon the human body while the natural heat is strong. Since this is so, who would deny that, for the prevention of pestilential contagion or of any impression whatever, every care must be taken to seek out those aids which can strengthen the innate heat? And since garlic has this property, every sane person will grant that it is rightly given to those who eat it without harm. As for those who have not used garlic, whether it is right to begin accustoming them to it during a pestilential season, I have not decided. For I should think that to start garlic in a pestilential season would be inconvenient for those of warm temperament, those of slender build, also for children and the weak, and in short for those whose bodies digest easily. But I believe that for those of thick build or cold temperament, who are slow to be released into vapours, especially in winter, it will bring the benefit others have gained from using it. To these add that garlic is an excellent preventive against gluttony and drunkenness, as Hippocrates and Galen have written. How much gluttony and drunkenness dispose bodies to take up any external impression is shown by the bad conditions that arise from them. So for those who live with disordered diet and stay in pestilential air, I judge it healthy to eat garlic. If you add to these the saying of Dioscorides, that garlic has great benefits against changes of water, to be granted not only as a means of prevention but for the sake of cure, you will rightly conclude that garlic is to be used. Perhaps you will assent to this opinion if you call to mind that this fever is so deadly that, as one of our physicians has said, remedies in this fever must be taken with rashness, and the rest of the cure must be committed to God. Yet physicians who use medicines do not hesitate to try everything, even rashly; why should it not be permitted to us, who try things with foods and deal with them with less harm to the human body if the outcome is otherwise? If we try by means of what long experience shows us strengthens natural heat, stirs the appetite of the stomach, sharpens digestion and the other natural actions, and does not let food rot, all of which we know garlic does, and if we see that bodies in pestilential fever suffer the opposite of all these, will you not judge that for the reasons already given it is right, without rashness, to mix garlic with the food of one who suffers from pestilential fever? If you consider that garlic dries out the stomach, as Dioscorides wrote of it, whereas in pestilential fever there is a bad moisture in the stomach by which all its actions are corrupted, especially the digestion of food and the retention of it, you will rightly judge that these benefits are not to be dismissed merely because garlic heats more than is right. Indeed, I for my part would not give up its use by others, knowing that those who suffer suffer less harm from added heat than from the putrefaction of the pestilence. For if garlic is of great benefit against changes of water because it strengthens natural heat, then for this same reason it is beyond doubt that it is also effective against pestilential changes of air. For when natural heat is powerful, it masters the natural moisture more strongly and resists the impression of external causes more firmly. Moreover, the heat of garlic lies not in its earthy part, as the heat of bitter things does, but in its watery part, which is at once dissolved into vapour, passing quickly from the inner parts to the outer. This contributes not a little in pestilential fever, as I shall show elsewhere. Nor should the saying of Hippocrates disturb you, that garlic produces wind, heat in the chest, heaviness of the head and loss of appetite. For Galen, taught by experience itself, asserts that it produces the opposite. Indeed he says that it relieves heaviness of the head if it is given after evacuation. Therefore I advise, as most wholesome, that the virtue of garlic be mixed into the food of all who suffer from pestilential fever, so that by its drying and by strengthening natural heat it may resist the corruption that spreads so deadly, and so that what has been corrupted may be driven off either by the urinary passages or by its own violent motion towards the outer parts. And not less for the sake of the stomach's symptoms, namely vomiting and loathing of food. But one must know that it should not be given in the same way or in the same amount to everyone, but to each according to his habit, the severity of the fever's heat, his age, temperament, and the season of the year.

units.la: Sed vt iis morem geramus, qui cum de aliqua re plura commoda & magni momenti audierint, ob aliquam etsi leuissimam qualitatem contrariam, eam tanquam infestam damnant, non considerantes difficile esse aliquid inuenire quod citra læsionem magnifice prosit, vt Galenus prudenter scripsit in libris de methodo medendi, libet igitur ea quibus alij caliditas refringitur referre. Quā ob rem illos ob id bona esse mente hortamur. Alij caliditas coctione plurimum euanescit, vt scripsit Arabum praecipuus medicorum Avicenna. Quare qui allio integro vti vult, citra aliam praeparationem simul cum cibis coquat. Quod si frangere quis velit, in acetum aut in succum acetosae die una infusum sinat, postmodum utatur. Nec silentio praetereundum est, commodum quod ab allio iij qui pestilenti febre detinentur habent. Formidinem pellere de eo proditum est, praecipue in decoctione oliuarum & nucis, vt tradidit dictus vir, qua vt ait vtuntur Christiani. Pro comperto est eos qui pestilenti febri detinentur, ab horrida concuti formidine quae omnium maximè animi motuum spiritus absumit. Quod inhibere modo quo possit curabit pius medicus. Iudico igitur allium in omnibus edulijs quae pestilenti febre laborantibus offeruntur commodè miscerì: Opinorque non solum fore innoxium, sed ex eo quàm pluri-mà sequi commoda, ad natiui caloris robur, & grassantis pestilentis contagij inhibitio-nem, & ad corrupti humoris ex omni parte cutem versus expulsionem.
units.tr: But to humour those who, having heard many advantages and things of great importance about something, condemn it as hostile because of some contrary quality, however slight, not considering that it is difficult to find anything that benefits greatly without some harm, as Galen wisely wrote in his books On the Method of Healing, I therefore wish to set out the means by which garlic's heat is tempered. For this reason we urge them to take it in good faith. Garlic's heat is for the most part dissipated by cooking, as Avicenna, the chief of the Arab physicians, wrote. Therefore whoever wishes to use whole garlic should cook it with the food without any other preparation. If anyone wishes to temper it, let him steep it in vinegar or in the juice of sorrel for a day, and then use it. Nor must we pass over in silence the benefit that those held by pestilential fever get from garlic. It is reported to drive away fear, especially in a decoction of olives and walnuts, as the said man taught, which, he says, the Christians use. It is established that those held by pestilential fever are shaken by a dreadful fear, which above all consumes the spirits of the animal motions. A pious physician will cure this in whatever way he can check it. I judge, therefore, that garlic should be conveniently mixed into all the foods offered to those suffering from pestilential fever. And I think it will not only be harmless, but that very many benefits will follow from it: to strengthen natural heat, to check the spreading contagion of the pestilence, and to drive the corrupt humour out to the skin from every part.

units.la: Vnus è nostris medicus sal commendát, dummodo tantum nō sit vt sitim inferat. sed paucis agendum est cum nostro medico. Si si-tim inducere noxium est, similiter ea censen-da sunt noxia quæ hanc nata sunt efficere. At talia sunt omnia quæ corpus exiccant. Ci-bos igitur qualitate exiccátes damnabit: qua-propter humidos laudabit, quos & ratio & experientia in pestilenti febre noxios esse monstrant. Cū igitur periti medici cibos exic-cantes laudarunt, necesse est, vt quod ex iis necessario sequitur non damnent. Quinimmò si rem exactius tractemus, inueniemus ea so-re exhibenda quæ ventriculum exiccare, & sitim inducere valeant. Exiccatio enim quæ effatu digna est, & sensu percipitur, sitim in-fert. Quæ citra hanc fit, parui aut nullius mo-menti est, vtpote ob imbecillitatem sensum immuimmutare non valens. Humectum autem et nimis laxum ventriculum prout in hac febre est, non vtcunque exiccare oportet, neque paulatim idagere tentandum. Nam ægritudo maximè exitialis (vt hæc est) præsentaneum exigit remedium. Exiccandi igitur eorū ventriculi adeò sunt, vt exiccatio sitim valeat inducere. Per hoc enim humiditates quibus pestilens contagium primo concipitur & aliis communicatur exiccabuntur. Humectus præterea præter modum ventriculus & relaxatione laborans, & ob id cibum cito euomens, tali exiccatione curabitur: meliusq; retinebit ea quæ ingeruntur ex cibis et potibus. quod non parui momenti est in huius febris curatione. Cuius gratia salitos piscesque supra concessimus, vt qui maximè ad vomitum valent, vt scripsit Rasis in hæc verba. Pisces (inquit) saliti calidi sunt et sicci, incidunt phlegma, & conferunt vomitui, eò quod emittunt phlegma viscosum de stomacho. Et quanto vetustiores tanto magis calidiores & sicciores. Sed laudabiles ij
units.tr: One of our physicians commends salt, provided it is not used in quantities that induce thirst. But this must be dealt with briefly, with our physician. If inducing thirst is harmful, then things that tend to produce thirst must likewise be judged harmful. All things that dry out the body are of this kind. So he will condemn foods that dry by their quality, and for that reason he will praise moist foods, which both reason and experience show to be harmful in pestilential fever. Since skilled physicians have praised drying foods, they must not condemn what necessarily follows from them. Indeed, if we treat the matter more exactly, we will find that those things should be given which can dry the stomach and induce thirst. For drying that is worth mentioning and is perceived by the senses produces thirst. Drying that happens without this is of little or no importance, since it is too weak to alter the senses. But a stomach that is moist and too lax, as it is in this fever, must not be dried in any haphazard way, nor should one try to deal with it gradually. For a disease that is as deadly as this one demands an immediate remedy. Therefore the stomachs of such patients must be dried so thoroughly that the drying can induce thirst. By this means the moistures in which the pestilential contagion is first taken up and then passed on to others will be dried out. Moreover, a stomach that is excessively moist and suffering from relaxation, and which therefore quickly vomits its food, will be cured by such drying, and will hold better what is taken in as food and drink. This is of no small importance in the cure of this fever. For this reason we have already allowed salted fish, since they are especially effective in provoking vomiting, as Rhasis wrote in these words: "Salted fish," he says, "is hot and dry; it cuts phlegm and helps vomiting, because it expels viscous phlegm from the stomach. And the older it is, the hotter and drier it becomes." But those that are seasoned with vinegar are praiseworthy.

units.la: 22. Conti nentis. sunt qui condiuntur cum aceto, Hæc ille. A- stio præterea facultatis quæ potum appetit sa litorum piscium siccitate acuitur. Vnde fit, ᴜt frigidam appetant, bibant & retineant, quæ non parũ ÿs prodest. Sunt præterea hui- ųsmodi exiccantia tanquam signum appeten tis facultatis quæ inventriculo est, nempe ut cognoscatur ᴜtrum illa superstes sit an mor- tua. Si enim adhibitis ÿs quæ exiccant & si tim ᴜalent inducere, laborantes nõ sitiant, si gnum est appetente ᴜentriculi facultate mor tuam esse: quod in pestilenti febre non raro cõ tingit. Vanum ergo est sitim ᴜereri in hac fe bre, ob id quod alÿs in febribus ægrotantibus sitire noceat. Neq; ideo quod cõtra sitim mul ta tradiderunt medici remedia, ᴜt Hippocra tes in libris de ratione ᴠictus in morbus acu- tis, in pestilenti febre ea prohibenda esse quæ sitim inducũt opinandũ est. Sed neq; obscurũ erat ex præceptis medicorũ intelligere, aliam fore in curatione pestilentis febris metho- dum obseruandum, ac longè diuersam ab ea quam alÿs in febribus tradiderunt. Quod ex cibis exiccantibus, et ex iis quae astringunt & ex crasso victu, & ex eo quod in hac febre ut comedant & bibant aegris persuademus. Quae omnia aliis in febribus diligenter prohibemus. Sal igitur tantum edulis miscendum est, quantum sano homini sitim inducere valeat. Unde Celso sitim excitandam esse in hac febre recte visum est. Sunt qui vinum prohibeant: alii qui suadeant, albumque consulant, sic temperantes. Vini pars una, aquae partes quinque. Qui exhibendum putant, dicunt familiare humanae naturae vinum esse, imbecillitatibus quoque subvenire, spiritus materiam abunde ministrans. Quapropter in pestilenti febre ubi magna fit spirituum exolutio ministrandum fore. Et quia calorem & commotionem timent ob id multa aqua diluunt. Ego vero potum quem solummodo morbus ipse indicat, referam. Quem enim aegrotantis vires, & consuetudo indicent, abunde in superioribus sub universali sermone tradidimus. Hic solum potum curante indicatione solummodo ab ipso morbo sumpta apponemus, ut in singulis febrium speciebus fecimus. Caeterum quicunque potum nosse cupiat qui Socrati quauis febre laboranti conueniat, percepta virium dispositione, & viri consuetudine, habito simul potu quem in singulis febribus apposuimus, ad tabellas quas supra scripsimus recurrat. Ab eis iuxta ea quae ibi tradidimus documenta facile conuenientem potu quiuis eliciat. Quapropter non est quod hic de potu disseramus, qui pestilenti febre imbecillitatis virium aut consuetudinis ratione conueniat. Curantem potum diximus eum qui morbo aut eius causae contrarius sit. Proinde cum iis quae supra diximus ostensum sit, curantem potum eum esse qui morbo aut eius causae contrarius sit, pestilentem q; febrem immoderatè calidum & humidu corpus humanum reddere & singulas eius particulas, potum frigidum & siccum conuenire huic febri sumpta solummodo indicatione ab ipso morbo haud dubium est. Non immeritò igitur nonnulli aquam cum aceto in potum pestilente febre laborantibus concesserunt. Ego succum maligranati acidi defæcatum, potum huic febri convenientem esse arbitror. Cui si aquam plantaginis aut acetosæ miscere velis, nihil nocueris. Modus sit ut aquæ partem unā, succi duabus misceas. Quod si succi maligranati non detur copia, sic agito. Capillorum veneris aut polytrichi man. duos, berberorum tres, coquito in decem libris aquæ ad tertias, ægrotanti propinato. Cæterum scire oportet in pestilenti febre laborantium virtutes semper vrgere, tum ob incessantes vomitus, tum maximè ob ingentè spiritus exolutionem. Hanc medicorum nonnulli respicientes vinum ministrandum suadent: ut Celsus, qui vinum calidum meratius dare iubet. Qui verò ad morbū magis mentem dirigunt, vinum rectè prohibent, aquāque mixtam cum aceto ministrant. Cæterum cum vrgentis virtutis aut consuetudinis ratione, vinum ministrare oporteat, cum succo maligranati aut aqua berberorum miscebimus. Aut cum aqua plantaginis, aut acetosæ, si illorum non detur copia. Modum iuxta rationem indicantiū ex tabellis inuenies. Ca- terum quia in pestilenti febre accidit labo- rantibus nauseante vt plurimū habere ven- triculum, ita vt statim quæ deuorant aut bi- bant vomitu eiıciant, incassum nostræ sorent de cibo & potu lucubrationes, nisi ea addi- derimus quæ extra posita ad retentionem ci- borum & potuum iuuent. Hæc autem sunt frigida astringentia, quæ non solum adid, ve- rùm ad infectionem pestilentem à ventricu- lo repellendam non parum proderunt. Succi cymarum tenerrimarum vitis, aut vuæ acer- bæ, partes tres, succi semperuiuæ maioris par- tes duas, aceti, decoctionis absinthÿ & mentæ partem vnam & semis, cinamomi parum, misceto. Apponito multoties spon- giam dictis succis frigidis madentem ventri- culo, ante cibum.
units.tr: 22. (Continued.) The action of the faculty that craves drink is sharpened by the dryness of salted fish. From this it comes about that patients desire cold drinks, drink them and keep them down, which is of no small benefit to them. Moreover, such drying foods serve as a sign of the appetite of the faculty that is in the stomach, namely, so that one may know whether that faculty is still alive or dead. For if, when drying foods that are able to induce thirst have been applied, the sick do not feel thirst, this is a sign that the faculty of the stomach is dead, which in pestilential fever is not infrequently the case. It is therefore pointless to fear thirst in this fever on the grounds that in other fevers it harms the sick to be thirsty. Nor should we think, because physicians have handed down many remedies against thirst, as Hippocrates did in his books on the regimen of acute diseases, that in pestilential fever those things which induce thirst must be forbidden. Nor was it unclear, from the precepts of the physicians, that a different method must be observed in the cure of pestilential fever, one quite different from that which they gave for other fevers. We advise this because of drying foods, astringent foods, a thick diet, and the fact that in this fever we urge the sick to eat and drink, all of which we forbid diligently in other fevers. Therefore salt should be added to food only in such quantity as can induce thirst in a healthy man. Hence it seemed right to Celsus that thirst should be provoked in this fever. Some forbid wine; others advise it, and recommend white wine, tempering it thus: one part of wine to five parts of water. Those who think it should be given say that wine is familiar to human nature, that it also helps weakness, supplying abundant material for the spirits, and that therefore it should be administered in pestilential fever, where there is great loss of the spirits. And because they fear heat and agitation, they dilute it with a great deal of water. I, however, will mention the drink that the disease alone indicates. For what the patient's strength and habits indicate, we have already set out fully in the earlier general discussion. Here we will give only the drink that is indicated by the disease itself, as we did for each species of fever. As for anyone who wishes to know which drink suits Socrates, suffering from any fever, let him, once he has perceived the disposition of the strength and the man's habits, and at the same time has considered the drink we have prescribed for each fever, return to the tables that we wrote above. From those, following the instructions we gave there, anyone can easily work out a drink that suits. Therefore there is no need to discuss here the drink that suits pestilential fever on account of weakness of strength or habit. We have said that the curing drink is the one that is contrary to the disease or its cause. Accordingly, since it has been shown in what we have said above that the curing drink is that which is contrary to the disease or its cause, and since it is beyond doubt that pestilential fever makes the human body immoderately hot and moist, and each of its parts, a cold and dry drink, taken solely as indicated by the disease itself, suits this fever. Not without reason, therefore, some have allowed water with vinegar as a drink for those suffering from pestilential fever. I think the clarified juice of sour pomegranate is a drink suited to this fever. If you wish, you may mix with it water of plantain or sorrel; you will do no harm. Let the proportion be one part water to two parts juice. But if there is no supply of pomegranate juice, proceed thus: take two handfuls of maidenhair or polytrichum, three of barberries, boil them in ten pounds of water down to two-thirds, and give it to the patient to drink. Moreover, one must know that in those suffering from pestilential fever the strength must always be pressed, both because of the incessant vomiting and especially because of the great loss of spirits. Some physicians, looking to this, advise giving wine, as Celsus does, who orders undiluted hot wine to be given. Those who direct their attention more to the disease rightly forbid wine and give water mixed with vinegar. Nevertheless, since on account of the urgent strength or habit it is necessary to administer wine, we will mix it with pomegranate juice or with barberry water, or with water of plantain or sorrel if there is no supply of those. You will find the proportion, according to the reasoning of the indications, in the tables. Moreover, since it happens in pestilential fever that the sick usually have a stomach prone to nausea, so that they immediately vomit up whatever they devour or drink, our labours on food and drink would be in vain unless we added those things which, applied externally, help to retain foods and drinks. These are cold astringents, which will be of no small value not only for this purpose but also for repelling the pestilential infection from the stomach. Mix three parts of juice of the tenderest vine tendrils, or of sour grapes, two parts of juice of greater houseleek, one and a half parts of vinegar, decoction of wormwood and mint, and a little cinnamon. Apply to the stomach, before food, a sponge soaked many times in the said cold juices.

units.la: Panem assum vino odorifero madentem modico cinamomi superasperso, ventriculo apponito. Linteum multipliciter plicatū suc- co vuæ acerbæ madens desuper imponito.
units.tr: Apply to the stomach toasted bread soaked in fragrant wine, with a little cinnamon sprinkled over it. Lay over it a cloth folded many times and soaked in juice of sour grapes.

units.la: Præterea aceti acerrimi partes tres, olei ro- sarum sarum ex oleo immaturo partes duas, succi cytoniorum partem vnam, misceto tandiu donec crassescat, et permixtum sit, vtere vt supra, efficacissimū est. Vsum camphorae in ijs epithematibus quae ventriculo apponūtur non laudo. Ea siquidem quae præter modum refrigerant citra astrictionem, principi parti apponenda non esse, rationalis docet methodus. Sed de his alibi. Aceti acris vnciam vnam, pulueris reubarbari tosti drachmam vnam, misceto & ita esse finito per diem & noctem. Postmodum vtere cum aqua rosarū vt supra. Nec praetermittendum est eisdem epithematibus multoties vtendum non esse. Cunq; nouum epithema apponere volueris, exiccare ventriculum linteo oportet vt vestigium praeteriti non sit medicaminis.
units.tr: Furthermore, mix three parts of very sharp vinegar, two parts of rose oil made from unripe oil, and one part of juice of quince, and stir until it thickens and is well blended. Use it as above; it is most effective. I do not commend the use of camphor in those plasters that are applied to the stomach; reason teaches that things which cool beyond measure without astringency should not be applied to the principal part. But of these matters elsewhere. Take one ounce of sharp vinegar and one drachm of roasted rhubarb powder, mix them and let them stand thus for a day and a night. Afterwards use it with rose water, as above. Nor should it be overlooked that these same plasters should not be used too often. And when you wish to apply a new plaster, the stomach must first be dried with a cloth, so that no trace of the previous medicine remains.

units.la: Victum inquirit colliquantibus febribus conuenientem.
units.tr: He inquires into a diet suitable for colliquative fevers. ## CHAPTER XXI.

units.la: CAPVT XXI.

FEBRIS colliquantis victū infrigidantem & modice astringente & crassiorem quàm pro morbi ratione esse oportet. Id, sicut et reliqua, ab Hippocrate discimus, qui cum de febrium curatione ageret cum aluo liquida absumente & contabefaciente corpus, ijs sorbitiones frigidiores & crassiores exhibendas docuit: Potusq; vinosiores & astringentiores delirio non obstante propinare iubet. Unde colligimus, eum esse in colliquan te febre victum exhibendum, qui corporis dissolutioni valeat subuenire, etsi in morbum aut eius symptomata addere videatur. In tertio cum de mulsa agat nocumentis, signa liquefacientium febrium in hunc modum scribit. Biliosa quoque alui deiycit magis, interdum quidem bona, sed interdum quàm decet, redundatiora, spumantioraq;, quod biliosis magis & his quibus tumefacta sunt viscera contingit. Magis praeterea quae dilutior est spumum educit, magisque pulmonem lenit. Merácior vero spumosa excrementa atque plusquam conuenit valde biliosa calidioraque, quàm dilutior agit magis. Deiectiones autem huiusmodi habent quidem & alias quae gravues ues sunt offensas, neq; enim hypocundriorum extinguunt ardore, sed excitant, inquietatio neq; & membrorum iactationem faciunt, in testinaque & sedem exulcerant. Qui ergo in morbis huiusmodi relictis sorbitionibus mul sa potius alterius vice, vtetur, is si multa foe liciter consequutus fuerit, nonne & multa ei succedent praeter animi sententiam? Quibus in verbis Hippocrates duplici nomine taxauit antiquos medicos, tum quia sorbitiones liquefacientibus in febribus dimittebant, tum quia alterius potionis vice, mulsa vtebātur. Quod autem aliās in huiusmodi acutis, febribus exceptis liquefacientibus, sola mulsa ad indicationem vsque aegrotantes alat, Galenus docet in hac verba. Significauit & nūc "manifestissimè ad morbi vsque iudicationē, "sola vti mulsa cōsulens. nempe in solis qui col liquefaciunt morbis, vel in quibus hominum virtus ad morbi vsque iudicationem suffice- re non posit, ad prisanæ cremorem perueni- emus. In alijs verò sola mulsa est cōmodius. Quod autem fluxus ventris syncere biliosus spumosusq; liquefacientem febrem indicet, asserit Galenus in expositione illius, Quæ dilutior est sputu̅ educit magis, cu̅ inquit: Hippocrates igitur nō immemor, cu̅ vel ex mulsa epota vel absq; ipsa quis spumosa simul et syncere biliosa deiecerit, febrem sciueris esse quæ liquefaciat & ad tabe̅ perducat, &c. Quare hos tali cibo nutries, sumpta in præsenti à sola corporis dissolutione indicatione.
units.tr: A diet for a colliquative fever should be cooling, moderately astringent, and thicker than the nature of the disease requires. We learn this, as we learn the rest, from Hippocrates. When he treated fevers with a liquid bowel that consumes and wastes the body, he taught that cooler and thicker broths should be given, and he bids us give wines that are fuller and more astringent, even though there is delirium. From this we gather that in a colliquative fever one should give the diet that can help the dissolution of the body, even if it seems to add to the disease or its symptoms. In the third book, when he discusses the harms of mulsa (honeyed wine), he writes about the signs of liquefying fevers in this way: "Bilious stools also discharge more, sometimes indeed good, but sometimes more copious and frothy than is fitting, which happens more to bilious people and to those whose viscera are swollen. Moreover, the thinner stool brings out more froth and soothes the lungs more. Stronger stools, however, which are frothy and far too bilious and hotter than is proper, act more harshly than the thinner ones. Such evacuations also have other bad effects, for they do not quench the heat of the hypochondria but inflame it, and they cause restlessness and tossing of the limbs, and ulcerate the intestines and the anus. Therefore, he who, in such diseases, leaves off broths and uses mulsa in their place, if he has achieved much with little, will not many things also follow beyond his intention?" In these words Hippocrates censured the ancient physicians on two counts: because they dismissed broths in liquefying fevers, and because they used mulsa in place of the other drink. That in other acute fevers, apart from liquefying ones, mulsa alone nourishes the patients up to the crisis, Galen teaches in these words: "He has also indicated most clearly, advising the use of mulsa alone up to the judgment of the disease. Namely, in those diseases alone which liquefy, or in which the strength of men cannot suffice up to the judgment of the disease, we shall come to barley gruel. In other cases, mulsa alone is more suitable." That a bilious and frothy flux of the bowel clearly indicates a liquefying fever, Galen asserts in his exposition of that passage, "What is thinner brings out more sputum," when he says: "Hippocrates, therefore, not unmindful, when someone has passed frothy and purely bilious stools either after drinking mulsa or without it, you should know that this is a fever which liquefies and leads to wasting, etc." Therefore nourish these patients with such food, taking the indication for the present from the dissolution of the body alone.

units.la: Victu̅ verò iuxta febris acumen conueniëtem, ex ijs quæ in superioribus diximus colliges. Quæ dissolutioni corporis obstant triplicia sunt, nempe quæ corpus & quæ humore̅ respiciunt, & quæ vtrunq;. Ad primum modum spectant ea quæ multum præstant corpori nutrimentum, & facilis coctionis sunt: Quæcunque potestate infrigidant, ad secundum. Infrigidantia verò cibaria quæcunq; astrictoria participant vi, ad tertiu̅. Optimus igitur in colliquatibus febrib. cibus fuerit is, qui corpus nutriat, infrigidet, & modicè astringat. Capu̅ igitur iuuene̅ crassu̅ ita coquito. Hordei excorticati mā.tres, vuæ acerbæ, portulacæ, plantaginis, viridis coriandri, sin gulorum man. vnu, bulliant simul, deinde colato ius, cuius accipe partes tres, succi granato rum acidorum partem vnam, sorbitionem cum pane crassam conficito. Panis infusus in succum granati acidi conuenit.
units.tr: The diet suited to the sharpness of the fever you will work out from what we said above. The things that stand in the way of the body's dissolution are of three kinds: those that concern the body, those that concern the humour, and those that concern both. To the first kind belong those foods which give the body much nourishment and are easy to digest; to the second, whatever cools by its power; to the third, cooling foods which also share an astringent force. The best diet, then, in colliquative fevers will be one that nourishes the body, cools it, and astringes it moderately. So let a thick broth be cooked from a young capon thus: take a handful each of hulled barley, unripe grapes, purslane, plantain, and green coriander, let them boil together, then strain the broth, and take three parts of it with one part of the juice of sour pomegranates, and make a thick sop with bread. Bread soaked in the juice of sour pomegranate is suitable.

units.la: Ptisanam hordei non colatam parato in hunc modum. Duos pullos crassos coquito cum tribus hordei excorticati pugillis, portulacæ vno, modicum antequam ab igne amoueas, immittito granorum mali granati acidi pugillum vnu, sinito vt coquatur tandiu quoad rumpatur hordeum & tenerrimum fiat. extrahito deinde hordeum, & adiecto paucō zucaro administretur iis quorum virtutes ob imbecillitate laborant. Conuenientissimus cibus fuerit iis qui colliquantibus febribus laborant. Infrigidat, roborat, & facillima coctionis est. Aqua frigida commodissimus ipsis potus & remedium est, vtrumque respiciens & corpus & humorem. Ad quam exhibendam exiguæ coctionis signū spectandum esse nos docet Galenus quarto de ratione
units.tr: Prepare a barley ptisan, not strained, in this way. Cook two fat chickens with three handfuls of hulled barley and one of purslane; a little before you take it from the fire, add one handful of the seeds of sour pomegranate; let it cook until the barley bursts and becomes very tender. Then take out the barley, and, with a little sugar added, give it to those whose strength is weakened by feebleness. It is the most suitable food for those who suffer from colliquative fevers: it cools, strengthens, and is very easy to digest. Cold water is the most convenient drink and remedy for them, as it serves both the body and the humour. In giving this, Galen teaches us that one must watch for the sign of weak digestion, in the fourth book of his On the

units.la: victus, & in libris de Methodo. Melius ad- uersissimum esse ab eodem didicimus. Scien- dum praeterea rectam victus administratio- nem & frigida potum, praecipuum esse ad li- quefacientes febres remedium, parumq; au- xilij praestare medicamenta. Quare diligen- ter obseruandum est, ut boni sint nutrimen- ti, & facillimae coctionis cibaria, quae ijs osse- remus: quibus cum admiscere ea quae refrige- rare & parum astringere valeant utile erit. Optimusque omnium quem sciam, his cibus est, ptisana hordei eo quo diximus modo pa- rata. In ea siquidem omnia quae necessaria sunt, insunt. Boni nutrimenti est, facilis coctionis, infrigidat, parumque astringit. Quae enim in- signiter astrictiora vi pollent, ex eo incom- moda sunt, quod causam morbificam intra corpus detinent, cum ad omnem euacuatio- nem vias obstruant.
units.tr: Diet, and in the books On the Method. We have learned from the same author that what is best is most opposed to the disease. It should also be known that a correct management of diet and cold drink is the chief remedy for liquefying fevers, while medicines give little help. Hence care must be taken that the foods are of good nourishment and very easy to digest, to which it will be useful to add those things which can cool and slightly astringe. And the best of all that I know is this food, barley ptisan prepared in the way we have said. For it contains all that is necessary: it is of good nourishment, easy to digest, cooling, and slightly astringent. For those things which are strongly astringent in power are harmful, in that they hold the morbid cause within the body, since they block all the routes of evacuation.

units.la: Victum inuestigat qui morbillis & uario- lis competat.
units.tr: He investigates a diet suitable for measles and smallpox.

units.la: CAPVT XXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXII.

units.la: MORBILLVS & variola differunt. Morbillus in cute est instar morsus pulicum, à sanguine nimis bilioso ortum habens. Variola cutem magis in tumorem attollit, diuersíque coloris est. Albæ visuntur vt plurimum, quandoq; citrinæ, raro nigræ, plumbeæ. Morbilli consimiliter non vnu seruant colorem. Proinde variolæ à sanguine nimis aquoso fiunt. Inter morbillos & variolas in eo conuenit, quod vtraque pustula ab ebullitione sanguinis fit, natura prauum ab eo quod purum est separante, & ad cutem detrudente. Quapropter à tali expulsione naturam, crasso cibo aut multo aut duræ coctionis, tunc temporis distrahendam non esse recte quis colliget. Vt verò opus melius compleat, & ab internis ad cutem versus cõmodius noxios humores depellat, & ne in aliqua interiorum partium humor detineatur, cibum parũ infrigidantem leuiter astringentem his ministrare oportet. Qui enim huiusmodi est, particulas roborat, vt validius à se quod molestat depellant. Vim præterea repellendi calidum humorem habet. Quapropter ius Hispanarū lentium cum acetosa herba, viridi coriandro, oleo, aceto, & sale, & modico croci ijs conuenit.
units.tr: Measles and smallpox differ. Measles on the skin is like the bite of fleas and arises from blood that is too bilious. Smallpox raises the skin into more of a swelling and is of various colours. They are seen mostly white, sometimes lemon-yellow, rarely black or leaden. Measles likewise do not keep one colour. Smallpox therefore arises from blood that is too watery. Measles and smallpox agree in this: each pustule arises from an effervescence of the blood, nature separating the foul from what is pure and driving it down to the skin. Hence one may rightly conclude that during such an expulsion nature should not be disturbed by thick food, either plentiful or hard to digest. So that the work may be better completed, and the harmful humours may be more conveniently driven from the internal parts to the skin, and so that no humour is retained in any internal part, it is proper to give food that is slightly cooling and gently astringent. For such food strengthens the particles so that they may more vigorously drive off what troubles them. It also has the power to repel hot humour. Therefore a broth of Spanish lentils with sorrel, green coriander, oil, vinegar, salt and a little saffron suits them.

units.la: Cucurbita etiam cocta cum portulaca, agresta, oleo, aceto, & sale.
units.tr: Gourd also boiled with purslane, verjuice, oil, vinegar and salt.

units.la: Ptisana, prout parauimus supra in colliquantibus febribus, commodissima his sorbitio est. Fugienda omnia ea sunt quae aut sanguinis copiam augeant, aut in eius ebullitionem addant. Quare inter initia, dummodo vires constent, gallinaceorum iura vitanda sunt, & omnia dulcia et vnctuosa. Facta euacuatione totius, nisi copiose erumpant, bonum erit in cibis minuere ea quae astringunt, et eorum quae aperire valeant aliquid imponere, vt folia apij, aut petroselini. At cum eruptio subsidere iam incipit, bonum est in cibis ea quae ventrem leniunt miscere: Vt pruna, vio las, borraginem & similia. Prunis autem quae astringente participant facultate, cuiusmodi Gallica sunt & Hispana, per omne tempus vti licet decoctis cū polytricho, plantagine, aut aut portulaca. Potus aũt ijs qui patiũtur morbillos aut variolas, sit aqua hordei cum polytricho & malo granato cocta. Sunt qui lactucas decoctas in aceto, medullā citrulli, & anguriæ, ijs qui variolas aut morbillos patiuntur exhibeant. Sunt & qui aquam anguriæ in potum ministrent. Sed quantum sentio, huiusmodi cibaria his damno potius quàm iuuamento sunt. Quandoquidem expulsioni naturæ obstant, & eruptionem pustularum retardant sua vehementi frigiditate. Nam huiusmodi ab intro ad cutem expulsiones à natura fiunt, materia ob ebullitionem eò inclinata, vtpote iam in vaporem transeunte ob substantiæ eius tenuitatem. Quapropter sicut ijs quæ calida & fumosa sunt augenda ebullitio non est, sic nec ijs quæ valdè refrigerant extinguenda. Solum igitur ea ministranda sunt quæ modicum refrigerent & astringant. Vt per hæc roboratis siue in se collectis particulis melius fiat ab intro ad extra expulsio. Quapropter ficuum aridarum exhibitionem in ijs qui morbillis aut variolis laborant, ut pluribus nostrorum medicorum visum est, ob id quod malas materias extra pellunt, non probo. Nam ob id ipsum quod caricas commendant, ego damnarem. Aiunt ea ru̅ vsu materias ab intro ad extra pelli: cuius argumentum esse scabiem ex earum immodico vsu euenientem aiunt. Sed profecto, vt opinor ipsa decipiuntur experientia. Non enim id agunt caricæ quia malos humores ab intro ad extra pellunt, aut quia sanguine ̅ mundificat, vt opinantur, sed quia eum nimis calfacientes, ebullitionis modum ei præstat. Vnde accidit vt id quod in fumum aut fuligine̅ ob calfactum sanguinem versum est ad cutem à natura detrudatur. Quare non immeritò vulgus fert, caricas scabiem & pruritum peculiariter inducere. Quapropter eas pueris & iuuenibus prohibent. Quod autem nimis calfaciunt, docet Dioscorides, qui eas sitim inducere asseruit. Rasis etiam tertio Almansoris ex multo earum vsu fieri pruritum & pediculos affirmauit. Nec id alicui admirationi sit. Nam in ipsis est occultū lacticiniū, vt recte sensit Auic. Halyabbas etiam 5. theo- ricæ, cap.19. cas in cholericos mutari humo- res scripsit. At si in ventriculo humores su- perflui fuerint, inquit ille dura fit ad digeren- dum carica, & ad corruptionem mutatur. Et inflationem ventositatem generat, & pessimū sanguinem. Auicenna similiter idem asseruit in hæc verba: Et sicca quidem (in- quit) in suis operationibus laudabilis est, ve- rùm tamen sanguis generatus ex ea nõ est bo nus. Verum id est, aridas ficus nimis abster- gere, aperire & incidere. Quapropter com- mendantur à Galeno secundo alimentorum cap.7. præcipuè cum nucibus & amygdalis. Vtcunque res habeat, caricas ob earum su- perfluam calfactionem vitandas esse in mor- billis in caloris febrilis præsentia opinamur. Senibus tamen frigidis natura, vbi eruptio nimis diminuta est, vtiles sunt, et securè con cedi possunt, præsertim in remissione caloris febrilis. Sua enim arida ficus apertione, sub- tiliatione, calfactione, humores adeò atte- nuat vt ad cutem facilè ferantur. Vnde variolas tunc temporis absque laesione euocare solet. Quod Petrus Aponensis vir disertissimus asseruit, de morbillorum & variolarum curatione agens.
units.tr: Barley gruel, as we prepared it above in the wasting fevers, is the most suitable drink for these. All those things must be avoided which either increase the quantity of blood or add to its effervescence. Therefore at the beginning, provided the strength holds, broths of fowl must be avoided, and all sweet and oily things. Once the whole has been evacuated, unless the eruption breaks out copiously, it will be good to reduce in the food those things that bind, and to apply something of those that can open, such as parsley or celery leaves. But when the eruption begins to subside, it is good to mix into the food those things that loosen the belly: such as prunes, violets, borage and the like. Prunes that share an astringent quality, such as the French and Spanish kinds, may be used at any time, boiled with polytrichum, plantain, or purslane. The drink for those suffering from measles or smallpox should be barley water boiled with polytrichum and pomegranate. Some give boiled lettuces in vinegar, and marrow of melon and cucumber, to those suffering from smallpox or measles. Some also give cucumber water to drink. But as far as I perceive, such foods do them harm rather than good, since they hinder nature's expulsion and delay the eruption of the pustules by their strong coldness. For expulsions of this kind from within to the skin are made by nature, the matter being inclined thither by the effervescence, since it is already passing into vapour because of its thinness. Therefore just as the effervescence is not to be increased by things that are hot and smoky, so it is not to be quenched by things that cool strongly. Only those things should be given which cool and astringe moderately, so that through them the particles are strengthened or gathered together and the expulsion from within outwards is better accomplished. For this reason I do not approve of the giving of dried figs to those suffering from measles or smallpox, as seemed good to most of our physicians, on the ground that they drive bad matters outwards. Indeed, on the very ground on which they commend figs, I would condemn them. They say that by their use matters are driven from within outwards, and they claim that the proof of this is the scabies that follows their immoderate use. But truly, as I think, they are deceived by experience. For figs do not act because they drive bad humours from within outwards, or because they cleanse the blood, as they suppose, but because, by heating the blood excessively, they bring it to a state of effervescence.
