Hence it happens that what has been turned into smoke or soot by the heated blood is thrust by nature out to the skin. So the common people rightly say that figs especially induce scabies and itching, and for this reason they forbid them to boys and young men. That figs heat excessively Dioscorides teaches, who asserted that they induce thirst. Rhazes too, in the third book of his Almansor, affirmed that from much use of them itching and lice arise. Nor should this cause anyone wonder, for there is a hidden milkiness in them, as Avicenna rightly perceived. Haly Abbas also, in the fifth book of the Theorica, chapter 19, wrote that figs change the humours into choleric ones. But if superfluous humours are in the stomach, he says, the fig is hard to digest and turns to corruption, and it generates flatulence and wind, and the worst blood. Avicenna likewise asserted the same in these words: "Dry figs indeed (he says) are praiseworthy in their operations, but nevertheless the blood generated from them is not good." It is true that dry figs cleanse excessively, open and cut. Therefore Galen commends them in the second book On Foods, chapter 7, especially together with walnuts and almonds. However the matter stands, we judge that figs are to be avoided in measles while febrile heat is present, because of their excessive heating. For old and cold natures, however, where the eruption is too weak, they are useful and may safely be allowed, especially during the remission of the febrile heat. For dry figs, by their opening, thinning and heating, so attenuate the humours that these are easily carried to the skin. Hence they are wont to bring out smallpox at that time without harm. This Peter of Abano, a most learned man, asserted when treating of the cure of measles and smallpox.

units.la: Quòd usus salitorum piscium in uariolis sit secundum rationem : non item in morbillis.
units.tr: That the use of salted fish is reasonable in smallpox, but not in measles.

units.la: CAPVT XXIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIII.

units.la: ET vt speculationi huic nihil defit, non ab re fuerit de eo victu differere quo vulgus vtitur in variolis & morbillis, nempe salitis piscibus. Siue enim ab ipsa experientia percepto commodo, siue ratione id ostendente, apud Lusitanam plebem salitorum piscium vsus longaeuus obtinuit, vt parua aut nulla medicis fides adhibeatur contrariu sudentibus. Aliud tamen vnus e nostris medicus natione Italus sentit, piscium salitorum vsum in morbillis & variolis reprobans. Nam ait ille apud nonnullos e plebe Itala aut scholares opinionem esse, in variolis rectè minstrari. Verùm si ab Aristotele rectè dictum est, non vanam esse omnino famam quâ vulgus gus ferat, non vanum vtique erit inquirere, an ratione aliqua qui salitis piscibus in vario lis vtitur innitatur. Percipimus ex quotidiano vsu salitos pisces pruritum inducere. Siue id salitorum piscium substantiæ concedas, sine caliditati & siccitati eorum, quibus ebullitionem sanguinis excitant. In omni autem ebullitione constat crassos humores in tenues solui, tenues in fumū digeri, fumos & fuligines ad cutem migrare. Huncque esse modum quo generatim salita edulia pruritum ob qualitates inducant manifestas. Siue id eorundem substantiæ in vaporem digestæ rapidæ ad cutem lationi, ob salis incisiuam qualitatem & acutam penetrationem, tribuas: quod nonnulli caricis inesse firmiter credidêre. Siue vtrunque simul in causa sit. Verùm est salitorum piscium vsu, ab internis corporis partibus ad externas nonnullorum excrementorum lationem fieri. Quod cum ita sit, dubium non est quin aliquando in ijs morbis salitis piscibus locus sit. Nempe vbi natura seqniter opus expulsionis aggreditur. Id autem si præter naturæ imbe- cillitatem accidat, aut deferuescente ebulli- tione fiet, qua iuuatur natura vt melius ex- crementa ad cutem detrudat, aut ob crassos & lentos humores ad expulsionem talē ine- ptos, aut ob viarum occlusionem. Quodcun- que horum trium adsit, aut omnia, pisces sa- litos prodesse ratio demonstrat, & ob calidi- tatem & siccitatem salitorum piscium, & non minime ob eorum incisionem & acutā penetrationem. Cum ergo in frigido natura corpore non satis variolæ erumpant ob ali- quam trium dictarum occasionū, febrili ca- lore nō obstante, dandos esse pisces salitos cū plebe sentio. In succo tamen acetosæ per diem integrā eos prius macerare oportet: sitq; me- diæ ætatis salitura. quanto enim antiquiores sunt, eo calidiores & sicciores euadunt, vt supra ostensum est. Ad hæc pisces salitī par- tes corporis ob salis compressionem in se inui- cem collectas roborant, quod siccis ficubus non inest, quinimmò contrarium. Id vnum est ex iis quæ cumulatiorem efficiunt expul- sionem: sionem: quod cibis inesse qui in variolis ministrantur, supra optauimus. Præterea si eueniat, vt fit, pustulas intro erumpi, profecto nullo medicamine efficacius rumpes, saniem purgabis, exiccabis, putredinemq; inde emanantem nullo alio citius castigabis, ne vlteriore concipiat corruptionem. Sanas tandem particulas nullo alio quàm ex salitis piscibus cibo incolumius, ne emanantis corruptionis contagio afficiantur, seruabis. Nec ab re fuerit, vt cum intro erumpuntur, pro earum maturatione ficus aridas primo vorare, deinde piscibus vti. Meminisse tamen oportet in morbillis cauendum esse piscium salitorum vsum; & in iis qui calidi & sicci sunt natura.
units.tr: And so that nothing is lacking to this inquiry, it will not be out of place to discuss the diet that the common people use in smallpox and measles, namely salted fish. Whether from experience itself, having perceived the benefit, or because reason shows it, the Portuguese common people have long kept up the use of salted fish, so that little or no trust is placed in physicians who speak against it. One of our own physicians, an Italian by birth, thinks otherwise and rejects the use of salted fish in measles and smallpox. He says that among some of the Italian common people, or the scholars, there is an opinion that these foods are rightly given in smallpox. But if Aristotle was right that the report spread by the common people is not wholly empty, then it will certainly not be empty to inquire whether the use of salted fish in smallpox by those who give it rests on some reason. We perceive from daily use that salted fish induces itching. Whether you attribute this to the substance of salted fish, or to their heat and dryness, by which they stir up a boiling of the blood, the fact is that in every boiling thick humours are dissolved into thin ones, thin humours are digested into vapour, and vapours and soots migrate to the skin. This is the general way in which salted foods induce itching, because of their manifest qualities. Or you may attribute it to the substance of these foods, digested into vapour and carried swiftly to the skin, because of the incisive quality and sharp penetration of salt, which some have firmly believed to be present in dried figs. Or both may be the cause together. It is true, however, that by the use of salted fish a drawing of excrements occurs from the inner parts of the body to the outer parts of some. Since this is so, there is no doubt that salted fish sometimes has a place in those diseases, namely where nature slowly undertakes the work of expulsion. If this happens beyond the weakness of nature, or when the boiling subsides, by which nature is helped to push the excrements better to the skin; or because of thick and viscous humours unfit for such expulsion; or because of blockage of the passages. Whichever of these three is present, or all of them, reason shows that salted fish helps, both because of the heat and dryness of salted fish and not least because of their incisive and sharp penetration. Therefore, since in a cold body nature does not bring out the smallpox sufficiently for one of the reasons mentioned, despite febrile heat, I think salted fish should be given along with the common people's practice. Yet they must first be steeped for a whole day in the juice of sour fruit, and the salted fish should be of middle age, for the older they are, the hotter and drier they become, as shown above. Besides, salted fish firm up their parts, which are gathered together by the compression of the salt, and this strengthens them; dried figs do not have this, and rather the opposite. This is one of the things that make the expulsion more abundant, which we said above is in the foods given in smallpox. Moreover, if it happens, as it does, that pustules break out inwards, you will break them with no remedy more effective, purge the pus, dry it up, and check the putrefaction that comes from it more quickly than with any other means, lest it conceive further corruption. Finally, you will keep the sound parts safe by no food more wholesome than salted fish, lest they be affected by the contagion of the corruption that emanates. Nor will it be out of place, when the pustules break out inwards, to eat dried figs first for their maturation, and then to use fish. Yet it must be remembered that in measles care must be taken with the use of salted fish, and in those who are hot and dry by nature.

units.la: Vt igitur summatim dicam, vbicunq; eruptio incompleta est, si crassi & lenti humores, aut viarum obstructio in causa sint, febre non obstante, nec calido & sicco hominis temperamento, ficus aridas & salitos pisces audacter ministrato. Nec audienda est illorum sententia qui salitorum piscium vsum ægris non conuenire scribunt. Nam absurdum est putare contraria salitorū piscium qualita te ægros affici non posse. Præterea tertio Al-mansoris scriptum est, salitos pisces nullo mo-do fore ministrandos nisi in die quo aliquis si-bi medicari voluerit, hoc est non cibi sed me-dicinæ gratia commendandos esse salitos pi-sces. Quod Avicenna asseruit, cum dixit, V-num est quod ipsorum nutrimentum est ma-lum: unde plus via medicinæ sunt accipien-di, quàm via cibi. E piscibus salitis laudauit Gal.sardam, cum ait in tertio de facult. ali-mentorum: Pretiosissima est sardæ salitura.
units.tr: To sum up briefly: wherever the eruption is incomplete, if thick and viscous humours or an obstruction of the passages are the cause, despite fever and without a hot and dry constitution of the person, give dried figs and salted fish boldly. Nor should we listen to those who write that salted fish is not suitable for the sick. For it is absurd to think that the sick cannot be affected by the contrary quality of salted fish. Moreover, in the third book Almansor wrote that salted fish must not be given at all except on the day when someone wishes to medicate himself; that is, salted fish is to be recommended not for the sake of food but for the sake of medicine. Avicenna asserted this too, when he said: "It is one thing that its nourishment is bad; therefore salted fish must be taken by way of medicine rather than by way of food." Galen also praised salted sardine among salted fish, when he said in the third book On the Properties of Foods: "Salted sardine is most valuable."

units.la: Victum conuenientem hemitritæo docet.
units.tr: He teaches a diet suitable for hemitritaeus.

units.la: CAPVT XXIIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24

units.la: HEmitritæus verus, nempe quotidiana continua, & tertiana interpollata, me-dia rationis victum exposcit. Hunc dico qui subtilior sit quàm qui febribus interpollatis conuenit, crassior verò quàm continuis ab vno simplici humore: cum singularum qua-libet longior sit. Cunque naturæ duobus qua-litate & substantia contrarijs humoribus pugna sit, viribus et tempore indiget vt ambos vincat. Viriusque igitur causa, nempe vt adlongum seruetur tempus, & vt vires contra vtrunque hostem habeat, ampliori opus habet alimonia. Cunq; in superioribus in singulis febribus cibis ea miscuerimus quae peccantis humoris qualitates reprimant, oportebit in hemitriteo aut simul ea quae contraria rum sunt qualitatum, miscere, aut cibis vti temperatis. Ea quae alterum illorum solum re spiciunt administrare non licet. Nam vtriusque febris medicus sit solicitus oportet. Cibum temperatum dico qui à naturali calido solum patitur. Hunc hemitriteo laborantibus idoneum non esse ex eo intelliges, quod sanguinem qui ab eo in febribus generatur ruptiosa fore qualitatis necessum sit. Nam in tertiana febre ob bilis putrescentis calorem & acredinem, pars effectiua sanguinis extra naturalem temperiē est, nempe calidior & siccior. Quapropter cibus temperatus ob id quod à naturali calido solum patitur, nec particulae intemperiem contrarijs qualitatibus valet corrigere, eisdem afficietur. Quare sanguis qui ab eo generabitur calidior & siccior euadet, pro viscerum intemperie: qui statim breui momento in bilem vertetur. Simile iudicium in febre quae à pituita corpus praeter naturaliter humectum efficiente, ortum habet. Quapropter miscenda sunt in cibo, quae contrariarum sint qualitatum, aut id accipi endu in quo vtraq; qualitas reperiatur, quod magis probo. Quod si praeter haec incisuum id sit, ante alia eligendum. Simplicium medicamentorum vnum est acetum, quod praefatis sit facultatibus insigne. Vtriq; enim conuenit humori, partibus insuper tenuibus praeditum est, quibus incidit. Quapropter si id cum eo quod abstergere valeat miscueris, habebis id quod quaerimus. Moderate abstergentium zucarum vnum est, quod febricitantibus plus conuenit. Quare mixtionem ex zucaro & acri aceto, quam syrupum acetosum medici nuncuparunt, hemitritaeo maxime conuenientem esse putato, quo vteris in hunc modum:
units.tr: The true hemitritaeus, that is, the quotidian continuous and the interpolated tertian, requires a middling diet. I mean a diet subtler than that suited to the intermittent fevers, but coarser than that suited to the continuous fevers arising from a single simple humour, since each of the single fevers is longer. And since nature is at war with two humours contrary in quality and substance, it needs strength and time to conquer both. For the sake of both, namely that it may hold out for a long time and have strength against each enemy, it needs a more generous nourishment. In the earlier chapters, when we mixed into the foods, for each fever, those things that restrain the qualities of the offending humour, in the hemitritaeus we shall have to mix in either those things that are of contrary qualities, or use temperate foods. It is not permitted to apply only those things that deal with one of the two. For the physician must be concerned with both fevers. I call temperate food that which is affected only by natural heat. You will understand from this that it is not suitable for those suffering from hemitritaeus, because the blood generated from it in fevers must necessarily be of a ruptured quality. For in the tertian fever, on account of the heat and sharpness of putrefying bile, the effective part of the blood is outside its natural temperament, namely hotter and drier. Therefore temperate food, because it is affected only by natural heat and cannot correct the intemperance of the part by contrary qualities, will be affected in the same way. Hence the blood that is generated from it will become hotter and drier, in keeping with the intemperance of the viscera, and will at once in a brief moment turn into bile. A similar judgement applies to the fever which arises from phlegm making the body more moist than is natural. Therefore in the food there must be mixed those things that are of contrary qualities, or else one should take that in which both qualities are found, which I prefer. If, besides these, there is an incisive quality, that should be chosen first. Among simple medicines, one is vinegar, which is outstanding for the aforesaid powers. For it suits both humours, and moreover it is endowed with thin parts, by which it cuts. Therefore if you mix it with something that can wipe away, you will have what we seek. Of the moderately abstergent sweeteners, one is sugar, which is more suitable for feverish people. Therefore consider that a mixture of sugar and sharp vinegar, which physicians have called acetous syrup, is most suitable for the hemitritaeus, and use it in this way:

units.la: Thymi, petroselini, hordei ab vno cortice exuti, singulorum ma. vnum, passularum enucleatarum vnum, corticem vnum raphani linguam vellicantis, salis parum, bulliat cum pulla crassa quantum satis, huius decocti accipito lib. unā, syrupi acetosi acris quantum tolerauerit aegrotantis palatus. Iterum bulliant quousque misceantur, dato vt bibat cum oportuerit, ex reliquo fac sorbitionem.
units.tr: Of thyme, parsley, and barley stripped of one husk, each a handful; of one stoned raisin; one peel of radish, which stings the tongue; a little salt; boil with as much fat broth as is sufficient. Take one pound of this decoction, and as much sharp acetous syrup as the patient's palate can bear. Let them boil again until they are mixed; give it to drink when it is needed, and make a soup from the remainder.

units.la: Hac vtere ante accessionem vehementiore, et in eius inclinatione. in die verò mitiori eisdem vtitor, pullaeque extremitates aegrotanti ministrato. Syluestrem capum qui escā perrerrans quaeritet, coquito cum hordeo, radicibus apij, aceto, & sale, fac vt supra. Succi violarum mediae magnitudinis vncias tres, piperis nigri grosso modo contusi grana triginta, infundito in succum violarum, & ita esse sinito quousque transeant dies tres, postmodum cum iure misceto itavt ad uncias decem iuris, vnciam vnam succi imponas. Et quia violarum succus omni tempore haberi nō potest, succus simul cum pipere coaguletur, & ad formam trociscorum reddatur, vt singuli drach. vnam contineant. Mixtionem ex pipere & succo violarum magni esse iuua-menti in hemitritaeo in quo pituita & bilis pares habent vires compositio ostendit. In eo enim in quo alter humorum superat, nec verus, nec certus hemitritaeus dici potest. In quo vero bilis & pituita pares sunt robore, quem verum & certum vocamus hemitri-taeum, meminit Hippocrates in libro de mor-bis vulgaribus, horrificam febrem hemitri-taeum vocans, quia multoties in accessione vna febricitantes horrescant. Nam horror medius est, inter rigorem quem bilis, & fri-gus quod pituita inducit. Cunq; alter humo-rum superat, ita rigoris vel frigoris plus fit horror particeps. Quod si humor qui praeua-let in hemitritaeo pituita fuerit, hoc cibo vte-re. Pullam aut capum cum hordeo, radicibus apij & ciceribus, aceto & sale coquito, fac vt supra. Ptisanam cum radicibus apij cocta pipere & oxymelite optimam ijs esse sorbi-tionem indicato.
units.tr: Use this before the more vehement attack, and as it declines. On the milder day, use the same, and offer the patient the extremities of the broth. Boil a wild capon that wanders about seeking food with barley, parsley roots, vinegar, and salt, as above. Infuse three ounces of juice of medium-sized violets, and thirty grains of black pepper coarsely crushed, into the violet juice, and let it stand until three days have passed; afterwards mix it with the broth, so that you add one ounce of juice to ten ounces of broth. And since violet juice cannot be had at all times, let the juice be thickened together with the pepper and made into the form of lozenges, each containing one drachm. That the mixture of pepper and violet juice is of great help in the hemitritaeus in which phlegm and bile have equal powers, the composition shows. For in the case where one of the humours predominates, the hemitritaeus can be called neither true nor certain. But where bile and phlegm are equal in strength, we call it the true and certain hemitritaeus. Hippocrates mentions it in his book On Common Diseases, calling it the horrific fever, the hemitritaeus, because those who are feverish shiver many times in one attack. For the shivering is intermediate between the rigour that bile induces and the chill that phlegm produces. And when one of the humours predominates, the shivering partakes more of rigour or chill accordingly. But if the humour that prevails in the hemitritaeus is phlegm, use this food: boil a hen or capon with barley, parsley roots, and chickpeas, with vinegar and salt, as above. Indicate that a ptisan boiled with parsley roots, pepper, and oxymel is the best soup for these people.

units.la: Quod si bilis superior fuerit, ita vt horror plus ad rigorem accedat, pullam aut capum cum hordeo, hepatica, thymo, petroselino et apij radicibus sale & aceto coquito. Aqua hordei cum radicibus apij cocta, conueniens potus est verum patientibus hemitritæum. Iis vero in quibus pituita superior est, aqua decoctionis radicis apij, & seminis fœniculi dulcis. Potus vero qui hemitritæo laborantibus ratione virium & consuetudinis competat, ex potus tabellis quærendus est. Iis vero qui hemitritæum pituitosum patiuntur, si temperamento sint frigido, non abre erit radiculam zinziberis in cibis & potibus addere, vt simul integra bulliat. Est vnus ex Arabibus medicis qui hemitritæum patientem alit in die accessionis cucurbitis, spinacijs, attriplicibus, & similibus. Sed erat quantū sentio duplici ratione: Altera ab ipsa natura corporis sumpta, altera ab ipso cibo. In hora in qua natura intenta separationi est, frigida exhibenda non sunt cibaria, ne separationi naturæ obstent, & ne expulsionem periodicam quæ ab internis partibus ad exteriores fit, ad contrarium repellant po-rosq; occludant: quorum causa paroxysmus longior efficiatur: ut ijs qui diligenter ciba-riorum naturas quid singulis horis valeant efficere scrutantur manifestum est. Iis adde cibos qui ex herbis oleribus ue parantur cor-ruptioni obnoxios esse, ex eo quod aquosum generent sanguinem, qui promptissime calo-rem extraneum concipiat. Prudentis consilij igitur non est, huiusmodi cibos tunc ministra-re, cum causa corrumpens validior est: non aliter quàm si ignauum & imbecillem mili-tem strenuæ inimicorū cohorti obijcias. Sed de hoc abunde supra diximus, vbi ostendimus cibum ex herbis aut oleribus inutilem esse a-cute febricitantibus: eosque in ægrotantium damnum errare, qui citra occasionem her-bis in cibo frequenter vtuntur: grauius eos peccare, qui ante accessiones herbas aut ole-ra ministrant, putantes se scopum attigisse. Qua in re nostrorum medicorum plurimi quo-tidie labuntur. Quando autem herbis & ole= oleribus in cibo vti conueniat infrà Deo inspirante, dicemus.
units.tr: But if bile predominates, so that the shivering tends more towards rigour, boil a hen or capon with barley, hepatica, thyme, parsley, and parsley roots, with salt and vinegar. Barley water boiled with parsley roots is a suitable drink for those who truly suffer from the hemitritaeus. For those in whom phlegm predominates, the water of a decoction of parsley root and sweet fennel seed. The drink that suits those suffering from the hemitritaeus in regard to their strength and habit is to be sought from the tables of drinks. For those who suffer from the phlegmatic hemitritaeus, if they are of a cold temperament, it will not be out of place to add a little root of ginger to food and drink, so that it boils whole together. There is one of the Arab physicians who feeds the patient with the hemitritaeus on the day of the attack with gourds, spinach, orache, and similar things. But, as far as I perceive, this is wrong for two reasons: the first taken from the very nature of the body, the second from the food itself. At the hour when nature is intent on separation, cold foods must not be given, lest they obstruct nature's separation, and lest they repel the periodic expulsion, which goes from the internal parts to the external, to the contrary, and close up the pores; on account of which the paroxysm becomes longer. This is clear to those who carefully examine what each food can do in each hour. Add that foods prepared from herbs or vegetables are liable to corruption, because they generate watery blood, which very readily takes in foreign heat. It is therefore not the part of prudent counsel to give such foods at the time when the corrupting cause is stronger; it is no different from throwing a feeble and weak soldier at the vigorous cohort of enemies. But we have said enough about this above, where we showed that food of herbs or vegetables is useless for those acutely feverish, and that those who frequently use herbs in food without reason err to the patients' harm; that those who give herbs or vegetables before the attacks, thinking they have hit the mark, sin more gravely. In this matter very many of our physicians stumble every day. When it is fitting to use herbs and vege-tables in food, we shall say below, with God's inspiration.

units.la: Febri in qua exteriora frigent, & interiora calent, & econtra, quis cōueniat uictus.
units.tr: On the fever in which the exterior parts are cold and the interior hot, and conversely, what diet is suitable.

units.la: CAPVT XXV.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXV.

units.la: FEBRIS in qua exteriora frigent et calent interiora, à bili putrescente ortū habet. In qua febrili calore phlegmata crassa in exterioribus existentia dissoluente, accidit partes externas infrigidari, æstuantibus internis. Subtili ideo indigent victu, quia febrilis calor multoties in seipsum reduplicatur transpiratione prohibita. Quapropter periculo non vacat hæc febris, sicut cum à revocatione natiui calidi exteriora frigent. Cibus ijs conuenit refrigerans: cui misceantur ea quæ aperire & valenter incidere valeat.
units.tr: A fever in which the outer parts are cold and the inner parts hot arises from putrid bile. In this feverish heat the thick phlegm present in the outer parts is dissolved, and it happens that the external parts grow cold while the internal parts burn. Such patients therefore need a light diet, because the feverish heat is often redoubled within itself when transpiration is blocked. For this reason this fever is not free from danger, unlike the case where the outer parts grow cold from a recall of the natural heat. A cooling food suits them, with things added that can open and cut vigorously.

units.la: Post calidam & asperam totius corporis fricationem, hunc febricitanti cibum ministrato: Ptisanam cum radicibus apij & petroselini, et lenticula aquæ parato, coquitoq sufficienter. Et cum syrupo acetoso, aut oxy-melite ægrotanti si frigida sit natura ministrato.
units.tr: After a warm, rough rubbing of the whole body, give the feverish patient this food: a barley gruel prepared with roots of celery and parsley and with water lentils, and boil it sufficiently. Give it to the sick person with a vinegar syrup or oxymel if the nature is cold.

units.la: Aliud, Coquito pulla cu eisdem herbis, foliis raphani, hordeo & aceto, fac potionem et tenuem sorbitionem. Præterea infundatur in libra vna aceti acerrimi, ficuu siccarum lib. vnius tertia, sinito per diem et noctem, postmodum coletur. Huius aceti vncias tres accipito, aquæ decoctionis radicis apij, lenticulae aquæ, vncias quatuor, zucari quantum sufficit, coquito & fac syrupum acetosum ijs conuenientem. Cumque hæc febris ab vno simplici accidit humore, vt a pituita valde crassa, quæ putrescens exteriora non valet calfacere, aut suæ crassitiei aut leuis putredinis occasione, ad febres phlegmaticas aut melancholicas aut cholericas pro victu eliciendo recurrendum est. A singulis enim prædictorum humorum originem posse habere, doctissimis viris placitum est. Unde bene dixit Arabs, Tu vero, inquit, non debes ad paroxysmos respicere. nam potest esse quod sit quotidiana, tertiana, & quartana, & quae quinto et septimo periodicant. De iis vero quibus a reuocatione caloris ad intro, accidit infrigidari in febribus extrema, alibi nobis sermo erit.
units.tr: Another: boil a chicken with the same herbs, radish leaves, barley and vinegar, and make a thin potion or sup. Besides, steep one pound of very sharp vinegar with a third of a pound of dried figs for a day and a night, and afterwards strain it. Take three ounces of this vinegar, four ounces of the decoction of celery root and water lentils, sugar as much as is sufficient, boil them and make a vinegar syrup suited to them. And when this fever arises from a single simple humour, such as very thick phlegm which, putrefying, cannot warm the outer parts, either because of its thickness or because of a slight putrefaction, one must turn for the diet to the phlegmatic, melancholic or choleric fevers. For it has pleased the most learned men that the fever may have its origin from each of the aforesaid humours. Hence the Arab rightly said: "You, however," he says, "should not look to the paroxysms, for it may be that it is quotidian," tertian, and quartan, and those which recur every fifth and seventh day. But concerning those in whom the extremities grow cold in fevers because the heat has withdrawn inward, we will speak elsewhere.

units.la: Est alia febris in qua exteriora calent & interiora friget. Quae ab aliquibus hepiala nominatur, a nonnullis lipyria ab aliis tenedos. Sed nomina secundum Platonem contemnere oportet eos, quibus ipsarum rerum incumbit inuestigatio. Haec accidit cum a putrescente bile caloremque febrilem excitante, phlegmata crassa in interioribus concreta dissoluuntur. Accidit enim vt iis solutis partes internae frigefiant. Victus iis copiosioris alimoniae exhiberi potest. Minus enim periculosa haec aegritudo est, vtpote praeternaturali calido in externas solum saeuiente partes. Miscenda igitur ea sunt quae valenter incidant & abstergant cum mediocri calore. Quapropter iis cibis vtere, quos hemitritaeo phlegmaticae conuenire diximus.
units.tr: There is another fever in which the outer parts are hot and the inner parts are cold. Some call this the hepiala, others the lipyria, others the tenedos. But one ought to disregard the names, following Plato, for those whose concern is the investigation of the things themselves. This arises when thick phlegm gathered in the inner parts is dissolved by bile putrefying and stirring up the feverish heat. For when these are dissolved, the inner parts happen to grow cold. Such patients may be given a more copious nourishment. For this illness is less dangerous, since the unnatural heat rages only in the external parts. Therefore things should be mixed in that vigorously cut and cleanse, with a moderate warmth. So use those foods which we said suit the phlegmatic semitertian.

units.la: Gallus antiquus post longam dimicationem cum altero, occidatur. Coquaturque cum hordeo passulis enucleatis, pulegio, hyssopo, thymo, & violis, temperetur〉 cum oxyme lite acri, propinato quantum vno haustu sorbere possit, sorbitionem ne facias.
units.tr: An old cock, after a long fight with another, is to be killed. Let it be boiled with barley, raisins with the stones removed, pennyroyal, hyssop, thyme and violets, and seasoned with sharp oxymel. Give him as much as he can sip in one draught; do not make it into a thick broth.

units.la: Præterea in aqua hordei conficito sorbitio nem ex furfure & fermento, vt supra docuimus in febribus phlegmaticis. Sunt qui hanc quoque febrem à simplici pituita quæ non putruit secundum totum euenire affirment. Sunt & qui à melancholia. Quorum victus sunt ex supradictis petendi. Hoc tamen proprium iis febribus inest. Omnia nem pe quæ aperiendo exiccant iis febribus incommoda ideò esse, quòd materiam crassiore red dunt, tenuioribus partibus in halitus digestis. Cunque febrium quæ calorem & frigus simul operantur materias, crassos humores esse medici asserant, fit, vt qui iis cicerum et muriam iis concedunt, febricitantibus parum salubriter consuluisse videatur. Rectius profecto fuerit, iis vti, quæ humida existentia, abstergere & incidere possint. Cum igitur huic febri à simplici pituita dependente ob uiaueris niaueris, praesertim in homine frigidae naturae hunc cibum ministrato.
units.tr: Besides, make a broth in barley water from bran and leaven, as we taught above for phlegmatic fevers. There are those who affirm that this fever too arises wholly from simple phlegm which has not putrefied. There are also those who say it arises from melancholy. Their diets are to be sought from those described above. Yet this peculiarity belongs to these fevers: all the things that dry by opening are harmful in them, because they make the matter thicker, the finer parts being digested into vapours. And since physicians assert that the matters of fevers which work heat and cold together are thick humours, it seems that those who allow chickpeas and brine to such patients have not advised very wholesomely for the feverish. It would surely be better to use things that, being moist, can cleanse and cut. Therefore, since this fever depends on simple phlegm, give this food, especially to a person of cold nature.

units.la: Senescentem gallum praedicto modo defatigatum parato ad hunc modum, chamaemeli man. unum & semis, ficuum aridarum, passularum enucleatarum, singulorum man. unum, hordei ab uno cortice exuti mă. tres, coquito sufficienter & colato. Accipito iuris libram unam, adipis anatis recentis uncias tres, aceti albi è pulegio unciam unam, salis parum. bulliant iterum donec permisceantur. Dato calidum quantum uno haustu sorbere possit. Efficacissimum est ad crassos humores & lentos febrem generantes. Idem cum capo & pulla efficere possis sed ineffica cius. Dicatur haec sorbitio ex adipe anatis.
units.tr: Prepare an old cock, worn out in the aforesaid way, in this manner: a handful and a half of chamomile, a handful each of dried figs and raisins with the stones removed, three handfuls of barley hulled of its outer husk; boil sufficiently and strain. Take one pound of the broth, three ounces of fresh duck fat, one ounce of white vinegar with pennyroyal, a little salt. Let them boil again until they are mixed together. Give it warm, as much as he can sip in one draught. It is most effective against thick and sluggish humours that generate fever. You could make the same with capon and chicken, but it would be less effective. Let this broth be called the duck-fat broth.

units.la: Superest de ea in qua simul calor & frigus per totum sentiuntur, febre sermonem facere. Haec à bile putrescente similiter ortu habet. Calore febrili crassa phlegmata partes internas & externas occupantia dissoluente, accidit, ut aegrotantis sensus minimas non percipiens differentias, calorem & frigus in eadem parte esse iudicet. Victus ijs conueniens est, qui incidere, & abstergere, & exic care vtcunque valeat. Phlegmata siquidem in hac febre facilius dissoluuntur quam in prædi ctis. Signum est frigus intro & extra perceptum, quod lationem materiæ per omnes indicat partes. Latio vero, eius liquefactione, liquefactio obedientia materiæ (calori) dissoluenti. Phlegmata igitur cum in duritiem nō oc calluere, aliquali indiget exiccatione. Quapropter talem ijs victum ministrato.
units.tr: It remains to speak of the fever in which heat and cold are felt together throughout the whole body. This likewise has its origin in putrid bile. When the feverish heat dissolves the thick phlegm occupying the inner and outer parts, it happens that the patient, not perceiving the slightest differences of sensation, judges that heat and cold are in the same part. A diet suited to these is one that can cut, cleanse, and dry in whatever way. For in this fever phlegm is dissolved more easily than in the aforesaid. The sign is cold perceived within and without, which indicates the movement of matter through all the parts. Movement, however, comes from its liquefaction, and liquefaction from the matter's yielding to the dissolving heat. Therefore, since the phlegm has not hardened into a crust, it needs some drying. For this reason give them such a diet.

units.la: Gallum senem vt supra defatigatum coquito cum hordeo, radicibus apij, petroselini, passulis enucleatis, ciceribus. Hora vna ante quam ab igne amoueas, proïcito aceti albi è pulegio quantum satis, salis modicum, fac vt supra. Potus omnibus ijs sit aqua hordei cum semine fœniculi & radice apij cocta. Iis verò qui intus frigent & extra calent, vinum album prædicta aqua dilutū administretur.
units.tr: Boil an old cock, worn out as above, with barley, roots of celery and parsley, raisins with the stones removed, and chickpeas. One hour before you take it from the fire, add white vinegar with pennyroyal, as much as is enough, and a modest amount of salt; do as above. The drink for all these should be barley water boiled with fennel seed and celery root. But for those who are cold within and hot without, let white wine diluted with the aforesaid water be given.

units.la: Quando à symptomatibus sumenda sit victus ratio.
units.tr: When the regimen of diet is to be taken from the symptoms.

units.la: CAPVT XXVI.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVI.

units.la: SED quos nam victus exigant singulæ sebres, indicatione sumpta ab affectu, & ab eius causa abunde quidem dictum est: Nunc verò quos nam victus symptomatum simul habita ratione adhibere conueniat tempestiuum est percurramus. Nam quemadmodum symptomata curationis quandoque indicationem ad se trahunt, sic & victus rationem. Victus enim administratio pars curationis est. Id etiam, sicut & reliqua, ab Hippocrate didicimus, quem a symptomatu etiam natura & vehementia, victum conuenientem inuestigare obseruamus. Vt in eo, Vbi autem dolor aliquis vexauerit, oxymeli bibendum dabis, hyme calidum, & state frigidum. Quod si multa sitis fuerit melicrato v- tendum & aqua Galenus in expositione ita ait: Nempe quantum ad morbum spectat, oxymelite magis est vtendum. Verum si æger accepto multo oxymelite adhuc sitiuerit, melicratum dare oportet. Quod si ab ea re sitiuerit, aquam offerendam putato. etsi aqua per se pota culpa non careat. Præterea infra ratione
units.tr: But what kind of diet each individual fever requires, with the indication taken from the affection and from its cause, has been discussed fully enough. Now it is timely to run through what diet ought to be applied to the symptoms, taking them into account at the same time. For just as symptoms sometimes draw the indication for treatment to themselves, so they also draw the plan of diet. For the administration of diet is part of treatment. We have learned this, as with the rest, from Hippocrates, whom we observe also seeking a suitable diet from the nature and severity of the symptom. As in this passage: "Where some pain has troubled him, you shall give him oxymel to drink, warm in winter and cold in summer." Galen, in his exposition, says this: "Indeed, as far as the disease is concerned, oxymel is to be used more. But if the patient, having taken a great deal of oxymel, is still thirsty, honey-water ought to be given. But if he is thirsty from that, you should think water ought to be offered, although water drunk by itself is not without fault." Furthermore, below, in the reasoning

units.la: In 1. de ratione uict. Symptomatis superuenientis sorbitionis mo-dum mutare iubet, cum inquit: Postea si do-lor quispiam vel periculum comparuerit sor-bitionem dare oportet neque multam nequecrassam, &c. Sed inuestigare diligenter o-portet, qua symptomatis magnitudine muta-re victum oporteat. Initium huius inuestiga-tionis ab Hippocrate etiam sumendum est, viro sapientissimo. Ille enim victus ratione in sola effatu digna symptomatis magnitudineimmutare videtur, ut cum dixit: Ἐὰν δὲ πολλὰ σίτια ᾖ, μελικρήτῳ καὶ ὕδατι. Hoc est, Simulta sitis fuerit melicrato et aqua. Ratio id quoq; suadet ut non a symptomatu quacun-que magnitudine, sed ab ea quae effatu digna est, curationis scopus mutandus sit. Nam cum symptomata morborum effectus sint, abla-tione causarum euanescunt. Quapropter ut effectus sunt nullius sunt capacia indicatio-nis. Cum vero ad effatu dignam accrescunt magnitudinem, indicationem curationis prae-stant. Proinde cum effatu dignae symptoma-tum magnitudines, sicut & cuiusuis rei, in-numerae numeræ sint, sola ipsius magnitudinis ratione differētes, nisi aliquo signo magnitudinē sym ptomatum diffiniamus, incompletus & om- nino inutilis noster sermo esset. Sic igitur sym ptomatum magnitudo diffinienda est, ut eo- rum ratione victus mutetur, nempe cum ali cuius præter naturalis dispositionis sunt cau sa, quæ aut morbum addat, aut naturæ vi- res exoluat. Quodcunque horum in corpore eueniat symptomatis magnitudinis causa, iu- sto tunc symptomata victus rationem & cu ratiuam indicationem suppeditant. Vt pleuri tico parum sitienti oxymeli, aut melicratū, quæ ipse morbus exegerit offeres. Quod si mul ta siti vexetur, non ijs quæ morbum & eius causam respiciunt, sed ijs quæ sitim mitigant vteris. Nam multa sitis sputum exiccat, & morbum incoctibilem reddit, febrisque calo rem auget. Quapropter melicratum & aquā exhibebimus à symptomate indicatione sum pta. Nam aqua morbi gratia exhibenda non esset, ob id quod doloris maturationi aduersa est. Sic ergo symptomatum magnitudo diffinienda est, vt ab eis ratio curationis & victus indicationes sumantur. Caeterum huiusmodi symptomata cum ad dictam peruenniut magnitudinem, hoc est vicem habent causae ad morbum relata, aut vrgentis, aut causae sine qua morbus curari non possit vicem habent. Quapropter potior est quae ab eis sumitur indicatio quam a morbo, vt ex dogmate de complicatis affectibus colligitur. Hoc etiam manifestum est ex eo quod Hippocrates pleuritico valde sitienti aquam concessit. Qua si potiorem a morbo indicationem faceret non exhiberet. Manifestum igitur est ex doctrina Hippocratis, ut cum symptomata ad eam magnitudinem peruenient vt in morbum ad dant, aut vires naturae exoluant, ab eis potiorem sumendam victus esse indicatione. Danda nihilominus est opera, vt ea ministremus quae aut morbo si fieri posset conueniant, aut saltem incommoda non sint.
units.tr: In the first book of On the Regimen in Acute Diseases, Hippocrates orders the broth to be changed when a supervening symptom appears, when he says: "Afterwards, if some pain or danger appears, broth ought to be given, neither thick nor crude," etc. But we must carefully investigate by how great a magnitude of symptom the diet ought to be changed. The beginning of this investigation must also be taken from Hippocrates, that most wise man. For he seems to change the diet by the magnitude of the symptom alone, when it is worth mentioning, when he said: "If there is much thirst, [give] honey-water and water" [Ἐὰν δὲ πολλὰ σίτια ᾖ, μελικρήτῳ καὶ ὕδατι]. That is, if there is much thirst, honey-water and water. Reason also suggests that the aim of treatment should be changed not by a symptom of any magnitude, but by one that is worth mentioning. For since symptoms are the effects of diseases, they vanish when the causes are removed; as effects, therefore, they are capable of no indication. But when they grow to a magnitude worth mentioning, they provide an indication for treatment. Since the magnitudes of symptoms worth mentioning are innumerable, as with anything else, differing only in their size, unless we define the magnitude of the symptoms by some sign, our discourse would be incomplete and altogether useless. Thus the magnitude of the symptoms is to be defined so that the plan of diet is changed by reference to them, namely when there is some cause beyond the natural disposition, which either adds to the disease or wears down the strength of nature. Whichever of these occurs in the body as the cause of the magnitude of the symptom, then the symptoms rightly supply the rule of diet and the curative indication. So, in pleurisy, with a patient who is only a little thirsty, you will offer oxymel or honey-water, as the disease itself demands. But if he is troubled by great thirst, you should use not the things that look to the disease and its cause, but those that mitigate the thirst. For great thirst dries the sputum and makes the disease hard to concoct, and it increases the heat of the fever. Therefore we shall give honey-water and water, the indication being taken from the symptom. For water should not be given for the sake of the disease, because it is adverse to the maturation of the pain. Thus the magnitude of the symptoms is to be defined so that the indications of treatment and diet are drawn from them. Moreover, when such symptoms reach that worth-mentioning magnitude, they take the place of a cause related to the disease, either as an urgent cause or as a cause without which the disease cannot be cured. Therefore the indication drawn from them is more powerful than that drawn from the disease, as is gathered from the doctrine on complicated affections. This is also evident from the fact that Hippocrates allowed water to a pleuritic patient who was very thirsty; if he had made the indication from the disease more powerful, he would not have given it. It is clear, then, from the teaching of Hippocrates, that when symptoms reach that magnitude at which they add to the disease or wear down the powers of nature, the indication from them is to be taken as the more powerful in diet. Nevertheless, care must be taken to provide those things which are either suitable for the disease, if that is possible, or at least not harmful.

units.la: In uigilijs conuenientem uictum inuestigat.
units.tr: He investigates a suitable diet in wakefulness.

units.la: CAPVT XXVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVII.

units.la: Ebricitanti patienti vigilias à biliosò humore ortum habentes hunc cibum ministrato: Ex aqua hordei lac amygdalarum conficito mediocri crassitie, cunque semicoctum fuerit, man. vnum coriandri viridis in mortario conterito, addito modico croci simul in ollam projcito. Zucari quantum satis addito. Fac vt decenter coquatur ad lentum ignem semper cum cochleari agitando quousque mediocriter crassum reddatur. Ex trahito ab igne & linteis circumuoluito, et tepidum ministrato. Hac sorbitione vsus fui olim in Anglia. Erat Anglus dicturus coram Henrico Anglia rege inuictissimo, & regni primoribus: curabatque vt suo cum honore rem ageret. Cunque tempus instaret, paucis ante diebus immoderato studio, vigilanti cura, cerebrum adeo exiccauit, vt in vigilias incideret. Cunque apud amicos de ea re quaereretur, nec diacodion, nec syrupo de papauere nec aliis id genus quæ ei in remedium miserant somnum sibi conciliare posset: tertiusque dies instaret, qua sibi sano capite opus erat, cunque ob imbecillitatem quam vigilia induxerant parum sibi crede-ret, in maxima erat solicitudine quid ageret. Accedens forte amicus hominem salutandi gratia, rem audiens, consuluit ut mea utere tur opera. Repente ipse veniens, hominem in ueni praeter modum calfactum. Cunque arteriam tangerem, conieci parum abesse homi-minem a febrili dispositione, in eamque lapsurum nisi praesentaneo remedio ad propria re-uocaretur temperiem. Cunque haec ei retulissem, acclamauit ut omni diligentia id praesta re vellem. Cunque hominem bono esse animo iuberet, abij, sero rediens, sole iam occumben te hominem in capacissimo labro aquae tepidae sedere iussi, ibique hora una immorari permisi. Exiens lectum petiit, ibi cum parum quie sceret, homini lac supradictum exhibui, abijq. Pueris admonitis, ut strepitum vitarent. Sequenti die mihi accedenti occurrerunt famuli gratias agentes quod heri vigilias & famulorum vno remedio sanassem, (inquietabat enim eos) referentes herum solidam dormisse noctem. Quod si in conficiendo lacte micam panis in aqua rosarum infusam simul cum amygdalis teras, crassiorem efficies sorbitionem magis nutrientem & humectantem.
units.tr: For a patient who is drunk with wakefulness arising from a bilious humour, give this food: from barley water and almond milk make a preparation of moderate thickness; when it is half cooked, pound in a mortar one handful of fresh coriander, add a little saffron, and throw it into the pot together. Add sugar as much as is enough. Cook it properly over a slow fire, always stirring with a spoon, until it is of moderate thickness. Take it off the fire, wrap the vessel in linen, and give it lukewarm. I once used this broth in England. There was an Englishman who was about to speak before Henry, king of England, most unconquered, and the leading men of the kingdom; he was anxious to carry the matter off with credit. When the time was pressing, a few days before, through immoderate study and anxious care he had so dried out his brain that he fell into sleeplessness. When his friends asked about it, neither diacodion, nor syrup of poppy, nor other such remedies they had sent him could bring him sleep, and the third day was approaching, on which he needed a clear head; and since the weakness which the wakefulness had brought on made him trust himself little, he was in the greatest anxiety about what to do. By chance a friend came to greet him, heard the matter, and advised that he make use of my services. I came at once and found the man unusually heated. When I touched his pulse, I judged he was not far from a feverish condition and would fall into it unless his temperament were called back to its proper state by an immediate remedy. When I had told him this, he cried out that I should do it with every diligence. When I bade him be of good cheer, I went away; returning late, when the sun was already setting, I had the man sit in a very large basin of warm water and allowed him to remain there for one hour. On leaving, he went to bed; when he was not quiet there, I gave the man the aforesaid milk and left, after warning the boys to avoid noise. On the next day, as I approached, the servants met me giving thanks that I had yesterday cured both the wakefulness and the servants with one remedy, for it had been disturbing them, and reporting that their master had slept a sound night. If, when preparing the milk, you pound a crumb of bread steeped in rose water together with the almonds, you will make a thicker broth, more nourishing and moistening.

units.la: Quod si crassiori uti velis sorbitione hoc modo conficito: Panem purissimum medio cris ætatis in exiguas abrade particulas, tribusque aquis lavato, deinde amygdalarum succum ex aqua hordei extrahito, simulque cum pane coquito, ad lentum ignem semper agitando, cumque semicoctum fuerit, coriandri viride quantum manu capi possit in mortario cum pauco croco conterito, & cum sorbitione quæ ad ignem est dissoluto, adiecto zucaro, simul omnia coquito, quousque permisceantur, cochleari panem ad ollæ parietes atterens. Conueniens hic cibus est exiccato & supercalfacto cerebro, frigidos & humidos halitus ad caput mittit, naturæ cerebri nimium familiares. Lusitanarum quæ in ægrotantium commodum diligentiores sunt fœminæ, cum somnum conciliare student, sorbitionem sic parant: Micam panis post ab-
units.tr: But if you wish to use a thicker gruel, prepare it in this way: cut the purest bread of middle age into small pieces, wash it in three waters, then extract the juice of almonds from barley water, and boil it together with the bread over a slow fire, stirring constantly; when it is half cooked, pound a handful of fresh coriander in a mortar with a little saffron, dissolve it in the gruel that is on the fire, add sugar, and boil everything together until they are mixed, scraping the bread against the sides of the pot with a spoon. This food is suitable for a dried and overheated brain; it sends cold and moist vapours to the head, which are very familiar to the nature of the brain. The women of Portugal, who are more careful for the comfort of the sick, when they wish to induce sleep, prepare the gruel thus: they boil a crumb of bread after washing it in barley water,

units.la: Sorbitio crassior. lutionem in aqua hordei coquunt, butyri re-centis parum pro panis portione, aut oleum purissimu oliuarum eius loco iniiciunt. Cunque fere coctu est, coriandrum viride & croci parum conterunt, & in mortario cum sorbitio nis modico dissoluunt. Oui recentis (in aqua frigida horis tribus infusi) vitellum, cum sorbitione quae in mortario est cochlearis conquassatione permiscent, in ollam reiiciunt et cum zucaro simul coquunt, semper agitando cum cochleari donec percoctum sit. Valens hic cibus est ad conciliandum somnum. Attamen quia multi nutrimenti est, continuis febribus & acutis non convenit. Nisi facultatis imbe cillitas id suaderet. Febribus ijs quae periodi-ce intermittunt & quiescunt bono temporis interuallo concedi posset.
units.tr: Thicker gruel. They boil it in barley water, adding a little fresh butter in proportion to the bread, or in its place the purest olive oil. When it is nearly cooked, they pound a little fresh coriander and saffron and dissolve them in a mortar with a spoonful of the gruel. Fresh egg (infused in cold water for three hours), they mix the yolk with the gruel that is in the mortar, by stirring with a spoon, and return it to the pot and boil it together with the sugar, always stirring with the spoon until it is thoroughly cooked. This food is strong for inducing sleep. However, since it is rich in nourishment, it is not suitable for continual and acute fevers, unless the weakness of the strength required it. It could be allowed in those fevers which intermit periodically and remit within a good interval of time.

units.la: Lactucas quae mediae sunt aetatis in aqua coquito, cunque percoctae fuerint, aquam ab eis forti compressione extrahito, culltello in exi-guas portiunculas percute, oleo, aceto, sale, & zucaro pro portione inspersis, vigilias pa tienti dato ut cum pane devoret. Qui vero vigivigilias ob doloris vehementiam patiuntur, cibis somnum inducere ne speres, sed confestim relicta ea artis medicæ parte quæ victus rationem docet, ad utranque & quæ de medicamentis agit, & quæ circa manus operationem versatur te confer, ab illis quo homi-nem à dolore leues, auxilium petas, sciens in hora doloris cibum quemcunque culpa non vacare, Præcipuè qui facilè acescat aut in-sumum abeat. Utraque enim causa dolorē augnet. Nam ptisana quæ ab Hippocrate ut conuenientissimus cibus acute febricitantibus receptus est, in vehementia doloris ab eodem damnatur, in primo de ratione victus in morbis acutis, in hæc verba. Nisi quis (inquit) dolorem vel alui subductione, vel secta vena, pro utriusuis exigentia soluerit, et ptisanā ita affectis dederit, præcipitem aget in mortem. De reliquis cibis in hora doloris ita ait: Prehendunt hæc non solum si ptisana intempestiue utantur, verū & multo magis si quip-piam aliud quod ptisana inconuenientius sit, vel ederint vel biberint. Sed fortasse quis nobis obyciet Hippocratem in prædictis locis ptisanam prohibuisse sicuti & cibos alios, non doloris sed inflammationis membranæ succingentis costas rationę, de qua ei sermo erat, quam dolorem appellauit. Verè ita res habet, non ob id tamen aufertur quod diximus, nempe in hora vehementis doloris, cibum quemcunque & si leuissimum culpa non vacare. Quinimmò magno esse nocumento assero, hac ductus ratione. Dolor est ex iis quæ maximè virtutem corporis prosternut, vt Galeno visum: Ita vt nec ventriculus cibum recte coquat, nec hepar aut venæ hunc in sanguinem commodè mutent: Nec distributio prætera, nec appositio, nec excrementorum expulsio, nec vlla naturalium actionum commodè peragatur. Tum ob dolorem actiones lædentem, tum maximè ob id quod intenta natura ad id quod contristat, sanguinem & spiritus, qui commune ad omnes actiones instrumentum est, ad locum doloris mittat. Vnde fit vt loca coctioni deputata indigentiam patiantur. Quæ causa est vt cibus perperam perperam coquatur in ventriculo, hepate, et venis, facileque inde extraneum concipiat calorem. Et tandem additionis doloris causa fiat. Cum igitur loca coctioni deputata influentis calidi indigentiam patiantur, & obiectum in quod agunt calido extraneo obnoxium ob id (natura alio intenta) maneat, consulte medici agunt sanguinem in forti dolore mittere. Vt quantum natura a consueta deficit cura, tantum sanguinis imminuatur: iuxta illud, minori curae minus quod curet. Nec solum mittendus est sanguis, vt qui in iocinere & venis est, succum ab extraneo calore incolumē tueamur. Sed & cibo qui in ventriculo est consulimus, vomitum prouocantes. Cum haec ita se habeant, dementis consilij fuerit, cibum ea hora ministrare, qua eius a corpore eductio doloris remedium est. Qua in sententia Galenus est in expositione illius, Maius quidem malum est & c. Vbi ad hunc modum scribit: Contra autem qui ob dolorem vel morbi acumen, euacuatione interdum magis quàm repletione indigent. Immo qui cibum his exhibet, maximum operatur malu, &c. Caeterum cum dolorum plures sint differentiae, ita ut alij alternis invadant temporibus & remittant, alij perpetuo torqueant, horum nonnulli talem consecuti sunt vehementiam, ut in vigilias laborantes deducant: alij in inquietationes: non una victus ratio ab omnibus sumenda erit. Dolores igitur quicunque laborantes inquietant omnem cibum et potum abscindunt, ut in iis quae in primo libro diximus abunde dictum est. Vbi osten dimus morbum cui continua coniuncta est inquietatio intra dies quatuor terminari ob eius vehementiam, & omnimodam ei absti nentiam convenire. Vehementissimi quidem dolores sunt, qui laborantes in inquietationem deducant. De hoc locutus est citato loco Galenus, cum dixit, Qui alimentum his ministrat, maximum operatur malum. Quod manifestum est ex iis quae in initio expositionis scripsit, ubi vehementissimum dolorem ad hunc modum describit: Propter dolores saepe quidem laborantes sine pulsu fiunt, & animi deliquia incurrunt, & in nullo motu moueri possunt. Similia his ab acumine morbi euenient. Sunt autem quibus non propter id virtus laborat, sed ob vasorum quomodolibet facta euacuationem. Siue igitur ob excretionem sensui manifestam, siue ob διαφόρησιν, id est in hac litus digestionem, siue ob inediam, hi quidem alimento indigent & quam celerrime refici. Contra autem qui ob dolorem, vel morbi acumen, euacuatione aliquando indigent magis quam additione. Immo qui alimentum his porrigit, maximum malum operatur. Validum ex verbis Galeni sumitur argumentum, laboranti vehementissimo dolore cum robore virium, nullum exhibendum fore alimentum, cum in eos qui ob dolorem imbecilles admodum facti sunt, ita vt absque pulsu fiant & animi deliquio capiantur, maximum operari malum scribat. Per dolores qui proxime a vehementissimis degenerant, vnam decubitus formam seruare queunt laborantes, somnum tamen capere non possunt. Quare talis ijs victus ministrandus est, qualem morbis qui ad septimum terminantur cõuenire diximus. Vigilia enim continuæ, vt in primo libro ostendimus, vnũ est ex tribus symptomatibus quæ morbum ad septimum terminant. Iis igitur qui ob dolorem perpetuas patiũtur vigilias, victus per pocula conuenit. Sic Hippocrates, Vti vero potu oportet, si dolor aliquis affuerit, oxymelite, hyeme quidem calido, æstate vero frigi-do. Si vero multa sitis fuerit, & melicrato et aqua. Quo in loco Hippocrates victus for-mam ratione duorum symptomatum diffi-niuit, nempe a dolore & a multa siti, dicens:
units.tr: Boil middle-aged lettuces in water. When they are thoroughly cooked, press the water out of them firmly, chop them with a knife into small pieces, sprinkle them with oil, vinegar, salt and sugar in due proportion, and give them to the sleepless patient to eat with bread. But those who suffer sleeplessness from the severity of pain must not hope to induce sleep with food. Instead, leave at once that part of the medical art which teaches the regimen of diet, and turn to the other parts, both the one that deals with medicines and the one concerned with manual operations, and seek from them help to relieve the man of his pain. Know that in the hour of pain no food whatever is free of fault, especially one that easily turns sour or passes into flatulence, for either of these causes increases the pain. For the ptisane, which Hippocrates received as the most suitable food for those with acute fevers, is condemned by the same author in the midst of severe pain. In the first book of the Regimen in Acute Diseases he writes these words: "Unless one (he says) relieves the pain, either by evacuating the bowels or by opening a vein, according to what each case requires, and gives a ptisane to those so affected, he will drive them headlong to death." Concerning other foods in the hour of pain he says: "These things are harmful not only if the ptisane is used at the wrong time, but much more so if they eat or drink something else that is less suitable than the ptisane." But perhaps someone will object to us that Hippocrates, in the passages cited, forbade the ptisane, as he did other foods, on account of the inflammation of the membrane that surrounds the ribs, which was the subject of his discussion, and which he called pain. It is true that this is the case, but this does not refute what we have said: that in the hour of severe pain no food whatever, even the lightest, is free of fault. Indeed, I maintain that it is a great harm, for the following reason. Pain is among those things that most of all prostrate the strength of the body, as Galen thought. So the stomach cannot properly digest the food, nor can the liver or the veins convert it suitably into blood; nor is distribution, apposition, or the expulsion of excrements, nor any natural action, carried out properly. Partly because pain disturbs the actions, and most of all because nature, intent on what causes distress, sends blood and spirits, which are the common instrument of all actions, to the place of pain. Hence it comes about that the places appointed for digestion suffer a lack, and this is the reason that food is badly digested in the stomach, the liver and the veins, and easily takes on a foreign heat from there, and finally becomes a cause of added pain. Since, then, the places appointed for digestion suffer a lack of the innate heat flowing to them, and the material on which they work remains exposed to foreign heat for this reason (nature being intent elsewhere), physicians rightly act by letting blood in severe pain, so that as far as nature falls short of her usual care, the blood may be diminished accordingly, in line with the saying: less care leaves less to be cared for. Blood must be let not only because it is in the liver and the veins, so that we may keep the humours safe from foreign heat, but we also take thought for the food that is in the stomach, by provoking vomiting. Since these things are so, it would be the act of a madman to administer food at that hour, when removing it from the body is the remedy for pain. Galen is of this opinion in his commentary on that passage, "The evil is indeed greater," etc., where he writes in this way: "On the contrary, those who, because of pain or the severity of a disease, need evacuation rather than filling, sometimes need it more. Indeed, whoever gives them food does the greatest harm," etc. Moreover, since there are many kinds of pain, some attack and remit by turns, others torment continuously, and some of these reach such a degree of severity that they bring on sleeplessness, while others bring restlessness, one regimen of diet must not be used for all. Therefore, whatever pains cause the sufferer restlessness, all food and drink must be cut off, as was sufficiently said in the first book, where we showed that a disease accompanied by continuous restlessness ends within four days because of its severity, and that total abstinence suits it. The most severe pains are those that bring the sufferers into restlessness. Galen spoke of this in the passage cited, when he said, "Whoever gives food to these does the greatest harm." This is clear from what he wrote at the beginning of the commentary, where he describes the most severe pain in this way: "On account of pains, people often become pulseless without strength, fall into fainting fits, and cannot be moved in any motion. Similar things happen from the sharpness of a disease. But there are some in whom strength does not suffer for this reason, but because of an evacuation of the vessels in whatever way. Whether, then, from an evacuation manifest to the senses, or from diaphoresis, that is, digestion in this sense, or from lack of food, these need nourishment and to be restored as quickly as possible. On the contrary, those who, because of pain or the severity of a disease, sometimes need evacuation more than addition, indeed whoever offers them food does the greatest harm." From Galen's words a strong argument is drawn: that when a patient is suffering the most severe pain, while his strength remains, no food is to be given, since he writes that those who have become very weak through pain, so that they become pulseless and fall into a fainting fit, are harmed to the greatest degree. Patients who suffer pains that come close to the most severe can keep one posture in bed, yet cannot take sleep. Therefore the diet to be given them must be the kind we said suits diseases that end at the seventh day. For continuous sleeplessness, as we showed in the first book, is one of the three symptoms that end a disease at the seventh day. For those, then, who suffer continuous sleeplessness from pain, a regimen by drinks is suitable. So Hippocrates: "One must use drink if some pain is present: oxymel, warm in winter, but cold in summer; but if there is much thirst, then melicraton and water." In this passage Hippocrates defined the form of diet with regard to two symptoms, namely pain and great thirst, saying:

units.la: Χρὴ ἀὲ τοτῶ, ἡν ἀλγιμά τι ἔχῃ, ὀξυμελι-τι χειμῶνῳ μὲν ἰςεμῷ, θέρος δὲ ψυχῷ. ἐὰν δὲ πολλὰ ςῖλα ᾖ, καὶ μελικρήτῳ καὶ ὕδατι.
units.tr: Χρὴ δὲ τούτῳ, ἢν ἀλγήματί τι ἔχῃ, ὀξυμέλιτι, χειμῶνι μὲν θερμῷ, θέρος δὲ ψυχρῷ. ἐὰν δὲ πολλὰ δίψα ᾖ, καὶ μελικρήτῳ καὶ ὕδατι.

units.la: Vbi perperam quidam in hunc modum ver-tit: Vbi autem dolor aliquis vexauerit oxy-meli bibendum dabis. Non equidem id solum uult Hippocrates, vt oxymelite cum dolor aliquis affuerit vtamur. Sed duo nos in dictis verbis docet. Nempe cum dolor aliquis affue-rit victu per pocula vtendum esse. Secundo declarat nobis cõuenientem potum oxymeli esse. Si enim eadem fuisset Hippocratis mens ac traductor intelligit, breuius quidem sententiam protulisset ad hunc modum χρεὼν ἢ ἀξυμέλιτι ὡ ἀλγιμέχτι ἔχη &c. Hoc est, Vtitor vero oxymelite si dolor aliquis affuerit. Id praeterea facile erat ex media quietis signo quod dictioni ποτῷ, coniunctum est elicere. Sed quod semper dicere sum solitus, hic praeterire silentio haud æquû censeo. Solius Hippocratis scripta de verbo ad verbum transferenda fore, ut incorruptam grauissimi viri sententiam haberemus. Nullo quidem breuiloquus vir ocioso usus est verbo. Quicunque igitur in vertendo Hippocrate curant elegantiam sermonis, caveant ne divinas viri sententias corrumpant.
units.tr: Where someone has translated it wrongly in this way: "But when some pain troubles him, you will give him oxymel to drink." Hippocrates does not, indeed, want us to use oxymel only when some pain is present. He teaches us two things in these words: first, that when some pain is present, one must use a regimen by drinks; second, he tells us that oxymel is a suitable drink. For if Hippocrates had meant what the translator understands, he would have stated the sentence much more briefly, thus: χρεὼν ἢ ἀξυμέλιτι ὡ ἀλγιμέχτι ἔχη &c., that is, "One must use oxymel if some pain is present." This would also have been easy to elicit from the mark of the pause placed after the word ποτῷ. But I do not think it fair to pass over in silence here what I have always been accustomed to say: that the writings of Hippocrates alone should be translated word for word, so that we may have the unchanged opinion of that most weighty man. Indeed, that man never used a word idly, being very brief in speech. Whoever, therefore, in translating Hippocrates takes care for elegance of style, let them beware lest they corrupt the divine opinions of the man.

units.la: Ad propositum redeo. Cum dolor tali sit vehementia ut vigilias inducat, victum per pocula indicat, sorbitionesque tunc temporis ministrandas non esse. Sed forsan quis nobis obiciet. Hippocrates cum in dolore assiduo sorbitiones & cibum subtrahit, non doloris sed inflammationis & acutae febris ratione prohibet: Ut in primo de ratiõe victus, cũ scribit: Ad hæc si adhuc lateris dolor continuus fuerit, &c. Non solum vbi dolor acutæ febri coniunctus est, victus qui poculis sit crassior incommodus est, sed vbi dolor absque vlla sit febre. Quod cum ostendemus, manifestũ erit in dolore acutæ febri coniuncto, cibum & sorbitiones Hippocratẽ ratione symptomatis potius quàm morbi prohibuisse. Ille igitur in de victu sanorum ita scribit: Quibuscunq; dolores fiunt in visceribus, vel ex exercitatione,vel alia quapiam ambulatione, his confertsine cibo recreari. Potione verò vti, &c. Ex ijs quæ statim subiungit & apertius ex Galeno in expositione manifestũ fit, de ijs qui absque febre fiunt doloribus locutum fuisse. Si igitur scripta Hippocratis vigilanti lectione percurramus, nõ solũ cibum ijs prohibere qui cũ robore viriũ doloribus infestantur reperie mus sed in eos qui imbecilles ideo effecti sunt, si quis victus formã aut quantitatem ad magis augeat, magnum operari malũ affirmat, vbi adhunc modum scribit: Ingens siquidem malum est, si ob dolorem & acumen morbi imbecillitato porrigat quis potum vel sorbi- tionis plus, vel esculentum, imbecillitatem eam ex vasorum inanitione contigisse arbi- tratus, &c. Quo in loco potū, sorbitionem, et esculentū nō asserit male ijs exhiberi qui ob dolorem aut morbi acumen imbecilles fiunt, vt quidam opinatus est: sed solum damnat additionem victus formæ aut quantitatis quibus ante imbecillitatem æger vtebatur.
units.tr: I return to my purpose. When pain is so severe that it induces wakefulness, it shows that a diet of thick drinks must be avoided, and that sorbitions should not be given at that time. But perhaps someone will object to us. When Hippocrates withholds sorbitions and food in continuous pain, he forbids them on account of the inflammation and the acute fever, not on account of the pain, as in the first book on the regimen of diet, where he writes: "Besides, if the pain in the side is still continuous," and so on. A thicker diet of drinks is unsuitable not only where pain is joined with acute fever, but also where there is pain without any fever. When we have shown this, it will be clear that in pain joined with acute fever Hippocrates forbade food and broths on account of the symptom rather than the disease. He therefore writes thus in the book on the diet of healthy people: "Whatever pains arise in the viscera, either from exercise or from some other walking, these are to be relieved with food. But use drink," and so on. From what he immediately adds, and more clearly from Galen's commentary, it is plain that he was speaking of pains that arise without fever. If therefore we read the writings of Hippocrates with attentive reading, we find that he forbids food not only to those who are assailed by pains while their strength is intact, but he also affirms that it is a great evil to increase the form or quantity of the diet for those who have been made weak in this way. He writes in this manner: "For it is indeed a great evil, if on account of pain and the sharpness of the disease someone gives more drink, or broth, or solid food, having judged that the weakness came from emptying of the vessels," and so on. In this passage he does not assert that drink, broth and solid food are wrongly given to those who become weak on account of pain or the acuteness of the disease, as someone has thought. He only condemns the addition of a form or quantity of diet beyond what the sick man used before he became weak.

units.la: Vt si tribus aquæ mulsæ cyathis Socratem acuta febre, vehementi capitis dolore, laborantem nutrias, ob dolorem autem aut morbi acumen in magnam incidat imbecil-litatem, ita vt moueri nequeat & absque pulsu fiat, caueas vt huic aut sorbitionē, aut plus tribus cyathis mulsæ ministres. Nā hoc quidem magnū malum esse affirmat. Quibus autem signis imbecillitatem quæ à dolore aut morbi acumine & eam quæ à vasorum inanitione euenit discernere possimus supra ostensum est. Potus igitur quē ijs cōcedemus talis sit, vt aliquod præstet corpori nutrimentū, & doloris etiam causam respiciat. Vt oxy-meli quo utitur in lib.1. de ratione victus ad lateris dolorem, ut quod eius causam respici at. Et in libro de victu sanorum ad dolores viscerum absque febre, qui ab obstructione or tum habent, potione utitur cuius minimum in corpus ingrediens plurimum educat lotiu. Et quia hæc inuestigatio ad eam artis medicæ partem quæ morborum speculatur remedia (θεραπευτικὴ græcè dicitur) spectat, non est quod hic longiorem faciamus sermonem. Illuc te confer si quod reliquum huius speculationis est, quæris. Nos interim reliqua prosequamur propositi. Vigilia interdum ex penuria vaporosi halitus cerebrum humectantis euenit, & si quando ex defectu alimenti in ventriculo accidat, ut plurimum inclinante morbo fit. Iis præcipuè qui bona valitudine multum ingerere sunt soliti. In morborum incrementis aut vigore, raro ob hanc solam causam vigilia accidunt. Difficileque tunc id percipere, vi morbi vigiliarum magis perspicua causa illam obscurante. Cum ergo hanc esse vigivigiliarum occasionem intellexeris, cibum dato qui facilis sit coctionis, & substantiæ quæ dulces ex se emittat halitus. Vt pisces petrosi qui in hora vigeant, cocti cum anetho, petroselino, sale & aceto, oleo, aut butyro recenti, & succo vuæ acerbæ, aut eius loco berberibus. Hunc cibum ministraui cum essem in Anglia præclarissimo viro domino Guilelmo Cidne serenissimi principis Anglorum magno cubiculario dignissimo. Cum enim in clinante iam morbo vigilias pateretur, multaque in huius gratiam apparata nil quicquam proficerent, rogaui hominem an vellet fluuiatiles ad cœnam pisciculos, quos gudions vulgari sermone Angli appellant. An nuente inductoque coquo modum apparandi imposui, permisique vt eisdem ad libitum vesceretur. Abij, in crastinum rediens percepi hominem noctu dulces cœpisse somnos. Ad huius cognitionem me potissimum induxerunt hominis habitus & eius assuetudo. Iis accessit quod inclinante iam morbo nulla videbatur ad vigilias inducendas occasio. Quapropter diligenter oportet medicum contempla-ri actiones singularum corporis partiu, quan-do imminuuntur, aut deficiunt, ratione indi-gentiæ nutrimenti, & quando acuminis mor-bi. Cunque primum contingit, cibus illico dandus est: si fecundum, maxime prohiben-dus. Qua in re sæpe labuntur nostræ ætatis medici, non discernentes alterutram actio-num noxæ causam. Quod antiquis medicis pri-or Hippocrates obiecit in libro secundo de ratione victus in morbis acutis in hæc ver-ba.Neque sane horum ita peritos video medi-cos, qui ut oportet dignoscât eas quæ in mor-bis contingunt virium infirmitates, quæ obvaforum quam κυναγχὴν [?] Græci dicunt:etquæ ob aliam quampiam irritationem, & quæob πόνος, id est laborem, & quæ ob morbiacumen fiant.
units.tr: Thus, if you nourish Socrates, who suffers from acute fever and violent headache, with three cyathi of honey-water, but on account of pain or the sharpness of the disease he falls into such great weakness that he cannot be moved and has no pulse, take care that you give him neither a broth nor more than three cyathi of honey-water. For he affirms that this is a great evil. By what signs we can distinguish the weakness that comes from pain or the sharpness of the disease from that which comes from emptying of the vessels has been shown above. The drink we concede to them, then, should be such that it provides some nourishment to the body and also takes account of the cause of the pain. Such is the oxymel which he uses in the first book on the regimen of diet for pain of the side, since it takes account of its cause. And in the book on the diet of healthy people, for pains of the viscera without fever which arise from obstruction, he uses a drink of which a very small amount entering the body draws off a great quantity of urine. Because this inquiry pertains to that part of the medical art which considers the remedies of diseases (called therapeutic in Greek), there is no need for us to make a longer discourse here. If you seek what remains of this inquiry, betake yourself there. Meanwhile let us go on with the rest of our purpose. Wakefulness sometimes arises from a lack of vaporous breath moistening the brain, and if at any time it comes from a deficiency of nourishment in the stomach, it mostly happens when the disease is declining, chiefly in those who were accustomed to eat much while in good health. In the increase or vigour of diseases, wakefulness rarely arises from this cause alone, and it is then difficult to perceive, since the force of the disease obscures the more evident cause of the wakefulness. When, therefore, you have understood that this is the occasion of the wakefulness, give food that is easy to digest and of a substance that sends forth sweet vapours, such as rock fish boiled with dill, parsley, salt, vinegar, oil or fresh butter, and juice of sour grapes, or barberries in its place. I gave this food when I was in England to the most distinguished man, Lord William Cecil, most worthy great chamberlain of the most serene prince of the English. When he suffered wakefulness in a disease already declining, and many things prepared for his sake accomplished nothing, I asked the man whether he would like river fish for supper, which the English call "gudgeons" in their vernacular. With his assent, and the cook having been instructed, I gave the method of preparing them and allowed him to eat as much as he liked. I went away, and returning the next day I learned that the man had begun to sleep soundly at night. His character and his habits chiefly led me to this understanding. To this was added that, the disease now declining, there seemed to be no occasion for inducing wakefulness. Therefore the physician must carefully consider the actions of the individual parts of the body, when they are diminished or fail on account of a lack of nourishment, and when they fail on account of the sharpness of the disease. When the first occurs, food must be given at once; when the second, it must chiefly be forbidden. In this matter the physicians of our age often go astray, not distinguishing which of the two actions is the cause of the harm. Hippocrates objected to this earlier, to the ancient physicians, in the second book on the regimen in acute diseases, in these words: "Indeed I see few physicians skilled in this, who rightly distinguish those weaknesses of strength which occur in diseases, which the Greeks call kynanche [κυναγχή], and those which arise from some other irritation, and those which arise from labour [πόνος], and those which arise from the sharpness of the disease."

units.la: Victum docet qui sitienti infirmo cōuenit.
units.tr: He teaches the diet that suits a thirsty patient.

units.la: CAPUT XXVIII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXVIII.

units.la: SITIS febricitantium quandoque taliest vehementia ut indicationem curationis suppe suppeditet. Idhoc modo discernas. Cum igitur sitis morbi materiæ remoratur coctione, aut nimia sputum exiccatione inhibet, aut ab ea corpus arefit, rationabiliter ab ea victus ratio sumetur. Quare tunc dare operam medicum oportet ut sitim leuet. Idque fiet cibo & potu qui actu & potentia frigidi & humidi sint. Omnium maxime quæ sitim vincunt aqua frigida est, præcipuè quæ à medicis probatur. Secundo loco est aqua hordei. Tertio syrupus violaceus multa aqua dilutus, quem sic præparabis.
units.tr: The thirst of feverish patients is sometimes so intense that it dictates the course of treatment. You can tell as follows. When the thirst comes from the disease matter being held back from concoction, or is caused by excessive drying of the sputum, or when the body is parched by it, then a diet suited to dryness should rightly be adopted. The physician must then take care to relieve the thirst, and this is done with food and drink that are cold and moist both in act and in potential. Of all remedies for thirst, cold water is by far the best, especially the kind approved by physicians. In second place is barley water.
