Third is violet syrup diluted in plenty of water, which you will prepare as follows.

units.la: Aquam coquito in olla recenti ad unius quartæ partis absumptionem, ab igne amovens residere sinito. Deinde aquam à sedimine separato, cuius accipito partes viginti, syrupi violarum depurati aut cius iulep partem unam. Bulliant ad lentum ignem, donec permisceantur. Deinde sub dio exponito ad Septentrionem. Et frigidum exhibeto. Simili modo confici potest aqua zucari, qua nostri recentiores multoties utuntur. Sed considerare diligenter oportet ne in vehementi linguæ totiusque corporis squalore vtamur ea, nec abstergente vllo. Nam talia corpus siccius reddunt, vt me experientia olim docuit. Cum essem in Anglia Hispanum puerū periodica febre laborante inuisi, habitu gracili & præter modum squalido, eius linguæ præ nimio squalore arida vltra modum erat, vt vix loqui posset, indomitamque sitim patiebatur. Frigidam puero exhibere mihi visum est, zucarumque impositui vt aquarum crassitiem corrigeret. Cunque à potu frigidæ non leuaretur sitis, vitio aquæ illud tribuens aquam distillationis buglossæ vtpote in qua nil crassum est cum zucaro ministraui. Cunq; à copioso & crebro illius potu siccior etiam euaderet, intellexi tandem in vehementi squalore, nimium aduersa esse quæ abstergendi facultatem habent: ex eo quia corpus & humores siccicora reddunt. Nam quæ abstergūt adhibentur, quàm si lintea sordida absque aqueo humore sapone detersorio vnguento diligenter perfrices, vt sordes detergeas. Quanto enim plus detersorij adhibueris eo minus proficies. Nam sordes magis & tenacius impinges. Oportet enim lintea aqua prius macerare, ut sordities quam abstergere cupis humecta fiat. Ut consueuerunt fœminæ quæ doctiores in ea arte sunt, nam ut minores faciant expensas, diutius lintea in aqua macerari permittunt, rem illis usu monstrante. Cum igitur hominum corpora vehementer exiccata sunt, cauendum est ab usu abstergentium. Nō sunt enim eo tempore detergendi humores, sed potius humectandi. At cum humectos satis reddideris, abstergentibus secure uti poteris. Hoc postea ab Hippocrate intellexi in primo de ratione victus in morbis acutis ubi ita scribit: Verùm dandæ sorbitionis quantitas hoc observabitur modo, nempe si morbus siccior quàm ut quispiam existimet fuerit, non multum dare oportet, sed præbibere ante sorbitionem vel mulsam vel vinum, utcunque magis conueniet. Galenus in expositione signa commemorans quibus cognoscitur siccus affectus, ita scribit: Et sanè (inquit) superfluitatum nihil excernere, siccorum omnium morborum nota est. Non im merito igitur Hippocrates humectantium ali- quod ante ptisanam adsumi iubet, &c. Nec solum ea quæ abstergunt in dicto affectu su- gienda sunt, verum & quicunque cibus & sorbitio. Nam solo potu humectante vten- dum est in iis quorum linguæ totumque cor- pus vltra modum arida sunt. Si enim iis ci- bum aut sorbitionem dederis, partes sorbi- tionis quæ crassioris sunt substantiæ ventri- culi tunicis præ nimia earum siccitate adhæ- rentes à febrili calore deurentur potius quàm coquentur. Non aliter quàm cibus ollæ adhæ- rens comburi solet, humore aqueo deficiente.
units.tr: Boil water in a new pot until a quarter of it is used up, then take it off the fire and let it settle. Then separate the water from the sediment and take twenty parts of it and one part of purified violet syrup, or its julep. Let them boil over a slow fire until they are mixed. Then set it out in the open air facing north, and give it cold. In the same way water with sugar can be made, which our more recent writers use very often. But one must consider carefully that we should not use it when the tongue and the whole body are very foul, nor any cleansing agent. For such things make the body drier, as my experience once taught me. When I was in England I visited a Spanish boy suffering from a periodic fever. He had a thin build and was unusually filthy, and his tongue was dry beyond measure from excessive foulness, so that he could scarcely speak, and he suffered unbridled thirst. I thought it right to give the boy cold water, and I put in sugar to correct the thickness of the water. When the thirst was not relieved by the cold drink, I blamed the water, and gave him distilled water of bugloss instead, since in it there is nothing thick, with sugar. When, from his copious and frequent drinking of it, he became even drier, I finally understood that in intense foulness, things that have the power of cleansing are very harmful, because they make the body and humours drier. For cleansing agents are applied in the way that if you rub dirty linen thoroughly with soap, a cleansing ointment, and without watery moisture, to remove the dirt. For the more cleansing agent you apply, the less you will achieve, since you will rub the dirt in more and more stubbornly. For the linen must first be soaked in water, so that the filth you wish to remove is moistened. This is what women who are more skilled in that craft do; to lower their expenses they let the linen soak in water for a longer time, experience having taught them this. So when the bodies of people are very dried out, one must beware of using cleansing agents. For at such a time the humours should not be cleansed but rather moistened. But when you have made them moist enough, you may use cleansing agents safely. I later learned this from Hippocrates in the first book of the Regimen in Acute Diseases, where he writes thus: "The quantity of gruel to be given is to be observed in this way: namely, if the disease is drier than one would think, one should not give much, but should give drink beforehand, either mulse or wine, whichever is more suitable." Galen, recalling in his commentary the signs by which a dry condition is recognised, writes thus: "And indeed (he says) to excrete nothing of the superfluities is the mark of all dry diseases." Not without reason, therefore, does Hippocrates order that something moistening be taken before the barley drink, etc. Nor should only cleansing agents be avoided in the said condition, but also any food and gruel whatever. For in those whose tongue and whole body are dry beyond measure, one must nourish only with a moistening drink. For if you give them food or gruel, the thicker parts of the gruel, adhering to the coats of the stomach because of their excessive dryness, will be scorched by the febrile heat rather than digested. It is just as food sticking to a pot is burnt when the watery moisture is lacking.

units.la: Hæc vt arbitror fuit mens Hippocratis su- pra citato loco, cū morbo vltra modum siccò existente, ante sorbitionem præbibere mulsam vel vinū ægrotantes iubet: volens in tali asse- ctu solo potu humectante prius nutriendos esse laborantes donec ariditas soluatur, dein- de ad sorbitiones deuenire. Et hoc est quod intellexit cum dixit ἀλλὰ προπίνειν πρὸ τῆς φύμακτος, id est, sed præbibere ante sorbitionem oportet. Nec ideo quod Hippocrates mul-sam exhibere consulat, quæ melius ratione ab-stergere valet, in Hispani pueri affectu aquâ çucari præter rationem prohibuimus, quæ longè inferior est quàm mulsa in abstergendo. Nam cum Hippocrates in morbo vltra mo-dum squalido nec sorbitionem nec cibum a-lium quemcunque recte exhiberi ob iam di-ctam rationem opinaretur, potum concessu-rus magis nutrientem elegit. Sunt autem quatuor de quibus agit in libris de ratione vi-ctus. Nempe aqua hordei, mulsa, vinū, oxy-meli. In sicco affectu nec oxymelitis nec a-quæ hordei mentionem fecit. Alterum quia nimis incisiuum est sicco affectui non conue-nit. Aqua hordei prout potus est, parum nu-trit ob tenuitatem. Mulsæ autem & vinime-minit tanquam ea quæ magis nutriunt et hu-mectant. Electionem verò alterutrius medi-co relinquit, ac si intelligat in sicco affectu posse aliquando alterum lædere & eorum al-terum conuenire. Si enim à bilioso humore ob eius indomitam qualitatem siccus eueniat affectus vitanda magnopere est mulsa, vinum vero exhibendum quod citra abstersionem incisionemve humectat, et vires naturae ministrat. Quod si a nimis crasso humore coctrici facultati repugnante, morbus siccior evadat, mulsa potius quam vinum ministranda est. Tum ad humoris extenuandam crassitiem, tum ad humectandum corpus. Plus enim humectat mulsa quam oxymeli. Hanc fuisse Hippocratis mentem opinamur. Sed & illud certo scimus quod siccitas quae linguae & toti corpori adve-nit ob bilis ardentis qualitate multo validior est, quam quae a crassitie sola humorum provenit. Quapropter recte supra additum est in vehementi siccitate vitanda esse aquam zucari & quae abstergendi vim habeant, potuque solo humectante vrendum esse. Sentis ne studiose lector quam dicta mea cum Hippocratis conveniant scriptis, quem unum virum undequaque sapientissimum admiror. Sed rectius mihi quis objiciet, me in curatione pueri Hispani fuisse lapsum, febrem tertianam patientis cum validissima & & linguæ & totius corporis siccitate, qui eĩ aquam ẓucari ministrassem. nam manifestũ erat vehementem illam siccitatem à qualita te bilis acerrimæ ortum traxisse. Quapropter vino diluto nõ aqua ẓucari nutriendus erat.
units.tr: This, I think, was the intention of Hippocrates in the passage cited above, where, when the disease is dry beyond measure, he orders the sick to drink mulse or wine before the gruel. He wanted those suffering from such a condition to be nourished first with drink alone that moistens, until the dryness is relieved, and only then to proceed to gruels. And this is what he meant when he said "ἀλλὰ προπίνειν πρὸ τῆς φύμακτος" [but one must drink beforehand, before the gruel]; that is, "but one must drink before the gruel." Nor because Hippocrates advises giving mulse, which can cleanse more effectively, did I rightly forbid sugar water in the case of the Spanish boy, since it is far inferior to mulse in cleansing. For when Hippocrates thought that in a disease that is excessively foul neither gruel nor any other food should be given properly, for the reason already stated, he chose a drink that is more nourishing, to be granted. There are four drinks of which he treats in his books on the regimen: namely barley water, mulse, wine, and oxymel. In the dry condition he mentions neither oxymel nor barley water. The former, because it is too cutting, is not suited to a dry condition; barley water, as a drink, nourishes little because of its thinness. But mulse and wine he recommends as being more nourishing and moistening. He leaves the choice between these two to the physician, as if he understood that in a dry condition sometimes one of them can harm and the other be suitable. For if the dryness arises from bilious humour, because of its unbridled quality, then mulse must be avoided altogether and wine should be given, which moistens without cleansing or cutting, and supplies strength to nature. But if the disease becomes drier from a humour too thick, resisting the concocting faculty, then mulse rather than wine should be given, both to thin the thickness of the humour and to moisten the body. For mulse moistens more than oxymel. We think this was Hippocrates' intention. But we also know for certain that the dryness that comes to the tongue and the whole body from the quality of burning bile is far more powerful than that which arises from the thickness of the humours alone. Therefore it was rightly added above that in intense dryness water with sugar and things having a cleansing power are to be avoided, and that one must rely on drink alone that moistens. Do you notice, studious reader, how my statements agree with the writings of Hippocrates, whom I admire as the one man most wise in every respect? But someone may object to me more fairly that I erred in the treatment of the Spanish boy, when I gave sugar water to a patient with a tertian fever and the most severe dryness of tongue and whole body. For it was clear that that intense dryness had arisen from the quality of most acrid bile. Therefore he should have been nourished with diluted wine, not sugar water.

units.la: Sed bene valeant medicorũ errores quibus à tergo morosa coniuncta est pœnitentia, vt in posteru illud caueant attentioris̛ cura remediorum qualitates & affectus examinet. Ego verò vt moris est Lusitanorum genti, error rem meum ingenuè fateri pium esse iudico, eundemque scriptis mandare, vt posteros rei cautos reddam. Id enim est à vitio virtutem, bonum à malo, ab aliquo rectũ elicere. Scio enim hominis naturam talem esse vt facile labi possit. Quod si cum Homero sentiendum sit, intellectum hominis in terris talem esse qualem pater deorum atque hominum induxit in diem, medicorum errores profecto dignifunt venia, qui secretos corporum affectus rimantur. Quapropter cũ erroribus maxime sit medicus obnoxius, pij hominis officio eum vti iudico, qui Hippocratis in primo de morbis vulgaribus adimplere conatur præceptum dicentis:In hoc te exerceto vt saltem si non prosis nequid noceas.
units.tr: But let the errors of physicians fare well, since they are followed by a troublesome repentance, so that in future they may take care, and by more attentive care examine the qualities of remedies and conditions. For my part, as is the custom of the Portuguese people, I judge it right to confess my error frankly and to commit it to writing, so that I may make posterity cautious in this matter. For it is to draw virtue from vice and good from evil, to bring forth something right from something wrong. For I know that human nature is such that it can easily slip. But if one must agree with Homer that the understanding of men on earth is such as the father of gods and men has made it from day to day, then surely the errors of physicians, who search out the hidden affections of bodies, deserve pardon. Therefore, since the physician is especially liable to error, I judge it the duty of a godly man to use this, and to try to fulfil the precept of Hippocrates in the first book of the Epidemics, which says: "Exercise yourself in this, that if you cannot at least help, you do no harm."

units.la: Sed ad reliqua propositi reuertamur. In febre quæ cum validißima siccitate est, cibis parcendum est,solo humectante potu nutriendi sunt ægrotantes. Vinumque ijs exhibendum,quod natura aquosum sit. Item pul lam crassam cum hepatica,hordeo abvtroq; cortice exuto,prunis,passulis,floribus borra ginis & violis in copiosa aqua coquito, vt ius tenue fiat. Cunq; percoĉta fuerint,colato.
units.tr: But let us return to the rest of our subject. In fever accompanied by very severe dryness, food must be spared, and the sick should be nourished with a moistening drink alone. Wine should be given to them, since its nature is watery. Likewise, boil a thick pulse with liverwort, barley (husked of both outer coats), plums, raisins, borage flowers and violets in plenty of water, so that it becomes a thin broth. When it has been well boiled, strain it.

units.la: Ius ægrotanti tenue exhibeto, statimque vinum dilutum in quo supernatet frustulum panis quantum vno haustu bibere possit, dato. Ventriculo aliquid extra,quod humectare possit apponito. Quodsi siccitas remissior fuerit, ijs quæ infrigidant & humectant in cibis & potibus vtemur. Cucurbita coĉtaci bus est qui sitim cöpescit. Lactuca etiam eo quo supra parauimus modo vtilis est, cruda etiam cum eisdem devorata maximè sitim re primit. Oleum purißimum oliuarum immaturi maturi partem vnam, acetialbi partes duas, zucari tres, simul misce et cum pane vtitor. Ad sitim sedandam & ad alios quampluri-mos vsus confert. Panis praeterea refrige-rans conuenit prout paranimus supra cum de victu qui tertianae pure competit ageremus. cibus est maxime aptus sitienti febricitanti. Sed & sorbitio ex pane & aqua hordei & zucaro, quam communiter panatellam vocant, confert. Conferunt & cibaria ea que ex herbis et fructibus parantur, quorum omnium melones primum locum obtinet. Sunt qui ad sitim sedandam aquis destillatis endiuiae, cichorij, buglossae, cum syrupo rosarum vel violarum aut iulep vtuntur. In febribus quae a causa calida ortum habent absque pituitae mixtione, estate praecipue, communis vsus amplectendus est. Caeterum latere no[n] oportet vbicunque crudi humoris de pituitae genere coctionem quaerimus, vt febri medea-mur, magis ladere potum aquae destillatae quam aquae naturalis. Illa quidem si frigida offeratur duplici nomine infrigidabit, actu & potentia. Magis praeterea penetrat in corporis interiora ratione qualitatis igneae. Vnde ab huiusmodi aquis magis pati natiuum calorem, quàm à naturali manifestum est. Qua propter in causa frigida & ijs qui alicuius interiorum viscerum imbecillitatem patiuntur, vitandas esse destillationum aquas opinamur.
units.tr: Give the sick person the thin broth, and straightaway give diluted wine in which a small piece of bread floats, as much as he can drink in one gulp. Apply something outside to the stomach that can moisten it. If the dryness is milder, we use in food and drink those things that cool and moisten. Cucumber is good for those who suppress thirst. Lettuce, prepared in the way we described above, is also useful, and eaten raw with the same, it especially checks thirst. Mix together one part of pure olive oil, from unripe or ripe olives, two parts of white vinegar and three of sugar, and use it with bread. It serves to allay thirst and for many other purposes. Cooling bread is also suitable, as we prepared it above when we dealt with the diet that suits tertian fever. It is a food most fitting for a thirsty feverish person. A sop of bread, barley water and sugar, which they commonly call panatella, also helps. Foods made from herbs and fruits help too, of which melons hold the first place. Some, to allay thirst, use distilled waters of endive, chicory and bugloss, with syrup of roses or violets, or with julep. In fevers that arise from a hot cause without any admixture of phlegm, especially in summer, the common practice should be adopted. Moreover, it must not be overlooked that wherever we seek to cure a fever by the concoction of raw, phlegmatic humour, drinking distilled water does more harm than drinking natural water. If it is offered cold, distilled water will cool doubly, in act and in potency. Furthermore, by reason of its fiery quality it penetrates more deeply into the interior of the body. Hence it is evident that the native heat suffers more from such waters than from natural water. Therefore, we think distilled waters should be avoided in cold cases and in those who suffer weakness of some internal organ.

units.la: Sed non praetermittendum est sitim quandoque à ventriculo, quandoque ab iocinere & pulmone & renibus euenire posse, vt à Galeno in libris de locis affectis scriptum est. Quae à pulmone ortum habet, aqua hordei cum syrupo violarum sedat. Ab hepate aqua destillata frigida. A ventriculo, potus aqua frigida. A renibus, aqua decoctionis liquiritiae compescit.
units.tr: But it must not be passed over that thirst can arise sometimes from the stomach, and sometimes from the liver, the lungs and the kidneys, as Galen wrote in his books On the Affected Parts. Thirst that has its origin in the lungs is calmed by barley water with syrup of violets. From the liver, cold distilled water. From the stomach, cold water to drink. From the kidneys, a decoction of liquorice checks it.

units.la: Ad inducendam appetentiam quae conueniant cibaria.
units.tr: Which foods are suitable for inducing appetite.

units.la: CAPVT XXIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX.

units.la: PAtiuntur febricitantes aliquando deiectionem appetentiae vt eorum corpora arescant atrophia. Cunque multiplices habeat causas nullus cibus simpliciter commendandus est ad inducendam appetentiam. Sed prius causa inuestiganda est, vt quod vtile ægro tantibus sit inueniamus. Cæterum omissis primarijs causis appetentia deijcitur deficiente aliquo eorum quæ ad inducendam appetentiæ necessariæ sunt. Appetimus secundum naturam homines hoc causarum ordine. Corpora nostra à vi continentis in halitus perpetuò diffluntur. Huic effluxui vt remedium restauratio à singulis nostri corporis particulis quæritur. Restauratur verò id quod effluxu est, ab ea substantia quæ singulis partibus apposita vnica transmutatione in substantiam simplicis mutatur, (cambium medici vocant.) hæc rursus ab ea quæ in osculis tenuium venarum est, instauratur, non à rore vt aliqui opinati sunt. Quæ in exilibus vasis est, à sanguine qui in magnis continetur vasis renouatur. Vasa ab iocinere, hic tandem à ventriculo per meseraicas venulas, quas manus hepatis recte quidam nuncuparunt, fugit. His trahentibus ad os ventriculi suctus peruenit. Hunc partiũ eius aliqualis constrictio excipit. Huius constrictionis sensus, fames est. Tres igitur summatim causæ consequentes in fame naturali apparent. Attractio, constrictio, & sensus oris ventriculi. Appetētia igi tur quocunque horum deficiente diminui & prosterni potest. Cæterùm prima causa ē tribus deficiente, remediũ ab ea artis parte quæ morbos curat petendum est. Minimam scias vim tunc inesse cibis cũ naturalis totius corporis attractio deest: aliquam, sed exiguam, si tertia. Magnam verò, si secunda. Non solũ igitur intemperies oris ventriculi cibi appetentiam deĭcit, sed & humor quicunque sit qui aut sensum oris hebetet, aut constrictionem partium eius prohibeat. Intemperies autem quæ vt in pluribus cibi fastidium generat calida est, cum vtraq; contrarietate sicca et humida, humori coniuncta & absq; eo.
units.tr: Feverish patients sometimes lose their appetite, so that their bodies waste away in atrophy. Since this has many causes, no food can be simply recommended for restoring appetite. First the cause must be investigated, so that we may find what is useful for the sick. Moreover, leaving aside the primary causes, appetite is lost when one of the things necessary for inducing appetite is lacking. Naturally, we humans desire in this order of causes. Our bodies are constantly dissipated into vapours by the power of the containing part. The remedy for this outflow is sought in restoration from each particle of our body. What has flowed out is restored from that substance which, applied to each part, is changed by a single transmutation into the substance of the simple part (physicians call this cambium). This in turn is renewed from what is in the mouths of the fine veins, not from dew, as some have thought. What is in the slender vessels is renewed from the blood contained in the large vessels. The vessels draw from the liver, and the liver at last from the stomach, through the mesaraic venules, which some have rightly called the hands of the liver. As these draw toward the mouth of the stomach, the suction arrives. A certain constriction of its parts receives it, and the sense of this constriction is hunger. So, in summary, three consequent causes appear in natural hunger: attraction, constriction, and the sense of the mouth of the stomach. Appetite therefore can be diminished and overthrown when any one of these is lacking. But when the first of the three is lacking, the remedy must be sought from that part of the art which cures diseases. Know that there is very little force in foods when the natural attraction of the whole body is lacking; some, but a small amount, if the third is lacking; and much, if the second is lacking. Therefore, not only the intemperature of the mouth of the stomach diminishes the desire for food, but also whatever humour it is that either dulls the sense of the mouth or prevents the constriction of its parts. The intemperature which, in most cases, produces loathing of food is hot, with both contrarieties, dry and moist, joined with humour and without it.

units.la: Cæterùm cum caliditas & humiditas causa sunt deiectionis appetentiæ, cappares cum aceto, condite oliuæ, & ius lentium, prosunt. Sed cum siccitati coniuncta est caliditas & appeappetentiam deïcit, aqua frigida maxime iuuat, nisi quid prohibeat. Lactuca, cucurbita, citrulli, melones, & id genus fructus maxime prosunt. Qua de causa æstate his primus ad mensam vtimur, vt calorem & siccitatem ventriculi reprimamus. Vnde ab ijs nosmetipsos ad cibos promptiores sentimus. Multa præterea sunt frigida & humida ciba ria huic proposito conuenientia quorum supra meminimus. Sed quæ à fructibus petuntur & ad appetentiam inducendam et ad sitim sedandam efficaciora sunt.
units.tr: Moreover, since heat and moisture are the cause of loss of appetite, capers with vinegar, pickled olives and lentil broth help. But when heat is joined with dryness and appetite is lost, cold water helps most, unless something prevents it. Lettuce, cucumber, citrons, melons and that kind of fruit help most. For this reason we set these first at table in summer, to restrain the heat and dryness of the stomach; hence we feel ourselves readier for food. Moreover, there are many cold and moist foods suited to this purpose, of which we have made mention above. But those taken from fruits are more effective both for inducing appetite and for allaying thirst.

units.la: Deïcitur etiam ob defectum constrictionis partium oris ventriculi. Huic contraria dispositio est quam quidam recentiorum medicorum ventriculi remollitionem aut relaxationem dixerunt. Hæc non solum actionis facultatis appetentis sed & reliquis ventriculi actionibus aduersatur. Ortum habet ab humore pituitoso diu ventriculo insidente, & eius tunicas irrigante, cuius meminit Galenus septimo de methodo, vbi in remedium huius vitij absinthij potionem concedit. Hæc relaxatio supersiciem ventriculi læuem reddit, vnde appetentiam deïcit. Hæc enim aut sensus exasperantis rei est, aut ex eo nascitur. Quam ob rem absinthium rectè appetentia inducere dicitur. Nam sua siccitate laxũ ven triculum corrigit, amaritudine & astriction ne lœuem eius supersiciem exasperat. Quam ob rem cum ob relaxationem ventriculi de- ïciatur appetentia, absinthio vtemur. Vnde ad hunc sensum rectè à Dioscoride commen datum est, ad discutienda fastidia. Sed & cappares & oliuæ hoc modo appetentiã ex- citant. Pisces quoq; saliti efficacissimi sunt ad deiectam appetentiam suscitandam. Vnde supra cum de variolis nobis sermo esset & de pestilenti febre salitos pisces appetentiam excitare asseruimus, teste Rasi.
units.tr: Appetite is also lost through lack of constriction of the parts of the mouth of the stomach. The opposite condition is what some recent physicians have called softening or relaxation of the stomach. This works against not only the action of the appetitive faculty but also the other actions of the stomach. It arises from pituitous humour lying long in the stomach and moistening its coats, which Galen mentions in book seven of his Method, where he prescribes a potion of wormwood as a remedy for this defect. This relaxation makes the surface of the stomach smooth, and so appetite is lost. For this is either a property of something that roughens, or arises from it. Hence wormwood is rightly said to induce appetite. For by its dryness it corrects the relaxed stomach, and by its bitterness and astringency it roughens its smooth surface. Therefore, since appetite is lost through relaxation of the stomach, we use wormwood. Hence Dioscorides rightly recommended it for this purpose, namely for dispelling loathing of food. Capers and olives also excite appetite in this way. Salted fish too are most effective in rousing a lost appetite; whence, when we spoke above of smallpox and of pestilential fever, we asserted that salted fish excite appetite, as Rhazes testifies.

units.la: Fit & aliquando vt humor crudus ven- triculi tunicis diu inhærens fastidium indu- cat. Quæcunq; ergo hunc excernendi et ven- triculum exasperandi facultatem habent, appetentiam proprie inducere dicũtur, ob id quod vt plurimum à iam dicta causa nascuntur cibi fastidia. Talia sunt in calidis allium & cepa. Allium siquidem excernendi vim habet, ventriculumque mordet, & exiccat vt asseruit Dioscorides. Vanum est quod de eo dicitur flatuosum esse, & cibi fastidia inducere. Nam experientia quotidiana scimus, aduersus flatum non leue remedium esse, & appetentiam excitare: cuius sententiæ astipulatur Galen. quarto de ratione victus in morbis acutis. De allio supra à nobis habitus est sermo, vbi ostendimus omnes naturales ventriculi actiones roborare. Quicunque igitur à crudis humoribus diu ventriculo insidentibus cibi fastidium patiuntur, allio in succo vnæ acerbæ aut acetosæ macerato efficacissime vtentur. Sed & cepæ expurgandi vis inest, iuxta Dioscoridis sententiam, ventriculumque mordet. Qua de causa apperentiā inuitat. Quicunque igitur ob exercitij defectum aut ob debilem expultricem, obdormientem oris ventriculi sensum habent, hacque occasione cibum fastidiunt, cepa cruda vtiliter vti possunt, cum aqua sale et pipere in tenues laminas incisa, unde apud Hebræos in prouerbio est, Cepa absque pane cor scrutatur. Si napi etiam aceto & pane contusum sensum ventriculi acriorem reddit, excrementa eius transferendo. Petroselinum cum cibo coctu, aut in visceribus capi qui ad ignem coquitur immissum, citra eam quæ à manifestis sumitur qualitatibus actionem, appetentiam excitat. Crudum item cu aceto & pane in mortario contusum mirum in modum prodest. Unde Angli petroselini carnibus assis infixi nidore delectantur. Recte quidam ex recentioribus de eo sentit, calido & frigido conuenire ventriculo.
units.tr: It also sometimes happens that raw humour clinging long to the coats of the stomach induces loathing. Therefore whatever has the power of expelling this humour and roughening the stomach is properly said to induce appetite, because loathing of food mostly arises from the cause just mentioned. Among hot things, garlic and onion are such. For garlic has the power of expelling, bites the stomach and dries it, as Dioscorides says. What is said of it, that it is flatulent and induces loathing of food, is false. For we know from daily experience that it is no slight remedy against wind and that it excites appetite; Galen agrees with this opinion in book four of On the Regimen in Acute Diseases. We discussed garlic above, where we showed that it strengthens all the natural actions of the stomach. Therefore those who suffer loathing of food from raw humours long lodged in the stomach may use garlic steeped in the juice of some sour or acid thing, with the greatest effect. Onion too has a purging power, according to Dioscorides, and bites the stomach; for this reason it stirs appetite. Therefore those who, from lack of exercise or from a weak expulsive faculty, have a dulled sense of the mouth of the stomach and on this account loathe food, may use raw onion cut into thin slices with water, salt and pepper to good effect. Whence among the Hebrews there is a proverb: "An onion without bread searches the heart." If turnip too is pounded with vinegar and bread, it sharpens the sense of the stomach by moving its excrements. Parsley, cooked with food, or put into the insides of a capon roasted at the fire, excites appetite apart from any action arising from its manifest qualities. Raw parsley pounded in a mortar with vinegar and bread also helps wonderfully. Hence the English delight in the smell of parsley stuck into roast meats. Some of the more recent writers rightly judge that it suits the stomach both hot and cold.

units.la: Cum ergo à calore & siccitate prostrata est appetentia aqua frigida summu est remedium. Olei immaturi partes duas, aceti partes tres, simul misceto. Mixtis utere cum pane.
units.tr: When the appetite has been prostrated by heat and dryness, cold water is the best remedy. Mix two parts of unripe olive juice with three parts of vinegar. Use the mixture with bread.

units.la: Cum à calore & humiditate ortum habet, oliuæ, cappares, uua acerba & similia prosunt.
units.tr: When it arises from heat and moisture, olives, capers, sour grapes and similar things help.

units.la: Cu vero à relaxatione partium oris ventriculi, triculi, salitipisces, cappares, & reliqua cibaria quæ ventriculum exiccantia exasperant. Allia verò feruefacta cum succo vnæ acerbæ aut acetosæ, relaxatiõi frigido humori coniunctæ non inutilia sunt. Quod srob hebetê ventriculi sensum, cibũ fastidiant ægrotantes, cepa cum aqua sale & pipere iuuat. Sinapi præterea cũ pane & aceto contusum prodest. In summa omnia quæ discutereva leant, & mordendi facultatem habeant.
units.tr: But when it arises from a relaxation of the parts of the mouth of the stomach, salted fish, capers and other foods that dry and roughen the stomach are useful. Garlic boiled with the juice of a sour or tart grape is not useless when the cold humour that relaxes the stomach is present. Where the stomach's sense is dulled and the sick loathe their food, onion with water, salt and pepper helps. Mustard crushed with bread and vinegar also helps. In short, all things that disperse and have the power to bite.

units.la: Est vnus ex Arabibus medicis qui ita scribit: Et ex eis quæ conferunt illis quorum appetitus prostratus est, propter debilitatem, sicut coualescentium, aut propter materiam humidam viscosam, est vt comedant olivas & aliquid de piscibus salitis. Sed re vera si- cut oliuæ læsioni sunt iis, quorum ventres humido & viscoso humore abundant, ita & pisces saliti conualescentibus iis, qui ob debilitatem cibum fastidiant. Nam iuxta huius medici sententiam propter sanguinis penuriam iis deiicitur appetentia. Et subdit sa tim, vt coualescētibus accidit, aut iis qui euacuantur plurima euacuatione. Vtrisque cum cibum fastidiunt, piscium salitorum vsum potius incommodo fore, quàm adiumento opinor. Sed neque oliuæ conditæ hos meliores reddent. Sed si succum perdicis ijs obtulisset, offamque panis in vino odorifero madentem et similia, citius his appetentiā reduceret, cum à prædictis causis cibū fastidirent. Sed indistinctè admodum multa postmodum connumerat quæ fastidium discutiunt ad hunc modum. Ex prouocantibus appetitum sunt cappares præparatæ, menta, cepa, oliuæ, piper, caryophylli, galanga, acetum, acetosa, almuri, allia, cepa, opoponacum & mel. Hæc ille, quibus in verbis multa absque vlla methodo connumerauit remedia, quibus cōueniant dispositionibus ea non adaptans. Quorum alia ex eo quia exiccant & exasperant appetentiam inducunt, vt cappares præparatæ & menta. Alia ob id quod astringendo exiccāt, vt acetum, acetosa, muria, & condita oliua. Alia quia exiccando excrementa à ventriculo excernunt, vt allium, piper. Alia quia mordendo oris ventriculi sensum acutiorem reddunt, ut cepa, si quando ab excrementis expultricis facultatis aut coctricis vitio redundantibus hebes fiat. Hoc profecto docere est, remediorum nempe unumquodque singulis causarum à quibus morbus ortum habet contrarietatem observantes adaptare. Sed inter ea quae indistincte numerat mellis meminit. Quod nec ratione nec experientia appetentiam posse inducere comperio. Nisi id mel li concedas ob id quia abstergendi vim habet. Hoc quoque modo plura sunt quae appetentiam inducunt, quam quae experientia ostendat.
units.tr: One of the Arab physicians writes thus: "Among the things that help those whose appetite is prostrated through weakness, as in convalescents, or through a viscous, moist matter, is to eat olives and some salted fish." But in truth, just as olives are harmful to those whose stomachs abound with moist and viscous humour, so salted fish are harmful to convalescents who loathe food through weakness. For according to this physician's opinion, their appetite is lost through a lack of blood. And he immediately adds: "as happens to convalescents, or to those who are purged by a great evacuation." In both cases, when they loathe food, I think the use of salted fish will be more of a hindrance than a help. Nor will pickled olives make these people better. But if he had offered them partridge broth, a morsel of bread soaked in fragrant wine, and similar things, he would more quickly have restored their appetite, since they loathe food from the causes mentioned. Yet he then lists, quite indiscriminately, many things that dispel loathing in this way. Among those that provoke appetite he names prepared capers, mint, onion, olives, pepper, cloves, galangal, vinegar, sorrel, brine, garlic, onion again, opopanax and honey. These are his words, in which he has listed many remedies without any method, without fitting them to the conditions they suit. Of these, some induce appetite because they dry and roughen, such as prepared capers and mint. Others do so because by astringing they dry, such as vinegar, sorrel, brine and pickled olives. Others, because by drying they expel excrement from the stomach, such as garlic and pepper. Others, because by biting they make the sense of the mouth of the stomach sharper, such as onion, when the stomach has become dull from excess of excrements or from a fault in the expelling or concocting faculty. Indeed, this is to teach: to fit each remedy to the particular causes from which the disease arises, observing their contrariety. But among the things he lists indiscriminately he mentions honey. I find that honey can induce appetite neither by reason nor by experience, unless you grant it this because it has a cleansing power. In this way there are more things said to induce appetite than experience shows.

units.la: Qui ad sedandam tussim prosit victus.
units.tr: A diet to calm a cough.

units.la: CAPVT XXX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX.

units.la: TVSSIS in febribus cum à caliditate & siccitate absque humore ortum habet, hoc victu vtere: Aquae hordei libram vnam, syrupi violarum aut eius iulep partem decimam, misceтo & vtere.
units.tr: A cough in fevers, when it arises from heat and dryness without moisture, call for this diet: take one pound of barley water and one tenth part of syrup of violets or its julep, mix and use.

units.la: Portulaca cocta cum aqua et zucaro confert. Valde etiam prodest panis in aqua frigida infusus, mucharo violarum superasperso. Fiat ptisana hoc modo: Hordei ab utroque cortice exuti man. quinque, violarum recentium, portulacae & prunorum ana man. unum & semis. coquantur in aqua copiosa cum duobus pullis crassis parvulis, donec rumpatur hordeum & tenerrimum fiat. Coletur tandem & modico zucaro penidiarum addito, bullire hordeum cum decocto iterum finito donec permisceantur, utitor cum oportuerit. Sunt qui hunc cibum hordeatum nun cupent. Multum prodest calidae & siccae intemperiei iocineris, & pulmonis. Multum etiam his conuenit expressio quatuor seminum frigidorum (emulsionem medici vocant) ex aqua hordei cum zucaro penidiarum & modico coriandri viridis integri in ebullientem succum proiecti. Cum vero a phlegmate crasso ortu habet, sorbitione furfuracea utere. Utere & iure galli antiqui prout supra paravimus.
units.tr: Boiled purslane with water and sugar helps. Bread soaked in cold water and sprinkled with violet mucilage is also very helpful. Let a ptisan be made in this way: take five handfuls of barley with both husks removed, and one and a half handfuls each of fresh violets, purslane and plums. Boil them in plenty of water with two small plump chicks until the barley bursts and becomes very tender. Strain at last, add a little fine sugar, and boil the barley again with the decoction until they are mixed, and use it as needed. Some people do not care for this barley food. It greatly helps a hot and dry intemperie of the liver and lungs. The expressed juice of four cold seeds (physicians call it an emulsion), made from barley water with fine sugar and a little whole green coriander, thrown into the boiling juice, also suits these conditions well. But when it arises from thick phlegm, use a bran gruel. Use also the broth of an old cock, as we prepared above.

units.la: Ad obstructiones iocineris & lienis quae co- petant cibaria.
units.tr: Foods suitable for obstructions of the liver and spleen.

units.la: CAPVT XXXI
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: LIB. III. CAP. XXXI.
units.tr: BOOK III, CHAPTER XXXI.

units.la: Ad obstructionem iocineris sorbitionē {a}è furfure ad hunc modum parato, capillorum veneris recentis man.tres, aquæ è fonte libras tres, coquito in testa recenti quousque aqua fuluum nacta sit colorem. Colatoque & in colatorram furfuris è recenti tritico man.tres lintco excepti infundito, & toties exprimito donec decoctum albescat, fermenti trium dierum in æstate & vnius hebdomadæ in hyeme vncias tres similí modo in decoctum infundito, & toties exprimito quousque aqua candidior appareat. Cum zucaro tandem coquito tandiu quoad ad crassitudinem sorbitionis perveniat. Obstructionibus iocineris plurimum valet & lienis, præcipuè addito scolopendrio vt simul cum capillari herba coquatur. Valet & ad alios plurimos vsus. Tussi à crassa pituita ortum habenti mirum in modū prodest cum hyssopo. Febribus etiam phlegmaticis, & ijs qui colico dolore vexantur, cum chamæmelo. Aluum ciet, renes mundificat, calculos & arenas potenter pellit. Hoc vnū huic
units.tr: For obstruction of the liver, make a sorbition{a} from bran prepared in this way. Take three handfuls of fresh maidenhair (Venus' hair), and three pounds of spring water. Boil them in a new earthen pot until the water takes on a tawny colour. Strain it, pour it over three handfuls of fresh wheat bran held in a linen cloth, and squeeze repeatedly until the decoction turns white. Then pour in three ounces of ferment, three days old in summer or one week old in winter, in the same way, and squeeze repeatedly until the water appears whiter. Finally boil it with sugar, for as long as it takes to reach the thickness of a sorbition. It is very effective against obstructions of the liver and spleen, especially if scolopendrium is added so that it is boiled together with the maidenhair herb. It has many other uses as well. For a cough arising from thick phlegm it works wonderfully when combined with hyssop; for phlegmatic fevers, and for those troubled by colic, with chamomile. It loosens the bowels, cleanses the kidneys, and powerfully expels stones and gravel. The only drawback of this sorbition is that its frequent use dulls the appetite.

units.la: {a} Sorbitio furfuracea. sorbitioni incommodum est, quod appetentia deijcit creber eius vsus. Confert & ius cicerum vt supra parauimus, adiecta hepatica si hepar afficiatur, aut ceterach, si lien. Sorbitio praeterea ex capite arietis decocti cū chamaemelo, passulis, & reliquis, cuius supra meminimus, maxime prodest ad antiquas et induratas obstructiones.
units.tr: {a} Furfuraceous sorbition. Likewise the broth of chickpeas, prepared as we described above, helps; add hepatica if the liver is affected, or ceterach if the spleen is. Moreover, the sorbition made from a ram's head boiled with chamomile, raisins and the rest, which we mentioned above, is especially useful for old and hardened obstructions.

units.la: In fluxu uentris quae uictus ratio sit obseruanda.
units.tr: What diet is to be observed in a flux of the bowels.

units.la: CAPVT XXXII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXII.

units.la: FLVXVS ventris si statim inter morbi initia eueniat, sistendus ideo videtur esse, quia eo tempore vi morbi potius quàm naturae actione regulariter agentis euenit. Proinde cum speculatio hæc ad curatiuā methodum spectet, solum ea quae ad victus rationem attinent dicemus. Cæterùm cum alvus liquida inter febris initia à vi morbi irritata natura fiat, necesse est vt ex eo labore et virium iactura sequantur. Quarum enim natura per seipsa auctor est effluxionum, non morbi initio, sed post crisim fiunt. Roborare igitur naturam à morbi violentia oppressam expedit cibo crassiori, quàm pro morbi acuminis ratione. Nam symptomati illud indulgendum est. Vt si Socratem ponas causo laborare cum aluo liquida, non potu solo ( quem victum aliâs exposcit ) sed sorbitiuncula exptisanæ cremore hunc nutries. Hoc voluit Hippocrates quarto de ratione victus de causi alio genere agens, quem nothum Galenus appellat, vbi sorbitiones attractorias dari iubet. Idem ab eodem in tertio cum de deiectionibus biliosis puris & spumosis ageret disci-mus. Sed de iis satis in primo libro diximus. Sic ergo manifestum est ex dictis Hippocratis & Galeni quibuscunque in febribus alvus ab initio liquida est crassiori victu febricitantes quàm morbi acumen exposcat, alendos esse. Nam vt plurimum huiusmodi ventris fluxus inter morbi initia eueniëtes si permanent, corpus absumunt contabefaciunt q. Quam ob rem colliquantium febrium indicia sunt & effectus. Quod à Galeno in quarto de ratione victus in expositione illius, Qui bus aluus per febres &c. Scriptū est in hæc verba. Nam vt cætera omittam cum aluus liquida esse possit, tum propter phlegmonem, tum propter contabesacientem colliquantemque febrem, frigidæ potus phlegmonæ contrarius est, &c. Sed forsan quis nobis illud Hippocratis secundo de ratione vistus ob ųciet: Ingens siquidem malum est, si ob la-borem morbisque acumen imbecillitato por-rexerit quis potum vel sorbitionem, &c.
units.tr: If a flux of the bowels occurs at once, at the very beginning of the illness, it seems it should be checked, because at that time it comes about through the force of the disease rather than through the regular action of nature. Therefore, since this inquiry concerns the method of cure, we will speak only of those things that pertain to diet. Moreover, since a liquid discharge from the bowels at the onset of fever is produced by nature irritated by the force of the disease, weakness and loss of strength must necessarily follow. For nature, which of itself brings about the discharges, does not produce them at the beginning of the illness but after the crisis. It is therefore expedient to strengthen nature, oppressed by the violence of the disease, with food thicker than the sharpness of the disease requires, for that symptom must be indulged. For example, if you suppose Socrates is suffering from liquid bowels, you will nourish him not with drink alone (which his condition otherwise demands) but with a little thin gruel of barley broth. Hippocrates intended this in the fourth book of On Diet, where, treating of another kind of cause, which Galen calls spurious, he orders attractive sorbitions to be given. We learn the same from the same author in the third book, where he discusses bilious, pure and frothy evacuations; but we have said enough about these in the first book. Thus it is plain from the sayings of Hippocrates and Galen that in whatever fevers the bowels are liquid from the start, the feverish must be fed with thicker food than the sharpness of the disease demands. For usually such flows of the bowels occurring at the beginning of an illness, if they persist, consume the body and waste it away. Hence they are signs and effects of colliquative fevers. Galen writes this in the fourth book of On Diet, in his commentary on the aphorism "Those whose bowels are liquid through fevers, etc.", in these words: "To omit the rest: since the bowels may be liquid both on account of phlegmon and on account of a wasting, colliquative fever, cold drink is contrary to phlegmon, etc." But perhaps someone will cite to us that saying of Hippocrates in the second book of On Diet: "It is a great evil if, through labour and the sharpness of the disease, weakness has so seized someone that he takes drink or sorbition, etc."

units.la: Duplicem imbecillitatem in febribus contin gere posse dicimus: alteram quæ ex sola spi- ritus substantiæ resolutione fit: de qua intel- lexit Galenus cum loco citato dixit. Ob do- lores sæpius ægri sine pulsu sunt animiqúe de- liquia incurrunt, & nullo pacto queunt mo- ueri. Alteram verò ex defectu materiæ ad eo- rum generationem, quam tetigit loco citato sub ijs verbis. Sunt autem (inquit) quibus non ob hæc virtus offenditur, sed ob vaso- rum quomodolibet factam euacuationem.
units.tr: We may say that a twofold weakness can occur in fevers: one that arises from the mere dissolution of the substance of the spirits, of which Galen spoke in the passage cited, when he said: "Because of pains, patients are often without pulse, and fall into swoons, and cannot in any way move." The other arises from a lack of matter for generating the spirits, which he touched on in the same passage under these words: "But there are (he says) those in whom the power is not offended by these things, but by whatever evacuation of the vessels has been made."

units.la: De primo imbecillitatis modo intellexit Hip- pocrates cum dixit, Ingens siquidem malūest &c. &c. Vbi ostendimus secundum mentem Galeni, qui laborantibus huiusmodi imbecillitate cibum exhibent, maximum operari malū. Eos verò qui ob defectum materiæ ad generationem spiritus infirmiores fiunt, cibari quàm celerrimè opportet. Immo si quis tenui victu hos alat, non parum lædet. In febribus autem quæ cum aluo liquida imbecillitates fiunt, eas partim ab evacuatione illa ortum habere suspicari medicum æquum est. Quapropter quantū evacuationi occasionis dat, eo tantum (eò magis) tenui victui parcendum est, & crassiori indulgendum. Sed nō ab re fuerit Angliæ mulieris curationem referre, quæ ad iam dictorum intellectum non parum proderit. Pharmacolæ Hispani vxor ardenti febre correpta est. Aluus perpetuò liquida erat, vigilias patiebatur, & ventriculi immoderatum ardorem. Deiectiones febrilem æstū non extinguebant. Huic aquâ hordei solum propinandam fore aliqui suadebant, morbi nanque acumen crassiorem victū nō exposcere judicabant. Alij medicaminibus peracuti morbi vim compescere melius esse. Alij immoderatum ventris profluuiu, ijs quae astringerent sistendum fore existima bant, eade causa quia nullum ex eo aegrotans leuamen perciperet. Mea quidem prævaluit sententia, vt nec astringentibus fluxus ventris cohiberetur, nec ad vlla medicamina tunc adesse occasionem, nullo-que alio eos tempestiui us vti posse remedio, quàm crassiori pro mor bi ratione victu, laborantis natura mrobo-rare. Posse siquidè eo modo citè alui symptoma minori ferre incommodo. Quapropter crassa sorbitione ex pulla gallinacea conue-nientibus herbis temperata, mulierem per ali-quot dies nutriui, nullo alio vtens remedio. Sic quidem illa acutum morbum euasit, solo competenti victu. Vnde collegi in febre acuta cum immoderato ventris fluxu, saluberri mum esse id solum medicum curare, vt natu ram crassiori victu roboret. Sed quando astringente cibo & potu vtendum sit, deinceps considerandum est. In acutis febribus morbi effectricem causam extra corpus pelle re modis omnibus damus operam. Cum au-tem aliqua euacuatio sponte euenit & si in-tempestiue fiat, ideo sistenda non est, quia no xÿ humoris superabundantis excerni portio nem suspicandum est. Et si in huiusmodi in-tempestiuis alui deiectionibus multum eius quod vtile & naturae conueniens est euacua ri certò sciamus, non ob id compescere aluū citam oportet. Nam maius ex retentione pra ui humoris solet incommodum sequi, aucta febre & increscentibus ob id symptomati-bus robur virtutis denorătibus, quàm sit im becillitatis damnum, quod contrarium operantes vererip ossent. Quapropter consulen-tes febri & eius symptomatibus fluxum ven tris non sistimus, virium robori crassiori vi ctu prouidentes. Intelligendum tamen est, quod in solo eo qui ob liquefacientes febres fit fluxu, sorbitiones frigidiores & crassioris substantiae offerimus, potusque qui astrictio ra participat facultate, vt liquefactioni plus obstent, non vt alium sistant. Quod enim iam dissolutum ex membris est à violento febris incendio, retinere intra corpus consilium non est. Ob id diuinus Hippocrates cum in libris de ratione victus multis in locis meminisset fluxus alui in febribus, semel tantum potus astringentis, & crassioris substantiæ sorbitionis meminit. Nempe cum aluus liquida fuerit & liquefaciens. Videtur mihi (inquit) sorbitiones frigidiores & spissiores offerendas esse & potus qui sistant vinosiores vel etiam astringentiores. In reliquis autem aliquando purgationem adhibere suadet, tantum abest vt fluxus eos inhiberi consulat. Vt in eo, Liquidam aluum habenti &c. Præterea in eo, Sorbitiones attractorias. Quandoque pedes calefacere iubet caeromatis & fascijs obuoluens, ita vt reliquo corpore frigidiores non sint. Cæterum scire oportet omnem ven tris fluxum à duabus euenire causis, nempe à noxa facultatis expultricis aut retentricis. Vbi igitur aluus liquida ab irritata expultri ce fit, fluxu astringentibus compescere haud tutum est, in morbis præsertim acutis. Cuve rò ab imbecillitate retentricis aluus liquida fit, cibo et potu astringentibus cohibenda est in omni febre et in omni morbo. In colliquan-tibus igitur febribus ob id quod liquefactio retentricis imbecillitatem magis quàm ex-pultricis fortitudinem aut irritationem ar-guit, nõ immeritò Hippocrates crassiores sor-bitiones frigidioresq;, & potus qui sistant vinosiores astringentioresque ministrare iu-bet. Quibuscunque igitur in morbis aluus li-quida ob retentricis imbecillitatem fiat, a-stringenti cibo & potu uti oportet, à sym-ptomate potiore quàm à morbo sumpta indi-catione. Cum ijs tamen prius experiri oporte-bit, quæ moderatè astringant, non penitus ne-gleCta ea quæ à morbo sumitur indicatione.
units.tr: Hippocrates understood the first kind of weakness when he said, "It is indeed a great evil, etc." etc. Here we have shown, according to the mind of Galen, that giving food to those labouring under this kind of weakness does great harm. But those who become weaker through a lack of matter for generating spirit must be fed as quickly as possible; indeed, if someone nourishes them with thin diet, he does no small harm. In fevers, however, which are accompanied by liquid bowels and weakness, it is fair for the physician to suspect that the weakness arises partly from that evacuation. Therefore, the more the evacuation gives occasion for it, the more thin diet must be spared and thicker food indulged. But it will not be out of place to relate the cure of a certain English woman, which will greatly help the understanding of what has been said. The wife of a Spanish apothecary was seized by a burning fever. Her bowels were constantly liquid; she suffered sleeplessness and an immoderate burning of the stomach. Her discharges did not quench the feverish heat. Some advised that only barley water be given her, judging that the sharpness of the disease did not call for thicker food. Others thought it better to restrain the force of the very acute disease with medicines. Others believed the immoderate flux of the bowels should be stopped with astringents, for the reason that the patient got no relief from it. My own opinion prevailed: that the flux should be checked neither with astringents, nor were there then any occasion for medicines, and that nothing else could be used at that time as a remedy than strengthening the patient's nature with thicker food suited to the disease. For in that way the symptom of liquid bowels could be borne with less harm. Therefore, I nourished the woman for several days with a thick sorbition seasoned with chicken broth and suitable herbs, using no other remedy. Thus she came through the acute disease by suitable food alone. From this I concluded that in acute fever with immoderate flux of the bowels, the most wholesome thing for the physician to do is this alone: strengthen nature with thicker food. But when astringent food and drink should be used must be considered afterwards. In acute fevers we take pains to drive the cause of the disease out of the body by every means. But when some evacuation happens spontaneously, and if it occurs untimely, it must not be stopped, for one must suspect that a portion of the superabundant humour is being discharged. And if, in such untimely evacuations of the bowels, we know for certain that much that is useful and suited to nature is being voided, we should not on that account check the rapid bowel movement. For greater harm usually follows from the retention of a noxious humour, when the fever increases and the symptoms growing from it wear down the strength of the powers, than from the loss of strength, which those acting the opposite way would fear. Wherefore, caring for the fever and its symptoms, we do not stop the flux of the bowels, providing for the strength of the powers with thicker food. Yet it must be understood that only in the flux which occurs in colliquative fevers do we offer colder and thicker sorbitions, and drinks which share an astringent quality, so that they may resist the liquefaction more, not that they may stop the other. For to hold within the body what has already been dissolved from the limbs by the violent heat of the fever is not a sound plan. Therefore divine Hippocrates, when in the books On Diet he mentioned the flux of the bowels in fevers in many places, mentions only once drinks of an astringent kind and thicker sorbition: namely when the bowels are liquid and liquefying. "I think (he says) colder and thicker sorbitions should be offered, and drinks that check, more wine-like or even more astringent." In other cases he sometimes advises the use of purgation, so far is he from advising that the flux be checked. As in that passage: "For one who has liquid bowels, etc." And in that: "Attractive sorbitions." Sometimes he orders the feet to be warmed, wrapping them in cerecloths and bands, so that they are not colder than the rest of the body. Moreover, it must be known that every flux of the bowels comes from one of two causes, namely a fault of the expulsive or of the retentive faculty. Therefore, where liquid bowels arise from an irritated expulsive faculty, it is not safe to restrain the flux with astringents, especially in acute diseases. But where liquid bowels arise from weakness of the retentive faculty, they must be restrained with astringent food and drink in every fever and every disease. In colliquative fevers, therefore, since liquefaction indicates weakness of the retentive faculty more than strength or irritation of the expulsive, Hippocrates not undeservedly orders thicker and colder sorbitions, and more wine-like and more astringent drinks, to be given. Therefore, in whatever disease the liquid bowels arise from weakness of the retentive faculty, astringent food and drink must be used, the indication being taken from the principal symptom rather than from the disease. Yet with these one must first try those which astringe moderately, without wholly neglecting what is indicated by the disease.

units.la: Iis igitur cibarijs potissimè utemur, quæ le-uissimæ sint coctionis, & bonum præstent corpori alimentum, parumq; grauent ventri-culum. Ob defectu primi, carnes bouinæ non cõpetunt, ob secundi, lentes, ob tertij, rizum utile non est. Hepata gallinaceorum satis assa in vino austero infusa non inutilia sunt. Diu tamen in ventriculo immoratur, quapropter assa in vino infusa in sorbitiones dissoluere expediet. Sic enim efficacius retentricem facultatem roborabunt. Succus perdicis satis assa omnia quae exegimus habet, eo tamen vti cum pane aegrotanti commodius erit. Phasianus simpliciter optima caro est, & magis nutrit quam perdix, minus tamen imbecilles particulas roborat. Caro enim phasiani media est inter perdicem & pullam gallinaceam. Quae nam victus forma et qualitas iis qui liquefacientibus detinentur febribus conueniat, supra dictum est.
units.tr: So we shall chiefly use those foods which are very easy to digest, give the body good nourishment, and weigh lightly on the stomach. Beef is unsuitable because of the first defect, lentils because of the second, and rice is not useful because of the third. Chicken livers, well roasted and steeped in dry wine, are not unhelpful. Yet they linger a long time in the stomach, so it will be expedient to dissolve livers roasted and steeped in wine into broths. In this way they will strengthen the retentive faculty more effectively. Partridge juice, if the meat is well roasted, has all the qualities we have listed, but it will be more suitable to use it with bread for a sick person. Pheasant is simply excellent meat and nourishes more than partridge, yet it strengthens the weaker parts less. For pheasant flesh lies midway between partridge and a young chicken. What manner and quality of diet suits those held by colliquative fevers has been said above.

units.la: INDEX IN IAC. SYLVII LIBRUM de morborum curatione, & Brudi Lusitani de ratione victus febricitantium. C. littera curationē significat, in libro Syluij quaerendam secundum numerum paginarum. Br. verò Brudum, sequentibus duobus numeris, quorum prior librum, posterior caput significat. fere enim is argumentum unum per caput integrum tractat. Libelli de pulsibus & urinis indice alphabetico non indigere visi sunt.
units.tr: INDEX TO JACOBUS SYLVIUS'S BOOK on the cure of diseases, and to Brudus of Lusitania's book on the regimen of feverish patients. The letter C signifies curatione (cure), and is to be looked for in Sylvius's book by the number of the page. Br. stands for Brudus, and the two numbers that follow denote, the first the book, the second the chapter; for he treats each subject fully within a single chapter. The short treatises on pulses and urines did not seem to need an alphabetical index.

units.tr: Those who during the beginnings of diseases use a thinner diet, even when the stage has been reached where a more solid diet is needed, grievously sin to the harm of the sick, Br. 2.15.

units.la: Victu tenue Anglis ægrotantib. nō offerendu esse, sumpta indicatiōe à cōsuetudine, regio- ne & cœli temperie Br. 1.17. & deinceps vsque ad finem libri 2.
units.tr: A thin diet should not be offered to English patients, the indication being taken from custom, region and the temperature of the air, Br. 1.17, and onward to the end of book 2.

units.la: Victus qualis sit exhibendus febricitanti- bus vnde sumatur Br. 2.5. Qualitatem à tribus sumi 2.8.
units.tr: What sort of diet should be given to feverish patients, and whence it should be taken, Br. 2.5. That the quality is to be taken from three things, 2.8.

units.la: Victus an apponi debeat intemperiei æquali gradu contrariæ qualitatis Br. 2.7
units.tr: Whether diet should be applied with an equal degree of contrary quality to the intemperance, Br. 2.7.
